items.b: If someone you know would benefit from receiving this bulletin, here’s a link to the signup form.

items.h: Batley and Spen by-election updates
items.b: Jo Cox’s sister, Kim Leadbeater, has been selected as Labour’s candidate in the upcoming election . The Conservative Party has announced it has selected Harewood councillor and Leeds city councillor Ryan Stephenson as its candidate. Corey Robinson has been selected by the Yorkshire Party to contest the election.
items.why: this matters democratically because the selection of candidates by competing parties is the mechanism through which voters are offered genuine electoral choice in a by-election.

items.h: Full ward-by-ward breakdown of May’s UK election results from Britain Elects
items.b: Ben Walker at Britain Elects has collated a comprehensive dataset of every ward result across the country. If you choose to use this resource, remember to cite Britain Elects.
items.why: this matters democratically because detailed, verifiable ward-level results data underpins public scrutiny of how votes translate into electoral outcomes.
items.note: Treated as election administration/transparency resource rather than pure sector logistics.
links: comprehensive dataset of every ward result

items.h: Metro mayoral election dataviz
items.b: Centre for Cities’ latest data tool visualizes the outcomes of mayoral elections across England. Explore the data here . Their latest City Minutes podcast delves into the meaning of the election results for England’s cities, with CfC Chief Executive Andrew Carter.
items.why: this matters democratically because visualising mayoral election outcomes helps the public understand the results of devolved decision-making elections.
items.note: Local/regional election structure and outcomes fall under elections per boundary rules.

items.h: Tell me what you want, what you really, really want
items.b: Democracy Club (DC) report back on the feedback they received throughout the election period. In short, it’s glowing, one user remarked DC are “simply the best”, people also really love polling station maps. But there’s always room for improvement, in this case with the provision of whether or not a polling station has disabled access.
items.why: this matters democratically because tools like polling station maps and disabled-access information affect the practical accessibility of voting for all citizens.

items.h: Electoral Commission to investigate ‘blatant electoral deceit’ at the Holyrood election
items.b: A new party with no online presence run by ex-BNP far-right activists called Independent Green Voice (IGV) took thousands of votes off the Scottish Greens in several areas, argue the Scottish Greens. The Electoral Commission is due to investigate the claims.
items.why: this matters democratically because an investigation into deceptive party naming and vote-splitting tactics goes to the integrity and fairness of the electoral competition.

items.h: Dark money and electoral rule violations by pro-Unionist campaigns tarnish Scottish election, reports openDemocracy
items.b: openDemocracy’s Peter Geoghegan reports concerning online political advertising rule violations by Unionist tactical voting campaigns throughout the recent Holyrood elections, with the Young Unionists reportedly spending as much as £20,000 on Facebook ads, all lacking details of who paid for them , with £5,000 of that amount being spent in the final days of the campaign.
items.why: this matters democratically because undisclosed 'dark money' spending on political advertising undermines campaign finance transparency rules that safeguard fair electoral competition.
links: all lacking details of who paid for them

items.h: The3million team celebrates election wins
items.b: Over the last three months, the Young European Network ran a campaign to promote voter registration amongst resident EU citizens. Together with the3million, they report the successful election of at least 15 EU citizens who ran for their local council and were elected on May 6th, including the first ever Romanian-British County Councillor, Cllr Alex Bulat . After the election they’re now focused on protecting and securing the voting rights of European citizens in the UK.
items.why: a campaign to register and elect resident EU citizens directly affects the inclusiveness of the franchise and representativeness of local elected government

items.h: Centre for Constitutional Change Scottish election highlights
items.b: The team at CCC has gathered together a great selection of blogs, media articles and tweets that they authored and contributed to throughout the recent Scottish Parliament election.
items.note: A self-curated roundup of the organisation's own commentary, not substantive new reporting on the election.

items.h: New electoral offences and overseas voters
items.b: In a pair of new House of Commons Library briefings, Neil Johnston outlines the background of the new offence of intimidation of candidates and voters , and provides some history and detail on the government’s ending of the 15-year overseas voting limit, introducing new ‘ votes for life ’ for expats.
items.why: new offences protecting candidates and voters from intimidation and the extension of overseas voting rights directly change the machinery of electoral integrity and suffrage
links: new offence of intimidation of candidates and voters

items.h: Rotten Boroughs are back, claim Electoral Reform Society
items.b: Reflecting on the recent elections Josiah Mortimer, Head of Communications at the Electoral Reform Society, provides some insight into England’s winner-takes-all voting system.
items.why: critiquing first-past-the-post outcomes concerns the fairness and representativeness of the electoral system itself

items.h: Do you have experience of organisational strategy development processes with participative elements?
items.b: Juliet Michaelson , Deputy CEO at Economy, is undertaking research to inform the process of their next 3–5 year long term strategy. They’re interested in hearing from people who’ve developed strategy processes and included participatory elements, or perhaps had a strong diversity, inclusion or anti-oppression focus.
items.note: A call for input on an organisation's internal strategy process, not a public democratic mechanism.

items.h: New mySociety climate job and seminar for councillors
items.b: Myf at mySociety announces a new vacancy for an Outreach and Networks Coordinator at mySociety, and an upcoming event for local councillors to learn more about how they can take urgent action on the climate emergency.
items.note: A job vacancy and a councillor seminar on climate policy, not on democratic participation or governance mechanisms.

items.h: Bitizen and real-time public sentiment of political activity
items.b: Co-Founder at Bitizen , Andrew Marshall is building a new platform designed for political participation, with data aggregation creating new real-time views of public sentiment towards political activity right across the political spectrum. They’re currently testing their new app with their founders community.
items.why: launching a new platform intended to aggregate and surface public political sentiment creates a new means for people to engage in political life
items.note: Sector capacity-building rule applied: a new participation tool/platform counts as a democracy story.

items.h: Join the upcoming cohort of the Landecker Democracy Fellowship
items.b: Humanity in Action’s Landecker Democracy Fellowship is now open to applications until July 11. Running from November 6 2021 to November 7 2022, this year’s cohort will focus on social cohesion, with applicants tasked to develop projects bridging the gulf between those who are increasingly drifting apart in societies across the globe.
items.why: a fellowship programme building civic capacity to bridge social divides creates new means for participants to engage in democratic and civic life
items.note: Treated under the sector capacity-building rule for programmes that expand participation.

items.h: Women in Parliament
items.b: This new briefing paper by Richard Kelly at the House of Commons Library provides a list of all the women who have ever been elected to the House of Commons.
items.why: a record of women's historical representation in the Commons bears on the representativeness of the elected legislature

items.h: Women 2 Win announce their Summer Party
items.b: Penned for the 21st July, the Conservative Party’s women’s network annual event will feature guests Suella Braverman MP and their months-old daughter Gabriella. Get in touch here to find out more.
items.note: A social event announcement for a party women's network, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.h: Can Democracy Safeguard the Future?
items.b: Graham Smith celebrates the launch and publication of his new book . Graham is Professor of Politics at the University of Westminster and Director at the Centre for the Study of Democracy.
items.note: Book launch/author promotion is organisational news, not a mechanism story.

items.h: Sheffield Festival of Debate
items.b: Colin Miller of Deeper Democracy recommends the Festival of Debate currently ongoing virtually in Sheffield throughout the month of May and into June, which is hosting some great discussions such as the Crisis of Democracy session on June 3 between Peter Geoghegan (Democracy for Sale), Klina Jordan, CEO of Make Voters Matter, and Neal Lawson of Compass.
items.note: Event listing for a debate festival, sector logistics.

items.h: TicTec 2021: That’s a wrap
items.b: With the last event on Tuesday covering empowering communities through geospatial tech, the TicTec 2021 programme has come to an end. You can view all previous events at this link , though Tuesday’s session may take a few more days to be uploaded.
items.note: Event wrap-up/listing, sector logistics.

items.h: Final decision on Commons restoration to be taken in 2023.
items.b: Commons leader Jacob Rees-Mogg has said the full costings and plans will be put before Parliament in early 2023 and it will be up to MPs to approve or reject it. Dr Ruth Fox, Director of the Hansard Society, makes their case for decanting Parliament.
items.note: Concerns building restoration/facilities logistics for Parliament, not exercise or scrutiny of power.

items.h: PolicyMogul launches free political monitoring
items.b: The PolicyMogul free plan allows you to monitor mentions of up to five keywords from anywhere in the political landscape, and is perfect for individual campaigners or small organisations with narrow interests. If you’re into political monitoring, also see Polimonitor .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new low-cost means for campaigners and small organisations to monitor and engage with the political process.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building: a new tool enabling political participation and monitoring.

items.h: VocalEyes announces successful funding raise
items.b: Susan Rodaway , Operations Director at VocalEyes Democracy CIC, reports they’re almost at 100% of the extended £350k target on their social bond raise, a huge achievement! They’re now recruiting a Sales Lead Generator and open to collaboration on projects, particularly where they involve supporting marginalised communities in exercising their voice.
items.note: Organisation's own funding raise announcement, excluded as org admin.

items.h: Changes at Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust
items.b: JRCT release their initial action plan for addressing dynamics of power and privilege within their organisation, they welcome anonymous feedback via this link . JRCT also answer questions on the origins of their endowment and the impact of the Rowntree business. The Trust announces new power for its grantmaking committees, with committees now able to disburse up to £120,000 without board approval. They also announce six new committee members to help guide their work, you can find out more here . View their last grantmaking round of over £2.5million worth of grants.
items.note: Internal governance and committee changes at a charitable trust, organisational admin.

items.h: Democracy Funding Opportunities Database
items.b: Molly and James from the Centre for Democracy team report they’ve now finished scouring democracy funding organisation websites and newsletters and have produced this Airtable list of available funding opportunities . If they’ve missed anything, add the funding opportunity, incubation or paid fellowship here .
items.note: A funding-opportunities database for organisations is sector logistics, not a tool for public democratic participation.
links: Airtable list of available funding opportunities

items.h: The latest in participatory grantmaking
items.b: Social Change Agency interviews Hannah Paterson, Senior Portfolio Manager — Innovation, Policy and Practice at the National Lottery Community Fund, on the latest developments in participatory grantmaking and democratising funding.
items.note: General interview discussing developments in participatory grantmaking without reporting a concrete new mechanism or change.

items.h: Modern Grantmaking pre-orders available
items.b: Gemma Bull & Tom Steinberg’s new book on transforming grantmaking, replete with practical tips for grantmakers and grantees, is now available to pre-order .
items.note: Book pre-order announcement, organisational/publication news.

items.h: Get your free 1password for Democracy account
items.b: 1password are offering fully complementary accounts of their password manager free to election candidates and those working around elections, from election staff to supporting candidates to run. Shout out to Matthew Shipton at Democracy Club for telling us about this.
items.why: free security tools for election candidates and staff lower practical barriers to standing for office and running elections safely
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource enabling participation rather than mere logistics offer.

items.h: Supporting young people into careers in politics and public policy
items.b: I Have A Voice just added a new interview to their careers hub on helping young people into public policy careers. Rebecca Deegan, Founder at IHAV, reports that the third stage of their current mentoring scheme for 10 young people from under-represented backgrounds is currently underway, delivered in partnership with the Public Relations and Communications Association.
items.why: a mentoring scheme and careers hub builds pathways for under-represented young people into political and policy careers, widening who can take part in shaping public power

items.h: Amending the Higher Education Bill
items.b: Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters is currently in the process of progressing an amendment to the Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Bill on political literacy. You can view and comment on the amendment, here .
items.why: embedding political literacy in higher education legislation aims to build citizens' capacity to understand and engage with democratic life

items.h: Constitution Unit Conference on Constitutional Reform
items.b: The Constitution Unit announces their new two day conference . Held across the 17th and 18th of June, the conference will bring together policy makers, academic experts and politicians to discuss what progress has been made and what lies ahead.
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not substantive reporting on a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Top Conservatives call voter ID plans “illiberal” and “politics as performance”
items.b: Britain’s Chief Brexit negotiator David Davis MP and former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson criticised voter ID proposals and mocked the idea that this is a legislative priority.
items.why: voter ID requirements affect who can practically exercise their franchise and are a live electoral integrity/access debate

items.h: Conservatives launch new pledge site Back the Bill
items.b: The Conservative Party launches a new campaign and website, Back the Bill , to muster public support for the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill. The bill is currently in committee stage . If you’re working on the bill or looking for more information, sign up to Liberty’s intermittent email bulletin list on the Police Bill here .
items.why: the bill being campaigned for includes new policing and protest powers that bear directly on freedom of assembly and state coercion
items.note: Classified by the substance of the bill (policing/protest powers) rather than the campaign mechanics.

items.h: Online Safety Bill (OSB) is finally published
items.b: Carnegie Trust have been tracking work around the bill, like Fair Vote UK and so many others. We highly recommend their summary and analysis of the OSB in their recent newsletter . Paul Goodman of ConservativeHome also provides a short brief on the background and content of the bill. DCMS Minister Oliver Dowden MP’s op-ed in the Telegraph on the Bill can also be found here .
items.why: the Online Safety Bill will shape what online content and speech is permitted, directly affecting the public information environment

items.h: Major concerns with the new Online Safety Bill
items.b: In a joint op-ed for Grazia with the Antisemitism Policy Trust, Glitch Founder Seyi Akiwowo, writes that the proposals don’t reflect the gendered nature of the problems around online harms.
items.why: critiques of the Online Safety Bill's treatment of gendered online harms bear on how the regulated information environment protects or fails different groups' ability to participate in debate

items.h: Bursting the democratic ‘bubble’
items.b: Ellen Judson writing for Demos focuses on the impact of the exemption of “content of democratic importance” in the new Online Safety Bill, i.e. cordoning off certain topics and viewpoints in a ‘bubble’ as protected no matter how harmfully expressed, is not a democracy enhancing strategy.
items.why: analysis of the 'content of democratic importance' exemption concerns how the Online Safety Bill shapes what political speech is protected or moderated online

items.h: Open Rights Group kickoff campaign against ‘digital police state’
items.b: As the Cabinet Office proposes a dramatic expansion of Police data-matching powers via the National Fraud Initiative, as covered in previous issues of Democracy Bulletin , ORG is rallying its supporters to oppose the move.
items.why: expanded government data-matching powers raise surveillance and privacy concerns that bear on citizens' freedom from unwarranted state intrusion

items.h: Taking stock of the deliberation landscape in the UK
items.b: This April Involve’s Deliberative Democracy Practitioners Network reflected on the state of play of deliberative democracy in the UK, mapping opportunities for change, forces providing resistance and an exploration of what practitioners can do now to make the most of the changing landscape — thanks to Maddie Gough, Involve’s Project and Inclusive Practice Officer, for providing a thorough breakdown of the work. Find out more about the Practitioners Network here .
items.why: it maps the state of deliberative democracy practice, a mechanism for collective decision-making beyond elections.
items.note: Deliberative processes are filed under elections & decision making per framework rule.
links: reflected on the state of play

items.h: Launching the Global Democracy Initiative
items.b: This Saturday Barnaby Flynn, Founder of Global People Power , is working to launch the Global Democracy Initiative (GDI). The GDI met for the first time in November 2020 and since then has brought together many of the global democracy organisations to work together synergistically.
items.note: Launch of a global network of organisations is organisational news, not UK democratic mechanism change.

items.h: Coalitions and progressive alliances on the cards at all levels across the country
items.b: As Jonathan Bartley tells Keir Starmer “you have my number — give me a call”, Labour and the Liberal Democrats in Milton Keynes announce a Progressive Alliance . Labour and Greens organise to run Sheffield Council as a ‘ co-operative administration ’ and Labour, Lib Dems and Independents form a coalition on Cambridgeshire county council after not standing candidates against each other and taking seats from the Conservatives as a result.
items.why: cross-party alliances and coalitions at local level shape political competition and representativeness in elected local government.
links: Labour, Lib Dems and Independents form a coalition

items.h: Fresh report from the LGIU’s new Local Democracy Research centre & new councillor support resources
items.b: Centred on the key challenges facing local democracy around the world, the paper argues the time is right for a radical restructuring of power, politics and policy around the needs of local places, and that the UK needs a new “settlement for place”. Join the launch of the new research centre and a discussion on their latest paper on the 16th June. The LGIU also published new councillor support resources for newly elected representatives.
items.why: the report and new resources concern the structure and powers of local government, a core decision-making tier.
items.note: Local government structure stories are filed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Evaluation of devolved institutions
items.b: A new report from BEIS , produced by Warwick Economics and Development, takes stock of the institutional processes of devolved institutions across England. The research will feed into government policy decisions on future devolution.
items.why: the evaluation of devolved institutions will inform government decisions about the structure of devolved decision-making.

items.h: Why Scotland’s election result is unlikely to hasten a referendum
items.b: Michael Keating of the Centre on Constitutional Change argues the 50/50 independence split in Scottish society is now clearer than ever, and that with such a close margin and the requirements of a UK Government sanctioned order to allow a referendum, it is unlikely we’ll see much real movement on this issue for some time, despite the hype.
items.why: prospects for an independence referendum concern the machinery of direct popular decision-making.
items.note: Referendums are filed under elections & decision making.

items.h: What do the elections in Wales and Scotland mean for their cities?
items.b: Senior Analyst Anthony Breach at the Centre for Cities proposes that politicians in the devolved nations take inspiration from the success of the English metro mayors and embark on a new wave of urban devolution .
items.why: the argument for further urban devolution concerns the structure and powers of local and regional government.
items.note: Local/regional devolution structure is filed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Mary Fitzgerald steps down as Editor-in-Chief of openDemocracy
items.b: Mary led the team at OD for 7 years and worked to build OD into the investigative journalism powerhouse it is today, as attested to in their recent annual report .
items.note: Staff departure from a media organisation is organisational news, not a democracy story.

items.h: Preparing for the biggest survey of independent news in the UK… ever!
items.b: Joe Mitchell, Prog. Mgr at Public Interest News Foundation, is working on the launch of the PINF Index 2021 , the largest survey of indie news outlets in the UK to date. They’re also looking into a new programme of work on local news and democratic engagement, how they’re linked and how they can better support one another.
items.why: a comprehensive survey of independent news outlets and a new programme linking local news to democratic engagement affects the plurality and health of the public information environment.

items.h: Elections? There’s an app for that
items.b: Tactical Tech’s Data & Politics Project have written up a series of four incisive articles on the ‘appification’ of politics, elections and issue campaigning, and why it’s important to investigate this new domain of political activity.
items.why: the rise of apps in political campaigning changes how voters encounter political information and are targeted during elections.
items.note: Technology/digital democracy is a cross-cutting lens; classified by underlying mechanism of political information and campaigning.

items.h: Hacked Off
items.b: The new Online Safety Bill proposes exemptions for news platforms that Hacked Off say would amount to ‘safe havens for those responsible for racism, hate and abuse online’.
items.why: it concerns how the state regulates online platforms and who controls the information environment people use to debate public affairs.

items.h: “A world leader amongst democracies when it comes to censorship and state control”
items.b: Those were the words of Big Brother Watch’s Mark Johnson commenting on proposed changes in the Online Safety Bill, where the bill restores the old gatekeepers of speech whilst creating a new regime of restrictions and censorship for the wider population, argues Mark in the Spectator.
items.why: it concerns proposed state restrictions on online speech and who is permitted to gatekeep public expression.

items.h: New seminar for teachers: House of Lords: Scrutiny… and reform?
items.b: The UK Parliament Education Service and the Political Studies Association have teamed up to provide an insightful seminar for educators with keynote speaker Professor Meg Russell, Director of the Constitution Unit. Register here .
items.note: An event listing for teachers rather than a change to democratic practice or a new participation resource.

items.h: We know what you did during lockdown
items.b: A new Financial Times film , funded by Luminate, explores how Covid-19 has exposed the tensions between the need for data to support health interventions, and the right to privacy and justice.
items.why: it examines the tension between state data collection powers and individuals' rights to privacy and legal redress.

items.h: Involve announces new Network for Democracy
items.b: The Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust (JRRT) and Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust (JRCT) have awarded Involve £350,000 to establish a network for the democracy sector over the next three years. Last year’s Networking for Democracy report, commissioned by JRRT and produced by The Centre for Democracy’s Joe Mitchell , found that establishing a network to support better connections within and outside the democracy sector was a priority. Outgoing Director Tim Hughes will act as interim chair of the new network until the new Involve CEO Sarah Castell assumes the post in the coming months. We look forwar…
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates new infrastructure to strengthen connections and capacity within civil society organisations working on democracy.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building (a new network) rather than organisational news about Involve itself.

items.h: Higher Ground Labs publish Political Technology Landscape Report
items.b: Interviewing 50+ expert technologists, practitioners and campaigners across the political tech space, the report details trends, opportunities and learnings . Whilst focused on the US, the approaches and findings have the potential for translation in a UK/European context.
items.note: A US-focused landscape report with no direct UK democratic mechanism engaged.

items.h: Boundary Commission for England reports on changes
items.b: The number of constituencies in England will rise from 533 to 543 , at the expense of Scotland (-2) and Wales (-8). The UK-wide rejig will resize constituencies to average populations of 73,400 registered voters. The boundary map is planned for completion by 2023. Welsh and Scottish boundary commissions due to report next month.
items.why: This matters democratically because changes to constituency boundaries directly affect the representativeness and equality of votes in UK elections.

items.h: Constitution Unit Conference on Constitutional Reform
items.b: Co-organised by the Constitution Unit , the Dept of Politics & IR at the University of Oxford and UK in a Changing Europe (UKICE) , the conference will take place on the 17th and 18th of June. The conference will bring together policy makers, academic experts and politicians to discuss what progress has been made and what lies ahead — click here to register.
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not substantive reporting.
links: Dept of Politics & IR at the University of Oxford

items.h: Compass + Unlock Democracy plan to push Labour on democratic reform
items.b: The long term project aims to shift Labour to a stronger position on constitutional and democratic reform by the time of the next election, reports Frances Foley , Deputy Director at Compass. Compass is hiring for a new Operations Officer — check it out, deadline June 18th.
items.why: this matters democratically because civil society organisations are campaigning to shape a major party's platform on constitutional and democratic reform ahead of an election.
items.note: Distinguished from the embedded hiring notice, which is organisational admin and excluded.

items.h: Open Government Network working to co-create the UK’s next National Action Plan for Open Government
items.b: Kevin Keith , Chair of the Open Government Network, is working to bring together civil society organisations to work with civil servants and co-create the UK’s next National Action Plan for Open Government , as part of the UK’s membership of the Open Government Partnership (OGP). Earlier this year, the UK Government was placed under review by the OGP. Help shape the UK’s policies on transparency.
items.why: this matters democratically because civil society is working with government to shape transparency commitments that hold public institutions answerable, under international review.
links: National Action Plan for Open Government

items.h: How to do a referendum on Irish unification
items.b: The Constitution Unit leads an international consortium of academics to research how to conduct future referendums on the constitutional status of Northern Ireland.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns how a future binding referendum on Northern Ireland's constitutional status would be designed and conducted.
items.note: Referendums are classified under elections & decision making per the revised framework.

items.h: Electoral Integrity Bill and the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Fair Vote UK are developing a strategy around these bills. They’re pulling together an organisation-level survey, mapping which organisations are working on the bills, and at what level. If you’re working on these, contact Director kyle@fairvote.uk
items.note: This is an organisational mapping/survey exercise rather than substantive reporting on the bills themselves.

items.h: Open strategizing at The National Lottery
items.b: Gemma Cossins notes how people at The National Lottery and other funders seem to be thinking out loud a lot more than usual.

items.h: The Politics Project run well attended Post-Election Debrief
items.b: Partnering with the UK Democracy Fund, ERS Cymru and Democracy Classroom, more than thirty organisations came together to share their election experiences, some of which are covered in this bulletin, including experiments with paying young people for election content creation and the first 16 & 17 year old ‘booster’ poll sample. You can view the notes and slides from the event here .
items.note: Event recap/listing rather than substantive findings.

items.h: Acorn experiments with boosting renter voter turnout
items.b: Tom Scott at Acorn ran digital election hustings and tested different types of adverts on renters to boost voting turnout throughout the pre-election period, in collaboration with a team of researchers from LSE and Kings. We look forward to seeing the results of the RCT when they’re validated and will publish the results in a future issue of this Bulletin.
items.why: this matters democratically because it tests interventions designed to raise voter turnout among renters, a core electoral participation mechanism.
items.note: Turnout-related stories are always classified under elections & decision making.

items.h: Democracy Volunteers break records
items.b: The recent elections saw Democracy Volunteers mobilise a record number of election observers across the UK, with over 2,000 polling stations visited .
items.why: this matters democratically because independent election observation safeguards the integrity and proper administration of voting.

items.h: House of Commons Library publish briefing on the recent metro-mayoral elections
items.b: Elise Uberoi , Statistics Researcher at the House of Commons Library, has run the numbers on the recent combined authorities elections: “Labour candidates won five out of the seven combined authority (metro-)mayor elections in May 2021, with the Conservative candidates winning the remaining two. Labour mayors now govern combined authorities covering more than 8.5 million people and Conservative mayors govern areas covering more than 3.6 million people. The Green Party came third in all five elections they contested, ahead of the Liberal Democrats. In three elections, the winning candidate won …
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports on the outcomes and mechanics (preferential voting, representativeness) of combined authority mayoral elections.

items.h: Polish Migrants Organise for Change break outreach records during May elections
items.b: There’s good reason for POMOC to celebrate , they campaigned in more cities, brokered dozens of partnerships and taught more political education workshops than ever before. The POMOC community even crowdsourced the first bilingual open source handbook for the 2021 elections!
items.why: it builds the civic capacity and political education of a migrant community to engage with and participate in UK elections
items.note: Organising and civic education workshops are participation-building rather than the electoral machinery itself.

items.h: Chloe Smith to answer questions on government strategy for the Union
items.b: Chloe Smith, as Minister of State in the Cabinet Office with responsibility for the Constitution and Devolution, will be answering questions from Akash Paun, Senior Fellow at the Institute for Government, on the government’s strategy for the Union in Wales and Scotland following the recent elections. You can sign up here .
items.note: Event/webinar sign-up notice rather than a reported development.

items.h: Request: list of climate-focused councillors or council officers
items.b: mySociety is planning a new climate programme aimed at local government, to offer them useful data and tech. Can you help Myf Nixon contact climate-focused councillors or council officers?

items.h: The Local Authority Podcast
items.b: FutureGov are teaming up with Local Government Chronicle to produce a new podcast bringing together leaders from the sector to explore the most pressing topics and challenges to LAs. First episode arrives in the next few weeks, stay tuned.
items.note: Podcast launch announcement without a clear participatory or informational democratic mechanism.

items.h: New Local asks: What do councils actually do?
items.b: The second part of New Local’s Local Government Explained series, Jessica Studdert unpacks the role and activities of councils in the UK.
items.why: it explains the structure, role and powers of local councils, the decision-making tier closest to citizens
items.note: Explainer on council structure and powers falls under local government per the boundary rule.

items.h: A timeline of UK community development
items.b: The Local Trust brought in social historian David Boyle to develop this interactive timeline tracking the history of community through more than 300 events that have shaped our collective social organism over the last century, from the Blitz to the pandemic.
items.note: Historical community timeline lacks a direct mechanism tied to public power or democratic participation.

items.h: EHRC rules UK government violated freedom of the press through mass spying programme on journalists
items.b: The ruling was the result of an eight-year landmark privacy case brought by The Bureau of Investigative Journalism and human rights orgs. The government and GCHQ must now seek independent permission prior to accessing confidential journalistic material, the court ruled. GCHQ acted illegally for years, the court said, and would never have come to light without Edward Snowden’s actions.
items.why: it constrains state surveillance of journalists, protecting the conditions for a free press and public-interest reporting on government

items.h: Substack awards cash to local independent newsletters
items.b: Joe Mitchell , Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation, finds it interesting to see Substack using its revenues to help boost civic reporting . The Manchester Mill is an example of one of the local publishers benefiting from the award.
items.why: it supports local independent journalism, sustaining plural sources of public-interest information
items.note: Treated as media-plurality support rather than organisational funding news since it funds outlets rather than the reporting organisation itself.

items.h: Votes for Schools polls school children
items.b: Lizzy Lewis and the Votes for Schools team polled more than 21,000 school children on the impact of local elections, here are their results . Their next poll will survey 100,000 school children on climate.
items.why: it engages young people in reflecting on and discussing elections, building civic engagement and political literacy

items.h: Political Literacy Day
items.b: Danielle Vaughan , Campaign Coordinator at Shout Out UK, is currently working on making Political Literacy Day a reality on November 4th. We’re excited to hear more!
items.why: it creates a new campaign aimed at building political literacy and civic engagement among the public
items.note: Sector capacity-building campaign counts as a democracy story under the participation beat.

items.h: Course: What Does My Political Future Look Like?
items.b: Elect Her ’s course, specifically created for BAME women, will take place on 14th and 21st June, with the first session earlier this week. The course is for women who strive to be more politically active and want to understand how they can make that a reality. There will be a second run of the course on 6th, 13th and 20th July. Register here .
items.why: it creates a new means for underrepresented women to build the capacity and confidence to participate in political life.

items.h: First parallel Senedd election for young people aged 11–15
items.b: Children’s Commissioner for Wales’ Project Vote ran the large-scale parallel mock Senedd election, with voting in 36 out of 40 Welsh constituencies. More than 1 in 20 young people took part, 59% of which said they were more likely to engage in future elections when they’re old enough.
items.why: it builds young people's civic capacity and willingness to engage with future elections through a hands-on democratic education exercise.
items.note: Mock election used as a civic engagement tool rather than an actual electoral process, so filed under participation with elections as secondary.

items.h: Welsh Election Study run first ever booster sample of 16–17 year olds
items.b: Jac Larner and the team at the Welsh Election Study polled over 4,000 people prior to and after the 2021 Senedd election, including a booster sample of over 250 16 & 17 year olds. Among other findings, the study found that those in predominantly Welsh speaking schools or youth groups were much more likely to have discussed the election than those predominantly speaking English in similar settings. View the findings here .
items.why: it produces new evidence about young people's engagement with and discussion of elections, bearing on future electoral participation.
items.note: Filed under elections per the turnout/participation rule covering willingness to engage with elections.

items.h: Mandate Democracy looks to expand to the UK
items.b: Mandate Democracy (MD) is a US based non profit focused on voter education and empowerment with strong international links. The MD team are keen to offer their resources, tools and technology and build partnerships with UK based organisations. Contact Hope , Head of UK Operations.
items.note: Announcement of an organisation's intent to expand and seek partnerships, not a concrete new means of participation yet created.

items.h: Democracy Club does Biscuit Politics
items.b: Democracy Club have released their biscuit poll of polls . According to their data encompassing 1500 2021 election candidate’s preferred biscuits, custard creams would win in a FPTP biscuit election, but if the election were conducted by PR, a coalition of many biscuit types would be inevitable, most likely led by the combined varieties of digestives (14.3%) or hobnobs (14.1%). Kate Seary is also leaving the Democracy Club team after 6 months as their Devolved Elections Assistant, for a full time role with the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales .

items.b: We hope you’ve found the Democracy Bulletin newsletter to be a useful resource. Please take a moment to complete this survey , which will take you no more than 5 minutes. Thank you very much for your time.

items.h: Involve hiring new Democracy Network Coordinator
items.b: Tim Hughes and the team have drafted a job description for the new role and are requesting feedback. You can comment directly into the Google Doc or send your feedback directly via DemocracyNetwork@involve.org.uk .
items.note: Organisational hiring news, not a change in democratic mechanism.

items.h: Launch of the Local Democracy Research Centre
items.b: A new initiative by the Local Government Intelligence Unit (LGIU) launched last week. The centre brings together academics and local government practitioners to generate insight, research and collaboration.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new research and collaboration hub aimed at building the capacity of academics and practitioners to strengthen local democratic decision-making
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building (a new 'hub') rather than mere organisational launch.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society begin implementing their new strategy
items.b: Josiah Mortimer, Head of Comms at the Electoral Reform Society (ERS), reports they are finalising a new report due out next month celebrating two decades of PR in Scotland, Wales and London. ERS is arrayed on many fronts, working on a Voter ID coalition with Fair Vote, tracking plans to impose FPTP on Mayors and PCCs, responding to the Government’s Electoral Commission plans and implementing a new strategy for the organisation.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns campaigning on voter identification, the electoral systems used for directly-elected Mayors and PCCs, and oversight of the Electoral Commission, all core to competitive and well-run elections

items.h: Labour’s National Policy Forum consultation launches
items.b: The consultation precedes the primary work of the NPF through its policy commissions. Are you trying to influence the Labour Party and its policy? Have your say by Monday 19th July 2021.
items.note: Internal party policy consultation does not itself concern acquisition, exercise or constraint of public power.

items.h: ConservativeHome acts to balance partisanship of public appointments
items.b: Tax Payers’ Alliance reports half of appointees to public bodies were Labour aligned, with less than a third for the Conservatives. ConservativeHome now reserve a space each week in their newsletter for links to new public appointment vacancies to better advertise these positions.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the political balance and fairness of appointments to public bodies, a standards-in-public-life accountability mechanism
links: ConservativeHome now reserve a space each week

items.h: Elect Her rolling out new workshops & hiring freelancer
items.b: Hannah Stevens, Director at Elect Her , is running 8 online workshops over the next few weeks to motivate, support and equip women to stand for elected office across the UK. Do you know a freelancer who’d like to help develop Elect Her’s downloadable resources? Reach out to Hannah to find out more.
items.why: this matters democratically because training programmes that help women stand for elected office directly affect candidate access and the representativeness of elected institutions
items.note: Classified as elections/candidacy capacity-building given the explicit focus on standing for office, rather than general civic participation.

items.h: Co-producing policy platforms through legislative theatre
items.b: A specialist in Legislative Theatre (LT) , Katy Rubin , is currently leading LT projects in Greater Manchester, Glasgow , Coventry and Islington, on a range of issues including homelessness and climate policy. Working with local and combined authorities, youth groups and participatory democracy partners such as Shared Future CIC , these projects aim to co-produce policy platforms.
items.why: this matters democratically because legislative theatre is a deliberative process used with local and combined authorities to co-produce policy, a form of collective decision-making machinery beyond elections
items.note: Deliberative/participatory policy-making processes are filed under elections & decision making per the boundary rule on deliberation.

items.h: Vote for Policies need volunteer developer to help improve their surveys
items.b: They’re rebuilding their survey so it’s faster, cheaper to run and easier to update at election time. They have a small team working on the upgrade, but could use an extra hand or two. If you have experience with React, Typescript, Node.js or CSS, email Matt Chocqueel-Mangan .
items.note: Volunteer/developer recruitment for an organisation's own tool is operational, not a new participation mechanism being launched.

items.h: Talk Shop are looking for volunteers in Bristol and Liverpool for their ‘Win-Win Workout’
items.b: Perry Walker is currently running trials of Talk Shop’s Win-Win deliberative process on the fate of the Colston Statue in Bristol.
items.why: trialling a deliberative process to resolve a contested public decision is part of the machinery of collective decision-making
items.note: Deliberative processes are filed under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, though this reads mainly as a volunteer call.

items.h: George Bolton keen to reach out to democracy practitioners for PhD research
items.b: George aims to collaborate with Young Citizens, Shout Out UK and the Political Literacy APPG on the design, evaluation and trialling of a new intervention aimed at 16–18yr olds.

items.h: NEON offers free trainings on polling and focus groups
items.b: The two free workshops, led by ICM and Survation, will be capped at 20 people, so please only commit if you are sure you can make it. Book here for polling and focus groups .
items.why: a free training that builds campaigners' capacity to run polling and focus groups expands the practical means available for civic and political participation
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation, per the newsletter's stated rule.

items.h: Government announces plans to strip Electoral Commission of prosecution powers
items.b: Outlined as part of a new elections bill, the plans remove the commission’s ability to prosecute criminal offences under electoral law on the basis that this “wastes public money”. Proposals announced so far include a move to allow politicians — rather than the Electoral Commission’s board — to set the priorities of the independent watchdog. The commission responded, remarking that these changes will place a ‘fetter’ on their work.
items.why: removing the independent electoral watchdog's prosecution powers and letting politicians set its priorities weakens a safeguard of electoral integrity
links: remove the commission’s ability to prosecute

items.h: Curbs on protest in policing bill breach human rights law, warn JCHR
items.b: The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) says clauses which allow restrictions to be imposed on protests because of the noise they generate, create powers to limit one-person demonstrations and increase penalties on people who breach conditions placed on protests should all be scrapped . They say the policing bill contains provisions that are unnecessary and disproportionate and confer unacceptably wide and vague powers to curb demonstrations on the Home Secretary and police.
items.why: new powers to restrict protest on grounds of noise or solo demonstration curb the freedom of assembly needed to contest and criticise state power
items.note: Protest story concerns legal restriction and policing powers, so filed under rights not participation.

items.h: Joint Committee on Human Rights investigates voter ID plans
items.b: The committee urged the government to focus on the ‘real problems’ in British elections, such as non-voters and introducing automatic voter registration. Members of the panel concluded that without universal ID provision, voter ID plans here look similar to Republican voter suppression efforts in the US.
items.why: voter ID requirements affect who can practically exercise the franchise and thus the fairness of elections

items.h: Constitution Unit Conference on Johnson’s Constitutional Reform Agenda
items.b: Last week’s conference featured gripping discussions on a range of topics, from devolution to digital campaigning. Highlights included John Pullinger , the new Chair of the Electoral Commission , signalling their interest in paying close attention to matters of digital campaigning in the future as a result of the discussions.
items.why: the Electoral Commission signalling closer scrutiny of digital campaigning bears on the regulation of election campaign practices
items.note: Conference summary is largely an event report but includes a substantive regulatory signal.

items.b: Adam Tomkins , Professor of Public Law at the University of Glasgow and a former Conservative MSP, remarked on his previous confidence in the survival of the Union but that this is now in question with the UK government’s policy to combat Scottish nationalism with English nationalism, or ‘muscular unionism’.
items.why: the stability of the Union and devolution settlement determines how governing power is distributed and exercised across the UK's nations
items.note: Borderline: mainly political commentary on nationalism, but bears on devolved decision-making structures.

items.b: Though the frankest remarks came during the concluding session from Peter Riddell , Commissioner for Public Appointments, Tim Bale , Professor of politics at Queen Mary University, and Dominic Grieve , former Attorney General, highlighting serial rule breaking by the current government and the severely diminished role of parliament, warning that the UK’s democratic system is not inherently self-correcting.
items.why: serial rule-breaking by government and a diminished parliamentary role weaken the checks that hold executive power answerable

items.h: Policy Exchange host Chloe Smith MP, Minister of State for the Constitution and Devolution
items.b: During the talk, entitled Defending Democracy, Chloe reaffirmed their commitment to the Electoral Integrity Bill. Questions to the minister included the issue of foreign interference in elections, ongoing challenges for returning officers and lack of representation and engagement in the work of the Lords. You can watch the session recording here .
items.why: it concerns safeguarding electoral integrity and addressing foreign interference in UK elections, alongside scrutiny of unelected chamber representation.

items.h: Lords call for immediate action to slim down second chamber
items.b: Five years ago the Burns Report on the size of the House of Lords recommended non-legislative reform to reduce the size of the House, capping members at 600, a two out, one in system, 15-year non-renewable fixed term limits with appointments linked to election results. Earlier this year the House reached 800 members. The Lord Speaker’s Committee on the Size of the House new report considers that piecemeal voluntary non-legislative approach no longer viable.
items.why: the size and composition of the legislature affects its capacity for effective scrutiny of the executive.
items.note: Lords reform concerns Parliament's structure and effectiveness rather than elections themselves.
links: Lord Speaker’s Committee on the Size of the House

items.h: ERS Scotland and Sortition Foundation ramp up calls for a ‘House of Citizens’
items.b: The push follows recent revelations of a Conservative Party donor funding the party £500,000, just after being made a peer . 22 former donors to political parties have been given peerages in the past 12 years, with donations totalling £50.4m. In Scotland, pressure is growing for a ‘House of Citizens’ — similar to the recent Citizens’ Assembly of Scotland.
items.why: it proposes new deliberative decision-making machinery to replace an appointed chamber, tied to concerns about donor influence over public appointments.
items.note: Citizens'-assembly-style proposals are filed under elections/decision-making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: just after being made a peer

items.h: Nesta join three year collective intelligence research project, COLDIGIT
items.b: Collective Intelligence through Digital Tools (COLDIGIT) will be running three participatory budget pilots in Trondheim, Gothenburg and Helsinki. Oli Whittington and the Nesta team will be leading investigations into blockers and enablers for scaling and adoption of collective intelligence methods, tools and advice.
items.why: it develops participatory budgeting and collective intelligence tools that expand practical means for citizens to take part in public decisions.

items.h: Are voters influenced by the results of citizens’ assemblies?
items.b: Steve Sloman, Daniella Kupor and David Yokum’s study sees a shift in opinion for a range of policies when participants are told about the results of an assembly. Their work concludes that citizens’ assemblies and other deliberative events can be more impactful by simply telling an electorate about its results.
items.why: it produces new evidence on how deliberative processes like citizens' assemblies can shape and legitimate collective decision-making.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections/decision-making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Democratic backsliding: could it happen here?
items.b: Stephan Haggard of the School of Global Policy and Strategy & Robert R Kaufman at Rutgers University launch a new book on their study of democratic backsliding across 16 countries, with an accompanying summary for the Constitution Unit blog .
items.why: it examines the mechanisms by which checks and balances on executive power erode, informing debate on whether such backsliding could occur in the UK.
items.note: Genuinely borderline given its general, comparative academic framing rather than a specific UK mechanism.
links: summary for the Constitution Unit blog

items.h: House of Commons Library boundary review briefings
items.b: Elise Uberoi and Neil Johnston at the House of Commons Library publish a pair of briefings on the rules and procedures for boundary changes , and how the public can have a say in the changes .
items.why: boundary rules and public input mechanisms directly shape how constituencies and electoral representation are drawn.
links: rules and procedures for boundary changes
how the public can have a say in the changes

items.h: openDemocracy wins transparency court case against secretive government FOI unit
items.b: The judgement marks a significant legal victory against the UK government, forcing transparency on Michael Gove’s ‘Orwellian’ Clearing House unit .
items.why: a court has forced a secretive government unit to be answerable and transparent about its FOI-handling practices.
items.note: FOI story concerns an institution being held answerable, per the standing distinction.

items.h: UK Parliament opens investigation into Michael Gove’s FOI unit
items.b: Following the openDemocracy legal victory, both openDemocracy and the Campaign for Freedom of Information had written to PACAC asking the committee to investigate. The public administration and constitutional affairs committee (PACAC) is now to launch an inquiry probe into the Cabinet Office’s controversial ‘Clearing House’. The exact terms of the probe have yet to be confirmed. It is expected that a short, targeted inquiry will be held either directly before or after the summer recess. Michael Gove is expected to be called to give evidence.
items.why: a parliamentary committee scrutinising a Cabinet Office unit exercises legislative oversight of executive conduct.

items.h: Concern rising over patient data handover plans say Big Brother Watch
items.b: Senior GPs have called on colleagues to refuse to hand over patients’ personal data to NHS Digital. The automatic transfer of medical records to the NHS Digital central database has been fraught with oversight concerns . These include the sole independent advisory group on collecting GP data, GPES IAG, the group that first raised concerns about the data plan being abolished without replacement .
items.why: it concerns privacy safeguards over government collection of citizens' personal data and the removal of independent oversight of that process.
items.note: Privacy/surveillance concerns are filed under rights and freedoms rather than accountability, though oversight-body abolition also touches accountability.
links: refuse to hand over patients’ personal data

items.h: mySociety explores the effectiveness of Freedom of Information
items.b: Alex Parsons, Researcher at mySociety, shows off their new FOI minisite , presenting up-to-date statistics on FOI requests across Government.
items.why: it creates a new tool to monitor how effectively Freedom of Information is holding government bodies answerable for their decisions.
items.note: FOI here is treated as an accountability mechanism rather than an information-environment story, per the standing distinction.

items.h: COVID contract winners go on to donate £615,000 to Conservatives
items.b: More than £600,000 has been donated to the Conservative Party by firms and individuals that have been awarded some £400 million in public contracts during the Coronavirus pandemic, reveals the Byline Times .
items.why: it reveals potential undue influence of private donors who received public contracts over a governing party, raising conflict-of-interest concerns central to standards in public life.

items.h: Calls for peers to bring new research agency within scope of FOI
items.b: The Advanced Research and Invention Agency, as it stands, will have a budget of more than £800m for “ high risk, high reward ” projects, but will be exempt from FOI. The Campaign for Freedom of Information are now calling for peers to act and bring ARIA within the scope of FOI .
items.why: exempting a large publicly funded body from FOI reduces the ability to hold it answerable for how public money is spent.
links: The Campaign for Freedom of Information
bring ARIA within the scope of FOI

items.h: NetPol and rights groups report concern over aggressive police tactics at G7
items.b: Netpol highlighted police confusion over their duty to protect the right to peaceful protest in the run up to the event. Police designated protest sites 23 miles from the G7 area and reportedly engaged in heavy surveillance and house raids on members of non-violent activist groups prior to the event. During the event the protest camp of climate group Animal Rebellion was raided, arresting 29 activists on conspiracy charges, including the owner of the farm the camp was sited on. Many were later released more than 100 miles from their arrest location and bailed out of the entirety of Cornwall.
items.why: aggressive policing, surveillance and restriction of protest sites limits people's ability to exercise freedom of assembly and challenge power publicly.
items.note: Classified under rights rather than participation because the story concerns policing and legal restriction, not willingness to protest.
links: released more than 100 miles from their arrest location

items.h: Election candidates are copying Trump election disinformation tactics, First Draft reports
items.b: Leading Peruvian political scientist, Adriana Urrutia, criticises Keiko Fujimori’s attempts to derail (Spanish) the Peruvian presidential election with unfounded claims of election fraud. Netanyahu likewise claimed his election loss was the result of “the greatest election fraud in the history of the country, in my opinion in the history of any democracy.” Netanyahu failed to provide evidence for his claims.
items.why: the spread of unfounded election-fraud disinformation tactics erodes public ability to trust and interpret information about electoral outcomes, a risk relevant to UK elections as comparative evidence.
items.note: International material included as comparative evidence on a disinformation tactic relevant to UK elections.

items.h: Batley and Spen by-election vote next week
items.b: All eyes are on Batley and Spen over the next few days as the contest, widely seen as a key test for Keir Starmer’s leadership, plays out. The election to replace the new Mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin , will be held on July 1st.
items.why: a competitive by-election is the mechanism by which voters choose their representative.

items.h: Public confidence in elections at record high
items.b: The Electoral Commission’s annual public attitude research focuses on how people feel about the process of voting and democracy. This year’s report found record public confidence in the running of elections and with the process of voting and registering to vote — though just 14% felt that political financing was transparent, down from 37% in 2011. 7 out of 10 people think online political ads should be transparent and two thirds say voter ID would increase their confidence in the security of the voting system.
items.why: public confidence in the administration and integrity of elections, including views on campaign finance transparency and voter ID, directly reflects the perceived legitimacy of the electoral process.
links: Electoral Commission’s annual public attitude research

items.h: Government response to consultation on digital imprints for online campaigning material
items.b: Last week the government published their response to the consultation on how digital imprints should be implemented. Minister of state for the Constitution and Devolution, Chloe Smith MP, made an accompanying written statement .
items.why: digital imprint rules govern transparency of who is funding and behind online campaign material, a core safeguard for fair and transparent electoral competition.
items.note: Digital imprints sit at the boundary between campaign finance (elections) and political advertising transparency (information).

items.h: Democracy Club write to the new Chair of the Electoral Commission, John Pullinger
items.b: The letter petitions the EC to deliver more digital services and provide a trustworthy source of good information for elections, that the Commission should bring DC’s services in-house and appoint a new Chief Digital Officer. Peter Keeling is preparing Democracy Club’s report on the 2021 elections.
items.why: the letter seeks to improve the Electoral Commission's capacity to provide trustworthy election information and digital services, affecting the quality of electoral administration.

items.h: House of Commons Library briefing on recall elections
items.b: The briefing explores the Recall process and its history since introduction in 2015. A recall special election has been triggered just once, to recall Peterborough Labour MP Fiona Onasanya after their 2018 conviction and prison sentence.
items.why: the recall mechanism is part of the machinery allowing constituents to remove an elected representative between general elections.

items.h: TheProgAlliance working to boost awareness of the upcoming Batley and Spen by-election
items.b: Jon Morter and the team spent the last month building awareness of the Chesham & Amersham by-election, which is becoming markedly more difficult they report, now that Twitter is “coming down much harder on those with ‘additional’ Twitter accounts.”
items.why: it concerns efforts to raise voter awareness and turnout for a parliamentary by-election, part of the machinery of electoral participation.
items.note: Turnout and awareness campaigns for elections are always classed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Cabinet Office ordered to disclose polling on the Union and spend
items.b: Tommy Sheppard MP, the SNP constitutional affairs spokesperson, sent an FOI request seeking information on government polling on public perceptions of the Union since January 2018 and how much the UK government has spent on it. The Cabinet Office refused the request, but has now been ordered to disclose the information requested .
items.why: a Freedom of Information order compels government disclosure of spending and polling activity, holding the executive answerable for its use of public funds and information.
links: now been ordered to disclose the information requested

items.h: Launch of cross-border campaign for Scottish independence
items.b: Campaign for Scottish independence, the People United , launches. Bringing together founders of the former Radical Independence Campaign, Catalonian movement organisers and figures from across the British left, the project aims to internationalise the cause for Scottish independence and contest the SNP’s leadership of the independence cause.
items.why: the launch of a new cross-border campaign group creates a fresh vehicle for civic mobilisation around a major constitutional question.
items.note: Campaign group formation for a constitutional cause sits between civic organising and the machinery of a future referendum.

items.h: The Local Authority Podcast
items.b: FutureGov have teamed up with Local Government Chronicle to produce a new monthly podcast bringing together leaders from the sector to explore the most pressing topics and challenges to LAs. The first episode covers the topic of democracy and remote meetings with guest star Jackie Weaver.
items.note: A sector podcast for local authority professionals is organisational content, not a change to democratic participation.

items.h: House of Commons Library Briefing on the Northern Ireland Bill 2021–2022
items.b: The NI Bill implements aspects of the New Decade, New Approach agreement (NDNA) . The NDNA restored the government of the Northern Ireland Executive after a three-year hiatus following the Renewable Heat Incentive scandal. Read the briefing .
items.why: the Bill restructures the powers and functioning of the Northern Ireland Executive, a devolved decision-making institution.

items.h: Home Rule for Scotland?
items.b: Kenny MacAskill , former MSP, MP and Scottish Cabinet Secretary for Justice, puts forward the case of Home Rule for Scotland .
items.why: the proposal concerns the distribution of decision-making powers between Scotland and Westminster, part of devolved governance structures.

items.h: Carnegie evaluate the Online Safety Bill
items.b: The Carnegie Trust have been digging into the detail of the bill and have published their initial analysis . Other organisations have published their initial reactions in the past few weeks including Hope Not Hate , Hacked Off , Impress and legal firm Osborne Clarke . Just to recap, the House of Commons Library published an updated briefing note at the end of May, with helpful chronological detail marking the evolution of the bill.
items.why: the Online Safety Bill will shape the rules governing online speech and the public information environment.

items.h: Join Public Interest News Foundation for the launch of their 2021 UK Index
items.b: Launching July 8th , the Index is the first ever comprehensive survey of the independent news sector in the UK.
items.why: a comprehensive index of the independent news sector maps media plurality and local journalism capacity, key to a healthy information environment.

items.h: New analysis on electoral integrity from Technology and National Security APPG
items.b: The APPG for Technology and National Security has published an analysis of the impact of misinformation and disinformation on electoral integrity; and Darren Jones MP, the APPG’s Chair, wrote an op-ed for Red Box on the findings
items.why: the analysis examines how misinformation and disinformation affect the integrity of elections.
items.note: Electoral integrity is explicitly anchored to elections & decision making even though disinformation is the vector.
links: APPG for Technology and National Security

items.h: Despite what they say, TikTok isn’t free from partisan ads — Mozilla report
items.b: TikTok have long claimed they’ve banned all political advertising. Mozilla’s investigation reveals how political influencers are flying under the radar on the platform.
items.why: undisclosed political advertising on a major platform undermines transparency and plurality in the public information environment.

items.h: Ofcom publishes their annual Online Nation research
items.b: The research is supplemented by two detailed reports on misinformation from LSE and consulting firm Yonder .
items.why: it examines the scale and nature of online misinformation shaping the public information environment in which political debate occurs.

items.h: How to help civil society disinformation researchers flourish
items.b: Samantha Bradshaw and Lisa-Maria Neudert of the National Endowment for Democracy’s International Forum for Democratic Studies analyse how civil society organisations (CSOs) play a central role in addressing disinformation’s growing impact on democracy. The research highlights clear paths forward for enhancing capacity to combat disinformation, such as community building amongst CSOs, better access to social media data and an improved skills base.
items.why: civil society capacity to research and counter disinformation affects the integrity of the public information environment underpinning democratic debate.
items.note: Research/analysis piece rather than a new tool or programme, but the topic is squarely the information environment.
links: National Endowment for Democracy’s International Forum for Democratic Studies

items.h: Votes for Schools polls school children
items.b: Lizzy Lewis , Head of Impact at Votes for Schools , reports they poll roughly 30,000+ children and young people every week. Results are in for last week’s vote on the refugee crisis. They also announced the winners of the Student Voice Awards .
items.note: Ongoing polling activity and award announcement, not a newly created mechanism for participation.

items.h: New advanced course on post-legislative scrutiny at the University of London
items.b: Westminster Foundation for Democracy and the Institute of Advanced Legal Studies at the University of London (IALS-UoL) announce a new Advance Certified Course on Post-Legislative Scrutiny. The course is intended for MPs, senior parliamentary staff and academics, the course will run throughout July. Read the syllabus and sign up here .
items.why: training MPs and parliamentary staff in post-legislative scrutiny strengthens Parliament's capacity to hold the executive accountable for the implementation of law.
items.note: New capacity-building course, but aimed at the specific accountability function of legislative scrutiny rather than general public participation.
links: Read the syllabus and sign up here

items.h: The double edged sword of legislative change
items.b: Amy Gibbs at Sheila McKechnie Foundation blogs about the unintended consequences of success and legislative change.
items.note: Too abstract a reflection on legislative change to identify a specific democratic mechanism.

items.h: Big Tent Ideas Festival returns next month
items.b: Trin Gong , Events Assistant at the Big Tent Foundation , reports that their in-person political festival will run on Saturday 10th July in Coventry. The theme of the festival is Healthier, Cleaner, Creative Growth to Build Back Better.
items.note: Event listing/sector logistics rather than a reported change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Learning from the 1997 Blair-Ashdown Tactical Voting Deal | Get PR Done!
items.b: Thursday 24 June, 7pm Neal Lawson, Director at Compass, spills the beans on the largest and most productive tactical voting programme ever launched in the UK. Register for the event here .
items.note: Event announcement about historical tactical voting strategy, not a reported change or new mechanism.

items.b: We hope you’ve found the Democracy Bulletin newsletter to be a useful resource. Please take a moment to complete this survey , which will take you no more than 5 minutes. Thank you very much for your time.
The draft bill is about to enter a 12 week pre-legislative scrutiny (PLS) period, likely concluded in the autumn.
items.why: the Online Safety Bill will regulate online platforms and speech, shaping the information environment citizens rely on for political debate.
items.note: Legislative process on internet regulation falls under information & public debate rather than pure legislative scrutiny.

items.b: Following PLS, the Bill is expected to come before Parliament in early-mid 2022.
items.why: the timing of the Online Safety Bill's parliamentary passage affects how soon rules governing online speech and platforms will take effect.

items.b: OFCOM will then begin a process of drafting guidance for companies, likely taking a further 6–12 months, followed by a period for companies to perform their own risk assessments.
items.why: Ofcom's guidance-drafting process will determine how platform regulation affecting public debate is implemented and enforced.

items.b: The Online Safety Bill will likely ‘go live’ by early 2023 at the earliest.
items.why: the timeline for the Online Safety Bill going live determines when new rules shaping online political speech and platform accountability take effect.

items.h: Digital Action request orgs sign Online Safety Bill public joint statement by COB Thurs 8th July
items.b: Ruth Dunlop Price and the Digital Action team have worked up a public joint statement . The letter welcomes progress on the Bill, highlights the areas of concern or where clarification is needed, and gives parliamentarians key questions to ask during pre-legislative scrutiny. If you would like to add your organisational name to the statement, contact Ruth ASAP.
items.note: A call to sign an advocacy statement is sector logistics, not itself a democracy story.

items.h: LSE host in-depth briefing on the Online Safety Bill this Thursday 8th July
items.b: The briefing will provide an overview of the draft OSB, featuring contributions from Full Fact, Ofcom, DCMS, CCDH, parliamentarians and academics. Register here .
items.note: Event listing/briefing announcement, not substantive reporting.

items.h: For more in depth analysis on the Online Safety Bill
items.b: See Carnegie , Demos , Glitch/Anti Semitism Policy Trust , Hope Not Hate , Hacked Off , Impress (regulator), Osborne Clark (legal) and a new HoC briefing note including chronological overview of the bill’s evolution.
items.note: A list of links to external analysis is a resource roundup, not a democracy story in itself.

items.b: Links to comment include: Graham Smith on OSB implications for journalism , David Davis on OSB as the “censors charter” .
items.note: A list of links to opinion pieces is not itself reporting a democratic mechanism.
