items.h: Applications open for new Democracy Network Coordinator role
items.b: Involve are looking for a coordinator for their new democracy network — the role spans three years and will lead on efforts to co-create and develop the network. View the new job posting .
items.note: Job advertisement for an organisation's own role, excluded even though the organisation works on democracy.

items.h: Shared Future looking for new Project Officer to work on Citizen’s Juries and Assemblies
items.b: Jez Hall and the team at Shared Future CIC are looking for someone keen to bring communities together with a passion for citizen participation to help them deliver a series of deliberative sessions across the North West of England.
items.note: Job advertisement, excluded as organisational admin rather than a change in participation opportunities.

items.h: Centre for Policy Studies publish landmark survey of British values
items.b: Dr Frank Luntz has spent the summer working with CPS on a landmark survey of the British public’s language and values. Headline findings include: Britain is not as divided as the USA, voters are just as fed up with business as with politicians, Tory and Labour supporters are united by their values — but divided by their policies.

items.h: 50% OFF this Saturday’s Big Tent Ideas Festival
items.b: Big Tent Ideas is back with their first in-person festival this Saturday 10th July in Coventry. Thanks to Trin and the team, you can enjoy the festival with this 50% off discount code: BIGTENT21
links: first in-person festival this Saturday 10th July

items.h: Constitution Unit’s Monitor: constitutional uncertainty on multiple fronts
items.b: Published three times a year, the UCL Constitution Unit’s Monitor is the democracy sector’s academic ‘newspaper of record’, unpacking the last four months of democratic and constitutional updates. The current issue prioritises the current climate of constitutional uncertainty, echoed in their recent conference on constitutional reform last month.
items.note: Announcement of an academic publication's existence, not substantive reporting of a change, treated as sector logistics.

items.h: SMK announce new dates for their Open Training Programme
items.b: The fully online training programme covers a range of topics, from influencing parliament to self-care and campaign evaluation. Signup for the new courses on their website .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new practical means for people to learn how to influence Parliament and run campaigns, expanding capacity for civic participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building resource counted per framework rule.

items.h: PSA EPOP deadline extended to this Wednesday 7th July!
items.b: The Political Studies Association’s Elections, Public Opinions & Parties (EPOP) conference have extended the deadline of their Call for Papers. This year’s face-to-face covid secure conference will be held on 3–4 September. If you’re a democracy researcher, don’t miss out on EPOP’s range of funding opportunities and awards .

items.h: NCCPE announce dates for Engage Conference
items.b: The National Co-ordinating Centre for Public Engagement’s Engage Conference is due to be held online on the 1st and 2nd December. The conference will be a mix of plenaries, networking opportunities, and opportunities to get involved with the Engage Unconference.

items.h: Political Studies Association announce their annual conference, Call for Papers open
items.b: The theme for this year’s November conference is Parliament at a Critical Juncture , focusing on the pressures placed upon parliaments during this period of compounding crises. Call for Papers are now open .

items.h: Questions of Accountability Conference, Call for Papers open
items.b: The University of Worcester and the University of Sheffield are organising a conference/exhibition entitled Questions of Accountability between 1–5 November 2021, full details of which can be found here .

items.h: New House of Commons Library briefings
items.b: Richard Kelly, Sarah Priddy and the team have published briefings covering the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Bill , MPs who’ve withdrawn or been suspended from the Commons Chamber, and apologies by MPs to the House .
items.note: Announcement of library briefings' publication, not substantive reporting of their content or a change.
links: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Bill
apologies by MPs to the House

items.h: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill passes third reading
items.b: The controversial bill was voted through on Monday evening with 365 MPs backing the bill and 265 opposing. The Joint Committee on Human Rights recently condemned the legislation as a breach of human rights law. In March, democracy orgs united to denounce the new laws , with particular focus on the new powers to impose conditions on protest and the implications of new trespass laws on GRT communities.
items.why: this matters democratically because new statutory powers to restrict protest and target trespass by GRT communities directly narrow citizens' freedom of assembly and expression against the state.
items.note: Protest restriction via policing/legislation falls under rights and civic space rather than participation willingness.
links: united to denounce the new laws

items.h: Make Votes Matter plan cross-party Day of Action for Equal Votes for July 31st
items.b: The Make Noise for PR Day of Action aims to bring national focus around PR. MVM are planning awareness raising activities including banner drops and street stalls. Get in touch with the MVM team to find out more here .
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns campaigning for proportional representation, a change to the electoral system that would affect how votes translate into political power.
items.note: Campaign for PR falls under electoral systems within elections & decision making rather than generic civic participation.

items.h: AEA say voter ID cards should be delivered by local authority, not election staff
items.b: Peter Stanyon, Chief Executive of the Association of Electoral Administrators, warned that whilst it is clear photographic voter ID will be necessary as a result of the new legislation, responsibility for producing voter ID cards should rest with the local authority, not over-stretched Returning or Electoral Registration Officers. Mr Stanyon also remarked that the cards should be nationally funded, with no additional cost burden pushed onto councils.
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns the administration and funding of voter ID requirements, which affects the accessibility and integrity of voting.

items.h: Urgent action required on size of the Upper House, says Lord Speaker’s Committee
items.b: We mentioned this in our last issue , though here, the Chair of the Committee, Lord Terry Burns, writes for the Constitution Unit blog , arguing that it is essential party leaders now “put aside short-term interests and agree plans to reduce its numbers”.
items.why: This matters democratically because the size and functioning of the legislature's upper chamber affects Parliament's capacity to scrutinise the executive effectively.
links: writes for the Constitution Unit blog

items.h: North Ayrshire’s experiments with youth-led participatory budgeting
items.b: Demsoc covered the work here , in conversation with Donna Anderson, Participation and Democracy Officer and Youth Work Lead for North Ayrshire Council. They’ve evolved their practices from participants physical ‘spending’ of tokens in a market stall environment, to moving into a fully online environment, which has brought increased engagement.
items.why: This matters democratically because participatory budgeting creates a direct mechanism for citizens, including young people, to take part in allocating public resources.

items.h: RebootGB to launch new podcast on their work building for a Progressive Alliance
items.b: Liz Crosbie and the team at RebootGB will be podcasting for the first time. They’re also on the lookout for someone to help develop and improve their website.
items.note: This is organisational news (a podcast launch and volunteer request), not a change affecting democratic participation.

items.h: Chatham House on strengthening youth participation in public affairs
items.b: Martina Carlucci, Anar Bata and Jacqueline Rowe at Chatham House note that whilst young people have been at the forefront of civic movements in recent years, they are consistently underrepresented in discussions around human rights and how to monitor their protection and defence.
items.why: This matters democratically because it addresses the underrepresentation of young people in civic and political engagement processes.

items.h: UK Government spends COVID-19 emergency funds on Union polling
items.b: Following a court order , the Cabinet Office released spending documents showing officials had been instructed to use emergency covid contract funds to commission political research on “attitudes to the UK Union”. SNP Westminster leader Ian Blackford has called for a public inquiry into the matter.
items.why: This matters democratically because it reveals potential misuse of public emergency funds for politically motivated polling, raising questions about executive accountability and transparency.
items.note: Court-ordered disclosure and calls for inquiry point to accountability rather than redress mechanisms.
links: Ian Blackford has called for a public inquiry

items.h: All party inquiry finds police breached fundamental rights during Clapham and Bristol Kill the Bill protests
items.b: The APPG on Democracy and the Constitution, supported by independent counsel and the Institute for Constitutional and Democratic Research (ICDR), condemned the unnecessary and disproportionate use of force used by officers at the Sarah Everard vigil and the Bristol Kill the Bill protests earlier this year. The report contradicts the findings of Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire and Rescue Service (HMIC), which argued that the police had acted proportionately in their use of force. HMIC’s claim to impartiality was recently questioned by whistleblower and civil servant Alicia O…
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns the lawfulness of police use of force against protesters, bearing on citizens' freedom of assembly and protection from state coercion.
items.note: Protest policing is classified under rights & freedoms per the boundary rule on legal restriction and state coercion; the inquiry itself also engages accountability scrutiny.
links: condemned the unnecessary and disproportionate use of force

items.h: mySociety release new tool to help challenge FOI refusals
items.b: The new automated notice on FOI refusals via WhatDoTheyKnow helps users identify potential exemptions which may have been applied to their request. The tool presents a series of questions which help establish whether or not you can take further action and what that action might be.
items.why: This matters democratically because the tool strengthens citizens' ability to use Freedom of Information law to hold public institutions answerable.
items.note: FOI tool is classified as accountability since its purpose is challenging institutional refusals, per the FOI boundary rule.

items.h: Institute for Government asks: Is it time to overhaul rules on adviser appointments?
items.b: Following the Matt Hancock affair, the problems of how publicly funded government advisors are appointed — and the access they get — is not a matter the government can consider closed, argues Catherine Haddon , IfG’s resident historian.
items.why: This matters democratically because the appointment and access of publicly funded advisers bears on standards in public life and conflicts of interest in government.

items.b: Writing for the Constitution Society , the Institute for Government’s Tim Durrant highlights the IfG’s recent report, Updating the Ministerial Code , setting out the steps the prime minister can take to strengthen both the ministerial code — the rules that govern ministers’ behaviour during and after their time in office — and how it is enforced.
items.why: it concerns how ministerial conduct is regulated and enforced, a core standards-in-public-life accountability mechanism.

items.h: Three new reports from Westminster Foundation for Democracy
items.b: Doing anti-corruption democratically by Heather Marquette; Rethinking strategies for an effective parliamentary role in combatting corruption by Phil Mason; and Post-legislative scrutiny of climate and environment legislation: Guide for parliamentary practice by David Hirst.
items.why: the reports address parliamentary strategies for combating corruption and scrutinising legislation, both accountability mechanisms.
links: Rethinking strategies for an effective parliamentary role in combatting corruption
Post-legislative scrutiny of climate and environment legislation: Guide for parliamentary practice

items.h: Death threats, abuse and arson against candidates and campaigners in Batley and Spen and elsewhere
items.b: Labour activists were ‘ kicked and egged ’ in Batley and Spen. In Lanarkshire, a Conservative councillor suffered a devastating arson attack and Minister Chloe Smith reports having received death threats .
items.why: intimidation and violence against candidates and campaigners threatens the ability of people to stand for and participate in genuinely competitive elections free from coercion.
items.note: Classified under elections because the threat is specifically to candidates/campaigners during an election process, though personal security also touches rights.

items.h: Whilst public confidence in elections is at record highs, the opposite holds for fairness
items.b: Jonathan Rose, writing for the Constitution Society , interrogates national election studies dating back to 1997, finding that public perceptions of whether or not elections are being conducted fairly are at an all time low. Last month the Electoral Commission found public confidence in the running of elections at record highs .
items.why: public perceptions of whether elections are conducted fairly speak directly to the legitimacy and clean-election dimension of the democratic process.

items.h: PM facing legal action over appointment of Tory Party former co-treasurer to the Lords
items.b: The independent watchdog, the House of Lords’ Appointment’s Commission was over-ruled by Johnson to award the seat to the now-Baron Cruddas, reportedly the first time the watchdog’s advice has been actively over-ruled. Lawyers on behalf of the Good Law Project argue the timing of donations by Baron Cruddas to the Conservatives represent ‘bias’ in the process . The Electoral Commission recorded a £500,000 donation to the party three days after taking his seat last February.
items.why: a prime minister overruling an independent appointments watchdog, amid allegations linking the appointment to a large party donation, raises standards-in-public-life and undue-influence concerns.
items.note: Primary beat chosen as public appointments/standards; campaign finance donation angle noted as secondary elections concern.

items.h: House of Commons Library briefings on extent of franchise, electoral intimidation and women members
items.b: The new research briefings from Neil Johnston and Richard Kelly outline voting rights for different types of elections in the UK and the expected new offence of intimidation of candidate and voters, as well as an update of the electoral offence of undue influence and a new review and listing of all the women who’ve ever been elected to the Commons.
items.why: these briefings cover suffrage extent, candidate/voter intimidation offences and representation history, all core to how elections are administered and contested.

items.h: Jackie Weaver’s campaign to hold abusive councillors to account
items.b: Compassion in Politics Ambassador and Zoom sensation Jackie Weaver has launched a campaign to ensure that abusive councillors can be removed from their posts. As it stands, there is no national provision to ensure that a local councillor who acts abusively towards colleagues or constituents can actually be forced to step-down.
items.why: the absence of a mechanism to remove abusive councillors is a gap in accountability for locally elected officials.
items.note: Local government conduct/accountability treated as government_accountability rather than the structural elections_decision_making beat since the issue is disciplinary accountability, not electoral structure.

items.h: LGIU release their primer series for new local councillors
items.b: The primers are designed to help new councillors get on top of the complexities of some of the difference services that LAs provide. New primers will be released in the coming weeks and months. The primers are exclusively for LGIU members. Are you a councillor and not sure if your council is an LGIU member? Check here .
items.note: Practical training resource for councillors' administrative duties, not a mechanism affecting democratic participation itself.

items.h: LGIU launch the Future of Local Government Review
items.b: The first step is this survey to gauge what’s important to those working across local government.
items.why: a review into the future structure and role of local government engages the machinery of local decision-making.
items.note: Local government structure review placed under elections_decision_making per boundary rule despite being only a survey stage.

items.h: Participatory democracy and local government
items.b: Originally published as part of the Improvement Service Thought Leadership series, Lynn Sharp unpacks a range of perspectives on the effective use of participatory democracy in local government.
items.why: it examines how participatory democracy mechanisms operate within local government decision-making structures.
items.note: Participatory/deliberative democracy content assigned to elections_decision_making per framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Index of Independent News Publishing Report launches Thursday July 8th
items.b: The report marks the UK’s first ever comprehensive survey of the independent news sector. Join them for their launch event with PINF Executive Director Jonathan Heawood, Shirish Kulkarni of TBIJ, Emma Meese of the Independent Community News Network and Dame Frances Cairncross, author of the Cairncross Review: a sustainable future for journalism.
items.why: a comprehensive survey of the independent news sector documents the health of media plurality that underpins public access to diverse political information.
items.note: Treated as substantive research on media plurality rather than mere organisational news.

items.h: Common Weal’s Source Direct ceases publication
items.b: For nearly six months we’ve enjoyed reading Source Direct’s updates on Scottish politics, James Foley’s daily blog helped provide the bulk of our Scottish updates for this bulletin. In other news, Common Weal’s podcast last week hosted a discussion with Kevin Anderson from the Evidence Group of the Scottish Climate Assembly, they unpacked the deliberation process and evidence-hearing processes of the Assembly.
items.note: Item is about a publication ceasing operations, which is organisational news rather than a democracy mechanism.

items.h: Shout Out UK, Political Literacy Oversight Group developing political literacy amendment to HE Bill 2020
items.b: Titus Alexander, SOUK and PLOG are working to insert the following clause to the HE Bill:
items.why: an amendment to embed political literacy in higher education would create new means for people to understand and take part in democratic life.
items.note: Sector capacity-building initiative aimed at fostering civic participation.

items.b: Reach out to Titus to find out more and get involved. You can find the link for the amendment here .
items.note: Purely a call-to-action/logistics fragment with no new substantive content.

items.note: Event highlight video listing, not substantive democracy reporting.

items.b: Mihail Chiru and Lieven De Winter have published an article, The Allocation of Committee Chairs and the Oversight of Coalition Cabinets in Belgium , in Government & Opposition.
items.note: Academic publication announcement about Belgium, not UK-relevant reporting with a clear democratic mechanism.
links: The Allocation of Committee Chairs and the Oversight of Coalition Cabinets in Belgium

items.b: Fair Vote building ‘Democracy Defence’ coalition of organisations — sign up now Kyle Taylor and the team at Fair Vote UK want to know whether democracy orgs are planning to engage on either the Online Safety Bill or Elections Bill and to what level so they can work towards a coalition approach. Dozens of orgs have already completed their brief survey to help map what’s happening! Reach out to Kyle to sign up or fill out their survey by Friday 23 July.
items.note: A call for organisations to sign up to a coordination survey is sector organising, not itself a reportable democratic mechanism.
links: Reach out to Kyle to sign up

items.h: Petition to scrap Voter ID reaches 100,000 threshold for parliamentary debate
items.b: MPs across the political spectrum, from David Davis to Dawn Butler, have expressed their opposition to the scheme. With 100,000 signatures on the government’s e-petition site, the issue will now be considered for debate in Parliament.
items.why: public power is contested through a formal petition mechanism that compels Parliament to consider debating a grievance affecting voting rights
items.note: The petition-threshold mechanism sits under participation, though its subject (voter ID) is an elections matter.

items.h: Young Europeans Network in talks with MPs on Elections Bill amendments
items.b: Lara Parizotto , Co-Manager at Young Europeans Network, is in talks with MPs Clive Lewis and Cat Smith for a potential amendment to the Elections Bill focused on residence-based voting rights — see their briefing paper . The amendment will likely call for a similar approach in England as currently exists in Wales and Scotland that saw residents vote in the May elections regardless of where they come from .
items.why: who is entitled to vote in UK elections is a direct question of suffrage and franchise
links: regardless of where they come from

items.h: Hands Off Our Vote campaign launches
items.b: Freddie Mallinson and Jack McAteer launched the new campaign , taking aim at voter ID. Rumour is they’ll be starting a new mailing list focused on voter ID in the next few weeks. Be sure to show your support and give them a follow !
items.why: the campaign contests a proposed restriction on who can practically exercise the right to vote
items.note: Campaign launch is a participation mechanism, but its target (voter ID) is squarely an elections matter.

items.h: PACAC inquiry into the work of the Electoral Commission held oral evidence sessions
items.b: On the 20th July the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee heard evidence from Dr Jess Garland, Director of Policy and Research at the Electoral Reform Society, Peter Geoghegan, Investigations Editor at openDemocracy, Lord Hodgson, and Chloe Hardy, Director of Policy and Comms at SMK, amongst others. You can review the meeting here .
items.why: a parliamentary committee scrutinising the Electoral Commission's work is a check on an institution responsible for running elections
items.note: Parliamentary scrutiny of an electoral management body sits at the boundary of accountability and elections.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society briefing on Voter ID
items.b: Earlier this month ERS posted a full briefing on voter identification, laying out the key arguments and evidence against the current proposals.
items.why: voter identification requirements directly affect people's practical ability to cast a vote

items.h: Elections Bill financial rules a ‘trojan horse’ opening up UK elections to outside influence
items.b: Tom Brake, Director of Unlock Democracy, Dr Jess Garland, Director of Policy and Research at the Electoral Reform Society and Cat Smith MP, Shadow Minister for Democracy, warn the Elections Bill is being used as a ‘trojan horse’ to funnel donations from non-domiciled sources outside the UK into our elections, opening up British elections to outside influence.
items.why: campaign finance rules determine whether elections remain free from undue foreign or non-domiciled influence
links: Elections Bill is being used as a ‘trojan horse’

items.h: DCMS issues comment arguing against requiring photo ID for social media verification, but…
items.b: With 3.5m without photo ID in the UK, the Cabinet Office is proceeding with voter ID for elections.
items.why: requiring photo ID to vote affects the practical ability of millions of citizens to exercise the franchise

items.h: MPs held Westminster debate on Voter ID plans
items.b: You can view the TheyWorkForYou Hansard entry for the 13th July Voter ID Westminster Hall debate here . The debate seemed to go unnoticed by those in the press, outside democracy campaigning circles.
items.why: a parliamentary debate on voter ID scrutinises a proposed change to who can practically vote

items.h: Koreo report organisations can still access a grant to cover a part time role
items.b: Jonny Chambers , Senior Consultant at Koreo and part of The Centre for Democracy , says there are still plenty of grant opportunities available for the government’s Kickstart scheme. You can access a grant to hire a 16–24yr old currently on Universal Credit, covering 25 hours per week at national minimum/living wage and all contributions. Lots of democracy organisations have already taken up this opportunity — reach out to Jonny to find out more.

items.h: Make Votes Matter National Day of Action — 31st July
items.b: With an apparent growing momentum for electoral reform amongst UK left-of-centre parties, this year’s day of action slogan is: Make Noise for PR . MVM are calling on supporters across the country to get the word out for PR, through banner drops, marching bands, street stalls and more.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns campaigning to change the electoral system used to elect representatives.
items.note: Electoral system reform campaigning is filed under elections per framework anchors on electoral systems.

items.h: Clear the Lobby are experimenting with Reddit
items.b: Sebastien Salek runs the fantastic weekly email newsletter (when Parliament is sitting) explaining the laws MPs are voting on the following week. Seb is now experimenting with a new subreddit to allow people to suggest ideas for new laws, build support and get help to pass them in Parliament. Show your support and join the new subreddit — they’ll start when their members hit 1,000.
items.why: this matters democratically because a new tool is being built to help citizens propose and build support for legislation, creating a new means of participation.

items.h: LabourList report Labour Party’s finances in severe disarray
items.b: The Labour Party is reportedly down to one month’s fiscal reserves and has offered voluntary severance to all NEC funded staff. General Secretary David Evans reports this is due to falling member numbers and antisemitism legal costs.
items.why: this matters democratically because the financial collapse of a major political party threatens its capacity to compete and offer voters a viable political alternative.

items.h: George Bolton working to experiment with young people on methods to build trust in democracy
items.b: George is an incoming PhD student at the University of Southampton, working with the university’s Centre for Deliberative Futures . They have been actively networking with democracy organisations with young people and are keen discuss their work and collaborations. You can get in touch with George via their email .

items.h: Women’s Equality Party host WEPstock — a new festival for feminist community building
items.b: The virtual festival is centred around building and developing communities, featuring educational interviews, quiz sessions and panel discussions. Tickets are now on sale .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new space for community building and engagement among people organising politically.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new participation opportunity rather than organisational admin.

items.h: Reboot plans a new series of webinars, podcasts and a newsletter
items.b: Holding their first webinar this past Monday focusing on learning from the recent Lib Dem win in Chesham & Amersham, Liz Crosbie and the team are launching a new podcast and newsletter for supporters.
items.note: This is organisational content output (webinars/podcast/newsletter) rather than a new means of public participation.

items.h: More in Common launch ‘The Endless Sea’ project
items.b: Inspired by the words of Antoine de St. Exupéry, The Endless Sea is an experimental narrative project to help shape the positive narratives of tomorrow. The project aims to assess whether this narrative approach can contribute to More in Common’s stated goals to help unite divided societies.
items.why: this matters democratically because the project aims to build societal cohesion and shared narratives, a condition for healthy civic participation.
items.note: Borderline: framed as narrative/comms experiment rather than a concrete participation mechanism.

items.h: Government sets firm precedent for supremacy of the executive
items.b: Lord Falconer highlights the Government’s use of a Written Ministerial Statement to override an Act of Parliament last week, which is likely enforceable by judicial review. The supremacy of Parliament is conventionally expressed through legislation. Lord Falconer argues that this government action now means that in practice supremacy is now exercised through government motion, the supremacy of the executive.
items.why: this matters democratically because the executive is reported to have overridden an Act of Parliament by ministerial statement, shifting constitutional supremacy away from the legislature.
links: highlights the Government’s use of a Written Ministerial Statement to override an Act of Parliament

items.h: Robert Buckland introduces new Judicial Review and Courts Bill
items.b: Rt Hon Robert Buckland QC MP, Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice, delivered a keynote speech at Policy Exchange on judicial review ahead of the parliamentary introduction of the new Judicial Review and Courts Bill this Wednesday. As part of the Constitution Unit’s conference last month the Secretary of State argued for the courts to narrow their remit, that they are “reading too much into the law”. Expect to hear more on the bill in coming weeks.
items.why: this matters democratically because new legislation and ministerial argument seek to narrow the courts' power to review executive action, affecting judicial constraints on government.
links: keynote speech at Policy Exchange on judicial review

items.h: Liberty highlight actions to take to reject the Police Bill in their latest PCSC newsletter
items.b: The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill will move to the Lords stage after the Summer Recess, according to Liberty’s latest intel. Liberty highlight that the bill will face significant opposition in the Lords and may even be defeated, owing to the composition of the Lords, and that its ranks include former senior judges, lawyers and campaigners with human rights experience. Sign up to Liberty’s newsletter on the Police Bill here .
items.why: it concerns parliamentary scrutiny in the Lords of a bill that constrains protest rights, testing checks on executive-driven legislation.
items.note: Focus is on legislative scrutiny of a bill rather than the underlying rights themselves.
links: The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill

items.h: Unlock Democracy & Compass kickstart new project to persuade Labour on electoral reform
items.b: Awarded a new grant of £80,000 from the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust, Unlock and Compass are now working to complement, network and grow upon existing efforts to shift Labour on electoral reform.
items.why: it concerns advocacy to change the electoral system used to elect Parliament.
items.note: Grant funding is incidental; the substantive story is electoral reform advocacy, not organisational funding news.

items.h: 83% of Labour members back shift to PR new poll finds
items.b: A new poll of 1,000 Labour Party members conducted by YouGov for Labour for a New Democracy found only 10% of party members say the party should not support the switch from FPTP to a form of PR. A previous YouGov survey in December 2019, prior to the election, found 76% of party members supporting a shift to PR. The results reflect the success of the Labour for a New Democracy campaign amongst Constituency Labour Parties (CLPs), with more than a third of CLPs passing motions in support of PR .
items.why: it provides evidence of shifting internal party support for changing the electoral system.
links: third of CLPs passing motions in support of PR

items.h: Shout Out UK and Titus building support for political literacy
items.b: As the Higher Education Bill enters the committee stage, Titus Alexander and the team at Shout Out UK are working to build support for a political literacy amendment to the bill. Get in touch with Titus and the team for more information. Titus also suggests identifying an MP to table an EDM to rally support for the HE Free Speech Bill , view and comment on the draft here .
items.why: it concerns efforts to build political literacy, a civic capacity that affects people's ability to engage in democratic life.

items.h: English Votes for English Laws (EVEL) to be scrapped, Government announces
items.b: Michael Gove has reported that together with Leader of the House, Jacob Rees-Mogg, they have reviewed the system of EVEL and have decided to scrap the procedure in order to simplify the legislative system. The system, suspended since April 2020, was established to address the West Lothian Question .
items.why: it changes the legislative procedure governing how laws affecting only England are decided, altering representational structures within Parliament.
items.note: EVEL concerns the machinery of legislative decision-making tied to territorial representation.

items.h: What do you know about the Scandinavian two-bloc system?
items.b: Electoral Reform Society guest writer Dylan Difford breaks down the bloc system of Scandinavian politics . The bloc system is a fascinating and unwritten rule of countries in the region with a long history, with the benefit of democratising and transparentising the government formation process.
items.why: it offers comparative evidence about alternative electoral and government-formation systems relevant to UK electoral reform debates.
items.note: Foreign system explainer with only indirect bearing on UK reform debate.

items.h: Progress on the UK Government’s next National Action Plan for Open Government is well underway
items.b: Kevin Keith , Chair of the UK Open Government Network , shares their progress on the next National Action Plan (NAP). Member governments of the Open Government Partnership must complete an NAP plan every two years. As the 2019–2021 NAP runs it course, Kevin and the OGN are working on co-creating the next plan with civil servants and civil society. At the moment, commitments (policies) for inclusion in the 5th NAP underway include Open Justice, Open Contracting / Procurement, Algorithmic Transparency, Open Health, and Natural Resources / Climate Change. Civil society leads have been appointed f…
items.why: it concerns government transparency commitments that make institutions more answerable to citizens.

items.h: Check out Crony Connect — helping you to identify politically connected individuals
items.b: Using data from Companies House, the Electoral Commission and MP’s Register of Financial Interests, Crony Connect is a new tool (in beta) that searches for associations between target individuals, their associated companies and any connected donations in financial interest databases.
items.why: it creates a tool to expose politically connected individuals and financial ties, supporting scrutiny of conflicts of interest and corruption.
items.note: New tool for civic scrutiny of political influence, bridging accountability and civic capacity.

items.h: FOI responses suggest Priti Patel misled Parliament on aspects of the Police Bill
items.b: During a 15th March parliamentary debate on the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill , Priti Patel, Home Secretary, said she had worked closely with the Police Federation. A FOI response reveals she did not consult the Police Federation , with the federation responding: “ We did not provide a written submission nor were we consulted on issues of protest-related legislation.” This follows senior police officers remarks earlier this month that they did not ask for the powers and former officers remarking the bill ‘is harmful to democracy’ .
items.why: it concerns whether a minister misled Parliament, a core mechanism of ministerial accountability.
links: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill
FOI response reveals she did not consult the Police Federation
did not ask for the powers

items.h: Green Party leaders Jonathan Bartley and Sian Berry step down triggering leadership race
items.b: Sharing the leadership for the past three years, Bartley and Berry have stood down and removed themselves from the upcoming ballot, citing their intention to help the future co-leaders settle into the role prior to a potential snap election. Berry mentioned apparent tensions at the top of the party over trans-rights as a key reason for her resignation. Bartley says he will now focus on building a progressive alliance. The Greens are also currently celebrating the election of a new party executive.
items.note: Internal party leadership transition is organisational personnel news rather than a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society launching new report highlighting the success of PR in Wales, Scotland & London
items.b: On the anniversary of the Scottish and Welsh referendums of 1997, and as Make Votes Matter launch their day of action on PR, ERS launch their new report comparing the new proportional representation elections in the Senedd, Holyrood and London Assembly with previous elections to those bodies, to show how PR achieves better and fairer outcomes.
items.why: it presents evidence about how electoral systems (PR vs FPTP) shape the fairness and representativeness of elected institutions.

items.h: House of Commons Library briefing on the 2021 Senedd elections
items.b: The briefing provides a full breakdown of the 2021 elections in Wales.
items.why: it documents the administration and outcomes of a national election.

items.h: Welsh Government confirms their longstanding commitment to a federal UK
items.b: Under the label of ‘entrenched devolution’, Mark Drakeford has set out his stall for reform of the union. The recently published strategy paper Reforming our Union: Shared Governance in the UK June 2021 highlights the diminished nature of inter-governmental relations and processes, noting that not one single meeting of the Joint Ministerial Committee has been convened since the current PM took office.
items.why: it concerns proposed changes to the structure and powers of devolved government within the union.
items.note: Devolution structure is filed under elections & decision making per the boundary rule; the intergovernmental accountability angle is secondary.
links: Reforming our Union: Shared Governance in the UK June 2021

items.h: Greater London Authority research project on civic participation — share the survey via your networks
items.b: Dr Elisabeth Pop , Citizenship and Integration Officer at the GLA, is running a new London wide survey on civic and democratic participation mechanisms to build trust and greater engagement between the city and the communities that make up the city. The survey is designed to highlight structural barriers, help shape best practice on civic and democratic participation and inform recommendations for what funders, local authorities and the government can do differently to support work and advocacy in this area.
items.note: This is a call to share a survey, sector logistics rather than a reported democratic mechanism or new participation tool.

items.h: Constitution Committee held Oral Evidence on Future Governance of the UK
items.b: Michael Gove MP, Minister of the Cabinet Office, and Sue Gray, Permanent Secretary to the Cabinet Office, provided oral evidence to the committee.
items.why: parliamentary committee scrutiny of ministers over the future governance of the UK is a core accountability mechanism.

items.h: What might an injection of news journalism do to an area’s civic engagement?
items.b: Joe Mitchell and the team at Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) are designing a potential programme around London 2022, experimenting how civic engagement might be affected by an increased dose of news journalism. PINF are also looking out for applications for their Autumn Leadership Programme for news publishers .
items.why: it explores whether increased local news journalism strengthens the public information environment and civic engagement.
items.note: Programme is still in design stage, and includes a leadership programme call that is closer to sector logistics.
links: Autumn Leadership Programme for news publishers

items.h: What Facebook gutting CrowdTangle means for misinformation
items.b: First Draft highlighted the demise of social media analysis tool CrowdTangle in recent weeks. The tool is critical for misinformation researchers and journalists for its access and data on trending topics, public accounts, communities and viral posts across a range of platforms. Speculation is now growing that the tool will be closed down , similar to the fate of Graph Search in 2019 — another tool critical for journalists and researchers. First Draft says analysts should consider ways to move toward purpose-built tools not reliant on the goodwill of platforms, such as The Markup’s Citizen Bro…
items.why: the loss of a tool used to research misinformation affects the ability of journalists and researchers to monitor the public information environment.

items.h: Institute for Strategic Dialogue report TikTok gives new virality to misinformation
items.b: ISD analyzed 124 TikTok videos featuring vaccine misinformation , finding that anti-vaccination audio tracks have gone viral as a ‘chain message’, with the original claim and post hidden by TikTok. Though TikTok has reportedly cracked down on COVID-19 misinformation, the report’s findings are likely the tip of an iceberg — an iceberg that is currently near-impossible to analyse at scale with current tools and access.
items.why: it documents how platform design enables viral spread of political/health misinformation, affecting the public information environment.
links: ISD analyzed 124 TikTok videos featuring vaccine misinformation

items.h: The National Lottery Community Fund announces first round of Growing Great Ideas funding
items.b: Growing Great Ideas offers long term, multi-year funding to initiatives they believe are capable of delivering transformative change.
items.note: A funding call announcement, sector logistics rather than a democracy story.

items.h: Remembering Mo Mowlam and Robin Cook
items.b: During the Thatcher years, two leading figures within the Labour Party at the time were also strong and talented campaigners for electoral reform and PR. With more than 200 Constituency Labour Parties now in favour of PR, Alan Yearsley celebrates their contribution to democratic reform efforts in the UK in this piece for The Chartist .
items.note: A nostalgic tribute piece rather than a report on a current democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: The Local Trust on Community Power
items.b: Responding to social historian David Boyle’s recent and provocative work on community power for the Local Trust, Colin Prescod — an academic sociologist and documentary filmmaker of Black British community struggles, examines how community development plays out through social upheaval and community action .
items.note: Discussion of community power/development is commentary rather than a mechanism affecting public power or participation opportunities.

items.h: Parline — global data on national parliaments
items.b: The Inter-Parliamentary Union’s new Parline resource has comprehensive data on all national parliaments across the world!
items.note: A data resource announcement about parliaments generally, not a UK democracy mechanism or capacity-building tool for participation.

items.h: Worth a look: Future Now
items.b: Future Now combines a political-action committee, advocacy group and the Future Now Fund. Acting from a ground-up approach, focusing activity within states and local communities, they aim to enact a far reaching policy agenda by 2030 across the United States.
items.note: US-focused organisation profile, not UK-relevant and not a change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Democracy organisations coming together under new umbrella campaign to amplify impact
items.b: Fair Vote, Electoral Reform Society, Unlock Democracy, Open Britain, Best for Britain and others are co-developing a sector wide campaign framework for the Elections Bill. If your org is not yet in the loop and wants to be, you’ll need to add your contact details to this list by 5pm on Thursday 12 August.
items.why: a coordinated civil society coalition forming to campaign on electoral legislation reflects and builds the capacity of civil society to engage with democratic decision-making processes.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building (a new campaign/network), not mere organisational admin.

items.h: How will the umbrella campaign work?
items.b: Kyle Taylor, Director at Fair Vote, notes general agreement on building a broad ‘brand’ for democracy campaigns, that issue-based coalitions emerge, but they will “fly the flag” that they are part of the “democracy defence initiative”, or whatever name the campaign later decides upon.
items.why: describing how a civil society coalition will organise itself to campaign on elections legislation bears on the capacity and coordination of civic engagement.
items.note: Elaboration of the same coalition-building story as item 6; borderline internal strategy detail.

items.b: Shared Contact List If you haven’t already popped your contact details into this list , do so before Wednesday 11th August, when the list will become invite-only to maintain privacy. Fair Vote and the other orgs suggest using this list to connect with other orgs working on the same issues as you, to set up coordinating calls etc.
items.note: Purely operational instruction to join a contact list, akin to sector logistics excluded by the framework.

items.b: Elections Bill Slack A new Slack group has been set up by Best for Britain as a hub for fast communication. Channels are being set up for each aspect of the bill.
items.note: Internal coordination tool (Slack) for organisations already engaged, not a new means of public participation.

items.b: Weekly Zoom “Office Hours” Fair Vote UK will be facilitating a weekly session every Thursday at 12pm open to drop-ins. Email kyle@fairvote.uk for the calendar invite.
items.note: Event/logistics listing, not substantive democracy content.

items.h: Immediate campaigns you can join:
items.b: Below are timely opportunities to collaborate, add your name to things, etc:
items.note: Generic call-to-action header with no substantive content.

items.b: This past Saturday 7th August was one month exactly to the second reading: Josiah Mortimer from ERS helpfully suggested orgs consider making noise to highlight the scale of collection action around this bill. Pop that in the diary!
items.note: Sector coordination reminder rather than reported democracy content.

items.b: Joint submission to PACAC inquiry into Elections Bill : Unlock Democracy is facilitating a joint submission to PACAC. If you’re interested, follow the link and fill in details per the document prompts. Remember you can also “add your name” to boost impact if you don’t have resource to fully participate. Deadline is the end of this month.
items.note: Call to sign a joint submission; treated as sector logistics per guidance on sign-on calls.
links: Joint submission to PACAC inquiry into Elections Bill

items.b: Civil Society sign-on for voter ID petition delivery to Downing Street : #HandsOffOurVote is doing a petition delivery to Downing Street on 7 September. Fair Vote UK is helping organise a parallel civil society org letter to be delivered at the same time. The text is fixed but if you’re keen to add your org/name, you can do that directly in the doc. Deadline is 2 September.
items.note: Call to sign a joint letter/petition delivery; sector logistics rather than reported news.
links: Civil Society sign-on for voter ID petition delivery to Downing Street

items.b: ConservativeHome’s Paul Goodman provides a full rundown to the Elections Bill, reporting that Michael Gove MP will likely present the bill at Second Reading on September 7th, whilst Chloe Smith MP — Minister for the Constitution and Devolution — will lead, with Julia Lopez MP in support.
items.why: it reports on the legislative progress, timetable and ministerial ownership of a bill that will reshape UK electoral administration.

items.b: Hannah Swirsky and the Centenary Action Group are investigating the relevance of Section 106 of the Equality Act with reference to the Elections Bill, they’re also ensuring that female MPs across the spectrum are aware of the impact of the bill upon women and that it’s on their radar.
items.why: advocacy work aims to ensure the Elections Bill's impact on women's equal representation in politics is scrutinised by lawmakers before it passes.
items.note: Equality here concerns representation within elections legislation, so filed under elections rather than participation.

items.b: Jess Blair and the team at ERS Cymru are working up case studies at the moment to show the effects of the Elections Bill in action. They also report that the Senedd is quite likely to attempt to block the Elections Bill.
items.why: the Senedd's potential move to block the Elections Bill concerns the distribution of electoral decision-making power between devolved and UK institutions.
items.note: Devolved government structure/powers falls under elections & decision making per boundary rule.

items.h: GLA gearing up for London Voter Registration Week
items.b: Elisabeth Pop and the team at London Voter Registration Week (LVRW) working with a wide array of London based civil society organisations and grassroots community groups across the city. Last year LVRW boosted voter registration in the capital by 14% across all demographics, and by a huge 25% among young people. London perennially suffers from high voter registration churn, due to its diverse, young and transient communities.
items.why: voter registration drives directly affect whether eligible people can exercise the franchise, especially in areas with high registration churn.
items.note: Turnout and registration campaigns are always classed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Democracy Club invite feedback on their website and services
items.b: Does your project or local authority embed or use Democracy Club’s services? Peter Keeling and the team have put together a stakeholder survey to find out more about how people use their tools. Let them know about how you use their services via the survey form .
items.note: A stakeholder feedback survey about an existing organisation's tools, not a new means of participation created.
links: Let them know about how you use their services via the survey form

items.h: COLDIGIT looking for local government members to interview as part of their research programme
items.b: Collective Intelligence Through Digital Tools is a new joint research project bringing together Nesta, the Economic & Social Research Council, SINTEF, NordForsk, University of Helsinki and Gothenburg University. Senior Researcher Oli Whittington is looking for members of local government to inform their work, get in touch if you’d be interested in taking part.
items.note: Recruitment call for research participants, not a democratic mechanism or new participation tool.

items.h: Climate Assembly UK deemed a success by independent evaluators
items.b: A group of experts including Jayne Carrick and Stephen Elstub of Newcastle University, David Farrel of University College Dublin and Patricia Mockler of Queen’s University, have judged the deliberative process a success, concluding that the UK Parliament should seek to establish more citizens’ assemblies in the future. The evaluation was funded by the UKRI QR Strategic Priorities Grant, with additional funds from a variety of academic sources.
items.why: it reports an independent evaluation of a citizens' assembly, a deliberative decision-making mechanism, recommending Parliament expand their use.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classed under elections & decision making per the revised framework.

items.h: Titus Alexander is promoting the idea of a ‘Democracy Mission’ for Higher Education
items.b: Will academics act together to strengthen democratic participation and governance, or will they just chronicle its decline, Titus asks. Their brief explanatory note on the idea of a “democracy mission” makes the case for universities to increase education and support for citizens to better develop the permanent experiment of democracy.
items.note: An advocacy idea being promoted, not a launched programme or concrete change to participation.

items.h: PolicyMogul offering free political monitoring
items.b: Unlock Democracy have embedded a real-time feed of political updates directly on their homepage, powered by PolicyMogul. Elliot Robinson from the PolicyMogul team claims that theirs is probably the most accurate source in the country for up-to-date information on democratic reform. You can sign up for this free service here .
items.why: it creates a new free tool helping people follow and engage with live political developments.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building: a new resource that helps people take part in civic life.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society launch new strategy and new report Two Decades of PR
items.b: ERS Chief Executive Darren Hughes lays out ERS’ new strategy for 2021–2024 . The strategy builds on their recent successes and draws upon wide-ranging conversations with members, supporters, councils, politicians and campaign groups across the UK. Key takeaways include: ERS aims to build a network supportive of democratic reform, persuade one of the two main parties to back PR, increase the salience of democracy and PR among key voter groups.
items.note: An organisation's own strategic plan announcement, not a concrete change to how power is exercised or contested.

items.b: On Tuesday 10th August ERS published their new report , detailing the deployment and successful implementation of STV in Wales, Scotland and London. Two Decades of PR cites fairer and more proportionate electoral outcomes, improved voter agency and cross-party working as key benefits where STV has been rolled out.
items.why: it presents evidence on how proportional electoral systems have performed in UK devolved and local elections, bearing on debates over electoral system design.

items.h: Make Votes Matter celebrate their Day of Action and prepare to hire two new roles to help build their alliance
items.b: On 31st July MVM activists marched, sang, samba drummed and dropped banners right across the UK as part of a national Day of Action to promote proportional representation. MVM Co-Director Klina Jordan reckons the Day of Action was their biggest yet. Make Vote Matters are preparing to hire two new part-time roles to help develop their Alliance. The Alliance for Proportional Representation started back in 2016 and is a cross-party grouping of 71 organisations and parties, ranging from Conservative Action on Electoral Reform to Plaid Cymru. If you would like to sign the Good Systems Agreement and…
items.why: it reports collective public action (a day of action) demonstrating willingness to campaign for electoral reform.
items.note: Protest framed as willingness to take part, per boundary rule, with electoral reform as secondary topic.

items.h: YEN and POMOC launch new #OurHomeOurVote campaign
items.b: The Young Europeans Network and Polish Migrants Organise for Change have teamed up to re-launch their Our Home Our Vote campaign for residence-based voting rights. The campaign aims to bring Northern Ireland and England into line with Scotland and Wales, where voting rights are based on residence not citizenship. Find out more their website or get in touch with one of their Voting Rights Champions .
items.why: it campaigns to extend voting rights based on residence rather than citizenship, directly affecting the franchise.

items.h: APPG on Political Literacy holding third meeting
items.b: Shout Out UK are convening a third meeting of the APPG on September 14th, with discussion between Simon Fell MP, Lord Ian McNicol, Nickie Aiken MP and Cat Smith MP. This session has a different approach to previous meetings, focusing on transatlantic comparisons between US and UK attitudes to political and media literacy and examples of international best practice.
items.why: it discusses efforts to build political and media literacy, which affects citizens' capacity to engage in democratic life.
items.note: Meeting of an APPG on literacy sits at the boundary of participation and information beats.

items.h: Updated Cabinet Manual needed to maintain public trust
items.b: Together with the Nolan Principles for Public Life , the Cabinet Manual, the Ministerial Code and the Civil Service code are an important part of the UK’s constitutional framework. Baroness Taylor of Bolton, Chair of the House of Lords Constitution Committee, in a new report emphasises that the Cabinet Manual must be regularly updated so that it does not lack authority and risk constitutional confusion.
items.why: it concerns whether constitutional conventions governing ministerial and civil service conduct remain clear and authoritative constraints on executive power.

items.h: Committee on Standards in Public Life recommends digital election finance changes
items.b: In their new report, Regulating Election Finance , they recommend changing the law to require parties and campaigners to provide the Electoral Commission with more detailed invoices from digital suppliers, ie content used, regions of the country where the advert was targeted etc. They also recommend legislation to require social media platforms to create advert libraries where they permit election adverts, with precise spend figures and detailed metrics of the adverts.
items.why: transparent digital campaign spending and advertising data enable meaningful scrutiny of electoral competition and campaign finance.

items.h: AEA calls for sweeping changes to election delivery
items.b: In a new blueprint for electoral reform, the Association of Electoral Administrators — the UK body representing election professionals, requests decisive action to bolster capacity and resilience in UK elections , and in the process lessening the increasing pressures on election officers and workers across the UK. The report calls for new legislation to modernise core electoral processes, a 30 day electoral timetable, earlier deadlines for absent voting applications, full review of electoral funding to reduce the burden on LAs and a full re-evaluation of electoral registration including consid…
items.why: the administration, timetabling and registration processes of elections directly determine how well-run and accessible they are.
links: decisive action to bolster capacity and resilience in UK elections

items.h: Democracy Club publishes 2021 Elections Report
items.b: The new review highlights the amazing strides Democracy Club over the last election cycle , with vastly expanded polling station finder coverage, high and consistent levels of engagement with local government (over 90% of councils provided data and more than 50% embedded DC’s widget!), WhereDoIVote got a Welsh language upgrade and so much more. Congratulations to the team for all their fantastic work! Remember, you can join the conversation and keep in the loop with all things election related on the Democracy Club Slack .
items.why: tools that help people locate polling stations and register to vote directly affect practical access to voting.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building affecting voter access mechanics rather than mere organisational news, though it borders on an annual self-report.
links: highlights the amazing strides Democracy Club over the last election cycle

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny have published the full results of their Local Government annual survey
items.b: The new survey and report shine a light on how councils have fared throughout the pandemic, drawing attention to the fault lines in support provided to governance and scrutiny.
items.why: the capacity of councils to exercise governance and scrutiny functions determines whether local government can be held to account.

items.h: Launch of the 2021 Cllr Awards
items.b: Run by the Local Government Information Unit and the CCLA, the Cllr Awards are the only national awards to celebrate the vital work of councillors across England and Scotland. Nominations are now open for the awards until the 24th September.
items.note: Awards nominations are organisational/sector admin, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: Changes to the Official Secrets Act mean investigative journalists could face 14 years in prison
items.b: The Home Office has just ended a consultation to change the Official Secrets Act. Proposed changes include suggesting that journalists should be treated as those who commit espionage offences and leak information (undisclosed disclosures). The consultation also proposes increasing maximum sentences for such offences from two to 14 years in prison. Rachel Oldroyd , editor of the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , added : “Sources, leaks and whistleblowers are all crucial to holding power to account — including our Government. Removing the public interest defence for such disclosures is deeply…
items.why: criminalising journalistic handling of leaked information and removing public interest defences chills investigative journalism and public access to information about power.
items.note: Whistleblower protection also implicates rule of law but the press-freedom framing dominates.
