items.note: A call to join an insider Slack rather than a genuinely new means of public participation in shaping the Elections Bill.

items.h: Sir David Amess MP
items.b: Westminster is in a state of shock at the murder of sitting MP David Amess, just 5 years on from the death of Jo Cox. On Monday, Parliamentarians of all hues paid tribute to the memory of the veteran Southend MP. The Queen has now granted Southend on Sea city status in his honour, in recognition of David’s tireless campaign to boost the then-town’s status. Democracy organisations and political parties have ceased campaigning for the time being out of respect.
items.why: political violence against a sitting MP threatens the personal security that elected representatives need to serve, and the suspension of campaigning directly affects the electoral process
items.note: Personal security of an elected official sits at the boundary of rights/civic space and rule of law; classified here as a civic-space/security matter given no state actor is implicated.

items.h: More in Common publish report on UK public attitudes to democracy and politics
items.b: The new report, Democratic Repair: What Britons expect from their democracy , is based on polling and focus groups based on their 7 segments . The research found that most take pride in Britain’s democratic system and felt that the democratic system is not in crisis, though the research highlighted signs of potential disrepair and decay. View More in Common’s paper and their recommendations here .
items.why: the polling reveals how much public confidence and perceived legitimacy underpins support for the democratic system, a condition for civic participation.

items.h: Police Bill Alliance update
items.b: The Police Bill had its Second Reading in the House of Lords, and is scheduled for Committee on 20th, 25th, and 27th October. From 10–17 October 2021, Amnesty UK, Liberty, Stonewall, Freedom from Torture, the British Institute for Human Rights, Equally Ours, The End Violence Against Women Coalition, the Quakers and The Humanists held a Week of Action for Human Rights in the UK. If you have any questions regarding the Police Bill Alliance or would like to join Liberty’s Police Bill Alliance email updates, please email Kathleen Christie .
items.why: the Police Bill's progress through Parliament directly affects legal restrictions on protest, assembly and civil liberties.

items.h: Democracy Pioneers legislative theatre performance this Saturday in Glasgow
items.b: A winner of the Nesta Democracy Pioneers award, a new legislative theatre project by Katy Rubin, Glasgow City Council and Shared Future CIC, has brought young Glaswegians together throughout the summer to explore and develop a play around transport and accessibility. Their final performance is this Saturday, October 23rd!
items.why: the legislative theatre project creates a new participatory mechanism for young people to engage with local policy on transport and accessibility.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation.

items.h: Shared Future CIC are on the lookout for Citizens’ Jury participants
items.b: Alex King at Shared Future CIC is looking for people based in Furness-in-Barrow in Cumbria and Southwark in London, to join Climate Change Citizens’ Juries in their area. The deadlines are on the 25th and 27th October respectively. Meanwhile, the Social Housing Tenants’ Climate Jury is due to launch their recommendations on Tuesday 2nd November at the Northern Housing Consortium’s 2021 Summit .
items.why: recruiting participants for citizens' juries constitutes new deliberative decision-making machinery on climate policy.
items.note: Citizens' juries classified as decision-making machinery per boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society working with Politics for the Many to build support within trade unions for PR
items.b: After last month’s Labour Party Conference vote, organisations pushing for electoral reform have re-focused on the trade unions as the last major obstacle to securing the Labour Party’s commitment to PR. Electoral Reform Society council elections are also currently ongoing. If you’re a member — or know anyone who is — make sure to vote!
items.why: the campaign to secure trade union support for proportional representation targets the electoral system used to choose representatives.

items.h: Josiah Mortimer starts their first week as City Hall Editor of MyLondon this week
items.b: Stepping down as Head of Comms at the Electoral Reform Society, Josiah is keen to hit the ground running in their new role. Please drop them an email or tweet to discuss any London democracy issues, campaigns, research and story tips.

items.h: ‘Jessie meets’ — the new Democracy Network Coordinator has been meeting & greeting democracy projects and attending events across the UK and democracy sector. Here is a summary of some of those meetings:
items.b: Hannah Stevens at Elect Her — Formerly known as The Parliament Project, Elect Her is active across England, Scotland & Wales and is a non-partisan organisation working to motivate, support and equip women in all their diversity to stand for political office in Britain. Nearly 5000 women have attended their workshops to date and are soon to be beginning a major project in Wales funded by the Welsh government. Simon Duffy at Citizen Network is a global cooperative working for equality and justice around the world. It exists to celebrate human diversity and stand up for human equality, encouragin…
items.note: Describes existing organisations rather than a new programme or change affecting participation.

items.h: Big update from Sortition Foundation: second chamber in Scotland, citizens assembly on democracy and more
items.b: James Robertson , Campaigns Director at Sortition Foundation , is currently in the midst of a campaign pushing for a “House of Citizens” as a second chamber in Scotland, first envisioned by the 2019 Citizens’ Assembly of Scotland. Sortition are also working to convene a new major coalition of groups, including Make Votes Matter, Compass, ERS and Unlock Democracy, running a series of events and supporter mobilisations at COP26, testing the waters for a new potential cross-sectoral campaign for a CA on democracy in the UK. But that’s not all, they’re also running a series of focus groups looking…
items.why: campaigning for a sortition-based second chamber and a national citizens' assembly concerns the structure of collective decision-making institutions.
items.note: Citizens' assembly and second-chamber campaigns classified as decision-making machinery per boundary rule.

items.h: London Assembly member expected to pass a motion in favor of residence-based voting rights
items.b: Whilst it’s unclear who on the assembly will pass the motion, Mayor Sadiq Khan has approved of RBVR in the past.
items.why: extending voting rights to residents changes who holds suffrage in local elections.

items.h: Liz Crosbie highlights lack of democracy sector readiness for a potential snap General Election in 2022
items.b: This week’s Democracy Check-In session centred on how ready the UK democracy space is for a potential election in 2022. What are the steps we need to take right now to begin? How is your organisation campaigning affected by the Elections Bill? Shaun Roberts of Unlock Democracy, Liz Crosbie of RebootGB and Jon Morter of the Progressive Alliance, suggested an immediate summit. Other interesting aspects of discussion centred on how do we prevent the tactical vote “mess” that occurred in GE 2019.
items.why: discussion of sector readiness for a snap election bears on the administration and competitiveness of that election.

items.h: I Have A Voice and Votes for Schools team up for the kids
items.b: In the run up to COP26, Votes for Schools are working partner organisations including UNICEF UK to explore with children climate change and its effect on their rights. There will be a free package of resources to facilitate a debate at Primary, Secondary and 16+, and the chance for children and young people to vote and comment on the question. Find out more here .
items.why: it creates a new resource enabling children and young people to debate and vote on a public policy question, building civic participation skills and voice.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation, even for a pre-voting-age audience.

items.h: Don’t miss: UK Democracy Fund Conference
items.b: Bringing together researchers, campaigners, policy makers and practitioners, UK Democracy Fund looks to assess the potential impact of the Elections Bill, the stalling of the Every Vote Matters agenda , and how we might build solutions to under-representation. Register for the conference here .
items.note: Event listing/conference announcement, not a reported change.

items.h: Champions of free expression celebrated at Index on Censorship awards
items.b: The winners of Index on Censorship’s 2021 Freedom of Expression awards have been announced at a ceremony in London. The Freedom of Expression Awards, which were first held in 2000, celebrate individuals or groups who have had a significant impact fighting censorship anywhere in the world. Winners join Index’s Awards Fellowship programme and receive dedicated training and support. This year’s awards are particularly significant, coming as the organisation celebrates its 50th birthday. Find out who won here .
items.note: Awards ceremony/organisational recognition, not a democratic mechanism story.

items.h: MP Kemi Badenoch is now likely to be the relevant minister for the Elections Bill
items.b: Recently the grapevine informed us that Chloe Smith’s replacement was to be Chris Pincher. Alas, the grapevine AKA Fair Vote’s Election Bill Office Hours session, now considers Kemi Badenoch the likely successor to carry forth the Elections Bill. If you’d like to join the weekly Election Bill Office Hours Zoom sessions, pop email Matt an email .
items.note: Personnel speculation about a ministerial role, not a substantive accountability mechanism.

items.h: Labour not tabling Electoral Commission amendments
items.b: The amendments to increasing fining power or allow for criminal prosecutions are not being tabled by the Labour Party, though they continue to push all voter ID amendments.
items.why: it concerns whether the Electoral Commission's enforcement powers over electoral fraud and violations will be strengthened through legislative amendment.

items.h: MLMS Young Leader Maddy Dhesi organises open letter for Welsh MSs and MPs against voter ID
items.b: If you’d like to assist Maddy in gathering signatures, please consult this spreadsheet .
items.why: it involves citizens organising a collective petition to influence legislators on voter ID rules, exercising the right to campaign and seek redress.
items.note: Campaigning/petition mechanism placed in participation, with voter ID subject matter noted as secondary elections beat.

items.h: Tom Brake clarifies the significance of Holyrood and the Senedd refusing legislative consent
items.b: “ The UK Parliament must ask the Scottish Parliament for consent if it is passing a Bill that affects Scotland. This is included in the Scotland Act 2016. However, the UK Supreme Court decided in 2017 that the Scottish Parliament does not have a “legally enforceable veto”. This means that if the Scottish Parliament votes against a legislative consent motion, it can still become the law ”.
items.why: it clarifies the legal mechanics of legislative consent between the UK Parliament and devolved legislatures, bearing on the structure of devolved decision-making.
items.note: Devolved government structure and powers falls under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: Carnegie Trust Online Safety Bill Update
items.b: Carnegie argue that the draft OSB provides too many powers to the Secretary of State over too many things. Last month’s reshuffle cleared out all of the previous tech, digital and data ministers at all levels, meaning that all those who had a hand in writing the current version of the OSB have now moved on. The Bill’s Joint Committee has been hearing evidence over the last few weeks and is picking up pace, Carnegie published their own submission here . You can view a more full account of committee submissions here . End Violence Against Women and Girls , supported by Glitch and others, have pu…
items.why: it concerns how much unilateral power the Secretary of State will hold over regulation of the online information environment.
links: cleared out all of the previous tech, digital and data ministers
End Violence Against Women and Girls

items.h: MPs vow to “radically toughen up” online safety bill in reaction to Sir David Amess’ death
items.b: Mark Francois, the MP for Rayleigh and Wickford, who lost a close friend and mentor in Sir David Amess, has called for radically toughening up the new draft bill , remarking in their tribute : “I suggest that if we want to ensure that our colleague didn’t die in vain, we collectively all of us pick up the baton, regardless of our party and take the forthcoming online harms bill and toughen it up markedly.”
items.why: it reports political momentum to strengthen regulation of online platforms that shape public debate and can incite harm.
links: radically toughening up the new draft bill

items.h: Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen will speak before MPs on 25th October
items.b: All eyes will be on the Joint Committee on the draft Online Safety Bill next Monday as Haugen gives evidence to MPs on Facebook’s failure to act on the evidence of harm on its platform.
items.why: whistleblower testimony to a parliamentary committee scrutinising a platform's failure to address harm bears directly on the integrity of the public information environment.

items.h: Lord Vaizey and William Hague share thoughts on the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Ed Vaizey has provided a comprehensive interview to TechCrunch , covering his candidacy for the Ofcom Chair vacancy and his thoughts on the OSB, meanwhile William Hague has written why social media algorithms are harmful to democracy .
items.why: the story concerns how social media algorithms and online safety regulation shape the plurality and quality of political information people encounter.
items.note: Focuses on algorithms/information environment rather than an individual's speech rights.
links: social media algorithms are harmful to democracy

items.h: New Information Commissioner expresses support for FOI charges
items.b: John Edwards, the current New Zealand Privacy Commission is due to take over the UK’s Information Commissioner on the 31st October. At a recent meeting of the DCMS Committee, Mr Edwards, unprompted , suggested he thought it was legitimate to charge some FOI requesters, seemingly unaware that the ICO had always opposed the introduction of charges.
items.why: the incoming Information Commissioner's stance on FOI charges affects the practical ability of citizens and journalists to hold public institutions to account through freedom of information requests.
items.note: FOI framed here as an accountability mechanism via the regulator, not the information environment itself.

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny announces Annual Scrutiny Conference

items.note: Organisational event announcement, not a change affecting democratic participation.

items.h: Keep up to date with the work of the Election Bill Coalition
items.b: The Democracy Defence Coalition’s calendar can be found here .
items.note: Sector logistics/calendar notice, not substantive news.

items.h: Elections Bill coalition open letter to the new Elections Minister
items.b: Unlock Democracy, ERS, Open Britain, Best for Britain and Hands Off Our Vote have penned an open letter to the new Elections Minister Kemi Badenoch. Add your organisation’s name in support of the letter here .
items.note: Call to sign an open letter is sector campaign logistics rather than reported news.

items.h: Elections Bill update
items.b: Michela Palese , Research and Policy Officer at the Electoral Reform Society, reports committee stage finished last week. The Democracy Defence Coalition now awaits the report stage which is due to be announced, whilst ERS and other groups prep for reports and the Lords stages of the bill.
items.why: the Elections Bill's progress through committee and report stages determines future rules for electoral administration and integrity

items.h: New CSPL blog on the Electoral Commission Strategy and Policy Statement
items.b: The Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL) have published a new blog by Dr Alistair Clark, a Reader in Politics at Newcastle University. The blog is an indepth review of the UK Government’s new strategy and policy statement on the Electoral Commission. Worth a read .
items.why: the government's strategy and policy statement affects the independence of the Electoral Commission, the body responsible for electoral integrity
items.note: Touches both EMB independence (elections) and regulator oversight (accountability); classed by its focus on the Electoral Commission.
links: The Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL)

items.h: 63% of London-based CSOs reject voter ID
items.b: Almost two thirds of London civil society organisations surveyed by the London Voices Project oppose the move, with the figure rising to 74% among groups representing BAME Londoners. The survey was funded by the Trust for London , on behalf of the Citizenship and Integration Initiative, and the UK Democracy Fund, a Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust initiative.
items.why: voter ID requirements affect who can practically exercise their right to vote, a core electoral integrity and access issue

items.h: Going to COP26? Join the Democratise to Decarbonise bloc
items.b: Join Democratise to Decarbonise for the Global Day of Action for Climate on 6th November in Glasgow and London. James Robertson and the crew need some help with flyering and talking to people at the march about the new campaign, but fear not — those helping out in Glasgow also get free entry to the Day of Action Afterparty at Civic House in Glasgow.
items.note: Event promotion for a climate protest, not a report on a democratic mechanism.

items.b: Talking to people at the demonstration and handing out flyers:
Glasgow: 11.15–12.45pm Meet Kelvin at Pocket Cafe (72 S Woodside Road, Glasgow)

items.h: Votes for Schools and UNICEF UK aid 48,000 children in vote on climate change
items.b: The question “Will climate change affect children’s rights?” was discussed in hundreds of classrooms across the UK. Detailed in a new report for COP26, the vote found 95% are concerned about climate change, 89% think not enough is being done and 81% feel young people aren’t listened to.
items.why: the initiative creates a new mechanism for young people to express political views and feel heard, building civic engagement capacity
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation for children rather than a formal election.

items.h: mySociety pushing Climate Action Plans Explorer ahead of COP26
items.b: According to Myf Nixon , Comms Manager at mySociety, the team will be running around handing out stickers at COP26 pointing to their Climate Action Plan Explorer . Besides that, there’s been a lot of updates from mySociety in recent weeks, including changes to party comparisons on TheyWorkForYou , research on TheyWorkForYou’s alerts, MS’s submission to PACAC clearing house inquiry. In other news, Myf also spent every day of the last month drawing a notable protest placard, check them out here . Pop Myf a DM for the high-res versions (they’re REALLY good).
items.note: Mixed sector promo roundup (climate tool, stickers, minor updates) without a single clear democratic mechanism.

items.h: Coming up this week: Political Literacy Day, 4th November
items.b: Danielle Vaughan , Campaign Coordinator at Shout Out UK (SOUK), reports that SOUK have organised Political Literacy Day as part of Parliament Week. During the course of the day, SOUK, Unlock Democracy, I Have A Voice and others have organised a series of panels for which you can find the details here . The day will close with SOUK’s fourth APPG meeting on Political Literacy — which will focus on the news that they are launching the largest report on teachers and parents attitudes to political literacy since 2000.
items.why: a new report and educational panels on political literacy build capacity for people to understand and engage with democratic life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building via a new report/resource rather than a mere event listing.
links: fourth APPG meeting on Political Literacy

items.h: Watch Make Votes Matter’s new film promoting fair votes\
items.b: Alex Toal, Klina Jordan and the team at Make Votes Matter have been hard at work on this one, a new film featuring dozens of leading voices from across the UK (and Greece!) calling for votes that matter. Watch the film here .
items.note: Promotional advocacy film akin to a 'call to sign/watch', not itself a new participatory mechanism or reported change.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund Conference
items.b: Shocking, I know — but the UK Democracy Fund plan on holding a real life, physical conference on the 23 November. The conference will cover recent research on the age divide in UK politics, electoral participation of BAME communities and migrants, reports from Votes at 16 in Wales and more. RSVP here .
items.note: Event listing/RSVP notice, not a substantive democracy story despite relevant conference topics.

items.h: Jessie Joe Jacobs inviting orgs to form initial steering group for new network
items.b: The new steering group and council of reference will assist and advise with the creation of the new Democracy Network. Jessie is also organising new Christmas democracy drinks, can’t wait! Get in touch with Jessie here to find out more about the new Democracy Network.
items.why: forming a new steering group and network creates new infrastructure for civil society coordination and civic engagement.
items.note: Applied sector capacity-building rule: launching a new network counts as a democracy story.

items.h: Early bird catches the tactical vote
items.b: Josh Russell , Forward Democracy, and Jon Morter , Progressive alliance, are starting early tactical voting advice data collaboration between the different websites that operated in GE 2019. The plan is to have an evergreen resource that works to build consensus from different analysis, polls, and local intel. Previously, with just a few weeks in a snap election cycle it’s been a rush to put together, and as a result conflicting advice was published. They hope to build consistency between the different operations and therefore credibility when a general election inevitably hits. Contact Josh o…
items.why: a coordinated tactical-voting resource shapes how voters act strategically within the electoral system ahead of a general election.
items.note: Tool concerns voting strategy/electoral competition, so filed under elections rather than generic participation despite being a new 'resource'.

items.h: Notwestminster is back!
items.b: Notwestminster is a community of people who really care about building a more constructive, more compassionate local democracy. Like most communities and conferences, Notwestminster put everything on pause whilst the plague ravaged. Diane Sims and the team are now looking to February 2022 for their next physical annual event in Huddersfield.
items.note: Announcement of resumed annual event/conference; event listing, not a substantive change.

items.h: I Have A Voice is growing
items.b: Rebecca Deegan and the team are happy to announce they’ve been able to hire three of their own youth ambassadors to their team to develop the programme further — amazing news!
items.note: Organisational hiring news, explicitly excluded as org-as-organisation news.

items.h: Joe Powell on Britain’s democratic leadership
items.b: Writing for the Foreign Policy Centre, Powell, Deputy Chief Executive of the Open Government Partnership, summarises the democratic backsliding of the last 15 years across the world, including in the UK and the US. As the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office chooses to prioritise open societies and human rights as part of its new agenda, this new strategy can only be successful, Powell argues, if Britain turns the page on the recent democratic turmoil — draconian new police powers, voter ID, new changes to the Official Secrets Act, political polarisation and other aspects.
items.why: the piece assesses whether UK institutions and policies uphold democratic standards domestically, affecting Britain's credibility and practice as a democracy.
items.note: Broad opinion piece spanning several mechanisms; classified by its overarching theme of democratic governance and backsliding.

items.h: Unite backs new voting system for UK general elections
items.b: Unite passes motion at its policy conference that commits the Labour-affiliated trade union to opposing FPTP and supporting moves to “explore, select and introduce a new voting system for the UK”. Unite’s new General Secretary Sharon Graham backed the move, saying “Our political class has failed working people and our system is broken. It is time to change our democracy.” The vote signals a major shift across the British labour movement with regards to electoral reform. September’s Labour Party conference vote to back PR only failed through a lack of union support, despite 80% of local parties…
items.why: a major trade union formally backing proportional representation shifts political momentum for changing the electoral system used to choose the UK's government.
links: commits the Labour-affiliated trade union to opposing FPTP

items.h: Young Europeans Network launch open letter on Residence-Based Voting Rights
items.b: Lara Parizotto and the team at the Young Europeans Network are calling for improvements to voting rights, in particular the normalisation of residence-based voting rights across the UK that have already been secured across Scotland and Wales. Sign and share the open letter here .
items.why: expanding residence-based voting rights changes who is enfranchised to elect representatives
items.note: Campaign is advocacy for suffrage expansion rather than an enacted change.

items.h: UK Constitutional Reform Tracker launched
items.b: Constitutional reform at the current time is not being approached in a unified manner, through a single Bill, but rather in a haphazard way through many different bills at different times through different departments. This makes it difficult to track what is going on. The Constitutional Reform Tracker is an attempt at trying to help, providing a searchable list of key constitutional events under the current Government. View the Public Law Project’s Tracker here .
items.why: tracking piecemeal constitutional reform helps hold the executive accountable for changes to how power is exercised
items.note: New scrutiny tool counts as a sector capacity-building resource for accountability.

items.h: New Constitution Society report — Northern Ireland and Brexit: An Explanation
items.b: The new Constitution Society paper argues that Northern Ireland’s present situation and role in Brexit can only be fully understood in reference to its contested constitutional history and unique contemporary constitutional structure.
items.why: understanding Northern Ireland's contested constitutional structure bears on how devolved government and power-sharing arrangements function
items.note: Explanatory report on constitutional structure rather than a reported policy change.

items.h: British Social Attitudes Survey finds trust in the Government at highest levels since 2007
items.b: The survey found 23% now trust the Government to put the needs of the nation above the interest of their own party. 32% feel the system of government in the UK couldn’t be improved, or only marginally. However, these levels of trust are largely confined to those who voted for Brexit in 2016.
items.why: public trust in government to act impartially reflects whether accountability mechanisms are perceived to be working

items.h: New Demos research shows people prefer more agency than more money when ‘levelling up’
items.b: The research finds 77% of the general public and 79% of the former Red Wall think that local people should be involved in decisions around how government money is used in their area. This preference is so strong that both surveyed sets prioritise this democratic control over increases in funding.
items.why: public preference for local control over funding decisions reflects demand for devolved and participatory decision-making structures
items.note: Preference for local decision-making agency ties to devolved decision-making machinery.
links: 77% of the general public and 79% of the former Red Wall

items.h: Institute for Government to hold conference on standards, 4th November
items.b: As the news of MP and former Cabinet minister Owen Paterson hits the headlines, the IfG’s one day conference looks at how the UK standards system can be strengthened. The sessions are looking at whether UK ethics watchdogs are effective, what the UK can learn from others and how the appointments process be improved — with a keynote from Lord Evans, Chair of the Committee on Standards in Public Life.
items.why: strengthening the standards system determines whether officials who break ethics rules can be held to account

items.h: Commons vote on Wednesday on whether to suspend Owen Paterson
items.b: The Committee on Standards in Public Life found that he broke rules on lobbying . A suspension is serious because it triggers a recall petition, if just 10% of his constituents sign it, he will be removed as an MP.
items.why: suspending an MP for breaching lobbying rules triggers a recall mechanism that lets constituents remove them from office

items.h: Police attempt to recruit BLM activist as informant
items.b: After the recent deaths of two men in police custody and Black Lives Matter’s campaigns over them, Lowri Davies was approached by officers and asked to spy on her fellow activists . This is not the first time, Paul Stephens, an ex-police officer turned Extinction Rebellion activist was approached by Met Police in 2019 and asked to become a covert human intelligence source. The Public Inquiry into Undercover Policing is now in its sixth year and only 1/6th the way through their work.
items.why: police attempts to recruit activists as informants chill the freedom of association and assembly needed to organise and protest
items.note: Ongoing public inquiry into undercover policing raises a secondary rule-of-law redress angle.
links: asked to spy on her fellow activists

items.h: Public Interest News selecting grantees to boost hyperlocal journalism
items.b: In a bid to understand about whether funding to hyperlocal journalism boosts democratic engagement, PINF are currently selecting grantees for the investment. Joe Mitchell and the team held a small retreat last week with orgs that support the independent news space, the retreat focused on next steps to building better networking infrastructure.
items.why: funding hyperlocal journalism sustains local news capacity that underpins an informed and plural public information environment
items.note: Sector capacity-building grant-making counts as creating new means of participation in the information environment.

items.h: Media & Information Literacy Alliance (MILA) launches new website
items.b: Media and Information Literacy Alliance is a new project set up in the summer of 2021 by the library and information association, CILIP. MILA aims to grow into an effective membership organisation supporting media and information literacy.
items.note: Website launch reads as organisational growth news for the alliance rather than a new public-facing resource.

items.h: Hacked Off’s IPSO campaign garners over 5,000 signatures
items.b: The campaign has released a new video about the campaign, watch it here . Find out more about Hacked Off’s campaign highlighting the failure and inaction of IPSO.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether the press regulator effectively holds the media to account for public-interest journalism standards, shaping the information environment.
items.note: Focus is on press regulation and media accountability, closer to information environment than institutional accountability.

items.h: Good Information Inc
items.b: A new billionaire-backed venture will fund local news and disinformation-fighting newsrooms. Wealthy investors such as George Soros and Reid Hoffman are behind the public interest company.
items.why: this matters democratically because new funding for local news and disinformation-fighting newsrooms expands the plural, reliable information available for public debate.

items.h: Since 2011 278 journalists have been murdered for their work worldwide
items.b: New data from the Committee to Protect Journalists shows that 226 of those cases, or 81%, recorded complete impunity, ie, no one has ever been connected with the crimes.
items.why: this matters democratically because impunity for murdering journalists undermines the safety conditions necessary for a free press and public debate.
items.note: International data used as comparative evidence bearing on press freedom generally.

items.h: Citizens’ Network publish map of voting systems around the world
items.b: The new map produced by Adam Sundle is a quick and easy way to see where the fairest voting systems are being used.
items.why: this matters democratically because comparing electoral systems worldwide bears on how competitive and representative voting systems can be designed.
items.note: Light offbeat item with no direct UK hook, but topic is core to electoral systems.

items.h: Democracy Defence Coalition preparing week of action for 27th November
items.b: Based on current information of the bill’s timeline, the Coalition is focusing their efforts on the week commencing 27th November, including an in-person rally led by Make Votes Matter at Parliament Square. Contact Emma Knaggs at Make Votes Matter to find out more about the rally and how you can participate.
items.why: it reports civic groups organising a rally and week of action to mobilise public pressure on electoral legislation, reflecting people's readiness to take part in democratic contestation
items.note: Protest framed as willingness/organisation to participate, not policing or legal restriction, so filed under Participation per boundary rule.

items.h: Cat Smith MP indicates government may push back Election Bill report stage
items.b: It is currently unclear when the report stage and Lords stage of the bill will progress, Cat indicated the possibility down to the Conservative Government wanting to distance themselves from the ongoing sleaze narrative.
items.why: it concerns the progress and potential delay of legislation governing elections, with the delay itself reportedly tied to avoiding parliamentary scrutiny amid a sleaze controversy

items.h: Don’t forget — if you’re working on the Elections Bill, join the weekly office hours discussion
items.b: Every Thursday at noon, Kyle and the team at Fair Vote convene a space to coordinate and share information for working on the bill. Contact matt@fairvote.uk if you’d like to be included in the Office Hours Zoom, or any of the wider Coalition activities.
items.note: This is internal coordination logistics for advocacy groups rather than a new mechanism of public participation.

items.h: Notwestminster 2022 first ticket release sells out — more tickets available on 25th November
items.b: Notwestminster is back on February 26th in Huddersfield. Diane Sims and the team are looking for people to host workshops on the day around their 2022 theme: “ The future is unwritten”. They’re also looking for sponsors for the event, and for their online event later next year. Find out more here & pop 25th November in your diary if you want to grab your free ticket!

items.h: Elect Her is hiring!
items.b: Hannah Stevens and the team are looking for a new Community & Comms Officer and a Programme Coordinator — deadline for the new roles is 6th December, check it out and apply here .

items.h: Less than ⅓ of secondary schools offer weekly lessons in politics or citizenship, says new report
items.b: Oliver Walkden at Young Citizens’ highlights the concerning findings of the recent Political Literacy APPG report surveying more than 3,300 secondary school teachers across the UK. The report found that less than one third of secondary schools offer regular weekly lessons on politics or citizenship — with just 1% of teachers feeling prepared to teach politics and 60% of teachers feeling responsible for developing their students’ political literacy skills. According to teachers, their training reportedly provides no preparation for teaching political literacy, despite declining youth voter turn…
items.why: low levels of political literacy education affect young people's capacity and confidence to engage with politics and civic life later on
items.note: Civic/political literacy education is treated as a condition for future participation rather than a rights or elections matter.

items.h: Shared Future CIC planning new Climate Change Citizens’ Juries
items.b: Having recently released the recommendations of their North of England social tenants climate jury bringing together 30 social housing tenants to advise the Northern Housing Consortium on the best ways to retrofit their homes and green their neighbourhoods, they’re now planning new juries in Southwark, Furness and Copeland. Check out the video on the jury from the Northern Housing Consortium here .
items.why: citizens' juries create new deliberative machinery through which people can shape binding local policy decisions.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies/juries are classified under decision-making machinery, not participation, per framework boundary rule.

items.h: Titus Alexander suggests engagement with Biden’s Summit for Democracy
items.b: President Biden’s Summit for Democracy is taking place this 9/10th December. Titus suggests petitioning Parliament to form an all-party Joint Committee on Strengthening Democracy to engage with the summit. See Titus’ suggestion document here . The International Coalition for Democratic Renewal writes here how the Biden summit has the capacity to push back on democratic backsliding of recent years and develop a common agenda to confront the new autocrats.
items.note: This is a call to petition/engage with an event rather than a concrete change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Jon Alexander writing new book on the Citizen Story
items.b: Jon’s new book, CITIZENS: Why the Key to Fixing Everything is All of Us hits the shelves early next year. Jon has put in the hard graft in an effort to change the story of the individual in society from consumer to citizen — but he’s also involved a lot of people from our community along the way, sharing ideas, reviewing drafts. Grab yourself a discount or pre-order a copy here .
items.note: A book announcement about an individual's work, not a new participation mechanism or institutional change.
links: CITIZENS: Why the Key to Fixing Everything is All of Us

items.h: Reboot GB launch Democracy Hubs™
items.b: Democracy Hubs ™ is a new initiative by RebootGB to provide spaces for people to discuss politics and build trust without being pressured to join anything long term. Find out more and sign up here .
items.why: the new Democracy Hubs create fresh physical spaces for people to engage in political discussion, expanding practical means of civic participation.

items.h: Join mySociety in responding to the DCMS data consultation
items.b: mySociety have submitted a response to the DCMS consultation, recommending a board position in the new ICO for FOI issues and focusing on FOI more generally. If you want to piggyback on their submission or make your submission, the deadline is this Friday — see here for more info .
items.why: the consultation response concerns whether the ICO can hold public bodies answerable for freedom of information compliance.
items.note: FOI framed around institutional accountability (ICO oversight) rather than the public information environment.

items.h: Unpicking the standards system one part of wider assault on our democratic system, argues Toby James
items.b: Writing for The Conversation, UEA Professor of Politics and Public Policy, Toby James, argues that the sleaze affair of recent weeks, with the government within spitting distance from unravelling the carefully crafted standards systems, should not be viewed in isolation — but is part of a wider attack on our democratic institutions , including taking back control of the independence of the Electoral Commission. Toby recently submitted evidence to the Standards, Procedures and Public Appointments Inquiry on the Elections Bill.
items.why: weakening the standards system and Electoral Commission independence erodes checks on executive power and electoral integrity oversight.
links: part of a wider attack on our democratic institutions

items.h: Novara Media temporarily pulled by YouTube, receives support from across the political spectrum
items.b: Novara Media’s YouTube channel was deleted without warning or provocation on 26th October. Novara Media is an independently regulated media publisher and amongst the top 50 most watched news and politics channel in the UK. After the deletion Novara Media received support from political commentators across the political spectrum.
items.why: unexplained removal of a widely-watched political media channel by a platform affects media plurality and public access to political debate.

items.h: Independent Media Association (IMA) receives new grant, launches new strategy
items.b: The Independent Media Association , formerly known as The Media Fund, is a cooperative focused on promoting the work of independent media. With their new £10k funding they’re looking to boost the work of independent media with short and snappy training on key topics including marketing and organising parliamentary briefings.
items.note: Primarily organisational funding and strategy news rather than a change to public participation or the information environment.

items.h: Democracy Volunteers funded £150k to scale up their observer capacity
items.b: Democracy Volunteers provide a valuable service in observing elections, with the likely issues caused by voter ID an expansion of volunteer observers of the UK makes sense, though not previously thought required, until now.
items.why: scaling up independent election observation strengthens safeguards against electoral fraud and irregularity, particularly around new voter ID rules.

items.h: IPPR awarded £65k for democratic renewal push
items.b: It’s thought that the Institute for Public Policy Research have been looking into the possibilities of, and funding, a new Commission on Democracy — very exciting if true!
items.note: Speculative funding/organisational news about a possible future commission, not yet a concrete democratic mechanism.

items.h: Fawcett Society funded to research the causes of women dropping out of Parliament
items.b: The £38k funding boost will allow Fawcett to investigate the causes of women MPs choosing to leave political life.
items.why: understanding why women MPs leave Parliament bears on the representativeness of elected institutions and gender balance in political office
items.note: Funding is for research capacity-building; beat assigned by topic (representativeness of parliament) rather than generic participation.

items.h: Spotlight on Corruption — Standards in Public Life
items.b: A new campaign is to be set up by Spotlight on Corruption having received £35,000 to promote integrity and the strengthening of standards regulating public life in the UK.
items.why: a campaign to strengthen standards in public life targets mechanisms for holding officeholders to account and curbing corruption

items.h: British Youth Council receives £18k to boost the case for Votes at 16
items.b: With Scottish and Welsh young people able to cast their votes at 16, attention now turns to England as the last holdout nation on the mainland. The new funding for BYC will help develop MP’s support for Votes at 16 in the UK Parliament.
items.why: extending the franchise to 16-year-olds changes who is entitled to vote in UK elections

items.h: #HandsOffOurVote receive a £7.5k boost
items.b: The voter ID campaign Hands Off Our Vote will utilise the new cash to provide coaching and training on developing impactful campaigns, as well as supporting mapping across the sector.
items.why: campaign capacity-building on voter ID rules bears directly on ballot access and electoral integrity safeguards

items.h: Fair Vote UK benefit from a £7.5k for a dedicated comms manager for the Election Bill Coalition
items.b: Part funding the role, the new role holder will significantly increase the capacity of the Democracy Defence Coalition at this critical inflection point in the campaign.
items.why: increased capacity to campaign on the Elections Bill affects rules governing voting and electoral administration

items.h: Open Rights Group get £7.5k to amp up their work on the Online Safety Bill
items.b: ORG will deploy the funding for a short five month campaign to inform and mobilise public activist against government and regulatory overreach through the Online Safety Bill.
items.why: campaigning on the Online Safety Bill concerns how the public information and online expression environment is regulated
items.note: Treated as the information environment rather than individual liberty, per the freedom-of-expression boundary rule.

items.h: TheatreState gets a £7k boost for inspiring the leaders of the future
items.b: Focused on reimagining political life, TheatreState’s new tranche of funding will help them deliver their programme Influencers for Change: a practical and creative journey into UK politics for the leaders of the future.
items.why: a new programme creates a means for young people to engage creatively with UK political life, expanding participation opportunities

items.h: New research charts a path for creating openings for civic space in authoritarian settings
items.b: John Gaventa, Professor at the UK’s Institute of Development Studies (IDS) , notes how a focus on developing capable democratic leaders working to push reform in their own countries, coupled with other measures detailed in their research , may chart a path forward — reversing the last decade’s global democratic recession .
items.note: Research concerns civic space in authoritarian states generally, without a clear bearing on UK democracy despite the UK-based author.

items.h: Involve’s Democracy Network
items.b: With the conclusion of Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust’s significant £300,000 funding round earlier this year, we saw Involve take the reins of a new democracy network project, with Jessie Joe Jacob’s the new network’s coordinator holding their first steering group of key stakeholders this Tuesday. With this major injection of funds into the sector, we can expect great things over the next year as the Democracy Network builds upon the foundations of this meetup and the work of the Centre for Democracy and other groups.
items.why: a newly funded network coordinating civil society groups creates new infrastructure for people and organisations to take part in democratic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building (new network/programme) rather than mere organisational news, though the funding-round framing is borderline.

items.h: Democracy Defence Coalition
items.b: We’ve seen a strong response from the sector to the Conservative Government’s plans this year, with collaboration between a wide range of organisations, including a Slack group, a weekly Zoom and weekly updates digest — and now a new website . Election Bill aside, this is great news for the health of the sector and our capacity to unite around key issues.
items.why: the formation of a cross-sector coalition with shared infrastructure builds civil society's capacity to organise and respond collectively to legislative threats
items.note: Classified as civil-society capacity-building rather than the underlying Election Bill policy content itself.

items.h: Proportional Representation shot to the top of the agenda this year
items.b: With 80% of Labour CLPs backing the vote at Labour Party Conference, with only unions holding out — and even then, mostly because they hadn’t held their own policy conferences due to COVID-19 — conference very nearly backed PR, thanks to Labour for a New Democracy’s tireless campaigning on the issue this year. This is a major step forward for proponents of fair votes and hopefully we’ll get a win in 2022.
items.why: a shift in a major party's internal position toward proportional representation bears directly on the electoral system through which representatives are chosen

items.h: Kirklees Council create new shared strategic outcome for active citizenship
items.b: Working with over 100 organisations and local citizen groups, Kirklees Council has developed Shaped By People, a new foundational outcome, written by the citizens of Kirklees describing what local people want for the future. It’s part of keeping the promise made by the Kirklees Democracy Commission to make active citizenship a shared strategic priority for the region.
items.why: it creates a new co-produced strategic outcome to embed active citizenship as a shared priority, expanding institutional support for civic participation.
items.note: Local government activity here concerns civic participation outcomes, not structure/powers/elections, so it sits in participation rather than elections.

items.h: Citizens Juries and Assemblies continue in 2021 despite the plague
items.b: Shared Future CIC, Involve, Democratic Society and others saw the citizens assemblies and juries running in Newham, Southwark, Furness, Jersey States’ and more, including the publication of the report of last year’s Scottish Citizens’ Assembly . The People Vs Climate Change marked a powerful moment for the UK democracy movement.
items.why: citizens' assemblies and juries are deliberative decision-making mechanisms that shape how binding or influential collective decisions are made.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies/juries are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: We also saw the launch of the All Party Parliamentary Group on Political Literacy
items.b: Launched in January the APPG is an all-party forum to discuss the provision of citizenship and political education in schools. The APPG published their latest report last month The Missing Link: An Updated Evaluation of the Provision, Practice and Politics of Democratic Education in English Secondary Schools . Covered in our November 18th bulletin, the report found that the vast majority of teachers feel responsible for developing young people’s political literacy, but completely lack the resources to do so and feel wholly unprepared, with just 1% feeling in a position to confidently do so.
items.why: political literacy education affects people's capacity to understand and engage in democratic life, and the APPG's work and report examine gaps in that provision.
links: The Missing Link: An Updated Evaluation of the Provision, Practice and Politics of Democratic Education in English Secondary Schools

items.h: Not one, but two democracy newsletters!
items.b: This year also marked the launch of two UK democracy newsletters, this very UK Democracy Bulletin, and Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust’s Democracy Action .
items.note: This is organisational news about newsletters as publications, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: A message from Jessie Joe Jacobs, Democracy Network Coordinator:
items.b: What a few months — It has been an exciting first two months as I began my role as Coordinator for a new Democracy Network. The Democracy Network is a new initiative funded by Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust to bring together people and projects from across the UK who are passionate about democracy. Our first past the post representative political system is out of date and hasn’t really changed since it’s inception. It is not geared up to govern the modern world. We need new ideas to rebuild democracy with all of us working together from all walks of life to shape what happens to us and around us…
items.note: Introductory message about a new coordinator role is organisational news, not a reported change in democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Civility in Politics Awards reminder — deadline 8 December 2021
items.b: Kicked off in the thick of the pandemic in 2020, the Civility in Politics Awards are back for 2022. The Awards focus on highlighting people in politics act with courtesy and decency to one another. There are four categories — Politician of the Year, Co-operation of the Year, Campaigner of the Year and the Daniel Stevenson Award. The deadline for submissions is 8th December 2021, so if you think there’s someone out there that deserves some praise, nominate them for an award .
items.note: Award nomination reminder is organisational admin, explicitly excluded.

items.h: Make Votes Matter crowdfunding, planning Election Bill protests, action days and preparing for the annual Democracy Awards
items.b: Holly Morgan-Davies and the team at MVM are currently preparing a cross-party demonstration in Parliament Square, as well as further protests around the country, likely early February — in addition to this, they’re planning their next Action Day on the 11th December, themed “Shine a Light on PR”. The day will be focused on promoting local actions, street stalls and online activity, for anyone interested in getting involved email the team at team@makevotesmatter.org.uk . MVM have also launched their new funding drive and are crowdfunding here, check it out and donate here . Lastly, MVM are plan…
items.note: Primarily fundraising, event and campaign-day logistics for an organisation rather than a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: mySociety charting a “new, slightly altered course”
items.b: Though still with a firm focus on democracy, Chief Executive Mark Cridge has set forward the new direction across three new blog posts . The blog posts serve as a thoughtful and careful examination of mySociety’s place within the democracy sector, what the climate crisis means for their work, and how they can use their strengths and skills to best impact society as a whole.
items.note: Organisational strategic repositioning, not a democracy story.

items.h: Liberty publish briefing on Police Bill last minute amendments
items.b: The draconian bill just got even more pointed, with last minute amendments brought in at a very late stage of the Bill’s passage. According to Kathleen Christie, Convenor of the Police Bill Coalition, there is considerable concern that last week’s Lords Committee stage had little opportunity for substantive review of these new additions to the Bill. The amendments include 51 week max prison sentences for a range of conventional direct action tactics, even for legal observers. The Bill now includes a new legal device, Serious Disruption Prevention Orders, effectively protest bans — for those in…
items.why: new legal restrictions and orders targeting protest and direct action narrow the freedom of assembly and expose participants, including legal observers, to criminal sanction.
items.note: Protest-related legal restriction and policing falls under rights & freedoms per the boundary rule.

items.h: Bad news gossip on Police Bill
items.b: Ask any Westminster contacts how much pressure they are getting about the Police Bill and they’ll say next to none, says senior climate lobbyist. We’ve asked several of our contacts to confirm this news and it seems to hold up.
items.note: Anecdotal gossip about lobbying pressure lacks a clear democratic mechanism.

items.h: Peers call for rebalance of powers
items.b: Two little known committees in the House of Lords, the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee and the Secondary Legislation Committee , joined forces last week to publish reports of critical constitutional importance. The reports Government by Diktat and Democracy Denied? examine the role of statutory instruments made by ministers under delegated powers, and whether bills give ministers inappropriate powers. The two committees are chaired by Conservative peers of long tenure, with the reports themselves being uncharacteristically blunt.
items.why: it concerns whether ministers are accumulating delegated powers that escape effective parliamentary scrutiny.
links: Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee

items.h: Alliance of Democracies offering Democracy Tech Entrepreneur Fellowship
items.b: Applications are open until December 15th, so act fast! The fellowship programme offers a six month programme that seeks to equip people from emerging democracies with the tools they need to start and scale successful democratic ventures. Applicants should come from one of the target countries: Ukraine, Georgia, Moldova, Armenia, and Venezuela.
items.note: International fellowship for non-UK emerging democracies, not UK democracy and reads as sector programme logistics.

items.h: Notwestminster 2022 is coming, 26th February
items.b: Next year’s participant-led event titled The Future is Unwritten will be held on the 26th February with a range of democracy workshops. If you’re interested in pitching an idea, pitches are open until 6th December, or until their programme is full. Get in touch with Diane and the team via their website or directly at Notwestminster@gmail.com .
items.note: Event listing/call for pitches, not a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Launch of new Local Climate Engagement programme
items.b: Today applications opened for local authorities and partnerships in England to join the new Local Climate Engagement programme. LCE will enable local authorities and partnerships to plan, commission and deliver high quality public engagement in their climate decision-making. The programme is an exciting new opportunity for local authorities to work with Involve , UK100 , Democratic Society , Shared Future and Climate Outreach . All are amongst the UK’s leading organisations in the fields of local government, public participation in climate decision-making, and climate communications and advoca…
items.why: it creates a new programme enabling local authorities to design public engagement in climate decision-making, expanding practical means of participation.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund launch three new reports
items.b: The reports include, Making Votes at 16 Work in Wales , The democratic participation of ethnic minority and immigrant voters in the UK , and Closing the Gap: Engaging the missing millions in electoral participation .
items.why: the reports address electoral participation and turnout among under-represented groups, which the framework always places under elections.
items.note: Turnout and electoral participation research is always classified under elections per the standing rule.
links: Making Votes at 16 Work in Wales
The democratic participation of ethnic minority and immigrant voters in the UK
Closing the Gap: Engaging the missing millions in electoral participation

items.h: New Electoral Commission chair joins Institute for Government for discussion, 6th December
items.b: Discussing the challenges to UK democracy, former statistician John Pullinger, the new EC chair since May this year, will share his reflections on voters, parties, the UK democratic system and his ideas for a way forward. Register for the session .
items.note: Event registration notice rather than substantive reporting of a change.

items.h: Shared Future CIC kicking off two new citizens juries on climate change
items.b: Alex King, Comms & Marketing Associate at Shared Future CIC, reports on Shared Future’s latest efforts, including two new citizens juries starting in the London Borough of Southwark and Furness in Cumbria. Their highlight of the past year has been hosting the Social Housing Tenants’ Climate Jury, commissioned by the Northern Housing Consortium. The jury saw 30 social tenants from across the North of England come together over 10 weeks until September 2021. The report on the process was published last month, but there’s also this brilliant video talking with participants about the jury, if you’…
items.why: it launches new citizens' juries, a deliberative decision-making mechanism that the framework anchors to elections and decision making.
items.note: Citizens' juries are deliberative processes, which the revised framework files under elections & decision making rather than participation.

items.h: Lead Fellow of the Citizen Network, Gavin Barker, is developing a citizen charter
items.b: Modelled on the original Chartist document, the citizen charter will call for a permanent transfer of power from Westminster to the regions. The charter is aiming for a spring 2022 launch. You can find out more about this initiative via the Citizen Reform Twitter , or emailing Gavin directly .
items.why: the charter calls for a permanent transfer of decision-making power from Westminster to the regions, altering the structure of devolved governance.
items.note: Devolution/power-transfer proposals are filed under elections & decision making per the local/regional government boundary rule.

items.h: Titus Alexander engaging with Biden’s Summit for Democracy
items.b: US President Biden’s Summit for Democracy is being held on 9/10 December this year. Titus is calling for a petition campaign to Parliament on the erosion of democratic norms in the UK, calling on Parliament to actively engage with the conference and use the year of action to create a new All Party Joint Committee on Strengthening Democracy. You can find Titus’ draft petition proposal here .
items.why: it is an effort to petition Parliament for redress and to create new institutional means of engaging with democratic reform.
items.note: Petitioning for redress of grievances sits explicitly within participation & civic life.

items.h: Talk Shop running workshop on digital democracy tool Pol.is, 6th December
items.b: Pol.is is used by groups around the world to identify common ground among large numbers of people. In Taiwan, Pol.is has been used extensively by the government there to crowdsource legislation. Perry Walker at Talk Shop has organised a seminar session with Andy Paice, which you can RSVP to join by email .
items.note: Workshop about an existing digital tool; 'digital democracy' technology is a cross-cutting lens, not a beat, and this is an event listing.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation focusing on fundraising
items.b: Whilst it’s small scale to begin with, PINF hopes that their Impact Fund shows what’s possible with funding local journalism. Public Interest News are now focusing on fundraising and finalising their survey of indie news publishers that’ll go out early next year.
items.note: Org fundraising/administrative update, not a change to public participation.

items.h: Manifesto for a People’s Media
items.b: Eliz Mizon and the team at the Media Reform Coalition have been busy the last few months coalescing and finalising their new Manifesto for a People’s Media . The manifesto draws on conversations with dozens of organisations and individuals, and 9 Town Hall events attended by nearly 30,000 people. It includes proposals for a People’s BBC and Channel 4, which would be radically transformed to become devolved and participatory. It also includes proposals for an Independent Media Commons — an ecology of participatory newsrooms, community radio stations, digital innovators and cultural producers, s…
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes restructuring public service media ownership and governance to broaden plurality and public control over the information environment
items.note: A manifesto proposing future reform rather than an enacted change, but concerns media plurality and public control of broadcasting.

items.h: Global State of Democracy report published
items.b: Published last week by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance in Stockholm, the Global State of Democracy Report 2021 reports of a number of democracies continuing the trend of democratic backsliding. Brazil, India, the US, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia have all seen these declines, with the pandemic prolonging, and likely exacerbating an existing trend, the report argues.
items.why: this matters democratically because it provides comparative evidence of global democratic backsliding across electoral integrity, executive constraints and civil liberties that contextualises assessments of UK democratic health
items.note: International report not UK-specific, included as comparative evidence per scope rules.
