items.h: Activity around the Policing Bill intensifies ahead of the Lords Report Stage debate
items.b: With civil society seemingly awakening to the threat of the Policing Bill since the recent last-minute amendments, there is now a strong pushback across campaign groups against Parts 3 (protest provisions) and Part 4 (criminalising nomadic communities). An 800,000 strong cross-platform petition is due to be handed in to the Home Office on Monday 17th ahead of the Report Stage debate.
items.why: the Policing Bill's protest provisions and criminalisation of nomadic communities directly restrict freedom of assembly and movement, core civic freedoms needed to contest public power.
items.note: Story concerns legal restriction on protest/assembly, so filed under rights not participation despite mention of a petition.

items.h: Climate groups are urging the Labour Party to oppose the Bill
items.b: Groups including Greenpeace, Extinction Rebellion, UK School Strike and Green New Deal Rising are calling for Labour to step up and oppose the Policing Bill and whip his MPs and peers to vote against the legislation, which they say is a “devastating attack on our democratic right to be heard”.
items.why: civil society groups mobilising a political party to oppose legislation restricting protest rights is an exercise of civic campaigning capacity that shapes democratic contestation.
items.note: Focus is on campaigning activity/willingness to organise rather than the legal restriction itself.
links: calling for Labour to step up

items.h: Do you have strong Lords links? Ask that they attend the Lords vote on 17th January
items.b: If your organisation has strong links with peers, Kathleen Christie and the Police Bill Alliance suggest encouraging them to turn up to vote at Part 3 Report Stage on 17th January. A range of issue-specific letters are going to peers this week from alliance members and influential supporters, including Unlock Democracy, UK21, Friends of the Earth and The Quakers.
items.why: organised lobbying of legislators to influence a vote on a bill affecting civil liberties is a form of civic participation in the legislative process.
items.note: Mechanism is civic mobilisation/lobbying rather than the substantive legal restriction.

items.h: Business Declares organise open letter to the House of Lords about the Policing Bill
items.b: The letter, warning against the criminalisation of protest and urging the Lords to act , has gained the attention of a range of significant operating in the UK including Innocent Drinks, Patagonia, Ben & Jerry’s, The Body Shop and others.
items.why: businesses organising a public letter to influence legislators on a civil-liberties bill reflects civic mobilisation shaping democratic decision-making.
items.note: Focus is on organised advocacy rather than the restriction itself.

items.h: Update on the timing and passage of the Policing Bill
items.b: According to the Police Bill Alliance, following the Lords Report Stage debate on the 17th, ‘ping pong’ will likely occur either the week of Feb 7th or Feb 21st, with the bill being enacted soon after.
items.why: this tracks the legislative progress of a bill through Parliament, part of the scrutiny process by which laws affecting public power and civil liberties are enacted.
items.note: Purely procedural timing update on a bill with civil-liberties implications, so beat is uncertain.

items.h: Josh Russell launches new platform to lobby the media to cover key bills
items.b: Hey News offers a quick and easy way for people concerned with the Elections and Policing Bills to reach out to media outlets and demand they report on these two key political developments.
items.why: a new campaigning tool creates a means for citizens to press media outlets to cover consequential legislation, expanding avenues for civic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building: a new platform/tool for engagement.

items.h: mySociety kick off the new year with a reflection on the old
items.b: Their annual review is both comprehensive and heartfelt, covering everything from their new partnership with Climate Emergency UK to their new strategic shift . mySociety are also on the lookout for a researcher to help them understand more about the intersection of Net Zero and local government, if this sounds like you, the call for proposals closes on the 21st January.

items.h: Democracy Club take stock of their work with a strategy for 2022
items.b: The last time Democracy Club thought about a five year plan, events got in the way . In their new strategy update for 2022 they discuss their desire to address the barriers around engaging with local government, to double down on their role as a foundational information layer, work with third parties to distribute their information better, and most importantly — ensuring that their core work and services continue and are well maintained. If you haven’t already, make sure to join Democracy Club Slack — the home for all things elections.
items.note: Organisational strategy review, not a launch of a new resource or mechanism.

items.h: JRRT recruiting new Head of UK Democracy Fund
items.b: The new role holder will work alongside the previous Head of Fund in a job share. Find out more and apply on JRRT’s website .

items.h: Switching parties, not Get Out The Vote, is key driver of electoral change, says new study
items.b: There is strikingly little research on the drivers of electoral change. Jon Mellon, Associate Professor at the University of Manchester, has brought together 104 inter-election panel surveys across 18 countries to determine the impact of turnout switching (GOTV), population replacement (generational change) or party switching. Across the datasets, Jon found that party switching was the most important factor in 97% of elections represented. Previous research emphasising turnout, he says, is focused on the atypical case of recent US elections, which doesn’t generalise to most electoral contexts.
items.why: the research bears on what actually drives electoral change and turnout, which is core evidence about how electoral competition and participation function.
items.note: Turnout-related research is always classified under elections per the standing rule.
links: found that party switching was the most important factor

items.h: Democracy Network considering democracy festivals and Northern Ireland networking
items.b: Jessie Joe Jacobs, Democracy Network Coordinator of Involve’s new Democracy Network , is currently continuing their long-running consultation and chat with the sector, considering plans for a Northern Ireland network and a potential democracy festival. Jessie is also in the process of setting up a council of reference for the network as a sounding board for the project. If you haven’t already, reach out to Jessie and say hello!
items.note: Only 'considering' plans, not an actual launch of a new participatory resource or network.

items.h: Have you heard of Aldermanic elections? Probably not.
items.b: Aldermanic elections in the City of London are a rare thing, and to quote Peter Keeling at Democracy Club “it’s all a bit silly”. The Alderman need only stand down once they’ve served their six year term, or turn 70 years old. As a result elections are on a rolling basis that’s staggered over the years. There are nine Aldermanic elections that are due to be held this coming year, but the Alderman haven’t decided when they will be. According to the City of London, it’s never the case that all 25 Alderman will be up for election at once.
items.why: this concerns the electoral mechanism by which representatives (Aldermen) are chosen and the structure and timing of those elections.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation researching community groups across London & Birmingham
items.b: Joe Mitchell , Programme Manager at PINF, and the team, are trying to discern a baseline of democratic engagement in five wards across the two cities. If you know of any active community groups in Birmingham, Newham, Southwark or Barnet please do get in touch with Joe.
items.why: the research aims to establish a baseline of civic engagement and community group activity, informing understanding of civil society's health and participatory capacity.
items.note: Research into community group activity treated as bearing on civil society participation rather than mere org news.

items.h: The Centre for Democracy are hiring a new Research Assistant to assist in composing this very Bulletin
items.b: If you know anyone that might fit the bill, please do send them our way . Applications close today (Friday 14th) at 11.59pm.

items.h: New Democracy Classroom monthly meetups start next week
items.b: These meetings will be an opportunity for partners to come together, share their work and discuss opportunities for collaboration in the upcoming Local Elections 2022. You can register for their first two meetups on Eventbrite and find out more about Democracy Classroom on their website .
items.note: Routine networking meetup among partners, not a new means of participation or public-facing resource.

items.h: Labour’s affiliated unions join the campaign to stop the Elections Bill
items.b: As pressure builds on the government, Labour’s trade unions start a new campaign and petition against the Elections Bill.
items.why: it concerns organised political opposition to legislation that changes the rules governing elections.

items.h: Ballot Box Scotland will be publishing local sit reps on each local council across Scotland
items.b: These situation reports will be written by local people, one per local council across Scotland. The reports will be an opportunity for young writers to have their work published on wide and fairly prominent platform. Contributors will be paid £40 for a 500–600 word assessment on their area. Find out more via Ballot Box Scotland . They’re also fundraising for this work and more, see their GoFundMe for more info.
items.why: it creates new public-interest reporting on local council elections that informs the electorate.
items.note: Treated as a new civic-journalism resource rather than pure sector logistics.

items.h: Connection Coalition reflects on two years of the pandemic
items.b: Zoe Cumberland, Manager of the Connection Coalition, runs through the challenges, opportunities and reflections on their work in 2021 with a view to outstanding questions for 2022. The Connection Coalition was founded by the Jox Cox Foundation in April 2020 at the very start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Realising the UK was facing an immediate crisis of connection, the Foundation worked to provide a space for communities and organisations focused on building connection across the country to connect and learn from each other.

items.h: Votes for Schools Student Voices Awards, ‘Welcome to your vote week’
items.b: Working with the Electoral Commission, Votes for Schools are developing a new resource for ‘Welcome to your vote week’, which starts on the 24th January. This year’s Student Voices Awards are now open, reports Lizzy Lewis, Head of Impact at Votes for Schools. The awards celebrate students who exhibit good democratic values and practice , such as confidently presenting informed judgements, listening to others and taking account of their views, or engaging in democratic action, supporting others to have a voice.
items.why: it is a campaign and resource designed to encourage young people's electoral participation and voting engagement.
items.note: Turnout-related campaigns are always filed under elections per the framework rule.

items.h: The Hansard Society Audit of Political Engagement
items.b: Joe Mitchell notes the last time the Audit of Political Engagement was published by the Hansard Society was back in 2019. The Audit is one of the very few and key bits of longitudinal data we have on political engagement. Will we see a return of the Audit for 2022?
items.why: it concerns whether a key longitudinal measure of citizens' political engagement will continue to exist.

items.h: Find out what politicians are talking about with Govtracker
items.b: Govtracker uses a natural language processing algorithm to track what UK politicians are talking about and their themes of conversation.
items.why: it creates a new tool for the public to access meaningful information about what politicians are discussing.

items.h: Small Charities Coalition to close
items.b: Unable to continue funding the charity, the trustees of the SCC have taken the decision to wind up operations this spring. The SCC has been a key source of support for charities across the UK for more than 13 years, to help find the information and support they need to start up and get on with their important work. The Charities Commission has produced this research on the impact of COVID-19 on charities across the UK.
items.note: Organisational closure news, not a change in democratic mechanisms.

items.h: UK Government publishes Voter ID policy
items.b: The latest policy paper confirms the government’s position on the new ID cards, though notably whilst 60+ railcards and other ID are now acknowledged as acceptable forms of ID, young people’s railcards, student IDs and other common forms of identification for young people are not included.
items.why: it sets the identification requirements that determine who can practically exercise their right to vote.

items.h: PACAC call for the Government to stop the passage of the Elections Bill
items.b: In a new wide-ranging report published before the Christmas break, members of the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee say the reforms ‘lack evidence base, consultation, and transparency’.
items.why: a parliamentary committee is exercising legislative scrutiny over a government bill for lacking evidence and transparency.
items.note: PACAC's scrutiny function is the mechanism, though the bill's content concerns elections.

items.h: It’s official: Sortition Foundation are the fairest at selecting participants for a Citizens’ Assembly
items.b: They run a pretty heavy-duty piece of code to sort through and select participants for citizens’ assemblies. This year, Nick Gill and the team are really keen to share all that they’ve learned and promote best practice around recruitment to CAs.
items.why: this matters democratically because fair participant selection determines whether citizens' assemblies genuinely represent the public in collective decision-making processes.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are filed under elections & decision making per the framework, not participation.

items.h: The next stage for climate assemblies — designing for impact
items.b: Graham Smith, Professor of Politics and Director of the University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy, reviews the extent to which national level climate assemblies have had an impact. Graham notes that not enough attention has been placed on coupling the citizens’ assembly format with the relevant policy systems of the relevant state. The blog considers the effectiveness of these assemblies so far in responding to the systematic challenges of climate breakdown, in that climate assemblies usually provide policy recommendations, as designed — rather than engaging in systems chan…
items.why: this matters democratically because it examines whether deliberative democratic mechanisms like citizens' assemblies actually translate into effective policy influence.
items.note: Deliberative processes are anchored to decision-making machinery, not participation.

items.h: An academic specialising in deliberative democracy was invited to a citizens’ assembly — here’s what happened next
items.b: John Boswel, Associate Professor in Politics at the University of Southampton, was surprised to be selected for the Kingston-Upon-Thames Citizens’ Assembly, having spent so much time writing and reading about democratic innovation and deliberative democracy. John’s reflections on the process are a must-read for any practitioners of deliberative democracy.
items.why: this matters democratically because it offers first-hand insight into how citizens' assemblies function as a deliberative decision-making mechanism.
items.note: Citizens' assembly process falls under elections & decision making per framework.

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us this week for Democracy Check-Ins. This week we were joined by Myf Nixon of mySociety, Natasha Fox of the Electoral Reform Society, Josh Russell of Forward Democracy, Joe Mitchell of Public Interest News Foundation, Lizzy Lewis of Votes for Schools, Jon Morter of the Progressive Alliance, Peter Keeling of Democracy Club, Nick Gill of the Sortition Foundation, Kathleen Christie of the Police Bill Alliance, Perry Walker of TalkShop, Jessie Joe Jacobs of the UK Democracy Network and David Stoker.

items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding and Molly Hudson of The Centre for Democracy . Read by 280+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : hello@centrefordemocracy.org.uk
Updates from Kathleen Christie — Police Bill Alliance Convenor:

items.h: PSCS Bill passes Lords Committee phase, 14 amendments voted down
items.b: According to UCL, this vote represents the single biggest Lords vote against a government since 1999. The amendments voted down related to Part 3 / Protest.
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports a legislative check on proposed state restrictions on the right to protest, with Parliament's upper chamber constraining executive-backed legislation
items.note: Protest legal restriction via legislation is coded to rights per boundary rule, with the Lords vote itself relevant to legislative constraint on the executive.

items.h: The Senedd votes to reject proposals to criminalise trespass
items.b: Following a powerful campaign by Welsh Gypsy, Roma and Traveller groups, the Senedd has voted to withhold legislative consent on Part 4 of the bill related to the criminalisation of trespass.
items.why: this matters democratically because a devolved legislature used its consent powers to block criminalisation of trespass, a coercive measure affecting a minority group's basic freedoms
items.note: Devolved legislative consent machinery is elections_decision_making territory, but the substantive issue is a rights-restricting criminal provision.

items.h: Police Bill Alliance strategy over next critical weeks
items.b: Kathleen Christie reports that all efforts are now turning to the parliamentary ‘ping pong’ which is expected to take place week beginning 7th Feb or 21st Feb. The Police Bill Alliance’s strategy will follow a constituency based approach, targeting backbench Conservatives where the MP is most likely to rebel or where alliance partner local groups are strongest. Focus will remain on Part 3 / Protest. These alliance partner groups include: Grassroots for Europe; Quakers in Britain; Friends of the Earth; Amnesty International UK; Greenpeace; Christian Aid and a new ethical business alliance with …
items.why: this matters democratically because it describes civil society coalitions organising and lobbying MPs to shape legislative outcomes, a form of political participation and campaigning
items.note: Campaigning/coalition strategy is coded to participation, while the underlying protest provisions are a rights matter.

items.h: Notwestminster — it’s coming
items.b: Diane Sims and the team at Notwestminster are in the final stages of preparations for this year’s free, friendly, open, volunteer-run, physical, in-real life, face-to-face day of workshops on local democracy. Notwestminster 2022: The future is unwritten will be held at the University of Huddersfield on Saturday 26th February, grab your ticket now !
items.why: this matters democratically because it is a new civic event creating opportunities for people to engage with and learn about local democracy

items.h: London Funders — Why 2022 is an important year for democratic engagement
items.b: London Funders have published a briefing on why this year is a key year for funders to step forward and back democratic engagement projects and initiatives. The briefing unfortunately vastly overstates the funding going towards democracy projects — suggesting £165m in London alone! We can but dream.
items.note: A commentary/critique of a funding briefing rather than a newly created resource or programme for participation.

items.h: Citizens’ Assembly on Democracy in the UK provides stark public outlook for integrity in British politics
items.b: Sarah Castell, CEO of Involve, highlights the fresh interim findings of their recent partnership with UCL’s Constitution Unit. After six weekends of intensive discussions, assembly members produced a range of concerning statements concerning the state of British democracy. The strongest theme was dissatisfaction and concern over a perceived lack of integrity among politicians . Alan Renwick, Director of The Constitution Unit, summarised the findings, ‘almost every member of the assembly, regardless of their political allegiance, was angry and frustrated and wanted their elected representatives…
items.why: this matters democratically because a citizens' assembly, a deliberative decision-making process, produced findings on public confidence in the integrity of elected representatives
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are coded to elections_decision_making per the revised framework, though the substance touches standards in public life.
links: dissatisfaction and concern over a perceived lack of integrity among politicians

items.h: Demos interviewing activists on the impact of the pandemic on their activities
items.b: In order to better understand the political impact of the pandemic , Demos are interviewing activists from across the spectrum who were involved in the powerful movements and moments that shaped our political experience of the pandemic, from mutual aid groups to Black Lives Matter and Insulate Britain. If you’d like to find out more about this piece of work, get in touch with Ciaran Cummins , Researcher at Demos. On a slightly separate note, if you’re up for it — Ciaran is pretty keen on setting up a democracy book club/irl meetup.
items.note: Research interviews with activists, not a new participation mechanism; sector logistics.

items.h: Frances Scott nominated for UK Diversity Awards
items.b: Director of 50:50 , Frances Scott, has been nominated for the UK Diversity Awards in Liverpool next week on 4th February. Good luck Frances!
items.note: Award nomination for an individual, excluded as organisational news.

items.h: Are you working in a UK government policy team? TPXimpact needs you!
items.b: Deliberative Democracy Lead at TPXimpact (previously FutureGov), Kelly McBride, is soon to be on the lookout for 12 people working across government policy teams to participate in a series of workshops assessing the impact of climate assemblies on public policy. Find out more and get in touch with Kelly here .
items.note: Recruitment for internal workshops assessing assemblies, not a new participation mechanism itself.

items.h: Big Tent Ideas is back
items.b: Trin Gong, Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent, is currently setting up the ticketing for this year’s festival in Bristol. The festival will be held on 11th June and the theme is Transitions. Stay tuned for more .
items.note: Event ticketing logistics.

items.h: Reflecting on last year’s Pew attitudes-to-democracy research
items.b: Joe Mitchell , democracy flâneur and Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation, highlights last year’s research revealing more than 87% of UK citizens in early 2021 wanted changes to the political system — and 52% think that complete reform or major changes are needed — that’s massive!
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports levels of public support for and confidence in the political system, a condition for democratic legitimacy and engagement.

items.h: Compassion in Politics working on a debate and survey report on standards and lying in politics
items.b: Matt Hawkins , Co-Director at Compassion in Politics , and their team, are working on writing up the results to a deep-dive survey into the culture of politics amongst MPs and their staff, in partnership with The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development . The results will be presented to their APPG and will form the basis for a new campaign. CiP are also working with Plaid Cymru on a debate on standards and lying in politics, starting with this EDM .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns standards of honesty and conduct among elected representatives, a core accountability mechanism in public life.
links: The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development

items.h: Naked Politics working to develop democratic participation in marginalised young people
items.b: Director and Founder of Naked Politics , Banseka Kayembe, is working to provide educational sessions, guidance and in-depth support to 18–25 year olds across the UK, focused on the importance of democracy and how they can exercise their democratic rights. But more importantly than that, they’re providing a space for young people to be heard and get them interested in politics.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new means for marginalised young people to understand and exercise their democratic rights, expanding capacity for participation.

items.h: Scottish Government responds to the Scottish Climate Assembly
items.b: The Scottish Government has responded in full to the 81 recommendations made by Assembly members at the Scottish Climate Assembly.
items.why: this matters democratically because it shows how government responds to recommendations from a deliberative citizens' assembly, part of the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the revised framework.

items.h: Titus Alexander looking to commission development of a ‘democracy gateway’
items.b: A public portal for interacting with the myriad organisations, projects and networks that make up the democracy sector, the Democracy Gateway would aim to make it easier to find the people and organisations that can help citizens take part in democratic processes. Titus is now seeking to commission the design and development of the portal. Contact Titus for more information.
items.why: this matters democratically because it aims to create a new tool helping citizens find and access organisations that support democratic participation.

items.h: Democracy Research Collaboration Toolkit
items.b: Graham Smith, Director at the Centre for the Study of Democracy , George Bolton, PhD University of Southampton, and Jessie Joe Jacobs, Coordinator of the Democracy Network , have teamed up to better understand the opportunities and barriers to collaboration between democracy organisations and academics, and how we might build a more productive relationship between the two.
items.note: Concerns collaboration infrastructure between democracy organisations and academics, not a mechanism affecting public participation directly.
links: Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: Climate Change Citizens’ Juries active across the UK
items.b: Citizens in Furness and Southwark are currently considering the question of addressing climate change in their area, reports Alex King , Comms & Marketing Associate at Shared Future CIC. The jurors are currently listening to expert advice before forming their recommendations.
items.why: citizens' juries are a deliberative democratic mechanism for taking binding or advisory collective decisions on public policy
items.note: Deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: Participatory budgeting in Blaenavon with VocalEyes
items.b: Susan Rodaway and the team at VocalEyes are kicking off a co-produced participatory budgeting project in Blaenavon, working with the Town Council, Unitary Authority, Local Health Board and others. Susan also announces that VocalEyes have rebranded and launched a new website .
items.why: participatory budgeting creates a new mechanism for residents to directly influence public spending decisions
items.note: Participatory budgeting is explicitly filed under participation & civic life rather than decision-making machinery.

items.h: Deaton Review of Inequalities publish draft paper on political equality
items.b: In this hefty draft text, Pablo Beramundi of Duke University, Tim Besley of LSE and Margaret Levi of Stanford University, focus on equal consideration as an ideal for political equality in democratic settings .
items.why: the paper examines equal consideration as a condition for fair political participation, bearing on equal access to power
links: equal consideration as an ideal for political equality in democratic settings

items.h: Sheila McKechnie’s annual survey out soon
items.b: Word on the grapevine says the survey will show that the sector is increasingly worried with ongoing political developments and direction of travel, but also determined to keep campaigning.
items.note: Speculative mention of an upcoming sector survey with no substantive findings yet.

items.h: Conservative MPs accuse party whips of blackmail
items.b: PACAC Chair William Wragg reports claims include having money pulled from constituencies or a promise of funding for the ‘right vote’ . Former Conservative MP Christian Wakeford also made blackmail allegations, claiming that whips told him his constituency would lose funding for a new school unless he voted with the government . Downing Street is seemingly refusing to investigate the accusations , saying they would ‘look carefully at the evidence presented to them, but were not seeking it’. Regardless, William Wragg is currently preparing to meet the Metropolitan Police to discuss the No 10 bl…
items.why: alleged coercion of MPs' votes via funding threats undermines legislative accountability and standards in public life
links: promise of funding for the ‘right vote’
unless he voted with the government
Downing Street is seemingly refusing to investigate the accusations

items.h: Cabinet Minister states Partygate has ‘damaged our democracy’
items.b: Sajid Javid, Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, admits that the string of parties said to have taken place in Downing Street over the course of the pandemic have ‘damaged’ democracy in the UK.
items.why: a minister's admission reflects on public confidence in government and standards in public office

items.h: Blackmail claims further erode Britain’s reputation overseas, amidst global democratic backsliding
items.b: UK’s democratic standing and position as a role model for developing democracies at risk, say experts. Recent allegations of blackmail and corruption compound the damaging behaviour of the Prime Minister in recent years, including the threat to break international law . Amongst those warning of the change were Douglas Alexander, former Minister and now Senior Fellow at Harvard University’s Kennedy School, who sought to link the behaviour of the Government in recent years and the damage it has caused against the backdrop of encroachment by alternative models put forward by Russia and other stat…
items.why: perceived corruption and rule-breaking by government erodes standards in public life and the UK's credibility as a democratic model

items.h: YouGov poll shows Britons overwhelmingly think corruption is present in British politics
items.b: Boris Johnson has said the UK is “not remotely a corrupt country”, but the British public resoundingly disagree. According to polling, 40% of the public think there is ‘a lot of corruption’ , with a further 40% who perceive a ‘fair amount of corruption’ in British politics.
items.why: public perceptions of pervasive corruption reflect on trust in government and political accountability
links: 40% of the public think there is ‘a lot of corruption’

items.h: 99 days to the local elections… and no sign of promised funds for COVID-safe local election delivery
items.b: Whilst last year’s rules for more flexible proxy votes to take account of the pandemic continue, Becca Crosier, Deputy Director of the Whitehall Elections Division, said there has been ‘no firm conclusions’ (paywall) on funding this year, when extra COVID safety measures are still expected to be required. In addition, the Deputy Director also ruled out any experiments or shifts to online voting in the short term, saying ‘there isn’t a way of doing it is that is sufficiently secure’.
items.why: funding and safety arrangements for local elections directly affect whether elections can be well-run and accessible

items.h: Boris Johnson no confidence vote looms
items.b: As reports trickle in of Conservative MPs submitting letters of no confidence to Graham Brady, Chair of the Conservative 1922 Committee, over the Partygate scandal, leadership contenders drop subtle hints as to their intentions — with Jeremy Hunt, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak as the likely front runners.
items.why: a no confidence vote concerns the orderly transfer of power and leadership accountability within the governing party
items.note: Treated as elections & decision making per the 'orderly constitutional transfer of power' anchor.

items.h: David Gauke argues to abolish the role of the Tory Party membership in electing their leader
items.b: As talk of leadership elections to replace the ailing Prime Minister heat up, David Gauke, writing for Conservative Home, makes the argument for the abolition of the role of the party faithful in deciding their next leader . His argument is that for a party whose leader is more often than not the sitting PM, that the country cannot wait ~4 weeks for a decision to be made, especially in the case of the death of the PM. For information on the process of any leadership elections, the Institute for Government produced this handy guide .
items.why: it concerns how a political party selects the person who may become Prime Minister, a core mechanism of political competition and elected government.
items.note: Party leadership selection process falls under elections/decision-making machinery.
links: abolition of the role of the party faithful in deciding their next leader

items.h: New report from Demos on Relational Local Government
items.b: The Social State calls for a system of relational public services to better bring together and knit local communities with the community at large and those who provide public services. The first part of a major new research programme at Demos, the project aims to build a credible policy agenda for 21st public services with citizen experience at the centre. The report includes lots of new research on public attitudes to democratic engagement in the design and delivery of local services.
items.why: it examines how citizens can be brought into the design and delivery of local public services, a form of civic engagement and participatory capacity-building.
items.note: Focus is on citizen engagement in service design, not local government structure or powers.

items.h: Petition for councils in England to meet remotely growing
items.b: The Association of Democratic Services Officers (ADSO) and Lawyers in Local Government (LLG) are petitioning for councils in England to have the right to meet remotely, based on local circumstances. The law does not currently allow for this. Find out more and sign the petition here .
items.why: it concerns the legal rules governing how local councils can conduct their decision-making meetings.
items.note: Local government meeting practice is treated as decision-making machinery per the boundary rule.

items.h: Citizen Network prepare to launch new constitutional charter
items.b: End Westminster Rule outlines 10 key demands for radical reform based on the charter of the Chartist movement. Simon Duffy and Gavin Barker of the Citizen Network , report a provisional date for the launch of the charter is spring 2022. The document will be submitted to main parliamentary parties asking for a response.
items.why: it proposes changes to the UK's constitutional and decision-making structures, submitted to parties for response.
items.note: Constitutional reform charter treated as decision-making machinery rather than mere campaigning.

items.h: New OECD policy paper on institutionalising deliberative democracy
items.b: The paper makes eight recommendations for how public officials and policy makers can create structures that allow representative deliberation to become an integral part of how certain types of decisions are taken. Read the policy paper .
items.why: it addresses how deliberative processes can be institutionalised as part of formal decision-making structures.
items.note: Deliberative democracy is classified under elections & decision making per framework rule.

items.h: Democratic Yorkshire launches
items.b: Supported by Citizen Network , a new campaign Democratic Yorkshire has launched — calling for a new citizen-framed constitutional settlement for Yorkshire, including a regional parliament, a regional executive, tax and spend powers and autonomy within the government of the UK.
items.why: it campaigns for a new regional tier of government with its own parliament, executive and fiscal powers.
items.note: Regional government structure/powers placed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Government announces BBC license fee to be frozen and abolished completely by 2027
items.b: The changes announced by Culture Secretary Nadine Dorries announced last week will leave the corporation with a funding gap of more than £250 million, according to BBC Director General Tim Davie .
items.why: it affects the funding and viability of a major public-service broadcaster that underpins the plural information environment citizens rely on.

items.h: Coordinating opposition to the BBC License Fee freeze
items.b: Sam Guiness, Founder of the Coalition Against Digital Coercive Control, is pushing to bring together a campaign against the BBC License Fee freeze. Sam has drawn up a document of data and arguments on the significance of the BBC and its impact on British and global cultural life.
items.why: it organises opposition to a funding decision affecting public-service media central to the information environment.

items.h: Pegasus spyware used to spy on Polish opposition parties, what does this mean for elections?
items.b: Notes From Poland editor Stanley Bill, Senior Lecturer and Director of the Polish Studies Programme at the University of Cambridge, talks with John Scott-Railton, Senior Researcher at Citizen Lab , whose work recently uncovered the use of spyware to hack the phones of people connected to Poland’s opposition.
items.why: covert surveillance of opposition politicians undermines fair political competition and the integrity of electoral contests.
items.note: International case used as comparative evidence bearing on electoral integrity.
links: recently uncovered the use of spyware

items.h: Big Changes at Democracy Club
items.b: With the new year, comes a new team, reports Peter Keeling , who oversees voting information at Democracy Club. Four new members are joining the DC team, including Eleesha Taylor-Barrett as their 2022 Elections Assistant and Mevan Babakar — who is stepping into the role of interim CEO, having been a member of the Democracy Club board since 2018. But if two new core members wasn’t enough, they’re also onboarding two new board members — Ashley Hodges — Chief Executive of Young Citizens and formerly of Speakers for Schools , and Susan Simmonds — a strategic communications and capacity building co…
items.note: Staff and board appointments at an organisation are excluded even though the org works on democracy.

items.h: Massive turnout for Elections Bill protests
items.b: From London to Manchester, Make Votes Matter and democracy organisations across the UK came out on Saturday 5th Feb in a show of support for a fairer voting system, against the provisions of the Elections Bill. Take a look at the photos from the day over on the Democracy Defence Coalition’s Twitter.
items.why: it reports people's willingness to publicly demonstrate against proposed changes to electoral law, a form of civic mobilisation around the machinery of elections
items.note: Protest turnout is classed as participation when the story is people's readiness to take part, with the underlying Elections Bill subject as secondary.

items.h: Democracy Network hiring, readying a Development Day
items.b: Democracy Network Coordinator Jessie Joe Jacobs is preparing a day of ideation to draw out some key themes and ideas for the new network. The workshop will aim to understand what the sector’s vision is for a better democracy and how to better coordinate and resource activities within the sector. Jessie also highlights they’re currently recruiting a Communications and Advocacy Officer to assist in the delivery of the Democracy Network.
items.note: Internal sector hiring and an organisational strategy day, not a new means of public participation.

items.h: Notwestminster asks: What’s your one best hope for local democracy?
items.b: With Notwestminster just around the corner on February 26th, they want answers to the question: What’s your one best hope for local democracy. They’re collecting responses to this question across this month to share with the wider network. Register now and join Diane Sims and the team for a day of participant-led workshops and lightning talks on local democracy in Huddersfield.
items.why: it creates a means for people to voice their hopes for local democracy and take part in participant-led workshops shaping local civic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of civic engagement rather than local government structure itself.

items.h: Civic Power Fund wants to hear from community organisers
items.b: Civic Power Fund (CPF) is the UK’s first pooled donor fund dedicated to community organising (CO). They’re investing in CO directly, building the infrastructure and leadership that CO needs to thrive. Are you involved in community organising? Do you know of brilliant projects or people that Civic Power Fund should be speaking to? Get in touch with Martha Mackenzie , Executive Director of the CPF.
items.note: This is an outreach/networking call for an existing fund, not a new capacity-building launch or reported change.

items.h: Grab your early bird ticket now for RADIX Big Tent Ideas Festival, Bristol June 11th
items.b: Big Tent Ideas are back! Well known for their annual festivals composed of rich discussions and workshops involving those from across the UK political spectrum, they’ve been on pause since the pandemic hit and have now teamed up with think tank Radix. For a taster of their events, they’ve got an event on the Northern Ireland Protocol coming up later this month. Register now for your Big Tent Ideas Festival early bird ticket .
items.note: Event ticket promotion counts as sector logistics.
links: event on the Northern Ireland Protocol

items.h: House of Lords once again try to abolish Hereditary Peer By-Elections
items.b: Lord Bruce Grocott has put another bill before Parliament to abolish the by-elections through which hereditary peers are replaced. Despite widespread support on both sides of the Lords, the current bill, and Lord Grocott’s previous bills introduced in 2016 and 2017, will not and have not so far been able to proceed through the Commons. For more information, see David Beamish’s Constitution Unit blog post .
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns how members of a chamber that shapes legislation continue to be selected, via hereditary by-elections rather than democratic mandate.
items.note: Composition of the legislature via non-electoral means is treated as elections/decision-making machinery.

items.h: House of Lords demands culture change
items.b: The House of Lords Select Committee on the Constitution publishes major new report following its inquiry into future UK governance. The report, Respect and Co-operation: Building a Stronger Union for the 21st century , draws on evidence from the Yorkshire Devolution Movement , the Electoral Reform Society and the APPG on Deliberative Democracy , amongst others. The Committee says there is a ‘clear opportunity to reset relationships and achieve a better functioning union’, calling on the Government to ‘articulate a compelling vision and narrative for the UK in the 21st century — and an end to t…
items.why: This matters democratically because it addresses the structures and relationships governing devolved and central decision-making across the UK union.
items.note: Devolution and intergovernmental structure falls under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Joe Mitchell ponders a Democracy Observatory
items.b: Last week Joe Mitchell , Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation, had a chat with Migration Observatory (MO) about the prospects for a Democracy Observatory. According to Joe, they felt it wasn’t a bad idea, but that for the MO they built upon an existing need — people were talking about migration. The problem according to Migration Observatory is that not many people talk about democracy! This isn’t the first time Joe’s considered a Democracy Observatory . Sound like a good idea to you? Get in touch with Joe .
items.note: This is speculative discussion about a possible future project, not a launched resource or reported change.
links: This isn’t the first time Joe’s considered a Democracy Observatory

items.h: Institute for Government and the Bennett Institute for Public Policy launch joint review of the UK constitution
items.b: With Brexit and COVID-19 placing strain on the already beleaguered British system, the new review will look at what works, what doesn’t and how we can improve the situation. Their first paper looks at three key relationships, between citizens and the state, the different tiers of government across the UK and the government, parliament and the judiciary. IfG and the Bennett Institute will explore these problems over the next 18 months, making recommendations for reform where necessary. For a complete picture of the review, see Maddy Thimont Jack’s recent Twitter thread on the review.
items.why: This matters democratically because it examines how power and accountability are structured between citizens, tiers of government, and the branches of the state.

items.h: New Commission on Political Power announced
items.b: The Commission aims to generate a national debate on legislative and structural form of the UK political system. The Commission on Political Power are expecting to publish a White Paper in Spring 2022. The commission has received funding from Julian Richer of Richer Sounds.
items.why: This matters democratically because it seeks to generate debate on reforming the legislative and structural form of the UK political system.

items.h: Democratic wellbeing under threat, Carnegie UK
items.b: The new report argues we should aim to measure ‘collective wellbeing’ based on social, economic, environmental and democratic outcomes — contrasted to the ONS’ which focuses on the social and economic. Carnegie found 41% of people in England say ‘democracy is not working’ and that the biggest threats to democracy are a ‘loss of trust and corruption’.
items.why: This matters democratically because it measures public trust and perceived legitimacy of democratic institutions, which underpin people's willingness to engage in political life.
items.note: Public trust and perceptions of democracy are treated as participation-related outcomes, not a standalone corruption story.

items.h: Responses to the Levelling Up White Paper
items.b: Involve and Demos have published responses to the Government’s Levelling Up White Paper. The two responses lauded the ambition of the new policy, to bring about a more ‘united society’, but highlighted the absence or lack of emphasis in certain areas, including the absence of plans for large scale fiscal transfers between rich and poor areas, the lack of proposals to strengthen relationships between communities and institutions, and in short — a lot of talk about the importance of local leadership, but limited practical policy that will make the vision a reality.
items.why: This matters democratically because the responses critique the powers, resources and community-institution relationships central to local and regional decision-making structures.
items.note: Local government powers and structure fall under elections & decision making; the equality/resource critique is a secondary participation dimension.

items.h: 50:50 preparing for International Women’s Day
items.b: Frances Scott , Founder of 50:50, is working with UN Women, the Fawcett Society and the Women in Parliament APPG for a special International Women’s Day event in Parliament. The event is being supported by Lloyds Banking Group.
items.note: Event preparation announcement counts as sector logistics rather than a reported democratic change.

items.h: Biden’s Democracy Summit — Next Steps
items.b: The December 2021 Summit called for a year of action by participant countries to make democracies more responsive and resilient, and to build a broader community of partners committed to global democratic renewal. A follow up event is planned for December 2022.
items.note: International summit announcement with no concrete UK democratic mechanism; sector event notice.

items.h: Newspeak House hosting event on product development in collective decision making
items.b: Run by the Chaitin School of Software Engineering , the event at Newspeak House will see attendees working together to ideate and design a new piece of software for collective decision making. Could this event birth a new Pol.is or Consul ? Find out and register for the event via Meetup .
items.note: Speculative event listing about ideating future software, not a launched tool or resource.

items.h: People Powered’s new Guide to Digital Participation Platforms
items.b: With so many digital participation platforms to choose from the team over at People Powered have produced a full guide to their use and execution, including a set of comparisons for ‘complex’, ‘simple’ and ‘speciality’ platforms from across the globe. View the full guide and platform ratings .
items.why: This matters democratically because producing a comparative guide to participation platforms creates a practical resource that helps organisations set up new means for people to take part in collective decisions.
items.note: Counts as sector capacity-building: a new resource that expands practical participation tools.

items.h: Centre for Democracy mulling a special local elections event
items.b: It’s early days but we’re currently planning a special elections event at Newspeak House. Stay tuned.
items.note: Early-stage event planning teaser with no concrete content yet.

items.h: Keir Starmer subject to intimidation following Jimmy Savile smears
items.b: The Labour leader was bundled into a police car to escape an angry group of protesters. The incident followed spurious comments made by the Prime Minister last week that Keir Starmer failed to prosecute Jimmy Savile in his former role as the head of the Crown Prosecution Service. Starmer has now laid blame on the PM’s comment for inciting the group that harassed him.
items.why: This matters democratically because political leaders must be able to operate free from intimidation and violence, and incendiary rhetoric from the head of government that incites harassment threatens the basic security needed for fair political competition.
items.note: Personal security of a political leader under threat of mob intimidation, linked to executive rhetoric.

items.h: Boris Johnson survives
items.b: With the release of the Sue Gray update detailing twelve UK Government parties during the height of the pandemic, including one in the Prime Minister’s own residence , Boris Johnson faced a wave of senior letters of no confidence , including the resignation of five key advisors. The previous week saw the defection of Bury South Conservative MP, Christian Wakeford to the Labour Party.
items.why: This matters democratically because the episode tests whether a prime minister can be held to account by his own party and Parliament for serious breaches of standards, through confidence letters, resignations and defections.
items.note: MP defection touches party competition but the core story is executive accountability.
links: one in the Prime Minister’s own residence
defection of Bury South Conservative MP, Christian Wakeford

items.h: Decline into illiberal democracy on the cards, former TI head warns
items.b: Professor Robert Barrington warns that the ongoing actions of the Johnson Government risk accelerating Britain’s democratic-backsliding even further , highlighting the Prime Minister’s co-option of the Metropolitan Police and failure to follow established codes of conduct. Robert Barrington is Professor of Anti-Corruption Practice at the Centre for the Study of Corruption in the University of Sussex and was formerly the head of Transparency International UK.
items.why: This matters democratically because alleged politicisation of the police and disregard for codes of conduct erode the checks that constrain executive power and preserve institutional independence.
items.note: Commentary warning of a trend rather than reporting a specific new event.

items.h: Labour leader cleared of lockdown rules breach
items.b: Durham Constabulary said they do not believe any offence was committed in April 2021 when Sir Keir was pictured with a bottle of beer in the office of City of Durham MP Mary Foy. The image of the Labour leader was brought to light last month as public focus on partygate intensified.
items.why: This matters democratically because consistent, even-handed application of the law to political leaders, regardless of party or position, is essential to public confidence in impartial law enforcement.
links: they do not believe any offence was committed

items.h: Disregard for integrity has become marked feature of Johnson’s premiership, claims Andrew Ryder
items.b: Author of Britain and Europe at a Crossroads: The Politics of Anxiety and Transformation , Andrew Ryder, argues that the Partygate scandal runs much deeper than the work culture at the heart of government or Johnson’s personal failings — it is emblematic of a decline in public standards that has sharply escalated since the 2016 referendum. Andrew Ryder is an Associate Professor of Sociology at Eötvös Lorànd University in Budapest.
items.why: This matters democratically because a sustained decline in standards of public conduct in government weakens the norms that constrain and hold accountable those who exercise executive power.
items.note: Opinion piece asserting a longer-term pattern rather than reporting a specific new development.
links: Britain and Europe at a Crossroads: The Politics of Anxiety and Transformation
emblematic of a decline in public standards

items.h: Kill the Bill riot charges prompt alarm over civil liberties
items.b: Dozens of young people are currently facing serious charges of riot over the protests last year, in what amounts to the biggest use of the public order offence since the 1980s. The charges have given some the impression of ‘revenge policing’ , similar to the actions of the officers involved in the protests allegedly using illegal tactics following several nights of violent clashes.
items.why: This matters democratically because the use of serious public order charges against protesters, seen by some as politically motivated 'revenge policing', raises concerns about state power being used to curtail the right to protest and freedom of assembly.
items.note: Protest policing is classified under rights and civic space per the boundary rule on legal restriction and state coercion.

items.h: Northern Irish power-sharing institutions saved from collapse
items.b: Alan Whysall, Honorary Senior Research Associate at the Constitution Unit, argues that the foundations of the Good Friday Agreement are at serious risk of crumbling . Last week DUP First Minister Paul Givan resigned over the Northern Ireland Protocol, just hours after DUP Agriculture Minister Edwin Poots instructed border staff to halt NI Protocol checks on goods at Northern Irish ports. Alan remarks that it appears we are witnessing the making good of DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldon’s threats to collapse the institutions over the Protocol, in part at least to force London’s gaze to resolve the is…
items.why: it concerns whether Northern Ireland's power-sharing executive and assembly, the core devolved decision-making institutions, can continue to function and be held accountable
items.note: Devolved government structure and collapse-prevention legislation falls under elections & decision making.
links: foundations of the Good Friday Agreement are at serious risk of crumbling
DUP First Minister Paul Givan resigned
instructed border staff to halt NI Protocol checks

items.h: Demos developing their vision for ‘relational local government’
items.b: Continuing from their recent landmark report The Social State , Demos have been setting out the detail of this vision. Ciaran Cummins , Researcher at Demos, argues that this relational local government has three key pillars: genuine power sharing, spaces for connection and consistent and open communication.
items.why: it proposes changes to how local government structures power-sharing and communication with citizens, affecting the machinery of local decision-making
items.note: Local government structure/vision falls under elections & decision making per boundary rule.

items.h: British Broadcasting Challenge
items.b: A new initiative backed by Sir David Attenborough to promote a public discussion on the future of UK public service broadcasting has launched. View or support the campaign .
items.why: public service broadcasting shapes the plurality and quality of information citizens can access about public affairs

items.h: The Bureau joined by new CEO and Editor-in-Chief, Rozina Breen
items.b: A champion of diversity and inclusion in newsrooms, Rozina has a wealth of experience to bring to the Bureau team, most recently heading up BBC News in the north of England.
items.note: Staff appointment news is excluded even at a democracy-relevant organisation.

items.h: Talking Politics are winding down
items.b: After 6 years and 300 episodes, Talking Politics are muting their mics. Whilst their archives will remain accessible, and they’ve still got a handful of episodes to go, they wanted to finish the project on a high note. If you missed Talking Politics, you’ve got a huge back catalogue of discussion and analysis to get through!
items.note: Organisational/programme wind-down notice, not a change in democratic participation or debate.

items.h: Don’t miss out on this great democracy podcast
items.b: Untelevised have put out a great little mini-series on all things democracy. We love their presentation style. Give it a listen now .
items.note: A content recommendation rather than creation of a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Daya Eseonu on Afrofuturism and deliberation on the PSA blog
items.b: Ciaran Cummins at Demos recommends this brilliant blog by Daya Eseonu’s on Afrofuturism and knowledge production in participatory and deliberative spaces published on the Political Studies Association’s blog.
items.note: A blog recommendation, not itself a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters, Joe Mitchell — Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation & The Centre for Democracy, Jessie Joe Jacobs — Coordinator at Democracy Network, Louise Crow — Programme Director at mySociety, Frances Scott — Founder at 50:50 Parliament and Alex King — Associate at Shared Future CIC.

items.h: Government rejects Lords amendments to Police Bill, MPs back the bill
items.b: Priti Patel wrote to MPs urging them to back the controversial anti-protest legislation. Last month peers inflicted a string of defeats on the government’s measures. The Bill now faces an extended round of parliamentary ping-pong.
items.why: the Police Bill's anti-protest measures restrict citizens' legal capacity to assemble and demonstrate, a core civic freedom underpinning democratic contestation.
items.note: Protest law is Rights & freedoms because the mechanism is legal restriction and state coercion, not willingness to protest.

items.h: Updates from the Democracy Defence Coalition:
items.b: Electoral Commission changes and Voter ID seem to be the two biggest issues for peers with the Elections Bill, with some mention of third party campaigning. Many peers have notably been using Democracy Defence Coalition (DDC) messaging and language in their speeches.
items.why: changes to the Electoral Commission's oversight and voter ID requirements directly affect the integrity and accessibility of UK elections.

items.h: Mega thread on the Lords 2nd Reading of the Elections Bill
items.b: Jessica Metheringham , Chair of Unlock Democracy , tracked developments in the House of Lords throughout the 2nd Reading. Must read for anyone working on the Elections Bill. The Bill now moves forward to Lords Committee stage, sitting on the 10th March.
items.why: tracking parliamentary scrutiny of the Elections Bill concerns the machinery and rules governing how elections are conducted.

items.h: Anti-Elections Bill Digital Billboard tours Westminster
items.b: Last week, the Democracy Defence Coalition drove a digital billboard truck around Westminster , if you’d like to use the photos, they are free to use .
items.why: a civic coalition's public campaign against the Elections Bill is an act of civic mobilisation aimed at influencing electoral legislation.
items.note: Campaigning activity classified under participation rather than elections since the mechanism is civic mobilisation, not the bill's content itself.
links: Democracy Defence Coalition drove a digital billboard truck around Westminster

items.h: Lord Wallace of Saltaire’s op-ed against the Elections Bill
items.b: Writing for The Times’ Red Box, Lord Wallace conjures an image (paywall) of where the Elections Bill leads us, further down the ‘Trumpian path’ where elections are neither fair nor free.
items.why: the op-ed argues the Elections Bill threatens the fairness and freeness of UK elections, engaging directly with electoral integrity.
items.note: Treated as elections content despite media format, since the substantive claim concerns electoral fairness.

items.h: Democracy Volunteers to join ENEMO Network
items.b: Democracy Volunteers’ Director Jon Ault has begun talks to join the European Network of Election Monitoring (ENEMO) , an international group focusing on observing elections in central & eastern Europe to ensure the quality of democracy in the region. ENEMO has condemned the invasion of Ukraine , citing attempts to destroy democracy in the country. For more of ENEMO’s work, see their recent report into Ukraine’s 2020 local elections .
items.note: UK organisation's international network membership for monitoring elections abroad does not clearly bear on UK democracy; reads as organisational news.

items.h: Concerns over influence of Conservative Party’s Russian donor links
items.b: According to Labour Party & SNP calculations, the Conservative Party has raised between £1.9m — £2.3m in party donations from Russian oligarchs since 2019. In a 2019 analysis openDemocracy found that the Conservatives had received more than £3.5m from Russian sources since 2010. In 2020, the so-called ‘Russia Report’ by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee expressed concern over the role of Russian money in UK political life. The Foreign Office has responded to recent probing of Tory donors saying it is “wrong and discriminatory to tar them with the same brush”.
items.why: foreign-sourced political donations raise concerns about transparent party financing and undue foreign influence over UK democratic institutions.
items.note: Campaign finance links to foreign powers touches both elections (transparent financing) and accountability (foreign influence).

items.h: Ukrainian Parliament continues to meet despite invasion
items.b: Ukrainian MP Kira Rudik reports from Kyiv that the country’s parliament is partially functioning again and will vote on key matters, including a formal appeal for Ukraine to join the European Union.
items.why: it shows an elected legislature continuing to exercise its constitutional functions and take binding decisions even under existential threat, testing the resilience of democratic institutions.
items.note: International case included as comparative evidence on institutional resilience, not routine war reporting.

items.h: Foreign property owners lose their anonymity through new laws in effort to combat UK’s role as money laundering hub
items.b: Foreign owners of British property will have to disclose their identities for the first time under new legislation designed to crack down on Russian oligarchs laundering their wealth. Transparency International revealed this month that £1.5billion of UK property had been bought since 2016 by Russians accused of corruption or with close links to the Russian government.
items.why: new disclosure requirements curb the ability of foreign actors to use anonymous UK property ownership to exert hidden influence over the political system.

items.h: Open Government Partnership condemns Russian actions
items.b: The Open Government Partnership has condemned the attack on Ukraine , a member of the OGP since 2011.
items.note: An international body's condemnatory statement is not itself a democratic mechanism affecting UK power.

items.h: Votes for Schools developing information pack for school children on Ukraine
items.b: The team at Votes for Schools are developing an informational lesson on the situation in Ukraine. They’re offering the guidance pack to any teachers that would find it useful in their classrooms.
items.note: A classroom information pack on a current event is general education rather than a mechanism of democratic participation.
links: offering the guidance pack to any teachers

items.h: Partygate seemingly swept under the rug amid Ukraine crisis
items.b: Last week the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was questioned by the Metropolitan Police.
items.why: it concerns whether a Prime Minister is held answerable for potential law-breaking, a core test of accountability to the electorate and the law.
links: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

items.h: Democracy comes to NOW PLAY THIS Games Festival
items.b: NOW PLAY THIS is a festival of experimental game design. This year’s festival theme is focused on the relationship between game design and democracy. Whilst submissions for the festival have now closed, The Centre for Democracy has put in a submission for a workshop on group decision making, where we will demonstrate different methods. The submission is currently pending approval.
items.note: A pending festival submission is event/sector promotion, not a confirmed new participation resource.

items.h: Democracy in a Pandemic Book Launch at Newspeak House
items.b: On March 10th at Newspeak House in Central London, Professor Graham Smith , Director of the Centre for the Study of Democracy at the University of Westminster, will be hosting an evening of drinks and talks in partnership with Involve’s Democracy Network to celebrate the launch of the book. Register now on Eventbrite . The book by Tim Hughes and Graham has been released under Open Access , free for you to read.
items.note: Book launch event listing, not itself a change to democratic mechanisms.
links: Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: 50:50 to host International Women’s Day event in Parliament
items.b: On the 8th March, Frances Scott and the 50:50 Parliament team are hosting a special event commemorating International Women’s Day, supported by Lloyds Banking Group. Contact Frances to find out more.
items.note: Event notice/admin rather than a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Democracy Network hosts Democracy Drinks Belfast
items.b: As part of the Imagine festival and as part of Democracy Day, Involve’s Democracy Network will be hosting the first session of Democracy Drinks Belfast on the 25th March. The event will feature lightning talks and an opportunity to network and make connections. Register now for the event in Belfast on Eventbrite.
items.note: Networking event listing, not a democracy story.

items.h: Democracy Network survey, Development Day
items.b: The Big Democracy Network Survey aims to better inform Involve’s Democracy Network team how they can help strengthen organisations across the UK democracy sector. Answer the survey and have your say. On March 21st, Jessie Joe Jacobs and the Democracy Network team will be hosting a full day co-creation workshop. This is your chance to have your say over how the Democracy Network should develop, what it should focus on and how it should engage with the sector. Sign up here to take part, the session will run from 9.30am to 3pm on Zoom.
items.note: Internal organisational survey and development day, not public-facing participation creation.

items.h: Democracy Happens Where You Are
items.b: Inspired by citizens across Kirklees, Diane Sims and Michelle Ross partnered up with Fettle Animation to produce this wonderful video . The video was previewed as part of this weekend’s Notwestminster festival of local democracy.
items.note: Promotional video/event preview, not a created participation mechanism.

items.h: Join Demos and Jon Alexander for the launch his new book, Citizens
items.b: Polly McKenzie, Chief Executive of Demos , and Jon Alexander, the author of the new book Citizens, will be hosting a launch event in Demos’ offices in London on the 17th March. The book explores the rise of the ‘citizen story’ across business, civil society and communities across the UK. Polly will be using the opportunity to reflect on their own Making Democracy Work series. Register now for the breakfast book launch.
items.note: Book launch event listing, organisational news.

items.h: Shared Future CIC jam packed schedule of events coming up
items.b: On the 10th March, the Southwark Climate Change Citizens’ Jury makes its public debut, register for the launch . On the 17th March Shared Future are hosting workshops on youth participation and PB, where they will be launching the Youth PB Accelerator Toolkit, find out more . If that wasn’t enough they’ve also teamed up with DemSoc, Involve and UK100 to design training and guidance for local authority officers on planning, commissioning and delivering high quality climate decision-making. Also, relatedly, check out the Greater Manchester Local Energy Markets Citizens’ Jury being run by Carbon …
items.why: citizens' juries are a deliberative decision-making mechanism and the PB toolkit creates new means for people to take part in budgeting decisions.
items.note: Citizens' juries are filed under elections/decision-making per the deliberation rule; the PB toolkit launch is capacity-building for participation.
links: Greater Manchester Local Energy Markets Citizens’ Jury

items.h: BBC should have a democracy correspondent, argues Joe Mitchell
items.b: With climate news desks quickly becoming a standard for big news companies, democracy desks seem like the next big step — and would be a huge filip for the sector, says Joe Mitchell, Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation. The Washington Post recently launched their own democracy news desk .
items.why: dedicated journalistic coverage of democracy would shape the public information environment through which people understand and scrutinise political power.

items.h: RECLAIM thinking about infrastructure for youth activism space
items.b: Roger Harding, Chief Exec at RECLAIM , is currently thinking about what new infrastructure is needed in the youth activism space. If that sounds like something you’d like to feed in on, get in touch with Roger .
items.note: A call for feedback on possible future infrastructure, not a created resource yet.

items.h: Compassion in Politics enjoy a team weekend
items.b: The team at Compassion in Politics (CiP) spent the weekend together hatching plans and strategies for developing a more inclusive, cooperative and kinder politics in the UK.
items.note: Internal organisational team-building, not a democracy story.

items.h: SMK survey finds recent culture war attacks on charities strengthened their support with the public
items.b: An annual survey of social campaigning by the Sheila McKechnie Foundation has found that many charities feel increasingly emboldened to speak out on contested issues, despite recent attacks. High profile attacks on charities including The National Trust by rightwing politicians backfired, galvanising support for the organisations. The charities were accused of a breach of charity laws, but were cleared of wrongdoing . The National Trust has since reported record numbers of new members.
items.why: the capacity of civil society organisations to speak out on contested political issues without being deterred by political attack is a matter of freedom of association and civic space.
items.note: Freedom of association for civic organisations is filed under rights/civic space per the boundary rule.
links: many charities feel increasingly emboldened to speak out

items.h: mySociety on the anti-corruption benefits of FOI
items.b: Alex Parsons takes note of the exclusion of the new Advanced Research and Invention Agency from FOI and that it’s exclusion and other similar attacks are a part of a broader attack on a key pillar of good governance.
items.why: excluding a public body from Freedom of Information obligations narrows a key mechanism for holding institutions answerable for how they exercise public power.
items.note: FOI framed as accountability mechanism rather than public information environment.

items.h: Does the public have a right to know about potential criminal activity?
items.b: No, says the UK Supreme Court — which has ruled a case against Bloomberg for naming a businessman being investigated for wrongdoings before he had been charged. Commentators have described this as punishment of investigative journalists for tabloid excesses, claiming it “creates a serious risk of legitimate media investigation being suppressed and wrongdoing going unreported”.
items.why: a court ruling limiting the ability to report on suspected wrongdoing before charge constrains investigative journalism's capacity to inform public debate about the exercise of power.
items.note: Court ruling concerns press freedom/information environment rather than adjudication process itself.
links: No, says the UK Supreme Court

items.h: Citizen Network awarded two years funding by Lankelly Chase
items.b: Simon Duffy, President of the Citizen Network, is celebrating the excellent news!
items.note: Organisation's own funding award, excluded per organisational-news rule.

items.h: I Have A Voice secure funding to deliver career training
items.b: IHAV have received funding from The Walcot Foundation to run a free 2 week training programme for 24 trainees to support their efforts to pursue careers related to informing the policymaking process e.g. government affairs, public affairs and research. IHAV have teamed up with a range of employers to provide at least 6 paid internships after the training course, which will run in April. If you know anyone who might benefit, share this link with them.
items.why: it creates a new training and internship pathway to help people build careers in influencing public policymaking, expanding practical means of civic participation
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new participation pathway rather than mere funding news.

items.h: Graham Smith wins a small grant for work to bolster the relationship between democracy sector and academia
items.b: Professor Graham Smith at the Centre for the Study of Democracy at the University of Westminster has won a small grant from the university to co-create guidance on democracy organisations and academics can foster better relationships.

items.h: Blagrave Trust open funding call to support young people with making policy change
items.b: Roger Harding, Chief Exec at Reclaim, reports that Blagrave have recently opened several funding rounds , one of which is now closed, on young people in policy making, and funding youth policy change and campaigning. Worth a look.
links: Blagrave have recently opened several funding rounds

items.h: Check out the New Economy Brief
items.b: Recommended by Jessie Joe Jacobs, this isn’t exactly democracy related, but presents a useful weekly digest of all things economics and levelling up.

items.h: Of By For
items.b: Debuting in 2022, this documentary delivers a bold new vision for democracy in the United States — one without politicians, parties, or campaigns.
