items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Molly Hudson and Max Roche of The Centre for Democracy . Read by 280+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : hello@centrefordemocracy.org.uk

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Carrie Deacon — Senior Advisor at UK Democracy Fund, Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters, Myfanwy Nixon — Communications Manager at mySociety, Sam at Votes for Schools, Trin Gong — Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent, Kyle Taylor — Director at Fair Vote UK, Shaun Roberts — Head of Campaigns & Digital at Unlock Democracy, Oli Whittington — Researcher at Nesta, Peter Keeling — Voting Information at Democracy Club, Perry Walker at Talk Shop, Hannah Stevens — Chief Executive at Elect Her, Oli Walkden …

Remaining committee dates are the 15th and 17th March, with the coalition pushing key amendments — you can view the amendments tabled so far. Kyle Taylor, Director at Fair Vote UK , says the government is getting dangerously close to running out of parliamentary time before prorogation, so a tactic at this stage is to introduce as many amendments as possible and ensure they are all vigorously debated!
items.sec: Democracy Defence Coalition is full speed ahead on Elections Bill, reports Kyle Taylor
items.why: the Elections Bill directly shapes the rules governing electoral administration and competition, and civil society amendments to it affect how those rules are set

items.h: Michael Gove questioned by PACAC, door is open for more types of voter ID
items.b: Dr. Elisabeth Pop highlights Michael Gove’s recent grilling by the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) , which raised the prospect of government being open to more types of voter ID than those currently in the works.
items.sec: Democracy Defence Coalition is full speed ahead on Elections Bill, reports Kyle Taylor
items.why: voter identification requirements directly affect who can practically exercise the franchise, and select committee questioning of the minister is a mechanism holding government to account for that policy
items.note: Primary beat is voter ID as an electoral mechanism; PACAC scrutiny is secondary accountability angle.
links: Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC)

items.h: Online Safety Bill coalition in the works
items.b: Kyle Taylor also reports that the Online Safety Bill (OSB) is building up steam, and with the invasion of Ukraine disinformation and the media lens are back in focus — Fair Vote will be co-steering a coalition around that bill also — stay tuned for more info on that. If you haven’t already, sign this open letter on the Online Safety Bill calling on the Culture Secretary to back a more robust OSB.
items.sec: Democracy Defence Coalition is full speed ahead on Elections Bill, reports Kyle Taylor
items.why: the Online Safety Bill will shape the regulation of disinformation and the public information environment that underpins political debate

items.b: The Policing Bill has been the subject of major political contention in recent weeks. Following attempts by MPs to reinstate a number of measures rejected in the House of Lords, the bill is now in ping-pong. For more analysis of the bill and its implications on democratic rights, check out the following blog from the Network for Police Monitoring (Netpol) — Resisting the Police Bill.
items.sec: Policing Bill moves into parliamentary ping pong
items.why: the Policing Bill concerns legal restrictions on protest and assembly, directly affecting citizens' capacity to organise and dissent
items.note: Protest story framed around legal restriction and policing, not willingness to participate, so filed under rights rather than participation.

items.h: UK faith leaders ask the government to rethink ‘discriminatory’ borders bill
items.b: Over 1000 faith leaders from across the UK have asked the government to amend the proposals laid out in the Police and Borders Bill. The government has already been criticised for a lacklustre approach to the Ukrainian refugee crisis, and faith leaders are now warning that those arriving via irregular routes to the UK could be criminalised rather than protected. The Bill is currently in the report stage in the House of Lords.
items.why: proposals to criminalise people based on their route of arrival raise questions of equal treatment and discrimination under public power
items.note: Treated as an equal-protection/discrimination rights story rather than an electoral or accountability matter.

items.h: Titus Alexander is working to encourage and support Russians seeking independent news resources
items.b: They are using all manner of ways to evade the Russian media lockdown and censorship, from posting questions to Google Maps reviews, to emailing schools, businesses etc and encouraging others to reach out any way they can. For more information see this Google Doc .
items.note: Concerns Russian citizens' access to information rather than UK democracy, so falls outside the UK-focused scope.

items.h: MPs push through Economic Crime Bill to intensify sanctions on Russian oligarchs
items.b: Economic sanctions facing Russian oligarchs are set to intensify following the fast-tracked Economic Crime Bil l that passed its third reading late Monday night. The long-awaited bill will allow the government to more rapidly sanction Russian oligarchs and firms by allowing them to automatically sanction anyone who has had assets frozen by the EU, US or Canada. The bill now passes to the House of Lords.
items.why: This matters democratically because it restricts the ability of sanctioned oligarchs and foreign-linked wealth to exert undue influence over UK political and economic institutions, a core accountability safeguard.

items.h: War in Ukraine highlights need for democratic unity to combat kleptocracy
items.b: Oliver Bullough has launched a working paper for the International Forum For Democratic Studies warning of the threat posed by transnational kleptocracy. In their paper: ‘An Offshore Cold War: Forging a Democratic Alliance to Combat Transnational Kleptocracy’ , they suggest we need greater collaboration amongst democracies to tackle the networked nature of transnational kleptocracy.
items.why: This matters democratically because unchecked transnational kleptocracy allows powerful private and foreign interests to distort accountability and undermine the integrity of democratic institutions, including in the UK.
links: ‘An Offshore Cold War: Forging a Democratic Alliance to Combat Transnational Kleptocracy’

items.h: National Endowment for Democracy (NED) funds volunteer action in Ukraine
items.b: A wave of volunteers has mobilised in Ukraine in response to the Russian invasion. The Ukrainian Volunteer Service (UVS) has been connecting activists across the country since 2017 and promoting opportunities for democratic community engagement. Within days of the outbreak of war, UVS had “200,000 caring people ready to help and connect”.
items.note: This concerns Ukrainian civic mobilisation with no bearing on UK democracy and is not comparative evidence about it.

items.h: Russian visits to BBC news increase by 225%
items.b: The BBC Russian news website has seen a surge in use following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Given the state’s regulation of information and heavy-handed propaganda, increasing numbers have looked to the BBC for more impartial reporting. BBC director-general Tim Davie commented saying “we will continue giving the Russian people access to the truth, however we can.”
items.note: Concerns Russian audiences' access to alternative information rather than the UK's own information environment.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund looking to fund ideas around broadening electoral participation
items.b: Carrie Deacon , Senior Advisor at the UK Democracy Fund , is eager to get in touch with people working on ideas to grow the number registered and participating in the next General Election, particularly those who don’t currently participate in elections. The Fund has recently released its funding priorities in a Funding Framework , alongside their next three funding deadlines, on the 16th May, 22nd August and 31st October 2022. If you think you have an idea that could help the Fund reach their goal of one million more voters taking part in the next election, get in touch with Carrie.
items.why: This matters democratically because expanding voter registration and turnout among underrepresented groups strengthens the inclusiveness and legitimacy of elections.
items.note: Turnout-related participation is classified under elections per the framework's standing rule.

items.h: Democracy Classroom kicks off new Election Countdown programme
items.b: Starting this week, Harriet Andrews and the team at Democracy Classroom are releasing resources week by week up until the election. To access these resources sign up for their weekly updates — don’t miss out!
items.why: This matters democratically because providing schools with ongoing resources ahead of the election builds young people's capacity and motivation to engage in civic and political life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of civic engagement rather than a turnout mechanism itself.
links: sign up for their weekly updates

items.h: What’s up for election in 2022, Democracy Club asks
items.b: Peter Keeling and the team at Democracy Club have counted all the seats up for grabs this May. They’re also recording all hustings events, which will be promoted on WhoCanIVoteFor . If you’re running an event, or know of one, report it to DC via this form .
items.why: This matters democratically because tracking which seats are contested and where hustings occur helps ensure voters can access the information needed to engage in electoral competition.

items.h: Elect Her preparing election toolkit
items.b: Hannah Stevens , Chief Executive at Elect Her , and the team, are designing a toolkit for women to support local candidates, engage in hustings and GOTV. They’re also supporting more than 50 women candidates with peer support, skills training and advice.
items.why: This matters democratically because supporting women's candidacies addresses the representativeness of elected institutions, a core measure of fair political competition.

items.h: Celebrate our first anniversary with a Democracy Co-Working Day!
items.b: It’s been over one year since we launched the Centre for Democracy . In that year we’ve held more than thirty meetups and published as many of these Bulletins. Now physical events are a real possibility, we’d like to celebrate by inviting you to a day of co-working together with other democracy folks at Newspeak House in East London. If you’d like to join, please register here to give us an idea of numbers — looking forward to seeing you there!
items.note: This is organisational anniversary and event admin, explicitly excluded even though the organisation works on democracy.

items.h: Centre for Democracy welcomes new Research Assistant Max Roche to the team
items.b: Max joined the team last week and will be helping to compose future bulletins (including this one!) alongside James Moulding and Molly Hudson. Welcome Max!

items.h: Big changes at mySociety
items.b: mySociety appoints interim Chief Executive, Louise Crow, following news that Chief Executive Mark Cridge is soon to move on. Having led the organisation for more than seven years, Mark Cridge has played a key role in it’s recent successes. We wish Mark every success in their future adventures. This now means that mySociety is a women-led and woman-majority organisation for the first time in its history.
items.note: Staff/leadership change at an organisation is org admin, not a democracy story even when framed as a milestone for gender representation.

items.h: Act Build Change publish guidance on hybrid organising
items.b: As COVID-19 restrictions continue to ease, vulnerable and cautious members of the community may feel themselves locked out of events. As a result many groups are turning to hybrid events as a halfway-house solution. Act Build Change have published a series of reflections on how to plan, prepare and deliver a hybrid event following their first community meet-up. Relatedly, the campaign #KeepFestivalsHybrid is seeking to ensure that events continue to consider remote accessibility for disabled and vulnerable people.
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates practical guidance that helps disabled and vulnerable people continue to take part in community and civic events despite pandemic-era barriers.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation.

items.h: Compass are looking for Board Members
items.b: Compass are seeking Board Members to join them from Spring 2022. Board Members will be in charge of overseeing the legal, financial and strategic direction of the organisation and supporting their efforts to shape a more democratic society. Check out the job listing for more information.
items.note: Board recruitment is organisational admin.

items.h: Activate to announce winners of grants for women in politics
items.b: This spring Activate will give out two grants supporting women’s engagement in politics. Teaming up with Elect Her through their Equip Her partnership , the first grant covers the personal and campaigning costs for political candidates preparing themselves for the elections in May. The second funding scheme helps women activists tackle issues in their local area. Activate are in the final stages of awarding the grants so be sure to follow them on Twitter for updates on who’s won.
items.why: This matters democratically because the grants fund women's political candidacy and local activism, expanding who has the practical resources to take part in electoral and civic life.
items.note: Capacity-building funding scheme counted as participation_civic_life even though tied to candidates for elections.

items.h: Join Unlock Democracy for an event recalling the Great Reform Act
items.b: This Wednesday 16th March Shaun Roberts and the team at Unlock Democracy will be joined in conversation by Nan Sloane, the author of Uncontrollable Women . Together they’ll be discussing the importance of the Great Reform Act of 1932 and what we can learn from it. Register your ticket here .
items.note: Event listing/talk announcement, not a new resource or mechanism.

items.h: Votes for Schools hosting 2022 Student Voice Awards in April
items.b: You can find out more about the awards on their website , or contact lizzy@votesforschools.com .
items.note: Awards event listing/promotion.

items.h: Grab your early bird ticket now for RADIX Big Tent Ideas Festival, Bristol June 11th
items.b: Big Tent Ideas are back! Well known for their annual festivals composed of rich discussions and workshops involving those from across the UK political spectrum, they’ve been on pause since the pandemic hit and have now teamed up with think tank Radix. For a taster of their events, they’ve got an event on the Northern Ireland Protocol coming up later this month. Register now for your Big Tent Ideas Festival early bird ticket .
items.note: Ticket sales/event promotion.
links: event on the Northern Ireland Protocol

items.h: Liberty publishes free guide ‘I Know My Rights’
items.b: According to Liberty , the government’s new Bill of Rights will water down the rights of British citizens. In response they have published a free guide outlining our fundamental rights as citizens.
items.why: This matters democratically because the guide helps citizens understand and exercise their legal rights at a moment when a proposed Bill of Rights may narrow those protections.
items.note: Sector capacity-building resource rule applied, though content concerns rights rather than participation mechanics.

items.h: Newspeak House hosts event on digital tools for public participation
items.b: Newspeak House, the London College of Political Technology, is hosting an event on digital participation on March 30th. The evening will include a series of short talks from Colin Megill, Co-founder of Pol.is , Sarah Castell, CEO at Involve , Oliver Whittington, Researcher at Nesta , Simon Parker, Director of Transformation and Policy Capability at the Department for Education , and Akshaya Satheesh, Developer at the Centre for Analysis of Social Media at Demos . Be sure to register for what promises to be a fascinating series of talks and a great opportunity to network with others working in …
items.note: Event listing discussing participation tools, not itself a new tool or resource created.

items.h: Nesta event explores reimagining democracy and our role as citizens
items.b: Topping off the month, Nesta have organised a conversation between Claudia Chwalisz, Innovation Citizen Participation Lead at the OECD , and Jon Alexander, Co-Founder of the New Citizenship Project and author of Citizens . The event will explore the emergence of the ‘citizen narrative’, alongside innovative participatory and deliberatory methods, and how these are changing the way we respond to challenges — and the multiple compounding crises we now face. Register your free ticket for the lunch time event.
items.note: Event listing/discussion, not a new participation resource or reported change.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society report urges greater devolution in England
items.b: England continues to typify a ‘Westminster knows best approach’ to national governance putting it at odds with much of the rest of Europe. This heavy centralisation also goes against the steady devolution of power seen across the UK over the last two decades. In a new report titled Democracy Made in England , the Electoral Reform Society sets out proposals for how to strengthen local democracy as well as a framework for how power could be decentralised.
items.why: it proposes restructuring how power is decentralised to local and regional government, directly bearing on the machinery of sub-national decision-making
items.note: Devolution/local government structure is classified under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: Green New Deal UK launch their Rising Leadership Programme
items.b: Green New Deal UK has opened applications for their Rising Leadership Programme which is a fully-funded 6-month training programme for 40 people aged 18–30. The initiative is a chance to gain vital campaigning skills and will set the foundation for a new generation of climate leaders.
items.why: it creates a new funded programme building young people's capacity to campaign and take part in political life
items.note: Sector capacity-building counts as a participation story under the framework's carve-out.

items.h: Young Citizens running their Big Legal Lesson, panel event on legal education
items.b: Every year, Young Citizens , a charity specialising in the delivery of citizenship programmes and designing teaching resources for primary and secondary schools, runs their Big Legal Lesson . The Big Legal Lesson is their hallmark campaign to get teachers delivering at least one lesson on the law and rights. On the 17th, they’ve also organised a panel event on the importance of legal education in schools, with I. Stephanie Boyce, President of the Law Society and other legal experts.
items.why: it builds civic and legal literacy among young people, a resource intended to support future democratic participation
items.note: Recurring annual campaign; borderline against event-listing exclusion but treated as capacity-building resource.

items.h: Call out for participation in project on climate citizen assemblies
items.b: Knowledge Network on Climate Assemblies (KNOCA) are looking to create more knowledge and guidance on how we can implement climate citizens assemblies. They have commissioned four ‘Knowledge Development Projects’ and are looking for input from organisations or individuals that want to take part in producing knowledge on this topic.
items.note: A call for participants/input into a knowledge project, closer to a sector call-out than a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Renew teams up with Gina Miller’s True and Fair Party
items.b: Renew has teamed up with Gina Miller’s True and Fair Party to combat what they see as our ‘increasingly corrupt’ and ‘outmoded’ political system. They will be focussing on cleaning up politics and arguing the case for proportional representation.
items.why: a new political alliance forming around electoral reform and party competition affects the plurality and prospects of political parties
items.note: Political party alliance falls under elections & decision making per the free-political-parties anchor.
links: Renew has teamed up with Gina Miller’s True and Fair Party

items.h: IMPRESS appoints Richard Ayre as new Chair
items.b: Richard Ayre will become the new Chair of IMPRESS . They take over from Walter Merricks CBE, who has led the IMPRESS board for the last seven years since its creation.
items.note: Organisational appointment news, explicitly excluded.

items.h: Byline Festival returns 29th April — 1st May in London
items.b: Byline Festival is back in April to host what promises to be an exciting set of panel discussions with investigative journalists, whistleblowers, authors, specialists and first-person voices. Topics will cover everything including current affairs, rights and equality, the culture wars, the climate crisis and more.
items.note: Event listing for a journalism festival, not itself a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation Report suggests campaigning climate becoming increasingly hostile
items.b: The Sheila McKechnie Foundation (SMK) have published their annual temperature check on the state of UK campaigning and the results make for grim reading. Their survey of 118 national campaigners found that 79% said attitudes from politicians towards civil society campaigning had become more negative over the last year — up from 63% in 2020.
items.why: deteriorating political attitudes toward civil society campaigning signal a narrowing operating space for civic organisations to organise and criticise power

items.h: Parliament websites activate bot-protection measures causing issues for civic tech activists
items.b: Matthew Somerville at mySociety notes that with Parliament adding Cloudflare technology to their websites, it makes it that much harder for web scrapers to extract vital information from parliamentary sites. If you’re having trouble accessing the Register of Members’ Financial Interests and other sites, see Matt’s short blog on the issue .
items.why: new technical barriers restrict civic tech access to parliamentary transparency data such as the Register of Members' Financial Interests, weakening a mechanism for holding officials answerable
items.note: Framed as institutional access to accountability data rather than the broader media information environment.

items.h: Health and Care Bill prompts fears over lack of scrutiny, campaigners say
items.b: A coalition of organisations including Reboot GB, EveryDoctor, Open Britain and Nurses United have penned an open letter to parliamentarians outlining why the Health and Care Bill represents a threat to public health institutions. They claim the bill, if passed unamended, would give ministers unprecedented power to control the direction of the healthcare system with reduced scrutiny.
items.why: it concerns delegated powers being expanded with reduced parliamentary and public scrutiny over executive control of health institutions.

items.h: Words to Win
items.b: Are you interested in all things election turnout? Shaun Roberts of Unlock Democracy recommends this podcast episode on how the Democrats nabbed Georgia in 2020.
items.note: A podcast recommendation link is sector content, not a reported democracy event.

items.h: Climate activism to reach fever pitch in coming months
items.b: Hot on the heels of Insulate Britain, Just Stop Oil — a new direct action movement rumoured to be blockading oil refineries across the UK, are readying themselves for their debut direct action in the first few weeks of April. Following that, Extinction Rebellion’s latest Rebellion will kick off hot on their heels. Just in time for a new coalition of climate orgs, led by Zero Hour — to mark the third anniversary since Parliament declared a climate emergency, calling on the government to accelerate their efforts at decarbonisation.
items.why: it reports on people's readiness to organise and take direct action to influence government policy, a form of civic participation.
items.note: Framed as willingness to demonstrate rather than policing or legal restriction, so classed under participation not rights.

items.h: Sign the Centre for Democracy’s Ecosystem Pledge
items.b: With one year since we launched the Centre for Democracy , it is one year since we launched the Ecosystem Pledge, now backed by 69 signatory organisations, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more. If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email p…
items.note: This is inter-organisational networking among democracy groups rather than a new means of public participation.

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Myf Nixon — Comms Manager at mySociety, James Clarke — Head of Outreach at True & Fair, Katy Rubin — Legislative Theatre Practitioner, Trin Gong — Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent, Matt Hawkins — Compassion in Politics, Roland Storti — Founder & CEO at Minfo UK, Jessie Joe Jacobs — Coordinator at Democracy Network, Josh Russell — Forward Democracy, Ciaran Cummins — Researcher at Demos, Will Snell — Chief Executive at Fairness Foundation, Grace Barnett — Unlock Democracy, Sam Welsh — Partnerships…

items.h: New coalition forms around the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Kyle Taylor, Matt Gallagher and the Fair Vote UK team are busy pulling together a new coalition on the Online Safety Bill (OSB) . The OSB coalition will differ from previous work on the Elections Bill. By comparison the Elections Bill is relatively straightforward, whilst the OSB is a much broader and more nuanced piece of legislation, where organisations across the UK democracy space may agree or disagree on certain aspects. However, Kyle and the team suggest working on where collaboration is possible, developing a conceptual space to boost overall campaigning on the OSB and share collective …
items.why: the Online Safety Bill will shape rules governing free expression, content moderation and the online information environment that underpins public debate
items.note: Coalition-building is sector coordination, but the underlying legislation concerns the information environment.
links: sign up via this Google Form

items.h: OSB Coalition makes recommendations to Secretary of State
items.b: A coalition of organisations have written to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Secretary, Rt Hon Nadine Dorries MP urging that the Online Safety Bill protects free speech, tackles the true drivers of online harm, and ensures transparency in digital regulation. If you want to be part of this initiative, fill in this Google form.
items.why: the recommendations concern how the Online Safety Bill will balance free speech, online harms and transparency in digital regulation, shaping the public information environment

items.h: Democracy Defence Coalition sends briefing to non-Conservative peers ahead of report stage
items.b: With the Election Bill’s report stage coming up, the Democracy Defence Coalition is sending this briefing out to peers today. The aim here is to bring everyone together to support the peers briefings and shut down the government on key areas of the Bill, as happened with the Police Bill. In other news, the Government has conceded Clauses 25 and 27 relating to 3rd party campaigning.
items.why: the Elections Bill's rules on third-party campaigning determine who can participate in and fund election campaigning, and the government's concession changes those rules

items.h: Share Unlock Democracy & Shout Out UK’s new video
items.b: The new video fact checks the government’s claims that photo ID will make our elections fairer and more secure. Can your organisation share the video and help push back on photo ID?
items.why: voter ID requirements affect who can practically exercise their right to vote and the integrity/accessibility of elections

items.h: Good summary of Nationality and Borders Bill from Refugee Action
items.b: Refugee Action have tweeted a summary of the Nationality and Borders Bill that is well worth reading, complete with its implications for asylum seekers. Refugee Action recently published a new report, All Punishment, No Protection , on how the proposed changes could impact asylum claims in the UK.
items.note: Concerns immigration/asylum policy for non-citizens rather than a mechanism of UK democratic power.

items.h: Full Fact express concerns over Online Safety Bill
items.b: The government introduced the Online Safety Bill to Parliament on Thursday 17th March. The bill will usher in a number of new laws designed to protect the public from harmful online information. Full Fact have raised a number of concerns however, criticising what they see as its failure to “tackle harmful misinformation and protect freedom of expression”.
items.why: regulation of online misinformation and expression shapes the public information environment citizens rely on for political debate

items.h: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) speak out against the Nationality and Borders Bill
items.b: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have condemned the Commons vote on the Nationality and Borders Bill on Tuesday 24th as “shameful” after just four Conservative MPs voted against the government. They suggest that if the bill passes, the UK will become “one of the most anti-refugee countries in the world” .
items.note: Concerns treatment of asylum seekers rather than a UK democratic mechanism.
links: “one of the most anti-refugee countries in the world”

items.h: Scale of humanitarian catastrophe laid bare in recent weeks
items.b: European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backs a new EU probe into reported Russian war crimes in Ukraine. The EU is understood to be sending Eurojust investigation teams on the ground to support the Ukrainian Prosecution Services. The International Court of Justice launched an investigation late February into the war in Ukraine, and countries around the EU backed the ICJ probe. Russia has denied accusations of war crimes.
items.note: International war crimes investigation does not bear on UK democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Global protests mark one month since Ukraine invasion
items.b: President Volodymyr Zelensky called for a worldwide show of support to mark one month since Russia invaded Ukraine, and the world answered. Hundreds of thousands turned out in London on the 26th March, with similar scenes in cities around the world.
items.why: mass turnout at demonstrations reflects people's willingness to take part in political and civic life
items.note: Protest framed as willingness to participate rather than as legal restriction, so filed under participation not rights.

items.h: Ukrainian activists circumvent Russian information embargo
items.b: Activists and campaigners in Ukraine are attempting to break Russia’s tight regulation of information by using ‘pop-up’ notifications and Facebook ads to tell the real story of the invasion to ordinary Russian citizens. With international press organisations like the BBC banned from operating in Russia , these activists are attempting to keep access to information open in whatever form possible.
items.note: Concerns Russia's information environment, not UK democracy or comparative evidence about it.
links: BBC banned from operating in Russia

items.h: Economic Crime Bill gains Royal Assent
items.b: The new Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act received Royal Assent on Tuesday 15th March ushering in new laws allowing quicker and more readily available sanctions to combat Russian oligarchs and the flow of ‘dirty money’ around the UK economy. The government has also established a new ‘Kleptocracy Unit’ to investigate assets belonging to Russian President Vladimir Putin in London.
items.why: new sanctions and anti-corruption powers curb undue influence by foreign actors and illicit money over UK political and economic life
links: government has also established a new ‘Kleptocracy Unit’

items.h: It’s SOPN Day! Can you help Democracy Club record all the candidates in their database?
items.b: Candidate lists are being released today, check out Democracy Club’s Twitter for info on how you can help! Democracy Club are also recording all hustings events across the UK, which will be promoted on WhoCanIVoteFor . If you’re running an event, or know of one, report it to DC via this form . Likewise, if you’ve seen an election leaflet, upload it here .
items.why: transparent, publicly-tracked candidate nomination processes underpin the credibility and administration of elections
items.note: Crowdsourcing candidate data is election administration capacity-building.

items.h: Back the pledge on political advertising
items.b: Reform Political Advertising and Compassion in Politics have teamed up for an election pledge this year on ‘ensuring that claims made in political adverts are fact-checked, reliable and traceable’, and for campaigners to seek to improve the conduct of our politics. If your organisation would like to back the pledge, please contact Matt Hawkins at Compassion in Politics.
items.why: fact-checked and traceable political advertising affects the reliability of information voters encounter during campaigns
items.note: Political advertising integrity sits within the information environment per framework anchors.

items.h: Labour press government to stop expatriates donating to political parties and voting in elections
items.b: The Labour Party continues to oppose the Election Bill. The bill currently includes proposals to make it easier for expatriates that were born in the UK but that have lived abroad for most of their lives to donate to political parties and vote in UK elections. Labour opposes what they see as the exposure of the electoral system to outside influence, citing recent allegations of Tory party links to Russian funds as a key example of the overseas financialisation of British politics.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns who can vote and donate in UK elections, touching franchise and campaign finance safeguards.
links: allegations of Tory party links to Russian funds

items.h: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Bill receives Royal Assent
items.b: The Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Bill received Royal Assent on the 24th of March. The new legislation overturns the 2011 Fixed Term Parliamentary Act meaning the Prime Minister will once again be able to call an early election at a time of their choosing. The power this brings to the executive and ruling party has been met with concern by some.
items.why: this matters democratically because it changes the executive's power to call elections, affecting the balance between government and legislature.
links: Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Bill

items.h: Gina Miller launches new political party
items.b: True & Fair is a new political party led by Gina Miller arguing for a ‘radical modernising’ of the machinery of government, a ‘cleaning up’ of our politics and a ‘multidimensional’ approach to policymaking. You can watch Gina’s launch speech on YouTube.
items.why: this matters democratically because it expands political competition through the creation of a new party contesting for votes and representation.

items.h: Orbán election win sets stage for more EU battles on democracy
items.b: Hungarian conservative nationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has won a fourth consecutive term in elections this weekend. More than 53% of Hungarians voted in favour of Fidesz in the national list, according to the results, with the Orbán’s party taking 88 of 106 available voting districts across the country. With reports of bussing voters and election fraud rampant in the country, the results portend a continuation of Fidesz’s policies to undermine democratic norms in the country.
items.why: this matters democratically because it provides comparative evidence of electoral integrity and fraud concerns bearing on wider debates about democratic backsliding relevant to UK democracy discourse.
items.note: International item included as comparative evidence on electoral integrity and democratic norms, per scope rules.

items.h: Democracy Network host development workshop
items.b: Last month more than 40 people from as many organisations came together to help chart a course for the fledgling network, trying to answer questions around purpose, structure and networking approaches. You can find Jessie Joe Jacob’s follow up Interim Report in our Dropbox here .
items.note: Reports on the network's own internal organisational development rather than a new means of public participation.

items.h: Pilar Girvan joins the Democracy Network team!
items.b: Joining Involve’s Democracy Network as an Advocacy & Communications Officer, Pilar will be primarily involved in the development of the Democracy Network.
items.note: Staff appointment/org admin, not a democracy story.

items.h: Call out for Democracy Research Collaboration Guide
items.b: George Bolton , Centre for Democracy, and Graham Smith , Centre for the Study of Democracy, invite democracy orgs to take part in a new project recently funded by the University of Westminster. The project involves co-producing a Democracy Research Collaboration Guide, aimed at facilitating a better working relationship between academics and practitioners across the democracy sector. The project involves two core stages, interviewing to explore the problems and challenges, and then two workshops with participants to co-produce the Guide, based on insights from the interviews. If you’ve previou…
items.note: Sector research collaboration project among academics/practitioners, not public-facing participation mechanism.

items.h: Centre for Democracy’s Co-Working Day goes down a treat
items.b: What a fantastic day! Thank you to everyone that joined us over the course of the day in central London to celebrate the Centre for Democracy’s first anniversary. Some even joined us from as far away as Land’s End and Peterborough. So much fun and so many great discussions & connections, we may have to organise another! Check out the pictures!
items.note: Anniversary/social event write-up, org admin.

items.h: Onward and Create Streets to hold conference on strengthening democracy and community building
items.b: Onward and Create Streets are set to hold Restitch: The Social Fabric Summit . The conference will be in London on May 24th and Halifax on May 27th and will explore themes of how to rebuild our communities in the face of the increasing polarisation of politics and society. Check out the event page and sign up for an important discussion on how we can rebuild society from the ground up.
items.note: Event listing/conference announcement, not a created participation mechanism.

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation Report encourages new way of thinking about power and social change
items.b: A new report, It’s All About Power , from the Sheila McKechnie Foundation offers a new way to think about power within social movements and how we can create more equitable partnerships with groups with lived experience. Join SMK for a participatory workshop on the 19th of April to discuss how to put these principles into practice and create more effective forms of solidarity.
items.note: Report and workshop about power dynamics in social movements; 'power' is a cross-cutting lens, not a beat.
links: participatory workshop on the 19th of April

items.h: E-campaigning forum resumes in Oxford
items.b: The annual event of the Electronic Campaigning Forum (ECF) community of campaigners, fundraisers and basically everyone involved in campaigning — is this week on this week on the 5–7th April. It’s not too late to join, with many events and activities online. They also host an excellent jobs board and community forum .
items.note: Event/community forum listing for campaigners, sector logistics.

items.h: Westminster Foundation for Democracy host first-ever conference on Environmental Democracy
items.b: Westminster Foundation for Democracy held their first environment conference 29–31st of March discussing environmental democracy in the context of the rising tides of authoritarian politics and climate change. Check them out on Twitter for updates on what will have been a fascinating event.
items.note: Conference announcement/event listing.

items.h: Reflecting on Legislative Theatre
items.b: Katy Rubin , Legislative Theatre (LT) practitioner, and Charlotte Bamford, LT co-facilitator of the Glasgow Youth-Led Climate Crisis Legislative Theatre , wrote an article for The Forge — a US based journal on community organising. The piece considers the challenges and opportunities of engaging in creative participatory democracy in partnership with local government. The Manchester Meteor also recently wrote a piece on the outcomes of the 2020/2021 LT project focused on homelessness.
items.note: Reflective article on a past participatory project, not a newly created participation mechanism.
links: Glasgow Youth-Led Climate Crisis Legislative Theatre

items.h: Big Tent Ideas Festival headed to Bristol
items.b: Marked for the 10th & 11th of June, the public Bristol festival will focus on the future of the media, regeneration and net zero. There will also be an invite-only event, the Big Tent Summit, focused on city-led regeneration. If you’d like more information or an invite, contact Georgie at Big Tent.
items.note: Festival/event listing.

items.h: Rebecca Deegan considers political literacy metrics and evaluation
items.b: I Have A Voice’s Founder, Rebecca Deegan , is currently pondering measures, or a measure, of political literacy, and is plotting a roundtable on it this summer. If this sounds like something you’d like to chime in on, pop them a message .
items.note: Individual pondering metrics and planning a roundtable; no resource or mechanism yet created.

items.h: Demos on the Great British Inbox and upcoming Future of Activism report
items.b: Having conducted dozens of interviews with activists across the spectrum, Ciaran Cummins , Researcher at Demos , is in the final stages of polishing off their new report on the impact of covid upon activism and the challenges of new pressures and intensifying crisis on activists. But whilst you’re waiting for that to slide into your inboxes, here’s a blog post by Ciaran on the Great British Inbox aka Jacob Rees-Mogg’s strategy for public participation — and no, he isn’t making this up.
items.note: Sector research/blog announcement, not a new participation tool or reported change.

items.h: Fairness Foundation identify democracy as key focus issue of fairness in UK
items.b: Will Snell , Chief Executive of the Fairness Foundation (FF), is currently designing an annual UK ‘fairness index’ that will use external indicators to summarise the state of the nation in relation to FF’s five ‘fair necessities’ , with democracy emergies as a key focus issue for fairness.
items.note: Announcement of an in-progress index/report rather than a mechanism affecting democratic power.

items.h: DemSoc outline their Theory of Change for improving democracy
items.b: DemSoc have published their Theory for Change report highlighting the changing nature of democracy as well as their own ambitions for promoting change. The report outlines the need to build a ‘networked democracy’ in response to an increasingly digitised and globalised world.
items.note: Publication of an organisation's internal strategy document, not a participation mechanism.

items.h: Act Build Change hold online event on accountability in organising
items.b: Act Build Change held an online community meetup last week on the topic of accountability. Led by Alex Johnston of Transforming Together , the event explored the role and value of accountability in organising, as well as the tools available to implement proper community accountability. Follow them on Twitter for updates on future sessions.
items.note: One-off event recap, sector logistics rather than a new lasting participation resource.

items.h: UK “driving a world-leading project on trust in democracy”
items.b: Joe Mitchell , Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation, questions the sincerity of the UK Government’s statement of commitments to the US Summit for Democracy…
items.why: this matters democratically because it scrutinises whether the UK government's public commitments to democratic standards are genuine, bearing on accountability and public confidence in government.

items.h: KNOCA to hold introductory talk on Climate Assemblies
items.b: Knowledge Network on Climate Assemblies (KNOCA) are holding an introductory talk on April 20th exploring the key features of climate assemblies. The event will provide a great opportunity for anyone curious about democratic solutions to the climate crisis to come and ask questions and explore the potential of this model. Bjørn Bedsted, organiser of the Danish Climate Assembly , will host the event.
items.note: Event listing explaining a deliberative model rather than launching a new mechanism.

items.h: Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform discuss routes to proportional representation
items.b: Earlier this month Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform (LDER) held an online cross party session on the routes to proportional representation. The session was chaired by Unlock Democracy chief Tom Brake and you can catch the online recording on YouTube if you missed it.
items.note: Recap of a past discussion event on electoral reform, sector logistics rather than a reported change.

items.h: Local Trust launch new Podcast — The Community Power
items.b: Local Trust have teamed up with the Community Wealth Fund to produce a new podcast on the power of community organising . The podcast explores the potential behind giving people on the ground the power, resources and financial opportunities to bring about change on their patch.
items.why: this matters democratically because launching a new podcast platform aimed at building community organising capacity creates a new means for people to engage in civic life.
items.note: Counted under sector capacity-building rule as a new resource/platform for participation.
links: new podcast on the power of community organising

items.h: Founders of New Citizenship Project to discuss new book ‘Citizens’
items.b: Sheila McKechnie Foundation will host an online conversation with Jon Alexander and Irenie Ekkeshis to discuss the publication of their new book Citizens: Why the Key to Fixing Everything Is All of Us. Join in on April 27th for a deep dive into the ideas behind the book.
items.note: Event listing for a book discussion, not a new participation mechanism.
links: Citizens: Why the Key to Fixing Everything Is All of Us.

items.h: Largest annual politics festival returns to Yorkshire
items.b: The Festival of Debate returns to South Yorkshire this year with speakers including Jeremy Corbyn, George Monbiot, and the unmissable, Jackie Weaver. Events run from April to June so be sure to check out the event schedule and take your pick.
items.note: Festival event listing, sector logistics.

items.h: Anglia Ruskin University to hold event on ‘the wisdom of the crowd’
items.b: Join philosopher Henrik Schoeneberg for an in-person event in Cambridge on the roots of collective consciousness and the ‘wisdom of the crowd’. Can these ancient dynamics be applied to help build resilience in our modern democratic institutions? Get over to Cambridge to find out.
items.note: Academic event listing, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Hope Not Hate Report highlights lack of faith in UK democracy and political establishment
items.b: Hope Not Hate have published their annual State of Hate report which has found that over half of the population (57%) are not satisfied with the way democracy works in the UK and 44% think our political system needs major changes. The report also expresses fears that ‘Partygate’ and a number of bills currently passing through parliament will intensify this mistrust.
items.why: public dissatisfaction with how democracy works and low confidence in the political system reflects the health of popular support for democratic institutions.

items.h: UK Constitution Monitoring Group report warns of insufficient checks and balances on ministerial power
items.b: The biannual report from The Constitution Society was published last month raising concerns about the expanding power of the UK executive. The report suggests that the impending bills on the regulation of elections , the right to protest and the treatment of refugees would all ‘enhance the discretion of the UK executive in troublesome ways’.
items.why: the report warns that expanding executive discretion is eroding the checks and balances that constrain ministerial power.

items.h: Ian Lucas, former MP for Wrexham, publishes new book on the breakdown of democracy
items.b: Ian Lucas has recently published a new book, Digital Gangsters , in which they explore the breakdown of democracy in the context of the emerging ‘information war’. Lucas, a key figure in the investigation into the Cambridge Analytica scandal , tells the story of how the unbridled power of social media and harvesting of online data has reshaped and undermined the democratic process.
items.why: the book argues that social media data harvesting and information warfare have undermined the public information environment that underpins democratic choice.

items.h: Big Brother Watch release documentary on the rise of the ‘UK surveillance state’
items.b: A new documentary Pandemic Police State: The Rise of Authoritarianism in the UK from Big Brother Watch tracks what they see as the emergence of a surveillance state within the UK state apparatus. The documentary explores the new terrain of civil liberties that have emerged following an era of ‘coronavirus law-making’.
items.why: the documentary examines expanded state surveillance and civil liberties restrictions introduced under emergency law-making.
links: Pandemic Police State: The Rise of Authoritarianism in the UK

items.h: Democracy Made In England, new report from ERS
items.b: The Electoral Reform Society’s latest report on devolution charts why England lacks so far behind Scotland and Wales when it comes to devolution of power away from Westminster and electoral reform. The paper asks what now can be done for democracy in England , and why is the need now so acute?
items.why: the report addresses the structure and extent of devolved decision-making power in England compared to other UK nations.
items.note: Devolution structure is classified under elections & decision making per framework rule.
links: what now can be done for democracy in England

items.h: Localis question whether ‘Levelling-up’ will initiate a meaningful devolution of power
items.b: Localis have published their response to the government’s Levelling Up White Paper . In the report, The Medici Code — The Levelling UP White Paper: Reflections and Responses, visiting fellow at Localis, Professor Colin Corpus , suggests the government’s levelling up strategy will amount to a ‘decentralisation of a range functions’ rather than a meaningful devolution of power.
items.why: the report questions whether the government's levelling up policy genuinely devolves decision-making power to local tiers of government.
items.note: Devolution structure and powers fall under elections & decision making.
links: The Medici Code — The Levelling UP White Paper: Reflections and Responses,

items.h: New publication from LGiU explores representation in local government
items.b: The Local Government Information Unit have been exploring representation in local government amongst ethnic minorities and disabled groups. Highlighting the scarcity of information in these areas, their new publication offers a starting point from which to have more meaningful conversations about diversity in local politics.
items.why: the publication examines whether elected local government bodies adequately represent ethnic minority and disabled populations.
items.note: Representativeness of elected institutions is anchored to elections & decision making.

items.h: IMPRESS launch public consultation on proposed changes to Standards Code
items.b: IMPRESS are looking for feedback on proposed changes to the IMPRESS Standards Code and guidance . The changes will help shape a new code that is appropriate for the changing face of journalism. Respond to the consultation by April 8th and have your say on the future and accountability of journalism.
items.why: the consultation shapes the standards code governing journalistic accountability, affecting the quality of the public information environment.

items.h: Deputy Prime Minister launches call for evidence on SLAPPs
items.b: The UK currently has no law in place to tackle the use of SLAPPs — Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation , which allow powerful actors to bring crippling lawsuits to investigative journalists and independent media corporations. This could soon change however as the Deputy Prime Minister has launched a call for evidence on their use in the UK. This comes amidst reports that UK law firms have been involved in preventing legitimate scrutiny in Russian oligarchs through such means.
items.why: tackling SLAPPs protects investigative journalists from being silenced through abusive litigation, safeguarding public-interest scrutiny.
links: UK law firms have been involved in preventing legitimate scrutiny in Russian oligarchs

items.h: Minfo UK working on new disinformation app
items.b: Roland Storti, Founder of Minfo UK , is working on Reveals, a new app with a Shazam-like feature allowing you to identify any speaker in any media and pull up data on them from the International Fact-Checking Network . Minfo hope the app will play a role in counteracting recent disinformation trends.
items.why: it creates a new public tool for verifying media claims and countering disinformation, affecting the quality of the public information environment.

items.h: Culture Secretary Nadine Dorries presses ahead with Channel 4 privatisation
items.b: DCMS Select Committee Chair Juian Knight MP has questioned if the privatisation plans are a “revenge” for the channel’s relatively impartial coverage of Brexit over recent years. We Own It have started a petition against the plans. Lindsay Mackie, writing in response to the government’s then consultation on these plans in openDemocracy last September, lays out the context for the government’s actions. Journalists and senior Conservative politicians alike have come out strongly against the plans.
items.why: privatising a public-service broadcaster affects media plurality and the independence of a channel from government influence.

items.h: UNESCO report suggests worrying global decline in press freedom
items.b: UNESCO has published a report on global freedom of expression and media trends . The report warns of a worrying decline in press freedom with 85% of countries said to have experienced some sort of restriction on the freedom of the press over the last five years.
items.why: a global decline in press freedom bears on citizens' ability to obtain plural, meaningful information about public affairs.
items.note: International report treated as comparative evidence bearing on UK media freedom.
links: report on global freedom of expression and media trends

items.h: Newsquest buy out of Archant brings further centralisation to local media
items.b: Media Reform Coalition report that Newsquest will be taking over the 74 local news titles attributed to the Archant media portfolio. The takeover means Newsquest now owns 30.3% of the local and regional newspaper market. It also means 80% of local and regional news is now owned by five companies.
items.why: increased concentration of local news ownership reduces media plurality, narrowing the range of independent political information available to citizens.

items.h: Labour criticise appointment of Conservative Peer as next chair of OFCOM
items.b: The decision to appoint Conservative Peer, Lord Grade , as the next chair of OFCOM has been met with scorn by Labour’s shadow minister for media, Chris Elmore . With OFCOM possibly soon to receive greater regulatory power through the Online Safety Bill , Elmore suggests this is a dangerous example of the government appointing a party insider.
items.why: a partisan appointment to the head of a powerful regulator raises questions about independent oversight and public appointments free of party influence.
items.note: Appointment is a public-appointments accountability issue, though it also touches the media regulator's independence.
links: decision to appoint Conservative Peer, Lord Grade

items.h: Applications still open for Sounddelivery Spokesperson Programme
items.b: Sounddelivery are re-running their Spokesperson Training Programme which aims to bring visibility to voices typically excluded from the media. The programme will equip the 14 successful applicants with the expertise to harness their lived experience and become voices and changemakers within their community. Deadline for applications is April 8th.
items.why: the programme builds new capacity for people from underrepresented groups to participate as public voices, expanding practical means of civic participation.
items.note: Treated under sector capacity-building rule as creation of new participatory means, not organisation news.

items.h: Novara Media explores whether our democratic system is up to the task of combating the climate crisis
items.b: Jeremy Gilbert’s #ACFM podcast explores the anti-democratic shifts across the spectrum, what it means to be ruled by the people with an incisive take on whether our beleaguered democratic system is able to take on the climate crisis or whether we need to ‘intensify’ democracy.
items.why: the discussion concerns whether deliberative or intensified democratic decision-making mechanisms are adequate to address collective challenges like climate change.
items.note: Podcast discussion of democratic theory and deliberation, mapped to decision-making machinery per boundary rule.
links: our beleaguered democratic system is able to take on the climate crisis

items.h: Could we represent abstainers and non-voters with randomly selected citizens?
items.b: In this blog the author explores the suggestion of representing abstaining citizens with randomly selected citizens, worth a read .
items.why: it proposes a mechanism to represent non-voters via randomly selected citizens, engaging directly with turnout and deliberative representation of abstainers.
items.note: Combines turnout and citizens'-assembly-style representation, both anchored to elections & decision making.

This week we were joined by Pilar Girvan — Advocacy & Comms Officer at Involve, James Clarke — True & Fair Party, Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters, Myf Nixon, Communications Manager at mySociety, Holly Morgan-Davies — Alliance and Support Executive at Make Votes Matter, Jessie Joe Jacobs — Coordinator at Democracy Network, Oliver Walkden — Communications and Digital Marketing at Young Citizens and Trin Gong — Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent.
