items.h: New Online Safety Bill office hours weekly meeting
items.b: Each weekly meeting involves intel sharing and subgroup updates from across the OSB working group. If you’re working on the Online Safety Bill, this is a must-attend! Next meet is today at 3.30pm, contact Matt at Fair Vote for your invite.
items.note: Sector networking/meeting logistics, not a democracy mechanism itself.

items.h: House of Lords votes to turn back the clock on second preference voting in PCC & mayoral elections
items.b: Writing for MyLondon, Josiah Mortimer , previously Head of Comms at Electoral Reform Society, notes that the Lords failed to block a change to election law, meaning that second preference voting has now been abolished in English & Welsh mayor-led areas and PCC elections. Peers also rejected automatic voter registration, but did vote in favour of expanded lists of accepted ID for when new voter ID laws come in. Worth noting, of 168 Labour Peers in the second chamber, only 74 turned out to vote.
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports concrete legislative changes to electoral systems (abolition of second preference voting), voter registration, and voter ID rules that directly shape how elections are run and who can vote.

items.h: Labour calls for crackdown on environmental activists, rings alarm bells among campaigners
items.b: Last week the Labour Party called on the Government to act with urgency and ban environmental protests . Unsurprisingly this has reportedly caused alarm amongst party members and allied organisations, particularly those working around the Police Bill.
items.why: this matters democratically because a call to ban environmental protests concerns the legal restriction and policing of assembly rights that let people challenge power outside elections.
items.note: Protest framed as legal restriction/policing, not participation willingness, so classified under rights rather than participation.
links: Labour Party called on the Government to act with urgency and ban environmental protests

items.h: Liberty suggest ‘crunch time’ looming for ‘dangerous bills’ that threaten democracy
items.b: Following the Easter break Liberty have highlighted possible plans from the government to pass nine bills in nine days , or else risk them being dropped altogether. According to Liberty, the rush to pass them is the result of a series of delays caused by entrenched opposition to the bills. The bills are due to fall unless passed immediately due to Parliamentary recess. The bills affected include the Elections Bill, the Police Bill, Nationality and Borders Bill and Judicial Review Bill.
items.why: this matters democratically because rushing multiple significant bills through Parliament in days undermines legislative scrutiny and checks on executive power, even though the bills themselves also touch elections, justice and rights.
items.note: Primary beat chosen for the overarching scrutiny/process concern; the individual bills cut across several beats as secondaries.
links: highlighted possible plans from the government to pass nine bills in nine days

items.h: Carnegie UK & Demos provide resources to better understand the Online Safety Bill
items.b: The Online Safety Bill (OSB) can be a challenge to navigate. To help make sense of it all Carnegie UK have published this one page summary of the bill and DEMOS have put out a position paper going into greater depth on how the bill stacks up against various tests for successful digital regulation.
items.why: public understanding of a bill regulating online content and platforms shapes informed public debate and scrutiny of the information environment
items.note: Explainer resources on pending legislation are treated as capacity-building for informed public debate rather than mere sector logistics.
links: one page summary of the bill

items.h: Extensive ‘reading list’ released on the Online Safety Bill
items.b: The House of Commons Library have released a reading list of all things related to the Online Safety Bill . With in-depth analysis, reactions from organisations and charities, as well as media articles and opinion pieces, the list is a great starting point for anyone looking to deepen their knowledge of the bill.
items.why: a curated resource on a bill governing online platforms helps the public and civil society engage in informed debate about the information environment
items.note: Treated as a capacity-building resource rather than routine listing since it aids scrutiny of information-environment legislation.

items.h: Hope Not Hate highlight ‘genuine electoral threat’ from far right in this year’s locals
items.b: According to the team at HNH, whilst the far-right have been in the ‘wilderness’ for the past few years, this year they claim far-right parties at this year’s local elections are a ‘genuine electoral threat’, and are calling for people to send in far right leaflets they come across. Hope Not Hate are monitoring far-right candidates and sharing intelligence with local organisations to combat their rise, alongside data-driven attempts to boost turnout amongst young people and minority communities in areas where far-right candidates are standing. Find out more about how you and your organisation …
items.why: monitoring far-right candidates and boosting turnout among under-represented groups directly concerns the competitiveness and participation of elections

items.h: LGiU publish guide to local elections
items.b: The Local Government Information Unit have published their Ones to Watch guide to the local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. Stay up to date with all the local election news and gossip by signing up to their elections bulletin (but we’ll be regurgitating most of it here anyway!).
items.why: a guide helping people follow and understand local elections supports informed electoral participation
items.note: Treated as capacity-building resource for elections rather than pure promotional logistics.

items.h: Citizens’ Assembly on Democracy report launches, suggests voters care more about integrity than previously thought
items.b: 67 members of the public, carefully selected to represent the UK public, have agreed eight resolutions and 51 detailed recommendations on how to strengthen UK democracy. The Constitution Unit’s Citizens’ Assembly on Democracy, developed with Involve, found that integrity in public life commanded the most passionate support . Recommendations included making “lying or intentionally misleading parliament” punishable as a “contempt of Parliament”. The report builds upon the Constitution Unit’s major survey of public opinion , polling some 6,000 people late last year.
items.why: a citizens' assembly producing recommendations on democratic reform is part of the deliberative decision-making machinery the framework anchors to this beat
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.
links: integrity in public life commanded the most passionate support

items.h: Dramatic loss of faith in democracy amongst UK adults, says IPPR report
items.b: The report’s disturbing conclusions find that donors to political parties and big businesses are now commonly viewed by the electorate as the main drivers of government policy. The polling found just 6% of UK adults believe their views are the main driver of government policy. The report, Road to Renewal , suggests compounding political crises, such as the prorogation of parliament, lack of parliamentary oversight over the Brexit process, sweeping pandemic legislation without parliamentary censure, and ministers briefing the media before MPs, have played a key role in sharp decline.
items.why: declining public belief that one's views influence government policy reflects eroding public support for and efficacy within democracy
items.note: The report also touches on undue influence of donors/business over policy, which is a government & accountability concern.

items.h: Young Citizens highlight Lord Hodgson’s new report The Ties that Bind
items.b: A follow-up to the 2018 report that called for the appointment of a dedicated minister responsible for matters related to active citizenship and civic engagement, the new report states that current coordination of citizenship and civic engagement policy is “insufficient”. Young Citizens’ CEO Ashley Hodges, a contributor to the report, remarks at the apparent contradiction of a levelling up strategy aiming to put power in the hands of local people that delivers no resource and makes no time for building citizen capacity to engage with institutions of government. Short on time? Read the report s…
items.why: the report concerns the state of civic engagement policy and the resourcing of citizens' capacity to engage with government institutions

items.h: Climate Emergency UK are looking for a Campaigns and Policy Officer
items.b: Climate Emergency UK work with councils and residents to catalyse local level action on the climate and ecological emergency. The Campaign and Policy Officer will help create next year’s Council Climate Plan Scorecards to help measure how effective local action is in reducing emissions. Apply before 3rd May.
items.note: Job advert; organisational news, not a democracy story.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society host discussion on the future of local governance
items.b: Following the release of their Democracy Made in England report on the dynamics of local government, ERS hosted a live discussion exploring the question of ‘where next for local government?’ Explore all previous online discussions through their YouTube channel , and become a member of ERS to put live questions to panellists at future events.
items.why: discussing the future structure and dynamics of local government concerns the machinery of local democratic decision-making
items.note: Local government structure is filed under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: New research suggests minipublics could reduce political dissatisfaction if results are properly implemented
items.b: In the context of rising public dissatisfaction within democratic countries, research into deliberative minipublics as a potential antidote has seen a recent surge. A new paper from the European Journal of Political Research has found that minipublics received higher levels of political support than representative decision-making processes when recommendations were implemented. However, it also suggests they have the capacity to aggravate political dissatisfaction when recommendations are not followed.
items.why: research on whether minipublics increase or reduce political dissatisfaction bears directly on the design and legitimacy of deliberative decision-making processes
items.note: Deliberative minipublics are classified under elections & decision making, not participation, per the framework's boundary rule.
links: minipublics received higher levels of political support

items.h: Pact Pioneers handbook explores power and anti-racism in civil society leadership
items.b: A new handbook from Pact Pioneers is aimed at anyone holding a leadership role across civil society. Focusing on themes of power, accountability, connection and trust, the handbook provides a series of exercises and frameworks through which to consider how civil society organsations can overcome discrimination and harness collective power.
items.why: it builds civil society leaders' capacity to understand and share power, strengthening organisations' ability to participate effectively in democratic life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource under the participation beat.

items.h: 50:50 Parliament to hold recurring event for women faced with ‘higher hurdles’
items.b: 50:50 are reaching out to all women that have physical, mental, emotional, or other such requirements that could create additional hurdles on their journey in politics. They plan to hold a bespoke session every month to help women overcome those hurdles with their first event taking place May 23rd. 50:50 are also looking for an Events Coordinator, do you know the right person?
items.why: it creates a new recurring means of support for women facing additional barriers to entering political life, addressing unequal conditions for participation.
links: do you know the right person?

items.h: Get set for Radix Big Tent Festival this June
items.b: Trin Gong and the team at Radix Big Tent have got a treat in store this Summer. The two day festival titled ‘Transitions’ will hone in on a discussion of strategy and action for regeneration and renewal across all layers of government. Find out more and book your 2FOR1 tickets here .

items.h: openDemocracy lead campaign demanding greater governmental transparency
items.b: More than 110 MPs, journalists and campaigners have signed an open letter to the Information Commissioner’s Office highlighting concerns over governmental secrecy and lacklustre attempts to ensure transparent and accountable government. The letter states the Freedom of Information Act (FOI) is ‘clearly not working’ and comes following a number of revelations detailing Whitehall’s abuse of the act .
items.why: it challenges whether the Freedom of Information Act still functions as an effective mechanism for holding government answerable for transparency.
links: number of revelations detailing Whitehall’s abuse of the act

items.h: New Local host Stronger Things 2022 event on community power
items.b: At the end of March, New Local held their Stronger Things 2022 event bringing together a range of speakers to discuss the power of community and engaged citizenship. If you missed the event you can catch up on all the talks, including a conversation with Angela Rayner, on the New Local YouTube channel .

items.h: Involve are looking for a new Engagement Lead
items.b: The role of the new Engagement Lead will be to help build capacity inside and outside public institutions and imbed practices that will lead to greater levels of public participation in decision making. Check out the job description and apply before 16th May.
items.note: Job advert for an organisation, not a new participation resource itself.

items.h: Russian military targets Ukrainian democratic institutions
items.b: Reports have emerged of systematic violence and targeting of Ukrainian civil society. Abductions of mayors, local government representatives, journalists, activists, and other civilians have become widespread. UK mayors and local representatives have responded by organising a solidarity campaign calling on the UN to take decisive action. Local representatives can sign up by emailing 2022ukrainesolidarity@gmail.com.
items.note: Primarily war reporting on Ukraine with only tangential UK solidarity action, not a UK democracy mechanism.

items.h: Germany combats far right by bolstering democratic culture
items.b: MBTs (Mobile Counselling Teams Against Right-Wing Extremism) have been supporting citizens, labour unions and local councils in Germany to combat the growth of the far-right. The programme offers tools to communities on how to respond to and prevent the mobilisation of far-right groups through a process of reclaiming public spaces, both physical and online. The initiatives began work in the 90s and are still having positive effects .
items.why: it offers comparative evidence on civil society programmes that build democratic culture and counter far-right mobilisation, relevant to UK civic capacity-building.
items.note: Foreign example included as comparative evidence for the domestic civic sector.
links: MBTs (Mobile Counselling Teams Against Right-Wing Extremism)

items.h: Extinction Rebellion take to the streets, Just Stop Oil take to the refineries
items.b: Extinction Rebellion have been back on the streets of London these past weeks calling for urgent action to avert climate catastrophe, their demands feature an urgent call for a citizens’ assembly on the climate crisis. Stay up to date on XR’s latest escapades via their Twitter . In recent weeks XR splinter group Just Stop Oil have occupied critical fossil fuel infrastructure across the UK calling for a moratorium on fossil fuel investments and extraction in the UK. Significant disruptions to fossil fuel supplies were reported nationwide, with pumps dry across many forecourts in the South East.
items.why: it reports citizens exercising their willingness to protest and take direct action to influence public policy, including a demand for a citizens' assembly.
items.note: Classified under participation because the story centres on willingness to protest rather than legal restriction; citizens' assembly demand noted as secondary per decision-making machinery rule.

items.h: Media Reform Coalition outlines proposals for sustainable local journalism
items.b: In February this year the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport department put out a call for evidence on the future of local journalism. Media Reform Coalition have responded calling for new funding streams for local journalism, financed through levies on tech giants. They suggest these funds should go towards local interest journalism rather than to commercial news providers.
items.why: it proposes new funding mechanisms to sustain local journalism, which underpins public access to plural information about local government and public affairs.
links: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport department

items.h: Government confirms plans to go ahead with privatisation of Channel 4
items.b: Nadine Dorries has confirmed the government’s plans to privatise Channel 4 claiming government ownership of the organisation is holding it “back from competing against streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon”. A We Own It petition opposing the plans received 28,000 signatures in its first 24 hours.
items.why: privatising a public-service broadcaster affects media plurality and the public information environment that underpins democratic debate
items.note: Public ownership/broadcaster policy treated as media plurality issue under information & public debate rather than accountability.

items.h: Make Votes Matter awarded grant by JRRT, plans day of action
items.b: Inspired by the Great Pilgrimage of 1913, the “Get Moving for PR” national day of action will include draft motions people can send to their local councils to support PR for the House of Commons. The funding award from JRRT has allowed MVM to expand their team and ramp up their campaign.
items.why: the campaign seeks to change the electoral system used to elect the House of Commons, directly affecting how representatives are chosen
items.note: Electoral system reform campaign classified under elections & decision making per framework anchors on electoral systems.

items.h: Act for Change Programme comes to a close
items.b: Paul Hamlyn Foundation and Esme Fairburn Foundation have been busy funding youth social justice action. Their joint Act for Change Fund ran from 2018–22 and issued £3.6m to provide funds and resources for young people to tackle inequality and discrimination in their communities. Explore the full list of projects funded through the programme and check out the great work these organisations have been doing.
items.note: Reports the closure of a funding programme, which is organisational/funding news rather than a change to democratic participation mechanisms.
links: Explore the full list of projects funded through the programme

items.h: Elections Bill passes the Lords, Parliament prorogued
items.b: Last Wednesday evening the House of Lords finally gave up its fight to inflict setbacks on the Government’s Elections Bill. With the Government failing to give way, the Lords let the legislation pass. The unamended Elections Bill could now potentially give ministers new and unchecked powers over the Electoral Commission, undermining free and fair elections in the UK. Naomi Smith, CEO of Best for Britain remarked last Wednesday, “Tonight was the last chance to protect the independence of the elections watchdog and with it free and fair elections in the UK.” Attendance at last week’s critical vo…
items.why: the bill grants ministers new powers over the Electoral Commission, the independent body responsible for safeguarding free and fair elections in the UK.
items.note: Also touches executive control over an independent regulator, engaging government accountability.
links: just 67 of 167 Labour peers turning up

items.h: Civil society organisations mobilise in response to passing of Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Bill
items.b: On the 28th of April, the Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Bill was passed in parliament. The bill has been the subject of major contention and will give the police unprecedented new powers to restrict protests deemed “too noisy”. The Police Bill Alliance , a coalition of over 350 UK organisations opposing the bill, have called it a “dark day for democracy” . Other rights-based groups such as Liberty and NetPol have pledged to release legal advice, workshops, training and guides on how to stay safe in light of the new laws. We will continue to cover emerging advice in upcoming bulletins.
items.why: the new law expands police powers to restrict protests, directly affecting citizens' freedom of assembly and their ability to challenge and contest public power.
items.note: Protest restriction via policing and legal power falls under rights and civic space, not participation willingness.
links: Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Bill

items.h: Longstanding ‘ping-pong’ of Nationality and Borders Bill comes to an end
items.b: On Wednesday evening the Government successfully passed the Nationality and Borders Bill after the House of Lords dropped a series of proposed amendments. The new laws will legalise offshore processing of asylum seekers and will make it a criminal offence to knowingly arrive in the UK via an illegal route. More than 240 organisations have pledged to oppose the Government’s new laws stating that the bill “rips up internationally recognised rights for people fleeing war and persecution, and will criminalise thousands of refugees”.
items.why: the legislation criminalises certain routes of entry and removes established legal protections, altering the personal security and legal rights afforded under UK law.
items.note: Borderline: primarily an immigration policy story, but engages personal security and equal legal protection anchors.
links: 240 organisations have pledged to oppose the Government’s new laws

items.h: Media Reform Coalition outline concern over the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Ahead of the spring reading, the Media Reform Coalition has published a briefing on the historical context and key debates surrounding the Online Safety Bill . They suggest the clear need for greater regulation of our online space should not be used as a foundation for “ill-thought out” regulation that could excessively bolster the power of the governing party and simultaneously isolate the UK tech industry as a global outlier.
items.why: the Online Safety Bill's regulatory design could increase state control over online platforms, shaping the information environment that underpins political debate.
items.note: Classified under information & debate as the concern centres on regulation of the online information space, with a secondary accountability angle about executive power.

items.h: Democracy Network Development Day #2 coming May 25th
items.b: On Monday 21st March 2022, the Democracy Network held its first ‘Development Day’ — a workshop designed to involve larger numbers of participants in forming the Network’s approach, in advance of a major public launch in autumn 2022. The second Development Day is scheduled for May 25th. View the report from the first workshop . Jessie Joe Jacobs , the Network’s Coordinator, asks that if you would like the Network to host a briefing on your work, or if you would like to get more involved in the work of the Network, that you please complete this short survey .

items.h: House of Commons Speaker rebukes sexist Angela Rayner article
items.b: Last Monday, the Mail on Sunday published a sexist story targeted at Angela Rayner. Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle summoned the Mail on Sunday editor for a meeting over the article last weekend. “The story can only deter women who might consider standing for election,” Mr Hoyle told MPs in the Commons last Monday.
items.why: media conduct that deters women from standing for office affects the representativeness of who can seek and hold elected office.
items.note: Treated as elections & decision making because the story concerns candidacy and representativeness rather than a general discrimination claim.
links: summoned the Mail on Sunday editor

items.h: ElectHer are running Peer Support Circles to connect women in politics
items.b: From the 10th of May to the 21st of June, ElectHer will be facilitating a series of free online support circles to connect women in politics and create a space for learning, reflection and personal growth. If you’re thinking about embarking on a journey in politics, join these weekly sessions to gain encouragement and expertise from women on the same path.
items.why: programmes that build women's capacity and confidence to stand for office affect the representativeness of candidates for elected positions.
items.note: Classified under elections given the focus on candidacy for political office, with participation as a secondary capacity-building angle.

items.h: LGiU publish short report on public attitudes to local elections
items.b: Ahead of the local elections across the UK tomorrow, LGiU have teamed up with pollster Ipsos to explore what the UK public thinks about local elections, local councillors and local government. Explore all the findings from the research and check out their online facts and figures page for more information on how local government and local voting works.
items.why: public understanding of and attitudes toward local elections and councils affect participation in and legitimacy of local democratic decision-making.

items.h: Demos launch Post-Pandemic People Power project
items.b: Over the past few months, Ciaran Cummins and the team at Demos have been looking at the experiences of activists in the UK to provide insight into the future of British politics. Get in touch with Ciaran if you’re keen to talk about this!
items.note: Too thin an announcement of a research project to identify a concrete democratic mechanism at stake.
links: looking at the experiences of activists

items.h: Constitution Unit host webinar to discuss conclusions from citizens assembly on UK Democracy
items.b: Earlier this month The Constitution Unit launched a report based on insights from the UK’s first citizens assembly on democracy. Following-up on the report launch, The Constitution Unit held an online webinar last week to discuss the key conclusions. If you missed it, check out their YouTube channel to catch-up on the debate.
items.why: citizens' assemblies are part of the machinery of collective decision-making that lets people deliberate on binding public choices.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are anchored to elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Communication Workers Union pass motion calling for a fairer voting system
items.b: The Communication Workers Union have passed a motion declaring the current First Past the Post system is “an undemocratic election process” that has “left the UK exposed to extreme Tory governments elected by a minority of voters”. They join Unite , Aslef , the BFAWU , TSSA , Musicians and PCS , who have all also passed similar motions since October 2021. A number of other unions including Unison have said they will host similar debates in the coming months.
items.why: union support for electoral reform bears directly on how competitive and representative the electoral system is in translating votes into seats.

items.h: New study on class and political engagement among young people in Scotland
items.b: Young people are often the most politically disengaged demographic, compounded by social class differences within that grouping. Based on data collected around the Scottish independence referendum in 2014, Christine Huebner and Jan Eichhorn have identified that when rates of participation increase amongst young people, young people of all social classes were equally likely to be politically engaged. Overall, social class differences in political engagement were less pronounced amongst 16–17 year olds in Scotland than elsewhere in the UK.
items.why: class-based differences in youth political engagement affect who is practically able to take part in democratic life.

items.h: Trust the People to launch eight-week course on community organising
items.b: Starting on the 9th of May, Trust the People will be running an eight-week course on community organising . The course will be split over five in-depth modules covering a range of topics from one-on-one relationship building to successfully running community assemblies. It is free to sign up and upon completion, you’ll have the chance to join a ‘Hive’ support group with others who took part.
items.why: training people in community organising creates new means for people to take part in civic and democratic life.

items.h: 50:50 host monthly ‘Connect and Reflect’ sessions for women from ethnically diverse backgrounds
items.b: 50:50 Parliament host a regular monthly session to create a safe space for women from a range of ethnic backgrounds to help progress on their political path. This is a recurring event that takes place on the last Monday of the month and you can find updates on future sessions by following 50:50 on Twitter .
items.why: it creates a recurring programme designed to help women from underrepresented backgrounds build the capacity and confidence to participate in political life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building rather than a mere event listing.

items.h: Radix Big Tent coming June 11th in Bristol
items.b: The annual festival is back — get your tickets — view the programme .

items.h: New Local are on the lookout for a new Principal Practice Consultant/Lead
items.b: New Local have been working with councils and other civic bodies to make sure ‘community power’ is at the forefront of local planning and engagement. The new Principal Practice Consultant/Lead with help develop this exciting work which has picked up speed. If this sounds like the role for you then check out the job description and apply before 11th May.

items.h: Get PR Done! are looking for a new Treasurer
items.b: GPRD are on the hunt for a new treasurer to help with the financial and administrative running of the organisation. Get in touch via getprdone@gmail.com if you are interested.

items.h: Carnegie UK are looking for a new Chair of Trustees
items.b: Sir John Elvidge is reaching the end of their term at Carnegie UK meaning they are on the lookout for a new Chair of Trustees . The new chair will lead the board and implement a new company strategy to improve collective wellbeing in the UK and Ireland. Deadline for applications is May 11th.

items.h: Onward are hiring a Chief Operating Officer
items.b: The new hire will report directly to the Director and Trustees and will oversee Onward’s finances, relationships and operations. If you have a strong understanding of the British political landscape and would be happy to representing Onward at all levels, including at C-suite and Cabinet level, then check out the job description and apply before 8th of May.

items.h: Copenhagen Democracy Summit arrives 9–10 June
items.b: The Alliance of Democracies Foundation, founded in 2017 by former NATO Secretary General and former Prime Minister of Denmark, Anders Fogh Rasmussen, works to strengthen ties between democracies and build a worldwide intellectual movement for democracy. The June summit is an annual event, bringing together elected leaders and business executives. For more information see their website .
items.note: International event listing with no direct bearing on UK democracy.

items.h: Andy Burnham: We need a complete rewiring of Britain’s political system
items.b: Greater Manchester Mayor and former Labour front bencher Andy Burnham has called for the introduction of proportional representation (PR) for general elections and a wholesale reform of the House of Lords, according to Sam Bright at the Byline Times. Burnham is also a passionate advocate for regional devolution and a system for electing parliamentary representatives on a regional basis, arguing that the current system “prevents people from acting across a broad region.” Whilst a divergence from Labour Party policy, YouGov polling found an overwhelming 83% of Labour members surveyed supported t…
items.why: it concerns proposals to change the electoral system used to choose representatives and the structure of a legislative chamber, both core to how power is acquired and constrained.
links: called for the introduction of proportional representation

items.h: Dr Hannah White to discuss their new book, ‘ What’s wrong with the House of Commons?’
items.b: In light of recent smears to the reputation of politicians, Dr White’s new book explores how the House of Commons can reform to reinstall trust and accountability with the public. Register for the launch of their new book on May 3rd — Held in Contempt: What’s wrong with the House of Commons?, which will be discussed alongside a panel of experts to find out how parliament could change for the better. Dr Hannah White is the Deputy Director of the Institute for Government.
items.why: it engages proposals to reform how the House of Commons scrutinises government and maintains public accountability.
items.note: Treated as substantive debate on institutional reform rather than mere event promotion.
links: launch of their new book on May 3rd

items.h: Unlock Democracy write their own version of the Queen’s Speech
items.b: With the Queen’s Speech looming , Unlock Democracy have taken the opportunity to craft their own version , putting forward a series of key democratic reforms. The speech has been sent to all 650 MPs and a public petition has been launched demanding that the Queen’s speech on May 10th includes plans to modernise our democracy.
items.why: it uses a public petition sent to elected representatives to press for democratic reforms, exercising the mechanism of petitioning for redress and change.
items.note: Petition mechanism places this in participation even though its content concerns democratic reform.

items.h: MP convicted of sexually molesting child finally steps down
items.b: MP Imran Ahmad Khan, who has been expelled from the Conservative Party following his conviction , had ignored calls for him to resign his Westminster seat until last Friday. Local Conservatives have been growing increasingly alarmed at his refusal to step down .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether an elected representative can be held to account and forced to relinquish their mandate following serious wrongdoing.

items.h: Unlock Democracy want your views on government accountability
items.b: The Elections Bill passed on Wednesday evening following what Best for Britain described as a deliberate Government strategy to bypass scrutiny by scheduling the vote late into the evening and running hard up against the parliamentary deadline. Unlock Democracy have raised similar concerns over current checks and balances on government power and are canvassing public opinion on how to ensure the Government is more effectively held accountable by the House of Lords.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether Parliament can scrutinise government legislation and whether the Lords can effectively check executive power.
items.note: Elections Bill scrutiny process is about checks and balances, not the bill's electoral content, so classified as accountability.

items.h: Home Office abandons policy of refugee pushbacks
items.b: In the face of multiple legal challenges from PCS Union, Care for Calais and Free from Torture, the Home Office has rowed back on it’s controversial and dangerous policy, reports Channel Rescue .
items.why: this matters democratically because legal challenges forced the executive to abandon a policy, showing courts and legal action constraining government action.

items.h: Full Fact launch campaign calling for greater transparency in parliament
items.b: In light of the recent fines for the Prime Minister and Chancellor, Full Fact have launched a campaign demanding new rules to allow MPs to correct false claims or statements, and formal sanctions for those who don’t. The petition, signed by over 18,000 members of the public, has been sent to all MPs in a bid to improve honesty and transparency in parliament.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns mechanisms to hold MPs accountable for honesty and impose sanctions for misleading statements in Parliament.

items.h: Pwy alla i bleidleisio ar gyfer?
items.b: Democracy Club’s voter information services are now running at full steam across all election areas ahead of the 5 May vote, including Northern Ireland. They’ve also boosted their platform, adding support for the Welsh language . Add their election widget to your website now .
items.why: this matters democratically because it expands practical access to voter information, including in Welsh, affecting people's ability to participate in elections.
links: Add their election widget to your website now

items.h: High praise for quality and speed of French election reporting
items.b: Martin Stabe, Data Editor at the Financial Times, remarks at the speed and granularity of the French elections. With more than 35,000 communes reporting results in just five hours, distributed in machine-readable formats by one official source. Democracy Club has been campaigning for years for a similar approach to UK elections, find out more about how we can work towards that goal here .
items.why: this matters democratically because the speed and transparency of official election result reporting is part of well-run electoral administration.

items.h: Electoral Commission release voter information resources for upcoming local elections
items.b: In a push to increase awareness and encourage participation in the upcoming local elections, the Electoral Commission has released a guide for voters with information on polling station opening times, when elections are taking place, what to do if you need help voting, and much more. Share it around to encourage the public to get involved this month!
items.why: this matters democratically because voter information resources affect people's practical ability to vote and turn out in local elections.

items.h: Legal uncertainty over proposed Indyref2
items.b: The Scottish Government has been ordered by the country’s information commissioner to publish details of legal advice it has received over a potential second independence referendum currently scheduled by the Scottish Government for 2023. The Scottish Government has so far refused to make the advice public, arguing it would breach legal professional privilege. The UK Government has shown no sign that it is willing to give the formal consent that ensured the legality of the 2014 poll. A court battle between the UK and Scottish Government could result should Sturgeon press ahead with the plans w…
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the legality and process of holding a referendum, a core mechanism of direct popular decision-making.
items.note: Referendum legality is classified under elections/decision-making per framework; the FOI order also touches government accountability.

items.h: Revisiting Local Government Chronicle’s emerging devolution map
items.b: Last September, the Local Government Chronicle mapped the progress of potential devolution deals and processes across the UK , charting potential flashpoints and plans.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the structure and progress of devolution deals affecting local and regional decision-making powers.
items.note: Devolution structure falls under elections/decision-making per boundary rule, though this item merely revisits an existing map.
links: mapped the progress of potential devolution deals and processes across the UK

items.h: mySociety commission report on linking up citizens and local government for climate action
items.b: The climate programme at mySociety has been exploring how local authorities can implement strategies to reduce carbon emissions. Their new report highlights public attitudes towards net zero and local government, and the role local authorities have in reaching climate targets. Check out the seven key messages from the report.
items.why: this matters democratically because it explores how citizens can engage with and influence local government decision-making on climate policy.
links: seven key messages from the report.

items.h: Join the ranks of the BBC’s Local Democracy Reporters
items.b: The BBC is currently advertising vacancies nationwide, including Sheffield, Fife, Northamptonshire, Scarborough, Southampton, Shropshire, Stoke, London, Cardiff and Bath. There are currently 165 BBC Local Democracy Reporters across the UK, funded by the BBC and employed by local news organisations. Find out more and how to apply on the BBC website .
items.note: Job advertisement for an existing scheme, treated as sector logistics.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation finalising their 2022 Index of Independent News Publishing
items.b: The annual in-depth review covers more than 70 independent newsrooms across the UK and is due to be published soon. Joe Mitchell, Programme Manager at the Public Interest News Foundation , is looking out for interesting examples of good, bad and non existent coverage of elections in local media, pop them a message if you have any suggestions.
items.why: an index assessing independent and local news coverage of elections bears on whether citizens can access plural, quality information about public affairs

items.h: Elon Musk buys Twitter with aim to promote free speech and democracy
items.b: Musk bought the social media platform for $44bn on the 25th of April with plans to liberalise restrictions on free speech. The Centre for Countering Digital Hate have responded by opening a tip-line for any current or former Twitter employees to share concerns on what the takeover will mean for countering hate speech and misinformation.
items.why: a change in ownership and moderation policy of a major social platform affects the plurality and integrity of the public information environment
links: The Centre for Countering Digital Hate

items.h: Physical attacks on journalists increase according to new report
items.b: A new report, Defending Press Freedom in Times of Tension and Conflict , published by the Platform for the Protection of Journalism and Safety of Journalists , has found that attacks on journalists increased by 51% over the last year. The report also found that many of the attacks have taken place at public protests raising significant fears over the status of free expression in Europe. The report found journalists in the UK at risk of detention and imprisonment, being attacked by police during protests and facing harassment and intimidation.
items.why: rising physical attacks on journalists, including by police at protests, threaten press freedom and the safety of those who inform public debate
links: Defending Press Freedom in Times of Tension and Conflict
Platform for the Protection of Journalism and Safety of Journalists

items.h: European Alternatives host No More War Citizens’ Assembly on war in Ukraine
items.b: On the 27th of April, European Alternatives hosted an online, transnational citizens assembly uniting European citizens in opposition to the war in Ukraine. The initiative, due to recur on a rolling basis, will open up channels for individuals to discuss their own experiences and solidarity actions, as well as share thoughts on possible solutions to the war. Follow EuroAlt on Twitter to stay up to date with what’s coming up, or email them directly to sign up to future assemblies — euroalter@protonmail.com .
items.note: A transnational, informal assembly not tied to UK democratic decision-making machinery.

items.h: Citizens Assemblies on biodiversity loss and local government begin in Dublin
items.b: A joint meeting took place in Dublin in April as part of a new initiative to consult the local population on local government structure and biodiversity loss. The assemblies will continue to meet throughout the year placing people “at the heart of the consideration of proposals which could have a significant impact on the way we live our lives”, according to the chair of the biodiversity assembly, Dr Ní Shúilleabháin.
items.note: Irish citizens' assemblies with no bearing on UK democracy.
links: joint meeting took place in Dublin in April

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters, Simon Duffy — Director at Citizens Network, Pilar Girvan — Communications & Advocacy Officer at Involve/Democracy Network, Sam Welsh — Partnerships Coordinator at Votes for Schools, Trin Gong — Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent and Rebecca Deegan — Founder at I Have A Voice.
items.note: Contributor thanks, organisational admin.

items.b: With just over a year since we launched the Centre for Democracy , it is one year since we launched the Ecosystem Pledge, now backed by 71 signatory organisations, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: Pledge signatory count is organisational/coalition admin rather than a new means of participation being created.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.
items.note: Generic mission statement, not a concrete mechanism.

items.b: If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .
items.note: Call to action to sign a list, sector admin.

items.h: Sign up for new Online Safety Bill Office Hours
items.b: Similar to the previous Election Bill Office Hours, the team at Fair Vote are running weekly office hours to bring together organisations and individuals working on the Online Safety Bill. Email Matt Gallagher to join the mailing list and RSVP for the sessions.
items.why: the Online Safety Bill governs regulation of online platforms and speech, shaping the information environment in which UK political debate occurs, and this creates a new forum for civil society engagement with that legislation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building around legislation affecting the information environment counts under participation-of-organisations in the legislative process, but the substantive topic (platform regulation) anchors it to information_debate.

items.b: Carnegie UK draft amendment on OFCOM independence open for comment & indicative sign on. Engage via Matt as above.
items.why: OFCOM's independence as a regulator overseeing online platforms bears on checks and balances over an accountable independent body with power over the information environment.
items.note: Regulator independence is a government_accountability matter even though OFCOM's remit touches information_debate.

items.b: The Public Bill Committee is now accepting evidence ahead of upcoming scrutiny of the Online Safety Bill. Oral evidence sessions will take place on 24 and 26 May, with line-by-line scrutiny running on Tuesdays and Thursdays throughout June.
items.why: this reports Parliament exercising its legislative scrutiny function over a major bill regulating online speech and safety.
items.note: Procedural legislative scrutiny is treated as Parliament exercising its accountability function even though the bill's subject touches the information environment.

items.b: The Government has published a factsheet on the new Communications Offences in the Bill and the Independent Reviewer of Terrorism Legislation has published an analysis.
items.why: new communications offences directly shape what speech is criminalised in the public information environment.

items.h: Police Bill Alliance comes to an end
items.b: As the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act passes into law, the Police Bill Alliance is dissolving. The Police Bill Alliance coordinated over 350 organisations through their mailing list and coordination sessions, organising protests, op-eds, mobilising academia, businesses, former police officers, diplomats, parliamentarians and even ex-Prime Ministers — including a petition backed by more than 800,000 people. They succeeded in dragging out the Bill for 14 months and kicking some of the government’s plans into the long grass. With the new Public Order Bill announced during the Queen’s Sp…
items.why: this reports on the capacity of a large civil-society coalition to mobilise and delay contested legislation, a form of collective civic action.
items.note: Focus is on coalition capacity and campaign history rather than routine organisational admin, so it is treated as a participation story.

items.h: New Public Order Bill extends protest suppression provisions
items.b: Introduced in the Queen’s Speech, The Public Order Bill has been interpreted as an attack on the climate movement. The Bill introduces measures to criminalise key protest tactics such as ‘locking-on’, alongside new criminal offences for obstructing major transport networks and interfering with national infrastructure. Green groups have decried the move.
items.why: new criminal offences targeting protest tactics narrow the legal space in which people can assemble and demonstrate against government policy.

items.h: Defending the Right to Boycott
items.b: Friends of the Earth, Liberty, Quakers in Britain and others have signed a joint statement defending the Right to Boycott , in light of expected legislation to prevent public bodies from making decisions ‘counter to UK foreign policy’. It is expected that the Bill’s remit will encompass local government and both the Scottish and Welsh governments.
items.why: restricting public bodies' ability to take politically motivated procurement or investment decisions curtails a form of collective political expression and local autonomy.
items.note: Touches both civil liberties (boycott as expression) and local government decision-making autonomy; classed by the expression/association mechanism.

items.h: Netpol launch Defend Dissent campaign in response to PCSC Act
items.b: With the passage of the Police Bill giving police significant new powers to suppress demonstrations, the Network for Police Monitoring have launched their ‘Defend Dissent’ campaign to support grassroots groups and find new ways of challenging the Act “in the courts and on the streets”. They have also published a new guide to police surveillance detailing how protest movements can stay safe in the face of increased police intelligence gathering.
items.why: a campaign responding to expanded police powers over protest and surveillance directly concerns the legal and practical space to dissent.
items.note: The new campaign and guide are also a capacity-building resource for civic participation, but the driving issue is protest policing and surveillance.

items.h: Bill of Rights to hit minority groups hardest according to campaigners
items.b: Plans to replace the Human Rights Act with a new Bill of Rights ‘will hit marginalised communities hardest’ according to Liberty Director, Martha Spurrier, and will have wide-reaching ramifications on Black and ethnic minority rights who ‘ already face huge disparities in the criminal justice system ’, according to The Runnymede Trust .
items.why: replacing the Human Rights Act is reported as reducing equal legal protection for marginalised groups.
items.note: Equal protection/discrimination framing places this in rights rather than rule of law, though judicial redress is also implicated.
links: already face huge disparities in the criminal justice system

items.h: Levelling-up and Regeneration Bill promises to expand devolution settlement
items.b: Introduced with the aim of bolstering struggling regions and rebalancing regional inequality, the Levelling-up and Regeneration Bill promises to expand the existing devolution settlement throughout England to ‘every part of England that wants a strong devolution deal’.
items.why: expanding devolution deals changes the structure of local and regional decision-making power across England.
items.note: Devolution structure stories are classed under elections & decision making per the framework.

items.h: Online workshop: Better collaboration between academics and democracy practitioners
items.b: Prof. Graham Smith of the University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy and George Bolton at the Centre for Democracy , are running the second of two half-day workshops to help develop the tools and guidance needed for building long-lasting productive cross-sectoral relationships. You do not need to have participated in the first workshop to attend the second. Register your interest .
items.note: A professional networking workshop between academics and practitioners is sector logistics, not a mechanism affecting public power or participation.
links: Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: Sheffield talks the Future of Democracy
items.b: On 21st May at Sheffield Town Hall, Democracy Network, Citizen Network, Neighbourhood Democracy Movement, and so many more, are coming together to shine a light on our democratic futures . To top off the day, Dr Simon Duffy , President of the Citizen Network, will be speaking alongside Jackie Weaver and New Citizenship Project thinker Jon Alexander.
items.note: This is an event listing/discussion rather than a new tool, resource or mechanism that changes what people can do.
links: coming together to shine a light on our democratic futures

items.h: Democracy Drinks Sheffield, following the Future of Democracy Hub Day
items.b: Following on from the Future of Democracy Hub Day on 21st May, the Democracy Network will be hosting Democracy Drinks Sheffield at the Showroom Cinema (5.30–7pm). This is an opportunity to hear lightning talks from local organisations and speakers, as well as to connect and catch up with existing contacts within the democracy sector. Tickets are free and can be ordered here .
items.note: Social/networking event listing, not a democracy mechanism story.
links: Tickets are free and can be ordered here

items.h: I Have A Voice launch new campaign programme
items.b: Rebecca Deegan and their team at I Have A Voice are launching a new scheme ‘Changes Lives Take Social Action’ . The scheme is aimed at helping young people who live, work or study in Lambeth learn how to campaign and encourage others to take action in their communities. Starting in July, the programme is free to join.
items.why: this creates a new programme helping young people learn to campaign and mobilise others, expanding practical means of civic participation.

items.h: Apolitical report: Better Leaders, Better Democracies
items.b: Apolitical have launched their new report mapping actors and incubators that help shape political leadership around the world. The 10 month global research highlighted the role of Elect Her , Activate Collective and the Patchwork Foundation operating in the UK.
items.note: A mapping report about sector actors, not a resource or mechanism that changes what people can do.

items.h: Constitution Society book launch: ‘How Democracies Live’
items.b: Join the The Constitution Society next Thursday 26th May for Prof. Stein Ringen’s launch of their new book How Democracies Live: Power, Statecraft, and Freedom in Modern Societies . Prof. Ringen is a Visiting Professor with the Department of Political Economy at King’s College London. Register now .
items.note: Book launch event listing.
links: How Democracies Live: Power, Statecraft, and Freedom in Modern Societies

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation National Campaign Awards tomorrow
items.b: On the 19th of May the Sheila McKechnie Foundation will be hosting their National Campaign Awards to celebrate the best campaigns and campaigners across the UK. In anticipation of the event you can check out the full awards shortlist and can book a free place at the event to see who has made the most effective and creative change this year.
items.note: Awards ceremony event listing.

items.h: PSA Parliaments co-host launch of new book on accountability and the constitution
items.b: On Wednesday 8th of June, the Political Studies Association Specialist Group on Parliaments will co-host the launch of Chris Monaghan’s new book Accountability, Impeachment and the Constitution . The book explores the case for a modernised impeachment process to make politics more transparent and accountable. No registration is needed and the event is free so don’t miss out.
items.note: Book launch event listing, not itself reporting a change in accountability mechanisms.
links: Political Studies Association Specialist Group on Parliaments

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Foundation hiring three Principal Policy Advisors
items.b: JRF are looking for three Principal Policy Advisors to help them advance and shape the national conversation on poverty. The work will involve convening new ideas, agendas and perspectives on the drivers of poverty and helping JRF exert influence at the highest levels of government. Deadline for applications is May 30th.
items.note: Job advert, organisational news.

items.h: Onward looking for a paid intern to join them for six months
items.b: The intern will help out with policy research and data analysis as well as some events and marketing tasks. The successful candidate will get a chance to work across a wide range of programmes at Onward, so do share with anyone looking to make a start in policy research. Deadline is May 24th.
items.note: Job advert, organisational news.

items.h: Upcoming conference on democratic backsliding in Oxford this weekend
items.b: On the 21st of May, the University of Oxford will host an in-person and online conference on democratic resilience in Europe and the US. Three separate panels will focus on the growth of illiberal populism, the challenges to democratic participation, and strategies for democratic resilience. The event is free to attend so register your interest and save the date.
items.note: Academic conference listing/event notice.

items.h: CitizenLab publish guide on how to set up a community engagement committee
items.b: Brussels-based CitizenLab have released a new guide on how to set up a community assembly. In the guide you’ll find lots of information on the theory behind community engagement, how it reduces polarisation, and the steps involved in setting up a committee yourself.
items.why: this provides a practical resource for setting up deliberative community assemblies, a form of decision-making machinery beyond elections.
items.note: Deliberative/assembly-style processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework, though the capacity-building angle also touches participation.

items.h: Labour — Lib Dem electoral pact in the works?
items.b: Despite rebuttals by Keir Starmer and Ed Davey to any suggestion of a pact, the Liberal Democrats have declared their intention to campaign in only one of this summer’s byelections — Tiverton and Honiton, the seat of disgraced Conservative MP Neil Parish. Labour is expected to do the reverse, backing off in Tiverton and prioritising Wakefield, the former seat of another disgraced and convicted Conservative MP, Imran Ahmad Khan.
items.why: this matters democratically because informal pacts between opposition parties shape voters' choices and the competitiveness of elections.
links: campaign in only one of this summer’s byelections

items.h: Labour and Lib Dem pact could deliver majority without need for SNP, reports Best for Britain polling
items.b: New polling by the team at Best for Britain suggests Labour could fall short of a majority despite a drop in Conservative support in the wake of the partygate scandal and cost of living crisis. The report suggests that if opposition parties worked together at the next election, they would be able to comfortably command a majority and produce a coalition government, without the need for SNP support.
items.why: this matters democratically because polling on opposition cooperation bears on political competition and prospects of alternation in government.

items.h: Local Government Information Unit provide round-up of local election results
items.b: The LGiU have published an election results summary to help comprehend the impact and changes of the more than 6,000 councillors elected in recent weeks. You can also view their final election bulletin for more highlights and analysis of the elections.
items.why: this matters democratically because analysis of local election results speaks to the representativeness of elected local government.
items.note: Treated as substantive election-results analysis rather than mere event/resource listing.

items.h: Democracy Club publish English local elections data
items.b: Democracy Club’s election and candidate datasets cover all of the English local elections and the 111 individual parties that took part.
items.why: this matters democratically because open datasets on candidates and parties increase transparency of electoral competition.

items.h: First Past the Post voting warped local election results say ERS
items.b: The elections in England and Wales were marred by ‘the distorting winner-takes-all voting system’, according to the Electoral Reform Society . Beyond the immediate issue this system creates in terms of representation, ERS have also highlighted that ‘one-party councils’ could be wasting £2.6bn annually due to the lack of proper scrutiny over their procurement process.
items.why: this matters democratically because the choice of electoral system affects the representativeness of councils and, per ERS, undermines scrutiny of one-party administrations.

items.h: Reform Political Advertising publish 2022 local elections campaign ads report
items.b: Reform Political Advertising have published a full report of ads and campaigns that contained misleading information during the 2022 Local Elections. They have also set up an Election Advertising Review Panel, chaired by Lord Puttham, which will continue to review factual claims made during elections to judge whether they are being honestly and factually represented. Watch Lord Puttham talking about the project in this short clip .
items.why: this matters democratically because misleading campaign advertising and new oversight of it affect voters' access to accurate information during elections.
items.note: Political advertising is anchored to information_debate rather than elections despite the electoral context.

items.h: Bristol votes to abolish elected mayor
items.b: Just 10 years after voting to bring in the directly elected mayor, the role will now be scrapped and replaced with a committee system, the Bristol Cable reports . 59.3% of Bristol voters opted to abolish the current system with a 28.6% turnout. The anti-mayor campaign was a joint effort dominated by Green, Lib Dem and Tory councillors in the city. Freshly re-elected Bristol Mayor Marvin Rees, disappointed at the result, is concerned about the visibility and accountability of politicians in the city under the committee system. The Bristol Civic Leadership Project recently published a report on …
items.why: this matters democratically because a referendum changed the structure and accountability of local decision-making in Bristol.

items.h: Councils for PR launch next week
items.b: Make Votes Matter (MVM) & GET PR DONE! (GPRD) are teaming up for a new campaign — Councils for PR (C4PR) — to encourage councils to declare their support for proportional representation for Parliamentary elections. In a joint statement, Holly Morgan-Davies of MVM and Alan Story of GPRD have called for greater “co-operative and collaborative politics” within electoral reform projects to mirror the principles espoused by the movement. Join their launch event next Monday 23rd May .
items.why: this matters democratically because the campaign seeks to change the electoral system used for parliamentary elections.
links: Join their launch event next Monday 23rd May

items.h: British Youth Council teams up with the Body Shop to lower the voting age
items.b: The British Youth Council are renewing efforts to lobby politicians to lower the voting age to 16+. They’ve teamed up with the Body Shop to do so who are running their #BeSeenBeHeard campaign calling for a reduction to the national voting age and encouraging young people to speak out about issues that affect them.
items.why: this matters democratically because lowering the voting age would directly expand the franchise.

items.h: The Constitution Unit looks back on Labour’s 1997 constitutional reform programme
items.b: Lord Falconer, Baroness Chakrabarti and Professor Robert Hazell, founding Director of the Constitution Unit , with chair Meg Russell, current Director of the Constitution Unit, will be looking back on Labour’s constitutional efforts 25 years on from the election of Tony Blair’s first Labour government. Register now .
items.note: Treated as an event listing/registration notice rather than substantive reporting.

items.h: Save the date — Participatory Budgeting Conference 2022 this September
items.b: PB Scotland have announced their annual conference for 28th September. Find out more and register on their website .
items.note: Event listing/save-the-date announcement, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Votes for Schools conducts poll on Partygate, voters overwhelmingly think Boris should go
items.b: 73–80% of school voters from 7–18 years old aligned on the view that the Prime Minister should have resigned and should not have broken the rules. 76% of younger primary school voters aged 5–7 voted ‘no’ when asked “is it ever okay to break the rules?” Sam Welsh, Penny Lamb and the Votes for Schools team polled more than 35,022 school age voters between 22nd — 29th April.
items.note: A private poll of schoolchildren's opinions is not itself a democratic mechanism story.
links: polled more than 35,022 school age voters

items.h: Tory MP arrested on suspicion of rape and banned from Commons
items.b: A Conservative MP has been banned from the Commons after arrest on suspicion of rape. The MP is as yet unnamed. Scotland Yard reports , “a man was arrested on suspicion of indecent assault, sexual assault, rape, abuse of position of trust and misconduct in a public office.”
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether an elected official can be held to standards of conduct and lawful behaviour, and how Parliament responds institutionally to serious alleged wrongdoing by a sitting MP.

items.h: Simon Burall considers methods to involve the public in the Covid Inquiry
items.b: Senior Associate at Involve , Simon Burall , suggests a role for mini-publics within the UK Covid-19 Inquiry. The inquiry has just completed its draft Terms of Reference after a four week consultation with bereaved families and experts.
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes deliberative mini-publics as a mechanism for direct public input into the design of the Covid Inquiry, a form of collective decision-making machinery.
items.note: Deliberative/mini-public proposals are classed under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: Reports of police violence as protesters thwart alleged immigration raids in London
items.b: Weeks after the rushed-through Nationality and Borders Bill emboldened immigration enforcement, Londoners rallied together this Saturday preventing an alleged immigration raid on delivery drivers. Journalists on scene, including those from the Financial Times and New Statesman , reported the use of violence on the crowd. Nine were arrested on violent disorder charge, with Met Police also investigating the actions of officers present at the protest. This follows similar actions earlier this month in Edinburgh.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns policing and alleged state violence in response to lawful protest, bearing on citizens' practical freedom to assemble and demonstrate against government action.
items.note: Protest policing/coercion falls under rights & freedoms rather than participation.

items.h: Open Government Partnership launches revised Skeptic’s Guide to Open Government
items.b: Produced by the Open Government Partnership’s Support Unit, The Skeptic’s Guide to Open Government provides an overview of the impacts of open government practices and a deeper view into the impacts of specific open government policies. First published in 2018, the Skeptic’s Guide is based on peer-reviewed research and provides a range of case studies of open government.
items.why: this matters democratically because the guide creates a resource intended to help civil society and officials understand and pursue open government practices, building capacity for civic oversight and engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource launch rather than organisational news.

items.h: Historic first as Sinn Féin set to re-establish executive
items.b: Sinn Féin secured the most seats in the assembly election , a first for a nationalist party north of the border. As a result, Michelle O’Neill is set to become First Minister, should the DUP nominate a Deputy First Minister. Since the partition of Ireland in 1921, unionist parties have always been the largest in the Assembly, and previously, the Stormont Parliament. See this Constitution Unit Twitter thread for more details.
items.why: this matters democratically because an election outcome has, for the first time, given a nationalist party the largest share of seats and thus the right to lead the devolved executive, marking a shift in the transfer of power.
links: Sinn Féin secured the most seats in the assembly election

items.h: New podcast sheds light on politics and power-sharing in Northern Ireland
items.b: If you’re feeling a bit puzzled by the implications of the elections in Northern Ireland, or just want a deeper dive into how the political system works, then check out this new episode of the Uncovering Politics podcast from the UCL School of Public Policy. The new episode — Politics in Northern Ireland — tackles the question of whether power-sharing can return and what the election means for the future of Northern Ireland.
items.note: Podcast promotion is explanatory media content, not a capacity-building tool or reported change.

items.h: ERS: We can revive local democracy in Scotland
items.b: As part of the Our Democracy coalition, ERS Scotland director Willie Sullivan and James Mitchell, professor of public policy at the University of Edinburgh, co-authored a pamphlet By us and for us: How Scottish local democracy can build and strengthen community . The pamphlet sets out a vision of how citizens can revive local democracy in Scotland.
items.why: this matters democratically because the pamphlet sets out proposals to restructure and strengthen local government and community decision-making power in Scotland.
items.note: Local government structure and powers fall under elections & decision making per framework.
links: By us and for us: How Scottish local democracy can build and strengthen community

items.h: Shadow Minister for Levelling Up to discuss Labour’s plan for devolution
items.b: During a speech on inequality on the 25th of May, Labour’s Alex Norris, Shadow Minister for Levelling Up, will address the Labour Party’s approach to devolution. Tickets are free and the event will be streamed online.
items.note: Event listing announcing a future speech, not itself a substantive report on devolution policy or change.

items.h: Torbay Council Conservative leader ‘breached code of conduct’
items.b: A Torbay councillor who was found to have bullied a council officer in a Zoom meeting has “stepped back” from all their roles on council committees, with their party’s group leader also having been found guilty of breaking council code of conduct. Reported by BBC Local Democracy Reporter Joe Ives , the story has been picked up by the BBC .
items.why: holding an elected local councillor accountable for a code-of-conduct breach against a public officer tests whether standards in public life are enforced at the local government level.

items.h: Cummings exposes Cash for Content Scandal
items.b: Byline Times reports on new testimony from the Prime Minister’s former chief aide uncovering a special subsidy arrangement for the Mail group, Mirror group, Murdoch group and Telegraph group. “Dressed up as COVID relief”, the subsidies were awarded to the four wealthy newspaper groups at the height of the pandemic, budgeted at more than £35m for the first three months.
items.why: undisclosed government subsidies to major newspaper groups risk compromising media independence and the plural information environment citizens rely on to scrutinise power.
items.note: Touches both media capture (information) and undue government-private influence (accountability); classified by the media-independence mechanism.

items.h: British Library to host event on compassion and honesty in news media
items.b: The British Library will host a discussion on the 11th of June on how we can create a trustworthy, independent and compassionate media to meet the challenges of the present. Joined by a panel of speakers from different branches of the media, Jennifer Nadel, CEO of Compassion in Politics , will chair the debate on whether journalism can be de-toxified. The event will not be live streamed so book now for an in-person spot.
items.note: Event listing about journalism ethics, not a reported change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: 96% of the public the oppose privatisation of Channel Four
items.b: A public consultation on the privatisation of Channel Four received 56,000 public responses, with 96% opposing the government’s plans and favouring a continuation of public ownership. Channel Four has since released plans to relocate their HQ out of London as an alternative to privatisation in a bid to appeal to the government’s levelling-up agenda.
items.why: the ownership structure of a major public service broadcaster affects media plurality and public access to diverse, independent information.

items.h: New Manifesto for a People’s Media released by the Media Reform Coalition
items.b: Concentrated media ownership, commercial constraints and political interference present major challenges to the independence of UK media, reports Declassified UK . The newly released Manifesto for a People’s Media from the Media Reform Coalition seeks to address this with a new framework for a publicly owned, independent media commons. They suggest this new framework will help build a more participatory media orientated towards the public interest.
items.why: concentrated media ownership and political interference in journalism constrain the plural public debate that democratic accountability depends on.

items.h: JRRT back Proportional Representation work with funding surge
items.b: Make Votes Matter has been awarded £300,000 over three years to upscale their campaign. Labour for a New Democracy has received £150,000 for an 18-month period to boost their work on achieving a PR manifesto commitment from the Labour Party. Find out more about recent funding awards from the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust and apply today.
items.note: A funding award notice to advocacy organisations, treated as sector funding logistics rather than a new means of participation.

items.h: Racial equity and complex social issues funding by Lloyds Bank Foundation
items.b: Applications for Lloyds Bank Foundation’s unrestricted funding are still open. They’re offering funding for small and local charities in England and Wales. Visit the website to check eligibility and apply for funding under one of eleven complex social issue subjects, or racial equity. It’s specifically looking to fund charities led by Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic communities.
items.note: Funding call notice, sector logistics.

items.h: European Parliament elections reform backs pan-European MEPs, spitzenkandidaten process
items.b: In the first major European election reform for some time, EU citizens may soon be able to vote for pan-European candidates. With pan-Euro candidates means the increased visibility of pan-European parties and pan-European debate, proponents of the reform argue. Whilst the reform has the backing of the European Parliament, opponents of the measure are relying on the European Council to water down the proposals. The proposed rules include adoption of the Spitzenkandidaten process for president of the Commission.
items.note: European Parliament electoral reform does not bear directly on UK democracy and falls outside the geographic scope.
