Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Rebecca Deegan — Founder at I Have A Voice, Sam Welsh — Partnerships Coordinator at Votes for Schools, Myfanwy Nixon — Marketing & Communications Manager at mySociety, Titus Alexander — Founder at Democracy Matters, Harry Wells — Research Assistant at Commission on Political Power, Trin Gong — Events Assistant at Radix Big Tent and Perry Walker — Co-Founder at Talk Shop.
items.note: Thanks/attendee list for an org's own event, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.b: With just over a year since we launched the Centre for Democracy , it is one year since we launched the Ecosystem Pledge, now backed by 72 signatory organisations, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: A pledge among sector organisations to coordinate is organisational/networking news, not a new means of public participation.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.
items.note: Sector self-description of collaboration intent, not a democracy mechanism.

items.b: If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .
items.note: Call to action to sign a pledge with no substantive content; sector admin.

items.h: New research briefings on Public Order Bill
items.b: The Public Order Bill was recently introduced to parliament raising concerns from campaigners about what they see as a continued assault on the right to protest. The Network for Police Monitoring and The House of Commons Library have released detailed briefings on protest and police powers and what the new bill will mean for the relationship between the two.
items.why: this matters democratically because the Public Order Bill expands police powers over protest, directly affecting citizens' ability to assemble and dissent from government policy.
items.note: Protest policing framed as legal restriction/state coercion falls under rights, not participation.

items.h: Online Safety Bill opportunities for collaboration
items.b: Are you working on the Online Safety Bill? Be sure not to miss Fair Vote UK’s weekly digest of news and updates relating to the Bill’s passage. RVSP for their weekly OSB Office Hours Zoom calls and sign up to the digest by emailing Matt Gallagher .
items.note: Sector networking notice about a digest/office hours, not substantive reporting on the Bill itself.

items.h: Full Fact start letter writing campaign to highlight the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Full Fact has kicked off a ‘Write to your MP’ campaign on the OSB — Please amplify if you can
items.why: this matters democratically because it mobilises citizens to petition their elected representatives on legislation shaping the information environment.
items.note: Letter-writing campaign to MPs treated as civic petitioning/participation.

items.h: Spend a day working alongside fellow democracy organisations
items.b: On June 29th, The Centre for Democracy are hosting a Democracy Co-Working Day at Newspeak House in London. Our first co-working day was such fun — with more than 20 organisations joining to hang out and work together — that we’re putting on another one. Don’t miss out, RSVP now to give us a better idea of numbers on the day and add a calendar reminder .
items.note: Sector social/networking event among organisations, not affecting public participation.

items.h: The State of the Constitution: Constitution Unit Conference 2022, 22–23 June
items.b: In partnership with the Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law, UK in a Changing Europe (UKICE) and the Oxford Constitutional Leaders Forum , The Constitution Unit has announced its annual State of the Constitution conference. Free to attend and continuing to take place virtually, the programme touches upon Brexit and the NI Protocol, the Johnson Government’s approach to constitutional standards, the role of the courts, the decline of parliamentary scrutiny and the future of devolution — a packed schedule for a period of growing constitutional tension and unease. Book your ticket now .
items.note: Conference/event listing, not itself substantive reporting despite covering constitutional topics.
links: Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law,

items.h: Make Votes Matter to hold National Action Day for Proportional Representation
items.b: Make Votes Matter are holding a national day of action on Saturday June 11th . They’re teaming up with Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform to build grassroots momentum behind the shift to PR.
items.why: this matters democratically because it is a campaign to change the electoral system to proportional representation, affecting how votes translate into political power.
items.note: Electoral system reform campaign classed under elections rather than general participation.
links: national day of action on Saturday June 11th

items.h: I Have A Voice launch applications for mentoring, plan event on compulsory voting
items.b: On the 21st of June, I Have A Voice will be hosting a discussion with Kim Leadbeater, MP for Batley and Spen, on whether voting should be made compulsory. Email Rebecca , Founder of I Have A Voice, to book your spot for this London event. IHAV have just opened applications for their 9-month mentoring scheme, find out more .
items.why: this matters democratically because the launch of a new mentoring scheme creates a new means for people to build capacity for democratic participation.
items.note: Mentoring scheme launch counts as sector capacity-building; compulsory voting discussion is secondary turnout angle.

items.h: Votes for Schools looking for a Content Developer
items.b: The role involves planning for and developing weekly VotePacks on various issues, helping VfS deliver polls in hundreds of schools across the UK. Find out more and apply here , deadline June 10th.
items.note: Job advert, organisational admin.

items.h: Join mySociety’s upcoming TICTeC sessions
items.b: Whilst their last TICTeC sesion was focused on amplifying the reach of civic tech, their next is focused on climate and societal change, with the next after that on civic tech in hostile environments . mySociety are also hiring a Python Developer , deadline June 6th.
items.note: Event listing and job advert, organisational admin.

items.h: New report from Demos explores democratisation of digital infrastructure
items.b: All too frequently liberal democracies have failed to articulate the principles of a democratic digital infrastructure, according to DEMOS . So for the past eighteen months they’ve been exploring the question of what a ‘good internet’ looks like. Their latest report , part of the Good Web Project , explores how a publicly owned digital infrastructure could nurture a democratic internet culture that is vital to sustaining liberal democracy itself.
items.why: the ownership and structure of digital infrastructure shapes the plurality and openness of the information environment citizens rely on for public debate.

items.h: Talk Shop developing new decision making method
items.b: The Win-Win Workout is a new face to face decision making tool. They’re currently testing a version on nuclear power and net zero, with their first public outing at Radix Big Tent Festival on the 11th June (below). They’re planning a new session on the BBC License Fee.
items.why: new face-to-face deliberative decision-making tools create additional machinery through which citizens can take part in collective decisions.
items.note: Deliberative decision-making tools are classified under elections & decision making, not participation, per framework anchoring.

items.h: Radix Big Tent Festival is almost here
items.b: In Bristol, next Saturday 11th June — Check the programme and book your tickets now . Radix are also looking for a Virtual Office Manager, details here .
links: Check the programme and book your tickets now

items.h: DemSoc work with LSE Students’ Union to improve democratic engagement
items.b: LSE Students’ Union are undertaking a rigorous Democracy Review to improve the democratic structure of their organisation. DemSoc have been helping them organise a Democracy Summit to gather and learn from the experiences of students at the university which will now be reviewed and turned into a set of workable recommendations for a new and inclusive democratic structure.
items.why: creating a new democratic structure and process for student engagement expands the means by which members can take part in collective decisions affecting them.
items.note: Treated as civic-engagement capacity building rather than formal electoral machinery since it concerns an internal student union structure.

items.h: Alliance of Democracies’ Democracy Perception Index 2022 published
items.b: The Democracy Perception Index is the largest annual study on attitudes to democracy, covering more than 50 countries and polling over 50,000 people, representing more than 75% of the global population. More than 84% of those polled believe democracy it is important their country is a democracy, though 41% feel that there is not enough democratisation within their country. More than 91% of African respondents and more than 80% of Latin American respondents viewed corruption as a threat to their democracy. Economic equality topped the poll as the single biggest threat to democracy around the wo…
items.why: global public attitudes toward democracy, corruption and economic equality reflect the underlying support and perceived legitimacy that sustain democratic systems.

items.h: Commission on Political Power publish Head of State options paper
items.b: The Commission on Political Power , led by Frances Crook, Baroness Frances D’Souza and Graham Allen, is an independent commission tasked with reviewing the British political system and suggesting a new roadmap aimed at enhancing democracy and legitimacy within the system. The new options paper, Head of State , presents six potential paths for reforming the UK’s head of state.
items.why: proposals to reform the head of state role touch on the constitutional conventions and structures that constrain and legitimise executive power.
items.note: Head of state reform sits between constitutional accountability and decision-making structures; classified primarily as government accountability.

items.h: Republican groups mobilise around the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee
items.b: The Scottish cross-party group, Our Republic , are set to host a rally calling for the establishment of a Republic in Scotland after a poll found that only a minority of Scots support the retention of the monarchy. Meanwhile, campaign group Republic are due to host their first International Anti-Monarchy Conference .
items.why: organised rallies and conferences advocating constitutional change reflect citizens' willingness to mobilise and campaign within civic life.

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy table 2022 conference motion calling for Proportional Representation
items.b: The new motion demands that the Labour party commits to implementing PR in their next manifesto, that they change the electoral system to PR during their first term in office, and that an ‘open and inclusive’ process for deciding on an appropriate electoral system is introduced. L4ND are encouraging all other Constituency Labour Parties to back the motion.
items.why: a proposal to change the electoral system to proportional representation directly affects how votes translate into political power.

items.h: New Local Poll finds strong public support for locally-led solutions
items.b: A poll from New Local has found a widespread lack of faith in politicians to solve local issues. 79% said Westminster and Whitehall were taking decisions ‘about people and places they know little about’ whilst 73% said politicians should transfer more power to local areas to tackle issues themselves. New Local are one of a number of organisations that have pledged support for the New Community Power Act in a bid to provide greater regional autonomy. Finally, if you’re interested in joining the team at New Local, they are hiring a Senior Communications Officer.
items.why: public support for transferring power to local areas concerns the structure and authority of local and regional decision-making tiers.
items.note: Local/regional devolution story classified under elections & decision making per boundary rule on structure and powers of sub-national government.

items.h: ‘It’s a bad day for democracy’ — Sue Gray report released
items.b: The Sue Gray report released last Wednesday confirms that a culture of partying and impunity over lockdown measures derived from the top of Government. The senior civil servant wrote ‘the senior leadership at the centre, both political and official, must bear responsibility’ for the ‘culture’ at the ‘heart of government’. Will Walden, Johnson’s former press secretary, called it ‘a bad day for democracy’ , whilst opposition leader, Keir Starmer, said those involved had ‘treated the sacrifices of the British people with utter contempt.’ Unlock Democracy responded with launching a new petition ca…
items.why: the report exposes failures of ministerial and civil service accountability at the heart of government, undermining standards in public life.
links: ‘treated the sacrifices of the British people with utter contempt.’

items.h: #StopTheRot campaign kicks off calling for greater parliamentary accountability
items.b: The #StopTheRot campaign kicked off on Sunday 15th of May calling for an end to the ‘rotten politics’ in the UK and backing a petition to have the ministerial code re-written to allow greater scrutiny over the actions of a sitting Prime Minister. Organised by Open Britain , the petition currently has over 19,000 signatures.
items.why: it seeks to strengthen scrutiny mechanisms over the executive by rewriting the ministerial code that governs prime ministerial accountability.
items.note: Petition is the vehicle but the substance is executive accountability via the ministerial code.

items.h: Labour accused of breaking rules on selection of parliamentary candidates in Wakefield by-election
items.b: The Labour Party stands accused of breaking their own rules in the selection process of a new candidate for the upcoming Wakefield by-election after the local party received only one of five seats on the panels for longlisting and then shortlisting candidates. The entire 16-person executive of the Wakefield constituency Labour Party (CLP) has resigned over the handling of the process, stating that several strong candidates with local roots were overlooked in the selection process.
items.why: disputes over internal candidate selection processes affect the fairness and openness of political parties in choosing who can stand for election.
links: accused of breaking their own rules

items.h: Current Elections Act implementation timelines optimistic at best, undeliverable at worst, states AEA Chief
items.b: Peter Stanyon, Chief Executive of the Association of Electoral Administrators , has written to Minister Kemi Badenoch, the current minister responsible for elections. Mr Stanyon reports on the success of the elections process but reports ‘our already straining democratic systems are close to becoming undeliverable’. Read the letter here . Peter Stanyon also wrote to Mick Antoniw MS on the challenging years ahead for electoral administration in Wales.
items.why: strained electoral administration capacity threatens the reliable delivery of well-run elections.

items.h: Labour mulls removing council leaders to improve electoral performance
items.b: Stirring the ire of local party activists, the party announced plans to introduce Campaign Improvement Boards (CIBs) to deal with ‘underperforming’ local groups. Whilst the primary aim of the CIBs will be to support local groups that need improvement, NEC member Gemma Bolton has accused the party leadership of an ‘anti-democratic stitch up’, suppressing local party democracy.
items.why: internal party mechanisms for removing local leaders bear on the freedom and internal democracy of political parties contesting elections.
items.note: Concerns internal party democracy, which the framework files under free political parties.

items.h: Funding from Activate helps secure electoral success for women in local elections
items.b: Activate has been busy providing financial support for women in their local election campaign bids. Four of their grantees, Nanouche Umeadi , Simita Kumar , Martha Matthos Coelho and Jo Elson , were successfully elected and many more received assistance in their campaigns. Activate are also funding a number of women as part of their ‘Activists Fund’ — meet the recipients and check out the great work they are doing with the vital funding injection.
items.why: targeted campaign funding affects candidate access and the representativeness of elected bodies, including the proportion of women elected.

items.h: Comprehensive digest of Northern Ireland elections released
items.b: The House of Commons Library has released a detailed research briefing exploring the political context behind the Northern Ireland election. The Centre on Constitutional Change has released a new podcast exploring the significance and outcome of the election.

items.h: SNP and Green Party forge working agreement for running Glasgow City Council
items.b: May’s local elections saw the Scottish Green Party become the third largest on Glasgow City Council, gaining three seats and overtaking the Conservatives. Negotiations on a working agreement with the SNP will now see the formation of an SNP minority administration, with the Green Party taking on a number of key roles within the Council. Cllr Martha Wardrop, Glasgow’s Green Co-Convenor noted ‘With our largest ever group of Green councillors, we will hold a minority SNP administration to account while working collaboratively across party lines to deliver a fairer, greener and more inclusive Glas…
items.why: the formation of a council administration through inter-party agreement determines how local government power is exercised after an election.
items.note: Story concerns the structure of local government administration formed after elections.
links: formation of an SNP minority administration,

items.h: Local Government Association annual conference, 28–30 June
items.b: The LGA are holding their annual conference in Harrogate this year on the 28–30th June. The Association of Electoral Administrators , Association of Democratic Services Officers , Local Government Information Unit , Center for Governance and Scrutiny , DemSoc and Lawyers in Local Government will be delivering a new Democracy Hub as part of the conference. More details soon.

items.h: We’re Right Here publish plans for a New Community Power Act
items.b: The new act will ‘fundamentally change where power lies in this country’ , by establishing new community rights, creating a power-sharing arrangement between councils and communities, and establishing a Community Power Commissioner to ensure government action is taken. We’re Right Here have dubbed this ‘the missing piece of the devolution puzzle’ , as it will build a ‘clear and trusted track’ through which power can be devolved.
items.why: proposals to create new community rights and power-sharing arrangements would expand the practical means by which communities can take part in local decision-making.
items.note: Touches both community participation mechanisms and local government structure.
links: ‘fundamentally change where power lies in this country’
‘the missing piece of the devolution puzzle’

items.h: IMPRESS call on government to retain publisher protections
items.b: The Government recently announced plans to repeal section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act 2013 through the media bill. CEO of IMPRESS , Ed Procter, has urged the government to re-think their plans, suggesting the proposed changes will fail to protect both news publishers from ‘exorbitant lawsuits brought about by those with vast wealth and power’, and the public from intrusion from the press.
items.why: repealing publisher protections affects the ability of the press to operate free from costly legal threats, shaping the public information environment.

items.h: Index file Council of Europe alert as journalists excluded from Home Secretary’s visit to Rwanda
items.b: Journalists from The Guardian, Financial Times, The Mirror, and others were excluded from a press trip made by the Home Secretary to Rwanda in mid-April. A number of newspapers have criticised the move suggesting this was a deliberate attempt to limit journalistic scrutiny over a set of controversial policies. Index On Censorship have filed a Council of Europe alert to formally express their concern.
items.why: restricting journalist access to a ministerial visit limits the press's ability to scrutinise government policy, undermining the public information environment.
items.note: Press access restriction sits at the boundary of press freedom and government transparency; classified as information_debate given the focus on journalistic exclusion.
links: were excluded from a press trip
Index On Censorship have filed a Council of Europe alert

items.h: Media Reform Coalition publish briefing on White Paper on the future of the broadcasting sector
items.b: The Department for Media, Culture and Sport’s White Paper on the future of the broadcasting sector represents a ‘concerted ideological attack on public service media in the UK’, according to the Media Reform Coalition . In a new briefing , they outline the proposed upcoming changes and their implications for the sector.
items.why: changes to public service broadcasting regulation affect media plurality and the public's access to diverse political information.

items.h: Shortlist for Freedom of Expression Awards announced
items.b: Index on Censorship have announced their nominees for the Freedom of Expression Awards celebrating artists, journalists and campaigners who risk their personal safety and wellbeing in order to champion free expression. Awards will be categorised according to arts, journalism and campaigning and the ceremony will take place in London on the 27th of October.
items.note: Award nominations are organisational news, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.h: Esmée Fairburn Foundation funding stream closed until Autumn
items.b: Esmée Fairburn Foundation have postponed the re-opening of their ‘A Fairer Future’ funding scheme until the autumn. The scheme will work towards the twin goals of challenging structural inequality and creating a new inclusive generation of leaders and artists. Stay up to date on all funding developments and opportunities via their Twitter page.
items.note: Funding scheme administrative timing is sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust makes grants of £6m in latest funding
items.b: The latest round of grant-making at JRCT has seen £6m allocated to a range of social, political and democratic projects . Funding applications will now temporarily close until November whilst the trust undergoes organisational changes. Follow them on Twitter for updates on this process. JRCT are also hiring a Grassroots Movements Programme Manager (Job Share 3 days per week) to help co-design a new funding stream to support social movements.
items.note: Grant round and hiring notice are organisational administration, not a new participation mechanism.
links: £6m allocated to a range of social, political and democratic projects

items.h: UN warns of ‘total societal collapse’ due to breaching of planetary boundaries
items.b: A landmark report by the United Nations concludes that ‘global collapse’ is becoming more likely . Despite these alarming statements, a senior advisor to the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, on condition of anonymity, told the Byline Times that the recent GAR2022 report was watered-down before public release and the published version represents an ‘eviscerated skeleton of what was included in earlier drafts’.
items.note: Report concerns environmental collapse risk, not a UK democratic mechanism.
links: A landmark report by the United Nations concludes that ‘global collapse’ is becoming more likely

This week we were joined by Josh Russell — Co founder at Forward Democracy, Kathleen Christie — Former Police Bill Alliance Convenor, Myf Nixon — Communications Manager at mySociety, Peter Keeling — Voting Information at Democracy Club, Gavin Barker — Lead on Democratic Reform at Citizen Network, Pilar Girvan — Communications and Advocacy Officer at Involve, Sam Welsh — Partnerships Coordinator at Votes for Schools, Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters, Colin Gordon — Grassroots for Europe, Oli Whittington — Nesta, Alex King …

The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 72 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: A pledge of intent to collaborate among sector organisations is sector admin, not a new means of participation for the public.

If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .

items.h: Line-by-line scrutiny begins on Online Safety Bill
items.b: Carnegie UK’s submission to the Online Safety Bill Committee has now been published, alongside evidence from a wide array of civil society and tech representatives covering topics from protection of children , consumers, women and girls, through to democratic harms and journalism exemptions. The Chair of the Joint Human Rights Committee, Harriet Harman, has written to the Secretary of State for DCMS to ask for clarification on a number of points relating to the definitions and scope of illegal content, “legal but harmful” and the protections for freedom of expression.
items.why: the Online Safety Bill's provisions on illegal content, journalism exemptions and 'legal but harmful' speech will shape what information and viewpoints people can access and express online.
items.note: Focus is on freedom of expression/journalism protections in the information environment rather than parliamentary process itself.
links: submission to the Online Safety Bill Committee
written to the Secretary of State for DCMS

items.h: Online Safety Bill opportunities for collaboration
items.b: Are you working on the Online Safety Bill? Be sure not to miss Fair Vote UK’s weekly digest of news and updates relating to the Bill’s passage. RVSP for their weekly OSB Office Hours Zoom calls and sign up to the digest by emailing Matt Gallagher .

items.h: Sign on — Briefing on strengthening privacy and anonymity protections in the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Ellen Judson from Demos has shared a new briefing on the Online Safety Bill , if you would like to sign on please send Ellen your organisation’s logo by COB Wednesday 15th June.
items.note: This is a call to sign a briefing, which the framework treats as sector logistics rather than a reported story.
links: new briefing on the Online Safety Bill

items.h: Liberty poll finds strong opposition to increasing police powers
items.b: The government is going against the grain of public opinion, according to Liberty , with plans to introduce the Public Order Bill . Polling carried out by nfpResearch for Liberty found that 68% of the public think the government should tackle root causes of crime rather than expand police powers and 73% think the police should not use tactics that discriminate against people of colour. Liberty are also looking to hire a new Digital Content Assistant to support their Human Rights Act campaign #SaveYourRights .
items.why: public opinion on expanding police powers under the Public Order Bill bears directly on the legal limits placed on protest and assembly, a core civil liberty.
items.note: Focus is on police powers and policing of protest, not willingness to participate, so falls under rights rather than participation.

items.h: It’s time to shake up coalition campaigning, says former convenor of Police Bill Alliance
items.b: Kathleen Christie, Convenor of the Police Bill Alliance through the Bill’s turbulent passage, reports back on their learnings at the helm of the coalition. The Police Bill Alliance comprised some 350 organisations working to obstruct and oppose the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022.
items.note: A reflective account of one coalition's own campaigning practice, not a new participation mechanism or reported democratic change.

items.h: Democracy Network round up
items.b: On Wednesday 25th May 2022, the Democracy Network held its second ‘Development Day’ where members discussed key decisions on the direction of the network. Productive discussions around vision, mission, values and membership criteria are now being taken forward to be decided in advance of the major in-person public launch in autumn 2022. The network is also working on launching their social media channels and website for a digital public launch in the next few weeks.
items.note: Internal organisational governance and launch planning, not a democracy story.

items.h: Spend a day working alongside fellow democracy organisations
items.b: On June 29th, The Centre for Democracy are hosting a Democracy Co-Working Day at Newspeak House in London. Our first co-working day was such fun — with more than 20 organisations joining to hang out and work together — that we’re putting on another one. Don’t miss out, RSVP now to give us a better idea of numbers on the day and add a calendar reminder .

items.h: Votes for Schools hiring, reach 1 million votes across UK
items.b: Votes for Schools’ Partnerships Coordinator, Sam Welsh, reports that they have recently passed a major milestone of over 1,000,000 votes held in schools and colleges across the country. VfS are on the lookout for a Partnerships & Impact Manager, see more details here — deadline Wednesday 29th June.
items.note: Reports a milestone and a hiring notice for an existing programme rather than a new participation mechanism or democratic change.

items.h: Swap My Vote is back, crowdfunder launched
items.b: Josh Russell and the team at Swap My Vote have launched a new crowdfunder. As the summer by-elections approach, they’re looking to boost their impact, spreading the word via more channels, targeting local media and securing mainstream coverage of vote swapping. Give generously and share their crowdfunding appeal now .
items.why: Swap My Vote's relaunch and crowdfunder expands a tool that helps voters coordinate tactical voting around by-elections, affecting how electoral competition plays out.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating/relaunching a means of electoral participation.
links: Give generously and share their crowdfunding appeal now

items.h: Titus Alexander reflects on the work of the Democracy Matters coalition
items.b: Democracy Matters was set up in 2009 by Titus Alexander and a wider group of volunteers and partner organisations, including Unlock Democracy, Sheila McKechnie Foundation, the WEA, Involve and others. In this draft document , Titus reflects on the work of the coalition and how we can learn from it.
items.note: A retrospective reflection on a coalition's history, not a reported democratic change or new participation resource.

items.h: RebootGB are working on a new Alliance UK project
items.b: Alliance UK, a grouping of several democracy organisations, are aiming to bring together civil society actors, including the democracy community, to work out the aims and goals of a potential Progressive Alliance.
items.why: This matters democratically because forming an electoral alliance among parties would reshape political competition and voter choice.
items.note: Concerns early-stage coordination on party electoral strategy, so filed under parties/elections rather than participation.

items.h: Democracy Club are looking for a new CEO
items.b: Big changes at Democracy Club as they look for a new CEO to help them grow their reach into services that support everyday democracy. Democracy Club are also looking for a Python Developer to help improve their services ahead of the elections in May 2023. Deadlines for both roles are June 30th and there is a £500 referral bonus if you refer someone that ends up getting the job, so make sure you share far and wide!

items.h: The State of the Constitution: Constitution Unit Conference 2022, 22–23 June
items.b: In partnership with the Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law, UK in a Changing Europe (UKICE) and the Oxford Constitutional Leaders Forum , The Constitution Unit has announced its annual State of the Constitution conference. Free to attend and continuing to take place virtually, the programme touches upon Brexit and the NI Protocol, the Johnson Government’s approach to constitutional standards, the role of the courts, the decline of parliamentary scrutiny and the future of devolution — a packed schedule for a period of growing constitutional tension and unease. Book your ticket now .
items.note: Event listing, not a reported change or new participation tool.
links: Bingham Centre for the Rule of Law,

items.h: Journal of Democracy release 10 free papers from Co-founder Larry Diamond
items.b: The Journal of Democracy are marking the departure of co-founder Larry Diamond by releasing ten of his seminal contributions to the journal. Over a thirty-year period, Diamond penned numerous articles covering a wide range of democratic theory so be sure to check out these free papers as they are only available for a limited time.

items.h: New Local hiring for multiple roles
items.b: New Local are looking to hire a new Head of Policy and Research (23rd June deadline), Network Coordinator (June 29th deadline), Head of Network (30th June deadline) and a Head of Events (5th July deadline). Check out their job board for full details on all roles and how to apply.

items.h: Network for Police Monitoring and Article 11 Trust to hire Organising and Partnerships Coordinator
items.b: Netpol and the Article 11 Trust are looking for an Organising and Partnerships Coordinator to challenge and monitor the impact of the Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Act on the right to protest. The role will involve documenting the use of police power and creating campaign materials to promote the aims of the project. Deadline for applications is June 27th.
items.note: Job advert; organisational hiring news remains excluded even though the role concerns protest rights.
links: Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Act

items.h: Institute for Government host event on ‘Reinvigorating UK Democracy’
items.b: Earlier this week the Institute for Government hosted an event discussing how we can bridge the divide between citizens and representatives to include people more directly in decisions that affect their lives and communities. Sarah Castell, CEO of Involve , was joined by Miriam Levin, Programme Director at Engage Britain , Professor Jane Suiter, Director of Dublin City University’s Institute for Future Media, Democracy and Society , and Oli Whittington, Senior Researcher at the Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, Nesta , to explore some of the digital and political technologies that cou…
items.note: Report of an event discussion rather than a created tool, resource or reported change.
links: Dublin City University’s Institute for Future Media, Democracy and Society
Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, Nesta

items.h: First candidate comes forward for deputy leadership of the Green Party
items.b: Zack Polanksi, a London Assembly member since 2021, has announced they’re standing for position. Polanski’s pitch in the election focuses heavily on driving the party forward to achieve more representation in the House of Commons and in local government, as well committing to ‘embed diverse representation’ within the Green Party as a whole. A number of other candidates are expected to announce their intention in the next few days. Nominations for the deputy leader election close on June 30, with members voting throughout the summer.
items.why: This matters democratically because internal leadership elections determine how a political party is led and how competitive and representative it becomes.
items.note: Treated as party/electoral competition under Free Political Parties.
links: number of other candidates are expected to announce their intention

items.h: A flawed systems means a sense of fair play is missing in local elections, says Keith Best
items.b: Keith Best, Chairman of Conservative Action for Electoral Reform and a former Conservative MP, writes in Conservative Home on the impact of First Past The Post on electoral outcomes in local elections. Where Conservatives are gaining as much as 25% of the vote, such as in the borough of Oadby and Wigston, but only receiving 7% of the seats, a sense of fair play is missing. Local elections in England should be placed under review, argues Best, citing that ‘more competition is needed to drive up England’s democratic standards’. Well worth a read.
items.why: This matters democratically because the electoral system used in local elections determines how proportionately votes translate into seats and representation.

items.h: Shared Future CIC wins award
items.b: Their Social Housing Tenants’ Climate Jury , which they facilitated — led by Shared Future Associate Andy Paice — last year on behalf of the Northern Housing Consortium, was named Best Resident Involvement Initiative at this year’s Northern Housing Awards.
items.note: Award nomination/organisational news, excluded even though the underlying project involved a citizens' jury.

items.h: Councils for PR campaign gets off to a good start
items.b: On 23rd of May, Make Votes Matter and Get PR Done launched their Councils for PR campaign which aims to get local councils to back the shift to proportional representation. The event was attended by 195 people and C4PR report that their core group has nearly doubled to 22 members off the back of the launch. Email C4PR if you would also like to join the group, or follow them on Twitter for future updates from the campaign.
items.why: it concerns a campaign to change the electoral system used by local councils, directly affecting how representatives are chosen and political competition.

items.h: Add your organisation to Citizen Network’s Constitution Commission Public Letter
items.b: Back in December 2020 Gordon Brown reported that he had brought together Scottish and Welsh labour leaders and English mayors to work on a ‘new constitutional offer’ . Citizen Network’s public letter calls on Brown to divulge new information about the commission, and in particular, calls on Brown and the commission to consider utilising citizens’ assemblies where possible. If you/your organisation supports the devolution aims set out in the public letter , please consider signing it. Citizen Network are particularly keen on enlisting regional and local grassroots movements who see democratic r…
items.note: This is a call to sign a letter, which counts as sector logistics rather than a reportable democratic development.

items.h: Crowd Wisdom Project reports back on Pol.is conversations
items.b: Crowd Wisdom is a non-profit organisation specialising in the use of the Pol.is platform survey communities and to answer difficult questions. They have run over 30 Pol.is conversations, including 20 for just one area — Harrogate. Building on their experience with the Harrogate District Consensus project, Crowd Wisdom are now looking to franchise their model and increase the number of areas that can host Pol.is conversations in this way.
items.why: it involves expanding a deliberative platform that lets communities collectively work through difficult policy questions, which the framework treats as decision-making machinery.
items.note: Deliberative/consultative platforms are classed under elections & decision making, not participation, per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Citizens’ Panel deliberates home energy use and climate change
items.b: A Birmingham Citizens’ Panel is currently debating what the government and public can do to take action on climate change in their homes. The sessions have been administered by Shared Future CIC on behalf of Lancaster University and the Climate Change Committee who will use the findings to advise the government on policies to bring energy use in line with the need to tackle climate change.
items.why: a citizens' panel is a deliberative process feeding into government policy, which the framework anchors to decision-making machinery rather than participation.
items.note: Citizens' panels/assemblies are classed as decision-making machinery per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Participatory Budgeting Champions
items.b: A new SCQF Level 5 qualification — PB Champion — is now available to 750 young people to become PB champions in Fife, Scotland. Free places will be made available to those participants volunteering with PB and/or grant making processes in Scotland.
items.why: a new qualification creates a formal means for young people to take part in participatory budgeting and grant-making processes, expanding practical avenues for civic participation.

items.h: PB Scotland launches Green PB
items.b: Green PB aims to get people to make direct decisions about how budgets are spent, addressing climate change and reducing our carbon footprint.
items.why: it creates a new participatory budgeting scheme letting people make direct decisions over public spending, expanding practical means of civic participation.

items.h: Campaign to end deliberate lying by MPs is raised in parliament
items.b: A campaign has been launched by Compassion in Politics with over 200,000 signatures in support of new laws to prevent politicians from deliberately lying. Working with lawyers the group has drawn up a Lying in Politics Bill that would address accountability and trust in the House of Commons. Debbie Abrahams MP, Co-Chair of the All-Party Group for Compassion in Politics, recently raised the campaign in parliament calling for legislation that would “make lying to this House and to the people of this country, a sackable offence.”
items.why: a campaign for legislation against deliberate lying by MPs, raised in Parliament, concerns mechanisms for holding elected officials accountable and maintaining standards in public life.

items.h: Rob Ford makes the argument for why workers should back PR
items.b: British trade unions should back PR, argues University of Manchester political science professor, Rob Ford . Rob charts the growth of the PR cause within the trade union movement and its subsequent impact on similar political systems, such as New Zealand.
items.why: it argues for a change to the electoral system, which determines how votes translate into representation.

items.h: Support for British monarchy eroding, YouGov poll finds
items.b: According to a recent poll from YouGov , six in ten Britons (62%) think Britain should keep the monarchy, while just 22% say they want to transition to an elected head of state. Just 9% of Conservative voters think the monarchy should be replaced with an elected head of state compared to 37% of Labour voters, whilst 31% of 18–24 year olds also want to see the monarchy abolished. Although support for the continuation of the monarchy remains strong, YouGov highlight that the overall figure of 62% has come down from 75% in 2012.
items.why: public attitudes toward whether the head of state should be elected bear on the structure of elected government and constitutional decision-making.
items.note: Classified under elections & decision making because it concerns the elected-government question, not merely general political engagement.

items.h: Make Votes Matter identify 213 ‘Stale Seats’ since beginning of Queen’s reign
items.b: MVM have identified 213 ‘Platinum Stale Seats’ that have been represented by the same political party since the Queen became the ruling monarch 70 years ago. Commonly dubbed ‘safe seats’, equal votes campaigners argue that these seats stifle democracy by silencing voters and creating “a class of politicians who think they are above the scrutiny of voters.”
items.why: persistently uncompetitive 'safe seats' bear directly on electoral competitiveness and voters' ability to hold representatives to account through elections.
links: “a class of politicians who think they are above the scrutiny of voters.”

items.h: UK ranked 20th in Europe for electoral integrity
items.b: The Electoral Integrity Project have been researching the integrity and transparency of global elections to produce a set of regional rankings . Electoral integrity is assessed by experts in each country based on a series of metrics including electoral laws, electoral procedures, media coverage and campaign finance. The UK was ranked 20th in Europe for electoral integrity and 25th out of 35 liberal democracies. The US was the worst-ranked liberal democracy for electoral integrity.
items.why: this matters democratically because it provides comparative evidence on the integrity and transparency of UK elections relative to other democracies.

items.h: Johnson survives no-confidence vote, but new rules could mandate another vote within the year
items.b: Monday 6th of June saw Johnson narrowly win a vote of no confidence in his leadership — 211 votes for 148. This ‘decisive’ endorsement of his leadership, to use the Prime Minister’s words, could however prove short-lived. Current rules dictate that a year of immunity is afforded to any leader that survives a vote of no confidence, but Chair of the 1922 Committee, Graham Brady, has refused to rule out a change that would cut the period of immunity to six months.
items.why: this matters democratically because changes to the rules governing leadership challenges affect the constitutional conventions constraining and holding the executive to account.
items.note: Party leadership no-confidence rules are treated as a constitutional-convention accountability mechanism rather than an election proper.

items.h: Nicola Sturgeon formally launches fresh campaign for Scottish independence
items.b: Yesterday Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon insisted she planned to hold another independence poll before the end of 2023, remarking “Scots are ready to separate”. The first ‘scene setter’ paper was released yesterday outlining the Scottish government’s plans for independence. Sturgeon has claimed she will proceed with a vote even without a Section 30 Order temporarily providing the Scottish Government with powers reserved to the UK Government.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the machinery and legal authority for holding a referendum on Scottish independence.
items.note: Referendums and direct popular votes are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: proceed with a vote even without a Section 30 Order

items.h: Mumsnet open letter calls on the Government to allow hybrid working for councillors and councils in England
items.b: As the country went into lockdown in 2020, so too did councils and councillors, shifting to remote and hybrid forms of working. With the easing of COVID-19 the UK Government forced councils to return to physical meetings and proceedings, to the chagrin of those with accessibility requirements, children and those who had become used to the benefits that working from home brings. 87% of councillors want a return to more accessible ways of working. Sign the open letter here.
items.why: this matters democratically because the working arrangements of elected councillors affect who can practically serve in and access local government structures.
items.note: Treated under elections & decision making as it concerns the structure and functioning of local government tiers.

items.h: Devolution, Levelling-up and Local Leadership — In conversation with Andy Burnham on 21st June
items.b: The Institute For Government is hosting a series of events on devolution and levelling up with local leaders across England. On 21st of June, Andy Burnham will be hosted by Akash Paun, Senior Fellow at the Institute, to discuss the powers he wants to see devolved as part of the government’s Levelling Up agenda. There will be opportunities to put questions the mayor and attendees can join in person in Manchester or online via a livestream of the event .

items.h: £10k funding for literature review of research into media/information literacy
items.b: The Media and Information Literacy Alliance have opened a call for proposals. Find out more and apply here .
links: The Media and Information Literacy Alliance

items.h: New initiative from Public Interest News Foundation to tackle underrepresentation in the media
items.b: A report from the Edelman Trust has found that just 35% of people in Britain trust the media, whilst the NCTJ reports that 92% of the media come from white ethnic backgrounds. In a bid to build a more representative, inclusive and trustworthy media, PINF have launched a Transformation Programme which will offer work placements to aspiring journalists from under-represented backgrounds. Check out updates from the scheme via their Twitter .
items.why: this matters democratically because increasing diversity among journalists affects media plurality and the range of perspectives available in public debate.
items.note: Classified under information & public debate as it concerns representativeness of the media environment, with a secondary participation angle as a new career pathway.

items.h: IPPR to hold convention on creating a citizen-serving media
items.b: On Wednesday 13th July IPPR will host an in-person conference in London bringing together senior figures from across the media to explore the current challenges facing the sector and how a citizen-serving media could be shaped from the crises. Expect lots of opportunities for participation through interactive sessions, and networking breaks to connect after two years of virtual Oxford Media Conventions.

items.h: ‘The Art of Going Viral’ — with Owen Williams and the Democracy Network
items.b: Owen Williams, formerly Head of Social Media at BBC One and now Managing Director at Siml, will be leading an online session on ‘The Art of Going Viral: Your guide to social exposure and engagement’ on 28th June from 10.30am — 12.45pm. The event is being hosted by the Democracy Network as part of their growing programme of events, workshops and training. Register here to attend and please note places are limited so grab your tickets now!
items.note: A general social-media skills training session, not specifically tied to democratic participation mechanisms.

items.h: Hacked Off launch ‘Leveson Defence Fund’
items.b: Plans to repeal Section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act 2013 have been interpreted by Hacked Off as an assault on press freedom. According to CEO, Nathan Sparkes, “Section 40 was designed to shield regulated newspapers from costly lawsuits brought by the rich and the powerful, it is the only way to guarantee the freedom and accountability of the press”. In response, they have launched a ‘Leveson Defence Fund’ to shore up the current system for another two years until there exists a government “prepared to end corruption between politicians and the press, and act in the interests of the public.”
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the legal framework protecting press freedom and accountability against costly litigation, shaping the media's ability to scrutinise power.

items.h: We Own It push back against the privatisation of Channel 4
items.b: Jesse Norman, a former Minister and sitting Conservative MP, came out against Boris Johnson this week in relation to the proposed privatisation of Channel 4. Believing that the government’s efforts to privatise the channel show they don’t have their priorities in order he noted “privatisation of Channel 4 is an unnecessary and provocative attempt to address a political non-issue during a time of crisis, at significant cost to the independent UK film and TV industry”. We Own It are pushing back against the policy and are inviting others to do the same. You can join the push back here .
items.why: privatising a public-service broadcaster affects media plurality and ownership, shaping the pluralistic information environment citizens rely on for political debate
links: You can join the push back here

items.h: Best for Britain want your lockdown stories
items.b: As Johnson tries to draw a line in the sand under the law-breaking that went on in Downing Street, Best for Britain has other ideas. In the wake of the Sue Gray report, they’ve taken to Twitter asking the public to share their lockdown stories to draw contrast between the sacrifices made by the country whilst Number 10 indulged in a boozy culture of partying and rule-breaking.
items.why: the campaign seeks to hold government to account for breaches of its own rules and standards in public life during the pandemic
items.note: Treated as accountability campaigning rather than mere controversy since it targets ministerial rule-breaking directly.

items.h: Release the bats!
items.b: mySociety’s freedom of information service WhatDoTheyKnow sees its largest ever release of information — and it’s not what you might expect. National Highways has released 1.25TB of bat survey data, made up over 115,000 files. Requester Emma Tristam is using the data to campaign against the proposed Arundel Bypass that threatens an area of international importance for bats.
items.why: the mass FOI release shows a public body being made answerable for its decisions through statutory transparency mechanisms that citizens can use to scrutinise power
items.note: FOI classified as accountability since the story centres on an institution being made to disclose information, not the media environment.

items.h: New podcast explores stories of togetherness and civic innovation
items.b: Onward have teamed up with The Cares Family to create a new podcast called Building Belonging . The podcast will explore stories of civic innovators and the institutions they’re building to overcome disconnection and isolation within communities. With different guests each week the podcast will look at the relationship between these innovators and those in power to explore mechanisms for unlocking the potential of communities.
items.why: launching a new resource exploring civic innovation and the relationship between communities and power builds capacity for civic engagement
items.note: Counted under sector capacity-building rule as a new resource intended to foster civic participation.
