items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Alvin Carpio — Founding Director at School of Social Justice, Titus Alexander — Founder at Democracy Matters, Myf Nixon — Communications Manager at mySociety, Joe Mitchell — Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation, Sam Welsh — Partnerships Coordinator at Votes for Schools, Oliver Walkden — Communications Coordinator at Young Citizens and Jessie Joe Jacobs — Coordinator at Democracy Network.

The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 72 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: A pledge among democracy organisations to collaborate more is sector network-building, not a new means of public participation.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.
If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .

items.h: MPs debate lying in Parliament
items.b: Yesterday a Private Members Bill proposed by Plaid Cymru MP Liz Saville Roberts was heard and debated in the chamber. The Bill was sponsored by Caroline Lucas MP (Green), Claire Hanna MP (SDLP), Martyn Day MP (SNP), Wera Hobhouse (Liberal Democrat) and Dan Carden MP (Labour). The Bill aims to end the practice of wilfully lying in Parliament. See Compassion in Politics ’ feed for more on the day’s debate.
items.why: a cross-party bill to criminalise wilful lying in Parliament bears on ministerial accountability and standards in public life

items.h: Repealing Human Rights Act will make it harder to fight deportation flights, argue campaigners
items.b: Charlie Whelton, Policy and Campaigns Officer at Liberty, says the ‘bill will make it easier to deport refugees by almost completely blocking article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights’, thereby ‘refugees and migrants … will find it harder to defend their basic rights and challenge deportation’. Four parliamentary committees and more than 150 organisations have so far called on the Justice Secretary to submit the bill for pre-legislative scrutiny. He has so far refused.
items.why: this matters democratically because narrowing article 8 protections would restrict individuals' practical ability to use courts to challenge state deportation decisions, and government is resisting parliamentary pre-legislative scrutiny of the change.
items.note: Framed around courts/challenge mechanism rather than the underlying right itself, so filed as rule of law rather than rights.
links: the ‘bill will make it easier to deport refugees

items.h: The BIG Democracy Network Survey
items.b: The Democracy Network have just launched The Big Democracy Network Survey giving you the opportunity to share your experiences of the Democracy Network so far. This will allow the Network to continue to improve and tailor content and output to support and highlight your interests and involvement in democratic spaces. It also allows the Network to gain a better picture of its diverse potential membership, ensuring the Network is an inclusive and accessible space for all. The deadline is 22nd July 2022 and you’ll be offered a £5 high street gift voucher as a thank you for taking the time to comp…

items.h: Add your organisation to Citizen Network’s Constitution Commission Public Letter
items.b: Back in December 2020 Gordon Brown reported that he had brought together Scottish and Welsh labour leaders and English mayors to work on a ‘new constitutional offer’ . Citizen Network’s public letter calls on Brown to divulge new information about the commission, and in particular, calls on Brown and the commission to consider utilising citizens’ assemblies where possible. If you/your organisation supports the devolution aims set out in the public letter , please consider signing it. Citizen Network are particularly keen on enlisting regional and local grassroots movements who see democratic r…
items.why: this matters democratically because the letter concerns proposals for constitutional reform and the use of citizens' assemblies to shape devolved decision-making structures.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and devolution structure are filed under elections & decision making per the revised framework.

items.h: Bond reflects on the evolving situation for campaigners and activists
items.b: With the passage of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act, and with the Public Order Bill just around the corner, Police have a vastly expanded range of new powers to restrict and even criminalise protest. Rosemary Forest , Policy and Advocacy Adviser at Bond, unpicks what we can do about this new situation and how organisations and communities can support one another.
items.why: this matters democratically because new legal powers expand police ability to restrict and criminalise protest, directly affecting citizens' freedom of assembly.
links: what we can do about this new situation

items.h: Young Citizens hiring new Trustees, Project Coordinator & Senior Schools Coordinator
items.b: Among their three new Trustees, Young Citizens are on the hunt for a new Young Trustee (18–25). Find out more on the Trustees roles here . View the Young Citizens jobs page to apply.

items.h: What’s it like to be a parent in politics, asks Pregnant Then Screwed, 30th June
items.b: Pregnant Then Screwed (PTS) is a charity dedicated to ending the motherhood penalty, supporting tens of thousands of women each year, and successfully campaigning for change. PTS and 50:50 Parliament team up for a special session on how to balance parenthood and a political career. Join Rhiannon Evans, Head of Comms at Mumsnet, and a cross-party panel of councillors on the 30th June. Register now .
items.note: Event listing discussing barriers to political participation for parents, but no new mechanism or resource is created.

items.h: New online School of Social Justice launches
items.b: The school’s new stated mission is to train the next generation of Martin Luther King’s, says Founding Director Alvin Carpio . Find out more about the School of Social Justice and take a look at their growing range of interviews with global changemakers.
items.note: Launch announcement is too generic about 'social justice' training to identify a specific democratic participation mechanism.

items.h: Big Brother Watch are hiring
items.b: Big Brother Watch are looking for a Campaign Manager (deadline July 5th) and Digital Communications Manager (rolling deadline) to join them in the battle for greater privacy, freedom of expression and data protection rights. Check out their jobs board for more details on both roles.

items.h: Stir to Action’s Playground for the New Economy Festival is back
items.b: Returning for its fourth year, the festival is a celebration of the movement for democratic ownership , featuring talks and panels on topics ranging from community wealth building to democratic finance. Whilst full-priced tickets are £125, there are a number of sponsored tickets available for £25 for attendees from marginalised communities, young adults, disabled individuals and those coming from deprived areas. Find your tickets now .
items.note: Event listing for a festival, not a new participation resource or tool.
links: the festival is a celebration of the movement for democratic ownership

items.h: Association for Citizenship Teaching Conference 2022
items.b: ACT’s 20th anniversary conference will be a celebration of their work promoting excellence in citizenship education, and a reflection on the overwhelming challenges facing the next generation and how the citizenship curriculum can support transformational outcomes. The conference will be held next week, Tuesday 5th July — Register your ticket now .
items.note: Conference listing rather than a new civic education resource or programme change.

items.h: mySociety asks, are you using the Climate Action Plan Explorer?
items.b: Myf Nixon, Communications Manager at mySociety, wants to know if you’re using their Climate Action Plans Explorer tool. If you are, please get in touch so they can grill you on it for a new case study on the project.
items.note: Organisational request for case-study participants, not a change to participation or debate.

items.h: Democracy Messaging Guide Workshop (18th July)
items.b: Led by James Robertson of Sortition Foundation and hosted by the Democracy Network, the Democracy Messaging Guide online workshop will run on Monday 18th July (2pm — 4pm). On a mission to communicate in more compelling ways and build public support, in late 2020 a dozen democracy organisations teamed up to produce a messaging guide for the democracy sector. Based on rigorous testing and research, the guide outlines how to frame democratic reform in a way that works to shift public attitudes and behaviour. This jam packed workshop is for anyone trying to talk about changing the political system…
items.why: this matters democratically because it builds sector capacity to communicate about democratic reform in ways that shift public attitudes and behaviour, a new means of civic engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource rather than organisational admin.

items.h: Third of Green Party Women’s committee collectively resign
items.b: Earlier this month four members of the Green Party’s Women’s Committee stood down citing “numerous issues with process, procedures, and communication”. According to Bright Green the resigning members were from the wing seeking to make the Party more inclusive for trans people. Last year Green Party Co-Leaders Sian Berry and Jonathan Bartley resigned citing internal party conflict over transgender rights.
items.note: Internal party personnel dispute rather than a change to electoral or associational mechanisms.

items.h: Extinction Rebellion UK asks, what is a Citizens’ Assembly?
items.b: If you want more information on how Citizen’s Assemblies work, then check out these online sessions by Extinction Rebellion on the 5th and 14th of July. And if you’re looking for a deeper dive exploring global examples of how they have worked in practice, check out the online session on the 26th July .
items.why: this matters democratically because it builds public understanding of citizens' assemblies, a deliberative mechanism for binding or advisory collective decision-making.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are filed under elections & decision making per framework boundary rule.

items.h: Conservatives becoming more antagonistic towards the constitution, according to new blog
items.b: A new blog from Andrew Blick, Senior Advisor to The Constitution Society , suggests there has been a shift within the Conservative Party in how they approach the constitution, from a traditional defence of established institutions to a more open position of antipathy and antagonism. Also, if you missed it in April, check out the report from Constitution Society Research Fellow Daniel Skeffington, ‘The Political Constitution: An Idea Worth Protecting?’ which undertakes a somewhat more extended analysis of British constitutional thought. Worth a read.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns a shift in a major party's stance towards constitutional conventions and checks on executive power.
links: ‘The Political Constitution: An Idea Worth Protecting?’

items.h: UNISON backs Proportional Representation
items.b: UNISON’s National Delegate Conference has backed a motion in support of PR. Hailed as a major boost to reform efforts by campaigners, the results follow last October’s vote from Unite which also backed proportional representation. At last year’s Labour conference, opposition from trade unions defeated a motion backing proportional representation despite widespread support from members. The latest vote now sees UNISON — UK’s largest union — join Unite, ASLEF, the Musicians Union, CWU and TSSA in adopting pro-electoral reform stances.
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports a major union adopting a position on the electoral system used to choose representatives.
links: opposition from trade unions defeated a motion

items.h: Politics For the Many hold online rally to build momentum for Proportional Representation
items.b: Back on 9th June Politics For the Many hosted an online rally to discuss how First Past the Post makes it easier for the Conservative Party to win elections and how we can create a more equitable and fair voting system. Speakers included trade unionists, MPs and electoral reform campaigners, including Jessica Garland, Director of Policy and Research at Electoral Reform Society . If you missed the event you can watch it back via their YouTube channel.
items.why: this matters democratically because the rally campaigns to change the electoral system used to choose the legislature.
items.note: Treated as advocacy campaign on electoral systems rather than mere event listing.

items.h: Labour Women’s Network running #Selections4ThisMillenium
items.b: Labour Women’s Network demand changes to Labour’s selection processes to benefit women. Changes include four week selections, hybrid voting and easy access to postal votes. Find out more .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns candidate selection processes that shape who can access elected office and how representative Parliament becomes.

items.h: Centenary Action Group hosting event on women’s political representation, July 19th
items.b: The event will run from 10.30–1pm on July 19th in Parliament, with a panel of MPs followed by Q&A and networking. Email gibbons@careinternational.org to register for the event.
items.note: Event listing/networking notice rather than a new resource, tool or reported change.

items.h: IPPR report launch — How representative is Parliament? 4th July
items.b: Join IPPR for their new report launch on the 4th July in Parliament. Angela Rayner MP, Deputy Leader of the Labour Party, will give a keynote address to introduce the event, focusing on how well Parliament represents UK society and whether there is a growing representation gap. Register for the event . The session is being held in partnership with Friedrich Ebert Stiftung .
items.why: this matters democratically because the report examines how representative Parliament is of UK society, bearing on the representativeness of elected institutions.

items.h: First day of new policing powers, first target: Pro-EU campaigner Steve Bray
items.b: For those of you that have passed through Westminster in recent years, you might have met the eccentric pro-EU campaigner covered in EU flags, Steve Bray. Yesterday marked the first day of the new policing powers covered by the controversial Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act, which include powers to restrict ‘one-person’ protests and ‘noisy’ protests. Mark Johnson, Big Brother Watch’s Legal & Policy Officer reports Steve Bray as perhaps their first use of these new powers.
items.why: new police powers are being used to restrict a lone protester's ability to demonstrate, directly affecting the legal space for peaceful dissent.
items.note: Protest policing under new legal powers falls under rights/civic space, not participation, per boundary rule.

items.h: ‘Carriegate’ — Did Johnson attempt to appoint his wife as Chief of Staff at Foreign Office?
items.b: The Times recently ran an article claiming Boris Johnson, whilst in post as Foreign Secretary, attempted to appoint his wife as Chief of Staff at the Foreign Office. The story appeared in the first edition of the paper on Saturday 18th, but was removed from later editions following apparent pressure from Downing Street . CEO of Best for Britain , Naomi Smith, described the escapade as “a violation of press freedom at a time when public trust is already low”.
items.why: it alleges a minister used personal position for a spousal appointment and that government pressure led to a newspaper suppressing the story, implicating both standards in public life and press independence.
items.note: Combines an accountability/nepotism allegation with a press-freedom suppression claim; classified primarily on the appointment/conduct issue.

items.h: Guardian investigation points to monarch’s influence over Scottish laws
items.b: A Scottish government memo reveals that ‘it is almost certain’ that draft laws have been secretly changed to secure the Queen’s approval. Previously, the Queen’s representatives have refused to say how many times the Queen has requested legislative alterations as part of the monarch’s consent procedure, but as a result of this latest research by the Guardian — we now know this number totals at least 67 times. Since the start of her reign, the Queen and her son have vetted more than 1,000 laws enacted by the Westminster parliament under the Queen’s consent mechanism.
items.why: it reveals previously hidden influence by the monarch over legislation via the opaque consent procedure, raising questions about constitutional checks and transparency of lawmaking.
links: ‘it is almost certain’ that draft laws have been secretly changed

items.h: Lord Geidt resigns over ‘affront’ to the ministerial code
items.b: Johnson’s ethics advisor, Lord Geidt, has resigned over concerns that the government intended to take measures that would “risk a deliberate and purposeful breach of the ministerial code”. Geidt, the second ethics advisor to quit under Johnson, said he felt the request had put him in an “impossible and odious position”, forcing his resignation. The Labour Party has since lost a vote proposing that MPs should have the power to hold ministers to account in light of Johnson’s refusal to commit to appointing a successor to Geidt.
items.why: the resignation of an ethics adviser over a threatened breach of the ministerial code exposes weaknesses in mechanisms holding ministers to standards of conduct.

items.h: Civil society organisations sign open letter to Nadine Dorries over ‘rigged consultation’
items.b: More than 30 civil society organisations have written a letter to Nadine Dorries expressing their concerns over what they believe to be an unlawful consultation process for the Data Reforms Bill . The signatories, including Liberty , Index on Censorship and Big Brother Watch , say the government has refused to meaningfully engage with civil society organisations and take into account the views of those groups and sectors likely to be affected by the policy.
items.why: it concerns whether civil society groups can meaningfully engage in a government consultation process that shapes policy affecting them.
items.note: Classified as participation because the core complaint is about the consultation mechanism rather than a formal accountability failure.

items.h: Procedure Committee to investigate Parliament’s correction procedure
items.b: Full Fact report that a new inquiry will take place into Parliament’s correction procedure. Currently, there is no mechanism in place to allow an MP who is not a government minister to correct the parliamentary record if they make a mistake in the House of Commons. Full Fact hopes that the investigation by the procedural committee will yield an important change in how we approach honest political debate.
items.why: an inquiry into how MPs can correct the parliamentary record bears on the accuracy and accountability of legislative proceedings.

items.h: Major losses for Tories in Wakefield and Tiverton & Honiton byelections
items.b: In Wakefield, a 12.7% swing saw Labour retake the ‘redwall’ seat which they had held since the 1930s before Imran Khan’s win at the 2019 general election. Meanwhile, in Tiverton and Honiton, the traditionally safe Conservative seat was overturned by the Lib Dems in a 30% voter swing . In the early hours Oliver Dowden, the Conservative Party chairman, resigned saying someone needed to “take responsibility” for the defeat.
items.why: byelection results demonstrate genuine electoral competitiveness and the ability of voters to remove incumbents.

items.h: French leftist coalition performs well in elections — a lesson for ‘progressive alliance’ efforts in the UK?
items.b: In what was a damaging night for Macron, the coalition of leftist parties known as Nupes became the largest opposition force in the French parliament . The coalition scored no more votes than in the 2017 election, but the decision to jointly field candidates meant that overall, they won more than double their previous total. Compass have long argued this approach as a model that the ‘progressive alliance’ in the UK could emulate.
items.why: the French coalition's electoral strategy offers comparative evidence on how electoral alliances affect political competition, relevant to UK debates about a progressive alliance.
items.note: International item included as comparative evidence bearing on UK electoral strategy.
links: largest opposition force in the French parliament

items.h: Bright Green promise to bring increased coverage to all Green Party election nominees
items.b: According to Bright Green, previous internal Green Party elections have been more like ‘coronations’ rather than competitive races with the big name going on to win. That’s why this summer they’ve pledged to give significant media coverage to all runners in the deputy leadership elections to provide a detailed analysis of the options open to Green Party voters.
items.why: it concerns whether internal party elections are genuinely competitive, with candidates given fair visibility to voters.
items.note: Internal party candidate competition falls under elections per the 'Free Political Parties' anchor.

items.h: Onward report suggests mayoral devolution key to boosting Conservative electoral prospects
items.b: A new report from Onward , Give Back Control , urges the government to devolve significant regional powers to local mayors and regional policymakers to better tackle issues in their area. A key part of the government’s Levelling Up strategy, Onward suggest that a strategic program for devolution will be vital to boosting the Conservative’s chances at the next general election.
items.why: the report concerns the structure and extent of devolved regional and mayoral power, which shapes how local decision-making authority is distributed.
items.note: Devolution of powers to local/regional government is classified under elections & decision making per boundary rule, despite the partisan framing.

items.h: Scottish Government seeks Supreme Court ruling on independence vote
items.b: First minister Nicola Sturgeon yesterday told MSPs she wants to hold a second independence referendum on 19 October 2023. To proceed with a lawful vote, the UK Government must provide Holyrood the powers to do so under Section 30 of the Scotland Act. Boris Johnson’s government has so far refused to engage on the matter, forcing the Scottish Government to seek a ruling from the justices of the UK Supreme Court.
items.why: it concerns whether a devolved government can lawfully hold a binding referendum on constitutional change and who controls that decision-making machinery.
items.note: Referendums are classified under elections_decision_making per the revised framework, not participation.
links: forcing the Scottish Government to seek a ruling

items.h: Index of Independent News Publishing 2022 launch
items.b: This year’s Index, conducted by Joe Mitchell and the team at Public Interest News Foundation , is the result of more than 72 surveys from across the independent news sector. The report found that local publishers face significant challenges around revenue, staffing costs and social media giants, but despite this — publishers manage to reach 39m people a year across the UK digitally, with a total print circulation of nearly 300,000. View the full report .
items.why: the reach and financial health of independent local publishers affects the plurality of the information environment citizens rely on.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation announce two local news initiatives
items.b: In a bid to bolster local news outlets that add ‘democratic, economic and social value to communities’, PINF have announced two new targeted schemes. The Local News Plan will work with communities, civil society and local policymakers to create a shared vision for a new public news scene, whilst the recently launched News for All campaign will work to create a better news economy for the future.
items.why: new initiatives to sustain local news outlets preserve the local journalism capacity needed for informed public debate and accountability.
items.note: Classified under information_debate because local journalism is explicit territory there, rather than defaulting to participation_civic_life for capacity-building.

items.h: IPPR to hold convention on creating a citizen-serving media
items.b: On Wednesday 13th July IPPR will host an in-person conference in London bringing together senior figures from across the media to explore the current challenges facing the sector and how a citizen-serving media could be shaped from the crises. Expect lots of opportunities for participation through interactive sessions, and networking breaks to connect after two years of virtual Oxford Media Conventions.
items.note: Event/conference listing rather than a reported development.

items.h: Over twenty production companies launch bid to prevent privatisation of Channel Four
items.b: Twenty-seven production companies have come out against the proposed privatisation of Channel Four. The companies have teamed up with anti-privatisation group, We Own It , to kick off their new campaign — ‘Channel Four Ain’t Broke’ . The campaign comes as Tory opposition to the plans is on the rise. Former front bench Tory MP, Jesse Norman, even cited the plans in his letter of no confidence to the Prime Minister saying the “privatisation of Channel 4 is an unnecessary and provocative attempt to address a political non-issue during a time of crisis”.
items.why: the proposed privatisation of a public service broadcaster affects media plurality and the range of political debate available to citizens.

items.h: National and local media boycott Bristol Mayor’s press conferences after local democracy reporters banned from attending
items.b: Bristol24 / 7 , BBC, ITV and South West Local Voice have announced they will boycott the fortnightly mayoral press conferences after Local Democracy Reporters (LDRs) were banned from attending. The mayor’s office initiated the ban accusing LDR, Alex Seabrook, of unfair bias after he questioned the mayor on the irony of flying to Vancouver to deliver a 14-minute Ted talk on climate change . Bristol24/7 Editor, Martin Booth, called it a ‘slippery slope’ once the mayor can pick and choose which journalists they want to attend a briefing.
items.why: banning accredited local democracy reporters from a mayor's press conferences restricts journalists' ability to scrutinise and inform the public about elected officials.
links: BBC, ITV and South West Local Voice
boycott the fortnightly mayoral press conferences

items.h: Report finds growth of local ‘news deserts’ across the UK
items.b: A new report from The Charitable Journalism Project has found social media groups are increasingly filling a void left by collapsing local media outlets. Quick and helpful at times, unreliable and divisive at others, the reliance on social media networks means key news stories are going unreported and local authorities can act with increasing impunity.
items.why: the spread of local news deserts reduces the plural, reliable information citizens have about local governance, leaving authorities less scrutinised.

items.h: RSA & UKRI funds available for public engagement projects
items.b: In collaboration with UK Research and Innovation, the Royal Society of the Arts is offering funding to support pilot projects that challenge the boundaries of conversations between the public, researchers and policymakers. The total value of the fund is £480,000. Find out more and apply here .
items.note: Funding call, excluded as sector logistics.

items.b: SMK has been awarded a five year grant from Oak Foundation to lead a participatory ‘power and capacity building programme’ for their grantees working to prevent housing injustice and homelessness across the UK.
items.note: News about an organisation's own funding, not a change to what people can do.

items.b: This year’s Alliance of Democracies’ Democracy Summit saw democracy activists, civil society, political and business leaders come together on the issues of the moment. Read the summary of this month’s Summit or view the YouTube playback .

items.h: Online Safety Bill dropped from Commons business next week, pushed back to autumn
items.b: Eleanor Langford at PoliticsHome reports that the OSB has been dropped from Commons business to make way for a motion of no confidence in the government due to be put to the House on Monday. Opposition parties claim that the Government has “ given up on governing ” due to the leadership race, creating a political vaccum.
items.why: a major piece of legislation's passage through Parliament is being disrupted by a political crisis, showing how executive instability can stall legislative scrutiny
items.note: Story is about parliamentary business scheduling, not the bill's substance, so classified under legislative accountability rather than information debate.
links: reports that the OSB has been dropped

items.h: Online Safety Bill coalition warns OSB amendment risks becoming ‘disinformation laundromat’
items.b: More than 57 organisations joined the open letter sign-on , including Demos, Hacked Off, Fair Vote UK, Hope Not Hate and Foxglove, amongst others, and has received great coverage including City AM , The Evening Standard , Yahoo News and The Times (paywall). Help promote the campaign by RTing Fair Vote’s Twitter thread or if you’d prefer to do your own post on socials, the group has pulled together a social media toolkit here .
items.why: civil society groups are warning that a legislative amendment could weaken safeguards against disinformation, affecting the public information environment
links: 57 organisations joined the open letter sign-on

items.h: Online Safety Bill Report Stage debate: what’s happening?
items.b: Liron Velleman at Hope Not Hate highlights a mega-thread from Carnegie’s Maeve Walsh on where we’re at with the Online Safety Bill.
items.why: tracking a bill's progress through Report Stage is part of parliamentary scrutiny of legislation shaping the information environment
items.note: Focus is on legislative process/status rather than substantive content, so filed as parliamentary scrutiny with information debate as secondary.

items.h: Reminder: Online Safety Bill opportunities for collaboration
items.b: Are you working on the Online Safety Bill? Be sure not to miss Fair Vote UK’s weekly digest of news and updates relating to the Bill’s passage. RVSP for their weekly OSB Office Hours Zoom calls and sign up to the digest by emailing Matt Gallagher .

items.h: The Politics Project wins ‘Organisation of the Year’ at the Association for Citizenship Teaching (ACT) awards
items.b: Hattie Andrews , Director at The Politics Project (TPP), and their team have run over 180 of their award-winning Digital Surgery sessions with teachers, students and politicians this year alone! Since The Politics Project’s founding in 2015, they’ve worked with more than 200 teachers, 5000 young people and more than 170 politicians in delivering high quality democratic education to the next generation.
items.note: Award recognition for an organisation is organisational news, not a democracy story.

items.h: Applications for 2022 Newspeak House residential programme are now open
items.b: Newspeak House is the London College of Political Technology, a hub for communities working to change society with technology, spanning all kinds of civic institutions, from government, politics, activism, charities, journalism, think tanks, NGOs, philanthropy, to academia. At the heart of Newspeak House is its residential programme, running since 2015. Seven residents spend a year immersed in these communities, enjoying the chance to meet thousands of people and attend events held on their doorstep. Find out more and apply here .
items.note: A professional fellowship programme for civic-tech insiders, not a tool created for public democratic participation.
links: Find out more and apply here

items.h: Post-Johnson: Where do we go from here?
items.b: This Monday Democracy Network and the Centre for Democracy created a space for democracy organisations to come together to reflect and discuss next steps after the collapse of the Johnson Government. Participants voiced concern, trepidation and confusion over the current state of politics, but at the same time marked a notable bloom in discourse around constitutional and democratic reform throughout last week — that there has been significant discussion of a written constitution and ministerial codes. View the shared notes from the session .
items.why: this matters democratically because it reflects sector discussion of constitutional constraints on executive power, such as written constitutions and ministerial codes, prompted by a change of government.
items.note: Reports discourse about accountability mechanisms rather than an actual institutional change.
links: View the shared notes from the session

items.h: Democracy Network’s Pilar steps back, Involve hiring Project Administrator role
items.b: Pilar Girvan, Involve/Democracy Network’s Communications and Advocacy Officer, is taking a step back to pursue an exciting new PhD on land use and protest in the Highlands and Islands. Whilst she won’t be leaving Involve entirely, the team at the Centre for Democracy will be sad to see her go. Pilar has been an amazing help, working alongside us to jointly produce this newsletter since she joined the Democracy Network team in April. In her stead, Involve are now looking for a Project Administrator (1–0.8FTE) to work on the Democracy Network. The role also includes a small amount of communicati…
items.note: Staff departure and hiring notice is organisational admin, excluded even for a democracy-sector body.

items.h: Swap My Vote launch new crowdfunder
items.b: Preparing for a snap general election at any moment, Adam Spiers, Josh Russell, Tom de Grunwald and the team at Swap My Vote have launched a new crowdfunder to invest in the platform and massively upgrade their existing services for tactical voters. Swap My Vote has been used by hundreds of thousands of voters in elections since 2015, support their crowdfunder now and RT their fundraiser .
items.note: A crowdfunder to upgrade an existing service is treated as organisational fundraising rather than the launch of a new participation tool.

items.h: Democracy Volunteers publish their May 2022 local elections report
items.b: Democracy Volunteers deployed more than 200 Electoral Commission accredited observers to more than 1,723 polling stations through the voting period. Observers noted significant levels of Family Voting in 25% of polling stations, i.e where one person has oversight or control of another person’s vote. Dr John Ault, Director of Democracy Volunteers, has since called on UK legislators to act to prevent the practice in polling stations. Read the full report or listen to the podcast .
items.why: this matters democratically because independent election observation exposing practices like family voting bears directly on the integrity and freedom of the ballot.

items.h: Updates on the Democracy Network
items.b: The Democracy Network has gone live with their new Twitter this week so look out for lots of content and follow for news, updates and events. They’re also inviting people to fill in the Big Democracy Network survey and there’s even a £5 thank you voucher for doing so. It should take less than 10 ten minutes to fill out and your insights would be greatly appreciated by their team. In addition, the Democracy Messaging Workshop, led by Sortition Foundation, is now just a few days away on 18th July, you can sign up here .
items.note: Social media launch, survey promotion and workshop signup are sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: Demos asks, how can we renew democracy?
items.b: Last week Demos hosted an event to discuss new ways of doing politics and policy making that listens more directly to people. During the event Marcial Boo, author of The Rules of Democracy, Polly Curtis, Interim Chief Executive, Demos and Björn Leví Gunnarsson, Icelandic Member of Parliament, gave their take on how we can revamp democracy and boost faith in politics. Head over to their YouTube channel for a recording of the event in case you missed it.
items.note: Event recording promotion without a reported concrete change or new mechanism.

items.h: mySociety are looking for new board members
items.b: There are a number of vacancies currently going on the boards of mySociety and their subsidiary, SocietyWorks . They are looking for trustees, a new Treasurer and Non-Executive Directors to help steer the direction of the organisation. Check out their job page for more details on each of the roles.
items.note: Board recruitment is organisational admin, excluded even for a democracy-sector body.

items.h: Shared Future kickstarting new Local Climate Engagement (LCE) programme
items.b: Alongside Involve, UK100, DemSoc and Climate Outreach, Shared Future are working with local authorities across England to deliver high-quality public engagement projects on climate policy, as part of a new nationwide programme to train councils in engagement-driven climate policymaking. You can read about the project here . Shared Future are also hiring a Communication and Marketing Associate to help them get the word out (deadline 18th July).
items.why: a new nationwide programme trains local councils to run public engagement on climate policy, creating new means for citizens to take part in local decision-making
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new participation infrastructure rather than mere event/job listing.

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation are hiring for multiple roles
items.b: SMK have been on a mission in recent years to become experts in social change exploring how change happens and championing civil society campaigners. If this mission resonates with you then check out their upcoming vacancies which include a new Operations and System Manager, Knowledge and Insight Manager, and Head of Programmes. All have a deadline for Monday 18th July.

items.h: Elect Her to hold webinar on the importance of lived experience in politics
items.b: On Thursday 21st July, Elect Her will host a women-only webinar to discuss how marginalised women have historically had a limited capacity to be politically active, and how we can begin to shift our mindset to recognise the importance of lived experience in politics. Speakers at the event will include MPs, councillors and activists who will discuss their own lived experiences, as well as how we can overcome the barriers to political participation for women with low or no income. Find out more .
items.note: An event listing/webinar announcement rather than a new participation mechanism or reported change.

items.h: New essay on ‘Platformation’ explores the potential behind changing organisational structures
items.b: A new essay from Koreo , in collaboration with Stephanie Sherman from design studio Supervisions, looks at how civil society organisations can redesign their structure to unlock individual and collective potential. The essay suggests that most organisations are restricted by hierarchical structures that consolidate power and in fact a more dynamic and on-going conversation about organisational forms is needed to unleash the power of civil society organisations. As well as the full essay, you can explore their motivations behind the project in this shorter summary of their work.
items.note: Concerns internal organisational design of civil society bodies, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Check out all the highlights from this year’s Festival of Debate
items.b: The largest UK annual politics festival, The Festival of Debate , took place across April and May with a huge variety of speakers debating all things politics. The festival might be over but you can still catch a number of recordings of the events on their YouTube channel .
items.note: An event recap/listing with no reported democratic development.

items.h: Liberty publish guide on how the right to protest is changing
items.b: The 28th of June saw several public order provisions on the right to protest come into effect as part of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act. In response, Liberty has published this explainer on the main changes to protest law and what they mean for protesters.
items.why: new statutory public order provisions restrict the legal conditions under which people can protest and be policed while doing so
items.note: Classified under rights/civic space as the story concerns legal restriction and policing of protest, not willingness to protest.

items.h: Government legislates to allow agency workers to replace striking workers
items.b: Ministers have approved controversial plans to drastically reduce the impact of industrial action by allowing agency workers to fill the gaps during a strike. Critics of the plans say it is akin to a “scab charter”. As trade unions rely on the impact of withdrawing labour in order to bring employers to the table to secure pay deals and workers’ rights, these changes mark a significant shift of power away from working people.
items.why: legislation weakening the effectiveness of strike action curtails the practical power of trade unions to organise and act collectively
items.note: Freedom of association for a trade union is classified under rights, freedoms & civic space per the boundary rule.

items.h: Polly Toynbee and Alexandra Hall Hall debate the Future of the Monarchy
items.b: The Commission on Political Power recently published an ‘Options Paper ’ examining six possible pathways for the future of the monarchy and head of state. They followed this up yesterday (12th July) with a public discussion between Polly Toynbee and Alexandra Hall Hall on the future of the British monarchy. Check them out on Twitter for updates on how the conversation went.
items.why: debating pathways for the future of the monarchy concerns whether the UK's head of state is chosen and held accountable through elected or hereditary means
items.note: Treated under elections & decision making as it concerns the structure of elected government/head of state, not merely constitutional convention.

items.h: Government breaks precedent refusing Labour time to debate no-confidence motion
items.b: Downing Street has refused to allow parliamentary time for the motion it had tabled. Long standing convention is that, if the leader of the official opposition tables a motion of no confidence, the government makes time for it to be debated and voted on. Update: UK Government have now tabled a no-confidence vote in their own government .
items.why: the government breaking a long-standing convention on debating no-confidence motions weakens Parliament's ability to hold the executive to account
links: Update: UK Government have now tabled a no-confidence vote in their own government

items.h: Transparency International monitoring Tory leadership statements, reaching out to candidates
items.b: Rose Whiffen, Research Officer at Transparency International UK (TI UK), is calling on Conservative leadership candidates to commit to restoring trust in politics by defending both integrity in public life and national security. As Daniel Bruce, Chief Exec at TI UK, said: “Britain’s reputation for the rule of law and stable, fair governance has long made us a reliable ally on the world stage and a safe place to do business. Hostile states have long sought to undermine these strengths by exploiting failures of integrity in Westminster and the City to influence our democracy and wash the proceed…
items.why: monitoring political leadership candidates' commitments on integrity and foreign interference bears on standards in public life and safeguards against corruption
links: calling on Conservative leadership candidates to commit to restoring trust in politics

items.h: Index of Independent News Publishing 2022 launch
items.b: This year’s Index, conducted by Joe Mitchell and the team at Public Interest News Foundation , is the result of more than 72 surveys from across the independent news sector. The report found that local publishers face significant challenges around revenue, staffing costs and social media giants, but despite this — publishers manage to reach 39m people a year across the UK digitally, with a total print circulation of nearly 300,000. View the full report . In other news, Joe also published his review of PINFs leadership programme , bringing together 14 independent publishers.
items.why: the health and reach of independent local news publishers affects whether people can access plural, meaningful information about public affairs.
items.note: Sector research index treated as bearing on the information environment rather than as organisational news.
links: published his review of PINFs leadership programme

items.h: Johnson leaves a severe public mistrust in politics, according to campaigners
items.b: Boris Johnson resigned as leader of the Conservative Party on Thursday morning following a torrent of resignations from within his cabinet and the rest of the Conservative Party. Tom Brake, Director at Unlock Democracy , was one of a number of civil society campaigners to speak out saying ‘Johnson leaves a deeply damaging legacy for our democracy, with trust in politics at an all-time low, rocked by scandal, lies and rule-breaking.’ A number of other campaigners have called on the incoming prime minister to rebuild trust, and re-establish a sense of honesty and integrity in UK politics.
items.why: a prime minister's resignation amid scandal and collapsing public confidence tests mechanisms of ministerial accountability and standards in public life.

items.h: Honesty in Politics Bill introduced to Parliament
items.b: MP Liz Saville Roberts has introduced the Elected Representatives (Prohibition of Deception) Bill to Parliament with the aim of preventing MPs from deliberately lying in parliament. MPs from Labour, the Lib Dems, Greens, Alba, SDLP, and the SNP have all agreed to support the Bill and polling from Compassion in Politics suggests 3 in 4 members of the general public also support it. The Bill will have its second debate in October, and is supported by Compassion in Politics and Reform Political Advertising .
items.why: a bill to prohibit deliberate deception by MPs directly targets standards in public life and ministerial/parliamentary accountability.

items.h: Whistleblower reveals Uber secretly lobbied top levels of government during expansion
items.b: The leak consists of emails, iMessages, WhatsApp exchanges and other data between senior Uber executives and at least six Tory ministers, including then Chancellor George Osborne. Ministers failed to declare secret meetings at which they were lobbied by Uber , the files reveal. Uber pushed UK politicians to influence then Mayor of London Boris Johnson into diluting minicab regulations, which were then dropped in Jan 2016. The covert meetings expose a series of lobbying loopholes in UK guidelines. Last year, the Committee on Standards in Public Life recommended that “the government should revis…
items.why: covert corporate lobbying of ministers exposes loopholes allowing undue private influence over government decisions without public disclosure.
links: Ministers failed to declare secret meetings at which they were lobbied by Uber
Committee on Standards in Public Life

items.h: Transparency International UK launch new research on the property interests of parliamentarians
items.b: The report published by TI UK, ‘ Parliamentary Estates’ , charts the scale, value and geographical distribution of property assets owned by Members of Parliament. The research reports finding a concentration of assets, investments and employment that is far in excess of what can be seen in the wider population. Relatedly, Unlock Democracy have started a petition to restrict MPs’ second jobs, view and share the petition via their site .
items.why: research on MPs' property interests and a petition on second jobs concern conflicts of interest and standards in public life among elected representatives.
items.note: Petition mention is secondary to the main accountability research.
links: view and share the petition via their site

items.h: Minfo is looking for feedback on its initiatives to improve transparency and tackle dis/misinformation
items.b: CEO of Minfo , Roland Stori, is looking for feedback on their stealth dis/misinformation solution and Trust Index for persons of interest (politicians, news readers) and organisations of interest. If anyone is available to talk this over with Roland, please book a slot to chat via their daily calendar .
items.note: A company soliciting feedback on a commercial product is sector logistics, not a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Constitution Unit podcast explores how constitutional and democratic standards can best be upheld
items.b: The Constitution Unit’s ‘State of the Constitution’ Conference took place in June exploring a range of political and constitutional issues. A new podcast taken from the first panel at the conference looks at how constitutional and democratic standards can best be upheld in a modern political era marked by democratic backsliding and parliamentary rule-breaking. Joined by politicians and academics, Professor Meg Russel chairs this discussion on whether norms of good and ethical behaviour can be maintained.
items.note: An event/podcast announcement discussing standing constitutional debates without reporting a change or new participatory resource.

items.h: Voter ID introduction before May 2023 in doubt, lack of paper for snap GE polling cards, say AEA
items.b: Peter Stanyon of the Association of Electoral Administrators , representing election delivery staff across the UK, states that it is no longer possible to introduce Voter ID in May 2023 due to a lack of key policy details and secondary legislation yet to be published. Stanyon warns of systemic issues, disenfranchised voters and inconsistent application of new requirements should ministers push ahead with the current timetable ahead of next year’s elections. The AEA also highlight a lack of paper stockpiles for the production of ballots should a snap general election be called.
items.why: delays and gaps in implementing Voter ID and ballot supply threaten well-run, accessible elections.
links: it is no longer possible to introduce Voter ID in May 2023

items.h: Conservative Leadership Election Policy Tracker
items.b: The consultancy PublicFirst have produced a comprehensive policy tracker for the Tory leadership election. View it here .
items.note: A policy tracker for an internal party leadership contest is a sector resource rather than a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Labour MP Sam Tarry highlights reselection issues
items.b: All ten Ilford South local Labour Party branches have voted to ‘trigger’ the seat for reselection. As the sitting MP, Tarry will automatically be on the shortlist. The news comes just days after Apsana Begum MP, a fellow Corbynite, was also told she will face a contest after all bar-one of her local Labour branches voted to ‘trigger’ her. Mr Tarry, a former Shadow Minister under Jeremy Corbyn, has raised concerns over the process given historical allegations of electoral fraud, the expedited process and foregoing rigorous membership checks.
items.why: concerns over the fairness and integrity of internal party reselection processes bear on candidate access and representativeness within the electoral system.
items.note: Treated as parties and candidate access under elections rather than participation, per the boundary rule on freedom of association for political parties.

items.h: Pathways to Scottish Independence — new animation maps possible routes
items.b: Nicola Sturgeon has announced plans to hold another referendum on Scottish Independence in October 2023. A new animation from the Centre on Constitutional Change maps the path to independence for Scotland, highlighting the likely steps and possible hurdles. Aileen McHarg, Professor of Public Law and Human Rights at Durham University, provides more in depth analysis on this here .
items.why: it concerns plans for a referendum on Scottish independence, a form of binding collective decision-making.
items.note: Referendums fall under elections & decision making per the framework's direct-democracy anchor.

items.h: Are councils working? The Ferret publishes first in series on democracy and local councils
items.b: The Ferret has been running a series of investigations in collaboration with The Herald to shed light on the key issues surrounding local government, councils and democracy. A new article, ‘Are councils working?’ , marks the first in the series with a number of other investigative pieces on the way. Follow The Ferret on Twitter for future updates in the series.
items.why: the series investigates whether local councils function as effective democratic institutions.
items.note: Focus is on the structure/functioning of local government rather than press freedom itself.

items.h: Bristol City Council announces it will only self-publish announcements
items.b: As the Bristol media boycott continues, Mayor Marvin Rees in refusing to back down now signals that the council will only publish announcements to its own websites and social media, rather than sending press releases. The boycott began after the authority decided to bar Bristol Post local democracy reporters Alex Seabrook and Adam Postans from his fortnightly briefings. Mr Rees claims the LDRs are not banned from the press conferences — instead insisting they are simply “not invited”.
items.why: a council barring local democracy reporters from briefings restricts the press's ability to hold local government to account and inform the public.
links: the council will only publish announcements to its own websites

items.h: Tánaiste Leo Varadkar says conditions for triggering a border poll on Northern Ireland should be clarified
items.b: The Constitution Unit’s Working Group on Unification Referendums on the Island of Ireland last year went into some detail on these complex issues. See the Twitter thread for the Unit’s response to Tánaiste Varadkar’s statement.
items.why: it concerns the conditions and process for triggering a border poll, a binding collective decision-making mechanism.

items.h: Inquiry into levelling up: submissions sought
items.b: The APPG for ‘left behind’ neighbourhoods is seeking written or video evidence across the Levelling Up White Paper’s policy focus areas and missions to support its Levelling Up inquiry. Submissions should assess the extent to which policy programmes align with the needs and aspirations of people living in ‘left behind’ areas, particular in light of challenges such as low levels of community capacity, depleted civic assets, and poor connectivity. You can access the submission page here.
items.why: the inquiry creates a channel for citizens and communities to submit evidence shaping levelling-up policy.
items.note: Treated as a participation mechanism (evidence submission) rather than a completed accountability act.
links: You can access the submission page here.

items.h: Decentralisation of power from Holyrood
items.b: Campaigners, including Alison Payne, Research Director at Reform Scotland , and Willie Sullivan, Director of Electoral Reform Society Scotland , are calling for reform of Scotland’s local authorities following a series of reports that ‘have uncovered a host of worrying issues with the way our local democracy works’, they claim. Decentralisation of power from Holyrood, full devolution of local taxes and directly elected mayors are among the proposals made by campaigners and politicians pushing for reforms to local government in Scotland.
items.why: it concerns proposals to restructure the powers and functioning of local government in Scotland.
items.note: Local government structure falls under elections & decision making.

items.h: Citizen Network calls for greater public consultation on devolution from the Labour Party
items.b: Labour leader Keir Starmer set up the Labour Constitutional Commission in 2020 with the promise of a ‘new constitutional offer’, however little is known about its progress or which groups have since been consulted. In the absence of this public consultation, Citizen Network , along with other campaign groups and regional parties, have written an open letter to the Labour Party urging them to consider using “citizens’ assemblies and other forms of deliberative democracy to kickstart a national conversation about what kind of democratic settlement people would like to see.” If you would like to …
items.why: it calls for use of citizens' assemblies and deliberative democracy to shape constitutional reform, a decision-making mechanism.
items.note: Deliberative democracy proposals are classed under elections & decision making per framework rule.

items.h: Power Now Project launch report on ‘new power’ and what it means for governance
items.b: The Power Now Project is a collaboration between Compass and Labour Together exploring concepts of ‘new power’. Bringing together academics, politicians, tech-specialists, activists, community organisers and front-line workers, they have been looking at how the government can devolve power to create a partnership between the state and wider society that can transform the country. Join them on Monday 18th of July for the launch of their new report and the chance to discuss how governments can implement beneficial power-sharing arrangements.
items.why: the project explores mechanisms for devolving power and building partnerships between state and society that affect civic participation.
items.note: Ambiguous between devolution structure and civic capacity-building; treated as participation given its focus on 'new power' sharing with communities.

items.h: Marta Wojciechowska asks: What is the role of the democratic megacity?
items.b: Writing in the Journal of Political Geography, Marta Wojciechowska, Lecturer in Politics at King’s College London, argues that large metropolises are engines of democratic and emancipatory potential. Find out more and follow Marta’s work here .
items.why: the piece examines how metropolitan governance structures can expand democratic participation and local decision-making capacity.
items.note: Academic/theoretical piece on local governance structure, only loosely tied to UK practice.

items.h: Conservative ministers tried to sway annual report to privatisation policy, claims Channel 4 head
items.b: Alex Mahon, Chief Executive of Channel 4, says the government tried to change the wording of the broadcaster’s annual report to fit its privatisation agenda. The controversial policy is opposed by Channel 4’s management and board, who — with their independent auditors, signed off on their annual report on 23rd May, but has yet to be made public. Mahon claims publication delays are due to DCMS’ attempts to alter the wording in line with government policy, he reported to the DCMS Select Committee.
items.why: alleged government pressure on a public-service broadcaster's reporting threatens its editorial independence and the plurality of the media environment.
items.note: Also touches government accountability given ministerial interference with an independent institution's transparency.
links: the government tried to change the wording of the broadcaster’s annual report

items.h: Media Reform Coalition briefing: Public Interest Journalism — Funding & Labour Issues
items.b: A new Media Reform Coalition policy brief finds that the public service of journalism, crucial to democracy, is at risk of ‘total collapse’, that the majority of frontline reporters, particularly in the regions outside London, are likely to be living near the poverty line. A damning report of the industry, unsurprising to those with some familiarity of the sector, the work highlights the crucial and currently fragile work of public interest journalism crucial for democracy to function.
items.why: a collapse in public interest journalism, especially regional reporting, undermines the public's ability to obtain meaningful information about public affairs and hold power to account.

items.b: View the full list of upcoming funding calls here — have we missed any? Add them via this form .

items.h: Funding of up to £5,000 available for Mutual Aid groups
items.b: The Social Change Nest CIC have teamed up with Changing Ideas to launch a UK Mutual Aid Fund . They are giving out grants of up to £5,000 to local mutual aid groups to develop their operations and continue serving the needs of their community. Funding will go towards upskilling members, creating greater operational capacity, supplying equipment, and more. Applications close on July 22nd.
items.note: A grant fund for mutual aid operational capacity is sector funding/logistics rather than a new mechanism of democratic participation.

items.h: ARTCRY recruiting funding decision panel
items.b: ARTCRY is a fund dedicated to responsive political art in the public realm. They are recruiting a panel of artists, activists and creatives to make decisions on applications for the next six months. If this sounds up your street, pop an email over to Kathryn Bllyard .
items.note: Recruitment notice for a panel role, not a democracy story.

items.h: CIVICUS publish 2022 State of Civil Society Report
items.b: CIVICUS has just published its global 2022 State of Civil Society Report , looking at how civil society is responding to an increasing number of regressive and volatile forces. The report includes a chapter on global developments in democracy which suggests that democracy is under attack from a rising tide of military coups, right-wing populism and electoral misinformation. The report does also recognise however that important positive changes are still being won by civil society organisations.
items.note: Coverage of an organisation's own report publication about global civil society trends, not a specific UK democratic mechanism.

items.h: Applications open to the World Forum for Democracy 2022 — Youth Delegation
items.b: Applications are now open for the World Forum for Democracy 2022 — Youth Delegation . The forum brings together global political decision-makers and activists to discuss the challenges facing democracies around the world, as well as explore experimental democratic initiatives and practices that can evolve democracy. Anyone aged 18–30 that is actively engaged in civil society democratic initiatives can apply (before August 2nd) for a place at this year’s conference which will take place this November in Strasbourg.
items.note: An open call for conference delegate applications is event/recruitment logistics, not a new means of participation created.
links: World Forum for Democracy 2022 — Youth Delegation

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Oli Whittington — Nesta, Rebecca Deegan — I Have A Voice, Zarino Zappia — Engage Liverpool CIC, Gavin Barker — Citizen Network, Ciaran Cummins — NatCen, Katy Rubin — Legislative Theatre, Jessie Joe Jacobs — Democracy Network and Pilar Garvin, Democracy Network.

The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 73 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Democracy Network, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: Intra-sector pledge to collaborate, not a new means of public participation, so treated as sector admin rather than a democracy story.
