If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .

items.h: The Death of Queen Elizabeth II
items.b: With the sad news of the Queen’s passing, we understand that during the period of official mourning legislation is likely to be paused for up to 10 days. Prince Charles as heir apparent has now acceded to the throne as King Charles III. The Constitution Unit produced this guide as to what happens next .
items.why: the death of the monarch triggers constitutional succession procedures that pause legislative business and affect how executive and parliamentary functions operate during the transition.
items.note: Borderline: covers constitutional convention and legislative pause rather than a standard accountability mechanism.
links: The Constitution Unit produced this guide as to what happens next

items.h: UK Govt announces Data Protection and Digital Information Bill
items.b: Terming the new Bill the ‘Data Oligarch’s Charter’, Open Rights Group claim the new legislation amounts to a ‘bonfire of our data rights’ that will turn the UK into a ‘digital police state’. The bill had a second reading in the House of Commons on September 5th.
items.why: new legislation reshaping data protection rights affects citizens' privacy and freedom from state surveillance, a core civil liberty underpinning democratic participation.

items.h: Proposed reforms to Electoral Commission draw significant criticism
items.b: Last month, the government released its draft statement outlining the new priorities for the Electoral Commission. The proposals have been met with significant criticism with former Electoral Commissioner, David Howarth, stating they are “precisely the kind of partisan interference with the Commission that we feared”. Meanwhile, Unlock Democracy has written to the Levelling Up secretary to voice their concerns, suggesting the move is an attempt to neuter the independence and potency of the commission.
items.why: government control over the Electoral Commission's strategic priorities risks undermining the independence of the body that safeguards electoral integrity.

items.h: Centre for Democracy and Democracy Network announce new partnership
items.b: Beginning this month, Democracy Network and the Centre for Democracy have agreed to work together in close collaboration. The two teams will work together to produce the fortnightly Democracy Bulletin , Democracy Meetups and maintain the jobs , events and funding databases.
items.note: Organisational partnership announcement, not a change to public participation.

items.h: Democracy Meetup moves to Thursdays, Centre for Democracy to launch new Democracy Map
items.b: As part of the new partnership Centre for Democracy are rescheduling Democracy Meetup sessions to Thursdays at 2pm every fortnight. Based on their research and work over recent years, the Centre for Democracy will soon be launching a new Democracy Map, charting all 750+ democracy organisations across the United Kingdom. If you’d like a preview, please email hello@centrefordemocracy.org.uk.
items.note: Rescheduling a meetup and launching a directory of organisations is sector admin/cataloguing rather than a new means of public participation.

items.h: Democracy Network launches website, planning conferences, new funding, hiring
items.b: Jessie Joe Jacobs, Coordinator of the Democracy Network , reports the launch of their new website . If you haven’t already, head over there now, sign up for their newsletter and join the network . But that’s not all — last month DN received a further £270,000 in funding from the Open Society Foundation , as a result they’re now looking to hire two new exciting roles (more soon). As conference season kicks off, Jessie and the Democracy Network team, will be speaking at the Labour Party and Conservative Party conferences, as well as the Democracy R&D conference in Berlin. But that’s not all — wo…
items.note: Organisational news (website launch, funding, hiring, conference attendance) about the org itself, not a democracy mechanism.
links: sign up for their newsletter and join the network

items.h: Mevan Babakar joins Google as their new News and Information Credibility Lead
items.b: Mevan Babakar is going back to their roots in misinformation as Google’s new News and Information Credibility Lead. Mevan has just served a term as Democracy Club’s Interim CEO, following on from their role as Deputy CEO & COO at Full Fact . Congratulations Mevan !
items.note: Staff appointment/career move, excluded as organisational admin.

items.h: Democracy drinks & coworking day brings together orgs across the UK
items.b: This week Democracy Network and the Centre for Democracy hosted their third democracy coworking day this year, with a lively democracy drinks session bringing together democracy organisations to collaborate and hatch plans.
items.note: Networking/social event among sector organisations, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy prepare for Conference
items.b: With a new 2022 conference motion , PR campaign Labour for a New Democracy set their collective eye on Labour Party conference. Join L4ND tonight for their pre-conference event setting out their plans.
items.note: Event/PR campaign listing without a substantive reported mechanism or change.
links: Join L4ND tonight for their pre-conference event

items.h: Join Nesta for their democracy innovation report launch
items.b: With trust in political representatives and our democratic system at an all-time low, the case for building more inclusive and participatory systems of governance is growing. Next week 13th September, Nesta are launching their new report What’s next for democratic innovation? Register for the event for free .
items.note: Report launch event announcement rather than a new participation mechanism or tool.
links: Register for the event for free

items.h: I Have A Voice ask: should voting be compulsory?
items.b: Earlier this week, Rebecca Deegan and the team at I Have A Voice held an event with Kim Leadbeater MP aimed at 16–25 year olds on whether voting should be a compulsory activity.
items.note: Report of a single discussion event, not a new mechanism, tool or change to participation.

items.h: How mySociety’s TheyWorkForYou quietly powers key democratic infrastructure
items.b: Myf Nixon, mySociety’s Marketing & Communications Manager, unpacks the vital role that TheyWorkForYou plays for civil society organisations, including the civil service. Noting that even MPs’ offices use their alerts services to stay up to date, whilst civil servants often scan their ministers’ pages to better understand their history and views. mySociety are on the lookout for volunteers to assist with their WhatDoTheyKnow FOI service, get in touch to help !
items.note: Descriptive piece about an organisation's existing tool plus a volunteer call, not a launch or reported change.
links: unpacks the vital role that TheyWorkForYou plays

items.h: DemocracyNext launches September 15th
items.b: Claudia Chwalisz, who until recently led the OECD’s democratic innovations group, is launching a new organisation called DemocracyNext. The organisation’s mission is to build democratic institutions and frameworks that will encourage more participatory forms of citizen engagement. Join them on September 15th, 17:00–18:30, for the official online launch of DemocracyNext.
items.why: a new organisation is being built specifically to design institutions and frameworks for participatory citizen engagement in collective decision-making, such as deliberative assemblies
items.note: Deliberative/participatory institution-building is anchored to elections & decision making under the framework, not participation.

items.h: Legislative Theatre trainings coming to a town near you, reports Katy Rubin
items.b: Katy Rubin is a Legislative Theatre (LT) practitioner, and brings news that a series of 2-day LT trainings has been commissioned and subsidised by the Lankelly Chase Foundation. The trainings are designd to be affordable and directed at anyone interested in weaving more creative techniques and exercises into participatory processes. The first weekend is 5–6 November, in partnership with Union Chapel in London .
items.why: a new subsidised training programme creates fresh capacity for people to run and take part in participatory democratic processes
links: The first weekend is 5–6 November, in partnership with Union Chapel in London

items.h: New NatCen series focuses on deliberative research
items.b: Ciaran Cummins, Senior Researcher at NatCen’s Centre for Deliberative Research , reports that their new ‘ Deliberate ’ series explores the theory and practice of deliberative research, its relationship to deliberative democracy and the impact it can have on citizens and policy. Take a look and watch their past events .
items.note: A research content series about deliberative democracy theory/practice, not a tool or programme that itself creates new participation capacity.

items.h: Engage Liverpool announce their new autumn seminar series
items.b: The events focus on local democracy and citizen engagement in Liverpool, how ordinary people — citizens — feel about the way their city is run and they think about the state of their local democracy and decision making processes. The talks feature Dr Camila Vergara and Jon Alexander and run from 13th October to 10th November, find your ticket here .
items.note: An informational seminar series about local democracy is an event listing rather than a tool that changes what people can do.

items.h: Mile End Institute conference celebrates women’s postwar contribution to politics
items.b: Thursday 15th to Saturday 17th of September will see the Mile End Institute host their ‘Breaking the Glass Chamber’ conference. The conference will celebrate the post-war contribution of women to British public and political life as well as exploring what politics has meant to women in the second half of the century. Check out the full list of panels across the conference.

items.h: ElectHer to host webinar series across September hearing from women in politics
items.b: Every Tuesday evening this September from 7:30–9 pm, ElectHer will host a webinar series exploring women’s experiences and journeys in politics. They will hear from women currently working in politics across the UK to discuss their roles and offer advice to other women taking their first steps into politics. Join them for the next session on September 13th which looks at what life has been like in the Scottish Parliament for three MSPs.
items.why: the webinar series is a capacity-building programme aimed at helping women take their first steps into political participation, creating new means for underrepresented groups to take part.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building rather than a mere event listing because its explicit purpose is to help women enter politics.

items.h: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss conventions of a Caretaker government
items.b: Since the announcement that Boris Johnson would resign as Prime Minister, the UK has widely been seen to be operating under a ‘caretaker government’. In a webinar on the 6th of October, The Constitution Unit will host a number of speakers to discuss the conventions surrounding such a government and ask whether they need to be clarified or reformed.
items.why: the conventions governing a caretaker government determine the limits on executive authority during a period without a settled mandate.
items.note: An event announcement, but its substance concerns constraints on executive power rather than pure sector logistics.

items.h: Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform are hiring
items.b: LDER are increasing their campaigning work to bring about a change to proportional representation ahead of the next general election. They are looking for funding and are also hiring three volunteer roles — Local Media Coordinator, Communications Coordinator, Video Editing and Publishing Manager — to help them in their efforts. Each role requires a few hours each month, so get in touch if you have skills in any of these areas.
items.note: Volunteer recruitment/job advert, organisational logistics rather than a change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation to host online discussion with authors of ‘Citizens: Why the Key to Fixing Everything Is All of Us’
items.b: On Thursday 22nd of September, authors of the book Citizens — Irenie Ekkeshis and Jon Alexander — will take part in an online event to discuss the ideas behind their work and what lessons can be learnt by campaigners. Attendees are invited to contribute as much or as little as they want throughout the evening so be sure to book your tickets asap for a chance to participate in what promises to be a lively discussion!
items.note: A discussion event about ideas in a book, not a new participation tool or capacity-building programme.

items.h: People Powered celebrates second birthday
items.b: People Powered is a global participatory democracy community hub spanning 73 members and 28 countries. They provide a range of in-depth resources for organisations and communities around the world, including a comprehensive multilingual resource hub, online training courses and a successful mentoring programme. Find out more .
items.note: An organisational anniversary notice, explicitly excluded even though the organisation works on democracy.

items.h: Policy Exchange report proposes changes to the machinery of government
items.b: This month, Policy Exchange is releasing a series of publications answering the question ‘What Do We Want From the Next Prime Minister?’ The second paper in the instalment puts forward a series of reforms the Prime Minister should implement to overcome the current structural and administrative inadequacies of government. With a focus on the civil service, ministerial capability, the machinery of government and public bodies, the report draws a roadmap to a more streamlined governmental structure.
items.why: proposed reforms to the civil service, ministerial capability and machinery of government would change how executive power is administered and held accountable.

items.h: Ian Byrne MP warned of threat to life
items.b: Earlier last month, Labour MP Ian Byrne was contacted regarding a possible threat to the life of their person, family and staff. A far right extremist who had made threats to the Jewish community and had previously made comments about the murder of Sir David Amess MP, said that Amess would not be the last to die, and was later spotted outside Byrne’s constituency office. This March Ian Byrne was awarded Member of Parliament of the Year by charity Patchwork Foundation.
items.why: threats to an MP's life are an attempt to intimidate an elected representative out of exercising their democratic role freely.
links: awarded Member of Parliament of the Year

items.h: Labour Commission on the Constitution due to publish report in autumn
items.b: Gavin Barker of Citizen Network reports on recent discussions with members of the Labour Party. The much-awaited report is due for release in autumn and is a key opportunity, Gavin says, for democracy organisations to give a very vocal collective response and use the report as a platform as a focus for constructive engagement.
items.why: a party commission's constitutional proposals could reshape the structures that constrain and hold government power to account.

items.h: Government prepare attack on right to strike
items.b: Despite their own workplace strike just weeks earlier against Boris Johnson, Transport Minister Grant Shapps and Conservative leadership contender Sunak and new Prime Minister Truss have outlined plans to drastically curtail the right of workers to strike for better pay and conditions. In new plans disguised as ‘modernisation’ , Shapps will work to stop co-ordinated industrial action, limit picketing further and institute a cooling-off period after strikes. As part of the leadership election Truss and Sunak outlined various plans to further restrict the right to strike, from banning strikes in…
items.why: restricting the legal right to strike narrows freedom of association, a civic freedom needed to organise and contest power outside elections
items.note: Trade union strike rights are freedom of association for a civic/labour body, placed in rights not elections.

items.h: Conservative plan to pack the Lords, Gordon Brown urges Starmer to abolish upper chamber if elected
items.b: New Tory plans have emerged to pack the House of Lords with up to 50 new peers . The plans, specifically designed to override key votes on controversial legislation, were designed by lobbying group CT Group , run by key Johnson adviser Lynton Crosby. Gordon Brown has urged the Labour leader to stick to his plans to abolish the House of Lords, warning that the plans ‘legitimise straightforward bribery’. Electoral Reform Society polling found a 54% majority of the public in agreement with Brown , with just 13% backing the move.
items.why: packing an unelected chamber to override votes on legislation weakens legislative constraints on executive power
links: New Tory plans have emerged to pack the House of Lords with up to 50 new peers
Gordon Brown has urged the Labour leader
54% majority of the public in agreement with Brown

items.h: Citizen Network rethinks Westminster rule
items.b: Gavin Barker and the team at Citizen Network are developing a Charter to End Westminster Rule , completing the work of the Chartists, they argue, that power be restored to local people and communities.
items.why: a campaign to restore power from Westminster to local communities concerns the structure and powers of local decision-making
items.note: Local government power structure falls under elections & decision making, not participation, per boundary rule.

items.h: Alliance Now working on Citizen Contract
items.b: Drafted by Reboot GB as part of Alliance Now , a new yet-to-be-launched grouping of civil society organisations, the Citizen Contract identifies 10 areas for reform.
items.why: a coalition of civil society organisations drafting a reform agenda is a new means of civic mobilisation around democratic change
items.note: Very vague item; classified as sector capacity-building under participation.

items.h: Trade unions threaten general strike in response to Conservative race to the bottom on workers rights
items.b: Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) secretary general Mick Lynch has said he would support a general strike and called for an ‘enormous response’ should Liz Truss move forward with their plan to crack down on unions in response to the escalating rail crisis. Frances O’Grady, TUC General Secretary appeared to back Lynch’s comments, hitting out the plans by Truss and Shapps, saying the proposals amount to a ‘fundamental attack on a fundamental British liberty’. Citing the death of Queen Elizabeth II, the RMT and CWU unions have called off their strikes over the next weeks.
items.why: unions threatening a general strike in response to curbs on industrial action concerns the exercise and defence of freedom of association
links: Mick Lynch has said he would support a general strike

items.h: Movement Forward launches new tactical voting campaign
items.b: Bringing together a coalition of tactical voting organisations from recent elections, the new campaign seeks to take tactical voting mainstream, to elect a new government and for that government to immediately legislate for proportional representation. Find out more and sign up here .
items.why: a coordinated tactical voting campaign seeks to shape electoral outcomes and push for a change to the electoral system
links: Find out more and sign up here

items.h: Liz Truss elected Prime Minister by Conservative Party
items.b: Winning the Conservative leadership election earlier this week, Liz Truss met with the Queen and has formed a government. Truss won 81,326 votes (57.4%) of Tory members to the former chancellor’s 60,399 (42.6%), a narrower victory than many had expected.
items.why: the selection of a new Prime Minister through a party leadership contest determines who exercises elected governmental authority

items.h: UK police chiefs issue secret orders to disclose relationships with journalists
items.b: Police officers ordinarily must disclose relationships with convicted criminals or extremists. The new order follows guidance from the College of Policing as part of apparent anti-corruption efforts. It is understood at the policing inspectorate, the HMICFRS , is behind the move . Ruth Smeeth, the chief executive of Index on Censorship , said “Index is increasingly concerned at the seemingly growing perception within the British police that journalists are seen as unsavoury or potentially disreputable individuals for officers to associate with.
items.why: treating journalist contacts as suspect risks chilling sources and undermining public-interest journalism that holds power to account

items.h: UK policing and border control infiltrated by war mentality, says NetPol report
items.b: The Network for Police Monitoring (NetPol) , in partnership with the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT) have published a new report on the increasingly blurred lines between the police and the military, and that key areas of counter-terrorism, gang policing, border control and anti-protest policing have adopted a war mentality. The report A Very British Problem: the Evolution of Britain’s Militarised Policing Industrial Complex published last month, explores these trends at home and their implications for foreign policing given Britain’s significant influence.
items.why: militarised approaches to protest and border policing bear on the lawful exercise of assembly and personal security against state coercion
links: A Very British Problem: the Evolution of Britain’s Militarised Policing Industrial Complex

items.h: Labour Party publishes Forde Report into antisemitism, sexism, racism and Islamophobia within the party
items.b: The Forde Report was commissioned by the Labour leadership following the leak of a document detailing private WhatsApp messages exposing acute factionalism in Labour’s efforts to combat antisemitism. The unpublished Labour Party document, leaked in April 2020, claimed that factional hostility towards Corbyn contributed to the party’s ineffective handling of antisemitism complaints and undermined its 2017 election campaign , showing senior officials from the party’s right wing, who worked at its HQ, channelled resources and efforts within the party to undermine a Labour election win in 2017.
items.why: factional manipulation of a party's internal processes to undermine an election campaign concerns fair political competition within parties
items.note: Party internal governance affecting electoral competition classified under elections rather than accountability.
links: claimed that factional hostility towards Corbyn contributed to the party’s ineffective handling of antisemitism complaints and undermined its 2017 election campaign

items.h: ByLine Times suggest Truss deliberately misled public on campaign trail
items.b: Liz Truss has been elected as the next Prime Minister of Britain after 81,326 Conservative party members (0.3% of the British electorate) voted for her. Tasked with re-establishing a sense of trust with the British public in the post-Johnson era, Adam Beinjov from the ByLine Times questions whether she is as honest and straightforward as she suggests exposing a number of false claims she made on the campaign trail.
items.why: a Prime Minister's misleading claims to voters undermine the accountability and honesty that public trust in government depends on
links: exposing a number of false claims

items.h: Constitution Unit report examines the independence of parliamentary watchdogs
items.b: The Constitution Unit has published the results of its landmark investigation into the independence and accountability of parliament’s watch dogs. Based on an in-depth study of five major watchdogs, the report looks at the role of these constitutional bodies in safeguarding our democracy and the ideal balance to be struck between independence and accountability in their relationship with parliament.
items.why: parliamentary watchdogs' independence determines how effectively Parliament can hold the executive to account

items.h: Full Fact to develop live fact-checking tool
items.b: Full Fact is developing a verification tool to fact-check the claims made by politicians in real time. The tool would enable facts to “flash in chyrons [on-screen graphics] under the faces of politicians and pundits debating on TV” and be checked live with minimal input from an operator. With recent financial backing from Google.org, Full Fact is looking to scale up the technology by using artificial intelligence before rolling it out on the global stage.
items.why: a live fact-checking tool changes the public's ability to assess the accuracy of political claims in real time
links: “flash in chyrons [on-screen graphics] under the faces of politicians and pundits debating on TV”

items.h: Netpol call on campaigners to help monitor impact of ‘anti-protest’ laws
items.b: As of July 2022, Netpol is starting a two-year effort to monitor, document and analyse the effects of the new ‘anti-protest’ legislation which was passed into law as part of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act. They are keen to understand how the new laws are being implemented by different police forces and are calling on campaigners across England and Wales to share and submit evidence.
items.why: monitoring how new anti-protest legislation is policed bears directly on the legal space for assembly and dissent
items.note: Protest policing and legal restriction sits under rights and freedoms per boundary rule.
links: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act.

items.h: Jury acquits Bristol policing bill protester
items.b: Facing charges of violent disorder and affray at Bristol Crown Court on 25th August, Ailsa Rauh was acquitted by a jury of their peers . Ailsa’s acquittal is an important reminder that self-defence is not an offence and that we do have a legal right to fight back against violent and disproportionate policing, Network for Police Monitoring say. Follow similar stories at #DefendDissent .
items.why: a jury's acquittal in a protest-policing case clarifies the legal limits on state coercion against demonstrators
items.note: Court outcome concerns protest rights as much as adjudication process, so both beats are engaged.
links: Ailsa Rauh was acquitted by a jury of their peers

items.h: PM Truss rules out Scottish referendum
items.b: Truss has moved beyond recent government arguments on the referendum, arguing instead that the Scottish Government’s recent Referendum Bill, currently up for consideration by the UK Supreme Court, is illegal. Truss’s statement lacks legal basis as the Supreme Court is yet to rule on whether the referendum bill proposed by the Scottish Government is within Holyrood’s competence. While matters which relate to the Union are reserved to Westminster, the holding of referendums is devolved. The Supreme Court is due to hear the case in October, around a year before the SNP’s proposed date for the ref…
items.why: a dispute over whether a referendum on Scottish independence can proceed concerns the machinery of direct popular decision-making and devolved competence

items.h: Landmark devolution deal for East Midlands draws criticism
items.b: A first-of-its-kind devolution deal has been announced for Derby, Derbyshire, Nottingham and Nottinghamshire which will see the four regions led by a single mayor as of 2024. Under the new Mayoral Combined County Authority (MCCA) plan, the region will receive £1.14bn in government funding as part of the Levelling Up agenda. Centre for Cities has criticised the model however, suggesting the merger will group together two counties with distinct economic needs making it hard for the new mayor to deliver a regeneration programme that works for both areas. Meanwhile, leaders in Leicestershire criti…
items.why: a new mayoral combined authority changes the structure and powers of regional government
items.note: Devolution deal concerns structure of local/regional government tier.

items.h: New Local report finds strong appetite for regional decision-making autonomy
items.b: Community Calling , a report from New Local , has found overwhelming support for localised policy solutions. An online survey with 2,000 members of the general public found that 79% think Westminster and Whitehall are making decisions about communities they know little about, whilst 75% think that giving communities more of a say in local decision-making is more effective than central planning.
items.why: public appetite for shifting decision-making power to local communities bears on the design of devolved decision-making structures
items.note: Survey evidence about local decision-making autonomy sits closest to the elections/decision-making beat per the devolution boundary rule, though it also touches political efficacy.

items.h: LGiU publish new report measuring decentralisation across the UK
items.b: The Local Democracy Research Centre brings together experts from local government and academia to produce practical research on local democracy around the world. In a newly commissioned project, researchers from the University of Kent have built and tested a model to assess the degree of decentralisation across different scales, geographies and policy areas within the UK. Check out the first two papers as part of the ‘Devometrics — measuring decentralisation’ series.
items.why: a new measurement framework for decentralisation informs assessment of local government's structure and powers

items.h: Institute for Government event explores the impact of devolution on Levelling Up
items.b: The government’s flagship Levelling Up agenda will involve a significant devolution of power to allow local authorities to best decide how funds are spent. On the 12th of September, the Institute for Government will host an in-person and online event to explore how exactly power ought to be devolved to local authorities and what the potential trade-offs might be with this approach.
items.note: Event listing about devolution policy discussion, not a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: State of the Union: Hansard Society event unpacks involvement of devolved institutions in UK Statutory Instruments
items.b: On the 29th of September, Hansard Society for Parliamentary Democracy will host an event with several parliamentarians from across the UK to discuss the role of devolved institutions in the development and approval of UK Statutory Instruments within their areas of devolved policy. The event is online and is free to join.
items.note: Event listing about devolved institutions' role in Statutory Instruments, not a reported change.

items.h: Government announces new anti-SLAPP measures
items.b: SLAPPs refer to the phenomenon whereby wealthy litigants use or abuse legal processes to silence critics and stories that could have damaging reputation effects. The anti-SLAPPs coalition has been pushing for government action on SLAPPs and has welcomed the news from Justice Secretary Dominic Raab that the government intends to introduce a host of legislation aimed at putting an end to their use.
items.why: SLAPPs abuse legal processes to silence journalists and critics, undermining the public information environment needed for scrutiny of power.

items.h: Emily Maitlis claims BBC news output is shaped by “active agent of the Conservative Party”
items.b: Former Newsnight reporter, Emily Maitlis, has claimed the BBC’s news output is being shaped by board member Sir Robbie Gibb, who previously worked as Theresa May’s director of communications and helped set up GB News. In her MacTaggart memorial lecture , she described Gibb as an “active agent of the Conservative Party”, suggesting he used his position as a BBC board member to influence the direction of BBC news coverage. She went on to suggest that this intimate relationship between the government and the BBC board has meant too often the BBC has sought to ‘pacify’ Number 10 when disputes over…
items.why: allegations of partisan influence over BBC editorial output bear on the plurality and independence of the public information environment essential for informed political debate.

items.h: Strike action brews over plans to close BBC News channel
items.b: With the BBC due to celebrate their centenary celebrations next month, corporation journalists have threatened strike action over new plans to merge BBC World News and the BBC News channel, arguing that this would significantly reduce newsgathering and airtime for domestic stories and affect UK democracy.
items.why: cuts to domestic newsgathering capacity at a major public service broadcaster affect the public's access to plural, quality information about political affairs.
links: threatened strike action over new plans

items.h: Democracy Network awarded £270,000 by Open Society Foundation
items.b: The team at Democracy Network and Involve have landed a major new funding award of £270,000 for the fledgling platform from the Open Society Foundation . This comes atop Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust’s earlier funding award of £300,000 over three years. It is understood that the new OSF funding has been largely earmarked for influencing work.
items.note: Organisation's own funding award, not a change to public participation mechanisms.

items.h: Civic Power Fund announces new Community Action Fund
items.b: A new Community Action Fund has been set up by Civic Power Fund to provide support to grassroots organisations that are building power in their community and campaigning for change. Grants will be awarded on a sliding scale between £2,500 and £20,000 and will prioritise organisations led by people with lived experience of injustice as well as those excluded from democracy. Civic Power Fund are also expanding their Board of Trustees and are looking for 3–4 additional trustees to join their founding team. The deadline for applications is 12th September.
items.why: launching a new grant fund to support grassroots organising by excluded communities expands the practical means by which people can take part in civic and political life.
items.note: Treated under sector capacity-building rule since it creates new means of participation.

items.h: Polly Curtis recommends: regaining voters’ trust
items.b: Demos Chief Executive Polly Curtis recommends this incisive article (paywall) in The Times on the long road to politicians regaining voters’ trust.

items.h: Podcast of the week: mySociety on democracy in a climate emergency
items.b: Myf Nixon and Siôn Williams of mySociety take to Delib’s Practical Democracy podcast to talk about how local authorities can play a critical role when it comes to both climate engagement and creating a liveable world for future generations. Meanwhile, scientists estimate that we are on the brink of five ‘disastrous’ climate tipping points .

items.h: Deliberation Naturalised
items.b: Ciaran Cummins, Senior Researcher at NatCen’s Centre for Deliberative Research , recommends this “superb” book by Ana Tanasoca — Deliberation Naturalized: Improving Real Existing Deliberative Democracy.

items.h: Misinformation failed to penetrate mainstream discourse during French elections, Institute for Strategic Dialogue reports
items.b: According to analysts at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue , the 2022 French election information ecosystem stood firm against misinformation attempts. In their report (in French) , ISD unpick the factors that came together to explain the resilience of the electoral system at this critical time.
items.why: evidence that an information ecosystem resisted misinformation during an election provides comparative insight into safeguards that protect voters' access to reliable information relevant to UK elections.
items.note: International case treated as comparative evidence bearing on UK democracy.

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Gavin Barker — Citizen Network, Paul Inskip — IC-UK, David Jubb — Sortition Foundation, Jessie Joe Jacobs — UK Democracy Network, Will Stringer — Sortition Foundation, Jon Morter — @TheProgAlliance, Mohammed Afridi — Civic Power Fund, Charlie Mansell — The Campaign Company and Colin Gordon — Grassroots for Europe.
items.note: Meetup attendance/networking notice, not a democracy story under the org-admin exclusion.

items.b: The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 73 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Democracy Network, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: Sector coordination pledge among organisations is admin/networking, not a new means of public participation.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.
items.note: Restates the pledge's intent; sector admin rather than a democracy story.

items.b: If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .
items.note: Call to action to sign a pledge; sector admin.

items.h: Online Safety Bill — Weekly Office Hours
items.b: Is your organisation working around the Online Safety Bill? Join the Online Safety Bill Office Hours — a weekly Zoom call to discuss emerging news and updates on this critical piece of legislation, hosted by Fair Vote UK . Get in touch with Kyle Taylor if you’d like an invite.
items.note: Event/call-to-action for a sector Zoom call, not itself a news story about the bill.

items.h: Liz Truss reportedly planning to ‘dilute’ the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Free speech concerns have been expressed from both left and right over wording in the Online Safety Bill saying speech that was ‘legal but harmful’ must be addressed. Truss says ‘tweaks’ are needed to protect free speech (paywall) .
items.why: changes to 'legal but harmful' provisions in the Online Safety Bill would alter what speech and content can circulate online, shaping the public information environment people rely on to debate politics.
items.note: Concerns 'legal but harmful' online content rules, which sits at the boundary of information environment and individual free speech; classified under information_debate as it concerns platform regulation.
links: ‘tweaks’ are needed to protect free speech (paywall)

items.h: Research Brief published on Data Protection and Digital Information Bill
items.b: The bill was announced over the summer to modernise the UK’s data protection framework. A new research briefing from the House of Commons Library outlines the background behind the bill and the future data protection framework being proposed.
items.why: a new data protection framework affects citizens' privacy against state and private data collection, which bears on freedom from unwarranted surveillance.
items.note: A background research briefing rather than a reported change, but the underlying bill concerns privacy protections.

items.h: Princes Charles proclaimed King Charles III
items.b: An Accession Council convened at St James’s Palace, the official residence of the sovereign, to proclaim the successor to Queen Elizabeth II.
items.note: Hereditary succession of the monarch does not engage a democratic mechanism of acquiring or exercising public power.

items.h: The Democracy Club announce new CEO
items.b: Shabira Papain, founder of People Street , has been announced as the new CEO of the Democracy Club. Shabira has a strong background in digital inclusion, recently as Head of Health Equalities & Digital Inclusion at NHSX, the digital arm of the NHS.
items.note: Staff appointment at a democracy organisation is organisational news, not a democracy story.

items.h: Political System Reform — A Messaging Guide
items.b: Over the summer, UK Democracy Network launched a new messaging guide on political system reform. Produced using a participatory cross-movement framing project led by Sortition Foundation involving over a year of workshops, focus groups and surveys, the guide is for campaigners, communications, press and spokespeople or anyone else trying to talk about changing the political system in the UK, in order to bolster democracy and increase public participation in decision making Check out the guide here .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new resource intended to help campaigners build public support for changing how political power is structured and increase participation in decision-making.

items.h: Sortition Foundation preparing new Citizens In Power resources
items.b: Citizens In Power is a new project by Sortition Foundation designed to support organisations to design citizen-led governance. Contact Will at Sortition Foundation to find out more. Read up on Sortition Foundation’s summary of the latest deliberative process / citizens’ assembly news across the world, not forgetting SF’s recent work on the Scottish Parliaments’s Citizens’ Panel on Participation .
items.why: this matters democratically because it develops resources to support the design of citizen-led governance and deliberative decision-making processes such as citizens' assemblies.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative process resources are filed under elections & decision making per framework rules, not participation.

items.h: Demos notes online abuse has changed from Johnson to Truss
items.b: Demos Junior Researcher Alice Dawson has identified clear sexist themes in recent weeks with the access of Liz Truss as Prime Minister, noting their intelligence is far more likely to be questioned and her appearance commented upon, as well as those of her female Cabinet colleagues, invoking typical gendered tropes about women in public life. Demos has also announced their programme of events over this year’s conference season.
items.why: this matters democratically because gendered abuse of women in public office is a form of unequal treatment that can deter women's exercise of political voice and office-holding.
items.note: Gendered abuse framed as discrimination is treated as a rights matter rather than participation capacity.

items.h: Nesta launch new Democratic Innovation and Digital Participation report
items.b: With trust in political representatives and our democratic system at an all-time low, the case for building more inclusive and participatory systems of governance is growing. Nesta’s report Democratic innovation and digital participation Harnessing collective intelligence for 21st-century decision-making is based on insights from global examples of digital democratic innovation, and in particular, three pilots from the COLDIGIT project : a citizens’ assembly in Trondheim, Norway; participatory budgeting in Gothenburg, Sweden; and participatory budgeting in Helsinki, Finland. The work is a coll…
items.why: this matters democratically because the report examines new digital and deliberative mechanisms, such as participatory budgeting, that expand how citizens can take part in collective decisions.
items.note: Report mixes participatory budgeting (participation) with citizens' assembly examples (elections & decision making).
links: Democratic innovation and digital participation Harnessing collective intelligence for 21st-century decision-making

items.h: Democratic Yorkshire launches
items.b: New alliance of Yorkshire-based democracy groups forms around electoral reform, written constitution and devolution issues.
items.why: this matters democratically because a new alliance forming to campaign on electoral reform, a written constitution and devolution directly concerns the machinery of collective decision-making.
links: New alliance of Yorkshire-based democracy groups

items.h: Republic calls for protests in lead up to King Charles’ coronation, condemns police action
items.b: Graham Smith, Chief Executive of republican campaign group Republic , criticised the actions of police against anti-monarchy protesters, announcing new protests around the coronation of King Charles III .
items.why: this matters democratically because police action against protesters and the announcement of further protests concern the legal and policing limits on freedom of assembly.
items.note: Protest policing is classified under rights & civic space per the boundary rule on legal restriction and state coercion.

items.h: Democracy R&D Conference, Berlin, 28–30 September
items.b: Held in Berlin, the annual conference of the Democracy R&D network is this year focused on three main streams: political buy-in, inclusive participation, and democracy in times of crisis. Find out more . Democracy Network will be in attendance.
items.note: Conference/event listing counts as sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: Citizen Network & Cornwall Compass to launch Cornwall Declaration of Democracy
items.b: Citizen Network are working with Cornwall Compass to engender cross party support in Cornwall for democratic renewal and the take up of proportional representation. Cornwall Compass are due to launch the Cornwall Declaration of Democracy , a document outlining the problems facing the county and garnering support for electoral reform as a solution. The two organisations are also planning a survey to assess the level of support for devolution in Cornwall.
items.why: this matters democratically because the declaration and survey aim to build cross-party support for electoral reform and devolution, directly engaging the structures of collective decision-making.

items.h: After Participation — new report seeks to expand modern democratic imaginary
items.b: In a new age where democracy is no longer the only option, they argue, the Untitled Group on Democracy including input from Demsoc, Alternative UK , Das Progressive Zentrum and others came together in Spring 2022 to discuss what practices and ideals are missing from our democratic imaginary. The new report, After Participation: Imagining Democracy in the Age of Conflict , outlines some of the sentiments held within those conversations, moving away from the idea that we simply need to add more participative processes to current structures, and examines what democracy could mean if we broadened …
items.note: A think-piece report on reimagining democratic concepts, not a concrete mechanism or new means of participation.
links: After Participation: Imagining Democracy in the Age of Conflict

items.h: Demsoc on the role of participatory ecosystems
items.b: Way back in February Demsoc examined participatory ecosystems as part of their quarterly ‘DemsocNext10’ series on the future of democracy. Where participatory ecosystems are similar to organic models, made up organisms interacting with each other, Demsoc spent time analysing how they relate to others as part of this democratic organism , inspired by Civic Square in Birmingham and Every One Every Day in Barking and Dagenham.
items.note: Sector commentary/analysis on participatory theory rather than a reported change or new participation mechanism.
links: spent time analysing how they relate to others as part of this democratic organism

items.h: Onward report looks at causes behind youth detachment from democracy
items.b: According to Onward , young people are more detached from society than ever before leading to a generational slide away from democratic norms and towards authoritarianism. In a new report, ‘The Kids Aren’t Alright’ , Onward look at the drivers behind this youth disenchantment and offers possible methods of driving greater social and political engagement.
items.why: the report presents evidence that young people's detachment from society is eroding their engagement with and support for democratic norms.

items.h: Women’s Equality Party Annual Conference to go online this November
items.b: WEP will host their annual conference on the 26th-27th of November. The conference has moved online due to concerns about the cost of living crisis and rising covid cases. Join them across the weekend for the chance to discuss the policies the party should be taking forward.
items.note: Organisational logistics about a party conference format, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: PSA Parliaments invites proposals for annual conference
items.b: This year’s PSA Parliaments Annual Conference will be held in Birmingham and online on 3–4 November 2022. The conference theme is ‘What next?’ and will consider a range of questions from the next scandal to hit parliament to what parliamentary reform practitioners should focus on next. There is an open call to submit papers on anything connected with this theme.
items.note: Call for papers/event listing, not itself a reported democratic development.

items.h: Sheila McKechnie Foundation host a range of training sessions this Autumn
items.b: SMK have a number of training sessions available this Autumn including sessions on devolved power and how to influence at a local level, how to get savvier with digital campaigning, and the power of community organising in achieving change. Check out the full range of trainings coming up this Autumn.
items.why: the training creates new capacity for people to organise communities and influence devolved and local power, expanding practical means of participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it creates new participatory skills/opportunities.

items.h: Will Snell, Chief Executive of The Fairness Foundation, announces launch date for The Fairness Tool
items.b: The Fairness Foundation will launch their online tool, The Fairness Index, with a webinar on 19th October. The tool, which aims to help social change organisations define and measure unfairness, analyses statistics by examining five key gaps in British society linked to the ‘fair necessities’.
items.note: A data/measurement tool for social change organisations, not itself a mechanism for democratic participation.

items.h: Stir to Action’s November community engagement course is open for booking.
items.b: A two day residential course by Stir to Action , Art of Invitation: creative approaches to community engagement , is being held by Selgars Mill from the 23rd to 25th November. Located in Mid Devon the course will cover topics such as approaches to engaging people in creative, collective responses to systemic challenges facing their communities, and creative processes and activities that can activate and inspire people to participate in bringing about change.
items.why: the course builds people's capacity and creative tools to engage collectively in community decision-making and civic action.
links: Art of Invitation: creative approaches to community engagement

items.h: Hear from global communities using deliberative assemblies at this year’s ReWorlding conference
items.b: The second edition of ReWorlding will take place from September 30th to October 2nd offering a chance to hear from communities in East Africa, Chile and Scotland on their experiences using deliberate assemblies or community-based decision-making processes. As well as looking at how and why they adopted these processes, the event will explore how these mechanisms challenge traditional power structures and help reinstate grassroots autonomy.
items.note: An event listing about deliberative assemblies elsewhere, not a reported UK democratic change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: The Campaign Company monitoring public impact of royal transition
items.b: Charlie Mansell and the team at the Campaign Company mainly work with local authorities, NGOs, charities and trade unions on community engagement, including citizens juries and PB. They are currently monitoring the public impact of the death of the Queen, in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Contact Charlie to find out more about what they’ve observed.
items.note: Promotional note about a firm's ongoing monitoring work, not a reported democratic development.

items.h: Grassroots for Europe organising around democratic issues
items.b: Whilst they primarily focus on the campaign for the UK to rejoin the EU, Grassroots for Europe — a coalition of more than 80 local citizen groups, now tends to spend their energy working with other democracy organisations on countering attacks on UK democracy through groupings such as the Police Bill Alliance or the Democracy Defence Coalition . They are currently organising a workshop on the impact of the invasion of Ukraine on UK democracy.
items.why: it reflects civil-society coalitions organising and building capacity to monitor and defend democratic norms in the UK.
items.note: Treated as civic-society organising/capacity-building rather than mere org news since it describes ongoing coalition activity and events.

items.h: Elect Her is hiring
items.b: Elect Her is looking for freelancers and new recruits to join its Board of Directors. Board members will serve a tenure of two years whilst freelancers will join for a range of projects running this Autumn. Find out more on their website.
links: Find out more on their website.

items.h: Liberty hiring investigative journalist
items.b: Working on Liberty’s new investigative journalism project focused on exposing and challenging abuses of power and violations of human rights, the role is full time and will focus on migrants’ rights and policing. Find out more and apply by 10th October .
links: Find out more and apply by 10th October

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation looking for a researcher
items.b: The role is focused on helping PINF with their 2023 PINF Index based on a large survey of 100 independent publishers across the UK. Find out more and apply .

items.h: Royal Society of the Arts hiring Head of Delivery
items.b: The RSA is hiring for a Head of Delivery for their new Design for Life strategy. Find out more on their website .
links: Find out more on their website

items.h: Kings College SU to hire a Democracy Development Coordinator
items.b: The Democracy Development Coordinator will work within the Community Engagement department to develop KCLSU’s democratic practices, policy and procedures. This is a full-time role and the application deadline is October 10th.

items.h: Perspectiva is hiring
items.b: Perspectiva is a group of ‘expert generalists’ exploring alternative forms of economic management and political cooperation. They’re currently on the hunt for a Director of Operations, Community Builder and Research Assistant to join their expanding team. They are also looking for new trustees and anyone with a background in audio-visual production to work with them on a consultancy basis. Get in touch for more details on the roles.

items.h: Labour may abolish House of Lords if it wins next election, leaked report reveals
items.b: The leaked constitutional review, seen by the Guardian , recommends abolishing the House of Lords and replacing it with an upper house of nations and regions, as well as handing sweeping new powers to local regions and devolved nations. Additional recommendations include, new tax powers for some devolved governments, powers for local people to promote bills in Parliament via democratically elected bodies, a constitutional guarantee of social and economic rights and powers for mayors on education, transport and research funding. The review recommends a crackdown on standards in central governme…
items.why: proposed abolition of the House of Lords and devolution of new powers to nations, regions and mayors would restructure how collective decisions are made and representatives are chosen across tiers of UK government.
items.note: Structural reform of upper chamber and devolved government placed under elections_decision_making per boundary rule; standards/Electoral Commission elements noted as secondary government_accountability.
links: leaked constitutional review, seen by the Guardian

items.h: Public opinion of King Charles III improves dramatically
items.b: Public polling of King Charles over recent years has remained fairly steady, but low, with a YouGov survey in May finding Britons split on his prospects at 32% for and 32% against whether or not he would make a good king. With the death of Queen Elizabeth II and his proclamation, his polling has shot up to 63% favourable, and just 15% disapproving.
items.note: A shift in public opinion of the monarch is not itself a mechanism of democratic power, contestation or accountability.

items.h: Letter to PACAC reveals key developments on implementation of Elections Act
items.b: Paul Scully MP, Minister of State for Levelling Up, has written to William Wragg MP, Chair of the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee providing new insight into the Government’s approach to the implementation of the Election Act. The letter indicates that due to the complexity of the implementation the full reforms are being implemented in phases through next year and finishing in 2024, to ease pressure on electoral services and to maintain the ‘no-fail’ nature of the UK’s electoral infrastructure.
items.why: the phased implementation of the Elections Act directly shapes the administration and reliability of electoral machinery in the UK.
links: The letter indicates that due to the complexity of the implementation the full reforms are being implemented in phases

items.h: A vision for a reformed political system is a vote-winner, argue Ruth Lister and Luke Williams
items.b: Writing for Labourlist last week, Ruth Lister, Board Member at Compass , and Luke Williams, Council Member at Unlock Democracy , argue that there is ‘overwhelming demand’ for Labour to ‘show more positive vision’ of how we can refresh our political system. With trust in politicians at record lows , there is a clear case to be made to ‘modernise the creaking political system that puts them in power and allows them to get away with so much’.
items.why: it advocates changing the electoral and constitutional system that determines how political power is allocated and held accountable.
links: trust in politicians at record lows

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy reports Labour Conference motions for PR top 140
items.b: Once again, PR motions top the table again at Labour’s annual conference with more than 140 CLPs backing motions, and more than 370 CLPs (some 60% of all CLPs in England) now have a policy in favour of PR, in addition to a majority of affiliated unions now in favour of electoral reform, L4ND are rightly excited about their prospects for Liverpool next week.
items.why: growing party support for proportional representation could change the electoral system used to allocate political power.
links: PR motions top the table again at Labour’s annual conference

items.h: Constitutional reform must be complemented with proportional representation, says Labour for a New Democracy
items.b: L4ND has published a new report , warning that Labour’s plans for constitutional reform will not deliver on its objectives unless they include plans to switch to a system of proportional representation for general elections. Writing for LabourList Caroline Osborne and Joe Sousek wrote : “If devolution alone could indeed mitigate Britain’s crisis of democracy, one would expect highly devolved countries with winner-takes-all systems (such as Canada, Australia and the US) to have healthier democracies. Yet…all such countries have experienced a similar long-term collapse in public satisfaction wit…
items.why: the report argues the electoral system itself must change alongside devolution for democratic reform to be effective.
links: Caroline Osborne and Joe Sousek wrote

items.h: Police face backlash as republican protesters arrested over royal mourning period
items.b: Civil liberties groups Big Brother Watch , Liberty and NetPol have criticised police over the arrests of anti-monarchy protesters over the royal mourning period. Arrests included a man heckling Prince Andrew, a man in Edinburgh arrested for shouting “who elected him?” and several protesters staging protests on the Royal Mile including a young woman holding a republican placard. In London, Paul Powesland, a barrister, held a blank piece of paper near Parliament and was threatened with arrest if he wrote ‘Not My King’ on it . Jodie Beck at civil rights group Liberty stated in response to the arr…
items.why: police use of arrest powers against political protesters directly restricts the freedom of assembly and expression needed to contest and criticise the state.
items.note: Protest policing is classified as rights/civic space per the boundary rule on legal restriction and state coercion.
links: threatened with arrest if he wrote ‘Not My King’ on it

items.h: Royal Wedding protester reflects on anti-royal dissent over the last decade
items.b: Writing for the Network for Police Monitoring , Hannah Chutzpah reflects on their arrest during the royal wedding period in 2011 and the effect this has had on them and their perception of the police. Hannah was arrested for dressing up in zombie fancy dress in a coffee shop some distance away from the wedding proceedings. More than 55 were arrested on the day of the royal wedding in 2011 using blanket stop and search powers, including 21 further ‘pre-emptive arrests’ the night before the wedding. The High Court later upheld these arrests .
items.why: a first-person account of pre-emptive arrests around royal events illustrates how policing powers can chill protest and dissent.
links: The High Court later upheld these arrests

items.h: Human rights law professor doubts police grounds for republican arrests
items.b: Professor David Mead at the University of East Anglia, specialist in UK Human Rights Law, analysed the legal arguments and ramifications of the recent arrests of anti-monarchy protesters across the UK . Professor Mead states that ‘without any evidence of likely violence, the police probably should not have acted … Even with heightened current public sensitivities, being provoked by a simple sign proclaiming “not my king” is probably not reasonable’. Mead suggests that the arrests may bring into question whether such open-ended common law policing discretion sits well in a liberal democracy.
items.why: a legal expert questioning whether police had lawful grounds for arrests speaks to predictable and lawful enforcement of the law against citizens.
items.note: Focus is on the lawfulness of state action rather than the freedom itself, placing it under rule of law.
links: analysed the legal arguments and ramifications of the recent arrests of anti-monarchy protesters across the UK

items.h: Automated policing helped kill Chris Kaba, argues Griff Ferris
items.b: Griff Ferris, Senior Legal and Policy Officer at Fair Trials , writing for Novara Media argues that Chris Kaba’s killing by police in London was a result of expanded automated policing, that the vehicle he was driving was linked to a previous “firearms incident” despite not being registered to Kaba. In the wake of Kaba’s killing fourteen rights groups wrote to Met Police Chief Sir Mark Rowley calling on him to end the force’s use of controversial automated policing technologies. A coroner’s inquest into Mr Kaba’s death is due to open on 4 October, the Met Police firearms officer involved has b…
items.why: the use of automated policing technology in a fatal police shooting raises questions about lawful and accountable state use of force.
items.note: State violence and policing lawfulness is anchored to rule of law & justice.
links: fourteen rights groups wrote to Met Police Chief Sir Mark Rowley

items.h: How the police map protest movements, new report from Parliament Security and Intelligence Committee
items.b: For the first time, a new report released by Parliament’s Security and Intelligence Committee has given us the Matrix (threshold and terminology matrix) that determines who is potentially categorised as an ‘aggravated activist’ and at what level. How campaigners are categorised will lead, in turn, to the kind of policing operation they can expect to have used against them.
items.why: a parliamentary report revealing how police categorise and surveil activists bears directly on the space available for people to organise and protest without state interference.

items.h: Stop and Search powers disproportionately target protesters, new figures reveal
items.b: The use of stop and search powers increased by more than a fifth during weekends where protests were taking place in central London. Big Brother Watch has revealed data from an investigation into the misuse of the policing tactic that, aside from special circumstances, can only be used for limited reasons. “Our research shows an alarming pattern of police disproportionately using existing powers to deliberately target people exercising their right to protest … The public order bill would grant officers new protest-specific stop and search powers which can be used without suspicion. This is a d…
items.why: disproportionate use of stop and search against protesters, alongside new suspicionless powers, restricts the freedom to assemble and dissent.
links: Big Brother Watch has revealed data

items.h: Byline Intelligence team maps Truss’s network of advisors and donors
items.b: Liz Truss has won the campaign to become the leader of the Conservative Party and the Prime Minister — but she relied on an extensive network of donors to do so. The Byline Intelligence team has mapped out who these donors are and have taken a look at her new advisors to get a sense of the interests and ideological positions that will have a stake in the current government. A further investigation has revealed that six cabinet members, including Truss herself, have funding ties to Conservative groups that are themselves heavily connected to The Mercer Family Foundation — a billionaire pro-Trum…
items.why: mapping the donor and advisor networks around a new Prime Minister exposes potential undue influence of private interests over government policy and appointments.
links: The Byline Intelligence team has mapped out

items.h: MP Paula Barker suggests centralised system of governance will lead to more scandals
items.b: During a Commons debate earlier this month MP Paula Barker argued the UK lacks any sophisticated or robust mechanism for upholding standards in public life and suggested a more thorough method of enforcing such standards is needed. Under the current system she said “far too much power is invested in the executive branch in an overly centralised system of governance — a centralisation of power that is incomparable to our counterparts — so I fear that the very nature of our democracy will inevitably see us lurch from scandal to scandal.” Barker also welcomed Full Fact’s commitment to providing m…
items.why: it concerns whether power is excessively centralised in the executive and whether adequate standards mechanisms exist to hold that power accountable.

items.h: Labour MP Rosie Cooper steps down, triggers byelection
items.b: The West Lancashire MP facing death threats from banned neo-Nazi groups has resigned. Taking the Chiltern Hundreds for the moment, the Speaker will soon issue a writ for a byelection for the 8,000 Labour majority seat.
items.why: a resignation triggering a byelection directly engages the mechanism by which representatives are chosen and replaced.
links: facing death threats from banned neo-Nazi groups

items.h: Zack Polanksi elected as deputy leader of The Green Party
items.b: Polanksi has been elected as the next deputy leader of The Green Party , although just 12.5% of the party membership took part in the vote. Polanski says he recognises the party ‘faces an enormous challenge with the first past the post voting system’, but with record gains in local councillor elections, he says he’s confident that there is an appetite amongst the electorate for a new kind of politics. Zack is a London Assembly Member and Chair of London’s Environment Committee.
items.why: it concerns an internal party leadership election and the electoral system's effect on political competition.
items.note: Political party internal elections are filed under elections & decision making per the freedom of association boundary rule.
links: Polanksi has been elected as the next deputy leader of The Green Party

items.h: Devolution deal for York and North Yorkshire scrutinised by IPPR
items.b: A new devolution deal was announced last month for York and North Yorkshire that will see a new combined authority with devolved authority governing the two regions. The new authority will gain specific devolved powers over education, transport, housing and more, with a regional mayor elected in 2024. IPPR takes a closer look at the new arrangement and considers what this means for the region.
items.why: it concerns the creation of a new devolved governance structure and elected mayoralty, altering how regional decisions are made and by whom.
items.note: Devolution deal structure and elected mayor place this under elections & decision making per the local/regional government boundary rule.

items.h: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council set to hold a People’s Jury on the Climate Change Crises
items.b: On the 26th September Shared Future are facilitating a People’s Jury in partnership with Darwen Borough Council. A representative group of 30 residents will look at what needs to be done in homes, businesses and in the local area to help tackle the climate change crisis.
items.why: a citizens' jury is a deliberative decision-making process that gives residents a formal role in shaping local policy.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes are filed under elections & decision making per the framework's revised boundary rule.

items.h: A shortlist of entries for the Media Freedom Awards due to be published in late September
items.b: UK Journalists championing the public’s right to know and holding power to account will be celebrated at an awards ceremony in London on 9th November. Awards will include News Media Organisation of the Year, Freedom of Information Award and Investigation of the Year and Campaign of the Year.
items.note: Award shortlist announcement is sector admin, not a mechanism of democratic power.

items.h: The Public Interest News Foundation begins its Autumn Leadership Programme
items.b: 15 independent newsrooms from across the UK will take part in the annual programme which aims to help publishers produce high quality content that meets people’s needs enabling better informed citizens and cohesive communities. If you’d like to know more or enquire about next year’s programme, contact Joe Mitchell .
items.why: training independent newsrooms to produce higher-quality public-interest journalism strengthens the plural information environment citizens rely on to hold power to account.
items.note: Capacity-building programme aimed at journalism quality is treated as information & public debate rather than participation, given its focus on the information environment.

items.h: European Union reveals plans for new media freedom laws
items.b: The European Union has announced plans to introduce a European Media Freedom Act. The Commission has criticised Slovenia, Hungary and Poland in recent years for limiting the freedom of their national media, but now they suggest there is a risk of political interference in more than 20 member countries. The new act aims to safeguard the freedom of the media across the continent by preventing state spying and state direction of the media, as well as secure funding for public service media and attempt to make media ownership more transparent.
items.why: EU-wide legislation to protect media plurality and prevent state interference in journalism is comparative evidence bearing on press freedom protections relevant to UK democracy.
items.note: International story included as comparative evidence on media freedom, not a direct UK development.
links: European Union has announced plans to introduce a European Media Freedom Act.

items.h: The sector needs more funders, says David Jubb, Sortition Foundation
items.b: Though democracy, the rule of the people, is the key bedrock of our society and political system — the systems, organisations and projects that seek to maintain, educate and advocate for democracy norms and practices have extremely limited resources. David Jubb, Co-Director at the Sortition Foundation, makes the comparison between the cultural sector and the democracy sector — the former receives approximately £1.5bn per annum, the latter receives a paltry £3–4m in total.
items.note: Commentary on funding levels for the democracy sector is organisational advocacy, not a reported mechanism change.

items.h: Russia strips independent media outlet of its licence
items.b: Novaya Gazeta, one of the few remaining independent media outlets in Russia, has been stripped of its media licence . The paper has been a stalwart of the media scene in Russia since it was established in 1993, carving out a reputation as the leading investigative paper. The new ruling amounts to ‘informational genocide’, says editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, and will make it far harder for the outlet to investigate and critique the Russian authorities.
items.note: Story concerns Russian state action against media with no direct bearing on or comparison to UK democratic mechanisms.
links: has been stripped of its media licence
