Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Oliver Walkden — Young Citizens, Perry Walker — TalkShop, Katy Murray — Cast From Clay, Jessie Joe Jacobs — Democracy Network, Louise Dunmore — Democracy Network, Calum Green — Involve, Charlie Mansell — The Campaign Company, Alex Bulat — Migrant Democracy Project, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Naomi Smith — Best for Britain, Bob Bater — Knowplexity Associates and Will Snell — Fairness Foundation.

The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 73 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: Sector pledge/alliance admin, not a report of change to democratic mechanisms.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.
items.note: Continuation of pledge statement text, sector coordination rhetoric.

items.b: If you would like to add you and your organisation’s name to the list of signatories, please email pledge@centrefordemocracy.org.uk .
items.note: Call to action to sign a pledge, sector logistics.

items.h: Online session to explore the Public Order Bill and implications for protest
items.b: Netpol and Garden Court Chambers are hosting an online event on October 11th to explore the upcoming Public Order Bill and its impact on the right to protest and civil liberties. The event will hear from a range of speakers including lawyers and campaigners and is free to attend.
items.why: the Public Order Bill would tighten legal restrictions on the right to protest, directly affecting people's ability to assemble and dissent.
items.note: Framed as an event listing but substantively concerns legislation narrowing protest rights.

items.h: Cast from Clay launches new report on impact of disinformation on research expertise
items.b: Democracy 2.0: Experts in the Age of Instinct explores how best policy experts — a discipline founded on reason and evidence — can continue to support democracies in this new age of misinformation and instinct where our information environment is under constant threat. Katy Murray , Insights and Relationship Lead at Cast from Clay , says they’re trying to get policy experts to recognise what they contribute to democracy and the risk of complacency.
items.why: disinformation degrading trust in evidence-based expertise undermines the quality of information available for public debate and policymaking.
items.note: Report launch counts as sector capacity-building on the information environment.
links: Democracy 2.0: Experts in the Age of Instinct

items.h: Young Citizens running Magistrates’ Mock Trials, celebrating 5 years of Quality Mark
items.b: Working for an active citizenship that they argue should be an essential part of children and young people’s education, Young Citizens work with thousands of schools each year to create practical experiences of ‘citizenship in action’. Their next programme on legal education are a set of Magistrates’ Mock Trials — applications are still open . Young Citizens celebrates 5 years of the Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural Development Quality Mark for schools.
items.why: the mock trials programme builds young people's practical civic capacity and understanding of legal institutions, expanding means of civic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of civic engagement for young people.
links: celebrates 5 years of the Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural Development Quality Mark

items.h: Stone King LLP running refresher on election law for charities and issue campaigns, October 13th
items.b: The law firm Stone King LLP will bring together speakers from the Electoral Commission, NCVO and their own in-house expertise to discuss changes to electoral law for future elections. Register now for the event on October 13th .
items.why: changes to electoral law affect how charities and campaigners can lawfully participate in election campaigning.
items.note: Event listing but substance concerns electoral law changes for future elections.
links: Register now for the event on October 13th

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project gathers steam
items.b: Alex Bulat & Lara Parizotto have registered a new company, the Migrant Democracy Project — a new home for their current residence based voting rights campaigns for migrants in the UK, including the re-launch of their campaign Our Home Our Vote . Head over to their Twitter now and give them a follow and show your support!
items.why: the campaign seeks to extend voting rights to migrant residents, a direct question of suffrage and who can participate in elections.

items.h: Best for Britain pushing back on Henry VIII powers, hiring
items.b: Naomi Smith, CEO at Best for Britain , reports that their team is focusing on achieving a cross party joint approach to pushing back on the Henry VIII powers in the Northern Ireland Protocol Bill . Best for Britain are also hiring for a Communities Manager , and possibly a PA soon too.
items.why: opposing Henry VIII powers in the Northern Ireland Protocol Bill concerns limiting executive power to bypass parliamentary scrutiny through delegated legislation.

items.h: TalkShop launching their Win-Win method
items.b: Having just completed training up the National Union of Students’ teams in how to shift their annual conference from motions, amendments and debates to a more dialogic, informal format, TalkShop will soon be launching their Win-Win method on November 2nd. Get in touch with Perry Walker to find out more.
items.why: the new dialogic method changes how a civil society organisation's members deliberate and make collective decisions, strengthening civic participation capacity.
items.note: Concerns internal civil-society decision-making method, not governmental deliberative machinery, so treated as participation rather than elections/decision-making.
links: Get in touch with Perry Walker

items.h: Democracy Network organising new Democracy Conference
items.b: It’s all hush-hush at the moment, but word on the Zoom-grapevine is that Jessie Joe Jacobs and Louise Dumore at Democracy Network are planning a new Democracy Conference for 2023, exciting! They’re also meeting with democracy organisations related to regional devolution, is that your focus? — then get in touch !

items.h: Sortition Foundation examine citizen assembly recruitment practices
items.b: The Sortition Foundation recently completed an analysis of two recent citizens’ assemblies they recruited for to explore just how inclusive they were. The research stems from concern that recruiting to targets such as age or gender will omit some important social demographics. Their analysis noted that the pool of respondents tended to over-represent those with higher educational attainment suggesting a hybrid recruitment strategy is needed to overcome this selection bias. Check out the full report on intersectionality and recruitment.
items.why: the research examines whether recruitment methods for citizens' assemblies produce socially representative deliberative bodies, bearing on the legitimacy of that decision-making machinery
items.note: Citizens' assembly recruitment is mapped to elections_decision_making per the boundary rule on deliberative processes, not participation.
links: Check out the full report on intersectionality and recruitment.

items.h: Fairness Foundation launching Fairness Index, 19th October
items.b: The new Fairness Index from Fairness Foundation is an online resource that aims to collate and explain the key data about how fair British society is today. Join their launch webinar on 19th October to find out more . Will Snell and the team at Fairness Foundation specialise in supporting other organisations to talk about fairness — to that end they also publish a curated set of resources for partners and a weekly email .
items.note: A general societal fairness index is not tied closely enough to a democratic participation or decision-making mechanism to qualify.
links: Join their launch webinar on 19th October to find out more

items.h: FrameWorks UK — framing strategies to help mission driven campaigns to support change
items.b: Charlie Mansell at the Campaign Company notes the great work being done at FrameWorks UK and their potential in assisting other organisations in reframing debates over democracy. Check them out .

items.h: Directory of Social Change to host event on influencing policy and policymakers
items.b: Whether it’s Westminster, Whitehall or local authorities, Engage’s annual event on the 18th of October will take a broad look at the policy landscape and explore all aspects of how to influence policymakers.

items.h: Nesta publishes report ‘Democratic Innovation and Digital Participation’ by Oli Whittington
items.b: The report discusses the barriers faced by democratic innovators alongside the need for democratic innovations and digital participation tools to remove the barriers to create inclusive decision-making systems.
items.why: the report examines barriers to democratic innovation and digital participation tools that determine who can practically take part in collective decision-making

items.h: Knowplexity offer free online course on citizens’ assemblies
items.b: Knowplexity launched their GreenPath learning portal in July, which includes a f ree online course on citizens’ assemblies . They’re planning to include new courses covering basic income, electoral reform and Doughnut Economics.
items.why: a new free course expands people's capacity to understand and engage with democratic innovation processes such as citizens' assemblies
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building under participation rather than as the deliberative process itself.
links: ree online course on citizens’ assemblies

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation welcomes Max Roche, fundraising
items.b: Joe Mitchell and the PINF team report that they’ve hired a new Researcher — none other than Centre for Democracy’s own Max Roche, who’ll be working with them a day work to lay the groundwork for next year’s PINF Index . In other news, they also report that their fundraising, possibly for a NewsMatch -style programme.

items.h: Demos are recruiting a Director of Policy and Impact
items.b: The Director of Policy and Impact will work closely with the senior leadership team at Demos and will lead the organisation’s policy work, helping to build funding routes to achieve it. The ideal candidate will be adept at identifying policy weaknesses and have a creative mindset on how to solve them. Deadlines for applications are w/c 7th Nov.

items.h: The Electoral Commission is hiring
items.b: The Electoral Commission is looking for a Senior Registration Advisor to work in their party registration team. Experience working in a regulatory environment is preferable and the deadline is this weekend! They are also on the hunt for a Monitoring Manager to lead the monitoring team and enhance the work of other teams in the regulation directorate. The closing date for this position is October 30th.

items.h: Forty democracy pioneers to take part in Climate Democracy Action program
items.b: Forty global policymakers and advocates with a vision of using participatory democracy to address the climate crisis have been selected to take part in the first Climate Democracy Action Programme. The individuals will receive training to help them deliver a climate-focussed participatory programme in their country of origin with two of the programmes eventually receiving a $20,000 implementation grant. Check out the full list of forty individuals that have been selected .
items.why: it creates new training and resources that build capacity for participatory democratic decision-making, expanding the practical means people have to take part.
items.note: Sector capacity-building programme counted per framework rule, though international rather than UK-specific.
links: full list of forty individuals that have been selected

items.h: New UCL report on social and psychological impacts of COVID-19
items.b: The report, ‘Tracking the Psychological and Social Consequences of the COVID-19 Pandemic Across the UK Population’ , by University College London provides an overview of the in-depth study which involved more than 70,000 participants over two years. The analysis includes population compliance levels with COVID-19 measures as well as barriers and facilitative elements that impacted on these numbers.
links: ‘Tracking the Psychological and Social Consequences of the COVID-19 Pandemic Across the UK Population’

items.h: Major win for electoral reform campaigners as Labour Party delegates back Proportional Representation
items.b: The campaign to introduce proportional representation gained significant momentum during the Labour Conference after party delegates voted in favour of ditching the first past the post voting system . The vote was hailed by Laura Parker from Labour for a New Democracy , as ‘an historic moment’, and comes following a year in which a number of key unions including UNISON and UNITE pledged their support for electoral reform. Campaigners and other parties including the Greens are now calling on Starmer to listen to the democratic voice of delegates and include PR as a manifesto pledge ahead of the…
items.why: it concerns a major party's internal position on the electoral system used to choose representatives.
links: party delegates voted in favour of ditching the first past the post voting system

items.h: Proportional representation will not be in a Labour manifesto pledge, says Starmer
items.b: Despite the historic Labour Conference vote to back a switch to proportional representation, Starmer has said electoral reform will not be a manifesto pledge at the next election . Writing for the New Statesman, Neal Lawson, Director at Compass , suggested the opposition to electoral reform from the Labour leadership stems from a fear that PR would expose them to unwanted electoral competition and perhaps a view that long periods of no power are preferable to sharing power.
items.why: it concerns whether a party seeking government will commit to changing the electoral system that determines how representatives are chosen.
links: Starmer has said electoral reform will not be a manifesto pledge at the next election
fear that PR would expose them to unwanted electoral competition

items.h: 51% of the UK want electoral reform, according to long-running survey
items.b: Since 1983, the British Social Attitudes survey has asked the public whether they want to keep the current electoral system or if they want to reform it ‘to allow smaller political parties to get a fairer share of MPs’. Since it was first asked the question has been put to the public over 20 times, but this year is the first time the balance has tipped in favour of reform . 51% compared to 44% voted in favour of electoral reform — a divide that is even starker amongst Labour voters with 61% vs 34% saying they want reform.
items.why: it reports public attitudes toward the electoral system that determines how votes translate into representation.
links: the balance has tipped in favour of reform

items.h: Briefing paper released on legal issues surrounding Scottish Referendum
items.b: The House of Commons Library has released a briefing paper tracing the Scottish Government’s attempts to legislate for a referendum. The paper outlines the constitutional development of the United Kingdom itself before examining the recent legal and legislative context behind the push for an independence referendum.
items.why: it concerns the legal and constitutional machinery governing whether a binding referendum on independence can be held.
items.note: Referendum machinery is filed under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: New report: Reimagining Whitehall: an essay by Dr Simon Kaye
items.b: Think tank Reform kicked off the start of their ‘Reimagining Whitehall’ programme with the publication of their eponymous paper which offers a high-level examination of the issues they believe must be resolved in order to deliver excellence that is suitable for the government apparatus of the future.
items.why: it addresses civil service capacity and the machinery of executive government, which affects how public power is administered and held accountable.

items.h: Compass asks: Is the cost of living crisis a crisis of democracy?
items.b: If people can’t afford the bare necessities because our political system stifles policies for change, what does this say about our democracy? In the first of a new three month podcast series, Compass are joined by Founder of the Tax Justice Network , Richard Murphy, to look at the current economic crisis and how it intersects with a crisis of our democracy.
items.why: it examines how economic hardship constrains people's practical ability to take part in and influence political life.
items.note: Cost of living framed as condition for participation rather than a rights claim.

items.h: Government ‘mini budget’ breaks with norms of good government, according to the Institute for Government
items.b: Truss and Kwarteng bypassed normal standards of parliamentary scrutiny after their budget was debated for just two hours, says the Institute for Government . Referring to it as a ‘mini budget’ or ‘fiscal event’ meant they were able to circumvent the standard five-day period of parliamentary scrutiny in which colleagues would be able to critique and amend the upcoming economic agenda. Furthermore, Kwarteng announced the proposals without first consulting the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), fuelling concerns that Truss’s leadership will be marked by a shirking of independent advice.
items.why: it reports the executive bypassing normal parliamentary scrutiny and independent fiscal advice, weakening checks on government power.
links: bypassed normal standards of parliamentary scrutiny

items.h: The Court of Appeals rule that the human rights defence is no longer valid for demonstrators
items.b: The Court of Appeal ruled last week that defendants in future instances resembling the Colston Four will not be allowed to raise human rights defences. In future protest cases human rights defences will only be considered in situations where there is perceived low value damage, a ruling which sways the scales of justice ever further against core human rights.
items.why: it narrows the legal protection available to protesters, affecting the practical freedom to assemble and dissent.
items.note: Court ruling addressed both as adjudication and as a restriction on protest freedom; classified by the freedom affected.
links: Court of Appeal ruled last week

items.h: News Media Association establishes new online public notice portal
items.b: The new Online Public Notices Portal , with funding from Google, supplements the existing physical public notice boards present across many towns and cities. This new online portal allows individuals and groups to view, comment on and share planned developments before decisions are made.
items.why: it creates a new digital means for people to view and comment on planning decisions before they are made, expanding practical avenues for civic participation.
items.note: Treated as new participation infrastructure rather than mere information provision since it enables commenting before decisions are made.

items.h: Ethics rules for the position of London Mayor must be strengthened, according to inquiry
items.b: An inquiry into the scandal around Boris Johnson and US businesswoman Jennifer Arcuri has suggested ethics rules for the position of London Mayor must be strengthened. The committee found that Johnson had opened himself up to “a perception of lack of due process and favouritism” in his dealings with Arcuri. The committee went on to suggest that London City Hall’s codes of conduct ought to specify clearly that public officials must declare personal relationships if public money is to go to that person.
items.why: it addresses whether standards in public life and conflict-of-interest rules effectively hold an elected office-holder answerable for favouritism.
links: ethics rules for the position of London Mayor must be strengthened.

items.h: Jacob Rees-Mogg comes under attack for abuse of governmental position
items.b: Jacob Rees-Mogg initially made headlines after handing a peerage and a job as a senior minister in Truss’s government to Dominic Johnson — a city businessman who co-founded Somerset Capital Management with Rees-Mogg and has donated over £250,000 to the Conservative Party. Rees-Mogg invited further criticism after an email leak to the Guardian exposed his attempts to bypass environmental and judicial scrutiny on upcoming fracking projects.
items.why: it concerns alleged cronyism in public appointments and a minister's attempt to bypass judicial and environmental scrutiny of a policy decision.
links: handing a peerage and a job as a senior minister

items.h: Unlock Democracy launch Take Action on Sleaze campaign
items.b: With trust in politicians at an all-time low, Unlock Democracy has launched a new campaign calling on the new Prime Minister to tackle sleaze, cronyism and rule-breaking. Amongst the campaign demands are calls for Truss to commit her government to obey international law, appoint an independent ethics advisor, and end cronyism in appointments to the House of Lords.
items.why: the campaign targets standards in public life, cronyism in appointments and compliance with international law as mechanisms for holding government answerable.

items.h: Climate activist receives compensation for unlawful arrest
items.b: Last year Extinction Rebellion activist Liam Geary Baulch was arrested outside Conservative Party Conference 2021 for holding a handmade sign reading ‘Priti Fascist’. Arrested for a ‘breach of the peace’, Liam later instructed ITN Solicitors to write to Greater Manchester Police to challenge the lawfulness of the arrest. Following this, GM Police have now provided Geary Baulch with compensation and legal costs following the unlawful arrest. Would you like to know more?
items.why: it shows a legal remedy being obtained for unlawful police action, demonstrating access to redress against state overreach.
items.note: Classified under rule of law because the mechanism reported is legal redress/compensation rather than the underlying protest policing itself.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Sheffield University auto enrols students onto Electoral Register
items.b: Did you know that Sheffield University ranks #1 for outstanding student voter registration practices? The University of Sheffield employs a novel method to the widespread problem of low student enrolment — integrating voter registration into the University’s start of term processes, so when you receive your Student ID — you’re also automatically enrolled on the electoral register. They’ve even been cited in Parliament as an example of best practice in achieving high student voter reg figures.
items.why: automatic enrolment onto the electoral register directly affects who can exercise the franchise and participate in elections.
links: Did you know that Sheffield University ranks #1 for outstanding student voter registration practices?

items.h: Meloni’s electoral success in Italy signals strengthening of ‘illiberal democracy’ bloc
items.b: Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy Party won the Italian national election last month with 26% of the popular vote. Victor Orban, who describes his regime in Hungary as an ‘illiberal democracy’, was quick to praise Meloni along with Le Pen, who suggested the Italian people had ‘woken up’. Meloni’s win has spread fear that civil liberties in Italy will be rolled back whilst strengthening a growing continental opposition to EU liberal democracy. ​​ Disillusioned Defectors report maps voters susceptible to populist rhetoric In light of the recent electoral success of several European populist par…
items.why: Meloni's election and analysis of UK voters' susceptibility to populist rhetoric bear on the health of competitive, liberal-democratic electoral politics comparatively relevant to the UK.

items.h: Wales is having a national conversation on its constitutional future
items.b: The Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales has been established by the Welsh Government. The commission has two broad objectives, to consider and develop options for fundamental reform of the constitutional structures of the United Kingdom — and develop progressive principal options to strengthen Welsh democracy and deliver improvements for the people of Wales. They are running an expansive consultation, ending in December — would you like to know more? Listen to this podcast by the Centre for Constitutional Change on the Commission.
items.why: the commission is examining the structures and powers of devolved and constitutional decision-making for Wales.
items.note: Devolved constitutional structures fall under elections & decision making per boundary rules.
links: The Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales
would you like to know more?

items.h: Elect Her Webinars through October
items.b: Throughout the month of October Elect Her are running six fantastic events including life as a community councillor, life as a councillor and life as an MSP.
items.why: the webinars build capacity for people, particularly women, to understand and pursue roles as elected representatives, creating a new means of participation.
items.note: Borderline event listing, but treated as capacity-building programme rather than mere logistics.

items.h: 2022 report on governance and scrutiny in local government is published
items.b: The Centre for Governance and Scrutiny surveys scrutiny officers, elected members and officers working in local government each year for their views on the effectiveness and impact of overview and scrutiny. Their 2022 annual report concludes that scrutiny is most effective when it’s properly resourced and supported by an executive that is open to challenge. The report also suggests local scrutiny could be improved in terms of approaches to risk, finance and oversight of commercial activity.
items.why: it assesses how effectively local government scrutiny functions hold executives answerable for decisions and spending.

items.h: Centre on Constitutional Change animation examines impact of Brexit on Devolution
items.b: In the wake of Brexit, the UK and devolved governments have had to agree to replace some EU rules with UK rules. A new animation and infographic from the Centre on Constitutional Change take a closer look at that process and the relationship between Westminster and the devolved assemblies in the wake of Brexit. Both animation and infographic are part of a research project being developed by UK in a Changing Europe , entitled A Family of Nations? Brexit, Devolution and the Union .
items.why: it explains how post-Brexit power reallocation between Westminster and devolved governments shapes the structure and authority of devolved decision-making tiers.
items.note: Devolution structure/powers falls under elections & decision making per the boundary rule for devolved government.
links: A Family of Nations? Brexit, Devolution and the Union

items.h: Hansard Society Event: What does the Retained EU Law Bill mean for Parliament?
items.b: The Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Bill was introduced to Parliament on the 22nd of September and could have far-reaching impacts on the relationship between Government and Parliament. On the 12th of October, the Hansard Society will host an event with leading parliamentary and legal experts to explore the devolved powers contained within the bill and what it means for parliamentary scrutiny.
items.note: Treated as sector event listing rather than substantive reporting on the bill itself.

items.h: Localis release local engagement policy toolkit designed for public organisations and local councils
items.b: Localis publish a toolkit designed for local councils seeking to engage in genuine public engagement and work in partnership with residents and communities. The toolkit is based on lessons learned from Kensington and Chelsea Council, during their journey to make meaningful public engagement their standard practice.
items.why: it creates a new practical resource enabling councils to build genuine public engagement mechanisms, expanding means of participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building resource counts as a participation story.

items.h: New Culture Secretary to reconsider plans to privatise Channel Four
items.b: Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today Programme , the new Culture Minister Michelle Donelan said, ‘we’re looking especially at the business case for the sale of Channel 4 and making sure we still agree with that decision.’ Their comments suggest the government could be considering a U-turn on the controversial plans, announced in April this year, to privatise the broadcaster due to concerns that public ownership was ‘holding it back in the face of a rapidly changing and competitive media landscape’.
items.why: the ownership status of a major public service broadcaster affects media plurality and the diversity of the UK's information environment.
links: Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today Programme

items.h: openDemocracy is looking for a News Editor
items.b: The News Editor will have a strong interest in using journalism to support democratic debate and will help lead the news coverage at openDemocracy. Deadline for applications is 24th October.
items.note: Job advert; organisational news, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.h: New media outlet The Canary has become a workers’ co-op, cites former owners toxic practices
items.b: The left-leaning new media outlet that rose to prominence during Labour’s Corbyn-era has found itself amongst turbulent waters in recent months, with workers and journalists at the site forced to investigate their bosses ‘toxic’ practices and financial ‘irregularities’, resulting in them staging their own revolution and resolving to become a workers’ co-op .
items.note: Internal organisational/labour dispute at a media outlet, not a systemic media plurality or public debate mechanism.
links: staging their own revolution and resolving to become a workers’ co-op

items.h: Accredited photojournalist ‘manhandled’ out of Conservative Party Conference
items.b: A video has emerged of accredited press photographer Tolga Akmen being forcibly removed from the convention centre by security staff during this week’s Tory Party Conference. A Conservative party spokesperson said: ‘We are aware there was an incident earlier today where a photographer was removed by venue security staff. We believe there may have been a misunderstanding and have been in contact with the photographer.
items.why: the forcible removal of an accredited journalist from a party conference bears on press access and the safety conditions needed for public-interest journalism.

items.h: One to watch: Poland’s first citizens assembly to discuss rising energy prices
items.b: Poland’s first citizens assembly will take place this month and across November to discuss the high cost of energy facing the country. 100 residents from across Poland will take part in the citizens assembly where they will be briefed by experts in social policy, energy and climate related fields before discussing possible solutions to the crisis.
items.why: citizens' assemblies are deliberative decision-making machinery, and this case offers comparative evidence relevant to UK debates on deliberative democracy.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the revised framework; foreign example treated as comparative evidence.

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Rosa Slater — The Politics Project, Penny Lamb — VotesforSchools, Diane Sims — Kirklees Council, Liz Crosbie — RebootGB, Katy Murray — Cast From Clay, Jessie Joe Jacobs — UK Democracy Network, Pilar Girvan — Involve, Myf Nixon — mySociety and Peter Gregory — Constituency Panels.
items.note: Meetup thanks/attendee list is organisational admin, not a democracy story.

items.h: Public Order Bill passes third reading in the House of Commons
items.b: The Bill has faced strong backlash from civil liberties groups, including from Tory MP Charles Walker who labelled the Bill ‘unconservative’ earlier this week. The Public Order Bill reintroduces earlier elements of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act that had been removed by the House of Lords, such as Serious Disruption Prevention Orders — which allow police to require any individual who has taken part in a protest within the last five years to wear an electronic tag and report to a police station on a regular basis — for two years — including barring those persons from entering part…
items.why: it expands state powers to restrict and surveil protest through tagging, exclusion zones and criminal penalties, narrowing the space to assemble and dissent
items.note: Protest restriction via policing/legal coercion sits in rights & civic space, not participation.

items.h: Online Safety Bill: will they, won’t they?
items.b: Fair Vote and the coalition of organisations working around the Online Safety Bill continue to be on tenterhooks over the Bill’s passage, next week’s leadership election and a potential general election look to mar the Bill’s final nod.
items.why: the Bill governs regulation of online platforms and content that shapes the public information environment

items.h: Economic Crimes Bill: democracy orgs working on amendments
items.b: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill seeks to tackle money laundering and other economic crimes, including seizure of cryptoassets and abuse of limited partnerships. Fair Vote UK are working on amendments that would seek to deal with funnelling money through trusts, foundations and offshore accounts into political party coffers. Stay tuned for more on this!
items.why: it concerns closing loopholes in campaign finance that allow opaque money to flow into political party funding
items.note: Political party finance falls under elections & decision making.
links: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill

items.h: New clause in Levelling Up Bill affording community right of appeal draws cross-party support
items.b: A clause in The Levelling-Up and Regeneration Bill affording a right of appeal for local communities against any new planning permissions has been met with approval by Conservative, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs. Lib Dem MP, Tim Farron, commented, “The ability to challenge a developer and a decision seems to be at the heart of democracy. To really level up, we must not just level up geographically, but level out the imbalance of power between developers…and local communities.”
items.why: a new right of appeal gives local communities a formal mechanism to challenge decisions affecting them, strengthening avenues for redress and voice
items.note: Community right of appeal against planning decisions is a participation/redress mechanism rather than an electoral or structural change to local government.

items.h: Save the date: Democracy Network Annual Conference, 7–8th December, London
items.b: Democracy Network’s first annual conference is coming to London on the 7th and 8th December — register now, limited tickets available .

items.h: Democracy Network head to Berlin for Democracy R&D Conference
items.b: Earlier this month Democracy Network Coordinator Jessie Joe Jacobs attended the Democracy R&D Conference in Berlin. Democracy R&D is a global network supporting and improving democratic outcomes. Jessie reports that the event showcased a wide variety of democracy practitioners from the Berlin government leading citizens assemblies, to small community based initiatives from across Europe. According to Jessie, there was a lot of awareness about the UK Democracy Network and a genuine desire to see the network and collaboration format replicated across Europe.
items.note: Report of staff attending a conference is organisational news, not a democracy story.

items.h: The Politics Project launching research on supporting politicians to engage with schools
items.b: On November 30th, The Politics Project are running their event Starting Powerful Conversations , launching their latest research into youth engagement with politicians based on more than 400 Dialogue sessions, bringing together young people and politicians from all levels of government across the UK. Don’t miss it — register now .
items.why: it builds a programme and evidence base for structured dialogue between young people and politicians, creating new means for youth political engagement
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building rather than mere event/research promotion.

items.h: Progressing Constituency Panels
items.b: Peter Gregory has made considerable progress in recent weeks with their Constituency Panels (CPs) concept. CPs are non-partisan panels designed to improve accountability and transparency between MPs and their constituents. Peter is currently penning a number of questions for a Survation Omnibus to determine public interest in the idea. Would you like to know more?
items.why: This matters democratically because it proposes a new mechanism for constituents to engage with and hold their MPs accountable, testing public appetite for a new form of political participation.
items.note: Early-stage concept still being tested via polling, not yet a launched tool.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Notwestminster planning their next gathering
items.b: Whilst the Notwestminster event is still in the planning stages with no date as yet, they’ll be on the lookout for people who are interested in hosting workshops about local democracy soon — they’re also considering an online gathering this autumn.

items.h: Citizen Network: new report, new democratic governance structure
items.b: You’ll have to stay tuned for more information on Citizen Network Coop, their new governance structure launching October 24th. In the meantime, Citizen Network are promoting a new report by Common Ground on democratic reforms showcasing some fantastic polling on a range of democratic transformations — check it out now .
items.note: New internal governance structure is organisational news; report promotion is too vague to assess as substantive content.

items.h: Festival of Debate — submissions open
items.b: Next year’s Sheffield based Festival of Debate will run from 12th April to the 26th May, with one of their three core topics for the event series being ‘how can we reimagine our citizenship and our democracy?’ Submit your ideas now for consideration for the 2023 programme .
links: Submit your ideas now for consideration for the 2023 programme

items.h: mySociety needs you
items.b: WhatDoTheyKnow enables thousands of organisations and individuals across the UK to seamlessly send Freedom of Information requests to more than 45,000 public authorities. However, sometimes these council contact emails need to be kept up to date. Myf Nixon, Comms Manager at mySociety , has shared a list of authorities with a missing email address and they need some help with finding them all. Can you help?
items.note: Volunteer request to maintain existing contact data is operational upkeep, not creation of a new means of participation.

items.h: Involve run Citizens’ Jury on Car Dependency in Northern Ireland, launch new report on housing
items.b: Earlier this month, Involve ran a weekend long citizens’ jury on car dependency. Commissioned by Queen’s University of Belfast, the event brought together 20 residents of Belfast where they heard evidence on car dependency and its impacts. The full report is out in November. See more about the NI citizens’ jury here . Next Wednesday 26th October, Involve are also launching a new report on housing in NI, produced in partnership with Housing Rights — register here .
items.why: This matters democratically because citizens' juries are a deliberative decision-making mechanism through which public input is formally incorporated into policy on transport and housing.
items.note: Citizens' juries are classified under elections & decision making as deliberative process, not participation.
links: See more about the NI citizens’ jury here

items.h: First UK-wide citizens assembly for nature to start next month following Government ‘attack on nature’
items.b: The idea for the assembly was developed by RSPB, WWF and the National Trust in response to the current government’s recently announced ‘pro-growth agenda’ which could see large swathes of environmental protections scrapped. The assembly will be facilitated in partnership with Involve , 89up , New Citizenship Project and Sortition Foundation and will run between November 2022 and February 2023, providing the opportunity for 100 citizens to have their say on how best to respond to the ecological crisis forming the basis of a set of ecological policy recommendations for the next government.
items.why: This matters democratically because launching a national citizens' assembly creates a deliberative process for citizens to shape environmental policy recommendations.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: ElectHer are running a three-part programme to help women kickstart their political career
items.b: The three-part series My Political Future , will explore key questions of what motivates women to be engaged politically. All women are invited to attend this free series, including non-binary people whose experiences or identities intersect with those of women.
items.why: This matters democratically because the programme builds women's capacity and confidence to participate in political life, addressing unequal conditions for taking part in politics.
items.note: Classified as participation because it concerns capacity-building for engagement rather than a rights claim or electoral mechanism.

items.h: Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform Annual Meeting on November 1st
items.b: Speaking after the formal AGM will be Wendy Chamberlain MP, Liberal Democracts for Electoral Reform President and Lib Dem House of Commons Chief Whip; and Christine Jardine MP, Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson, who will discuss the current prospects for electoral reform. All are welcome to register for the event to hear about the work of LDER and discuss future avenues for electoral reform.
items.note: Announcement of a party-affiliated group's AGM is sector event logistics rather than a substantive report on electoral reform.

items.b: On October 26th Constitution Unit will host a webinar to discuss the constitutional changes that will occur with the coronation of King Charles II and the implications for the Commonwealth now that several countries have announced their intention to become republics. The webinar is free to attend and there will be a number of expert speakers to debate the upcoming constitutional developments.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.why: This matters democratically because it addresses constitutional changes to the monarchy and Commonwealth relationships that bear on the structure and legitimacy of public authority.
items.note: Concerns constitutional convention and structure of the state rather than elections or rights, placing it under government & accountability.

items.h: The3million are looking for a new Head of Policy and Advocacy
items.b: The new Head of Policy and Advocacy will lead the Policy and Advocacy team at the3million , producing rigorous evidence-based research, writing policy development papers and designing and implementing a compelling advocacy strategy. Deadline for applications is November 6th.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.note: Job advert/organisational hiring notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: I Have a Voice are looking for a Voter Registration Ambassador
items.b: A great opportunity for someone in further education (sixth form of college) to gain paid experience in the democracy sector. The position is paid at London Living Wage — Get in touch with I Have a Voice for more details.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.note: Job advert for a paid role, not a change in participation infrastructure itself.

items.h: Scottish Greens to cut ties with Green Party of England and Wales over reported shortcomings on transphobia
items.b: Members of the Scottish Greens have voted to suspend their formal association with the Green Party of England and Wales (GPEW) due to their failure to tackle transphobia within the party. The vote comes following heavy criticism of a number of high profile figures who stand accused of making transphobic comments and actions. Despite deputy leader Zack Polanski’s powerful defence of trans rights at the Scottish Greens’ national conference, the speech was not enough to allay the party’s concerns who subsequently voted with a significant majority to sever ties with GPEW.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.note: Internal party organisational dispute over values, not a mechanism of democratic contestation, representation or rights.

items.h: Westminster Foundation for Democracy are hiring a Programmes Manager (Political Parties)
items.b: Westminster Foundation for Democracy are looking for an experienced Programme Manager to support the work of the Multi-Party Office team. The Programme Manager will lead on managing; programme systems and processes, quality assurance. Apply by November 1st.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.note: Job advert/organisational hiring notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: Chartered Institute of Public Relations explores impact of technology on UK politics
items.b: The way we hold elections, implement government policy, and campaign on topics is changing as a result of technology, they argue. Coinciding with their AGM, the Chartered Institute of Public Relations is hosting an event discussing how digitalisation may continue to alter politics and public relations in the years to come.
items.sec: Constitution Unit webinar to discuss constitutional change under the new monarch
items.note: Event listing about a general theme without reporting any concrete claim or change.

items.h: Sortition Foundation full steam ahead on their House of Lords campaign
items.b: Sortition Foundation happily reports that they’ve gone from dwindling finances to a full calendar of sortition selection work. Will, who led their Scottish House of Citizens’ campaign spent his final days with Sortition at the Scottish Greens’ annual conference talking up their democratic renewal motion which included a commitment to the House of Citizens! Sortition Foundation have been taking soundings on the House of Lords campaign with their press contacts and they are apparently ‘pretty hot for it’ — particularly the ‘frankly disgusting’ stories their researchers have uncovered about the H…
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns a campaign to change how members of the House of Lords, part of the legislature, are selected, touching on decision-making machinery and representativeness.
items.note: Sortition/citizens'-assembly style reform campaigns are anchored to elections & decision making per framework rules.

items.h: Landmark case on Scottish independence held in UK Supreme Court
items.b: A court case to decide whether the Scottish Government has the formal authority to hold an independence referendum has been unfolding in the UK Supreme Court. A senior lawyer acting for the UK government, Sir James Eadie KC, argued the attempt by Scottish ministers to secure approval for the independence referendum was unfounded as ‘the impacts and effects of Scottish independence would be felt throughout the UK’ , meaning all parts of the UK, not just Scotland have a stake in the issue. Dorothy Bain, Scotland’s top lawyer, countered these statements with the claim that the SNP has won success…
items.why: this matters democratically because the case decides whether the Scottish Government has legal authority to hold a referendum, a core mechanism of direct popular decision-making and devolved authority.
items.note: Referendums are classified under elections & decision making even though adjudicated by a court.
links: ‘the impacts and effects of Scottish independence would be felt throughout the UK’

items.h: Electoral Reform Society expects initial Gordon Brown Commission findings soon
items.b: Last month’s leaked report outlined a series of high profile constitutional departures, including abolition of the House of Lords and devolution of economic powers. Jess Garland and the team at the Electoral Reform Society expect the full findings to be released soon. Democracy Network, Citizen Network, ERS and others are poised to react to the new report.
items.why: this matters democratically because the Commission's proposals concern devolution of power and reform of the House of Lords, both matters of decision-making structure and legislative accountability.
items.note: Devolution of powers falls under elections & decision making; Lords reform touches legislative accountability.

items.h: Tory leadership race, Prime Minister Liz Truss resigns amid growing tensions within the Conservative Party
items.b: Truss resigned as Prime Minister after just 44 days in the job, triggering yet another Conservative Party leadership race. The new leadership race is due to be completed at an expedited pace by Friday 28th October, ahead of the Autumn Budget the following Monday.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the orderly (or disorderly) transfer of executive power following a Prime Minister's resignation, a core constitutional mechanism.

items.h: UK constitution is under increasing strain, warns Constitution Monitoring Group UK
items.b: A new report from the UK Constitution Monitoring Group covering the first seven months of 2022 identifies 90 instances in which the constitution has been eroded and degraded. The report details a host of instances in which ministers and civil servants failed to uphold standard principles of conduct and outlines a series of ill-considered legislation and attacks on the independence of the judiciary. The report calls for greater integrity amongst policy makers and across public life to create a healthier democracy.
items.why: this matters democratically because the report documents alleged failures of ministerial conduct, standards in public life and attacks on judicial independence that erode checks on executive power.

items.h: Labour MP Sam Tarry lambasts local deselection vote as a ‘manufactured circus’
items.b: Sam Tarry, Labour MP for Ilford South, has publicly criticised his deselection vote , calling it a ‘manufactured circus’ and demanding to see a list of votes to ensure the ‘integrity’ of the result. Tarry, who lost his position to local council leader Jas Athwal, said the result ‘does not reflect the feeling my campaigners met on the ground talking day in day out to members’. Tarry has suggested whether this was an orchestrated move by the party leadership to remove dissenting voices within the party.
items.why: internal party candidate selection processes determine who can stand for election and shape political competition within parties
items.note: Treated as party/candidate access under elections rather than a generic internal dispute.

items.h: 14% of all LLPs ever incorporated may have been used for financial crime, says Transparency International
items.b: New research from Transparency International UK suggests that 14% of Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) incorporated in Britain bear the hallmarks of shell companies that have been involved in major corruption and money laundering schemes. Much of the abuse has been linked to Russian individuals with significant personal control, underlining concerns about the flow of Russian ‘dirty money’ in the UK economy. Director of Policy at Transparency International UK, Duncan Hames, is calling for the expedition of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill (detailed above) to help tackle th…
items.why: widespread abuse of corporate structures for money laundering undermines the rule-based system meant to constrain corruption and hold economic power accountable
links: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill

items.h: Opposition parties call for immediate general election
items.b: Labour, Liberal Democrats, the SNP and the Green Party have all now called for an immediate general election, following the continued political and economic turbulence in recent weeks culminating (at least for now) in the resignation of PM Truss.
items.why: calls for an immediate election concern the transfer of power and opposition parties' ability to compete for government
links: Labour, Liberal Democrats, the SNP and the Green Party

items.h: General Election Strategy Planning Day with The Politics Project
items.b: Are you working with youth or education organisations? The Politics Project is hosting a general election strategy planning day with the Democracy Fund this January. If you’re interested, let Hattie know .
items.note: Event listing/logistics notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: Kirklees celebrates Local Democracy Week
items.b: Diane Sims and the team at Kirklees Democracy Commission are celebrating Local Democracy Week and giving out their first Democracy Friendly Schools awards this week. See what else has been happening on this Twitter thread .
items.why: new local awards and activities encouraging schools to engage with democratic institutions create new means for young people to participate in civic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new participation opportunities rather than mere celebration.

items.h: Jaime, 16, takes over as First Minister of Wales for a day as part of Day of the Girl
items.b: Teenager Jaime spent the day as Wales’ First Minister as part of International Day Of The Girl . Jaime opened a press conference, visited the Senedd chamber and spent the day behind the scenes getting to know more about the inner workings of the Welsh Government.
items.note: A single symbolic one-day shadowing event does not create or change any mechanism of democratic participation.
links: Teenager Jaime spent the day as Wales’ First Minister as part of International Day Of The Girl

items.h: Green MP criticises Government’s Investment Zone policy for bypassing local democracy
items.b: Caroline Lucas launched an attack in parliament on the Government’s Investment Zone plan for undermining environmental legislation, avoiding fair taxation policies and bypassing local democracy. The controversial new policy, modelled on Rishi Sunak’s freeport scheme, will see councils and combined authorities set up Investment Zones in which planning regulations are relaxed and business taxes reduced in an attempt to drive growth.
items.why: the policy changes the powers and planning role of local democratic structures by bypassing their normal decision-making authority
items.note: Story concerns the structure/powers of local government, placed under elections per the boundary rule rather than participation.
links: Caroline Lucas launched an attack in parliament

items.h: Demos polling highlights need for locally-led levelling up
items.b: With a new Prime Minister and a new politico-economic agenda in Britain, Demos teamed up with KPMG to poll the public on their thoughts towards the levelling up agenda and other flagship Conservative policies. Amongst their findings, it was clear that levelling up needs to be locally led with 71% saying local communities need a say in regional decisions. Meanwhile, just 16% thought the government understood local needs and 50% said they were unsatisfied with the amount of involvement currently offered to communities in policymaking.
items.why: public dissatisfaction with the level of say communities have in regional decisions reflects on people's practical ability and sense of voice to take part in governance
items.note: Framed as public attitudes/efficacy toward involvement rather than the formal structure of local government itself.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation run meetup for indie news publishers
items.b: PINF’s meetup in Leeds last weekend generated a number of new working groups formed by indie news publishers, including groups that will look at: networking between them, better measuring (and showing) impact, and a campaign for better public awareness of independent news — as well as continued thinking on community newsrooms. Good stuff! Would you like to know more?
items.why: new collaborative efforts among independent news publishers to strengthen local journalism support a plural and functioning public information environment
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building for journalism/media plurality.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Business Secretary Jacob Rees-Mogg accuses BBC of impartiality breach
items.b: During an interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, the Business Secretary claimed impartiality rules were breached by the BBC presenter suggesting market turmoil is linked to the mini-budget.
items.why: disputes over broadcaster impartiality bear on whether the public receives a fair and trustworthy information environment for political debate

items.h: Legal proceedings issued against UK media outlets by Khazakstani Endowment Fund
items.b: openDemocracy and The Bureau of Investigative Journalism are facing legal proceedings following an investigation into the financial ties of the Nazarbayev Fund, an endowment fund associated with the former Khazakstani Prime Minister Nursultan Nazarbayev, and Jusan Technologies Ltd, a UK registered company. According to their reporting, the Nazarbayev Fund held a controlling interest in the UK company via an intermediary, raising concerns as to why a UK company held Khazakstani wealth. In light of the legal action, a number of media organisations are calling on the UK government to expedite the…
items.why: legal intimidation (SLAPPs) against investigative journalists threatens the press's ability to hold powerful interests accountable and inform public debate.

items.h: Investigative journalist role opens at public interest news co-op in Bristol
items.b: The Bristol Cable , a co-operative news platform democratically owned by local people in Bristol, is recruiting an investigative journalist. Suitable for anyone keen to work in a community newsroom on more in-depth articles covering local issues — find out more and get an application in before October 31st.
items.note: Job advert, not a story about new democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Naked Politics secure £25k in funding from JRSST-CT
items.b: Naked Politics are due to be awarded just over £25k for the next year to maintain their online content and run workshops and training sessions in schools with predominantly young people of colour, on citizenship and civic action. Find out more about JRSST-CT and how you can apply for a grant.
items.note: Funding/organisational news maintaining existing activity, not a new participation mechanism.
links: Find out more about JRSST-CT and how you can apply for a grant.

items.h: Impetus secures £500,000 funding
items.b: Impetus , a non-profit organisation supporting young people from disadvantaged backgrounds to thrive in life, has successfully secured a three-year, unrestricted grant of £500,000 from the Inflexion Foundation . This will support Impetus in their crucial work closing employment and education disparities.
items.note: Organisational funding news about youth employment, not democracy-specific.

items.h: Power to Change offer funding community technology grants
items.b: Power to Change is a group that helps community-based enterprises create technology which delivers advantages locally, that can be held accountable by the community, and completely satisfies its users’ requirements. If your organisation makes and uses technology that benefits and gives power to your community, applications for their two-year funding programme, Community Tech: Makers & Maintainers , are open until 4th November.
items.note: Funding call for community tech grants; sector logistics rather than a launched participation mechanism.

items.h: Durham University event unearths the violent origins of English electoral democracy
items.b: Professors running a research project at Durham University on the causes and consequences of English electoral violence are hosting a talk introducing you to the dark side of electoral politics. Join them on the 24th of October to explore the first systematic database of violent events during all 20 general elections between 1832 and 1914 in England and Wales.
items.note: Event listing about historical research, not current democratic mechanism.
links: causes and consequences of English electoral violence

items.h: University of Geneva roundtable on democratic theory
items.b: Anticipated to be an engaging and comprehensive conversation with leading academics in the area about topics such as democratic theory, democratic models, and threats to democratic systems — the roundtable will be held at 3.15pm on Zoom, UK time — register here .
items.note: Academic event listing, not a democracy story.
