items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Will Snell — Fairness Foundation, Perry Walker — TalkShop, Jessica Metheringham — Unlock Democracy, Roger Wilson — Unite to Reform, Jessie Joe Jacobs — UK Democracy Network, Tom Brake — Unlock Democracy and Kevin Keith — UK Open Government Network.
items.note: Organisational thanks/meetup notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: More than 300,000 sign petition to halt Public Order Bill
items.b: Liberty and Greenpeace UK joined forces to deliver a damning public verdict on the controversial new public order legislation with over 300,000 people coming together to re-kill the Bill. The Public Order Bill resurrects those elements of the now Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act that were previously thrown out by the House of Lords.
items.why: it concerns legal restrictions on the right to protest and assembly, a core civic freedom, and public mobilisation against curbing it
items.note: Protest law framed as legal restriction/policing, so rights beat rather than participation.
links: Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act

items.h: Public Order Bill receives Second Reading in House of Lords
items.b: During the debate in the Lords, peers warned that tourists and members of the public could be caught up in the new restrictions. Labour peer Vernon Coaker warned of effectively unlimited stop and search powers in the vicinity of protest , whilst Lib Dem peer Brian Paddick–a former Police Commander–remarked that the new law further erodes ‘people’s right to assembly, free speech and peaceful protest’. The Public Order Bill is due for Lords committee stage on 16th November 2022.
items.why: it concerns expanded stop-and-search powers and restrictions on assembly and free speech near protests, a matter of state coercion over civil liberties
links: warned of effectively unlimited stop and search powers in the vicinity of protest

items.h: Labour Party appears to side with Government on Public Order Bill
items.b: In a wake up call to campaigners hoping for any future Labour government to roll back on controversial Conservative protest law, in an interview with radio station LBC, Keir Starmer argued that he supports longer sentences for those ‘who are gluing themselves to roads and motorways’.
items.why: it concerns whether political competition offers a genuine alternative on curbing protest rights, affecting civil liberties and the opposition's role
items.note: Party political positioning on a civil liberties bill; classified by the substantive rights issue at stake.

items.h: Online Safety Bill withdrawn due to limited parliamentary time
items.b: The Online Safety Bill has now been withdrawn in its current form from the Commons’ schedule. It is expected that a new ‘watered down’ version of the Bill will be proposed later this month by Culture Secretary Michelle Donelan. Civil society groups have criticised the move stating that its withdrawal leaves children at risk .
items.why: it concerns regulation of the online information environment and platform safety, affecting the conditions for public debate
items.note: Withdrawal also reflects parliamentary scheduling/scrutiny, noted as secondary.

items.h: Fears raised over lack of parliamentary scrutiny proposed in Retained EU Law Bill
items.b: Hansard Society have highlighted concerns over the ‘sunset clause’ in the Retained EU Law Bill , which would see any piece of EU retained law revoked by default at the end of December 2023 unless ministers actively decide to save it. Since becoming prime minister, Sunak has promised to tone down the government’s zeal for axing EU law due to fears it would severely restrict the machinery of government.
items.why: it concerns reduced parliamentary scrutiny of delegated powers used to revoke retained EU law by default

items.h: Help renew the UK Open Government Network
items.b: For the last decade the UK Open Government Network (UK OGN) has taken civil society into the heart of the UK government. Hundreds of reformers have worked with civil servants to secure policy commitments related to open government — yet now, the UK Government is ‘under review’ for failing to meet the 77 strong Open Government Partnership (OGP) criteria. Kevin Keith, Chair of the UK OGN, reports that they have not had the resources equal to the task over the recent period, and as a result civil society confidence is low precisely at a time when interest in open government is high, off the back …
items.why: it concerns the UK government being reviewed for failing open government transparency commitments and the civil society mechanism holding it to account
items.note: Mixed with organisational renewal appeal, but substantive point is government accountability on open government commitments.
links: help shape the UK Open Government Network and click here to sign up now

items.h: Democracy Awards nominations are now open
items.b: UK Democracy Network are hosting their first ever Democracy Awards dinner to recognise and champion outstanding work being done across the sector. Taking place at their first annual conference in December, the awards will cover five categories: Equality & Power, Democratic Innovation, Democracy Campaign of the Year, Outstanding Contribution to Democratic Change, Empowerpowerment, Transparency and Democracy Rights. Nominations close 21st November — make yours now .
items.note: Organisational awards nomination call, not substantive democracy content.

items.h: Fairness Foundation launches Fairness Index
items.b: Will Snell, Chief Executive at Fairness Foundation , reports that they launched their Fairness Index — a new online resource that brings together key data on the ‘fair necessities’: wealth, education, pay, tax and health, to build a comprehensive picture of how fair Britain is today. The Index includes a special page dedicated to democracy-related fairness matters . Sign up for updates from the Fairness Foundation here .
items.note: A general fairness data resource is informational content, not a tool that changes democratic participation.

items.h: Jessica Metheringham is creating a democracy board game
items.b: Avid boardgame designer at Dissent Games and Chair of Unlock Democracy , Jessica Metheringham, is looking for up to ten people to contribute to the design of a new democracy game. They’ll likely get started in the new, but if this sounds like your jam — get in touch .
items.note: Call for volunteers to help design a game, not itself a democratic participation tool yet.

items.h: #DemocracyDrinks arrives in London on 16th November
items.b: It is the UK launch of the UK chapter of #democracy drinks which are held in a number of countries around the world. Alice Stollmeyer, who has been setting these up throughout Europe, will be joining for part of the evening. The event will run from 5.30pm to 8pm and will be held at Boardroom, Second Floor, North Wing, 55 Broadway, London, SW1H 0BH. For more information contact Shaun Roberts at Unlock Democracy.
items.note: Social networking event listing.

items.h: Talk Shop launch Win-Win Workout
items.b: The new deliberative format launched last week by Perry Walker and Bob Bollen at Talkshop and aims to counter increasing polarisation in public life. Win-Win Workout emphasises common ground and shared solutions — find out more on their website . Their next event, focused on rewilding, using the Win-Win format will be held on the 7th December.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new deliberative format intended to help people reach collective decisions across divides, which the framework treats as decision-making machinery.
items.note: Deliberative processes are anchored to elections & decision making per the boundary rules, even outside formal government processes.

items.h: Democracy Action to become part of Democracy Network
items.b: Earlier this year Democracy Action went on pause to consider its next steps. They will now become part of the UK Democracy Network’s core activities producing their monthly newsletter.
items.note: Organisational merger/administrative news.

items.h: Elect Her crowdfunder to support women in the 2023 and 2024 elections
items.b: Elect Her has launched its first-ever crowdfunder to provide financial support for women in the upcoming 2023 and 2024 elections. They want to ensure women from all financial backgrounds can be represented.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new financial means for women from all backgrounds to stand as candidates, affecting who can compete for elected office.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society Cymru gearing up for their annual conference
items.b: Hosted in Cardiff next month, the ERS Cymru annual supporter conference will welcome Mick Antoniw MS, Counsel General and Minister for the Constitution, as keynote speaker for an action packed conference replete with workshops and updates on the Welsh government’s ambitious programme of democratic reforms. Would you like to know more?
items.note: Primarily an event/conference listing rather than substantive reporting on the reforms themselves.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Don’t miss: Koreo’s bi-weekly RADAR newsletter
items.b: Each fortnight, Jonny Will Chambers and the team at Koreo , take a moment to drill down what they’ve seen or heard into their RADAR newsletter, often touching on questions and topics of democratic transformation. Read last week’s issue and subscribe for your next read .
items.note: Newsletter subscription promotion, organisational self-promotion.

items.h: Institute for Government asks: Does the UK’s human rights regime need reform?
items.b: On Wednesday 16th November, the Institute for Government are hosting an online panel looking at whether the government should consider reform to how rights are upheld in the UK, a hot topic considering recent moves towards more authoritarian policing methods and attempts to usurp the Human Rights Act — Register now .
items.why: this matters democratically because it engages debate over whether the legal framework protecting individual rights and constraining state power, including the Human Rights Act, should be reformed.
items.note: Framed as an event listing but the substance concerns the standing legal architecture of rights protection.

items.h: New report unpicks causes of global democratic backsliding
items.b: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace have released a new report looking at the overarching causes behind the ongoing global decline in democratic values and practices. The paper focuses on three main types of backsliding: ‘grievance-fuelled illiberalism’, ‘opportunistic authoritarianism’ and ‘entrenched-interested revanchism’, and explores how civil society and international actors can respond to the crisis.
items.why: it analyses the mechanisms driving democratic backsliding worldwide and how civil society and international actors can respond, which bears on understanding threats to democratic institutions generally.
items.note: International/comparative report without specific UK mechanism, low confidence it clears the bar.

items.h: Citizen Network launch first global cooperative to foster citizenship
items.b: On Monday 24th October, the Citizen Network Cooperative was launched. Connecting twelve international organisations, the co-op will promote active global citizenship by creating a framework that supports individuals to take action in their community and learn from others around the world.
items.why: it creates a new international framework and cooperative structure intended to help individuals take civic action in their communities, expanding means of participation.

items.h: Demos hiring for multiple roles
items.b: Demos are still on the lookout for a Director of Policy and Impact . They are also now recruiting a Head of External Affairs and a Researcher . Check out the job descriptions for more details on all roles.
items.note: Organisational hiring notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: TPXimpact are looking for a Deliberative Democracy Officer
items.b: The exciting new role will involve working with the Democracy Lead and colleagues across TPXimpact (formerly FutureGov) to shape and deliver impactful projects that put people at the heart of their change-making process.
items.note: Job advert for an organisation, not a substantive democracy development.

items.h: Research Associate wanted for a project on Digital Campaigning and Electoral Democracy
items.b: The University of Manchester is looking to hire a Post-Doctoral Research Associate to work on the Digital Campaigning and Electoral Democracy Project (DiCED) directed by Professor Rachel Gibson. DiCED is a large-scale comparative project that studies the drivers and effects of digital campaigning in 5 countries and 7 national elections during the period 2020–2023.
items.note: Job advert for a research post, not a democracy story in itself.
links: Digital Campaigning and Electoral Democracy Project (DiCED)

items.h: Black Europeans, a new immigrant and Black-led organisation has been launched
items.b: Co-founder Ake Achi says: “As it stands, migrants are seen as victims who need to be saved, not as social innovators who are capable of standing up for ourselves.” Black Europeans stated goal is to monitor the EU settlement scheme, aiming to combat systemic racism post-Brexit and offer representation to all EU citizens from the Global Majority.
items.why: a new migrant-led organisation is being created to monitor a government scheme and build representation for a marginalised group, expanding civic capacity and voice.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building launch of a civic organisation rather than mere organisational news.

items.h: Hope Not Hate hiring five new roles
items.b: Senior Policy & Engagement Officer, Community Response Co-ordinator and Press & Communications Lead are just some of the roles Hope Not Hate are advertising for. Hope Not Hate is a leading organisation responding to and tackling far-right politics in the UK. Find out more and apply here .
items.note: Job adverts for an existing organisation, not a democracy story.

items.h: Charities too ‘respectable’ to win change, Janey Starling argues
items.b: Writing for openDemocracy last month, Janey Starling, Co-Director at LevelUp , says charities are too fixated on doing ‘good’ and being polite, that charities have stopped fighting for social justice . Janey states that ultimately ‘charities cling on to their service contracts, offering tepid policy briefs, while the government does whatever it wants’.
items.why: it concerns whether civil society organisations retain the capacity and willingness to challenge government and pursue structural change, a condition for a healthy civic sector.
items.note: Opinion piece about civil society's role and willingness to engage politically, not organisational admin.
links: charities have stopped fighting for social justice

items.h: Institute for Government publish new report on austerity in public services
items.b: The new report ‘Austerity’ in public services: lessons from the 2010s argues that the Chancellor’s expected push for austerity will be far more damaging to public services and harder to deliver than the coalition government’s 2010 austerity programme — in short, that there is no meaningful ‘fat to trim’ from existing budgets, many of which are still feeling the impacts of a decade of spending restraint and pandemic pressures.
items.note: Concerns the feasibility and impact of fiscal policy on public services rather than a democratic mechanism of accountability or participation.
links: ‘Austerity’ in public services: lessons from the 2010s

items.h: Proposed English boundary changes to be announced on 8th November
items.b: The Boundary Commission for England (BCE) has announced a new map of proposed boundary changes will be published on 8th November. The changes will aim to equalise the number of electors between constituencies. From 8th November, the final public consultation period will open for four weeks , ending on 5th December. The BCE will publish all comments received during the secondary consultation stage. Welsh constituencies are also undergoing review for which you can find more information here . Roger Wilson at Unite to Reform highlights the need for a shared baseline of GE2019 results ahead of new…
items.why: boundary changes determine how constituencies are drawn and thus how votes translate into representation, a core mechanism of electoral fairness.

items.h: Compass to launch new national campaign Win as One
items.b: The new national campaign from Compass seeks to make the case for a better political system, supporting a new generation of changemakers to step up and represent their communities in the next election. Win as One candidates will place particular emphasis on delivering electoral reform. More details to follow.
items.why: it involves recruiting and supporting candidates to stand for election on a platform of electoral reform, directly touching political competition and the electoral system.
items.note: Campaign supports candidates for election and pushes electoral reform, so filed under elections rather than participation.

items.h: New voting clause in Levelling-Up Bill rejected by UK Government
items.b: The voting clause allowing local authorities to choose the voting systems they operate in their areas has been rejected by the UK Government. Lib Dem Tim Farron MP remarked the clause was entirely reasonable if the government was serious about devolving power and trusted local people. Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Levelling Up, Deheena Davison, asked that the clause be withdrawn, stating, “the Government absolutely cannot accept it…Ensuring confidence in the voting system is paramount. Having different systems for neighbouring areas risks confusion for electors.”
items.why: it concerns whether local authorities can choose their own electoral systems, a matter of electoral system design and local democratic structure.
links: if the government was serious about devolving power

items.h: Centenary Action Group to host panel discussion on women’s representation in Parliament
items.b: The parliamentary event on 17th November will discuss how political parties can increase the number of female MPs and what cultural changes are required to retain them. The event is an in-person question and answer session with time for networking.
items.note: An event listing/panel announcement rather than a reported change or new participation mechanism.
links: discuss how political parties can increase the number of female MPs

items.h: Social Market Foundation make a democratic case for independent fiscal policy
items.b: A new briefing from the Social Market Foundation suggests that empowering technocrats to take charge of national fiscal policy could circumvent the current over-politicisation of macroeconomic policy. Following the move to make national monetary policy independent through the Bank of England, the briefing suggests that democratising fiscal policy would allow it to be decided on by independent experts, leaving elected officials to make allocative decisions.
items.why: it proposes shifting fiscal policy control from elected officials to independent technocrats, altering how executive economic power is exercised and held accountable.

items.h: 50,000 march on Westminster to demand a second referendum on Brexit
items.b: The National Rejoin March took place last month with thousands of protestors taking to the street calling for Britain to re-join the EU. Re-joiners argue that the current crises facing the country can be traced back to the 2016 referendum and call for a general election and a second referendum on Brexit.
items.why: it reflects citizens' willingness to mobilise and demonstrate to demand a change in how a major constitutional question would be decided.
items.note: Coverage focuses on the march itself (readiness to demonstrate) rather than policing/restriction, so filed under participation; the referendum demand touches elections.

items.h: Braverman reinstated as Home Secretary despite breaching ministerial code
items.b: Suella Braverman has been reinstated as Home Secretary six days after she was forced to resign for sending confidential government information to private email addresses. Dave Penman, head of the FDA civil servants’ union said the reappointment was a clear sign of ‘double standards’ and it shows that ministers can ‘act with impunity if it suits the prime minister’. Meanwhile, Keir Starmer accused Sunak of making a ‘grubby deal’ with Braverman, offering her a place in the cabinet in order to secure her support in his leadership bid.
items.why: it concerns whether a minister who breached the ministerial code faces real consequences, bearing on standards in public life and ministerial accountability.
links: accused Sunak of making a ‘grubby deal’

items.h: Labour MP Chris matheson resigns over ‘unwanted sexual advances’, triggers Chester byelection
items.b: The findings by Parliament’s bullying and harassment watchdog, as well as the standards commissioner, found Matheson had breached the sexual misconduct policy of the House of Commons . Whilst an independent expert panel then recommended his suspension from Parliament, Matheson said last Friday that he has instead decided to step down, triggering a byelection in his Chester seat following his appointment to the Chiltern Hundreds .
items.why: the MP's resignation over misconduct triggers a by-election, directly affecting representation and electoral competition in the seat.
items.note: Misconduct proceedings touch standards in public life, but the reported mechanism is the triggered by-election.
links: Matheson had breached the sexual misconduct policy of the House of Commons

items.h: Government to push ahead with Voter IDs ahead of May elections despite criticism
items.b: Peter Stanyon, Chief Executive of the Association of Electoral Administrators , has written to the Department for Levelling Up and Communities warning that it could not guarantee the May 2023 elections would run smoothly if the government went ahead with plans to introduce voter ID. Speaking to the Byline Times , Lib Dem peer Lord Chris Rennard said the scheme amounted to “a Trump-inspired form of voter suppression” that could prevent as many as 2 million from voting as they are unlikely to have to correct forms of ID. For more info on the scheme to introduce voter IDs, check out this House of…
items.why: the introduction of voter ID requirements directly affects who can exercise their right to vote and how elections are administered.
links: it could not guarantee the May 2023 elections would run smoothly

items.h: Onward polling reveals extent of collapse in Conservative electoral fortunes
items.b: New research from Onward has underlined the crisis facing the Conservative Party. The survey of more than 10,000 members of the general public at the end of August found that 35% rate their chances of voting Conservative as zero percent and 46% rate it as extremely unlikely. However, the majority of lost Conservative voters indicated that they don’t know who they will vote for at the next election, suggesting Labour still have some way to go to capitalise on the ongoing crisis within the Conservative party.
items.why: it reports on shifting party support and the competitiveness of the governing party, bearing on the health of electoral competition.
items.note: Borderline horse-race polling rather than a mechanism change, but falls under political competition territory.

items.h: New research suggests lower voting age improves voter turnout
items.b: New research from Germany has shown that allowing 16 and 17 year olds to vote in elections improved voter turnout among voters in their late teens and throughout their twenties. The research comes following a 2021 commitment from the new coalition government in Germany to lowering the voting age at a federal level for European Parliament elections. The findings add to a growing body of research from a number of international contexts that reducing the barriers to voter enfranchisement leads to greater levels of political engagement.
items.why: it provides evidence on how lowering the voting age affects suffrage and voter turnout, a core electoral mechanism.
items.note: Turnout and suffrage-related findings are always classified under elections per the framework's standing rule.

items.h: Localis release Policy Toolkit to improve engagement in the public realm
items.b: Public organisations and local councils are realising that there is more to be done in partnership with communities and residents, according to think tank Localis . Their new toolkit, The Connected Society , provides actions and policy options to enhance engagement based on the lessons learnt from recent work in Kensington and Chelsea Council. Localis are also celebrating their twenty-first anniversary in December — join them for a drinks reception at the Bishop Partridge Hall, Church House, Westminster on the evening of Tuesday 6 December from 6.00pm onwards.
items.why: it creates a new toolkit intended to help local councils and communities build sustained engagement mechanisms, expanding practical means for civic participation.
items.note: Anniversary reception mention is organisational admin and excluded from the assessment.

items.h: Twitter will become a ‘supercharged engine of radicalisation’ under Musk, warn civil rights advocates
items.b: Elon Musk has finalised his takeover of social media platform Twitter amidst concern over plans to liberalise content regulation in the name of ‘free speech’. President of the US-based company Media Matters said the platform would become a ‘supercharged engine of radicalisation under Musk, adding to pre-existing concerns about the growing inability of social media platforms to control the spread of misinformation.
items.why: changes to platform moderation policy affect the plurality and reliability of information citizens encounter about politics.

items.h: Join Impress for the launch of their News Literacy Report
items.b: Impress’ new report explores how the public interacts with news, their experience using different news mediums, trust levels of the public towards the news and how they feel about their own media literacy — as well as the role that regulation could play in improving journalistic standards. The new report will be launched on Zoom on the 30th November 11am, register now .
items.why: the report examines public trust and literacy regarding news, which shapes the quality of the public information environment underpinning democratic debate.
items.note: Presented as an event launch, but substantive content concerns the information environment.

items.h: BBC’s Chris Mason falsely reports on Johnson’s support in Tory leadership race
items.b: Political editor for the BBC, Chris Mason, came under fire last week for mistakenly tweeting that Johson had accrued the requisite 100 MPs to place him in the running to become leader of the Conservative Party. Writing in the Byline Times , former BBC reporter Patrick Howse criticised the ‘schoolboy error’ and considered the damaging effects on the BBC and UK political culture.
items.why: errors by a major broadcaster's political editor affect the accuracy of public information about a live leadership contest, bearing on the quality of political debate.

items.h: BBC local radio faces funding cuts
items.b: A fresh round of BBC cuts will see the 39 local radio stations across the UK share more shows, with sources telling the Guardian this could be the end of truly distinctive local platforms — creating 131 new local news jobs whilst cutting 179 other roles in the process. Media minister, Julia Lopez, said the government was ‘concerned’ and ‘disappointed’ by the planned cuts, and ‘serious questions’ would be raised if local content production was damaged.
items.why: cuts to local BBC radio reduce local journalism capacity, narrowing the plurality of information available to citizens about local public affairs.

items.h: Major new report into climate disinformation launches ahead of COP27
items.b: Are you a local or national journalist reporting on this month’s UN COP27 climate crisis conference? Climate Action Against Disinformation — a coalition of organisations pushing back against climate misinformation efforts — have published this critical new field guide for journalists to help navigate climate misinformation in reporting over the next period. Find out more on this month’s Drilled podcast talking to the report’s authors.
items.why: a field guide to help journalists counter climate disinformation strengthens the reliability of public information relevant to political debate.
items.note: International focus, included as it concerns journalistic capacity against disinformation.
links: critical new field guide for journalists to help navigate climate misinformation

items.h: Amanda Tattersall on negotiating big and small and and slow in campaigning
items.b: In this beautiful personal piece for Griffith Review, Amanda Tattersall the Co-founder of GetUp & Sydney Alliance and a major social change leader unpacks their experiences from community and political organising, a must read for any organiser.
items.note: A personal reflective essay on organising experience rather than a report of a democratic mechanism or change.

items.b: Join us for our Democracy Coworking Day on December 9th at Newspeak House as part of the wider Democracy Network Conference activities.

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . This week we were joined by Oliver Walkden — Young Citizens, Perry Walker — TalkShop, Myf Nixon — mySociety, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Martyn Harris — North Warwickshire Borough Council, Diane Sims — Notwestminster, Rebecca Deegan — I Have A Voice, Natasha Kaeda — 50:50 Parliament, Charlie Mansell — The Campaign Company, Ed Hammond — Centre for Governance and Scrutiny, Jessica Kennedy — New Economy Organisers Network and Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters.

The Ecosystem Pledge is a statement of intent, now backed by 74 signatory organisations from across the democracy sector, including Involve, Unlock Democracy, mySociety and 50:50 Parliament. Together, we pledge:
items.note: A pledge among sector organisations to talk to each other is sector admin, not a new mechanism of participation.

items.b: We are individuals and organisations working to improve democracy in the UK. We acknowledge that there are many other organisations working towards the same goal. We believe that, if we want things to change, we need to start talking to each other more.

items.b: We’re just three weeks away from Democracy Network’s first annual conference on Dec 7th & 8th in London. The conference will include a series of workshops, panels and activities, including the Network’s own Democracy Awards. Reserve your spot for the conference . If you’re interested in hosting a workshop or taking an exhibition space at the conference contact Democracy Network via their registration page .

items.h: Democracy Coworking Day, 9th December
items.b: As part of this year’s December democracy extravaganza, UK Democracy Coworking Day is back to top off the week’s programme of events, activities and awards. Coming down for the conference anyway? Spend your last day in London working alongside other organisations working on UK democratic reform, it’ll be a great opportunity to connect and reflect on the week’s events.
items.note: Coworking/networking event listing.

items.h: Democracy Network hires new Network Development Lead
items.b: Democracy Network hires new Network Development Lead to support Network Coordinator Jessie Joe Jacobs and the team in their work of strengthening connections across the UK democracy sector. James Moulding — currently Director at the Centre for Democracy — will be starting the new role just in time for the Network’s first Democracy Conference this December.
items.note: Staff hire announcement, organisational admin.

items.h: Democracy Meetup on pause until 15th December
items.b: Due to the changes above, the Centre for Democracy’s current projects and programmes will be brought under the aegis of the Democracy Network . Whilst we make the slight but necessary changes, we have paused this month’s remaining Democracy Meetup. Please join us again at the upcoming Democracy Network conference and at our next Meetup on the 15th December .
items.note: Internal programme restructuring/admin notice.

items.h: New directory of UK democracy organisations
items.b: The Centre for Democracy contributes to the upkeep and promotion of a UK directory of democracy organisations — an open database of more than 870 organisations and campaigns working to build a better democracy in the United Kingdom. The mapping includes legacy organisations that are no longer active, as well as those that have ceded from the democracy space. The map supports the development of a shared picture of the definition and size of the sector and helps people to connect with others working on similar issues and objectives. The UK directory has been developed using publicly available in…
items.why: a public directory mapping democracy organisations creates new means for people and groups to find and connect with others working to strengthen civic and democratic participation
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building tool per the explicit rule, distinct from organisational news about the Centre itself.

items.h: Stand with 50:50 on #AskHerToStand Day, 21st November
items.b: Natasha Kaeda, Frances Scott and the incredible team at 50:50 Parliament will be running a big social media campaign across all channels next Monday — find out more here and get involved! That’s not all, 50:50 and Elect Her are now working together on party-specific resources to help women progress in politics, exciting!
items.why: a campaign encouraging women to stand for political office builds new capacity for participation and bears on the representativeness of elected institutions
items.note: Campaign purpose is to help people take part in democratic life, per the sector capacity-building rule, with a secondary link to representativeness of elected office.

items.h: Notwestminster 2023 is coming
items.b: Join Notwestminster on the 18th Feb 2023 in Huddersfield for a celebration of local democracy and exploration of how to nurture active citizens — Want to host a workshop? Get in touch .
items.note: Event announcement and call for workshop hosts, treated as sector logistics rather than a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Democracy academic collaboration project nears completion
items.b: George Bolton, University of Southampton, and Dr Graham Smith, Centre for the Study of Democracy — University of Westminster, have been running a participatory research project focused on improving the collaborative working arrangements between academics and democracy practitioners in the UK. After seven months, the project Collaboration for Democratic Change is undergoing final review before publication. Email George Bolton to find out more .
items.note: An academic project about researcher-practitioner collaboration methods, not a change to public participation mechanisms.
links: Centre for the Study of Democracy
Email George Bolton to find out more

items.h: Young Citizens hiring
items.b: Big changes at Young Citizens as they hire a new Chair of Trustees, Director of Partnerships and Engagement and a Data and Communications Officer to assist in delivering their mock trials and active citizenship programmes. Find out more and apply now .
items.note: Job advert / organisational hiring notice.

items.h: Royal Society of the Arts opens consultation of their new strategy
items.b: RSA Fellow Titus Alexander draws some lessons for the RSA from their forty years of experience working with change agencies at the local, national and the global level. Read Titus’ analyses here .
items.note: Organisational strategy consultation and opinion piece, not a change affecting public participation.

items.h: Shared Future examine the difference made by a Climate Change Citizens Jury
items.b: Two years after Kendal’s first Climate Citizens’ Jury Shared Future returned to assess the progress made as a result of greater communication between local authorities, citizens, and the not-for-profit sector. With significant changes made in the two years, the Kendal Climate Citizens Jury demonstrates successful jury process, collaboration and community power in action.
items.why: this matters democratically because it assesses whether a deliberative citizens' jury process actually altered how binding local decisions were shaped through collaboration between citizens, local authorities and civil society.
items.note: Citizens' juries are deliberative decision-making machinery, filed under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: I Have A Voice are looking for a Community and Engagement Officer
items.b: Apply now to work alongside Rebecca Deegan and the amazing IHAV team opening up politics and policymaking.
items.note: Job advert / organisational hiring notice.

items.h: Over 3000 offensive tweets sent to MPs each day, BBC investigation reveals
items.b: An investigation by the BBC has unearthed the scale of online abuse facing MPs. Analysis of three million tweets directed at MPs over six weeks found that 130,000 were likely to be toxic and 20,000 ‘severely toxic’. All 20 MPs who received the highest levels of online abuse were in neither the cabinet nor the shadow cabinet. MP Jess Philips said criticism was a necessary part of the job but there now exists a culture in which politicians are scared to share their views for fear of online abuse.
items.why: this matters democratically because sustained online intimidation of elected representatives can chill their willingness to speak, engage and stand for office, undermining the personal security and expressive freedom that public political life depends on.
items.note: Framed as individual liberty/security of representatives rather than the media environment, so filed under rights & freedoms rather than information & debate.

items.b: On Wednesday 30th of November IPPR and Unlock Democracy are hosting an in-person event at Broadway House in London to discuss the current crisis of our political system. Joined on the night by Sir Ed Davey MP, Leader of the Liberal Democrats, Tom Brake, Director of Unlock Democracy and Carys Roberts, Executive Director of IPPR, attendees will hear about how we increase trust in politics and restore the foundations of our democracy.
items.sec: IPPR and Unlock Democracy discuss: Why isn’t our politics working and how can we fix it?
items.note: Event listing/promotional notice rather than reported news of a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Roundtable discussion on political literacy to be held on Monday 5th of December
items.b: On the 5th of December, Shout Out UK will be celebrating Political Literacy Day with an event in parliament to celebrate the work being done to improve political literacy amongst the youth and discuss the challenges and solutions to quality democratic education across the UK. Joined by the chairs of the APPG for Political Literacy and other civil society stakeholders, the talk will be followed by a roundtable discussion with the chance to join in person and online. Check out the full details and reserve a spot at the discussion.
items.sec: IPPR and Unlock Democracy discuss: Why isn’t our politics working and how can we fix it?
items.note: Event listing/promotional notice rather than reported news of a democratic mechanism.

items.b: The Electoral Reform Society is hosting its 2022 Conference and AGM in Cardiff on Saturday 3rd December where they’ll be joined by academic Professor Ailsa Henderson from the University of Edinburgh and Mick Antoniw MS, Council General and Minister for the Constitution. Across the day there will be a series of talks and workshops exploring the crises, challenges, and opportunities facing UK democracy, as well as plenty of networking opportunities. Be sure to register for the free conference asap !
items.sec: Electoral Reform Society to host their annual supporter conference in December
items.note: Event/conference notice about an organisation's own activities, not a democracy story.
links: register for the free conference asap

items.h: MP Richard Burgon proposes bill to allow public to directly call a general election
items.b: Richard Burgon, Labour MP for Leeds East, has proposed a new constitutional mechanism to allow the general public to directly call a general election in cases where they have lost faith in the governing party, calling it a ‘scar on our democracy’ that such a mechanism does not currently exist. Burgon aims to introduce the Bill in the coming weeks with details of a ‘right of recall’ which he believes will be fundamental to restoring faith and trust in democracy at a time when both are at an all-time low.
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes a new mechanism for the public to trigger a binding collective decision (a general election) outside the normal electoral cycle.
items.note: Treated as decision-making machinery akin to direct popular vote rather than general accountability.

items.h: Unlock Democracy calls for amended legislation to allow constituents chance to fire absent MPs
items.b: Following news that Matt Hancock could be absent for up to three weeks whilst appearing on I’m a Celebrity Get Me Out Of Here, Unlock Democracy has launched a petition to amend the Recall of MPs Act 2015. The amendment would allow constituents to recall absent MPs if 10% of constituents sign it, triggering a by-election and a docking of the MP’s pay.
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes amending electoral recall law that would trigger by-elections and alter how constituents can remove their representative.
items.note: Recall mechanism triggering a by-election is classed under elections machinery rather than accountability alone.

items.h: European Digital Democracy Database
items.b: An international volunteer effort composed of some 40 analysts have collected, composed and reviewed more than 1,000 digital democracy projects across Europe. Access the database .
items.why: this matters democratically because cataloguing digital democracy projects creates a new resource that can help people and organisations find and build means of civic participation.
items.note: Marginal: primarily a European resource, included as sector capacity-building rather than direct UK reporting.

items.h: New briefing outlines which seats will change under the 2023 boundary review
items.b: New research from Carl Baker and Elise Uberoi from the House of Commons Library looks at which constituencies are proposed to change under the 2023 Boundary Review. They’ve found that under current plans, one in seven constituencies would retain 99% of their current population, whilst one in nine constituencies would have less than 60% similarity to the successor constituency. Find out more .
items.why: this matters democratically because constituency boundary changes directly affect how votes translate into representation.

items.h: New mySociety research finds 1 in 10 people have made an FOI request!
items.b: Alex Parsons, Senior Researcher at mySociety , reports that newly commissioned polling by Opinium reports that 10% of UK adults have used Freedom of Information requests to try and get access to information. If inclusive of those using FOI for work, the figure increases to 14%.
items.why: this matters democratically because it measures the public's practical use of freedom of information to obtain information about public affairs.
items.note: Framed around public usage of the information environment rather than an institution being held to account, so filed under information & public debate.

items.h: Gavin Williamson resigns over bullying allegations
items.b: Gavin Williamson has resigned as Minister of State without Portfolio following a slew of bullying allegations in which he allegedly told a civil servant to ‘slit your throat’ and told another official to ‘jump out of a window’. In his resignation letter Williamson refuted the ‘characterisation of these claims’ but recognised that the controversy was drawing attention and resources away from the Government’s key priorities.
items.why: this matters democratically because a minister's resignation over bullying allegations reflects standards in public life and accountability for conduct in office.

items.h: Trust in British politics in freefall according to IPPR polling
items.b: According to recent polling from IPPR , two in three voters now say that politicians are ‘out for themselves’ rather than serving ‘the interests of the country’. This sentiment was consistent across a number of key demographics: leave voters 68%, remain voters 67%, Conservative 64%, Labour 69%, London 60%, the North 69%, Scotland 70%, middle class 65%, and working-class 66%. Trust in British politics has fallen by 9 percentage points over the last 18 months according to IPPR. By comparison, it took roughly 7 years for the previous fall of a similar scale and 42 years for the one before that.
items.why: this matters democratically because falling public trust in politicians and parties reflects the legitimacy and accountability of democratic institutions.

items.h: The Independent Monitoring Authority take the Government to court over EU citizen’s rights in the UK
items.b: The Independent Monitoring Authority, a statutory body set up to protect the rights of EU citizens settled in the country before Brexit, has taken the Government to court over their implementation of the Withdrawal Agreement. They argue that the way the Government has implemented the Withdrawal Agreement means people with rights enshrined in law will be denied these rights unless they reapply for permanent or settled status. This means 2.6m people with ‘pre-settled’ status risk detention or removal from the country unless they apply for the ‘upgrade’.
items.why: This matters democratically because an independent statutory body is using judicial review to compel government compliance with law protecting the rights of millions of residents, testing whether public power is exercised within legal limits.
items.note: Framed as a court challenge over government compliance with law, so rule_of_law_justice takes primacy over the rights content.

items.h: Postal voting will not be included in the Voter ID implementation for May 2023 elections
items.b: According to Martyn Harris, Head of Elections at North Warwickshire Borough Council, postal voting — or early voting — will not be included in the Voter ID implementation ahead of May 2023. Whilst postal voting is included in the Elections Act, its implementation will come later.
items.why: This matters democratically because the phased rollout of voter identification and postal voting rules directly affects the administration and accessibility of voting.

items.h: Byelections postponed as pre-election period begins
items.b: In those areas holding council elections in May 2023, byelections will now be postponed and superseded by the local elections. Note that local byelections in Wales, Scotland, London and areas not up for election in May will still be held as normal and ignore the 6-month pre-election period. Thanks to the Democracy Club Slack community and Martyn Harris for the legislative reference .
items.why: This matters democratically because rules governing the timing and conduct of byelections are part of the machinery of electoral administration.

items.h: It’s London Voter Registration Week 2022!
items.b: This week London’s City Hall teamed up with Shout Out UK for London Voter Registration Week. London Boroughs and organisations across the city including the East European Resource Centre , Lambeth Democracy and Tigray Youth Network , to name but a few, pulled together to highlight the importance of registering to vote over social media airwaves across the city and outside tube stations and public spaces. Lara Parizotto and the team at Migrant Democracy Project even took to Stratord in East London with their voter registration dance .
items.why: This matters democratically because voter registration drives directly affect people's practical ability to exercise the franchise.
items.note: Turnout and registration activity is always filed under elections per the standing rule, not participation.

items.h: Democracy Meetup spawns renewed discussions on Voter ID
items.b: Last week’s meetup saw a vibrant discussion on all aspects of the upcoming Voter ID implementation. During the discussion concerns were raised about democracy organisations trying to work on Voter ID awareness raising in a short time frame close to the election and that action should be taken now to think through ‘how to stop hares running’ and applying for a form of ID voters don’t need. Jess Kennedy, Director of Movement Building, New Economy Organisers Network , raised the spectre of campaign groups and local authority services saying competing things about the problems and issues facing vo…
items.why: This matters democratically because coordinated efforts to clarify and communicate new Voter ID rules affect whether eligible voters can successfully cast a ballot.
items.note: Framed as sector discussion but substantive content concerns electoral administration and access mechanics.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Officials warn of election chaos if voter IDs are mandated for May election
items.b: Election officials and councillors have called on the government to delay the introduction of Voter IDs due to fears that a short timetable and a lack of clarity over regulations could prevent thousands from voting. The rule that all voters would need to show ID became law under the Elections Act 2022 , passed in April this year. The Electoral Reform Society has joined with Unlock Democracy and Hands of Our Vote to call for an inquiry into the implementation of the voter ID by the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee.
items.why: This matters democratically because warnings about implementation timelines for voter ID bear directly on whether eligible citizens will be able to vote.
links: an inquiry into the implementation of the voter ID

items.h: Labour dissolves local selection panel in row over Camberwell and Peckham seat
items.b: The Labour Party has dissolved a local selection panel following accusations that the panel leaked details on the selected candidates to a local news website. The selection process for Harriett Harman’s seat had already come under scrutiny after anti-racism campaigner Maurice Mcleod was blocked from standing over reported concerns about his social media activity. Last week Kensington also had their selection committee dissolved in similar circumstances.
items.why: This matters democratically because disputes over candidate selection processes affect the fairness and integrity of party access to elected office.
links: Maurice Mcleod was blocked from standing

items.h: MPs increasingly hail from the constituency they represent, according to new research
items.b: New research (paywalled) from Queen Mary has revealed that the number of MPs born in the same constituency they represent has increased from 45–52% over the last decade.
items.why: This matters democratically because the local origin of MPs bears on the representativeness of elected institutions.

items.h: Freedom of Information Reform (Scotland) Bill published
items.b: The bill proposes extending Freedom of Information legislation in Scotland coverage to all bodies delivering public services, services of a public nature and publicly funded services, creating a role of Freedom of Information officer; increasing the proactive publication of information; improving enforcement where necessary and improving compliance with human rights law. Responses to the proposed bill are welcome until the 2nd February.
items.why: This matters democratically because extending Freedom of Information coverage to more bodies delivering public services strengthens the public's ability to hold those bodies answerable for how they exercise public functions.
items.note: FOI reform is filed under accountability because the story is about institutions being made answerable, not the information environment.
links: extending Freedom of Information legislation in Scotland

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny running webinars for local authorities
items.b: Ed Hammond, Acting CEO, Centre for Governance and Scrutiny , is preparing a series of webinars on scrutiny of local authority finances and health services for elected councillors. In addition to this they’re working on finalising a set of guides for councils on redrafting and improving their constitutional material to make it more accessible. Get in touch with Ed to find out more .
items.why: This matters democratically because building councillors' capacity to scrutinise local authority finances and constitutions strengthens the practical machinery of local democratic accountability.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building, which the framework files under participation regardless of the specific accountability topic.
links: Get in touch with Ed to find out more

items.h: Is it time for Wales to change its voting system?
items.b: In a report published by the Electoral Reform Society, Jess Blair makes a compelling case for changing the Welsh system by contrasting the First Past the Post elections in Wales with the proportional Single Transferable Vote elections in Scotland.
items.why: This matters democratically because the electoral system used determines how votes translate into representation and shapes political competition in Wales.
links: Jess Blair makes a compelling case for changing the Welsh system

items.h: Institute for Government asks: What tools do local areas need to boost regional growth?
items.b: On the 5th December Institute for Government are hosting an panel discussion exploring which powers could be devolved to regional authorities to aid local growth. Participants will also consider whether power should be devolved to councils or combined authorities and how the Government can empower subnational governments through the Levelling Up and Regeneration Bill .
items.why: This matters democratically because decisions about which powers are devolved to regional and local authorities determine the structure and reach of sub-national democratic decision-making.
items.note: Local/regional government powers are filed under elections & decision making per the framework's treatment of devolved structure.

items.h: UK Government announces new round of austerity with damaging impacts for local services
items.b: Polly Billington, Chief Executive at UK100 , remarks that the return to austerity will ‘alarm local leaders up and down the country still grappling with the effects of the first round of spending cuts almost a decade ago’. Last month, Local Government Association Chairman Cllr James Jamieson, voiced concerns over increasing council cost pressures and the impact on service delivery, saying ‘ reserves can only be spent once, a local service cannot be cut twice .’
items.why: This matters democratically because central government funding decisions constrain local authorities' capacity to exercise their powers and deliver services they are accountable for.
items.note: Classified under government accountability because the mechanism is fiscal power over local government capacity, not a change to structure, powers or elections of that tier.
links: reserves can only be spent once, a local service cannot be cut twice

items.h: IMPRESS to launch News Literacy Report on 30th November
items.b: In collaboration with the Universities of Leeds and Derby, IMPRESS have been researching public perceptions and attitudes towards the current news landscape. Their new report takes a closer look at the public experience of news mediums, levels of media literacy, trust levels, and more. On the 30th of November, IMPRESS will host a free online event to launch and discuss the report — don’t miss out .
items.why: This matters democratically because public understanding of and trust in the news landscape shapes people's ability to obtain meaningful information about public affairs.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation push ahead with UK Local News Map
items.b: Joe Mitchell and the team at PINF are preparing their directory of UK local news organisations, which will soon become a snazzy interactive map — they’re on the lookout for anyone with experience of Datawrapper / Flourish — Get in touch .
items.why: This matters democratically because a directory of local news organisations supports the visibility and sustainability of local journalism that underpins informed public debate.
items.note: Classified under information & public debate since the mechanism concerns the local journalism landscape rather than a participation tool.

items.h: Society of Editors ‘strongly condemn’ arrest of journalists covering Just Stop Oil protests
items.b: LBC reporter Charlotte Lynch, documentary filmmaker Rich Felgate, and photographer Tom Bowles are all reported to have been arrested whilst covering the recent Just Stop Oil protests. Dawn Alford, Executive Director of the Society of Editors, spoke out against the affront on press freedom saying ‘the protests are a source of legitimate public interest and journalists, filmmakers and photographers have a right to attend protests and report on behalf of the public. We strongly condemn the arrest of journalists in the course of their work.’ The press arrests received widespread coverage in nation…
items.why: This matters democratically because arresting journalists while they cover protests threatens press freedom and the public's ability to receive independent reporting on matters of legitimate public interest.
links: spoke out against the affront on press freedom

items.h: Culture Secretary promises to push ahead with repeal of Section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act
items.b: Speaking at the Media Freedom Awards, Culture Secretary Michelle Donelan confirmed that the government would be pushing ahead with plans to repeal Section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act 2013 as well as adding legislation to the Online Safety Bill to ‘protect journalists’. Plans to repeal section 40 were initially announced in the Queen’s speech in May and were met with scepticism from media campaign groups who maintain that the legislation is key to ensuring both press and public freedom.
items.why: This matters democratically because changes to press regulation law affect the incentive structures underpinning press freedom and public access to information about power.
items.note: Press regulation legislation is treated as information environment rather than accountability since the focus is on journalists and press freedom.
links: pushing ahead with plans to repeal Section 40
met with scepticism from media campaign groups

items.h: Byline Times examine Musk’s Twitter takeover with former Twitter executive
items.b: As Elon Musk continues to make headlines for his controversial Twitter takeover, Adrian Goldberg from the Byline Times has interviewed former Twitter executive Bruce Daisley on the company’s new owner and the threat to democracy he poses.
items.why: This matters democratically because ownership and control of a major social media platform affects the plurality and integrity of the public information environment.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund call for proposals: University support for electoral registration
items.b: The Fund plans to commission rapid research on the state of university support for students to register to vote and participate in elections in England. The resulting report will be used to highlight the need for improved student registration practices and higher rates of student voter registration and turnout. Please contact the UK Democracy Fund for more information .
items.note: This is a funding call for proposals (sector logistics), not itself a new participation mechanism or reported change.
links: Please contact the UK Democracy Fund for more information

items.h: Mehr Demokratie
items.b: Perry Walker at TalkShop recommends checking out German democracy organisation Mehr Demokratie . With more than 40 staff, 10,000 active members and more than 200,000 participants in their activities, MD is perhaps the largest NGO advocating for direct democracy and active citizenship worldwide. Mehr Demokratie pushes for the expansion of direct democracy across the federal states of Germany.
items.note: An offbeat recommendation to look at a foreign organisation, not UK-relevant or reporting a change.

items.h: Civil society groups accuse Egyptian officials of intimidation and surveillance at COP27
items.b: Members of civil society groups report being subject to intimidation and surveillance whilst attending COP27. Speaking anonymously to the Guardian, one individual said, “mentioning activism in conversation means you get ‘cleaners’ and technical staff coming over to you.” The issues described by numerous sources mirror the situation faced by Egyptian civil society groups who have reported a significant crackdown on their organising capacity in recent years.
items.note: Concerns civic space intimidation abroad with no clear bearing on UK democracy, so falls outside the geographic scope.
links: report being subject to intimidation and surveillance
