items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Louise Dunmore and Max Roche of the Democracy Network and Centre for Democracy . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : democracynetwork@involve.org.uk

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Meetup . We were joined by Katy Rubin — Legislative Theatre, Myf Nixon — mySociety, Prof. Graham Smith — Centre for the Study of Democracy, Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters, Gavin Barker — Citizen Network and Charlie Mansell — The Campaign Company.

items.h: Online Safety Bill returns to Parliament
items.b: The Online Safety Bill returned to parliament last week for a further round of debate. Last month, a coalition of campaign groups, including Liberty , Big Brother Watch and Index on Censorship , wrote to the UN Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression warning of the threat to free speech and privacy that would arise if the Online Safety Bill becomes law. In recent months, all aspects of the Bill concerning disinformation have been removed and key sections concerning privacy rights have been scaled back.
items.why: the bill's provisions on disinformation and privacy shape the plurality and safety of the online information environment through which people encounter political debate
items.note: Free speech/privacy concerns tied to online platform regulation are treated as information environment with a rights secondary for privacy.
links: warning of the threat to free speech

items.h: Elections (Proportional Representation) Bill has first reading in parliament
items.b: Cat Smith, Labour MP for Lancaster and Fleetwood, has introduced the Elections (Proportional Representation) Bill to parliament calling for PR to be implemented at all parliamentary elections, mayoral elections and local authority elections in England, and Police and Crime Commissioner elections in England and Wales. The Bill had a first reading in the Commons on the 29th of November and is set to have a second reading on the 20th of January 2023.
items.why: the bill would change the electoral system used to translate votes into seats across multiple tiers of UK government

items.h: The Public Order Bill has completed committee stage in the Lords
items.b: The Bill will be scrutinised at report stage in the New Year, which those working to improve the Bill believe to be crucial to amending it and removing the aspects they see as damaging.
items.why: the bill governs legal restrictions and policing powers over protest and assembly, affecting people's ability to organise and demonstrate
items.note: Protest legislation concerning policing/legal restriction is classified as rights, not participation.

items.h: Democracy Network Annual Conference
items.b: It has been just over a week since the Democracy Network’s Annual Conference and participants across the sector already can’t wait for next year . If you attended the conference be sure to provide feedback to the team on how it went for you. Check out the Network’s new video marking one week since the event here .
Frances Scott (50:50 Parliament), Matteo Bergamini (Shout Out UK), Mohammed Afridi (Civic Power Fund) and Ruth Hannah (People’s Powerhouse) at the Democracy Network Annual Conference

items.h: Notwestminster — February 18th, register now
items.b: Notwestminster is a free conference on building a more open, kinder local democracy. Based in Huddersfield the event will run on the 18th February 2023. Find out more and register now .
items.note: Treated as an event listing rather than the creation of a new participation resource.
links: Find out more and register now

items.h: Response to Gordon Brown’s ‘New Britain’ report
items.b: Whilst the report itself is covered later in this issue, those across the sector have spent the past week or so digesting a sector-wide response. Tom Brake, Director of Unlock Democracy , is penning a joint letter for organisations to sign in the next few weeks. Rich Wilson and others at the Democracy Network conference suggested that the response include an independent process facilitated by the Democracy Network to feed into Labour’s consultation, which may potentially build support for a wider range of reforms. Titus Alexander also suggested following in the footsteps of previous campaigns …
items.why: civil society organisations are coordinating a campaign response intended to build public and institutional support for proposed constitutional reforms
items.note: Sector logistics but purpose is building a participation campaign, so treated as capacity-building.

items.h: Democracy Defence Coalition resurrected
items.b: Over the last 18 months, the Democracy Defence Coalition (DDC) — an alliance of more than fifteen organisations across the sector — worked closely to oppose and limit the potential damage from the then Elections Bill. Whilst dormant since the inception of the Elections Act, the DDC is being given a new lease of life due to widespread concerns over the implementation of the Elections Act.
items.why: a coalition of civil society groups is mobilising to scrutinise how the Elections Act is implemented, affecting electoral administration and integrity safeguards

items.h: Involve on the lookout for new Trustees and Treasurer
items.b: Ed Cox, Chair at Involve , and their wider team are on the lookout for promising candidates to be their next Treasurer for the Board and Trustees. Find out more and apply here .

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust hiring new Grant Officers, Executive Governance Officer
items.b: The Trust is looking to hire two new Grants Officers and an Executive Governance Officer over the coming period. Applications close 8th January, apply now .

items.h: Seb Payne departs the lobby for Onward
items.b: Hailing their new role as ‘Westminster’s finest think tank’ Seb Payne has departed their role as Whitehall Editor at the Financial Times taking the helm at Onward as Director. Former Onward Director Will Tanner stood down earlier last month before moving into the №10 team as the PM’s Deputy Chief of Staff.

items.h: Civic Power Fund keeps the flame of Campaign Bootcamp alive
items.b: In recent months Civic Power Fund (CPF) won a bid to take ownership of Campaign Bootcamp’s assets, resources and website. In order to keep vital campaign resources available to activists and campaigners CPF opted to keep Campaign Bootcamp’s website up as a legacy website and archive. Campaign Bootcamp announced their closure this time last year after more than 8 years and 1,300 graduates of their powerful training programmes.
items.why: maintaining a training and resource archive preserves a means by which activists and campaigners can build skills to participate in democratic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since a participation resource is being preserved rather than merely organisational admin.

items.h: UK Open Government Network reinvigorated
items.b: Through Involve’s stewardship of the Open Government Network (OGN) reform agenda, they are looking to convene a sponsoring committee to provide bridge funding for a coordinator and help raise longer-term funding. This is as the UK Government start to turn their attention to Open Government National Action Plan 6, the deadline for which is 31 December 2023. The publication deadline for National Action Plan 6 is 31st December 2023 — Sign up to assist the OGN as a volunteer .
items.why: a civil society network is being rebuilt to coordinate input into the UK's open government commitments, sustaining a channel for public scrutiny of government transparency
links: Sign up to assist the OGN as a volunteer

items.h: New research briefing looks at the causes and prevalence of political disengagement in the UK
items.b: A new briefing paper by Neil Johnston and Elise Uberoi of the House of Commons Library looks at the causes behind political disengagement across the UK and the reasons why certain groups have lost faith in the democratic process.
items.why: understanding why groups disengage from politics and lose faith in the democratic process bears directly on people's willingness and ability to take part in civic life
links: looks at the causes behind political disengagement

items.h: Republic are on the lookout for a new Lead Campaigner
items.b: Republic has had a busy few months making the case for a democratic alternative to the monarchy and are now looking for an experienced campaigner to help grow their membership base and boost public support for republicanism in the UK. Apply before December 30th and help shape the debate around King Charles III’s coronation.
items.note: Job advertisement for an organisation's staff role, not a democracy story.

items.h: Graham Smith steps down as Chair of Foundation for Democracy and Sustainable Development
items.b: Prof. Graham Smith is handing over the leadership of the Foundation for Democracy and Sustainable Development to Peter Davies of Wellbeing of Future Generations (Wales) Act fame, who was also Wales’ first Future Generations Commissioner.
items.note: Leadership handover within an organisation is organisational admin, not a democracy story.
links: Foundation for Democracy and Sustainable Development

items.h: Tom Tugendhat discusses democracy in an age of state threats at Policy Exchange event
items.b: In a keynote speech, Minister for Security, Tom Tugendhat discusses the question of how to defend democracy in an age of state threats. Watch the full lecture on YouTube .
items.note: Event/lecture listing rather than a reported development in how democracy is defended or contested.

items.h: Starmer promises to abolish the House of Lords if elected
items.b: Labour leader Keir Starmer has revealed plans to abolish the House of Lords in an attempt to ‘restore trust in politics’, replacing it with an elected chamber. The plans aim to combat the growing public disillusionment with the political system by putting a stop to the practice in which outgoing prime ministers have appointed ‘lackeys and donors’ to the House of Lords. Labour Peers have, however, warned the Labour leader against the reforms , which they suggest would land him in a ‘constitutional quagmire’ and unable to push through key domestic reforms.
items.why: it proposes replacing an appointed chamber with an elected one, changing how legislative power is authorised and who can be chosen as a representative.
links: revealed plans to abolish the House of Lords
warned the Labour leader against the reforms

items.h: Gordon Brown publishes key report on constitutional reform and democratic renewal
items.b: The Brown Commission has released A New Britain: Renewing our Democracy and Rebuilding our Economy — a 40-point briefing outlining how our political system can be rebuilt to make the UK more prosperous, egalitarian and accountable. A significant decentralisation of power, an elected second chamber and improvements in standards of public life are at the centre of the proposals. The Electoral Reform Society , along with other pro-PR groups, have criticised the plans , however, for not proposing proportional representation for the Commons, which they describe as ‘a glaring hole in Britain’s new c…
items.why: it proposes decentralising power to local and regional tiers and replacing the House of Lords with an elected chamber, altering the machinery through which representatives are chosen and power is distributed.
items.note: Report spans multiple beats (electoral reform, devolution, standards); classified by its central proposals on elected representation and decentralisation.
links: A New Britain: Renewing our Democracy and Rebuilding our Economy

items.h: UK Supreme Court rejects authority of Scottish parliament to call independence vote
items.b: In mid-November, court proceedings over the question of Scottish independence finally concluded with the UK Supreme Court ruling unanimously that Scotland cannot hold another independence referendum without the prior approval of Westminster. Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has vowed this will not be the end of the referendum push however and has said she will treat the next general election as a de facto referendum with independence being a central theme of the SNP manifesto. For more information on the Supreme Court decision, see this research briefing from David Torrance at the House…
items.why: it determines whether a devolved legislature can call a binding referendum, directly shaping the machinery of direct popular decision-making.
items.note: Referendum authority is classified as elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, though the ruling itself is a judicial act.
links: Scotland cannot hold another independence referendum

items.h: Greater Manchester Legislative Theatre wins global participatory democracy award
items.b: Katy Rubin reports that earlier this month in Grenoble, France, Legislative Theatre for the Greater Manchester Homelessness Prevention Strategy was chosen out of 122 nominations to win the 2022 Award for Best Practice in Citizenship Participation from the International Observatory on Participatory Democracy . This is the first time that either the UK or the Legislative Theatre methodology have been honoured with this international prize.
items.why: it highlights recognition of a participatory practice that gives residents a direct role in shaping local policy, expanding the means through which people can take part in civic life.
items.note: Legislative Theatre is a participatory civic practice rather than formal deliberative decision-making machinery, so classified under participation rather than elections & decision making.
links: 2022 Award for Best Practice in Citizenship Participation

items.h: Assisted Dying likely to be legalised in Jersey following Citizens’ Jury
items.b: In a major landmark policy shift, the island of Jersey is likely to see Assisted Dying legalised on the back of a Citizens’ Jury recommendation . Parliamentary Select Committees have been reported as asking for input into an inquiry on the issue beyond Jersey. The jury topped off a process initiated in 2019, when more than 1800 islanders signed a petition which triggered an online public survey, a GP and doctors’ survey and a public meeting on the issue. Together these elements signalled widespread support for policy among islanders which led to the Jersey Government commissioning a Citizens’ …
items.why: a Citizens' Jury, a deliberative decision-making mechanism, directly shaped a major policy outcome.
items.note: Citizens' juries/deliberative processes are classified as elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Hansard Society Lecture looks to the future of the House of Lords
items.b: The Lord Speaker’s Parliamentary Affairs 75th Anniversary Lecture was delivered on the 7th of December exploring a range of issues related to the reform of the Upper House. During the lecture, the speaker Lord McFall of Alcluith, discussed the size and appointments system and the House’s role in wider society, stressing the need for reform whilst underlining the importance of the Lords’ scrutiny and revision roles.
items.why: it concerns how the House of Lords' composition, appointments and scrutiny powers shape legislative oversight of the executive.
items.note: Lords reform touches both chamber composition and scrutiny function; scrutiny role treated as primary.
links: Lord Speaker’s Parliamentary Affairs 75th Anniversary Lecture

items.h: Climate Change Committee experiments with deliberative engagement
items.b: Jake Ainscough, Senior Research Associate on the Climate Citizens project at Lancaster University, interviewed Climate Change Committee CEO Chris Stark on the Committee’s recent experiments with deliberative research.
items.why: it involves a public body experimenting with deliberative engagement as a mechanism for informing collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative process is classified under elections & decision making per framework anchoring.
links: interviewed Climate Change Committee CEO Chris Stark

items.h: Sunak rejects calls to overrule European Court of Human Rights over deportations
items.b: Downing Street has rejected a short bill introduced earlier this week by Tory backbencher Jonathan Gullis which would allow the government to deport asylum seekers even if the ECHR has explicitly ruled against it. Rishi Sunak has pledged not to contravene ECHR rulings despite calls from within his party to do so, although he failed to answer questions in the commons as to whether he would remove the UK from the ECHR altogether.
items.why: it concerns whether the executive will comply with binding international court rulings, a core test of government under law.

items.h: Report calls for increased powers to enable robust parliamentary scrutiny
items.b: A joint report from the Bennett Institute and the Institute for Government has found that the amount of time spent by MPs debating bills in parliament has declined over the past 20 years, now representing just a quarter of their time. The report suggests parliament’s powers have been eroded in recent years and calls on the government to empower parliament to allow proper scrutiny of legislation, checks on executive action and greater balance to the UK constitution.
items.why: it documents erosion of parliamentary time and powers for scrutinising and checking executive legislation.
links: parliament’s powers have been eroded in recent years

items.h: mySociety publish their annual review and WhatDoTheyKnow’s transparency report
items.b: Deep dive into the work of mySociety over the past year with their 2022 Annual Review . Meanwhile Sally Reader, Service Manager on WhatDoTheyKnow, reports back on a year of FOI requests through the platform — this year they racked up more than 109,653 requests made by more 239,540 WhatDoTheyKnow accounts (an increase of 16,217 this year!).
items.note: Treated as organisational annual review/self-reporting rather than a substantive change to FOI mechanisms.
links: reports back on a year of FOI requests

items.h: openDemocracy re-opens ‘Who Funds You’ campaign to investigate think-tank funding
items.b: The re-booted programme uses think tanks’ disclosed sources of income to position them on a scale of funding transparency. Their analysis gave nine out of the twenty-eight think thanks analysed the worst possible ranking as they found no, or negligible available information on their funding streams. These ‘dark-money’ think tanks, who often publicly claim to carry influence within government, had a total income of £14.3m.
items.why: it exposes opacity in the funding of think tanks that seek to influence government policy, bearing on accountability for undue influence.

items.h: Network for Police Monitoring reviews 2022: ‘the year it became okay to jail protesters in Britain’
items.b: ‘It has not been a good year for our right to dissent’ , report NetPol — the review lays bare the successive challenges and threats to civil liberties and basic political rights of expression by the Johnson, Truss and Sunak Governments over the course of 2022. This year saw the introduction of the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act, coming into force in the summer, the new Public Order Bill — and the National Security Bill — both taking aim at the right to demonstrate and dissent . This year saw the highest number of political prisoners incarcerated within British jails for decades, with…
items.why: it documents legal and policing changes narrowing the right to protest and dissent.
links: ‘It has not been a good year for our right to dissent’
taking aim at the right to demonstrate and dissent

items.h: Climate protestors may be classified as terrorists by police
items.b: According to secret documents seen by openDemocracy , intelligence on climate protesters who specifically target large companies is being handed over to counter-terrorism police (CTP) to see if it classifies as terrorist activity. Although public order and protest-related duties have been removed from the CTP remit since 2020, information is still being shared with the department, meaning protestors from direct action groups such as Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion may be assessed by the CTP.
items.why: it concerns state surveillance and potential coercive reclassification of protest activity as terrorism, affecting the freedom to dissent.

items.h: Report and blog explore scrutiny within local government
items.b: Megan Ingle, Researcher at the Centre For Governance and Scrutiny , has written an introductory guide on scrutiny, looking at the main facets of scrutiny and a summary of some of the key tools and skills needed to improve and enhance scrutiny in local authorities. A blog from Charlotte Cameron, Democratic Services Officer at Peterborough City Council looks at how to improve scrutiny from the perspective of a new Democratic Services Officer.
items.why: it concerns the scrutiny function within local government, a core accountability mechanism for holding local decision-makers answerable.
items.note: Scrutiny practice guidance is filed under accountability rather than participation since it targets the institutional scrutiny function, not public participation.

items.h: Labour retains seat of Chester with firm by-election victory
items.b: Samantha Dixon MP won the seat earlier this month with the party’s highest-ever vote share (61.22%) and a majority of just under 11,000. The Conservatives received 6,335 votes and a 22.4% vote share, their worst result in the constituency since 1832.
items.why: a by-election result reflects genuine electoral competition and representation of voters' choices.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society criticises government over voter IDs
items.b: The government finally published their list of voter IDs that can be used at the next election as part of the reforms introduced through the Elections Act . The Electoral Reform Society has criticised the list however, for offering the elderly significantly more options than young people, which could see young people discouraged from voting. For more information on Voter IDs, check out this research briefing from Neil Johnston and Elise Uberoi at the House of Commons Library.
items.why: voter identification requirements directly affect who can practically exercise their right to vote.

items.h: Government signs landmark £360m devolution deal with Cornwall
items.b: The Government has signed a £360 million devolution deal with Cornwall, creating a new directly-elected Mayor and giving the area greater control over transport, housing and adult skills. The deal now means that almost half of England is covered by some form of devolution deal. Give Back Control , a policy paper released by Onward over the summer, sets out 25 recommendations for giving these mayors deeper and broader powers, alongside bolstered accountability and increased capability.
items.why: the deal creates a new directly-elected mayor and restructures regional decision-making powers.
items.note: Devolution deals affecting the structure and powers of a tier of government are filed under elections & decision making per the boundary rules.

items.h: Bright Green speak to Welsh Green Party about the prospect of Welsh independence
items.b: In a recent interview with Wales Green Party leader Anthony Slaughter, Bright Green discusses Future Cymru Forum — a new body set up by the Welsh Greens and Plaid Cymru to make the case for Welsh independence. Listen back for updates on the Welsh independence campaign and the Welsh Greens’ prospects at the next election.
items.why: the story concerns a campaign for a future independence referendum, a mechanism of direct popular decision-making.
items.note: Borderline: mostly party political commentary but touches on the machinery of a prospective referendum.

items.h: Titus Alexander is developing a Scottish Sovereignty Index
items.b: The Scottish Sovereignty Index AKA ‘Independence Readiness Index’ is currently at 72% according to the first assessment. Titus and the team are looking for an organisation to host it and help promote the Index (for which they have funding). Contact Titus if you’re interested .
items.note: This is primarily a call for a hosting organisation, i.e. sector logistics, rather than a reported democratic development.

items.h: People’s Powerhouse launch their new film
items.b: People’s Powerhouse work to include the voices of ordinary Northerners in the decisions that affect their lives. Late last month they teamed up with Northern wordsmith Nathan Parker for their new film .
items.note: An organisation's own film launch is organisational news rather than a new mechanism for participation.

items.h: MPs vote through controversial National Security Bill
items.b: The Society of Editors has warned that the proposed new laws would ‘ride roughshod’ over established journalistic protections meaning journalists and campaign groups might be deterred from publishing information in the public interest. The society has joined a coalition of organisations demanding amendments to the bill to prevent the criminalisation of public interest journalism. The bill passed its third reading last month and now goes to the Lords for further scrutiny.
items.why: the bill risks criminalising public interest journalism, undermining the information environment necessary for public debate.

items.h: Editors and industry experts call on Dominic Raab to introduce anti-SLAPP legislation
items.b: Leading editors, lawyers, journalists, publishers and free speech organisations have written an open letter to Dominic Raab asking him to back meaningful anti-SLAPP protections. Pressure has been mounting over the last year to introduce legislation to protect the press from the ‘abusive legal tactics’ that are often employed to silence investigations.
items.why: the ability of journalists to investigate and report on the powerful without being silenced by abusive legal action is essential to a plural, functioning information environment.

items.h: Plans to privatise Channel Four could be scrapped
items.b: The UK Government appears to have dropped their plans to privatise Channel Four as they enter discussions with the broadcaster over alternative funding models that could avoid privatisation. Whilst ministers claim they are still considering all options, Culture Secretary Michelle Donelan told MPs: ‘I’ve been looking at other options on sustainability and discussing those with Channel 4 as to how feasible they are.’
items.why: the ownership and funding model of a major public-service broadcaster shapes the plurality and independence of the media environment citizens rely on for political information.
links: enter discussions with the broadcaster over alternative funding models

items.h: Institute of Welsh affairs publishes results of citizen-led research on Welsh media
items.b: In the summer of 2022, a selection of fifteen citizens from across Wales came together with a range of ‘expert witnesses’ to discuss and debate how the media in Wales can better serve its citizens. Led by independent facilitators, the meetings focused on three main areas; media regulation, democracy and citizenship education, and recognising Welshness. Check out the full report and all the recommendations put forward by how to improve the Welsh media.
items.why: it uses a citizens'-assembly-style deliberative process to produce recommendations on media governance, which the framework treats as decision-making machinery regardless of topic.
items.note: Deliberative/citizen-led process classified as decision-making machinery per boundary rule despite the media subject matter.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation report looks at link between local media and electoral turnout
items.b: In the run-up to local elections in London and Birmingham in May 2022, PINF provided funding to five news providers to increase levels of local journalist activity to see whether this would in turn increase democratic engagement. Although the project did not generate conclusive evidence that voter turnout or registration had improved, there were a number of other interesting insights around knowledge of local issues, opportunities for engagement and trust in local information. Would you like to know more? .
items.why: the research directly investigates whether local journalism affects electoral turnout, and turnout in any framing sits in elections and decision making.
items.note: Turnout is always classified under elections & decision making per the standing rule, even though the intervention was local media funding.
links: the project did not generate conclusive evidence
Would you like to know more?

items.h: New research from Impress reveals low levels of public news literacy
items.b: Impress recently surveyed 3000 members of the public for their beliefs, experiences, and perceptions of today’s news landscape. Their recently published report reveals a striking correlation between low levels of trust in journalism and a lack of knowledge about the news media industry more broadly. Improving trust in journalism means engaging more thoroughly with the public on news values and the role of regulation, said Impress CEO, Richard Ayre.
items.why: public trust in and understanding of journalism shapes whether citizens can meaningfully engage with plural sources of political information.

items.h: The Ferret launch new community newsroom in Glasgow
items.b: Thanks in part to crowdfunding donations from members, The Ferret will today (Friday 16th December) open a new community newsroom which they will share with Greater Govanhill Magazine . The newsroom will offer a space for community building and will allow hyperlocal, community-based journalism to collaborate with rigorous investigative journalism.
items.why: creating a shared newsroom space expands capacity for hyperlocal and investigative journalism that underpins public scrutiny and debate.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building (a new 'hub') that materially expands local journalism capacity.

items.h: Civic Power Fund’s Community Action Fund is now open
items.b: Civic Power Fund new Community Action Fund is aimed at supporting grassroots organisations that are building the power of their community and campaigning for long-term change. The fund aims to provide flexible, one-off grants between £2,500 and £20,000 — Apply now .
items.note: A funding call for grant applications, explicitly listed as sector logistics rather than a democracy story.

items.h: Unlock Democracy to receive funding for campaign on automatic voter registration
items.b: Shaun Roberts, Head of Campaigns and Digital, at Unlock Democracy reports that they have just had confirmation of funding for a new parliamentary campaign to support AVR.
items.note: Reports an organisation securing its own campaign funding, which is organisational news rather than a change in democratic mechanism.

items.h: Common Knowledge funded by Civic Power Fund
items.b: Not-for-profit tech worker cooperative Common Knowledge work closely with grassroots organisations across the UK to provide high quality digital and campaign support. They have worked to produce new brand identities, strategies and digital presence for campaigns such as 350, London Renters Union, StopWatch, Autonomy, GND UK, Generation Rent, Nurses United and more. Civic Power Fund are providing core funding for their work to support grassroots organisations.
items.note: This is funding/organisational news about a cooperative receiving core funding, not a new participation mechanism or change to public power.

items.h: German right-wing coup d’etat plot foiled
items.b: Earlier this month more than 3,000 police across Germany moved to arrest members of the far-right terrorist group Patriotic Union , part of the far-right Reichsbürger movement. Coup plotters threatened to violently seize Germany’s federal government and install Heinrich Reuss as monarch. A former Alternativ für Deutschland (AfD) MP was also implicated and arrested in the police action.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns an attempted violent overthrow of an elected government, directly threatening the orderly constitutional transfer of power that underpins democratic legitimacy.
items.note: International item included as comparative evidence about threats to constitutional transfer of power, despite not being UK-specific.
links: 3,000 police across Germany moved to arrest members of the far-right terrorist group Patriotic Union

items.h: Does our mental health affect democratic participation? The Practical Democracy Podcast investigates
items.b: Joined by Dr Antonis Kousoulis, Director of the Mental Health Foundation , a new episode of the Practical Democracy Podcast looks at the relationship between mental health and public participation, examining how issues such as financial instability and social inequality may impact someone’s capacity to involve themselves in the democratic process.
items.note: A podcast episode announcement discussing a topic is promotional content rather than a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: The Community Power podcast returns for a second series
items.b: The Community Power podcast is making a return for a second series, exploring what happens when you give local people the money, power and resources to become changemakers in their communities. Check out current episodes on community resilience, local regeneration and climate conversations.
items.note: A returning podcast series announcement is sector content promotion, not itself a new mechanism for participation.

items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Louise Dunmore and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : democracynetwork@involve.org.uk
