We were joined by Joseph Gaunt — E-lectorate Project, John Preston, Perry Walker — Talk Shop, Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters, Ed Hammond — Centre for Governance and Scrutiny, Diane Sims — Notwestminster, Amna Ahmad — UK Democracy Network, Alex Bulat — Migrant Democracy Project, Ed Watson, Harry Hayfield — Wales Green Party, Josiah Mortimer — Byline Times, Jéssica Kranz Barcelos — Mogi Das Cruzes, Ed Dowding — Represent.me.
items.note: Acknowledgement of event attendees, organisational admin rather than a democracy story.

items.h: Peers set to frustrate attempts to scrap thousands of EU laws by end of the year
items.b: Members of the House of Lords have raised concerns over the practicality of reviewing thousands of pieces of EU legislation by the end of 2023 and are preparing to slow down government attempts to do so. Downing Street has refused to reconsider the end of year deadline contained within the Retained EU Law Bill and on the 18th of January, the bill passed its third reading in the House of Commons. The bill now passes to the House of Lords for consideration.
items.why: it concerns Parliament's capacity to scrutinise and constrain a sweeping delegated-powers process for rewriting law within an arbitrary deadline.
links: Members of the House of Lords have raised concerns

items.h: Bill proposing statutory code of conduct has first reading in the House of Commons
items.b: Labour MP, Debbie Abrahams, has introduced the Elected Representatives (Code of Conduct) Bill to parliament with the intention of bringing in a statutory code of conduct for elected representatives. The bill also proposes that an independent body of legal experts is created to advise on this process. The independent body will be informed by a citizens’ assembly to give the public a say in how elected representatives should conduct themselves.
items.why: it proposes a statutory mechanism to hold elected representatives to enforceable standards of conduct.
items.note: Citizens' assembly element is secondary as it feeds into standards rather than being the core decision-making mechanism.

items.b: Under the new ‘anti-strike’ legislation , Secretary of State for BEIS Grant Shapps will decide new statutory minimum service requirements across a range of public services limiting the capacity of workers to strike. If the minimum service requirements are not met then striking workers could be laid off by the employer under the terms of the new bill. Mick Lynch called the legislation ‘an attack on human rights and civil liberties’ , whilst the Trade Union Law Group has said the new legislation breaches international treaties and the human rights convention . According to the law group, any att…
items.sec: UK Government introduces Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Bill across public services to quell strike action
items.why: it restricts trade union freedom of association and the right to strike through state-mandated minimum service levels and dismissal powers.
links: ‘an attack on human rights and civil liberties’
breaches international treaties and the human rights convention

items.h: Sunak tables amendment to Public Order Bill to crack down on ‘guerilla’ protest tactics
items.b: The new amendment would see tactics used predominantly by environmental protestors such as ‘slow walks’ criminalised . The Bill also contains new laws which would allow the police to crack down on planned protests before they have actually taken place. Campaigners have expressed outrage at the latest plans with Liberty Director Martha Spurrier remarking the new proposals ‘ should be seen for what they are : a desperate attempt to shut down any route for ordinary people to make their voices heard’. The bill entered the report stage in the House of Lords on 30th January 2023.
items.sec: UK Government introduces Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Bill across public services to quell strike action
items.why: it criminalises specific protest tactics and expands pre-emptive police powers against assembly.
links: tactics used predominantly by environmental protestors such as ‘slow walks’ criminalised
should be seen for what they are

items.h: Public Order Bill
items.b: Reports that Labour are wobbling on the Public Order Bill, potentially withdrawing support for key amendments. Efforts are now shifting from gaining Conservative and cross-bench support to focusing on Labour Lords and the shadow frontbench.
items.sec: UK Government introduces Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Bill across public services to quell strike action
items.why: it tracks the parliamentary contest over legislation that would restrict protest rights, affecting whether curbs on assembly become law.
items.note: Framed as legislative politics but substance is the protest-restriction bill itself.

items.h: Online Safety Bill passes third reading in House of Commons
items.b: The final Commons Report stage took place on January 17th. After a rebel amendment to the bill gained opposition support , the government agreed to amendments. The changes now mean senior managers at tech firms will face criminal charges if they fail to adequately protect children from online harm. The bill now passes to the House of Lords.
items.sec: UK Government introduces Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Bill across public services to quell strike action
items.why: it imposes new legal duties and liabilities on platforms shaping the online information and speech environment.
items.note: Content focuses on child safety rather than political speech, but falls under platform regulation territory.
links: rebel amendment to the bill gained opposition support

items.h: Notwestminster is coming, announces first workshops
items.b: If you haven’t already, you can still grab your free ticket to Notwestminster 2023: In Democracy We Trust on 18th Feb in Huddersfield — details of lightning talks and participant-led workshops are now available on the website. Ahead of the event they’re asking people who cherish local democracy to answer this one simple question: what helps you to trust?
items.note: Event/ticket announcement rather than a new tool, programme or change affecting participation.

items.h: The Politics Project host General Election Strategy Conference for democratic education orgs
items.b: The special event convened by The Politics Project saw dozens of organisations from across the UK descend upon the central London venue, showcasing the breadth and diversity of the democratic education and youth engagement space, with organisations ranging from the Northern Ireland Youth Forum, the Association of Colleges, to the UK Parliament Education and Engagement Team. The day centred around preparing for the upcoming General Election with discussions centred around voter registration, voter ID concerns and negotiating questions of political impartiality and neutrality whilst delivering q…
items.why: it builds sector capacity for voter registration and political education ahead of an election, creating new means for civic engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building rather than mere organisational news given its substantive focus on registration and political education.

items.h: Amna Ahmad begins work on supporting the sector to coordinate around the General Election
items.b: Amna Ahmad , UK Democracy Network’s new Campaigns and Advocacy Lead, is consulting sector organisations to coordinate action around engagement with political parties ahead of the GE. The first step involves engagement with the Labour Party’s National Policy Forum (NPF) process, following in the wake of the publication of the Gordon Brown Constitutional Review. The NPF consultation process is now open and reportedly closes on 17 March. Would you like to know more? Pop Amna an email .
items.note: Primarily staff/role news about a new hire's early activities, not a reportable change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny to host in-person conference in June
items.b: The conference will take place on 14 June 2023, at the King’s Fund and will bring together colleagues in the local government space to discuss the challenges and opportunities facing local democracy. Check out the full agenda and book your tickets now.
items.note: Event/conference listing, sector logistics.

items.h: Democracy Club’s Every Election gets a new lick of paint
items.b: Peter Keeling and the team at Democracy Club have been busy undertaking a comprehensive redesign of their Every Election (EE) database. The new site features a new design system, a revision of election IDs in light of the boundary reviews and voting system updates — but most importantly of all, maps! All election pages on EE now provide an interactive ‘leaflet’ map of the relevant area of division. Check it out .
items.why: it creates a new public-facing tool that helps citizens locate and understand elections and constituency boundaries, expanding practical means of electoral engagement.
items.note: Applied the capacity-building rule: a new resource aimed at helping people engage with democratic processes is filed under participation even though its content concerns elections.

items.h: Just two weeks left for applications for the New Institute’s Future of Democracy fellowships
items.b: The New Institute is an experimental initiative aimed at developing social imaginaries for future societies, combining academic rigour and innovative practice. The Institute hosts up to 35 fellows at their site Warburg Ensemble in Hamburg. They are currently seeking 21 fellows across three programme areas, including Depolarising Public Debates, Governing the Planetary Commons, and Conceptions of Human Flourishing. Find out more and apply here , applications close on 16th February.
items.note: International fellowship application call, not UK-focused sector logistics.

items.h: Charlotte Obijiaku moves on from Involve to take up new role at TPXimpact
items.b: Project Officer at the Involve Foundation , Charlotte Obijiaku will take up a new role at TPXimpact as a Deliberative Democracy Officer to support their growing portfolio of deliberative democracy projects.
items.note: Personnel move between organisations, excluded as organisational news.

items.h: 50:50 and Power Done Differently launch new podcast
items.b: The podcast sets out to explore why women should pursue roles in politics and how power can be reinvented by women. The podcast is streaming on all major platforms.
items.why: it launches a new media resource encouraging women's engagement and representation in political life, expanding conditions for equal participation.
items.note: Treated under the capacity-building rule as a newly created means of encouraging participation.

items.h: National Rejoin March is organising a pro-rejoin day in March
items.b: On Saturday 23rd of March, National Rejoin March is organising a day of pro-rejoin activity around the whole of the UK. They’re looking for volunteers to help coordinate activities in their local areas. Sign up on their website if you’re keen.
items.why: it mobilises volunteers and citizens to organise a nationwide day of political activity, reflecting willingness to take part in campaigning and public demonstration.
items.note: Focus is on willingness/organisation to demonstrate rather than legal restriction or policing, so filed under participation rather than rights.

items.h: Scottish Parliament’s Citizens’ Panel on Participation recommendations, consultation closing 10th February
items.b: As part of the Scottish Parliament’s development of its capacity to deliver deliberative engagement over recent years, Holyrood’s Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee have been running an inquiry into public participation. As part of that process, a Citizens’ Panel on Participation was commissioned and has since published their report detailing 17 recommendations. An 8-week consultation has now been launched on the Parliament’s Your Priorities platform , with a 10th February deadline for responses.
items.why: it advances a citizens' deliberative process feeding into how the Scottish Parliament structures public participation in its decision-making machinery.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per the revised framework, not participation.
links: Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee

items.h: POMOC and Involve win grants to deliver on London Civic Data Innovation Challenge
items.b: Polish Migrants Organise for Change (POMOC) and Involve have both won £10k grants to deliver key platforms of the Greater London Authority’s Civic Data Innovation Challenge. POMOC are delivering a pilot survey measuring the diversity of local councillors across London, whilst Involve will develop a toolkit which enables local decision makers to define what types of deliberative and participatory processes they are using, and to identify the impacts on themselves and local communities.
items.why: the funded tools aim to measure representativeness of local councillors and build capacity for deliberative decision-making processes, both part of the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative process toolkits are classified under elections/decision-making rather than participation per the boundary rule.

items.h: Make Votes Matter announce 24th May Lobby of Parliament
items.b: On Wednesday May 24th, the Make Votes Matter Alliance are pulling together to demonstrate public support for electoral reform. Their new campaign, Sort the System — the Public Lobby for Equal Votes will see a public launch in the next few months, with an aim to marshall the wide array of pro-PR organisations and lobby for PR at a time when political parties will be penning their manifestos ahead of the next General Election. Don’t miss MVM’s Democracy Loves Climate Justice session next Tuesday, grab your ticket .
items.why: the campaign seeks to change the electoral system to proportional representation, directly affecting how votes translate into representation.

items.h: Scottish Government opens online consultation on electoral reform
items.b: The Scottish Government’s consultation on electoral reform considers possible improvements to electoral law, such as whether 16–17 year olds should be allowed to stand for election, as well as being able to vote, as well as a number of possible changes to assist candidates in local elections, increase voter registration and accessibility in elections, including the possibility of Digital Polling Cards (Brighton & Hove tested this a few years back with positive results).
items.why: the consultation considers changes to suffrage, candidacy rules, voter registration and accessibility that shape who can vote and stand in elections.
links: Scottish Government’s consultation on electoral reform

items.h: Electoral Integrity Project publish new report The UK’s Electoral Data Democratic Deficit
items.b: Penned by Toby James and Paul Bernal of the University of East Anglia, the report outlines the electoral democratic data deficit and its wider consequences for UK democracy. The report found six key aspects behind the UK’s electoral data deficit, ranging from unworkable data formats (marked registers still being published in hard copy only) to the current electoral data infrastructure largely held up civil society groups (such as Democracy Club ) who lack secure funding, and whose work should really be the preserve of statutory public electoral bodies. You can read the report here . The report…
items.why: the report exposes deficiencies in the electoral data infrastructure that underpins electoral administration and public scrutiny of elections.

items.h: The Fawcett Society call for modernisation in parliament to make it more gender inclusive
items.b: The Fawcett Society has released a new report based on new survey data and interviews conducted with current and former Members of Parliament. They report that 69% of women MPs and 49% of all MPs have witnessed sexist behaviour in Parliament in the last five years and 73% of women MPs said they ‘do not use social media to speak on certain issues because of the abusive environment online’. They recommend a series of reforms towards the creation of a more inclusive parliament including calls for an amendment to the Online Safety Bill to better address the disproportionate levels of online abuse …
items.why: sexist behaviour and online abuse of women MPs constitute a discrimination and freedom-of-expression barrier that affects women's equal ability to participate in and remain in political office.
items.note: Gender equality as a rights/discrimination issue placed under rights rather than participation.

items.h: Represent.me v2 on the horizon
items.b: Ed Dowding, Product Innovation at Represent.me , is working with Frome Town Council and councils in Wales to establish what Represent v2 might look like. Ed and the team are looking for a pragmatic and finance focused cofounder. If this sounds like you, pop them an email .
items.note: Recruitment/organisational note about a cofounder search, not a launched participation mechanism.

items.h: Talk Shop experimenting with Pol.is, reflecting on predictive policing
items.b: Next Wednesday Perry Walker and the team at Talk Shop will be utilising their Win-Win Workout method to reflect on the emerging practice of predictive policing — join them and register for the event here . In other news they’re also looking into Pol.is to find common ground between political parties in the UK, stay tuned for more on this.
items.note: Event listing and speculative future exploration of a tool, not a concrete launch or reported change.

items.h: Starmer’s plans for Lords reform will create an ‘arm wrestle’ for power, says Speaker of the Commons
items.b: In an interview with LBC just before Christmas, Speaker of the House of Commons Lindsay Hoyle broke his traditionally neutral position to criticise Labour’s plans for an elected second chamber. He suggested the plans would create an ‘arm wrestle’ for power between the two chambers with both the House of Commons and the Lords vying for supremacy. For more information on Labour’s plans, check out this new research briefing by Richard Kelly of the House of Commons Library which takes a closer look at the government’s attitude towards House of Lords reform and the current system of peerage appoint…
items.why: proposed Lords reform would alter the balance of power and checks between the two chambers of the legislature.
items.note: Debate over an elected second chamber touches both legislative structure/checks (accountability) and elections.

items.h: Calls for the regulation of political adverts increase
items.b: Compassion in Politics has joined with Reform Political Advertising to call for greater regulation of political advertising after it emerged that the Conservative Party had put out leaflets bearing a striking resemblance with Green Party advertising. The campaign group wrote to the Conservative Party Chairman asking for reform following what they described as attempts to deliberately mislead voters.
items.why: political advertising that misleads voters affects the plurality and integrity of information people rely on to make electoral choices
items.note: Political advertising regulation is anchored to information & public debate, not elections mechanics.

items.h: Will Labour change the voting system? The New Statesman invites the Electoral Reform Society to find out
items.b: In the recent edition of the New Statesman podcast , Director of Policy and Research at the Electoral Reform Society , Jess Garland, joins Anoosh Chakelian to discuss all things voter reform. The pair unpick the significance of the past year in which support for proportional representation reached new heights, discussing where the main parties now stand on this issue.
items.why: a change in electoral system determines how votes translate into representation and political competition

items.h: Proportional Representation leads to greater income equality, says King’s College professor
items.b: Dr Sandher, Economist and Political Scientist at Kings, argues in an article for Progressive Britain that adopting proportional representation leads to greater levels of income equality .
items.why: the choice of electoral system shapes representation and, per this research, downstream economic equality that affects people's capacity to participate
items.note: Core subject is electoral system design, so filed under elections despite the equality angle.
links: adopting proportional representation leads to greater levels of income equality

items.h: Liberal Democrats for Electoral Reform set out their strategy for how to achieve proportional representation
items.b: LDER hosted an event on 17th Jan to discuss how PR can be achieved ahead of the next election and the implications of Labour adopting PR as a manifesto pledge. Check out the recording if you missed it, as well as this interview with Tom Brake, Director of Unlock Democracy , who discusses with the Editor of Bright Green why proportional representation is important and what a new democratic settlement should look like.
items.why: strategies to achieve proportional representation concern the electoral system through which representatives are chosen

items.h: E-lectorate building new digital democracy platform
items.b: Project Director Joseph Gaunt and the team at E-lectorate are working on a new digital direct democracy tool to increase democratic participation via digital tools. E-lectorate are currently looking for user testers, partnerships and feedback, if you’re interested email Joseph .
items.why: a new direct democracy tool creates a mechanism for citizens to take binding or advisory collective decisions outside standard elections
items.note: Direct democracy tools are anchored to elections & decision making rather than general participation per framework rule.

items.h: Tortoise Media’s Westminster Accounts release bombshell financial data
items.b: Sky News and Tortoise Media have released a new interactive database detailing the earnings and donations declared by any MP, political party, APPG or donor since the 2019 General Election. This is the first time such data has been made available, allowing the public to easily see the total sums of donations and earnings for individual MPs — something which was previously very difficult to collate and compare due to the way the registers are published.
items.why: public access to consolidated data on MPs' earnings and donations enables scrutiny of conflicts of interest and holds elected representatives answerable

items.h: UK drops to lowest ever position on Corruption Perceptions Index
items.b: The UK has dropped from 11th to 18th on Transparency International’s Global Corruption Index , with their overall point score falling from 78 to 73. Only five of the 180 countries assessed for the 2022 Index saw their year-on-year scores drop by five or more points: the UK (-5), Qatar (-5), Myanmar (-5), Azerbaijan (-7) and Oman (-8). CEO of Transparency International, Daniel Bruce, said the fall was a ‘powerful indictment of a recent decline in standards in government and controls over the use of taxpayer money.’
items.why: a falling corruption perceptions score reflects declining standards in government and weaker controls over the use of public power and money

items.h: Strasbourg designates UK Government’s failure to act on Russian democratic interference as ‘impact case’
items.b: Despite two Parliamentary committee reports ( DCMS , Intelligence and Security ) detailing the impact of and credible attempts by Russian-backed outfits to interfere with UK elections, the UK Government has ignored and failed to act on the findings. In response, last March a group of UK parliamentarians took the UK Government to the ECHR backed by journalist grouping The Citizens . The Strasbourg court has now requested the British Government respond in detail to the allegations by 26th April, designating the case as an ‘impact case’. Read the Byline report for more information .
items.why: unaddressed foreign interference in elections undermines the integrity of the electoral process, and the government's failure to act is now subject to international legal scrutiny and accountability
items.note: Combines electoral integrity, court redress and executive accountability; filed primarily under elections since interference in voting is the core issue.
links: Read the Byline report for more information

items.h: PM fires Nadhim Zahawi over tax scandal
items.b: Zahawi has been fired from his position as Conservative Party Chairman following an investigation by the new independent advisor, Sir Laurie Magus. They found a lack of openness in their tax affairs that meant it was untenable to keep them in position. Jake Berry, former Conservative Party Chair, has called for a new mechanism to allow for the suspension of ministers during ongoing investigations into their conduct — check out this article from Hannah White of the Institute for Government discussing the various pros and cons to this approach.
items.why: it shows a mechanism of ministerial accountability being exercised, with a minister removed following an ethics investigation and debate over whether stronger suspension powers are needed.

items.h: Labour Party facing high costs over legal actions
items.b: Whilst the ICO has told the BBC it will not be prosecuting three Jeremy Corbyn supporters accused of leaking confidential information due to ‘insufficient evidence’, the Party is taking five Corbyn supporters to the High Court for conspiring to put a leaked internal anti-semitism report into the public domain. The legal case could cost between £3–4 million according to the BBC, but as unions cut back on their funding for the party and Labour members subs are no longer swelling the coffers of the party due to collapsing membership figures , Labour’s funding gap is growing with a reported £5 mil…
items.why: it concerns party funding disparities and legal costs that affect the relative capacity of parties to compete for power, a core condition of political competition.
items.note: Classified under elections/party competition rather than integrity because the core issue is the widening funding gap between parties, not an accountability mechanism per se.
links: The expected date of the two-week trial could fall during the 2024 General Election

items.h: Unlock Democracy question authority of new ethics advisor
items.b: Unlock Democracy has penned an open letter to the Prime Minister’s new ethics advisor, Sir Laurie Magnus, welcoming their appointment but questioning the logic of appointing an ethics advisor without the power to initiate inquiries that haven’t already been signed off by the PM. Given that the PM will also decide on any sanctions for wrongdoing they question whether the new ethics advisor has any significant power.
items.why: it questions whether a key standards-in-public-life mechanism, the independent ethics adviser, has genuine power to hold the executive to account.

items.h: Transparency International’s Open Access UK tool: UK Government ministerial meeting oversight
items.b: Open Access UK is a central hub that allows you to understand who is meeting with government, when and for what purpose. The UK Government publishes the data, but it is scattered and difficult to understand. Transparency UK’s Open Access tool provides this data in an accessible format for you to interrogate. Find out more or contact TI UK if you’re interested in funding them to assist in expanding the provision of their data collection operation.
items.why: it creates a tool making ministerial meeting data accessible, strengthening transparency as a mechanism for holding government answerable.

items.h: Majority of voters consider the Conservative Party institutionally corrupt, according to new poll
items.b: A new poll carried out by Omnisis and commissioned by The Byline Supplement has found that 65% of the population now think Rishi Sunak’s party is ‘institutionally corrupt’ compared to just 18% who disagree with the statement. The poll also found that 72% think senior members of the Conservative party are ‘more interested in personal gain than serving the public’, with just 16% disagreeing.
items.why: public confidence in the governing party's integrity is a direct indicator of trust in institutions and their perceived susceptibility to corruption.

items.h: Conservative MP suspended from House of Commons over lobbying
items.b: MP Andrew Brigden was suspended from the House of Commons for five days in January after it was found that he breached parliamentary rules on paid lobbying and declaring interests. Brigden subsequently lost the Tory whip for spreading misinformation about Covid-19 and for comparing the vaccine rollout to the Holocaust.
items.why: the suspension enforces parliamentary standards on lobbying and declared interests, a core accountability mechanism for elected representatives.
links: suspended from the House of Commons

items.h: GLA teams up with Shout Out UK to boost voter registration in London
items.b: With just four out of ten London voters aware of the recent voter ID changes, the Greater London Authority have kicked off a new initiative with Shout Out UK , Migrant Democracy Project and others to ensure those across the capital do not lose their vote in this May’s elections.
items.why: the initiative aims to ensure eligible voters are registered and aware of new ID rules, directly affecting their practical ability to exercise the franchise.
links: just four out of ten London voters aware

items.h: Electoral Reform Society launch voter ID public awareness campaign as calls mount for legislation to be abolished
items.b: On the 9th of January ERS launched their voter ID public awareness campaign to help voters understand the forms of identification they will need to bring to polling stations to be allowed to vote in elections later this year. Opposition to the legislation continues to grow with Labour MP Richard Burgon saying it amounts to vote rigging , given warnings of significant voter disenfranchisement due to the limited time to properly implement the scheme. Last month the Guardian released a podcast on voter ID legislation and the risk it poses to free and fair elections.
items.why: the campaign addresses voter ID rules that affect ballot access and raises concerns about disenfranchisement in electoral administration.

items.h: Polish Migrants Organise hosting symbolic election for migrants in London
items.b: The POMOC symbolic vote will be a local level election on a local issue involving non-EU, non-Commonwealth migrants who cannot vote in council elections in Brent, London, despite paying council tax. To find out more you can reach out to the Migrant Democracy Project — if you know any Brent based migrant orgs let them know!
items.why: it dramatises the exclusion of long-term resident migrants who pay council tax from the local franchise, highlighting a gap in inclusive suffrage.
items.note: Symbolic election concerns suffrage/franchise rather than participation generally.
links: reach out to the Migrant Democracy Project

items.h: Voter Authority Certificates now available online, concern over low numbers of voter ID applications
items.b: Whilst an Electoral Commission marketing campaign launched at the start of last month raising awareness of voter ID linked to a website where voter ID applications were at the time not available except by post, the online service is now available . However, at the time of writing it is understood there have been only 10,000 voter ID applications requested , just 0.5% of the number who could need the document. Almost 2 million voters in Great Britain do not possess a form of valid photo ID. A Byline Times poll last month found that 60% of voters were not aware that they would need to bring ID t…
items.why: voter ID requirements and low uptake of the certificates needed to comply with them directly affect whether eligible citizens can actually cast a vote.
links: there have been only 10,000 voter ID applications requested

items.h: Citizens UK unveil new project for 100% registered schools
items.b: Taking a leaf out of their successful living wage campaign, Citizens UK recently announced at the Democratic Education General Election Strategy Day that they are kickstarting a new project for a voter registration traffic light system for schools across the UK.
items.why: a new school-based voter registration initiative creates a mechanism to raise electoral registration and future turnout.
items.note: Turnout/registration initiatives are classified under elections per the standing turnout rule.

items.h: Save the Children to run UK-wide parallel election
items.b: Similar to the work undertaken by the Children’s Commission for Wales project in the 2021 elections, Save the Children are planning a UK wide parallel election to support children’s rights to have a say over decisions that affect them. The mass campaign will be based on a similar Norwegian campaign run in 2021 Barnas Valg 2021 , involving child-friendly hustings and media partners working together to make a splash pre-election results night.
items.why: a parallel election for children who cannot vote highlights and rehearses the mechanics of democratic choice for a group excluded from the franchise.
items.note: Treated as decision-making machinery rather than general civic participation, consistent with the framework's treatment of symbolic/parallel votes.

items.h: Democracy Classroom gear up for their Election Countdown
items.b: Running over six weeks prior to the 2023 local elections, Democracy Classroom will offer up resources to teachers, youth workers and education practitioners across the country, with bitesize information tailored specifically to support young people who will be engaging with elections for the first time. Hattie and the team at Democracy Classroom will be working with democratic education campaigns across the sector to develop the readiness of the space for the upcoming 2024 General Election, with everything in place by this September — stay tuned for more!
items.why: resources aimed at helping first-time voters engage with upcoming elections bear directly on electoral participation and turnout.
items.note: Turnout-related engagement is classified under elections per the standing rule even when framed as youth education.

items.h: Northern Ireland local elections moved to avoid coronation clash
items.b: Initially planned for Thursday 4th May, the local elections will now be pushed back by two weeks to 18th May to avoid King Charles III’s coronation on 6th May. NI Minister Steve Baker MP sent a letter to the chief executives of the 11 councils about the change. Chief Electoral Officer Virginia McVea reported that the original date would ‘impede the smooth running of the election and cause difficulties for staff involved’ due to counts likely running into the day of the coronation.
items.why: rescheduling elections to avoid administrative clashes affects the smooth and credible running of electoral administration.
links: local elections will now be pushed back by two weeks to 18th May

items.h: Best for Britain poll suggests undecided voters will vote Conservative over Labour at general election
items.b: A poll surveying voter preferences during the Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak eras predicts that Labour’s current lead would secure them more than 500 seats at the 2024 general election. However, analysis from Best for Britain suggests their lead could in fact be far more fragile once you consider the voter profiles of those that answered ‘don’t know’. Redistributing the wavering votes based on their age and education profile, they found that many of those voters were more likely to swing towards the Conservatives which would slash Labour’s total to just 353 constituencies.
items.why: the poll bears on whether the opposition has a realistic prospect of forming government, a core measure of electoral competitiveness.
items.note: Borderline horse-race polling coverage rather than institutional analysis, but directly engages the 'opposition prospects' anchor.

items.h: Danny Beales to take on Boris Johnson as MP for Uxbridge and South Ruslip despite claims of Labour Party interference
items.b: Thirty-four year old Danny Beales will hope to overturn Johnson’s significant 7,210 vote majority at the next election. However, the appointment of Beales was highly controversial. The local selection committee was disbanded after they were seen to be promoting a particular candidate in a local newsletter meaning the selection process then passed to the London region. The move was decried by leftwing members organisation Momentum .
items.why: disputes over internal candidate selection processes affect the fairness and openness of political parties' access to the ballot.
items.note: Party candidate selection integrity falls under free political parties within elections & decision making.
links: Danny Beales will hope to overturn

items.h: Constitutional crisis deepens as Westminster blocks Scotland’s Gender Recognition Reform Bill
items.b: Westminster has blocked Scotland’s introduction of the Gender Recognition Reform Bill using a section 35 order approved by 318 Westminster MPs to 71 against. Pete Wishart, chair of the Scottish Affairs Committee called it the ‘single biggest attack on Scottish devolution and Scottish democracy since the establishment of the Scottish Parliament in 1999’, whilst the first minister for Wales said it was a ‘very dangerous moment’ that could be the start of a slippery slope.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns Westminster's use of powers to override the devolved Scottish Parliament's legislative competence, directly affecting the structure and authority of devolved decision-making.
items.note: Devolved government structure/powers routes to elections & decision making per boundary rule.

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny thinking hard about participation and deliberation
items.b: The Centre for Governance and Scrutiny (CFGS) provides corporate governance support to English local authorities, ranging from advice relating to accountability, transparency, decision-making etc. At the moment, Ed Hammond , Acting CEO of CFGS, is considering novel methods of participatory governance, involving a wider range of people than just experts and local politicians, and how that ‘docks in’ with traditional governance. In other news, they’re about to start recruiting for a new Chief Exec.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns how participatory and deliberative methods might be integrated into local government decision-making structures.
items.note: Deliberative process discussion routes to elections & decision making per boundary rule, though this is exploratory thinking rather than a concrete initiative.

items.h: Titus Alexander looking for a host organisation for the Scottish Independence Readiness Index
items.b: The Scottish Independence Readiness Index is a new initiative aiming to focus the debate over Scottish independence on more practical issues by creating a shared understanding of areas that need to be addressed if Scotland were to become independent, together with opportunities for the public to engage online. Titus is looking for a politically neutral, independent organisation or group of organisations with different positions on independence, to host the Index. Get in touch if you can help.
items.why: this matters democratically because it aims to create new means for the public to engage practically with the debate over Scottish independence.
items.note: Borderline between a new participation tool and machinery tied to a potential future referendum.

items.h: Institute for Government launch report on subnational governmental structure in England
items.b: A new report from the Institute for Government examines the unusually centralised system of governance in England and the impact this has in local decision-making. Drawing on comparative analysis from Germany and Japan the report considers the financial dependency local authorities have on Westminster and other aspects of devolved responsibility.
items.why: this matters democratically because it examines the centralisation of power away from local authorities and its impact on local decision-making capacity.

items.h: More support needed to halt damaging decline of local journalism, DCMS Committee warns
items.b: The House of Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee have just released their latest report Sustainability of Local Journalism on the sustainability of local media. The Committee recognise a significant decline in local media, noting the reduced quality of local journalism as a result of media ownership consolidation, and the ‘extreme vulnerability’ of independent local alternatives. The report has been welcomed across the independent news sector for including proposals that the government increase public funding to £10m for independent local journalism to aid local democracy and r…
items.why: this matters democratically because the decline of local journalism reduces the public's ability to obtain meaningful information about local public affairs and hold local power to account.
links: House of Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch 2023 survey of independent news providers
items.b: The survey will provide an in-depth look at the independent news landscape and provide crucial insights for PINF when advocating on behalf of the sector. Please do consider sharing this information directly with any independent news providers and send them a link to the survey .
items.note: Sector survey for internal advocacy purposes, not a change to public participation or information access.
links: sharing this information directly with any independent news providers

items.h: Josiah Mortimer seeks to make democracy key theme of Byline coverage
items.b: In their new role at Byline Times , Josiah Mortimer is keen to make democracy coverage a key plank in Byline’s future coverage. Over the next period they’ll be covering the voter ID rollout, the (anti-) Strikes Bill, Public Order Bill, as well as looking into various Tufton Street think tanks. Josiah’s keen to chat with anyone working in and around these issues, so be sure to pop them an email .
items.note: News about a journalist's new role and coverage plans is organisational personnel news, not itself a democracy story.

items.h: The Media Democracy Festival returns in March this year
items.b: Every year the Media Democracy Festival takes place to explore the media landscape, bringing together a network of academics, journalists and activists for a range of great debates. This year the festival will be held at Birkbeck University on Saturday 25th of March. Book your free ticket now!
items.note: Event listing/ticket announcement, sector logistics.

items.h: Impartiality of BBC chairman called into question over Boris Johnson loan
items.b: An investigation has been called into the appointment of Richard Sharp as chairman of the BBC following revelations that they helped Boris Johnson secure an £800,000 loan through way of an introduction to a wealthy Canadian businessman. William Shawcross was due to head the investigation but he has since recused themself due to concerns over his own impartiality — although Labour are questioning why it has taken him a week to reach this conclusion.
items.why: it concerns a public appointment to a major broadcaster being compromised by an undisclosed conflict of interest tied to a former Prime Minister's personal finances, undermining standards in public life and oversight of public institutions.
links: revelations that they helped Boris Johnson secure an £800,000 loan

items.h: Press Gazette analysis reveals increasing centralisation of local news provision
items.b: Recent analysis from Press Gazette indicates that the top four publishers within the UK now control 88% of the daily print market. This represents a significant shift in ownership from five years ago when the top four owned 76% of the daily news market and a decade ago when they controlled just 50%.
items.why: increasing concentration of local newspaper ownership reduces the plurality of sources through which the public can access information about public affairs.

items.h: Government scraps plan to privatise Channel Four
items.b: Culture secretary Michelle Donelan has announced the government is abandoning plans to privatise Channel Four . Rather than sell the broadcaster, the government has said they will allow it to borrow more money to make more programmes in-house. The decision has been welcomed by We Own It who have campaigned heavily to keep the broadcaster in public ownership ammassing 38,000 signatures behind their petition. However, the Media Reform Coalition have raised concern over the role of the new Media Reform Bill to both dilute the definition of public service broadcasting (PSB) and to reduce PSB oblig…
items.why: the decision preserves public ownership and shapes the obligations of a public-service broadcaster, affecting the plurality and quality of the information environment available to citizens.

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust launches a new Grassroots Movements Fund
items.b: JRCT has recently launched a £1m fund to support grassroots social movements. The fund will use a participatory grant-making process which means grant decisions will be put in the hands of communities affected by the fund. JRCT hope this will put more autonomy into the hands of those working to address inequality. Deadline for applications has now closed.
items.why: the fund creates a new participatory grant-making mechanism that gives affected communities direct decision-making power over resources supporting civic organising.

items.h: Civic Power Fund Community Action Fund closes 26th Feb
items.b: The Community Action Fund has been launched to support grassroots campaigning and community organising in the UK, providing one-off grants between £2,500 and £20,000. All successful applicants will be offered support beyond funding, including the Civic Power Fund Governance Hub and optional, bespoke cohort and capacity building opportunities. Deadline is 26th February 2023.
items.why: the fund creates new resources and capacity-building support that expand grassroots groups' practical ability to campaign and organise in civic life.

items.h: John Preston developing democracy micro-grants project
items.b: Democracy micro-grants aim to provide a small non-repayable grant to individuals and groups to allow them to participate in democratic activity. John held a meeting to kickstart the project last week and they are now looking for a fiscal host organisation. Interested? Contact John Preston .
items.why: the project is developing a new small-grants mechanism intended to enable individuals and groups to take part in democratic activity, expanding practical means of participation.

items.h: Esmée Fairbairn Foundation offers 10% uplift to grant recipients
items.b: The foundation aims to provide support for the long-term change needed and ease pressure on the organisations it supports. The uplift requires minimal reporting and admin, with the foundation using what it learns to inform future support. Find out more.
items.note: This is a grant administration change for existing funded organisations rather than the creation of a new means of democratic participation.

items.h: Following in Jersey’s footsteps, France holds national citizens’ assembly on assisted dying
items.b: Following a consultative process involving a citizens’ jury , Jersey is set to approve assisted dying measures this year. France’s national citizen assembly on assisted dying, organised by constitutional council CESE , has been running since 9th December 2022 and is set to run for 27 working days across four months. More than 25 researchers were invited to observe the proceedings, read the report so far (trans.).
items.why: citizens' assemblies and juries are deliberative decision-making mechanisms, and comparative evidence from France and Jersey bears on how such processes could inform UK collective decision-making.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections and decision making per the framework, even though this example is international.

items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Louise Dunmore and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : democracynetwork@involve.org.uk

Although cancelled due to illness, we’d like to thank everyone who contributed check-ins to last week’s Democracy Meetup shared document. We were joined by Jon Morter — The Progressive Alliance, Kathie Conn — Extinction Rebellion UK, Rebecca Deegan — I Have A Voice, Myfanwy Nixon — mySociety, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation and Rosie Trevill — Elect Her.

items.h: Significant defeats for the government on the Public Order Bill as Lords defend public protest
items.b: Peers voted 254 to 240 against legislation that would have allowed the police to preemptively shut down public processions and public assemblies. Liberty arecelebrating two significant wins; that suspicionless stop and search legislation has been removed as well as the ability of police to issue Serious Disruption Prevention Orders (SDPOs) without a prior conviction. SDPOs are effectively ‘protest-banning orders’ that can be imposed on individuals who have participated in at least two protests within five years, whether or not they have been convicted of a protest-related crime. The win in the…
items.why: the ability of citizens to protest and assemble without pre-emptive police restriction is a core civil liberty underpinning democratic contestation
items.note: Protest legislation classified under rights/civic space per boundary rule on policing and legal restriction of assembly.
links: briefing on the Public Order Bill from Liberty

items.h: Minimum Service Bill passes third reading in Commons despite lack of impact assessment
items.b: The ‘anti-strike bill’ , as it has been dubbed by opposition groups and trade unionists, has now moved to the House of Lords after passing its third reading in the Commons on January 30th. However, the government failed to submit an impact assessment to the Regulatory Policy Committee until the 2nd of February, prompting comments from the TUC General Secretary , Paul Nowak, that MPs were ‘voting blind’ on ‘far-reaching new laws’. Public opinion appears largely out of step with the new legislation, with a new report from the Fairness Foundation suggesting that almost three quarters of 2019 Cons…
items.why: restricting the ability of trade unions to strike affects freedom of association, a civic organisation right protected under democratic norms
items.note: Freedom of association for unions is classified under rights/civic space rather than participation.
links: failed to submit an impact assessment
comments from the TUC General Secretary

items.h: Modern Bill of Rights unworkable in current form, according to Constitutional Society report
items.b: Despite the reform of the Human Rights Act considered a key manifesto pledge in 2019, progress has been slow and criticism of the replacement — a modern Bill of Rights — has been widespread. A new report The ‘Modern’ Bill of Rights Bill from Joanna George at The Constitution Society highlights the unworkability of the bill in its current form, suggesting that it would introduce a series of constitutional contradictions and confusions at a time when constitutional coherence is fragile.
items.why: a poorly designed Bill of Rights would create constitutional incoherence and weaken the predictable legal enforcement of individual rights against the state
items.note: Treated as rule of law given focus on constitutional workability rather than a specific rights restriction.

items.h: Shock at resignation of Nicola Sturgeon as First Minister of Scotland
items.b: Following in the wake of Jacinda Ardern’s shock resignation last month, FM Nicola Sturgeon this week announced their decision to step down . Frances Scott, Director and Founder of 50:50 Parliament said Sturgeon’s departure ‘ makes a bad situation worse ’, remarking ‘It is sad to see these two female world leaders step down. They have been blazing a trail that others can follow.’
items.why: the orderly transfer of power at the head of a devolved government is part of the machinery by which democratic leadership changes hands
items.note: Classified under elections & decision making per the anchor on orderly constitutional transfer of power, applied to devolved government.

items.h: Notwestminster kicks off this weekend
items.b: Notwestminster is a free event for everyone who has something positive to say about local democracy and anyone who is up for the challenge of making it better. Whilst the fun begins this evening, the main event is this Saturday in Huddersfield. Grab your last minute tickets here!
items.note: Event listing, not a reported change to democratic practice.

items.h: Constitution Society to host event on the future of UK democracy
items.b: On Friday 24th of March, The Constitution Society will host an event in Putney, London, on the site of the famous 1647 Putney Debates , alongside academics and constitutional experts to discuss the crisis facing UK democracy. Panels throughout the day will focus on themes including devolution, electoral reform and the constitutional crisis. Tickets are free, but it is worth booking in advance for this one!
items.note: Event listing/announcement, sector logistics.

items.h: mySociety recruiting new Chair of Trustees, celebrate their 20th anniversary!
items.b: Myf Nixon and the team at mySociety are on the lookout for a new Chair of Trustees — they’re asking everyone to please spread the word to cast the net far and wide — see more details here . Meanwhile, last week saw mySociety turn 20! Read Louise Crow’s anniversary blog charting their journey since 2003. As TicTec Labs draws to a close, join the mySociety team for a special event to unpack the learnings and outputs from the 18 month programme.
items.note: Organisational admin (trustee recruitment, anniversary), not a change to democratic participation.
links: join the mySociety team for a special event

items.h: Elect Her kickstart their candidate support programme Equip Her with range of new events and workshops
items.b: Equip Her is a four month programme of support for women in our community who are preparing to be candidates in upcoming elections, taking place in 2023 and 2024. From now until the local elections Elect Her are creating spaces for women to access free resources, advice and community — so if you, or someone you know, are putting themselves forward as a candidate this election, get in touch . But that’s not all, Elect Her are offering a range of new events from My Political Future , designed for women who want to become leaders in their community, but aren’t sure where to start — to the Disable…
items.why: this matters democratically because it addresses candidate access and the representativeness of elected institutions by helping women overcome barriers to standing for office.
items.note: Candidate support programmes are filed under elections/candidate access rather than general participation.

items.h: People’s Jury in Blackburn launch climate recommendations
items.b: Community members in Blackburn and Darwen met for 30 hours during September and December 2022 to debate the question; What do we need to do in our homes, in business and our local area to respond to the climate change crisis? The process was facilitated by Shared Future CIC with the group providing recommendations to the local council on how to address the issue. Later this year Shared Future will be hosting a citizen’s assembly in Wandsworth to discuss how to tackle air pollution, and in Bude they will be running community engagement programmes on the climate flooding threat .
items.why: this matters democratically because a citizens' jury is a deliberative decision-making process feeding directly into local council policy.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework anchors.
links: met for 30 hours during September and December 2022
community engagement programmes on the climate flooding threat

items.h: Civic Power Fund is hiring for two new positions
items.b: Civic Power Fund is on the hunt for a Community Power Builder based in Greater Manchester who will lead their funding and organising across the region. They are also looking for an Operations Officer who can be based anywhere in the UK and will help streamline their admin and operations. The deadline for both roles is the 3rd of March.
items.note: Job advert; organisational hiring news does not itself change democratic participation.

items.h: The Politics Project flesh out General Election support
items.b: Following on from their 25th January General Election Strategy Day, Hattie Andrews and the team at The Politics Project have laid out their plan to support plans over the next year to prepare the GE. This involves support through convening and signposting, a monthly email round up of activities and opportunities, hosting online and physical meetups, developing a directory of people, organisations and projects — as well as a new shared hub for offers, needs and opportunities. If you’d like to know more, email Hattie .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new convening infrastructure (a hub, directory and meetups) to help civil society organise and participate around the general election.

items.h: Candid are reaching out to others working on election candidate datasets
items.b: Joe and the team at Candid are a new project working to build a more complete picture of election candidates. Find out more about them and get in touch .
items.why: this matters democratically because compiling comprehensive candidate data supports transparency and understanding of who stands for election.
items.note: Thin description of a nascent project; classified by its stated purpose of building candidate information.

items.h: Tech for Good Organisers host March 2023 Retreat
items.b: Are you involved in civic tech? Do you organise a tech for good project? Would you like to? Register for the Tech for Good Organisers 2023 Retreat this March 24th in London.
items.note: Sector networking event for practitioners rather than a resource created for public participation.

items.h: I Have A Voice running day of World Cafes’ and social action in Leeds and London, February 25th
items.b: Rebecca Deegan and the team at I Have A Voice are running two events, at the same time, in both Leeds and London — joined together via videolink, involving speakers Hilary Benn MP, Cllr Barry Anderson, Cllr Ria Patel and artivist Simone Yasmin . Find out more for Leeds and London .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a structured space for citizens to engage directly with elected representatives and take part in civic dialogue and action.

items.h: Twitter kills off backend service causing issues for Democracy Club and others
items.b: The change means that services such as Democracy Club will no longer be able to monitor Twitter as easily for spotting such changes as councillors and elected representatives changing their Twitter handles over time.
items.why: This matters democratically because losing a tool that tracks elected officials' public communications reduces the means available to monitor and hold representatives accountable.
items.note: Treated as an information-environment/accountability tooling story rather than mere sector logistics.

items.h: MP Watch set to publish report on generational political change
items.b: MP Watch is a campaign working to build a network of constituency groups to hold MPs accountable on their net zero commitments, notable for their work around Steve Baker MP among others. The new report provides an analysis of the changing demographics of UK constituencies, including detailed information on the expected dates a range of constituency areas become ‘majority millennial’. The report sets the stage for their next phase of work, maximising young voter engagement in priority areas.
items.why: This matters democratically because efforts to analyse and boost young voter engagement bear directly on electoral turnout and the representativeness of the electorate.
items.note: Turnout-focused campaigning is filed under elections per the standing rule.
links: notable for their work around Steve Baker MP

items.h: Women’s Equality Party are hiring for multiple positions
items.b: WEP are campaigning for a society in which there is equal representation in politics, business and everyday life. If you share that vision and want to get involved then check out some of these exciting news roles they’re hiring for; Campaigns Coordinator , Political Advisor , Finance and Membership Officer. Deadline for all three roles is February 20th.

items.h: Fito are providing resources and support to those building networks around social impact
items.b: Are you convening groups and networks around social change in the UK? Fito are a new project working to develop and support a network of networkers & convenors . Would you like to know more?
items.note: Generic social-impact networking support, not specifically tied to democratic participation mechanisms.

items.h: Massive increase in tactical voting Facebook Groups
items.b: Jon Morter and Josh Russell have reportedly overseen the growth of more than 200 local Facebook Groups focused on promoting tactical voting across the UK. Reach out to Jon for more info .
items.why: This matters democratically because a large-scale rise in organised tactical voting coordination reflects mobilisation aimed at shaping electoral turnout and outcomes.
items.note: Tactical voting mobilisation is filed under elections as it concerns electoral participation and outcomes.
links: Reach out to Jon for more info

items.h: Join 50:50 in Parliament to celebrate International Women’s Day
items.b: This year’s APPG Women in Parliament event is being hosted by Maria Miller MP and 50:50 . Following the success of previous years, Maria will host a panel of women talking openly about their experiences of standing for election and holding office, alongside senior guest speakers. The event is happening on the 1st of March, 5pm-7pm. Get in touch to find out more .
items.note: Event listing, not a reported change.
links: Get in touch to find out more

items.h: Constitution Society hiring Research Fellow
items.b: The Research Fellow will join The Constitution Society on a fixed-term 4-month contract and will research and write a paper on a contemporary UK constitutional issue of their choosing. The job is based in London and there is a salary of £2,000 pcm.

items.h: Power to Change is hiring a Democratic Ownership Manager
items.b: Power to Change is working to support greater community power and ownership across England through community business. The new Democratic Ownership Manager will work with partners who are campaigning for and delivering greater democratic ownership across the country. They are also looking for a Local and Regional Officer to join the policy and comms team. Both positions have a deadline of the 28th of Feb.
items.note: Job advertisement, organisational admin.

items.h: New Local and TPXimpact share findings from new community engagement project
items.b: The project is being organised by the Local Government Association (LGA) in partnership with New Local and TPXimpact to find and celebrate examples of innovative community engagement by councils with groups who are disadvantaged or underrepresented in local decision-making. A new blog from Polly Lord at New Local and Tom Chigbo from TPXimpact highlights some of the themes that emerged from a series of workshops they conducted as part of the wider LGA project.
items.note: Sector blog sharing workshop themes rather than a new participation mechanism or tool.

items.h: Has the pandemic impacted political participation? The Practical Democracy Podcast investigates
items.b: The latest episode of the Practical Democracy Podcast takes a closer look at how the pandemic has impacted political engagement, discussing how the pandemic has impacted public trust in the government and other political behaviour.
items.note: A podcast discussing the topic is content, not itself a democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: We’re Right Here responds to Gordon Brown’s report, reasserts need for Community Power Act
items.b: We’re Right Here welcomed Brown’s recent report , publishing a new briefing in response which sets out how Labour can implement a policy to support and build community power. WRH argue a Community Power Act will rebalance the scales of where power lies across the UK, establishing new community rights and bringing local people into decision-making. They are also looking for a Campaign Coordinator to join them on a 0.5 FTE contract to help build public support for the act. The deadline for the role is the 19th of February, apply now .
items.why: it advocates for a Community Power Act that would redistribute decision-making power and access to communities, affecting the practical conditions for civic participation.
items.note: Community power proposals sit close to local decision-making structures but the emphasis here is on equal access to power for communities.

items.h: Parliamentary Digital Service working to make it easier for people to find and use parliamentary procedural data
items.b: Chris Caden, User Researcher at Parliamentary Digital Service , is currently leading on a project to better understand what researchers, journalists, community groups and members of the public need from parliamentary data. To this end, they’re planning research interviews over the next two months to understand what these different groups need from openly published parliamentary data and what their current frustrations are from accessing that data. If you’d like to help Chris and the PDS team, pop them an email .
items.why: improving public and journalistic access to parliamentary procedural data affects whether people can obtain meaningful information about how public power is exercised.
items.note: Parliamentary data access sits at the boundary of accountability and public information; classified as information because the focus is on researcher/public access rather than institutional answerability.

items.h: Scottish Parliament’s Citizens’ Panel on Participation consultation ends
items.b: As part of the Scottish Parliament’s development of its capacity to deliver deliberative engagement over recent years, Holyrood’s Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee have been running an inquiry into public participation. As part of that process, a Citizens’ Panel on Participation was commissioned and has since published their report detailing 17 recommendations. An 8-week consultation ran until earlier this week, hosted on the Scottish Parliament’s Your Priorities platform . However, Researcher at Demos , Sophia Knight, still recommends checking out the portal which explores …
items.why: a citizens' panel on participation feeds recommendations into how the Scottish Parliament structures deliberative and participatory decision-making mechanisms.
items.note: Citizens' panels and deliberative consultations are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee

items.h: Equality and Human Rights Commission concludes monitoring of the Labour Party
items.b: The EHRC has now formally concluded their monitoring of the Labour Party which began in 2020 following accusations that anti-semitism was rife within the party. EHRC chief executive Marcial Boo said the EHRC were now ‘satisfied’ that Labour had ‘implemented the necessary actions to improve its complaints, recruitment, training and other procedures to the legal standards required’.
items.why: formal equality-body oversight of a political party's handling of discrimination complaints bears on equal protection and non-discrimination as democratic rights.
items.note: Could also be read as party standards/accountability, but the substantive issue is discrimination and equal treatment.
links: Marcial Boo said the EHRC were now ‘satisfied’

items.h: Big Brother Watch report reveals Government use of military brigade to monitor the public
items.b: A new report from Big Brother Watch reveals that UK government departments have been monitoring government critics online under the claim that they are tackling misinformation. The report includes findings with a whistleblower from the 77th brigade of the army claiming the government has been using the army to track citizens’ speech online, despite claiming the brigades were strictly directed overseas.
items.why: covert military monitoring of citizens' online speech implicates surveillance, privacy and the government invoking new threats to curb civil liberties.
items.note: Also touches government accountability given use of military/security apparatus domestically, contrary to stated purpose.

items.h: Jeremy Corbyn attacks decision to stop him from standing as Labour MP
items.b: Former Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn has said the decision from Keir Starmer to prevent them from standing as a Labour MP at the next general election is a ‘flagrant attack on the democratic rights of Islington North Labour Party members’ . Corbyn, who has been an MP in the area for 40 years, said it was up to party members, not party leaders, to decide who should represent them.
items.why: a party leadership decision to block a sitting MP from standing bears on candidate access and internal party democracy, which shapes political competition.
links: ‘flagrant attack on the democratic rights of Islington North Labour Party members’

items.h: Labour holds onto West Lancashire in byelection win
items.b: Labour has retained the seat of West Lancashire after Ashley Dalton won the local byelection on Thursday 9th of Feb. A 10% voter swing saw Dalton win a majority of 14,068 votes, with the Conservative candidate, Mike Prendergast, coming second with 5,742 votes. In their victory speech, Dalton said the win was a sign that the public has lost confidence in the Tory government.
items.why: it reports the outcome of a competitive election that determines who holds a parliamentary seat.
links: retained the seat of West Lancashire

items.h: Sturgeon’s resignation throws SNP independence strategy into disarray
items.b: SNP plans for a de-facto independence referendum appeared to be stalling this week after FM Nicola Sturgeon announced plans to step down as leader. Scottish Labour expect electoral benefits from the downfall of the highly popular former SNP leader. Check out this explainer from The Ferret on what happens in the near future now that Sturgeon has resigned.
items.why: it affects the prospects for a future independence referendum, a form of direct popular decision-making machinery.
items.note: Referendum strategy is filed under elections/decision-making machinery rather than participation.

items.h: Stormont election delayed by a year
items.b: As the ongoing stalemate continues, the UK Government is due to introduce legislation that will push the timetable for an election back to 18 January 2024.
items.why: it delays the timetable for elections to the devolved Northern Ireland Assembly, affecting when voters can choose representatives.

items.h: Demos lambasts Treasury moves to restrict capital spending on Levelling Up programme
items.b: With the anniversary of the Levelling Up White Paper this month, the Treasury announced it is restricting the ability of the Dept for Levelling Up to make decisions on capital spending without prior Treasury agreement. Demos has criticised the move saying the introduction of more bureaucracy on devolution means the country is being pushed further away from the ambition of localising power.
items.why: it concerns whether devolved and local structures retain real decision-making power over spending or are recentralised to Treasury control.
items.note: Story concerns the structure/powers of devolved decision-making, filed under elections & decision making per boundary rule.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation identify need for a community organiser post for independent journalism
items.b: Joe Mitchell and the Public Interest News Foundation team are beginning an analysis of their recent survey responses from across the indie news publisher sector, and it’s becoming apparent the sector would benefit from a community organiser, says Joe. Things to look out for later this year from the indie media sector: this new community organiser post, another Independent News Forum ( see what happened last October ) and possibly a co-created PR campaign for indie news .
items.note: This is an internal sector needs-assessment, not a launched resource or capacity-building initiative.
links: co-created PR campaign for indie news

items.h: Anti-SLAAPs bill introduced to parliament to protect investigative journalists
items.b: Last month Conservative MP Bob Seely introduced a private members bill that would allow the courts in England and Wales to prevent wealthy figures from using SLAPPs to silence investigative journalists , campaigners and watchdogs. Seely said the new bill would stop ‘unethical’ British law firms from working on behalf of oligarchs and politicians who attempt to ‘spy, snoop, smear and sue’ their critics. The bill will put additional pressure on the government to make good on their promise made in July 2022 that they would introduce legislation to tackle the use of SLAPPs. So far the government h…
items.why: it addresses legal mechanisms (SLAPPs) used to suppress investigative journalism and public-interest reporting on power.
links: prevent wealthy figures from using SLAPPs to silence investigative journalists

items.h: Lords add clause to Public Order Bill to protect journalists covering protests
items.b: A new clause has been added to the Public Order Bill by members of the House of Lords to ensure the police can’t prevent someone from observing or reporting on a protest. The clause was voted in with a 91 vote majority (283 to 192) and comes following the verdict from an independent review that the arrest of journalists at the Just Stop Oil protests in November 2022 may have constituted ‘unlawful interference’.
items.why: it protects journalists' ability to observe and report on protests, safeguarding public access to information about state-citizen confrontations.
items.note: Journalists' reporting rights filed under information & debate; protest policing context noted as secondary.
links: new clause has been added to the Public Order Bill

items.h: IMPRESS launch new standards code
items.b: IMPRESS has just launched a new standards code to meet the changing face of modern journalism. The new code has guidance on tackling misinformation in the media, discrimination in news reporting, the use of AI, child protection measures, and more.
items.why: it sets new standards governing press conduct, misinformation and discrimination in journalism, shaping the quality of the public information environment.

items.h: HackedOff report celebrates a decade of change in the UK media
items.b: A new report from HackedOff , 10 Years of Press Freedom , looks at the changes across the UK media since the 2011 Leveson Report which stressed the need for the media to become more accountable and transparent. According to the report, 186 publications are now regulated by IMPRESS — 67% of those publications are local or hyper-local organisations which now serve communities where larger publishers have pulled out.
items.why: it reports on the state of press regulation and plurality including local journalism coverage, which shapes the public information environment for democratic debate.

items.h: New Voter ID coalition funded by Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust for four months ahead of local elections
items.b: Under the Democracy Defence Coalition banner, Unlock Democracy, Fair Vote UK, Open Britain and Electoral Reform Society, have been awarded funding for a four month campaign to make the case for dropping voter ID, raising public awareness of voter ID requirements, as well as work to persuade local and central government to do more to make voters aware of the new requirements. Congrats!
items.why: the coalition campaigns on voter ID rules that affect people's practical ability to vote in elections.

items.h: Civic Power Fund Community Action Fund still open for one more week
items.b: The Community Action Fund has been launched to support grassroots campaigning and community organising in the UK, providing one-off grants between £2,500 and £20,000. All successful applicants will be offered support beyond funding, including the Civic Power Fund Governance Hub and optional, bespoke cohort and capacity building opportunities. Deadline is 26th February 2023.
items.why: the fund creates new resources and capacity-building support for grassroots campaigning and community organising, expanding means of civic participation.
