items.h: Community Powerhouse Map to launch map of change-makers across the North
items.b: The People’s Powerhouse is in the process of creating a map of organisations, movements and individual projects that are working towards community change across the North of England. If you’re running a project of this nature, add yourself to the map to connect with other important work happening across the region.
items.why: this creates a new tool connecting community change-makers, expanding the practical means for civic organisation and collaboration.
items.note: Sector capacity-building tool treated as participation under the framework's explicit rule.

items.h: Elect Her looking to fundraise to provide grants to women standing for office
items.b: Elect Her do amazing work getting women into elected office. They have already raised enough funds to give 12 women grants to help them run in the May local elections. Now they are looking for £6,000 more to help give grants to a further 24 women from marginalised backgrounds running in the May elections. If you know anyone who may be able to help — please contact hannah@elect-her.org.uk .
items.note: This is a fundraising ask/logistics item rather than a report of a new participation mechanism being created.

items.h: Independent watchdog criticises strike legislation as ‘not fit for purpose’
items.b: The Regulatory Policy Committee (RPC) , the government’s independent watchdog, has criticised the pending anti-strike laws as ‘not fit for purpose’ in a new assessment and issued the legislation a ‘red rating’. The committee said the Government has failed to follow its own policy for the timely submission of an impact assessment for scrutiny. The bill is currently under examination in the House of Lords.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether government follows its own scrutiny procedures (impact assessments) when legislating, a check on executive power.

items.h: European trade unions lambast anti-strike law
items.b: A number of unions from across the EU have criticised the strike legislation , suggesting it will ‘only drag the UK further away from democratic norms, risk violating international law, and tarnish its international reputation.’
items.why: this matters democratically because the legislation restricts trade unions' freedom of association and ability to strike.
items.note: Criticism of union rights restrictions falls under freedom of association for civic/labour organisations.
links: unions from across the EU have criticised the strike legislation

items.h: Public Order Bill enters ping pong following major defeats in the Lords
items.b: The Public Order Bill had its third reading in the House of Lords on the 21st of February with peers inflicting eight defeats on the government’s flagship anti-protest legislation. Lauren Nicolls, Researcher at the House of Commons Library, has written a briefing detailing the passage of the bill through the Lords and the key changes made since the bill was last in the Commons. The bill now enters parliamentary ping-pong where both houses will wrangle over the final details of the legislation. Expect the legislation to return to the Commons in early March.
items.why: this matters democratically because the bill restricts the legal space for protest and assembly, a core civil liberty for contesting public power.
items.note: Protest legislation is classified under rights per the boundary rule since the story concerns legal restriction, with parliamentary scrutiny as a secondary element.

items.h: National Security Bill enters report stage
items.b: This Wednesday 1st March, the National Security Bill entered report stage, reports Bond . Spotlight on Corruption defeated the government on an amendment to the bill requiring political parties to identify donations from foreign powers. Fears remain over the potential of the bill to limit the ability of the press to expose abuses of power by intelligence agencies or government failures. Government also expected to make some major concessions on the Foreign Registration Scheme .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns safeguards against undue foreign influence over political parties and government, and press ability to scrutinise intelligence agencies.
items.note: Multiple mechanisms (foreign donations, press freedom, foreign influence) touch several beats; foreign influence on government functions is primary.
links: requiring political parties to identify donations
limit the ability of the press

items.h: Immigration Bill delayed
items.b: The new Immigration Bill (unpublished) will significantly restrict asylum, leading to more people being deported — and may allow human rights abuse without recourse, reports Liberty. The government plans to push this bill as hard as it can, until it gets pushed back and likely make it an election issue next year, they say. Whilst the bill was supposed to be published a fortnight ago — it wasn’t. Conservative backbenchers and activists are frustrated over the delay .
items.why: this matters democratically because the bill may remove legal recourse for those subject to state action, undermining due process and access to justice.
items.note: Focus on removal of legal recourse places this under rule of law rather than rights as such.

items.h: Online Safety Bill not likely to progress until after Easter
items.b: Kyle Taylor of Fair Vote UK reports that the Online Safety Bill is unlikely to progress until after Easter — in other news, Kyle will be back in London for a brief hiatus from Tokyo this month.
items.note: Purely a scheduling note on a bill with no substantive content on its democratic mechanism.

items.h: Democracy Coworking Day returns next month at Demos, April 14th
items.b: Spend a day working alongside fellow organisations working on UK democratic reform at Demos’ offices on Whitehall. As usual, feel free to drop in at any part of the day, for all of it or just part of it — the more the merrier. We’ll be putting on tea & coffee, snacks and refreshments, including croissants and pastries for the early birds. Register now .

items.h: Democracy Drinks in London, March 22nd
items.b: This month, join Unlock Democracy and the UK Democracy Network for this month’s London democracy drinks at the Electoral Reform Society’s offices in Southwark. Catch up on the latest democracy gossip and meet new faces — register on Eventbrite .

items.h: Democracy Classroom launch #ElectionCountdown 2023
items.b: Launched this Monday, #ElectionCountdown is a wide-ranging programme to support young people navigate the busy election period and keep up to date with candidates and manifestoes, follow election news and get important knowhow on voter registration and voter ID. If you or your organisation would like to receive tailored learning resources, template emails, blogs and posters with information for young people — you can sign up here for the weekly newsletter.
items.why: it creates a new resource programme helping young people register to vote, meet voter ID requirements and follow election information, directly affecting electoral participation mechanics.
items.note: Voter registration and ID knowhow falls under elections per the turnout/registration rule, even though delivered as a youth engagement programme.

items.h: APPG event on race, elections and political participation this month
items.b: The APPG on Race and Community will host the upcoming event on the 20th March in Parliament. The event chaired by Labour MP Clive Lewis and SNP MP Kirsten Oswald will explore the democratic deficit faced by Black and minority ethnic groups. Sign up here .
items.note: An event announcement/sign-up notice rather than a report of a substantive change, despite touching on representation of minority groups.

items.h: V-Dem Institute’s 2023 report on democratisation launches
items.b: Every year V-Dem publish their comprehensive analysis on the trends for democracy and autocracy across the world. This year’s topline follows that more than 72% of the world’s population are now living under autocracies. You can watch the launch and read the new report Defiance in the Face of Autocratization .
items.note: A global report launch announcement without specific UK-focused analysis or mechanism.

items.h: Imagine! Belfast festival returns this month
items.b: Peter O’Neill is currently organising over 130 events for the Imagine! Belfast festival of politics and ideas between the 20th and 26th March. Guest speakers include Noam Chomsky, Francis Fukuyama, Shon Faye, George Monbiot and more. 24th March will be a special ‘ Democracy Day ’ strand, with events run by Involve , 50:50 NI , Northern Ireland Open Government Network and many more.

items.h: Titus Alexander welcoming contributions for a special issue of Frontiers in Political Science
items.b: Hot on the heels of Titus’ recent blog post for the European Consortium of Political Research , they are welcoming article contributions on the topic of Learning for Democracy , for the journal of Frontiers in Political Science . Get in touch with Titus .

items.h: NEON looking for Executive Director to cover parental leave
items.b: New Economy Organisers Network are hiring for a new Executive Director to cover for new-parent leave. The four-day-working-week role has a rolling application deadline and is also open to a job-share. The role extends to between 12–15 months. Apply now .

items.h: Constitution Society hiring new Research Fellow
items.b: The Constitution Society are looking out for a new Research Fellow for four months to write a paper on a major contemporary UK constitutional issue of their choosing. Applications close 31st March, apply now .

items.h: Liberty hiring Interim Director to cover maternity leave
items.b: The role at Liberty will last for 10–12 months, with applications closing on the 10th March. Apply here .

items.h: Refugee Action is looking for a new Head of Campaigns
items.b: The new Head of Campaigns will be responsible for developing and leading Refugee Action ’s campaigning strategy and will play an active role on the senior leadership team. Note — applications for this role are only open to people who identify as having lived experience of forced displacement due to war, invasion, persecution or human rights abuses. Deadline for applications is Sunday 5th of March so apply fast!

items.h: Institute for Welsh Affairs is looking for new board members
items.b: The Trustees of the Institute of Welsh Affairs (IWA) are looking for four new members for their Board. If you are interested in having an informal discussion about what the role entails, get in touch with Auriol Miller , IWA Director, to arrange a chat. The deadline to apply is 9am on Friday 17 March 2023.
links: get in touch with Auriol Miller

items.h: The Institute for Government is looking for a Communications Intern
items.b: The Communications Intern will join the Institute for Government on a year-long contract starting in September 2023. This is a salaried role and will provide a career-starter with a great chance to help promote the work of IfG to a wide audience.

items.h: APPG on Political Literacy AGM, 13th March
items.b: The All Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political Literacy aims to ensure all young people are politically literate by the time they finish their secondary education. On 13th March, Shout Out UK (SOUK) will be hosting the Annual General Meeting for the APPG on Political Literacy in Parliament. They will be presenting their ideas and thoughts to the APPG members on youth engagement and the ways in which the voices of young people can be used to inform policy and strengthen political literacy. Register now .
items.why: it concerns a programme aimed at building young people's political literacy and engagement, expanding the means by which they can take part in democratic life.
items.note: Event about political literacy capacity-building counts as participation under the sector capacity-building rule.
links: All Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political Literacy

items.h: Compassion in Politics to host discussion on honesty in politics
items.b: On the 7th of March, Compassion in Politics will host a discussion on how we can restore honesty in politics to safeguard the future of our already fragile democracy, featuring speakers including Lord Puttnam, Gina Miller, Jennifer Nadel, and Debbie Abrahams MP. Find out more .
items.note: A discussion event about honesty in politics is an event listing, not itself a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: Stir to Action to host ‘Demanding Democracy’ event in May
items.b: Stir to Action are hosting a lecture by Carne Ross on how we can revamp democracy to turn it into something ready to meet the challenges in the twenty first century. The event is taking place in May and is free to attend .
items.note: Event listing/lecture announcement, not a democracy story in itself.

items.h: International conference on democracy, political and civic participation to take place in June
items.b: The conference will bring together leading academics, researchers and industry leaders to discuss and share their knowledge on all things related to democracy, political and civic participation. The conference is being organised by The World Academy of Science, Engineering and Technology and will take place in London, June 22–23. There is also a call for papers on a range of democracy-related topics which will be presented at the conference.
items.note: Conference/event listing and call for papers, sector logistics.
links: The World Academy of Science, Engineering and Technology

items.h: New report explores the challenges and possibilities of community empowerment
items.b: Winning with Communities, new report from Unlock Democracy and Compass suggests a framework for greater community empowerment must revolve around four key principles; deepening democracy, supporting independent community action, underpinning social solidarity, and supporting community innovation and autonomy. Would you like to know more?
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes a framework to strengthen community-level participation, autonomy and resourcing for civic action.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource rather than mere organisational news.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: mySociety publish new report on fragmented public data
items.b: As part of a joint project between mySociety and the Centre for Public Data , they have written a set of simple principles on how to get the most out of publishing public data and a new report on the value of better data publication , including a set of minimum publishing standards to ensure value and impact.
items.note: Concerns data publication standards as transparency-for-its-own-sake, not tied to a specific accountability mechanism or information-environment claim.
links: new report on the value of better data publication

items.h: Former MP Ian Lucas publishes new book on ‘digital gangsters’
items.b: Former UK Member of Parliament Ian Lucas describes in the new book the ways in which so-called digital gangsters work to meddle in politics , polarise conversation and erode democracy. He takes particular aim at how we take democracy in the physical world for granted with certain protections, yet digital spaces are undefended and ill fit for purpose.
items.why: this matters democratically because it addresses how digital manipulation, polarisation and unregulated online spaces can distort political debate and public understanding.
links: new book the ways in which so-called digital gangsters work to meddle in politics

items.h: 25 English councils now back proportional representation, reports Councils for PR
items.b: Last week Sheffield City Council passed a motion in support of proportional representation, making the city the 25th council across England to back PR. William Relton and the team at Councils for PR are working to build momentum for PR across councils in England as a means of broadening political support for the measure. Councils for PR offer a range of support, guides and model motions for those looking to enrol their own council.
items.why: this matters democratically because it tracks growing institutional support for changing the electoral system used to choose representatives.

items.h: Unlock Democracy working on a campaign to promote overseas constituencies
items.b: With the Elections Act 2022 removing the 15-year electoral registration limit that had applied to British citizens who reside abroad, the numbers of eligible voters living abroad has ballooned from 233,000 registered overseas voters at the 2019 general election to as many as 3.5 million eligible voters. Working with New Europeans , Unlock Democracy are now working on promoting overseas constituencies to simply this significant administrative burden and better represent overseas voters. Read the draft Parliamentary Briefing .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns how overseas citizens' suffrage and representation are structured following a change in electoral registration law.

items.h: Votes at 16 manifesto unveiled this week
items.b: The British Youth Council , Body Shop and the APPG for Votes at 16 teamed up this week to present a new manifesto for youth participation. See more .
items.why: this matters democratically because it advocates extending the franchise to 16- and 17-year-olds, directly affecting who can vote.

items.h: How can we create a more gender-balanced democracy? Upcoming 50:50 event will discuss
items.b: 50:50 Parliament has set itself the target of having 100 more women in Parliament by 2030. A panel discussion hosted on 23 March 2023 will explore the progress made so far on female representation in UK politics and what more can be done to achieve a better, more gender-balanced democracy in the future. The event is free and will be held at Queen Mary’s University in London.
items.note: Event listing/notice rather than a reported change or new participation tool.

items.h: Polling for the Byline Times reveals public resentment of money in UK politics and appetite for Lords reform
items.b: Polling for the Byline Times has found a concerning level of discontent with the British political system. Two thirds (66%) of the general public now believe people or organisations with large amounts of money can ‘buy influence’ in UK politics and that political power is gained through the influence of money rather than the democratic wish of voters. Half of voters (48%) said they opposed the ability of Johson to hand out new peerages with a third of voters (31%) saying the House of Lords should be abolished altogether. If you have polling questions you think are newsworthy, get in touch with…
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports public perceptions that money rather than votes determines political power, bearing on corruption and the legitimacy of an unelected chamber's appointment process.
items.note: Covers both perceived corruption/lobbying (accountability) and House of Lords reform (elections & decision making).

items.h: Talkshop suggest changes based on Tuscany public participation policy
items.b: In force between 2008 and 2013, the law introduced a new Regional Participation Authority in Tuscany to institutionalise public participation and consultation into regional and local decision making. Perry Walker at Talkshop suggests the pioneering Tuscan model as a good case study for similar UK local government reform.
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes institutionalising deliberative public participation into local government decision-making structures.
items.note: Deliberative/participatory decision-making mechanisms are classified under elections & decision making, not participation.

items.h: Brown’s constitutional reforms will not be immediate, says Constitution Unit
items.b: A new blog from Meg Russel, Director at the Constitution Unit at UCL , takes a closer look at Gordon Brown’s ambitious reforms for the House of Lords, suggesting they are unlikely to materialise until at least the second or third year of a Labour government. Drawing on previous UK and international experience with constitutional reform and citing the need for a period of public consultation on the reforms, Russell suggests there are a number of logistical hurdles that will push back the possibility of immediate and concrete reform.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the pace and feasibility of reforming the House of Lords, a check on executive and legislative power.

items.h: Constitution Society event to explore their latest research on public attitudes to democratic reform
items.b: A seminar on Monday 13th March, hosted by The Constitution Society , will examine what the British public thinks about UK democracy and the options for reform. The Constitution Unit’s ‘Democracy in the UK after Brexit’ project has been examining this question in depth and will share some of the findings from their major survey conducted in August/September 2022. Sign up now .
items.note: Event listing inviting sign-up rather than reporting substantive findings.

items.h: Britain could be slipping into an ‘elected dictatorship’, says top parliamentary standards official
items.b: A new paper written by one of parliament’s most senior standards officials, Daniel Greenberg CB, has warned that Britain could be slipping towards a parliamentary dictatorship . The paper, ‘ Parliamentary Democracy and Parliamentary Dictatorship ’ , alludes to a general overreach by ministers and governmental bodies at a time when a number of pieces of legislation that could damage our democracy are passing through parliament. Although the paper was published on Greenberg’s personal website and is intended in a ‘purely private capacity’, Labour MP Clive Lewis said it should be understood as a …
items.why: this matters democratically because it warns that executive and ministerial overreach is weakening parliamentary constraints on government power.
links: Britain could be slipping towards a parliamentary dictatorship

items.h: Labour Party to appoint Sue Gray as LOTO Chief of Staff amid concerns
items.b: Senior civil servant Sue Gray, who oversaw the Partygate report, is pending appointment to Labour’s top team as Keir Starmer’s Chief of Staff. The appointment is subject to approval by the Advisory Committee on Business Appointments (ACOBA) due to Gray’s role in the recent inquiry that arguably brought down then PM Boris Johnson and their knowledge of sensitive information regarding government workings.
items.why: this matters democratically because it involves scrutiny of a senior public appointment with potential conflicts of interest through the ACOBA process.
links: pending appointment to Labour’s top team

items.h: Robert Jenrick admits the government is spying on human rights lawyers
items.b: The Minister of State for Immigration admitted during a debate in parliament on February 20th that the government is ‘monitoring’ human rights lawyers . After suggesting human rights lawyers ‘exploit and abuse our laws’, Jenrick commented, ‘we are monitoring the activities, as it so happens, of a small number of legal practitioners, but it is not appropriate for me to discuss that here.’ Human rights lawyers have reacted with dismay and expressed concern that the rhetoric around the need to monitor ‘lefty lawyers’ could exacerbate an already tense relationship.
items.why: this matters democratically because state surveillance of lawyers representing individuals against government action can chill the civic and professional space needed to challenge public power.
items.note: Surveillance of a professional/legal body sits at the boundary between civic space and access to justice.
links: the government is ‘monitoring’ human rights lawyers

items.h: Transnational Institute publishes new report Digital Power — State of Power 2023
items.b: Transnational Institute’s (TNI) 11th flagship State of Power report exposes the actors, strategies and the implications of the digital power grab — expanded surveillance, weakened workers’ rights and spiralling disinformation — and how movements are forming to bring back popular control.
items.note: General report launch on global digital power dynamics, not a UK-specific democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Labour rumoured to be considering Tendered Ballots in response to voter ID challenge
items.b: Tendered ballots are a special and uncommonly used measure to provide an opportunity to vote for people who allege that they have been subject to an administrative error. Tendered Ballots may be used to defuse potential disputes at a polling station and resume normal voting station operations. The ballots are issued in a form that allows later eligibility verification, as opposed to outright denying the voter to a possible eligible voter. The Labour Party are understood to be consulting lawyers and specialists on the topic.
items.why: a party considering a mechanism to resolve voter ID disputes at polling stations bears directly on electoral administration and access to the vote

items.h: Shout Out UK working with Greater London Authority on communicating changes to voting rights
items.b: Shima Langan, Public Policy Coordinator at Shout Out UK, reports that their work with the Greater London Authority on improving public awareness of the changes implemented through the 2022 Elections Act continues. The campaign is closely coordinated with the Electoral Commission’s own nation-wide voter awareness campaign in the run up to the local elections. With only a fraction of those requiring voter ID signed up in London, the campaign will focus on the acceptable forms of photo ID and how to apply for voter ID.
items.why: public awareness campaigns about new voter ID requirements affect whether eligible voters can actually cast their vote
items.note: Voter ID awareness campaigns are filed under elections per the turnout rule.
links: Electoral Commission’s own nation-wide voter awareness campaign

items.h: Local Government Association issues warning over voter ID concerns
items.b: With just two months to go until polling day, the Local Government Association (LGA) has issued a warning regarding concerns that the requirements to vote are too strict with too little effort spent on informing voters that the rules have changed. Conservative councillor and chairman of the LGA, James Jamieson remarked ‘Raising public awareness of these new requirements is crucial, and we remain concerned about the potential for electoral staff to be overwhelmed with enquiries and voter authority certificate applications when polling cards go out’.
items.why: warnings about voters being unprepared for new ID rules bear on whether eligible citizens can exercise their vote at the ballot box

items.h: Democracy Defence Coalition reconvenes ahead of the local elections, plans public engagement campaign
items.b: This week marked the first meeting of the Democracy Defence Coalition (DDC) since mothballing the project in the wake of the passage of the Elections Act last year. Reviving the effort, earlier this month the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust funded Unlock Democracy through a joint funding bid with other coalition partners with the aim of improving public awareness of the new changes to voting requirements. The group plans to use the new funding to hire a media partner to broaden public engagement on the issue beyond the democracy sector bubble. Get in touch with Matt Gallagher from Fair Vote to ge…
items.why: a funded campaign to raise public awareness of new voter ID rules directly affects turnout and access to voting
items.note: Turnout-related awareness campaigns are always filed under elections per the settled rule.
links: Get in touch with Matt Gallagher

items.h: Labour unlikely to repeal voter ID, sources say
items.b: Campaigners working on the issue in the sector have suggested that whilst unlikely that Labour will repeal voter ID in government, due to the head of steam the current government has built up around the topic — it is more likely they will reduce photo requirements and improve validation systems.
items.why: whether a major party will retain, reform or repeal voter ID rules shapes the accessibility of the franchise

items.h: New Electoral Commission guidance on accessibility at elections
items.b: Martyn Harris, Head of Elections at North Warks Borough Council, highlights the new guidance on accessibility from the Electoral Commission for the upcoming elections. The guidance provides key information for Returning Officers and their staff to help remove some of the barriers and challenges disabled people face when voting at polling stations. Check the guidance here .
items.why: new accessibility guidance for disabled voters affects the practical ability of citizens to exercise their franchise

items.h: Voter ID to cost up to £180 million this decade, says Electoral Reform Society
items.b: Electoral Reform Society has undertaken an analysis of the expected costs of the new controversial reforms, totalling some £180 million over the decade . It has been suggested that the funds would be better used to increase voter turnout.
items.why: the cost and resourcing of voter ID implementation bears on the administration and accessibility of elections

items.h: Calls on the government to postpone voter ID legislation increase as just 1% of voters without ID have signed up
items.b: As of this week just 24,500 voter IDs have been requested , marking just 1% of voters without ID. As a result the Labour Party claimed the government ‘ risked widespread disenfranchisement ’, with Lib Dem MP Helen Morgan remarking voter ID as a ‘thinly-veiled attempt to make it far more difficult for people to vote’. Furthermore, polling for the Byline Times suggests that just 52% of voters under the age of 40 are aware of the need to own a valid form of Voter ID, with that percentage rising to 63% amongst 18–24 year olds. For more info on the upcoming changes, check out this explainer from op…
items.why: low uptake of voter ID undermines universal and equal access to voting, risking disenfranchisement of eligible electors.

items.h: Hancock’s leaked messages further reveal government’s close relationship with the press during pandemic
items.b: Leaked WhatsApp messages between Matt Hancock and George Osborne, then editor of the Evening Standard, reveal further details of the intimate relationship between the government and established press during the pandemic.
items.why: leaked messages reveal an unusually close relationship between government ministers and press owners, raising questions about undue private influence over government communications and accountability.
items.note: Classified as accountability because the story centres on improper closeness between government and a private actor, not on the media environment itself.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch report on co-creational news models
items.b: A new report from PINF ’s Executive Director Jonathan Heawood and leading philosophy professor Fabienne Peter of Warwick University looks at the possibilities of creating a new model for the media with a greater commitment to public participation and social inclusivity. The report outlines what they believe to be a healthy democratic culture and how a news media governed by principles of accuracy and participation could be integral to upholding those values. On the 9th of March PINF is hosting a Zoom launch to discuss the project and anyone interested is welcome to join.
items.note: A research report and launch event rather than a new means of public participation being created.
links: PINF is hosting a Zoom launch

items.h: Sounddelivery programme is back this year and aims to diversify voices in the media
items.b: The Sounddelivery training programme makes a return in 2023 for its third year. The eight month programme aims to diversify voices in the media to make it more representative of society. Sounddelivery are looking for 14 new participants who will be united in using their lived experience to create a positive change in and for their communities. Applications close 24th of March.
items.why: a new training programme aims to diversify who gets to speak in the media, broadening the plurality of voices in public debate.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation in the media landscape.
links: Sounddelivery are looking for 14 new participants

items.h: Catalyst commissioning research on innovation and learning in distributed professional networks
items.b: Commissioned by Catalyst’s Collaborative Network Circle, the successful applicant will focus on surfacing and reviewing best practice and innovative approaches to distributed networks. The budget totals £3,000 with a rolling deadline, find out more .

items.h: Association Civic Tech Europe is fighting for recognition of Europe’s civic tech sector
items.b: Adrian Duguet, founder of Brussels-based Associate of Civic Tech Europe is working to bring together European civic tech professionals to promote the sector and raise awareness of civic tech at an EU level. They have so far brought together more than 20 partners, heads of networks and organisations. Adrian’s has an eye on the upcoming 2024 European elections as a big opportunity for European civic tech.
items.note: Focuses on an organisation building sector recognition rather than a mechanism affecting UK democratic participation.

items.h: James Moulding takes a moment to share his thoughts on why building stronger connections between organisations and individuals working on democracy is crucial to facing down the serious threats faced by democracy in the UK.
items.b: Democracy in the UK in 2023 is under assault. Whether by a dramatic attempt at curtailing judicial review, skewering of the independence of the Electoral Commission, decades of hard won gains on fair votes rolled back, an Online Safety Bill threatening free speech , or through new laws to crack down on protest and undermine the social contract. There are more than 700 organisations across the UK working against this to build a stronger and fairer democracy, but their work is too often poorly coordinated. Many individual organisations are unaware of research, funding, talent, or access that the…
items.why: it describes the creation of a new coordinating network intended to strengthen the capacity of civil society organisations working on democracy, which is a form of civic infrastructure-building.
items.note: Sector capacity-building (a new network) counts as participation even though the piece also references other beats' topics in passing.

items.b: “Relationships move at the speed of trust, and social change moves at the speed of relationships” - Jennifer Bailey
items.note: A standalone quote, not a substantive claim about democratic mechanisms.

items.b: At its core, a change-generating network’s impact will be determined by the strength and proliferation of relationships between its constituent members — or its ecosystem. This means that we work to create and develop opportunities and spaces for individuals to reach out across divides, collaborate, share information — and fundamentally, build trust in each other, empathy with each other’s viewpoints and perspectives, and a familiarity with the topics and touchpoints other organisations might be working around.
items.why: it describes deliberate efforts to build relationships and trust among civil society organisations, strengthening the capacity of the democracy sector to act collectively.
items.note: Describes ongoing capacity-building work for civil society as a sector, which is participation territory.

items.b: As catalysts of this network, we can foster this connectedness in practical and concrete ways — through programmes of intentional matchmaking — creating direct 1:1 connections between peers, performing a signposting role, facilitating learning circles — problem-solving in peer-to-peer groups, creating spaces for connection such as Democracy Drinks to the Democracy Meetups , providing coaching and buddying opportunities, and much more.
items.note: Describes internal sector networking activities among democracy organisations, not a mechanism affecting public democratic participation.

items.b: But the role of network leadership amongst such a sizable sector of 700+ organisations (and the thousands of amazing community-based organisations too) can only be so great, we can only have so many 1:1 meetings and run so many events. At some point we have to consider the question of connectivity — or the general amount and quality of connectedness in a system, and what we can do to maximise our impact.
items.note: Discusses network leadership capacity within the sector, not a democracy mechanism.

items.b: To use a common network analogy of the soil food web , if intentional matchmaking between organisations is akin to watering a pair of plants in a forest, then enhancing connectivity across an entire sector is working out how to feed those mycelial networks from which our shared endeavours grow.
items.note: Metaphorical discussion of sector connectivity, not a democracy story.
links: a common network analogy of the soil food web

items.b: Over time both those involved in the stewardship of the network itself and those who will have taken part in some of the activities outlined above, will have a much improved sense of who is doing what, who’s speaking to whom, who’s receiving what funding and where the bottlenecks and opportunities are. Combined with surveys and research interviews, this network mapping can provide us with a lay of the land, which parts of the network have the knowledge, skills and resources for impact — and which could benefit from more targeted capacity building efforts, ie. skill sharing and training on part…
items.note: Describes internal network mapping among organisations, akin to sector administration rather than public participation mechanism.

items.b: Underlining these efforts, and returning to that analogy again, we can provide much needed nutrients for those mycelial networks through a form of network mulch, or network infrastructure. By this we mean providing the foundational resource and information layer needed for people and organisations in the UK democracy space to thrive and for all networking efforts to build from.
items.note: Describes provision of sector infrastructure/resources to organisations, not a public-facing democracy mechanism.

items.b: In my previous role as Director at the Centre for Democracy, we made a great start on this, delivering the fortnightly sector newsletter, democracy map, sectoral calendar, meetups, jobs boards and funding opportunities lists. As the new Network Development Lead, I’ve brought these efforts over into the work of the Network, and we’ll be building on these too.
items.note: Describes organisational services (newsletter, jobs board, funding lists) for the sector itself, which is organisational admin rather than a democracy story.

items.b: The engagement of individuals and organisations across the democracy space through these varied activities will accrue many benefits. Stronger bonds between organisations mean they are more likely to collaborate on projects and reduce duplication. More densified networks can share information and knowledge more rapidly and effectively, the rapid growth of the Democracy Defence Coalition in early 2021, for example.
items.note: General claims about benefits of organisational networking, not a specific mechanism of public power or participation.

items.b: Networks also allow for knowledge exchange amongst groups that might otherwise not communicate directly. They allow for the spread of ideas and best practice, and for comparisons on performance for campaigns and organisations with similar goals. Administered well, they should engender cultures of openness and generosity across a sector. Similarly, diversity in networks reduces the risk of groupthink and increases the likelihood of fresh new ideas and innovations reaching a greater number of people. Crucially, they should build a sense of shared purpose.
items.note: Abstract discussion of network theory benefits for the sector, not a democracy story about public power or participation.

items.b: At the greater end, if the requisite trust, familiarity and empathy exist across a network, deeper levels of collaboration can take place, pooling resources and expertise of the network to achieve more together than they would working in isolation. This might include joint funding bids, campaigns, shared office space, shared operations functions or press lists, the list goes on, the ambition is palpable.
items.note: General reflection on sector networking benefits, not about democratic mechanisms.

items.b: Through our feedback, we’ve already seen the impact of recent, though nascent, networking efforts in the sector bear fruit, with many mentioning the improved coherence of parts of the sector, increased visibility of opportunities for connection and greater synergy, some collaboration around funding that may otherwise not have happened and importantly an improved responsiveness of the sector to the threats we face.
items.note: Describes internal feedback on sector networking, organisational rather than democratic mechanism.

items.b: “The future won’t be a new big, tower of power- but well trodden paths from house to house” - Raimon Panikkar
items.note: A standalone quote with no democratic mechanism identified.

items.b: 150 organisations have joined us on this journey, with hundreds more involved in networking efforts across the sector already — and we’re just getting started. If what we’ve outlined here has piqued your interest, get in touch to find out more about membership as part of the UK Democracy Network or sign up on our website .
items.note: Membership recruitment pitch for the network, organisational admin.

items.b: Networks are a slow burn, trust takes time to build, familiarity time to embed and empathy time to share. So if you were waiting for the right time to join the network — this is it.
items.note: Call to join the network, organisational membership admin.

items.h: Building a Youth Manifesto — UK Youth
items.b: UK Youth are keen to chat to anyone that is interested in building a youth manifesto for the next election. The aim of this piece of work is to produce a manifesto outlining what young people want to see from the Government at the next election, not just on youth policy but on all areas of policy from justice to health. For anyone interested, please contact kate.roberts@ukyouth.org
items.why: this creates a new mechanism for young people to articulate policy demands and engage with the political process ahead of an election.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation for youth in politics.

items.h: Association for Citizenship Teaching looking for collaboration on lobbying for politics and citizenship education
items.b: Association for Citizenship Teaching (ACT) are keen to chat to any organisations that might be interested in collectively lobbying for politics and citizenship education. For anyone interested in a chat about that work, please contact Liz via info@@teachingcitizenship.org.uk
items.note: Sector collaboration/networking call, not a change in participation opportunities.

items.h: Contributions welcome for new blog series The Loop
items.b: Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters is working alongside the European Consortium for Political Research on a new blog series The Loop . Titus has kicked off contributions to this new series with a challenge in his article Can political science save democracy? Contact Titus to get involved.
items.note: Call for blog contributions is sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: House of Lords passes single amendment to Public Order Bill, Bill heads back to Commons
items.b: Despite a vigorous debate in the House of Lords earlier this month, only one amendment was successfully passed by the Lords last week. The amendment tabled by Lord Coaker, to introduce two safeguards to suspicionless stop and search powers, was passed by a majority of 50 . The amended Bill now moves back to the House of Commons to be voted on again before proceeding quickly to Royal Assent (passing).
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns legal safeguards on state stop-and-search powers used against protesters, affecting freedom of assembly.
items.note: Protest policing power classified under rights/civic space per boundary rule.

items.h: Suspicionless stop and search re-inserted into the Public Order Bill in the Commons
items.b: Earlier this month suspicionless stop and search, previously removed by Lords amendment, was re-inserted into the Bill on a 281–236 vote, majority of 45.
items.why: this matters democratically because reinstating suspicionless stop-and-search powers expands state coercive power over protest participants.
items.note: Protest-related police power classified under rights/civic space per boundary rule.

items.h: Lords’ amendment to remove SDPOs from Public Order Bill rejected by House of Commons
items.b: Previously the House of Lords had amended the Bill to remove Serious Disruption Prevention Orders (SDPO) made otherwise than on conviction from the Public Order Bill. The Commons has now overturned this amendment on a 280–232 vote, majority of 48. This means that these protest banning orders can be imposed on members of the public regardless of whether they have been convicted, for more information on these draconian measures see this recent parliamentary briefing .
items.why: this matters democratically because it allows protest-banning orders to be imposed without conviction, restricting freedom of assembly.
items.note: Protest banning orders fall under rights/civic space as state coercion of assembly.

items.h: New clause added to National Security Bill to combat foreign financing of UK political parties
items.b: The Government has been defeated in the House of Lords over an amendment to the National Security Bill which will require political parties to publish policy statements to ensure any donations from foreign powers are identified and highlighted. The new clause will also require parties to provide annual statements to the Electoral Commission on risk management relating to donations from foreign powers.
items.why: this matters democratically because it introduces transparency requirements on foreign donations to political parties, a core campaign finance safeguard for fair political competition.
links: defeated in the House of Lords

items.h: Minimum Service Bill ‘almost certainly’ against international law, says leading labour lawyer
items.b: Jeffrey Vogt, co-Founder of the International Lawyers Assisting Workers Network (ILAW) — a global coalition of 900 workers’ rights lawyers — has said the government’s ‘anti-strike’ legislation will most likely be struck down as illegal under international law due its lacking a stated minimum service — a prerequisite under international law for introducing legislation of this nature.
items.why: this matters democratically because the legislation restricts trade unions' freedom of association and right to strike, a civic freedom protected under international law.
items.note: Trade union rights classified under rights/civic space per freedom-of-association boundary rule.
links: government’s ‘anti-strike’ legislation will most likely be struck down

items.h: Illegal Migration Bill passes second reading in House of Commons
items.b: The Government’s Illegal Migration Bill , which would see anyone arriving in the UK by so-called illegal means, passed its second reading by 312 votes to 250. A Labour amendment seeking to block the bill was defeated by 249 votes to 312. The Home Secretary acknowledged in a letter to Conservative MPs and Peers that there was a ‘50% chance’ that the legislation was incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights, but stated that the government intended to pass it nonetheless.
items.why: this matters democratically because the government is knowingly passing legislation likely incompatible with binding human rights law, raising questions about predictable and lawful exercise of public power.
items.note: Focus is on government's disregard for legal compliance rather than the migration policy itself.
links: ‘50% chance’ that the legislation was incompatible

items.h: Campaigners call on the government to scrap the Data Protection and Digital Information Bill
items.b: 25 civil society organisations including human rights campaigners, trade unions and criminal justice organisations, have written to the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, Michelle Donelan MP, calling for the Data Protection and Digital Information (DPDI) Bill to be scrapped. Abigail Burke, Policy Manager at Open Rights Group said, ‘the bill weakens data subjects rights and corporate accountability mechanisms, politicises the Information Commissioner’s Office, and expands the Secretary of State’s powers in numerous, undemocratic ways’.
items.why: expanding ministerial powers and politicising the independent data regulator weakens checks on executive authority and accountability mechanisms.
items.note: Overlaps with data privacy rights but core complaint is about executive power expansion and regulator independence.
links: written to the Secretary of State
Data Protection and Digital Information (DPDI) Bill

items.h: Pledge your support for the Elected Representatives (Code of Conduct) Bill ahead of second reading in Commons
items.b: On 24th March, Debbie Abrahams, Labour MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth, will present their Elected Representatives (Code of Conduct) Bill to parliament for its second reading. The bill aims to codify the Ministerial Code, empower the Commissioner for Ministerial Standards to independently oversee the code, establish a Parliamentary Standards Commissioner and launch an Independent Ethics Commission, with citizens assemblies to engage the public on the ongoing reform of our political system. Debbie, and the team at Compassion in Politics , are calling for signatures in support of the bill whi…
items.why: codifying the ministerial code and creating independent standards oversight bodies would strengthen the mechanisms holding elected representatives answerable for their conduct.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are mentioned only as a secondary engagement tool within a broader accountability bill.

items.b: Please add your updates to this week’s Check-In document . Our last fortnightly Democracy Bulletin will be published next week, before we move to our new monthly schedule. Please subscribe to the Democracy Network calendar and have our key network events, such as the Meetups, Democracy Drinks, Coworking, popped in your calendar every month automatically.

items.h: Democracy Drinks this wednesday, 22nd March
items.b: Join Unlock Democracy, Electoral Reform Society, UK Democracy Network and more at this week’s in-person London Democracy Drinks — register here .

items.h: Add key elections dates to your calendar
items.b: Thanks to Harriet Andrews , Director at the Democracy Classroom, for setting up this subscribable public calendar providing key election dates up until the 2023 Local Elections — add the dates to your calendar now .
items.why: a shared public calendar of election dates helps organisations and citizens track electoral events, supporting practical access to voting opportunities.
items.note: Treated as an access-mechanics resource under elections rather than general civic capacity-building.
links: add the dates to your calendar now

items.h: Democracy Network Voter ID event series
items.b: Join Democracy Network for their voter ID event series workshops starting this Friday 24th March. The first event is aimed at ensuring UK democracy organisations are all on the same page when it comes to voter ID guidance, with Martyn Harris, Head of Elections at North Warwickshire and Nuneaton & Bedworth Borough Councils, and Matteo Bergamini, Founder at Shout Out UK, providing the critical insight. There will two further events on the 30th March and 5 April, stay tuned for more on those — register now for Friday’s event .
items.why: aligning organisations on voter ID guidance affects how easily citizens can meet identification requirements to vote, a core electoral integrity and access issue.
items.note: Voter ID guidance is filed under elections & decision making even though delivered as sector capacity-building.

items.h: Democracy Classroom developing shared resources for civic education collaboration
items.b: Democracy Classroom have been working on developing databases of organisations and projects to aid with on-going collaboration across the civic education space. If you would like to find out more or take part in the new initiative, contact Harriet and the team . You can also view the ongoing list of offers and asks from Democracy Classroom and their partners on their new Sharing Hub .
items.why: building shared civic education resources and collaboration infrastructure expands the sector's capacity to help people engage in democratic life.
items.note: Counted as sector capacity-building creating new means of civic engagement rather than mere organisational news.

items.h: Civic Tech Field Guide are offering pro-bono democracy tech consultations
items.b: Civic Tech Field Guide has received grant funding from the National Endowment for Democracy and are portioning some of it to provide pro bono democracy tech consultations . If you are actively engaged in defending, improving, reforming or promoting democracy through a non-violent project or campaign, apply now for a chance to get personalised guidance on how you can harness technology to improve your democratic engagement. The deadline to apply is the 31st of March .
items.why: providing free technical support to democracy campaigns creates new practical capacity for civic and political engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building expanding participation resources, not organisational funding news.
links: The deadline to apply is the 31st of March

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation and Opus Independents hiring new network coordinators
items.b: Networks are apparently all the rage at the moment, with both Opus Independents and Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) hiring for new network coordinator roles.
items.note: Job hiring announcement for organisational staff, not a change to democratic participation.

items.h: Friends, Families and Travellers release new Police Act guidance, campaign on energy grants
items.b: The Gypsy and Roma and Traveller community has been hard hit by the new policing legislation, with the communities directly targeted by new powers involving, for the first time, prisonable offences. The new materials from Friends, Families and Travellers (FFT) aims to provide clarity on the new legislation for GRT communities across the UK. FFT have also started a new campaign at justice for GRT communities and itinerant live-aboard boaters who have been specifically excluded from receiving energy grant support .
items.why: this matters democratically because new prisonable police powers specifically targeting Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities raise questions of equal protection, personal security and discriminatory state coercion.
items.note: New legislation creating prisonable offences targeting a specific group is treated as a rights/discrimination issue rather than general policing logistics.
links: specifically excluded from receiving energy grant support

items.h: New Constitution Unit report suggests options for Lords reform
items.b: New report House of Lords reform: navigating the obstacles from The Constitution Unit Director, Meg Russell, takes a closer look at public opinion on the House of Lords, discussing the successful and unsuccessful proposals for reform in the past and considering what the contemporary key reform objectives should be. If they form the next government, Russell suggests Labour should implement a series of small-scale and immediate changes to the Lords that don’t require significant legislation, whilst opening a consultation on the options for larger reform.
items.why: this matters democratically because the composition and reform of the House of Lords affects the structure and constraints on legislative power within Parliament.
items.note: Lords reform concerns parliamentary structure and accountability rather than an election or devolved decision-making mechanism.
links: House of Lords reform: navigating the obstacles

items.h: Multiple opportunities to join the team at mySociety
items.b: mySociety is currently hunting for a new Chair of Trustees to help steer the board and the organisation as a whole. They are also looking for a Policy and Advocacy Manager to help shape their approach towards engagement with government and decision-makers and a User Support Officer who will respond to the various types of correspondence coming through their service. And for anyone more suited to a sales role, there’s an opportunity to join them as a Regional Business Development / Account Manager (North) .
items.note: Set of job vacancy listings, not a change affecting democratic participation.

items.h: Sortition Foundation is looking for a digital campaigner
items.b: The new Digital Campaigner role at Sortition Foundation will work with their campaign working group to drive multi-platform digital campaigns to help build a case for House of Lords reform and broader democratic renewal. Apply by Monday 27th of March.
items.note: Job hiring announcement, not a new participatory mechanism itself.

items.h: Are generative AI good for democracy? Demos investigates
items.b: According to ChatGPT’s own algorithm. ‘language models like ChatGPT have the potential to both support and undermine democracy, depending on how they are used and the context in which they are applied’. Join Demos on the 23rd of March for a deeper dive into whether generative AI really is good or bad for democracy. Speakers on the day will include Laura Giesen, Programme Manager, Democracy Technologies , Carys Afoko, Senior Director for Communications and External Affairs, Mozilla and Ellen Judson, Head of CASM, Demos .
items.note: Event listing/discussion announcement rather than a reported change or new participatory tool.
links: Join Demos on the 23rd of March

items.h: Compass to discuss the Labour Party’s Forde report
items.b: The Forde Inquiry involved sifting through thousands of submissions, finding ‘little evidence of mutual respect and a great deal of evidence of factionalism so deep-rooted that the Party has found itself dysfunctional’. Little has been done, however, to follow up and the findings of the report. Now Compass is hosting an event alongside Director of Compassion in Politics , Jennifer Nadel, Human rights academic, Francesca Klug OBE, and President of the US/Middle East Project Daniel Levy, to discuss the findings of the report and explore how our political culture needs to change to reinvigorate o…
items.note: Event listing about discussing an existing report, not itself a reported democratic change.

items.h: Act Build Change is hiring
items.b: Exciting new opportunities to join the team at Act Build Change . They’re on the hunt for a Programme and Operations Assistant to join them 3 days a week and a Collective Care Trainer to join them 4 days a week.
items.note: Job hiring announcement for organisational staff.

items.h: Byline Times festival returns in July
items.b: The Byline Times Festival returns this year in July for more music, talks, food, dancing and ideas about how the world could be changed for the better. Speaking at the festival this year will be a number of journalists from The Byline Times as well as politicians and various other political commentators. Book your tickets asap!
items.note: Festival event listing, not democracy mechanism news.

items.h: Democracy Club take a look at what’s up for election this year
items.b: Peter Keeling of Democracy Club takes us on a tour through the 8,519 councillors and four mayors who are to be election this year across England and Northern Ireland — making this the largest set of elections since 2019. Find out more over on Peter’s blog .
items.why: it informs the public about the scale and structure of this year's local council and mayoral elections, a core part of the electoral calendar in England and Northern Ireland.

items.h: Parallel Elections kick off meeting
items.b: This month Save the Children held a kick off meeting for organisations looking to collaborate on the national Parallel Election. They are continuing to hold meetings throughout this month to consult on the design of the project. If anyone wants to get involved, please contact Meg at Save the Children.
items.why: it creates a new civic engagement initiative, a 'Parallel Election', giving groups excluded from the franchise a structured means of political participation.

items.h: The Politics Project launch their #ElectionCountdown
items.b: This month The Politics Project launched their #ElectionCountdown programme for the local elections, with a range of resources and support for schools and youth groups. You can learn more and sign up to receive content packs through the campaign here .
items.why: it creates new educational resources and support to help schools and young people engage with the electoral process, building capacity for future democratic participation.
items.note: Classed as civic engagement capacity-building rather than a turnout drive since it targets schools/youth broadly, not specifically voter turnout.

items.h: My Vote My Voice Campaign Launch
items.b: This week United Response launched their #MyVoteMyVoice Campaign to encourage people with learning difficulties and autistic people to use their vote.
items.why: it is a campaign to raise electoral turnout among people with learning difficulties and autistic people, and turnout campaigns are always classified under elections regardless of framing.
items.note: Turnout campaigns are always Elections & decision making per framework rule.

items.h: Luke Temple and Ana Ines Langer working on democracy activism research piece
items.b: Luke Temple, University of Sheffield, and Ana Ines Langer, University of Glasgow, have produced a research paper examining the democracy activism scene in the 2017 and 2019 general elections. The piece is currently under peer review, and they have published a short briefing note on the work. For anyone interested in the details of the longer form piece, please contact Luke Temple .
items.why: it presents new research evidence on the democracy activism scene surrounding recent general elections, bearing on civil society participation and campaigning capacity.

items.h: New Channel 4 polling sees the Conservatives losing all 45 ‘red wall’ seats at the next GE
items.b: A new poll carried out by Channel Four has found that if an election was called tomorrow, the Conservatives would be ‘completely wiped out’ in all red wall seats. Check out this video for a quick digest of the poll.
items.note: Horse-race polling on likely election outcomes, not a mechanism of democratic power.

items.h: Dormant Asset Scheme finds £76m for social enterprises and community wealth funds
items.b: The government has announced community wealth funds will become one of the primary beneficiaries of the funding made available through the Dormant Asset Scheme . The funds will be controlled by local communities, with residents directing spending as they see fit to develop social infrastructure and social capital. Find out more here .
items.why: it channels dormant asset funding into community-controlled wealth funds, giving residents direct control over local resource allocation as a condition for practical participation.

items.h: New Localis report explores prospects for devolution and local government options
items.b: The new report Moving Through The Gears by Localis builds on conversations with local government leaders, experts and academics, on their thoughts and assessment of the future of devolved and local government finances over the next political cycle. Read the report .
items.why: it examines the future powers and financing of local and devolved government, a core part of the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Local/devolved government structure and finance falls under elections & decision making per the boundary rule.

items.h: UK human rights groups issue ‘distress signal’ to the UN
items.b: Over 60 charities, unions and campaign groups, including Liberty , Unison , JustFair and Mermaids , have penned a ‘distress signal’ letter to the UN warning of an erosion of human rights in the UK. The letter comes as the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (CESCR) begins its assessment of the UK’s human rights record. The letter refers to an attack on civil liberties through recent legislation such as the Police, Crimes, Sentencing and Courts Act, Public Order Bill and raises fears over proposed legislation to scrap the Human Rights Act.
items.why: it documents civil society claims that recent legislation curtails civil liberties, freedom of protest and human rights protections in the UK.
links: penned a ‘distress signal’ letter to the UN

items.h: UK Government monitoring human rights lawyers
items.b: Minister of State for Immigration, Robert Jenrick MP, has announced that the government is monitoring human rights lawyers within the UK and accused them of ‘abusing the law’.
items.why: state surveillance of lawyers representing rights claimants risks chilling the civic space and legal challenge function that hold public power accountable.
items.note: Overlaps rule of law (access to justice/lawyers) but the mechanism is state monitoring/intimidation of a civic actor.
links: government is monitoring human rights lawyers within the UK

items.h: Landmark independent report finds London Metropolitan Police institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic
items.b: Commissioned in the wake of Sarah Everard’s kidnap, rape and murder at the hands of serving Metropolitan Police officer Wayne Couzens, Dame Louise Casey’s 300 page independent report is a damning indictment on the operation of the force , with campaigner Andrea Simon of End Violence Against Women Coalition remarking the report ‘leaves the Met with nowhere to hide’ , even PM Sunak failed to back the Met Police on live TV when asked about his confidence in the force in the wake of the report.
items.why: institutional failures in policing bear on the lawfulness, fairness and accountability of a public body wielding coercive power over citizens.
items.note: Policing lawfulness placed under rule of law; discrimination findings also engage rights as secondary.
links: Dame Louise Casey’s 300 page independent report is a damning indictment on the operation of the force
Andrea Simon of End Violence Against Women Coalition remarking the report ‘leaves the Met with nowhere to hide’
PM Sunak failed to back the Met Police

items.h: CIVICUS Monitor downgrades UK civic space rating to ‘Obstructed’
items.b: The UK joins 39 other countries rated as ‘obstructed’ in the CIVICUS Monitor annual report on civic space People Power Under Attack . This puts the UK in the same categories as countries such as Hungary, South Africa, Poland, Brazil and Indonesia. The main factors warranting this downgrade CIVICUS cite include the extension of police powers introduced via the recent Police Act and Public Order Bill. In addition to the legislation, the report emphasises how climate and anti-racism protesters are being targeted by police, with legal observers experiencing high levels of intimidation, harassment …
items.why: an international monitor's downgrade reflects a documented narrowing of the legal space for protest, assembly and civil society activity in the UK.

items.h: Home Secretary may have broken ministerial code with attack on civil service
items.b: The Home Secretary stands accused of breaching the ministerial code for a second time after an email surfaced in which she accused ‘left wing’ civil servants of blocking her plans to crack down on boat crossings. In the email she said, ​​’we tried to stop the small boats…But an activist blob of left wing lawyers, civil servants and the Labour Party blocked us.’
items.why: an alleged breach of the ministerial code concerns whether ministers are held to standards of conduct and accountability while exercising public power.

items.h: Coalition of trade unions accuses government complicity in refugee attacks
items.b: A collection of UK trade unions including GMB , UNISON , RMT , have issued a joint statement criticising the government for inciting violence against refugees through their dangerous rhetoric and oppressive policies. In the statement they said, ‘anti-migrant politics are an attempt to divide working class people against each other…The people to blame for this are politicians, billionaires and big corporations, not migrant workers or refugees forced to live in temporary accommodation.’
items.note: A political statement criticising government rhetoric on policy is not itself a democratic mechanism story.

items.h: UK politics needs stronger independent regulation to uphold ministerial integrity, finds Constitution Unit report
items.b: A survey of 4,000 members of the public carried out by The Constitution Unit in August and September 2022 found half of participants (52%) thought politicians had lower ethical standards than ordinary citizens, whilst just 5% said they thought politicians had higher ethical standards. 79% said that reform is needed so that politicians are made more accountable and act with integrity, whilst just 6% said the system should stay as it is.
items.why: public confidence in politicians' ethics and calls for stronger independent regulation bear directly on mechanisms for holding officeholders to standards of integrity.

items.h: BBC backs down over Gary Lineker controversy, announces independent review
items.b: Earlier this month leading sports commentator and BBC freelancer Gary Lineker remarked on the British Government’s new asylum policy, leading to severe criticism from leading politicians , including the Home Secretary and the Labour Leader’s office. Following this the BBC required Lineker to step down, triggering fellow BBC sports commentators and personalities to withdraw their own labour in solidarity with Lineker, forcing the BBC to reduce and cancel its sports coverage of Premier League fixings. The BBC has now backed down, reinstating Lineker and announcing an independent review of the Co…
items.why: it concerns the BBC's editorial independence and a freelancer's freedom of expression under political pressure from government figures, shaping the public information environment.
items.note: Freedom of expression treated as information_debate since the story centres on public-service media policy, with individual liberty as secondary.
links: fellow BBC sports commentators and personalities to withdraw their own labour in solidarity
BBC has now backed down, reinstating Lineker and announcing an independent review of the Corporation’s social media guidelines

items.h: Jon Alexander suggests an independent BBC citizens’ assembly board
items.b: Echoing the Media Reform Coalition’s calls for a Peoples’ BBC and the Institute of Welsh Affairs’ citizens’ panel on media policy in Wales , as well as suggestions from the Voice of the Listener and Viewer on running a citizens’ assembly on a new funding model for the BBC — Jon Alexander suggests a randomly selected, representative citizens’ assembly board for the BBC reminiscent of Independent SAGE.
items.why: it proposes a citizens' assembly, a deliberative decision-making mechanism, to govern a major public institution.
items.note: Citizens' assembly proposals are classified under elections_decision_making per the framework's deliberation rule, even when applied to media governance.
links: Media Reform Coalition’s calls for a Peoples’ BBC
Institute of Welsh Affairs’ citizens’ panel on media policy in Wales
suggests a randomly selected, representative citizens’ assembly board

items.h: Index on Censorship is organising a hybrid day event on SLAPPs
items.b: On the 23rd of March, Index of Censorship will host an in-person and online day event to discuss all things SLAPPs — how they work, who tends to use them and what can be done to stop them. A collection of lawyers, journalists, academics, politicians, and campaigners, will be speaking on the day as well as from keynote speakers, UN Special Rapporteur Mary Lawlor. The conference is free so be sure to reserve a spot .
items.note: An event announcement rather than a reported mechanism change or substantive analysis.

items.h: Permanent citizens’ assemblies set up in Copenhagen and Brussels
items.b: A permanent citizens’ assembly is being trailed as part of a two-year pilot which will help inform the workings of Copenhagen’s municipal parliament. Over the next two years, two groups will be selected from the local population to work on themes relevant to the city’s development. Similar steps are being taken in Brussels where a 100-person citizens’ assembly is being set up to provide recommendations on climate change and how the city can transition.
items.why: it reports the establishment of permanent citizens' assemblies as ongoing deliberative decision-making machinery, comparative evidence relevant to UK debates on democratic innovation.
items.note: International item included as comparative evidence on deliberative decision-making structures.
links: permanent citizens’ assembly is being trailed
100-person citizens’ assembly is being set up

items.h: Fancy a political argument with a bot?
items.b: Then John Bryden has built just the thing for you — a prototype chatGPT derived political ‘argument clinic’ bot that’ll argue with you on political talking points — Go on, get arguing .
items.why: it creates a new tool intended to help people practise political argument, expanding informal means of civic engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of political engagement rather than an information-environment story.
