items.h: Have you got a story or news related to voter ID? Byline Times want to know
items.b: Byline Times have been covering voter ID closely over the past months, contact Josiah Mortimer via josiah@bylinetimes.com for anything and everything voter ID related.
items.why: this is a call for evidence on voter ID rules, which govern who can practically exercise the franchise and how electoral integrity safeguards operate.
items.note: Journalistic call for tips on voter ID counts as engaging electoral administration mechanics.

items.h: Joint Committee on Human Rights launches inquiry into Illegal Migration Bill
items.b: The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has launched a new inquiry into the Illegal Migration Bill and how it engages with the European Convention on Human Rights. The JCHR has written to the Home Secretary requesting that they appear before the committee to answer questions on the provisions contained within the bill and whether there has been adequate time for scrutiny. Meanwhile, more than 60 MPs, NGOs and academics have signed an open letter to PM Sunak urging them to withdraw the bill due to significant fears over the potential loss of human life as a result of its passing.
items.why: a parliamentary committee is scrutinising whether emergency legislation complies with human rights law and whether Parliament has had adequate time to examine it, a core check on executive power.

items.h: Lib Dems introduce last-minute bill to block voter ID legislation
items.b: On the 29th March Lib Dem MP Helen Morgan staged a last-minute intervention to try and stop the government’s voter ID scheme from going ahead, introducing the Elections (Voter Identification Requirements) Bill . The bill would reverse the obligation for voters to produce a valid form of ID at all future elections and is currently co-signed by 11 other Lib Dem MPs.
items.why: it concerns a legislative attempt to reverse voter ID rules that govern people's practical ability to cast a ballot.

items.h: Democracy Coworking, Friday 14th April at Demos
items.b: Don’t miss Democracy Coworking in Central London on Friday 14th at Demos’ office on Whitehall. Stay for the full day or just pop by, the more the merrier. Find out more and give us an idea of numbers on the day by RSVPing here .

items.h: Democracy Network voter ID resources
items.b: You can find Democracy Network’s new voter ID resources page here . This includes recordings of our voter ID meetings and links to further information. If you’d like to include your own resources then please contact amna@involve.org.uk .
items.why: a new resource hub is created to help civil society and voters understand and navigate voter ID requirements, expanding practical means of engagement.
items.note: Sector capacity-building rule applied since the item creates a new resource rather than reporting policy itself.

items.h: Flurry of great democracy-related jobs currently open for applications
items.b: Organisations hiring over the next month include Cast from Clay, The Small Axe, Institute for Government, British Youth Council, Public Interest News Foundation, Mozilla Foundation, Boundary Commission for England, New Economy Organisers’ Network, mySociety, FullFact, Demos, Young Citizens and more. See the full list of upcoming jobs on the Democracy Network’s Democracy Jobs Board . Follow our job updates on Twitter via #DemocracyJobs .

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project launch new campaign targeting directly elected mayors
items.b: Lara Parizotto and the team at the Migrant Democracy Project are asking all 26 directly elected mayors in England to sign their statement of support for residence-based voting rights (RBVR). Find out more about the campaign and get involved . Think you can assist? Get in touch .
items.why: the campaign seeks to extend voting rights (suffrage) to migrant residents in local elections, directly engaging the scope of who can participate in choosing representatives.
items.note: Classified under suffrage/elections despite being a sector campaign, since the substantive issue is franchise extension.
links: Find out more about the campaign and get involved

items.h: Sortition Foundation hosting ‘Peerless Symposium’ on Lords reform
items.b: James Robertson at Sortition Foundation is organising a special facilitated conversation event at a venue overlooking the Thames on the 26th April. Find out more and register now .
items.note: Treated as an event listing rather than a substantive report on Lords reform or deliberative democracy.

items.h: Miriam Levin has been appointed Chief Executive of Engage Britain.
items.b: Miriam Levin is currently settling in as the new CEO of Engage Britain , remarking that they are ‘excited to lead Engage Britain into our next chapter of putting people at the heart of policy making. We’ll carry on working on health and care, testing out some new ways of working, and we will be exploring other policy areas. I’m really looking forward to working more closely with the members of the Democracy Network and driving change together.’

items.h: Centenary Action Group to host panel on how we get more women into Parliament
items.b: The 12th May Centenary Action Group event will feature speakers including Maria Caulfield MP — Conservative Minister for Women, Yasmin Qureshi MP — Labour Shadow Minister for Women, Kirsten Oswald MP — SNP Spokesperson Equalities, Christine Jardine MP — Lib Dem Spokesperson for Women and Equalities, and Liz Saville Roberts MP, Plaid Cymru’s Spokesperson for Women and Equalities. The panel will discuss how we get more women into Parliament — register now .
items.note: Event listing/panel announcement, not a created participation mechanism or reported change.

items.h: People’s Powerhouse seek to expand their Racial Justice Network
items.b: People’s Powerhouse Racial Justice Network aims to provide a focal point for race equality issues affecting people of the North, by amplifying the voices of northern communities and ensuring that decision makers are held to account on matters of social and economic inclusion and racial equality. Find out more about the Racial Justice Network on their new website , or contact Ruth Hannan , Director at the People’s Powerhouse.
items.why: this expands a civil-society network's capacity to organise communities and hold decision makers accountable on racial equality, a condition for civic participation.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building resource (new website/network) rather than mere organisational news.

items.h: 50:50 NI run training programme at Imagine! Belfast
items.b: Last month 50:50 NI concluded their ‘So you want to be a councillor?’ training programme that worked to give women the skills, knowledge and experience they need to run for elected office in Northern Ireland. With the training complete, Aoife Clements and the team are now focusing on running a small campaign around the local elections in Northern Ireland.
items.why: training women to stand for local council seats affects candidate access and representativeness of elected office.
items.note: Candidate training tied to elected office access is filed under elections rather than participation.

items.h: Talk Shop run MozFest sessions, submit proposal to Wellcome Trust
items.b: As part of their work experimenting and finding the path forward to plug the ‘ deliberation gap ’, Talk Shop have put in a proposal to the Wellcome Trust through their recent call for proposals on creative approaches to policy making. Perry and the team were also on hand last month at Mozilla Festival running one of their Win-Win Workout sessions.
items.note: Reports the organisation's own grant proposal and festival session rather than a created public participation mechanism.

items.h: Newspeak House opens applications for their annual residency programme
items.b: Newspeak House , the London College of Political Technology, hosts an annual residential programme providing a valuable opportunity to engage with civic communities of practice and expert practitioners in senior positions across UK institutions. Applications are now open for their 2023–2024 cohort .
items.note: Routine opening of applications for an existing annual programme, treated as organisational admin.

items.h: I Have A Voice Youth Ambassador Scheme in full flow
items.b: Elisha Holt, Community Development at I Have A Voice , and the team, are currently running multiple campaigns on a range of issues alongside their youth ambassadors, from political education to fast fashion to voter registration drives. They’re also working with the NHS Confederation on sourcing interns for the Confederation’s paid placements over the summer .
items.note: Reports ongoing activity of an existing scheme rather than a new launch or concrete change.
links: Confederation’s paid placements over the summer

items.h: Institute for Government explore how to increase public engagement with constitutional issues
items.b: On the 17th of April, Institute for Government will host a panel discussion to explore the public understanding and interest in constitutional issues, with a particular focus on how to increase engagement on constitutional issues to empower citizens to become more active in this area.
items.note: Event listing about a panel discussion, not itself a reported democratic change.

items.h: Just 50,000 eligible voters have registered for a Voter Authority Certificate
items.b: According to the latest figures from the Democracy Defence Coalition , according to Shaun Roberts, Head of Campaigns and Digital at Unlock Democracy , just 50,000 people have registered for voter ID, leaving as many as 2,000,000 voters bereft of a means to vote in upcoming elections. Recent campaigning efforts by the Coalition saw voter ID feature on TV show Good Morning Britain and in local press. View the latest voter ID application data on the GOV.UK portal .
items.why: low uptake of Voter Authority Certificates threatens the practical ability of eligible citizens to vote, a core electoral administration issue.

items.h: Have you got a story or news related to voter ID? Byline Times want to know
items.b: Byline Times have been covering voter ID closely over the past months, contact Josiah Mortimer via josiah@bylinetimes.com for anything and everything voter ID related.
items.note: Call for tips/contributions to a journalist, not reporting on democracy itself.

items.h: New look polling cards drop through letterboxes nationwide
items.b: In the last week or so, polling cards have been posted to those eligible to vote in the upcoming local elections. Notably, this year’s polling cards feature a new design including repeated reminders and space given over to the requirements for voter ID in this May’s elections.
items.why: the design and content of polling cards directly affects whether voters understand and can meet new voter ID requirements to cast a ballot.

items.h: Nominations for English local elections close, help Democracy Club sort the data!
items.b: Nominations for elections closed yesterday at 4pm in England, after which time Statement of Persons Nominated (SoPN) began to be published. Northern Irish nominations close on 24th April, with the data released shortly afterwards. As usual, Democracy Club will collect this candidate data for publication on WhoCanIVoteFor.co.uk — they’re always looking for volunteers to help crowdsource, would you like to know more ?
items.why: publication of nominated candidates and crowdsourced election data affects voters' ability to know who they can vote for, a core election administration function.
items.note: Volunteer call is sector logistics but the underlying nomination/data event is genuine election administration.
links: would you like to know more

items.h: Democracy Classroom’s #ElectionCountdown in full swing
items.b: Hattie Andrews and the team at Democracy Classroom have been working with schools and youth groups to engage young people ahead of the local elections. As part of #ElectionCountdown, Democracy Classroom produces an excellent weekly campaign newsletter with a round up of resources and articles for the local elections — sign up here .
items.why: the creation of youth-focused resources and campaigns builds new means for young people to engage with an upcoming election.

items.h: Democracy Classroom hosting General Election Resources Day on 12th June
items.b: To support the creation of learning resources, Democracy Classroom is hosting a one-day in-person meetup for democracy organisations looking to develop learning resources for the General Election. Please contact Hattie via hattie@thepoliticsproject.org.uk if you would like to attend online or in-person, or learn more.
items.note: An event listing/meetup notice for organisations rather than a new participation resource or reported change.

items.h: Welsh Government consulting on new local STV rules — closes 7th April
items.b: The Senedd legislated to allow local authorities in Wales to choose their electoral system , between First Past the Post (FPTP) or Single Transferable Vote (STV). FPTP is currently in use for all 22 principal council elections and local authorities in Wales. The consultation seeks views on draft rules for the conduct of these new processes using STV, should local authorities opt to switch to the proportional method. View the consultation .
items.why: the choice between electoral systems for local councils directly shapes how votes translate into representation at the local level.
items.note: Local government electoral system change falls under elections & decision making per boundary rule.
links: The Senedd legislated to allow local authorities in Wales to choose their electoral system

items.h: Shout Out UK conclude their London voter ID engagement campaign
items.b: Shout Out UK have been working closely with the Greater London Assembly since January through to the end of March, supported by a pan-London coalition of some 200 civil society and democracy organisations and councils, who have been sharing SOUK’s resources online — would you like to know more?
items.note: Wrap-up announcement of a completed organisational campaign rather than launch of a new resource or reported change.
links: would you like to know more?

items.h: Labour Party’s blocks Jeremy Corbyn standing as Labour MP, sparks questions about democracy within the party
items.b: The Labour Party’s National Executive Committee has voted to block Jeremy Corbyn MP from standing as a candidate in the next general election. In response to the news activists, politicians and senior party figures raised questions around whether these actions set a precedent for the party to interfere with the democratic process of selecting candidates in the future.
items.why: internal party decisions over candidate selection affect the freedom of political parties and voters' ability to choose among competing candidates.
items.note: Party candidate access falls under elections & decision making per the free political parties anchor.
links: voted to block Jeremy Corbyn MP

items.h: Save the Children continue preparing Parallel Election for the General Election
items.b: Aiming to get greater input from the wider civic education community on the role of young people and youth organisations, Save the Children have held four thematic meetings on the Parallel Elections project in recent weeks. The UK wide youth Parallel Election is being planned for the General Election based on a similar Norwegian campaign run in 2021 Barnas Valg involving child-friendly hustings and media partners working together to make a splash pre-election results night.
items.why: it creates a new means for young people to practise and engage with the democratic process ahead of eligibility to vote, building civic engagement capacity.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new participation mechanism for young people, distinct from actual electoral administration.

items.h: Senior Labour figures cast doubts on reliability of post-election voter ID data
items.b: Alex Norris MP, Labour’s Shadow Levelling Up Secretary, has questioned the reliability of government data on non-eligible voters at the upcoming local elections. Current plans would see election officials stationed at the doors of polling stations to check if voters have the correct ID. However, those turned away at the door will not be logged as having been refused a ballot on the grounds of a lack of ID and will only be logged if they make it to the main desk and are refused there. Norris said in parliament on March 27th, he thought the scheme was “totally daft and will, of course, completel…
items.why: it concerns the reliability of data used to evaluate a new voter ID requirement that affects who can actually cast a ballot.
links: questioned the reliability of government data

items.h: Security staff could be deployed at polling stations in Newcastle
items.b: Bouncers could be sent to ‘hotspot’ polling stations across Newcastle due to fears from local councillors that arguments could break out over the ability of voters to cast their vote. Initial estimates last year suggested that approximately 3,900 voters in Newcastle would not have an appropriate form of ID to present on polling day, but it was later said that the true figure could be double or even triple that amount.
items.why: it concerns the administration and security of polling stations amid new voter ID rules that could affect people's practical ability to vote.

items.h: Sort the System mass lobby for proportional representation, May 24th
items.b: Make Votes Matter’s Sort the System rally on the 24th May will see large numbers from across the UK descend on Westminster with a message of immediate electoral reform — Find out more now .
items.note: Treated as an event listing/call to action rather than substantive reporting, per sector-logistics guidance.
links: Make Votes Matter’s Sort the System

items.h: People’s Plan for Nature launched after the first UK-wide citizens’ assembly on nature
items.b: The People’s Plan for Nature was launched in March setting out proposals for how the UK can protect and restore nature. The plan was drawn up following a two-stage process which included citizens from across the UK. The first stage was a ‘National Conversation’, in which 30,000 members of the public submitted their thoughts on nature and why we should value it. This subsequently informed a national citizen’s assembly made up of 100 members of the public who came together to create the People’s Plan itself which set out a manifesto for why and how we should protect nature. This landmark project…
items.why: a UK-wide citizens' assembly is a deliberative decision-making mechanism through which ordinary citizens directly shape public policy proposals.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are anchored to elections & decision making per the framework's deliberative process rule.

items.h: Democracy Network submit proposals to Labour Party’s National Policy Forum
items.b: The UK Democracy Network has submitted proposals calling on the Labour Party to undertake various democratic reforms. The reforms were signed by twenty-one democracy organisations and included calls for the Party to adopt proportional representation, devolve more power to communities, and break up media giants, amongst others.
items.why: civil society organisations are collectively petitioning a major political party to adopt democratic reforms, exercising organised civic voice in the political process.
items.note: Story's mechanism is civil-society campaigning/petitioning rather than the electoral system topics themselves.

items.h: Commission on Political Power sets out options for House of Lords reform
items.b: The new paper Creation of a Senate from the Commission on Political Power sets out a range of options for House of Lords reform , eschewing directly elected politicians. Frances Crook, Co-Convenor of the Commission, makes the point that direct elections will not necessarily provide improved democracy and that having more professional politicians may not enhance public confidence in the system — read the new report now .
items.why: it examines how the composition and structure of a legislative chamber should be reformed, bearing on parliamentary scrutiny and constitutional design.
items.note: Focus is on legislative structure and scrutiny rather than elections, since the report explicitly rejects direct election.

items.h: Public dialogue on sentencing policy tests new online methods
items.b: A public dialogue on sentencing policy is exploring innovative ways of engaging people online. The project, supported by UKRI and the Royal Society of the Arts , is a partnership between Involve , the University of Southampton and Nethood , and aims to challenge the boundaries of conversations between the public, researchers and policymakers. Stay tuned for more on this.
items.why: it tests new deliberative methods for involving the public directly in shaping policy, a form of decision-making machinery beyond elections.
items.note: Deliberative/public dialogue processes are anchored to elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Graham Smith preparing state of the art report on climate assemblies
items.b: Graham Smith, Director of the Centre for the Study of Democracy at the University of Westminster, is leading a Knowledge Network on Climate Assembly (KNOCA) workshop on a ‘playbook for climate NGOs’ on how to engage with climate assemblies, with the recording and slides available on the KNOCA site shortly.
items.why: it builds civic organisations' capacity to engage effectively with deliberative decision-making processes like climate assemblies.
items.note: Deliberative/citizens' assembly engagement is anchored to elections & decision making rather than participation.
links: Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: Constitutional turbulence calms under Sunak, according to Constitution Unit
items.b: A new blog from The Constitution Unit takes a closer look at the constitutional climate around Rishi Sunak’s government. In the article, Meg Russell and Alan Renwick suggest that Sunak’s premiership has been marked by a decline in constitutional turbulence compared to the recent past.
items.why: it assesses whether constitutional conventions and norms constraining executive power are being respected or eroded.

items.h: Fourth report of the United Kingdom Constitution Monitoring Group is published
items.b: The United Kingdom Constitution Monitoring Group (UKCMG) released its biannual report on the 23rd of March, warning that 2022 exposed a series of weaknesses in the UK constitution and the devolved systems of government. They also concluded that some UK ministers had exploited and aggravated these tensions highlighting that the constitutional abuses witnessed under Johnson were simply the beginning of a widening trend.
items.why: it documents ministers exploiting weaknesses in constitutional checks on executive power across the UK and devolved systems.

items.h: mySocietys asks, what if you could reshape democracy for the better — and you had 20 years to do so?
items.b: On 24th May at the Sheffield Festival of Debate (online and in-person) mySociety will be asking the question to an assembled panel and audience, inviting them to contribute their ideas to mapping the journey to democracy in 2043. RSVP now . But that’s not all — mySociety are busily preparing their big 20th anniversary event later this year, more on this soon.
items.note: Event listing and organisational anniversary promotion, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Potsdam researchers study effectiveness of three different deliberative participation formats
items.b: Researchers from the Research Institute for Sustainability (RIFS) in Potsdam undertook an analysis of three different deliberative participation formats around the same topic, with three-separate participant groups receiving the same briefing, working materials and tasks, but facilitated in three different ways — self-organised, a multi-method approach and the third through ‘dynamic facilitation’. Read more on the research here , thanks to Rebekah McCabe at Involve for highlighting!
items.why: it produces evidence on how different facilitation designs affect the quality of deliberative decision-making processes.
items.note: Deliberative process research is anchored to elections & decision making.

items.h: Is support for liberal democracy in crisis? A new study explores the trends and causes
items.b: A peer-reviewed Is Support for Liberal Democracy in Crisis? has been published in journal Political Insight and looks at the reasons and supporting data for the global drop in support for liberal democracies. The study examines how elements like populism, inequality, immigration, and media influence people’s perceptions towards democracy by analysing data from surveys, experiments, and social media.
items.why: it examines why public support for liberal democratic systems is declining, a core condition for democratic legitimacy and participation.
links: Is Support for Liberal Democracy in Crisis?

items.h: Humza Yousaf elected as SNP leader and Scottish First Minister
items.b: A total of 72,000 members were able to cast ballots in the SNP election, which was held both online and by mail. The winner, Humza Yousaf MSP , garnered 52% of the vote, with Kate Forbes MSP gaining 48%. Pro-independence Yousaf was widely considered the continuity candidate in the leadership election and has been described as socially progressive and as a Sturgeon loyalist.
items.why: it determines who leads a governing party and, consequently, who exercises the office of First Minister through an internal party election.

items.h: Former Chief Executive of the SNP arrested ‘as a suspect’ in SNP funding probe
items.b: Former Chief Executive of the Scottish National Party, Peter Murrell, has been arrested by Police Scotland ‘as a suspect’ as part of an ongoing inquiry into the fundraising and finances of the SNP. As husband to the former SNP party leader Nicola Sturgeon, the police’s actions are thought to include the search of their family home.
items.why: it concerns an investigation into a political party's campaign finances, bearing on transparency and integrity of party funding.
items.note: Party funding probes sit at the boundary of campaign finance (elections) and corruption (accountability).
links: has been arrested by Police Scotland

items.h: Men dominate 95% of local authorities in Britain, Democracy Club & Fawcett Society data shows
items.b: The analysis conducted by the Fawcett Society and Democracy Club reports that over 95% of local authorities are dominated by men , while only a third of local councillors are women and only 18 out of 382 councils have minimum gender representation parity. The data also shows that at a regional level, no council has gender parity and the proportion of women in councils has only grown by 2% since 2018. Fawcett Society partially attributes these low figures to sexism and harassment having been shown to be widespread throughout local councils, according to Fawcett research, as well as limited pare…
items.why: the underrepresentation of women in local councils affects the representativeness of elected institutions, a core measure of democratic legitimacy.
items.note: Proportion of women in elected bodies is an explicit elections_decision_making anchor rather than a general equality/participation issue.
links: 95% of local authorities are dominated by men

items.h: ‘Trailblazer’ devolution deal signed with Great Manchester Combined Authority
items.b: A ‘Trailblazer’ devolution deal has been signed by the Great Manchester Combined Authority transferring more control and influence over local economic policy. The deal involves changes to the ‘single funding settlement’ which will see Greater Manchester receive more money in the future and provide Mayor Andy Burnham and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority with more autonomy in how it’s spent. For Burnham’s reaction to the deal, hear him in discussion with Centre for Cities on the 12th of April. And finally, for a deeper dive into devolution frameworks, check out this report from The Nort…
items.why: devolving funding and policy control to a combined authority changes the structure and powers of local democratic decision-making.

items.h: Transparency International report lays bare revolving door between public and private office
items.b: Transparency International’s new report Managing revolving door risks in Westminster attracted front page attention last week with findings of over 170 ex-ministers and officials since 2017 taking jobs related to their old policy briefs . The comprehensive analysis sets out a range of policy recommendations to strengthen the scope of existing rules aimed at reducing the risk of corruption and damage to public confidence in government brought about by these behaviours, as well as suggestions to improve the oversight and enforcement of the revolving door — read the report .
items.why: the revolving door between public office and private interests raises risks of undue influence and weakens accountability mechanisms for those exercising public power.
links: Managing revolving door risks in Westminster
taking jobs related to their old policy briefs

items.h: 2022 was damaging for standards in public debate, according to Full Fact report
items.b: The new report entitled Informed citizens: Addressing bad information in a healthy democracy from political fact-checkers, Full Fact , raises concerns over voters’ access to good, reliable information last year. The report sets out 12 recommendations for politicians, media, and other organisations in public life to improve public trust, particularly around the issue of voting. These include calls for political parties to end ‘bullshit manifestos’ before the next general election and a new law to prevent deceptive campaign practices.
items.why: poor-quality information and deceptive campaign practices undermine the public's ability to make informed political choices.
items.note: Touches campaign practices but the core mechanism is the information environment, not electoral administration.
links: Informed citizens: Addressing bad information in a healthy democracy

items.h: First ever Whistleblowing Awareness Week held in parliament
items.b: WhilsteblowersUK held the first ever Whistleblowing Awareness Week in Parliament last month to raise awareness of the challenges faced by those who decide to speak out. They are pushing for new legislation to help protect individuals through the Protection for Whilsteblowers Bill . The bill intends to establish an Office of the Whistleblower to protect whistleblowers and aims to make it easier for people who can’t afford huge legal bills to speak out. The bill had its second reading in the Lords in December.
items.why: legal protection for whistleblowers enables exposure of wrongdoing and provides redress mechanisms essential to accountable governance.

items.h: Top UK lawyers refuse to prosecute climate activists
items.b: 120 top UK lawyers have signed a ‘Declaration of Conscience’ refusing to act in the interests of fossil fuel groups or prosecute climate activists for protesting against inaction on the climate crisis. The group recognise that continued fossil fuel development represents a ‘serious risk to the rule of law’, and called on fellow lawyers and the government to address the crisis. It is the first time in legal history that a collection of lawyers have engaged in a collective act of civil disobedience.
items.why: lawyers publicly refusing to prosecute protesters raises questions about the even and predictable enforcement of law against political dissent.
items.note: Also touches protest rights, but the framing centres on rule of law and enforcement discretion.

items.h: One-in-ten voters think Boris Johnson told the truth over partygate
items.b: Polling for the Byline Times has revealed that just one in ten voters think Johnson told the truth over Partygate and whether or not he broke lockdown regulations. Even Conservative voters have lost faith in the ex-Prime Minister with just 28% saying they thought he told the truth about the scandal. The poll suggests the routes back into public life for Johnson are becoming increasingly narrowed.
items.why: public confidence that a former Prime Minister lied to Parliament and the public bears on accountability of those who have exercised executive power.

items.h: Grants of up to £15,000 available for projects to support young people as active and engaged citizens
items.b: The new funding from the Institute for Community Studies (ICS) aims to support young people develop civic knowledge, skills, attitudes, behaviours and experiences — exploring how ‘policy scaffolding’ could better support them to become active citizens. Deadline is 11th April to apply — see more . ICS have also opened a Call for Evidence on their two-year Civic Journey programme exploring the ways in which young people get involved in civic life.
items.why: new funding creates concrete means for young people to develop civic skills and take part in democratic life.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating new participation opportunities counts under participation_civic_life.

items.h: Media Reform Coalition launch new membership offering
items.b: Deborah Grayson, Campaign Coordinator at the Media Reform Coalition , and their wider team, have developed a new membership structure for the community of passionate media activists and reformers working to build a healthier media system that serves the public interest in the UK. Membership is free, though donations to support their core activities are welcome. Join the Media Reform Coalition now .
items.note: Organisational membership admin, not a democracy story about changed participation mechanisms.
links: healthier media system that serves the public interest
Join the Media Reform Coalition now

items.h: Voice of the Listener and Viewer Spring Conference, 11th May
items.b: Their annual Spring Conference will be held on Thursday 11th May at the Geological Society in Piccadilly Central London. The event will include keynote speeches from Chair of the Lords Communications and Digital Committee, Rt Hon Baroness Stowell of Beeston MBE, and former Director General of the BBC, Lord Hall, CBE. Find out more on the Voice of the Listener and Viewer’s website .
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not a substantive democracy development.

items.h: Care about democracy? Worry about Twitter, says Joe Mitchell
items.b: Joe Mitchell, Programme Manager at Public Interest News Foundation argues that those that care about democracy should consider moving to decentralised platform Mastodon , highlighting social.coop, a democratically run cooperative instance of Mastodon as an ideal place to connect. Open Rights Group have even produced this video tutorial to how you might set up on Mastodon, check it out . (Democracy Club have set up their own Mastodon in the other place too — connect with them here )
items.why: it concerns whether concentrated corporate control of social platforms shapes the public information environment people rely on for political debate.
items.note: Advocacy piece about platform choice framed as bearing on media plurality.
links: social.coop, a democratically run cooperative instance of Mastodon

items.h: Surge in voters say BBC has a pro-government bias
items.b: New polling by Omnisis on behalf of the Byline Times found 41% of the public now think the BBC has a pro-government bias compared to 31% who said it was impartial. This figure has increased from 25% since the start of March, before the Lineker row. Asked who they trust the most to tell the truth out of Lineker, the BBC’s management, or the government, 39% picked Lineker, with just 11% picking the BBC’s management and 10% picking the UK government.
items.why: public trust in a major public-service broadcaster's impartiality affects the plurality and credibility of the information environment underpinning political debate.

items.h: Independent Community News Network partners with Google to enhance independent community journalism
items.b: A new partnership through the Independent Community News Network’s (ICNN) public interest news gateway, Ping News , will see Google partner with the independent news community. So far, forty-five independent news titles have signed up to the Google News Showcase allowing them to better connect with audiences. ICNN have said the financial support provided by Google will help build much-needed sustainability within the sector and will give greater exposure to local and hyperlocal titles.
items.why: sustaining independent local and community journalism affects the plurality and availability of public-interest information needed for democratic accountability.

items.h: Impress launch consultation to shape the future of independent media regulation
items.b: Impress has launched a six-week public consultation on its regulatory scheme and is looking for thoughts on a number of proposed changes. After a lengthy review process, Impress put forward a number of proposed changes, including to their membership eligibility criteria, transparency agreements and the investigations process. Respond to the consultation for a chance to shape the strategy of the UK’s only independent press regulator.
items.why: changes to the rules of an independent press regulator affect the structures that govern press freedom and accountability in the media environment.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation is looking for a Network Manager
items.b: Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) are hiring a Network Manager to help them maintain, grow and mobilise their network of news providers and support organisations across the sector. If you’re interested in supporting independent news providers and have a background in organising and capacity-building, apply before April 14th.
items.note: Job advertisement, organisational hiring news.

items.h: Extinction Rebellion’s The Big One four day action starts 24th April
items.b: With more than 70 organisations coming together to support the action, including Greenpeace, Friends of the Earth, PCS Union, to name a few, Extinction Rebellion’s next action kicks off at the end of this month, find out more . A core demand of the action includes a citizens’ assembly on the climate and ecological emergency.
items.why: it concerns citizens' readiness to mobilise and demonstrate, and includes a demand for a citizens' assembly, a deliberative decision-making mechanism.
items.note: Protest mobilisation framed as willingness to take part places it in participation; the citizens'-assembly demand touches decision-making machinery.

items.b: The UK Democracy Network maintains a full database of events from across the democracy sector.
View the database here — Have we missed something? Add it here !
Apply by 11th April: Creative Campaigner at The Small Axe (£31–39k)

items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Check-In . We were joined by Myf Nixon — mySociety, Rebecca McKee — Institute for Government, Jess Sargeant — Institute for Government, Rebecca Deegan — I Have A Voice, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Josiah Mortimer — Byline Times, Jessie Joe Jacobs - UK Democracy Network, Rosa Slater — The Politics Project, Laurie Moulton-Ulrich - Zero Hour, Susan Rosaway — Vocal Eyes CIC, Tom Brake — Unlock Democracy, Titus Alexander — Democracy Matters and Perry Walker — Talk Shop.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.h: Byline Times coordinating journalists on election day over voter ID concerns
items.b: With polling day coming up quick, Byline Times are organising journalists to report from polling stations across England on polling day to collate people’s experiences of voter ID. They want to hear from as many people as possible — if your org is working with voters or election workers/volunteers, get in touch!
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: voter ID requirements affect who can actually exercise their vote, and monitoring their real-world impact bears on electoral integrity and access to the franchise

items.h: Researchers for Fair Elections working to capture the stories of voter ID
items.b: Researchers for Fair Elections are a group of researchers who mission is to understand the qualitative impact of using voter ID in the UK, unaffiliated to any campaign or group. They are keen to hear the stories and experience of people using voter ID for the first time — share this survey through your networks and channels .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: understanding the practical impact of voter ID rules on voters bears directly on the accessibility and integrity of elections

items.h: The International Observatory on Participatory Democracy (IOPD) invites submissions for their best practice award
items.b: The annual IOPD Best Practice in Citizen Participation Award recognises successful experiences and public policies on citizen participation, community engagement, democratic engagement, public deliberation and open government. The deadline for submissions to the IOPD is May 31st — see more information .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: An award for others' participatory practices is sector admin/recognition, not a new mechanism for participation.
links: IOPD Best Practice in Citizen Participation Award

items.h: mySociety running a survey on their Freedom of Information tools
items.b: If you’ve used their WhatDoTheyKnow FoI service to discover something, or if you have memories of its earlier days, or if you just want to add your thoughts about its place in society, please fill in their survey .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: A feedback survey about an existing tool's history/reputation is sector admin rather than a change to participation or accountability mechanisms.

items.h: Government introduces anti-slow walking Statutory Instrument
items.b: In a bid to combat the threat of ‘walking slowly’ as a protest tactic by climate groups such as Just Stop Oil , the Government is bringing forward a Statutory Instrument to include the tactic as an example of ‘serious disruption’ . This is possible under the new powers granted by last year’s Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill to the Secretary of State, allowing them to redefine serious disruption by way of regulation .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: the government is using delegated powers to narrow the legal space for protest by redefining what counts as serious disruption, restricting citizens' ability to organise and dissent
items.note: Concerns legal restriction and state coercion of protest, so filed as rights/freedoms rather than participation.
links: climate groups such as Just Stop Oil
include the tactic as an example of ‘serious disruption’
redefine serious disruption by way of regulation

items.h: Public Order Bill coalition wrapping up
items.b: With the Public Order Bill (POB) due to receive Royal Assent today, the Public Order Bill coalition are wrapping up their regular meetings and updates on the passage of the Bill. Final updates and highlights from the coalition include:
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: the Public Order Bill receiving Royal Assent creates new legal restrictions on protest and assembly, narrowing the space for civic dissent
items.note: The coalition wrap-up itself is admin, but it reports the substantive change of the Bill becoming law.

items.h: Lords fail to pass two amendments to the POB suspicionless stop and search powers
items.b: The amendments would have introduced minimal safeguards for the stop and search procedures, requiring officers to provide their name, badge number and relevant details when conducting a search, as well as establishing a charter on the use of the powers setting out how they will be used, as well as an annual report on the use of the powers. The Lords refrained from making further amendments to the Bill.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this concerns whether suspicionless police stop and search powers over protesters carry safeguards against arbitrary state coercion
items.note: Stop-and-search policing power tied to protest is classified as rights/civic space per the policing-and-coercion boundary rule.

items.h: Some organisations from POB coalition will be convening a Civil Society Voice manifesto ahead of next year’s General Election
items.b: Please contact Amna Ahmad at the Democracy Network for more details on how to join the manifesto convening group. Liberty are creating a Know Your Rights resource for when the Bill passes.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: a civil society coalition is building new resources and a manifesto process to help people engage ahead of a general election

items.h: The Public Order Bill successfully secured the removal of Serious Disruption Prevention Orders without conviction from the Bill by way of government concession.
items.b: The threshold for SDPOs on conviction was also raised to two criminal offences/injunction breaches and the coalition removed the possibility of 24/7 electronic surveillance conditions being attached to them. Civil society groups also won important concessions on protecting journalists and legal observers.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: removing suspicionless protest-restriction orders and surveillance conditions changes the legal limits on state coercion over assembly rights

items.h: The Public Order Bill coalition also successfully threw out the Government’s attempts to introduce late-stage amendments
items.b: These conditions would have allowed police to impose conditions to pre-emptively restrict protests and further narrow the ‘reasonable excuse’ defence.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: defeating amendments that would let police pre-emptively restrict protests preserves the legal scope for freedom of assembly

items.h: Celebrating engagement and interventions speaking out against the Bill
items.b: In addition to cross-party parliamentarians across the Houses, five UN Special Rapporteurs , the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights , the Director of Public Prosecutions , former senior police advisors , health workers , environmental organisations , 20 faith leaders , and companies , all spoke out against the Bill — with more than 300,000 people signing a petition against the Bill too.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: widespread public and institutional mobilisation, including a mass petition, against a bill shows civic engagement in contesting legislative power over protest rights
items.note: Petitioning and public engagement filed under participation, though the underlying substance concerns civil liberties.
links: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights

items.h: Campaigners call for greater attention to women and girls in the Online Safety Bill
items.b: A joint campaign from Glitch and EE Hope United is calling for amendments to the Online Safety Bill to consider the specific risk of online abuse facing women and girls. In its current 262 pages, the bill fails to mention women and girls at all despite over half of the public (53%) thinking the internet is not a safe space for women. The campaign is calling on peers to support amendments to the bill, including a mandated Violence Against Women and Girls Code of Practice .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: the campaign seeks legal protection for women and girls from online abuse as a matter of personal security and gender equality as a right
links: Violence Against Women and Girls Code of Practice

items.h: Government waters down Retained EU Law Bill to just 800 pieces of legislation
items.b: The government has whittled down the proposed 4,000 pieces of legislation that might be scrapped by the end of the year as part of the Retained EU Law Bill to just 800. Opposition to the bill has been growing , with Tory peers recently announcing they would join a cross-party revolt in the House of Lords to oppose the legislation. With the prospect of lengthy delays to the passage of the bill, the recent concessions mean it is now expected to return to the House of Lords on the 15th of May.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: reducing the scope of executive power to unilaterally repeal retained EU law reflects a change in delegated powers and parliamentary constraint on the executive

items.h: Government forced to make concessions on the Strikes Bill
items.b: The government recently suffered a string of defeats in the Lords on the Strikes Bill , including that a consultation will have to be carried out and reviewed before the Secretary of State specifies minimum service levels.The bill is currently having its third reading in the Lords.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: Lords-imposed defeats requiring consultation before ministers can set minimum service levels constrain executive discretion and reassert legislative scrutiny

items.h: Register now for the Post-Election Debrief in London, May 24th
items.b: Join the Democracy Network for a series of lightning talks later this month to help unpack the elections. The hybrid event will feature brief talks from a range of those working on the frontlines of election delivery and campaigning — register now .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: Event listing/registration notice, not a democracy story.

items.h: New tactical voting tool StoptheTories.vote launches
items.b: The new tactical voting tool provides guidance for members of the public to help them tactically vote against the Conservative Party in their area. The tool also includes a vote reminder and a breakdown of this year’s contested seats by council .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new mechanism helping voters coordinate their choices in competitive elections.
items.note: New participation tool tied directly to voting mechanics, so filed under elections rather than general participation.

items.h: BBC launch new election widget
items.b: Resulting from a partnership between the BBC and Democracy Club , the new tool utilises Democracy Club data and API access to provide an accessible interface for voters to find out key information on elections in their area — check it out now .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new infrastructure helping voters access accurate information needed to exercise their vote.

items.h: Good Law Project preparing legal challenge over voter ID
items.b: Acceptable forms of voter ID have come to encompass the varieties of older persons photo ID, but specifically exclude the various forms of young person’s photo ID. Executive Director of the Good Law Project (GLP) , Jo Maugham KC, remarked that voter ID is ‘a needless act of sabotage against the universality of the franchise … an attempt to deny those likely to vote against the Government the ability to do so’. GLP’s team, led by a specialist King’s Counsel, will monitor the effects of voter on Thursday’s elections and bring a case against the Government to challenge these rules before the Gene…
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether voter ID rules unjustifiably narrow the franchise for certain groups of citizens.
items.note: Legal challenge mechanism noted as secondary, but core issue is franchise/voter ID scope.
links: will monitor the effects of voter on Thursday’s elections and bring a case against the Government

items.h: Green Party offers to sign up to an advertising code of conduct
items.b: Ahead of the General Election, the Green Party of England and Wales has offered to sign up to an advertising code of conduct in an effort to spur the major parties into pledging factual accuracy in electoral advertising, report Reform Political Advertising .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether political advertising during campaigns is held to standards of factual accuracy, shaping the information environment voters rely on.
items.note: Political advertising is anchored to information & public debate rather than campaign finance mechanics.
links: offered to sign up to an advertising code of conduct

items.h: Norwich Conservatives voter ID fiasco forces local party to rescind leaflet
items.b: Earlier last month, Norwich Conservative Federation distributed a leaflet designed by CCHQ telling voters that they don’t need ID to vote . After realising the apparent error, the local party suspended distribution of the leaflet design and promised to contact those who received the leaflet to correct the error. Local Tory leader Simon Jones described the affair as a ‘dreadful mistake’ .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because incorrect information about voter ID requirements can prevent eligible citizens from casting a valid vote.
links: telling voters that they don’t need ID to vote

items.h: Spotify run voter ID awareness campaign
items.b: Earlier this week music app Spotify ran a civic engagement campaign across their various platforms to raise awareness of voter ID requirements in this year’s local elections.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because raising awareness of voter ID requirements affects whether eligible citizens are able to vote.
items.note: Voter ID awareness treated as turnout/access mechanics under elections per standing rule.

items.h: Democracy Network host voter ID resources
items.b: Did you miss Democracy Network’s recent series of informative panel discussions focusing on voter ID? Fear not — you can view them now on DN’s voter ID resources page , alongside a range of other voter ID resources produced by democracy organisations.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because hosting voter ID resources helps ensure citizens understand and can meet requirements to exercise their vote.
items.note: Resource hosting treated as capacity-building tied to voter ID access, filed under elections.

items.h: Local Government Information Unit publish report on public attitudes towards local elections
items.b: The Local Government Information Unit (LGIU) has published a report in collaboration with Ipsos , producing polling data on public attitudes to local elections, the work of councillors and the role of local government. The report finds that 61% of the public want more information or a greater say in how decisions are taken at a local level. Read the report .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it measures whether the public feels informed and able to have a say in local government decisions and elections, bearing on the practical health of local democracy
items.note: Local government attitudes report sits between elections/local government structure and participation/sense of voice; classified under elections per the local-government boundary rule.

items.h: New report plots Labour’s path to power, whilst Onward discuss the future of Conservatism
items.b: Labour Together have published a new report assessing the possible paths to victory at the general election next year. The report outlines 6 core voter types Labour is targeting and their policy agenda for winning them over. Meanwhile, Onward are hosting the second of their debates on the ‘Future of Conservatism’ , discussing how the Conservative Party can meet the long-term challenges of their supporter base.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: Party strategy reports and internal debates about winning elections are political news rather than a democratic mechanism story.

items.b: The UK Democracy Fund are looking for a digital campaign consultant to assist in defining the bounds and activities of an effective digital voter participation campaign. View the advert for more information — deadline 22 May.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.b: Leeds Beckett Student Union (LBSU) are looking to take a fresh approach to how they represent and engage with their student body, and are soliciting support to develop a new democratic student engagement model. Find out more here .

items.h: Vocal Eyes Democracy CIC win Welsh Government democratic engagement grant
items.b: The Welsh Government has awarded Vocal Eyes CIC a democratic engagement grant to work with schools and families to increase engagement in community improvement and increase interest in local government and voter registration in the number one for lowest voter turnout and highest deprivation in Swansea.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it funds a programme to increase voter registration and local government engagement in an area with especially low turnout, expanding practical means of electoral participation
items.note: Framed as a grant win but describes a substantive new engagement programme touching voter registration, which is always classified under elections per the turnout rule.

If you can make it, please join us on May 22nd .

items.b: Also on May 24th, I Have A Voice are hosting an event and workshop as part of the Festival of Debate in Sheffield looking into how we might reverse declining trust and voter turnout trends — Sign up here .

items.note: Event listing/workshop announcement.

items.b: Next month the Democracy Network will be hosting Democracy Coworking in Edinburgh — stay tuned for more info, or subscribe to the Network’s newsletter for the latest updates.

items.h: Anti-monarchy protest set to disrupt King’s coronation as public support for the monarchy falls
items.b: Over 1000 anti-monarchy protesters will be heading to London this weekend to protest the coronation of King Charles. Campaign group Republic are organising the protest which they say will be ‘colourful and loud’ to make their presence heard despite the negligible coverage they expect to receive from the mainstream media. The protest comes as public support for the monarchy hits its lowest point yet.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because it shows citizens organising and turning out to publicly contest a state institution, reflecting willingness to take part in political life
items.note: Framed as protesters' organising and turnout rather than legal restriction or policing, so filed under participation rather than rights/civic space.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation hiring
items.b: Public Interest News Foundation are hiring multiple desk researchers and campaign coordinators for two consultancy projects. They’re also readying their 2023 Index of Independent Publishing in the UK for launch on May 24th, more news on that soon.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.b: Involve are on the lookout for a new Interim Director of Innovation and Practice . The successful candidate will take charge of their tendering process as well as leading on the delivery of projects for Involve. This is a six month appointment with full time, part time and flexible working options.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
links: Interim Director of Innovation and Practice

items.h: Olivia Blake MP to retable Climate & Ecology Bill
items.b: Oliver Blake MP (Lab) will be retabling the Zero Hour campaign’s Climate and Ecology Bill in the House of Commons on May 10th. The Bill includes provisions for the establishment of an advisory citizens’ assembly on the twin climate and ecological emergencies.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: this matters democratically because the bill would create a citizens' assembly, a deliberative decision-making mechanism, to advise on major policy
items.note: Citizens' assembly provision places this under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Mark the date — Sort the System: The Lobby for Equal Votes, 24th May
items.b: On the 24th May, Make Votes Matter , Electoral Reform Society, Politics for the Many, Open Britain, Compass, Unlock Democracy and Best for Britain are coming together under the banner Sort the System, holding a mass rally and mass lobby in Parliament Square for equal votes — find out more .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: This is an event/rally announcement (sector logistics) rather than reported change or new participatory infrastructure.

items.h: Institute for Government and Bennett Institute conducting Review of the UK Constitution
items.b: The Bennett Institute for Public Policy and the Institute for Government (IfG) are teaming up to conduct a major research programme into UK constitutional arrangements. Over the course of the review they will publish original research and guest papers, and will hold public events and private roundtable discussions across the UK. The programme includes an upcoming IfG paper on the constitutional implications of electoral reform, a paper by Meg Russell on Lords reform , and a final paper on embedding public engagement into constitutional change — contact Rebecca at the Institute for Government f…
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: a major research programme on UK constitutional arrangements, including Lords reform and constraints on executive power, informs how public power is structured and checked
links: a paper by Meg Russell on Lords reform

items.h: USDAW is latest Labour affiliate to back campaign for proportional representation
items.b: The Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers (USDAW) has become the latest Labour affiliated union to back the campaign for proportional representation , meaning two-thirds of Labour-supporting unions have thrown their weight behind the campaign. Caroline Osborne of Labour for a New Democracy states this now means there is an ‘undeniable consensus for a new electoral system’.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: growing union backing for proportional representation reflects shifting political support for changing how votes translate into seats, a core electoral system question
links: Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers (USDAW)
back the campaign for proportional representation

items.h: Wandsworth runs Citizens’ Assembly on Air Quality
items.b: A key manifesto pledge for the administration of the London Borough of Wandsworth, the Citizens’ Assembly forms a major part of their plans to review their Air Quality Action Plan and to set new targets to clean up the borough’s air. Fifty local residents have been brought together, selected by Sortition Foundation’s stratified selection processes, and facilitated by Shared Future , have been meeting on the weekends to deliberate a new plan . The process also included a five week pause between sessions to open up the discussions to the whole borough, using Pol.is .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: a citizens' assembly is a deliberative decision-making mechanism used by local government to shape binding policy
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's deliberative-process rule.

items.h: Constitution Unit ask — how can we fix our democracy?
items.b: Drawing on recent Constitution Unit research into public attitudes to democracy, Alan Renwick’s inaugural lecture will be discussing how we can work to heal our democracy. The hybrid lecture on the 16th May will be followed by a drinks reception and a chance to chat with other democracy enthusiasts — register now .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: This is an event listing (lecture and reception) rather than a reported change or new participatory resource.

items.h: Talk Shop setting up Win Win Workouts
items.b: Last month Talk Shop produced new discussion packs for Extinction Rebellion’s The Big One, for XR activists to collect, use and distribute locally. Perry and the team at Talk Shop are looking into setting up new in-person Win Win Workouts.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: creating new discussion packs and in-person deliberative workouts builds new means for people to take part in political and civic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new participatory tools.

items.h: Block on Scottish gender reforms to be challenged in court in watershed moment on devolution
items.b: Scottish ministers are launching a court challenge against Westminster’s veto of the Scottish Gender Recognition Reform Bill . Passed by MSPs last December, the Bill was then vetoed by the UK Government utilising Section 35 of the 1998 Scotland Act. The court case is being described as a ‘ watershed moment’ for Scottish devolution as constitutional experts fear Section 35 could be weaponised in the future to encourage further changes to Scottish legislation at the whims of Westminster.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: a court challenge over Westminster's veto of devolved legislation tests the constitutional balance of power between UK and devolved decision-making structures
items.note: Story concerns the structure and powers of devolved government, with a judicial review component.

items.h: Power to Change say government must devolve financial decision making to deliver impact on Levelling Up
items.b: A new report from Power to Change on the government’s Levelling Up strategy has found that just 11% of the public think the policy has had a positive impact , whilst 56% say it has had no impact at all, with a further 14% claiming a negative impact. The report makes a series of recommendations to improve upon the policy and deliver impact, including delegating financial decisions to those outside Whitehall.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: recommendations to devolve financial decision-making power away from Whitehall concern the structure of local and regional government decision-making
items.note: Devolution of financial decision-making structure falls under elections & decision making per the local/regional government rule.
links: 11% of the public think the policy has had a positive impact

items.h: Standards Committee demands tighter rules on APPG lobbying
items.b: The Committee on Standards is calling for tighter rules around All-Party Parliamentary Groups (APPGs) which are often funded by or closely linked to external organisations. A new report published by the committee recognised that APPGs can present ‘ a significant risk of improper access and influence by commercial entities or by hostile foreign actors ’, and is calling for annual income and expenditure statements to be produced by APPGs.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns lobbying transparency and conflicts of interest around parliamentary groups that can be used by commercial or foreign actors to gain improper influence over public power.
links: a significant risk of improper access and influence by commercial entities or by hostile foreign actors

items.h: Growing concerns over House of Commons scrutiny function, or lack thereof
items.b: ‘The Commons doesn’t really do the detailed scrutiny of legislation now,’ remarked Labour leader in the Lords, Baroness Angela Smith of Basildon to PoliticsHome . There is a purported growing unease amongst peers over the increasing workload of the House of Lords, with the Commons increasingly leaving the upper chamber to perform the bulk of scrutiny over government legislation, apparently as a result of a lack of trust of the Government in their own backbenches .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns whether Parliament is able to exercise meaningful legislative scrutiny over the executive.

items.h: Mile End Institutes reflects on Raab’s resignation as indicative of Minister-Civil Servant relations
items.b: Patrick Diamond and Dave Richards of the Mile End Institute take a look at what the resignation of Deputy Prime Minister Dominic Raab can tell us about current relations between ministers and civil servants, in particular the demise of the Public Service Bargain .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns the relationship between ministers and the civil service, which affects how executive accountability and administrative capacity function.

items.h: openDemocracy FOI request refused on public interest grounds
items.b: The government has refused to respond to a Freedom of Information request submitted by openDemocracy to ascertain the extent of their surveillance of human rights lawyers. Despite a public admittance from Robert Jenrick in February that the government is monitoring a ‘small number of legal practitioners’, the Home Office recently decided that revealing the full extent of their surveillance was not in the public interest.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns the use of freedom of information law to hold the government answerable for covert surveillance activity affecting legal practitioners.
items.note: FOI refusal treated as accountability mechanism per boundary rule, with surveillance of lawyers as a secondary rights concern.
links: refused to respond to a Freedom of Information request

items.h: Spotlight on Corruption report highlights government failure to implement ethics standards changes
items.b: Integrity Deferred? , a new report from Spotlight on Corruption , explores how the government has so far failed to implement crucial recommendations on upgrading ethics in government made by two major independent reports over 18 months ago. Sir Nigel Boardman’s report into the Greensill scandal and the Committee on Standards in Public Life’s Standards Matter 2 report , collectively outlined 57 recommendations for improving government ethics. The report states just 4 of the 57 recommendations (7%) have so far been implemented and 40 have had no action whatsoever.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns the government's failure to implement recommended reforms to ethics and standards regimes governing public office.
links: Committee on Standards in Public Life’s Standards Matter 2 report

items.h: Just Stop Oil protesters sentenced to nearly three years in prison
items.b: After scaling the QE2 Bridge in October last year, disrupting traffic for two days, Morgan Trowland and Marcus Decker will now spend three years and two and a half years in prison respectively, with Just Stop Oil remarking ‘ these are the longest sentences for peaceful climate protest in British history ’. Judge Collery KC handed down the sentence, commenting that the harsh sentence was due to deter copycat actions. There are currently two Just Stop Oil and five Insulate Britain activists serving time in prison for actions taken with the campaigns.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns the state's use of criminal sentencing to deter protest, bearing on the legal space available for assembly and dissent.
items.note: Protest sentencing treated under rights/civic space as it concerns legal restriction and state coercion, not willingness to participate.
links: these are the longest sentences for peaceful climate protest in British history

items.h: Richard Sharp quits as BBC chairman
items.b: The chair of the BBC, Richard Sharp, has resigned after a report found they failed to disclose potential perceived conflicts of interest during their appointment. Pressure has been mounting on Sharp to resign after it emerged that they helped facilitate a loan for Prime Minister Johnson who subsequently appointed them as chairman.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it concerns undisclosed conflicts of interest in a public appointment process for a body with responsibility for public-service media.
items.note: Primary is public appointments/standards; secondary reflects BBC's role in the media environment.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation to launch report on UK independent news provision
items.b: On Wednesday 24th of May, PINF will be launching their new report on the status of UK independent news provision . Now in its third year, the 2022–23 report received input from 100 independent news providers and provides a range of insights on revenue, staffing and impact across the sector. Join via Zoom to explore the key findings .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: it presents evidence on the health and capacity of independent news provision, which bears on media plurality in the UK's information environment.
items.note: Borderline between substantive research and event promotion; treated as democracy story due to its bearing on media plurality.
links: PINF will be launching their new report on the status of UK independent news provision
Join via Zoom to explore the key findings

items.h: Independent Media Association voices concern over Draft Media Bill
items.b: The Independent Media Association (IMA) has written to the government expressing concerns over the Draft Media Bill , specifically in relation to plans to repeal Section 40 of the 2013 Crimes and Courts Act . The IMA, a representative organisation for the independent media sector, asked why they weren’t consulted on the draft bill which could strip away key protections for independent news providers from the use of SLAPPs — a tactic of stifling investigative journalism with expensive legal actions.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: repealing legal protections against SLAPPs would let powerful actors use costly litigation to suppress investigative journalism that holds public power to account
items.note: SLAPPs and press protection framed as information environment issue rather than accountability mechanism itself.

items.h: Shocking slide in global media freedom revealed by new report
items.b: The World Press Freedom Index , published by advocacy group Reporters Without Borders , has found that media health is declining fast among an increasing number of countries due to the threats of propaganda, misinformation and artificial intelligence, including the UK. Would you like to know more?
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: declining global media freedom, including in the UK, weakens the plural information environment citizens need to scrutinise public power
links: found that media health is declining fast

items.h: World Press Freedom Day 2023
items.b: Today marks 30 years since the UN General Assembly proclaimed an international day for press freedom, held on 3 May every year — celebrating the importance of press freedom and freedom of expression. Dawn Alford, Executive Director of the Society of Editors said: ‘Now, more than ever, governments worldwide must look to uphold and strengthen their commitment to this vital human right’. Would you like to know more?
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.why: press freedom underpins the public's ability to access information and hold power to account, though this item is largely commemorative rather than substantive
items.note: Mostly a celebratory anniversary notice rather than reporting new developments.

items.h: Institute for Strategic Dialogue explore online support for proscribed groups in Northern Ireland
items.b: In recent months, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue ran preliminary scoping research across Facebook, TikTok and Instagram, finding a hive of activity amongst IRA, UVF, INLA, UDA, RHC and LVF proscribed groups — Read the report.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.note: Concerns proscribed paramilitary groups' online activity, a security/extremism issue rather than a democratic participation or information-environment mechanism.

items.b: The UK Democracy Network maintains a full database of events from across the democracy sector.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.b: View the database here — Have we missed something? Add it here !
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition

items.b: If you can’t make our monthly check-in, you can always drop in to the check-in document of the current month and add to it by going to democracymeetup.org.uk .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, 3rd May — Election Edition
items.sec: Featured Job Listings across the Democracy Sector

items.b: Fortnightly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Louise Dunmore and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : hello@democracynetwork.org.uk

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Check-In . We were joined by Kevin Keith — Open Government Network, Jessica Townsend — MP Watch, Ashok Viswanathan — PeoplePower, Calum Green — Involve, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Grace Barnett — Unlock Democracy, Shima Langan — Shout Out UK, Pip Eldridge — Voice of the Listener & Viewer, Natasha Kaeda — 50:50 Parliament, Myf Nixon — mySociety, Nancy Platts — Politics for the Many and Lara Parizotto — Migrant Democracy Project.
items.note: Event thanks/attendee list is organisational admin, not a democracy story.

items.h: Democracy Coworking
items.b: Spend a day working alongside other organisations working on UK democratic reform:
items.note: Generic coworking event listing without a specific participation mechanism created.

items.h: Launch of the Collaboration for Democratic Change Toolkit, 13th June 5.30pm — hybrid event
items.b: Join the UK Democracy Network on Tuesday 13th June for the launch of the new academic and practitioners toolkit. Hosted by the University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy , the evening will feature a panel discussion and roundtable discussions amongst practitioners, academics and funders exploring the challenges and opportunities for collaboration — Sign up now .
items.why: a new toolkit is launched to help civil society organisations collaborate more effectively on democratic reform, building sector capacity for participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource creation rather than mere event listing.
