links: University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: How to: AI & Democracy Workshop, June 29th 2.30pm
items.b: Join us on Thursday June 29th at 2.30pm for a special Zoom workshop focusing on how you can use new AI tools to supercharge your democracy work and campaigns — register now !
items.why: a new workshop equips campaigners with AI tools to strengthen their democracy work, expanding practical capacity to participate.
items.note: Sector capacity-building workshop counts as creating new means of participation.

items.h: PeoplePower running pilot constituency panels
items.b: Ashok Viswanathan of PeoplePower is setting up four constituency panels across the UK, in Islington North, Leeds East, Oldham & East Saddleworth and Uxbridge & South Ruislip. They are working to get endorsements on the pilot from MPs and similarly minded organisations, can you help?
items.why: new constituency panels are being created to give citizens a structured channel to engage with their MPs, expanding avenues for civic participation.
items.note: Constituency-level engagement structure counts as new participation mechanism, not an election itself.

items.h: Urgent call out for signatories against further restrictions to protest
items.b: The Public Order Act 1986 (Serious Disruption to the Life of the Community) Regulations 2023 will be voted on by peers on the 13th June, next week. Not only is this notable as another attempt to even further tighten the restrictions on protest, but also as unconstitutional in the way it is being brought forward, Dave Timms of Friends of the Earth argues, as these measures were already dismissed by peers during the passage of the Act, and are now being reintroduced through secondary legislation. Read the Liberty briefing here — Sign the open letter to Peers now — deadline 8 June. Contact Dave T…
items.why: proposed secondary legislation would further restrict the legal right to protest, narrowing the civic space for assembly and dissent.
items.note: Also raises accountability concerns as measures dismissed by peers are being reintroduced via secondary legislation to bypass debate.
links: Public Order Act 1986 (Serious Disruption to the Life of the Community) Regulations 2023
Sign the open letter to Peers now

items.h: DCMS launches pre-legislative scrutiny on the Draft Media Bill
items.b: The Media Bill will be the first time that the Communications Act has been updated since 2003. The deadline for pre-legislative scrutiny evidence closed 17 May. Pip Eldridge and the team at Voice of the Listener & Viewer have just submitted scrutiny evidence to the Committee.
items.why: the Media Bill will reshape regulation of broadcasting and communications, affecting the plurality and structure of the public information environment.

items.h: Government forced into concessions on Retained EU Law Bill
items.b: The UK Government has been forced into a number of concessions on the Retained EU Law Bill . The first amendment requires a schedule of any law that may be revoked to be referred to a Joint Committee of both Houses so that any possible revocation is debated and voted on by each House. A new clause has also been added to allow Parliament to prevent the revocation of any particular retained EU rights, powers and liabilities that are due to be revoked automatically at the end of 2023.
items.why: Parliament has secured new powers to scrutinise and vote on the revocation of retained EU law, strengthening legislative constraints on executive delegated powers.
links: new clause has also been added

items.h: Spotlight on Corruption dismayed at Government win on foreign donation law amendment
items.b: The government has voted down an amendment to the National Security Bill which could have tightened laws around foreign financing of political parties. Spotlight on Corruption say the move was a ‘badly missed opportunity to protect the next election from malign influences’ and is calling on parties to adopt their ‘Know Your Donor Policy’ to improve financial transparency.
items.why: it concerns whether campaign finance rules adequately prevent foreign influence over UK political parties and elections.
items.note: Campaign finance falls under elections & decision making even though framed as an accountability failure.

items.h: Republic forging ahead with plan to repeal the 2023 Public Order Act
items.b: Republic are working to bring together a coalition of organisations in an effort to get last year’s Public Order Act repealed in the wake of its apparent misuse at the King Charles’ coronation. If you’re interested in collaborating on this project, get in touch .
items.why: it concerns legal restrictions and policing powers affecting the right to protest and assemble.
items.note: Protest law is classified under rights & freedoms since the issue is legal restriction and policing, not willingness to participate.

items.h: UK has increasing levels of neighbourhood trust, says new KCL report
items.b: New research from the The Policy Institute at King’s College London has found that the UK has some of the highest global levels of neighbourhood trust . The report Love Thy Neighbour? found that 84% of the British public said they completely or somewhat trusted people in their neighbourhood — up from 78% in 2005.
items.note: General interpersonal neighbourhood trust is social capital, not a democratic mechanism.
links: UK has some of the highest global levels of neighbourhood trust

items.h: Open Government Network want ‘bold ideas’ for new National Action Plan
items.b: As part of the plan for their new 6th National Action Plan (NAP), the Open Government Network (OGN) are welcoming civil society input to propose and develop a platform of bold new ideas. These proposals will form the basis of discussions for a process of working alongside government to create new policy commitments ahead of the publication of the NAP at the end of the year. Reach out to Kevin Keith regarding any questions — or submit your ideas here .
items.why: it invites civil society to shape a formal government transparency and participation commitment, creating a channel for public input into policy.

items.h: 50:50 Parliament to host a commemoration of Emmeline Pankhurst 165th birthday
items.b: Hosted by Jess Philips at Westminster and run in partnership with Women in Public Affairs , the commemoration event of the suffragette leader will be held on Monday 17th July — stay tuned for more information . In other news, 50:50 are currently working on their GE strategy, to identify seats that could provide an opportunity for women to be selected and elected.
items.note: Mainly a commemorative event listing; the brief GE strategy mention is too incidental to carry the item.

items.h: Campaign Development Workshop update
items.b: Last week more than 40 member organisations of the UK Democracy Network came together to discuss proposals for joint campaigns on democracy in the UK. Participants considered four different types of campaigns. Look out for a full report in the coming weeks, but in the meantime, take a look at the event pre-read here .
items.note: Internal sector workshop discussion without a concrete new mechanism or change.
links: take a look at the event pre-read here

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project hiring Event Organiser
items.b: It’s full steam ahead at the Migrant Democracy Project , in preparation for a new voter registration programme they’re running with Shout Out UK and the Greater London Authority, they’re hiring a new Event Organiser — apply now . Meanwhile, the team at Migrant Democracy are focusing on trying to get Labour Party National Policy Forum representatives to table an amendment to the NPF paper on Residence-Based Voting Rights.
items.why: it involves a new voter registration programme and advocacy to extend voting rights based on residence, both matters of electoral participation and suffrage.
items.note: Hiring news itself is not a democracy story, but the registration programme and suffrage advocacy are.

items.h: Autonomy propose Universal Basic Income trial for England
items.b: Will Stronge, Director of Research at Autonomy , hopes the proposed pilot will ‘make the case for a national basic income and more comprehensive trials to fully understand the potential of a basic income in the UK’. Grange Big Local in East Finchley and Big Local Central Jarrow have led two years of community consultation to design a basic income pilot in their areas, the pilot would involve a £1,600 payment for two years. Find out more on the proposed pilot — Autonomy is now seeking funding for the research.
items.why: a basic income trial addresses the economic conditions and basic welfare that affect people's practical ability to participate in civic and political life.
items.note: Basic welfare and economic security are treated as egalitarian conditions for participation under this beat.

items.h: Shout Out UK running voter reg public awareness campaign with GLA
items.b: Partnering with the Greater London Authority on a large-scale public awareness campaign around voter registration and voter ID, Shout Out UK are currently recruiting focus groups with target demographics ahead of the main campaign.
items.why: a public awareness campaign on voter registration and voter ID directly affects people's practical ability to exercise the franchise
items.note: Turnout and registration campaigns are always classed under elections per the standing rule, even though this is sector capacity-building.

items.h: Joe Mitchell is Public Interest News Foundations’ new Deputy Director
items.b: Congratulations to Joe Mitchell, the new Deputy Director at the Public Interest News Foundation . Joe was formerly Head of Impact at PINF. They reflect on their two years of trying to bring about a healthier media culture in the UK, read Joe’s reflections .

items.h: Democracy Network are recruiting a campaigns officer
items.b: UK Democracy Network are recruiting a new Campaigns & Advocacy Officer (Maternity Cover) — the deadline has been extended for the role, apply by Sunday 11th 5pm .

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust is recruiting two new directors
items.b: The Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust is looking for two new directors to join the organisation and broaden the skills and diversity of the Board. A deep understanding of democracy is essential to the role and campaigning experience would be an added benefit. One of the two new Directors will chair the Trust’s Finance Committee monitoring the overall financial health of the Trust — Apply by June 11 .

items.h: mySociety run #Democracy2043 panel as part of Festival of Debate
items.b: As part of their 20th anniversary year, mySociety ran a fantastic discussion at the Sheffield Festival of Debate focused on looking ahead 20 years ahead to the world that might be, considering — what do we need to put in place now, to ensure a thriving future for all in 2043. Stay tuned for the livestream recording or follow mySociety on YouTube .
links: Stay tuned for the livestream recording

items.h: Unlock Democracy are tracking party manifesto development processes
items.b: Introduced by Tom Brake at the Democracy Network’s General Election Working Group, Unlock Democracy’s live document provides insight on the most recent intelligence and manifesto process from various parties — contact Tom Brake to view and access the document. Contact Democracy Network if you would like to join the General Election Working Group — the next GE Working Group meeting will be 26th June at 3pm on Zoom.
items.note: An internal working-group tracking document for sector advocacy, not a public-facing participation tool or reported change in party processes.

items.h: Senior Tory suggests voter ID scheme was a deliberative attempt to gerrymander elections
items.b: At the National Conservative Conference, Jacob Rees-Mogg suggested that voter ID was a ‘clever scheme’ by the party to swing voters in their favour. Rees-Mogg said ‘parties that try and gerrymander end up finding their clever scheme comes back to bite them, as dare I say we found by insisting on voter ID for elections’. Labour MP, Dawn Butler, is now calling for a parliamentary inquiry and possibly a police investigation to ascertain whether the scheme was indeed a deliberate and illegal way to swing votes. The Parliamentary Standards Commissioner noted that chamber conversations are not inclu…
items.why: allegations that voter ID requirements were deliberately designed to skew election outcomes go to the integrity and fairness of the electoral process
items.note: Also touches accountability via calls for a parliamentary inquiry, but the core mechanism is electoral integrity.
links: suggested that voter ID was a ‘clever scheme’

items.h: Local elections highlight failings of First Past the Post, say Electoral Reform Society
items.b: The Electoral Reform Society has unearthed a series of local councils with significant discrepancies between the vote share and final seat share. In Broxbourne, for example, the Conservatives gained 90% control of the council despite attaining just 50.3% of the vote. ERS said the First Past the Post system is ‘failing voters and failing communities’ , reiterating the need to introduce Proportional Representation.
items.why: disproportionate seat allocation relative to vote share under First Past the Post affects how fairly votes translate into representation
links: First Past the Post system is ‘failing voters and failing communities’

items.h: Voter ID chaos must not overshadow important electoral system reforms, says Institute for Government
items.b: Although voter ID grabbed most headlines in May, Peter Hourston at the Institute for Government highlights that these elections were the first in which the council mayor, metro mayor and police and crimes commissioner were elected via First Past The Post. Check out their blog for a range of local election takeaways that went unreported in the wider media.
items.why: it reports a change to the electoral system used to elect mayors and PCCs, altering how citizens choose these office-holders.

items.h: MP Watch prepares for new campaign in Lee Anderson’s constituency
items.b: Jessica Townsend and the team at MP Watch are currently recceing Lee Anderson MP’s constituency for a new campaign targeting the climate denialist MP, using similar methods to their well-known campaign Steve Baker Watch , in the constituency of the MP of the same name last year. They’re aiming for 100 of these campaigns by next year’s General Election. Contact Jessica to find out more .
items.why: it describes a civic campaign scaling up grassroots organising to scrutinise and hold an elected MP accountable to constituents.
items.note: Treated as civic capacity-building/organising rather than an accountability institution story since it is a campaign group's own expansion.

items.h: Hundreds descend on Westminster as part of mass lobby for equal votes
items.b: People joined the mass lobby from all over the country from Carmarthen to Cornwall, before joining Klina Jordan, Clive Lewis MP, Zack Polanski and others at a rally in the Emmanuel Centre. On the day of the mass lobby, a new poll found overwhelming support for changing the voting system , with only 1 in 5 Brits saying the system works well.
items.why: it concerns public mobilisation and evidence of support for changing the electoral system used to choose representatives.
links: joined the mass lobby from all over the country
overwhelming support for changing the voting system

items.h: Starmer hints at lowering the national voting age to include 16 and 17 year olds
items.b: Last month Keir Starmer made several comments hinting at possible expansions of the electoral franchise were Labour to win the next General Election. The Labour leader said it ‘does not pass the common sense test’ that EU nationals who have lived in the UK long-term can’t vote in general elections. He also remarked that allowing 16 and 17 year olds to vote was ‘not such an outlandish idea’, confirming that Labour is ‘looking at’ the option.
items.why: it concerns proposals to expand the franchise, directly affecting who can vote for representatives.

items.h: Lord Rennard calls for change in party finance regulation
items.b: Lib Dem Peer Lord Rennard highlights the growing arms race between the major parties over election campaign spend, as well as the corrupting influence of large donations — find out more .
items.why: it concerns campaign finance regulation, which governs fair competition for elected office.

items.h: Politics for the Many building the campaign for PR amongst the trade union grassroots
items.b: Politics for the Many is the trade union campaign for electoral reform and democratic rights. Nancy Platts and the team are collating a comprehensive list of trade union branches across the country to write to their members, invite them to events and involve them in the trade union campaign for proportional representation .
items.why: it concerns organising to change the electoral system, which determines how votes translate into representation.
items.note: Union organising is treated as secondary civic-society capacity building; the core topic is electoral system reform.

items.h: Involve launch call to use citizens’ juries to help set new rules for MPs
items.b: Calum Green, Director of Advocacy and Communications at Involve , reports that they are calling for new reforms to embed citizens’ juries at the heart of our democratic system , starting with juries to help set and evaluate new rules for MPs. Commissioning citizens’ juries to set these rules, check they work and even play a role in judging potential wrongdoing — as part of a wider effort — would help to rebuild trust in politics, they say , and it would appear economist Martin Wolf agrees .
items.why: it proposes using a deliberative process (citizens' juries) as new decision-making machinery to help set and enforce rules for MPs.
items.note: Per framework, deliberative processes like citizens' juries are anchored to elections & decision making even when the topic is MP standards.
links: embed citizens’ juries at the heart of our democratic system

items.h: Unlock Democracy launch new report on UK democratic backsliding, 26th June
items.b: Written by Professor Toby James of the University of East Anglia for Unlock Democracy , A New Charter to Renew Democracy: How Can We Reverse Democratic Backsliding in the UK? will document democratic backsliding in the UK since 2019, proposing a ten-point charter for how we might reverse this trend. Join the launch event online on 26th June at 6pm — Register now .
items.why: it concerns a report and proposed charter aiming to reverse erosion of checks and constraints on executive power since 2019.
items.note: Report covers broad, unspecified backsliding across multiple beats; classified under accountability as the closest overarching frame.

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny publish their ‘first look’ at the new Devolution Accountability Framework
items.b: The Centre for Governance and Scrutiny has taken a ‘first look’ at the English Devolution Accountability Framework , published by the government in March. The Accountability Framework has been anticipated since the issuing of the Levelling Up White Paper . This key contribution from CfGS takes a look at the framework’s key themes and components, outlining their impact on officials working in local and combined authorities.
items.why: it concerns the structure and accountability mechanisms governing devolved combined authorities, shaping how devolved power is exercised and checked.
items.note: Devolution structure/accountability framework falls under elections & decision making per the local government boundary rule.

items.h: Institute for Government explores the impact of devolution on regional growth
items.b: The Institute for Government has published a new report How can devolution deliver regional growth in England? looking at the link between devolution and economic performance. The report suggests the devolution of key economic policies — such as transport and skills — is a good start, but calls for an extension of the ‘trailblazer devolution’ deals agreed with Greater Manchester and the West Midlands to other combined authorities.
items.why: it examines which policy powers are devolved to sub-national government, affecting the structure of devolved decision-making.
items.note: Devolution structure/powers falls under elections & decision making.
links: How can devolution deliver regional growth in England?

items.h: Fiscal devolution is moving out of the wilderness, reports New Local
items.b: In an exciting turn of events for devolution wonks, Jessica Studdert’s new report talks fiscal devolution and how it is finally making a show after its long exile as being seen as too radical for the UK. Recently Leeds City Council Chief Exec Tom Riordan said fiscal devolution ‘isn’t about a zero-sum game of who raises the tax, it’s actually about doing it better and raising it more effectively’.
items.why: it concerns whether local authorities gain taxation powers, affecting the structure of devolved decision-making.
items.note: Fiscal devolution is treated as structure of local government under elections & decision making.
links: zero-sum game of who raises the tax, it’s actually about doing it better

items.h: Parliamentary scrutiny is becoming increasingly difficult, says the Institute for Government
items.b: ‘Legislating at speed’ during the Brexit and Covid crises has become a regular feature of government, Dr Alice Lilly from the Institute for Government writes in an article for PoliticsHome . Far more ‘skeleton legislation’ is now being introduced to parliament with limited time for MPs and Peers to effectively scrutinise and amend new bills, says Dr Lilly.
items.why: it concerns Parliament's diminishing capacity to scrutinise and amend legislation, weakening a core check on executive power.

items.h: Labour Party bars sitting directly elected mayor from re-selection
items.b: The party leadership has blocked sitting directly elected North of Tyne Mayor Jamie Driscoll from the long list for next year’s elections. The move has caused consternation amongst key party figures and union leaders , with Driscoll considering legal action against the Party. Labour justified the action on the grounds of anti-semitism .
items.why: it concerns a political party's control over candidate access to an elected office, affecting political competition ahead of an election.

items.h: Government ignored official warnings on overseas donations to political parties, openDemocracy reveals
items.b: Security Minister, Tom Tugendhat MP, ignored explicit written warnings from the Electoral Commission regarding election law loopholes that could be allowing backdoor donations from foreign actors to British political parties. A letter from the Chair of the Electoral Commission, obtained by openDemocracy through an FOI request, highlighted the need for stronger controls on donations to ‘address the risk of foreign interference in UK political campaigns’, but received no reply from Tugendhat.
items.why: it concerns loopholes in campaign finance law that could allow foreign interference in UK elections, and government inaction despite regulator warnings.

items.h: Coronation policing is an everyday experience for marginalised groups, say campaigners
items.b: The outcry over the Public Order Act and the policing of the coronation protests is long overdue, say campaigners. Zita Holbourne, human rights campaigner at African, Caribbean and Asian Lawyers for Justice , said minority groups face ‘heavy handed’ and ‘dispproportionate’ policing in everyday life, not just at protests. The civil society and media response to the use of the new laws is another reminder that some voices in society matter and are listened to more than others, they said.
items.why: it concerns disproportionate policing of protest and assembly rights among marginalised groups, a matter of state coercion and equal protection.
links: African, Caribbean and Asian Lawyers for Justice

items.h: Tory MP demands action to address sexual harassment in Parliament
items.b: In light of the suspension of Labour MP Geraint Davies and Julian Knight MP (now restored), Caroline Nokes, Conservative Chair of the Women and Equalities Commission, has reiterated the need for a formal mechanism to address sexual harassment in parliament. An Independent Complaints and Grievance Scheme does exist to allow staff to report misconduct, but Nokes wants MPs to sign a Code of Conduct committing them to losing the whip if they are found guilty of harassment.
items.why: it concerns standards of conduct and accountability mechanisms for elected representatives within Parliament.

items.h: Transparency International UK working with Labour on ethics commitments
items.b: Transparency International report that they are working with the Labour Party shadow team to influence Labour’s integrity and ethics commission commitment, with a view to engaging with parliamentary candidates on these areas in future.
items.why: it concerns civil society shaping a political party's future commitments on standards and integrity in government, which bears on accountability mechanisms once in office.

items.h: Growing concerns over facial recognition surveillance, argue Big Brother Watch
items.b: Biometric Britain: The Expansion of Facial Recognition Surveillance , a new report from Big Brother Watch , demonstrates the proliferation of facial recognition technology in the UK without democratic approval or oversight. The research details how law enforcement, businesses, technology companies, and even some schools are investing heavily in this intrusive technology.
items.why: unchecked expansion of facial recognition surveillance without democratic oversight threatens privacy and civil liberties central to citizens' freedom from unwarranted state and corporate monitoring.
links: Biometric Britain: The Expansion of Facial Recognition Surveillance

items.h: Culture of harassment and mishandling of complaints is producing surge in unionisation of MP’s staff, says GMB Union
items.b: Union membership amongst MP’s staff working in Parliament has increased by 1000% since the GMB Members’ Staff branch was relaunched in 2020. Jenny Symmons, chair of the branch, said the increase is due to a culture of harassment in parliament and the inadequate response to complaints from parliamentary authorities and political parties.
items.why: the surge in unionisation reflects staff exercising freedom of association to seek redress for workplace harassment within Parliament, a core civic freedom.
items.note: Trade unionisation of parliamentary staff is classed under freedom of association for civic/professional bodies, not participation.

items.h: New report unpicks the challenges and renewed importance of regulating political finance
items.b: As part of their review of the UK constitution, the Institute for Government and the Bennett Institute have published a report exploring political financing, which until the year 2000 was effectively unregulated. The Regulation of Political Finance: Choppier Waters Ahead? looks at the challenges presented by technological change, internationalisation and the growth of non-party actors, as well as how the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act can be updated to meet the changing landscape.
items.why: regulation of political finance directly governs how parties and candidates compete for power and how campaign funding shapes electoral fairness.
links: Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act

items.h: Civic Power Fund reflects on how grassroots community funding can be improved
items.b: Last month the Civic Power Fund and Joseph Rowntree Foundation came together with Martha Awojobi and JMB Consulting to discuss how funders can better support grassroots organisations working to shift the balance of power in society. Check out some of the reflections from Martha Mckenzie, Executive Director of Civic Power Fund, on how the funding process can be modernised with beneficiaries in mind.
items.note: A reflective discussion on funding practice without a concrete new resource, tool or mechanism created.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch State of the Sector Report — Index 2023
items.b: PINF have launched their 2023 report on the state of the UK independent media sector based on over 100 responses from small publishers across the country — read it here . But that’s not all — they’ll soon be launching their new UK Local News Map. In development since 2022, the Map outlines the independent news sector, listing more than 2,000 small news publishers across the UK. Stay tuned!
items.why: mapping and reporting on the independent local news sector documents the health of media plurality that underpins informed public debate.

items.h: Hack the Press is back — join the hackathon, 24 & 25th June
items.b: Hack the Press (HTP) is a community of technologists and journalists working together to create a healthier media landscape in the UK. This will be their first hackathon since before the pandemic — Take a closer look .
items.note: An event listing/call to join a hackathon rather than a report of a created resource or change.

items.h: Two-thirds of the British public believe the press acts unlawfully
items.b: A new poll from Omnisis has revealed that 63% of the public does not think the British press act within the law. This deep public mistrust was shared across the political divide, with all age groups, aside from those over 75, registering a concerning lack of trust in the mainstream British media.
items.why: widespread public belief that the press acts unlawfully reflects a breakdown in trust in the information environment that citizens rely on for democratic debate.
items.note: Poll on public trust in media, bordering on the excluded 'public trust' lens but tied to the information environment beat.
links: new poll from Omnisis has revealed

items.h: Progressive media outlets refused entry to National Conservative Conference
items.b: A number of left-leaning media outlets including openDemocracy , Novara Media and the Byline Times were refused entry to the NatCon Conference earlier this month. Despite applying in advance for press passes, the organisations were denied access due to ‘high demand and limited space’ — although openDemocracy later discovered other outlets were granted entry despite applying just days before the conference began.
items.why: selective denial of press access based on outlet viewpoint undermines plural media coverage of political events and journalists' ability to scrutinise power
items.note: Treated as press/media plurality issue under information_debate rather than a pure discrimination claim.
links: refused entry to the NatCon Conference

items.h: UK anti-SLAPP coalition launches their website
items.b: The UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition is an informal working group researching and documenting the use of SLAPPs as well as advocating for reforms to prevent their use. On the 24th of May they launched their website which will serve as a repository for everything related to SLAPPs , including the model UK anti-SLAPP law, case studies of SLAPPs, a resource library, and practical advice for those targeted with SLAPPs.
items.why: the launch of a resource hub creates new means for journalists and civil society to resist SLAPPs, which chill public-interest reporting and civic scrutiny
items.note: Classified as sector capacity-building (new tool/resource) though the underlying topic, SLAPPs, is anchored in information_debate.

items.b: The UK Democracy Network maintains a full database of events from across the democracy sector.
View the database here — Have we missed something? Add it here !

We are making some changes to the Democracy Map, Jobs, Events and Funding Airtable lists over the next month, whilst those changes are underway, the jobs and events lists may appear out of date, apologies for the inconvenience.
items.sec: Featured Job Listings across the Democracy Sector

items.b: Monthly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding, Louise Dunmore and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : hello@democracynetwork.org.uk

items.h: We’ve added new ongoing ‘Civic Tech’ & ‘Democratic Economy’ sections to this month’s Bulletin
items.b: You can join the UK Democracy Network as a member here . You can read and subscribe to the UK Democracy Bulletin on Medium . It’s time for the Democracy Network’s Annual Survey — take our survey and claim your £10 voucher
links: take our survey and claim your £10 voucher

items.b: Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Check-In . We were joined by Ellen Berry — UK Democracy Fund, Nathan Young — Viewpoints, Myf Nixon — mySociety, Edward Saperia — Newspeak House, Miriam Levin — Engage Britain, Joe Mitchell — Public Interest News Foundation, Flynn Devine — Alan Turing Institute, Liz Crosbie — Reboot GB, Zoë Wilkins — People Powered, Lara Parizotto — Migrant Democracy Project, Bartek Staniszewski — Bright Blue, Gloria Dawson — Research for Action, Mohammed Afridi — Civic Power Fund, Martyn Harris — North Warks & Nuneaton and Bedworth Councils, Arthur R…

items.h: Urgent call out for signatories against removal of EU citizens’ voting rights
items.b: Migrant Democracy Project has prepared an open letter to be sent to the Minister for Levelling Up regarding a draft Statutory Instrument to implement the removal of the voting rights of EU citizens. Sign the open letter here — contact Lara Parizotto and the team for more info.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether EU citizens retain the right to vote, directly affecting the franchise and suffrage.
links: contact Lara Parizotto and the team

items.h: Open Rights Group submit open letter calling for improvement of the Online Safety Bill
items.b: Open Rights Group have brought together dozens of organisations to submit an open letter calling for improvements to be made to the Online Safety Bill , which is now coming to the end of Committee Stage in the House of Lords. The letter focuses on key issues with the bill, namely the undermining of end-to-end encryption.
items.why: this matters democratically because undermining end-to-end encryption affects citizens' privacy and freedom from surveillance.
items.note: Classified under rights/privacy rather than information_debate because the letter's focus is encryption/privacy, though the bill also touches the information environment.
links: open letter calling for improvements to be made to the Online Safety Bill

items.h: International Labour Organisation says UK Govt must modify strike laws in line with international standards
items.b: The UN labour standards body, the International Labour Organisation (ILO), has told the UK Government they must seek technical assistance from the agency’s experts to ensure the Strikes Bill conforms to international rules on freedom of association. The ILO is urging the government to improve consultation with unions and limit government powers to ensure worker autonomy is not impeded.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether trade unions retain freedom of association and autonomy from government restriction.

items.h: SLAPP legal protections to be added to Economic Crime Bill
items.b: An amendment offering specific protections in law for journalists and individuals at risk of being targeted by Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs) is to be added to the Economic Crime Bill . The Society for Editors described the amendment as ‘a welcome and significant first step’ in tackling SLAPPs but suggested further protections and penalties are needed to deter the use of SLAPPs as an attractive vehicle for harassment.
items.why: this matters democratically because legal protection against SLAPPs affects journalists' ability to conduct public-interest reporting without intimidation.

items.h: Upcoming London Democracy Coworking
items.b: Democracy Network has been running a series of increasingly popular Democracy Coworking sessions every month since March 2022 — this month we’ll be heading back to Demos’ offices on Whitehall for 28th July . We’ll be pausing for August as the holiday season takes over, and then we’ll be running sessions in Manchester, Brighton, Cardiff, London and Edinburgh in September and October — Register now .
links: heading back to Demos’ offices on Whitehall for 28th July

items.h: Are you getting ready for party conference season? Democracy Network want to know
items.b: Democracy Network are tracking who’s doing what within the democracy sector this conference season , are you organising an event, canvassing party members, organising a conference vote? We’re looking to understand who’s doing what, to better understand how the wider democracy movement can help support them, the Network are looking to partner on events, contact Democracy Network Director Jessie Joe Jacobs if you’d like support, speaking opportunities or sponsorship — add your party conference activities into this sheet .
links: tracking who’s doing what within the democracy sector this conference season
contact Democracy Network Director Jessie Joe Jacobs if you’d like support, speaking opportunities or sponsorship

items.h: Launch of the Collaboration for Democratic Change Toolkit
items.b: This month Graham Smith, George Bolton and members of the Democracy Network gathered to celebrate the launch of the Collaboration for Democratic Change Toolkit. The toolkit outlines how practitioners and academics can more effectively collaborate and sustain relationships — to support this work, a new Network of Democracy Academics & Practitioners (NDAP) launched to carry forward and build on the work of the Toolkit — Download the Toolkit and contact Graham Smith to join the NDAP group .
items.note: This is sector organisational news about practitioner-academic collaboration rather than a new means of public participation.
links: contact Graham Smith to join the NDAP group

items.h: JRRT hiring new Grants & Learning Manager
items.b: This one’s hot off the press from Nicky Milstead and the team at the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust — they’re on the lookout for a new Grants & Learning Manager focused on democracy — deadline 3rd August. Apply now .

items.h: People’s Powerhouse Community Map
items.b: Are you a change making organisation or movement builder in the North of England? People’s Powerhouse want to meet you — add your organisation to their Community Map now!
items.why: This matters democratically because building a network map of change-making organisations creates new practical means for people to organise and take part in civic life.

items.h: Alliance Now launches
items.b: Bringing together 99% Rising, The 99% Organisation, Take Back Britain, Open Britain, Citizens Network and Reboot GB, the Alliance Now (ALL) coalition soft launched last week, releasing their two key documents: The Citizens’ Declaration and the Good Guide to Government . The ALL welcomes other organisations across the democracy movement to join them — Contact ALL Project Leader Liz Crosbie to find out more and get involved.
items.why: This matters democratically because launching a coalition and shared civic documents creates new infrastructure for collective participation in the democracy movement.

items.h: mySociety kick off new Repowering Democracy blog series, tell them about their first 20 years
items.b: In this series of blog posts, mySociety will hear from guest bloggers who think deeply about how our democracy works, and are at the frontlines of trying to improve it — read more about it and sign up here . mySociety also wants to hear from you if you’ve any anecdotes, stories or thoughts about their work over the past twenty years — get in touch here and let them know .
links: get in touch here and let them know

items.h: 50:50 Parliament to host a commemoration of Emmeline Pankhurst 165th birthday
items.b: Hosted by Jess Philips at Westminster and run in partnership with Women in Public Affairs , the commemoration event of the suffragette leader will be held on Monday 17th July — stay tuned for more information . In other news, 50:50 are currently working on their GE strategy, to identify seats that could provide an opportunity for women to be selected and elected.
items.note: Primarily a commemorative event notice rather than a created participation mechanism or reported change.

items.h: Power for Democracies looking to test effectiveness of democracy supporting organisations
items.b: Positioning themselves as a non-profit democracy charity evaluator, Power for Democracies are looking to build an evidence base on effective ‘pro-democracy activities’ and the ‘efficient NGOs carrying them out’ — based on this research the organisation will make recommendations for donors who want to support democracy as effectively as possible — one to watch .
items.note: Concerns evaluating democracy-support organisations as a sector, not a public participation mechanism.

items.h: Common Sense is looking for new freelancers and volunteers
items.b: Common Sense is about to commission a range of new documentaries, shows and projects and is looking for freelancers and volunteers to join the team. They have a wide range of vacancies available, so check out what’s on offer and complete their application form .

items.h: DemocracyNext to launch guide on setting up citizen’s assemblies
items.b: Next month, DemocracyNext will be sharing a new ‘Assembling an Assembly Guide’. The guide will walk visitors through the key design elements and principles of running a successful citizens’ assembly, and will offer guidance on adapting it to one’s community or context. Keep your eyes peeled for the release.
items.why: This matters democratically because a practical guide to running citizens' assemblies expands the means available for communities to conduct deliberative collective decision-making.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rules, not participation.

items.h: New Conservatives faction forms
items.b: A new right-wing Tory faction has emerged, the New Conservatives count 25 MPs among their number, entirely drawn from the 2017 and 2019 intakes. The new grouping is focused on cutting migration, law and order and ‘woke issues’.
items.note: Reports the formation of a parliamentary faction without engaging a specific democratic mechanism such as party competition rules or scrutiny powers.

items.h: Conservative Democratic Organisation launches
items.b: It’s a bumper crop of right-wing Tory factions this month, with a new grassroots-focused Conservative Democratic Organisation launching. The group, seemingly aimed at empowering the Tory grassroots and internal party reform, is allegedly funded by a prominent donor of the 2011 No to AV campaign, opposed to electoral reform.
items.why: This matters democratically because internal grassroots reform of a political party affects how that party selects leaders and candidates and thus shapes political competition.
items.note: Treated as elections/parties territory since it concerns internal party organisation and control, not general policy controversy.

items.h: New GLA Voter ID grants available, deadline 14th July
items.b: The Greater London Authority (GLA) is running phase two of their Voter ID Awareness Campaign Grants as part of its Civic and Democratic Participation Programme. There is a £556,900 funding pot for this work, with organisations able to apply for grants between £25,000 and £50,000 — Apply now .
items.why: This matters democratically because voter ID awareness campaigns affect people's practical ability to meet identification requirements and cast a vote.
items.note: Voter ID access mechanics fall under elections per the turnout/access boundary rule.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund seeking digital expertise for new voter participation campaign
items.b: Ellen Berry at the UK Democracy Fund is looking for ambitious and effective non-partisan digital campaigns focused on voter participation. The Fund is looking to potentially fund and seriously scale up their work to hit their target goal of one million more people from lower propensity voting groups to register and vote in the next General Election — contact Ellen for more information .
items.why: This matters democratically because campaigns to register and mobilise lower-propensity voters directly affect electoral turnout and participation.
items.note: Turnout and voter registration campaigns always sit under elections & decision making per the framework's settled rule.

items.h: Newspeak House spinning up project to help new MPs set up their offices effectively
items.b: Edward Saperia of Newspeak House — the London College of Political Technology , reports that they are undertaking the first phase of work on a new project to update and maintain best practice around setting up new MPs offices effectively, in light of changing technologies and organisational practices. The first phase, user research with MP office staff has started this month — so if you know any MP staffers that might be up for a chat, let Ed know — whilst they’ve received some small seed funding for this first phase, they are looking for funding opportunities for the remaining £85,000 to comp…
items.note: Helping MPs set up constituency offices is operational/administrative support, not a democratic mechanism of scrutiny or participation.
links: Newspeak House — the London College of Political Technology

items.h: VocalEyes looking for funding to upgrade their platform
items.b: VocalEyes CIC runs an amazing and long-running community participation and engagement platform. With a decade of success behind them they’re looking to the future and — importantly — a tech upgrade for their 10 year old platform. They’re looking for funding to expand, as well as to develop their tech stack, including the use of new generative AI. Can you assist them, or any have leads for them to follow up? Contact Arthur at VocalEyes . Multitudes Foundation offer € 10,000 ideation grants As part of a Europe wide fund, changemakers can apply for this Multitudes Foundation £10,000 grant to deve…
items.note: Funding requests to upgrade an existing platform and a generic ideation grant are sector funding logistics rather than a new participatory mechanism.

items.h: Power to Change Discovery Fund closes 21 July
items.b: Offering £10,000 to explore a community tech solution, with an additional £2,000 to fund capacity to engage with their community of practice, free courses including a structured design course and Open Working and Reuse course — the Power to Change Discovery Fund closes on 21st July — Find out more .
items.note: A generic funding call for community tech solutions, without a specified democratic participation mechanism.

items.h: People Powered launch new accelerator programmes on climate and digital policy
items.b: The People Powered accelerator programmes aim to support participants to design a participatory process, paired with a mentor and combined with an implementation grant of $15,000 on completion, with the possibility of a further $100,000 grant follow up award. The deadline of the call for applicants is July 15th — see the relevant pages on climate and digital policy to apply or contact Zoë Wilkins for more info.
items.why: This matters democratically because the accelerator programmes create new participatory processes through which citizens can help design and shape policy.
items.note: Counted under sector capacity-building since it launches new means for people to take part in participatory design processes.

items.h: Landecker Democracy Fellowship opens
items.b: With €15,000 available to support their ideas through the Fellowship programme , Fellows will also receive support from the Humanity in Action network and hands-on training. This year, Humanity in Action are looking to support projects in line with their theme of Democracy and the Politics of Memory — Apply now .
items.note: A fellowship funding call on a broad thematic area, without a specified participatory mechanism, treated as sector funding logistics.
links: €15,000 available to support their ideas through the Fellowship programme

items.h: Large scale democracy funding round from Open AI closes
items.b: Flynn Devine at the Alan Turing Institute reports that Open AI recently welcomed applications from across the world to apply for their Democratic Inputs to AI funding round, making £100,000 available to 10 projects exploring democratic processes for deciding what rules AI should follow. Winners will be announced by July 14th.
items.note: This is an international funding call announcement, not a UK democracy mechanism or a completed capacity-building resource.

items.h: Catalyst publish list of third sector funding opportunities
items.b: Catalyst has published a full list of third sector funding organisations — check it out now, we’ll be sure to add this to our new democracy resources libraries launching next month!
links: published a full list of third sector funding organisations

items.h: At least 14,000 unable to vote at local elections, according to Electoral Commission interim report
items.b: New research from the Electoral Commission has revealed that a minimum of 14,000 were unable to vote at the local elections because they lacked an acceptable form of ID. The actual figure is likely to be far higher, however, as almost 40% of polling stations used ‘greeters’, tasked with telling voters before they went in that ID was needed. Their full report releases in September following more extensive feedback from stakeholders, councils and civil society organisations.
items.why: it shows voter ID requirements are preventing eligible citizens from casting their vote, directly affecting electoral access and participation.
links: 14,000 were unable to vote at the local elections

items.h: Unlock Democracy are tracking party manifesto development processes
items.b: Introduced by Tom Brake at the Democracy Network’s General Election Working Group last month, Unlock Democracy’s live document provides insight on the most recent intelligence and manifesto processes from various parties — contact Tom Brake to view and access the document. Contact Democracy Network if you would like to join the General Election Working Group — the next GE Working Group meeting will be meeting at 10am 26th July on Zoom.
items.note: This is primarily a working-group networking notice with contact/meeting logistics rather than a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Association of Electoral Administrators publish post-poll report
items.b: The new report Under pressure: increased demand on the UK electoral system outlines concerns that only a major electoral failure will focus attention on the UK electoral system’s vulnerabilities. Launching the report, AEA chief executive Peter Stanyon said: “Stacking significant changes on endemic issues is increasing risk for all elections, but especially a high turnout general election.”
items.why: it highlights systemic vulnerabilities in the administration of elections that could undermine well-run, competitive polls.
links: Under pressure: increased demand on the UK electoral system

items.h: Councils begin planning for a snap General Election
items.b: According to Martyn Harris , Head of Elections at North Warwickshire and Nuneaton & Bedworth Councils, planning has begun for a potential snap General Election, as well as for the PCC and local elections in May 2024.
items.why: it concerns the operational readiness of election administration for a potential general election and other polls.

items.h: Best for Britain to launch tactical voting campaign as polling reveals Labour’s lead is in jeopardy
items.b: Polling from Best for Britain suggests that Labour’s potential 470 seat majority could be in jeopardy should Reform UK stand down candidates in target Conservative constituencies. In response, Best for Britain is planning their biggest ever tactical voting campaign ahead of the election to encourage voters to vote for the party most likely to beat the Conservatives.
items.why: it concerns campaign strategy and political competition aimed at shaping electoral outcomes.
links: planning their biggest ever tactical voting campaign

items.h: Boris Johnson resigns sparking wave of by-elections
items.b: Former Prime Minister, Boris Johnson, resigned as an MP in early June, preempting the outcome of the Privileges Committee Report into lockdown partying. Their resignation, along with allies Nadine Dorries and Nigel Adams, has prompted upcoming by-elections in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, Selby and Ainsty, and mid-Bedfordshire.
items.why: a sitting MP's resignation ahead of a scrutiny report triggers by-elections that determine representation and accountability.

items.h: Postal ballot ID requirements may lead older voters to ‘give up’, says Age UK
items.b: The newly announced rules requiring postal and proxy voters to show ID may disproportionately affect older voters and could prevent them from casting a vote, say Age UK . Director of Age UK, Caroline Abrahams, said the legislation may ‘erect additional barriers to older people exercising their democratic right to vote’ and expressed concern that the new rules have not been subjected to adequate parliamentary scrutiny.
items.why: new ID requirements for postal and proxy voting could create practical barriers to casting a vote, affecting electoral access and participation.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society praise Single Transferable Voting in Northern Ireland’s local elections
items.b: This year Northern Ireland held local elections using the Single Transferable Voting system. The system gives voters a group of local councillors to choose from which are representative of the political diversity of their ward itself and asks them to rank candidates in order of preference. Doug Cowan at ERS argued the system means voters in Northern Ireland were able to express ‘nuanced preferences’ and ensured voters don’t have to worry about ‘splitting the vote’.
items.why: the choice of electoral system (STV) shapes how votes translate into representation and political competition in local elections.

items.h: Welsh Government reviewing consultation on using the STV system for local elections
items.b: Principal councils in Wales are now able to choose to hold electing using the single transferable voting system. Ending back in April, the consultation is looking into the rules around conducting elections in this way — stay tuned for updates .
items.why: a government consultation on adopting STV for local elections would change the electoral system used to choose local representatives.

items.h: Labour For A New Democracy mobilises ahead of the National Policy Forum
items.b: The Labour Party’s National Policy Forum (NPF) is due to meet this week and throughout the month, culminating in its final weekend on 22–23 July to decide what will become Labour Policy. Labour For A New Democracy (L4ND) has mobilised unprecedented engagement with this process, compared to any past issue, from across the Labour movement, with 44% of all submissions to the NPF calling for PR. Alex Zur-Clark at L4ND says it helps to know about any potential interventions, press, events or campaigns you may have organised over the next four weeks that may relate to Labour and electoral reform, an…
items.why: advocacy within a major party for proportional representation bears directly on what electoral system will be used to choose representatives.
items.note: Focus is on electoral system reform (PR) rather than party organisational news, so classed under elections despite the campaign framing.

items.h: Gordon Brown unveils Alliance for Radical Democratic Change
items.b: Gordon Brown has launched a new alliance of Labour politicians backing democratic reform to meet the pressing challenges facing the UK. The new group includes Welsh First Minister Mark Drakeford, Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, West Yorkshire Mayor Tracy Brabin and Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar. The alliance is advancing ‘wide-ranging proposals’ to ‘ end the centralisation of power in Whitehall and Westminster ’ in order to create a ‘fairer, greener and wealthier Britain’.
items.why: the alliance advocates changing the structure and powers of devolved and local government, which is core decision-making machinery.
items.note: Devolution and decentralisation of power are classed as elections & decision making per the framework's treatment of local/regional government structure.
links: launched a new alliance of Labour politicians

items.h: Labour MP says party plans for House of Lords reform will take a back seat
items.b: The Labour Party’s promised House of Lords reform has suffered as part of the Party’s ongoing wave of u-turns in recent weeks, as Shadow Commons Leader Thangam Debbonaire MP remarks Lords reform ‘takes time and drains energy’ in an apparent bucket of cold water over growing hopes for wholesale reform of the upper chamber.
items.why: the prospects for reforming the House of Lords affect how the legislature is constituted and able to scrutinise the executive.

items.h: Institute for Public Policy Research explore how best to frame ‘democratic reform’
items.b: A new report by IPPR , Talking Politics: Building support for democratic reform , found just 6% of the public have full trust in the current political system, while 89% support constitutional reform. Based on a survey of 8,000 people, they concluded that democratic reform is strongest in the UK’s former industrial heartlands. The report discusses the most effective framing and politicisation of the ‘democratic reform’ to capitalise on this appetite for change.
items.why: public trust in and support for the political system shapes willingness to engage with and back democratic reform.
items.note: Report is about public trust/appetite for reform generally rather than a specific mechanism, placed under participation as popular support for democracy.
links: Talking Politics: Building support for democratic reform

items.h: Constitution Society report explores the impacts of party whips
items.b: A new report from Tabitha Troughton at The Constitution Society , Cracking the Whip: The UK’s Party Control System , takes a closer look at how whipping was used to significant effect in two landmark parliamentary votes — the invasion of Iraq and triggering of the EU referendum — underlining the implications for transparent democratic process in the face of pressure to toe the party line.
items.why: party whipping practices affect how independently MPs can scrutinise and check executive decisions in Parliament.
links: Cracking the Whip: The UK’s Party Control System

items.h: Research for Action plan launch of their new report on local government auditing
items.b: The new report by Gloria Dawson and the team at Research for Action looks at the collapse of the local government auditing regime over the past decade and its wider impact on local democracy. Find out more about the upcoming report by contacting Gloria and the team at Research for Action .
items.why: the collapse of local government auditing weakens a key mechanism for holding local authorities accountable for their use of public power.
items.note: Auditing is an accountability mechanism rather than an electoral or structural issue, so classified under government & accountability rather than local democracy structure.

items.h: Scottish First Minister unveils plans for a written Scottish Constitution
items.b: Scottish First Minister Humza Yousaf has argued that without a written Constitution, the UK parliament could choose to abolish the Scottish parliament , undermine the devolution settlement, and override decisions made in Scotland. The first minister said drafting a constitution would create ‘meaningful rights that put power in the hands of the people who live here’.
items.why: a written constitution would formally constrain how power over Scotland's devolved institutions can be exercised or withdrawn by Westminster.
links: UK parliament could choose to abolish the Scottish parliament

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Foundation and New Local report explore avenues for local-led policy making
items.b: A new report, Designing out the most severe forms of hardship in local areas , by JRF and New Local explores the link between enhanced local decision making and poverty alleviation. The report sets out a framework for how power can be shifted to communities and local decision makers to enable those with lived experience to shape a local policy framework that combats hardship.
items.why: shifting decision-making power to local communities changes who holds authority over policy affecting their lives.
items.note: Classified under decision-making structure per the devolved/local government rule, though it also touches egalitarian participation conditions.
links: Designing out the most severe forms of hardship in local areas

items.h: Orxit? Orkney votes for motion to explore leaving current UK governance settlement
items.b: Fed up with long-running underfunding and neglect by Edinburgh and London, Orcadian councillors have voted to explore alternative forms of governance . Whilst Orkney is unlikely to make the switch, locals think the move will focus attention on their ailing ferry services.
items.why: a council voting to explore leaving the current governance settlement concerns the structure and allocation of local decision-making power.
links: Orcadian councillors have voted to explore alternative forms of governance

items.h: UK still lacking anti-corruption champion, say Transparency International
items.b: Transparency International and the UK Anti-Corruption Coalition have been working on a joint campaign to encourage the Government to appoint a new anti-corruption champion — as the post has been empty for a year now, reports Rose Whiffen of Transparency International.
items.why: the absence of an anti-corruption champion reduces oversight of standards and abuse of office in government.

items.h: Big Brother Watch pursue legal action against UK Counter Disinformation Unit
items.b: Big Brother Watch has launched a crowdfunder to pursue legal action against the UK Counter Disinformation Unit — the first ever legal action in Europe against a government’s counter disinformation activity. The campaign group has been spurred to action following recent news that Caroline Lucas MP has been repeatedly logged by the Counter Disinformation Unit for criticising the government.
items.why: government surveillance and logging of an MP's critical speech risks chilling the freedom to dissent and criticise those in power.
items.note: Framed as a rights/liberty issue (chilling effect on speech) rather than the information environment itself, though the disinformation unit context is relevant.

items.h: Mayor Jamie Driscoll banned from standing for re-election by National Executive Committee
items.b: The Labour Party is in the midst of another internal row over candidate selection after the Labour NEC blocked North Tyne Metro Mayor Jamie Driscoll from standing for re-election. In a joint letter to the NEC, Driscoll, Manchester Metro Mayor Andy Burnham, and Liverpool Metro Mayor Steve Rotherham, said the decision to exclude a sitting mayor from a selection process with no right of appeal was neither democratic, transparent or fair.
items.why: blocking a sitting elected mayor from standing for re-election through an opaque internal process affects fair candidate access and political competition.
links: NEC blocked North Tyne Metro Mayor Jamie Driscoll

items.h: Institute for Government praises Privileges Committee ruling on Johnson
items.b: Hannah White, Director of the Institute for Government , praised the Privileges Committee for upholding one of the key parliamentary mechanisms underpinning our democracy. In their ruling on Johnson’s Partygate scandal, White says the Committee has cemented the principle that politicians must tell the truth as well as the Committee’s fundamental role in upholding parliamentary transparency.
items.why: the Privileges Committee ruling reinforces parliamentary mechanisms holding ministers accountable for truthfulness to Parliament.
links: Committee has cemented the principle that politicians must tell the truth

items.h: Lowest ever percentage of FOI requests granted by Sunak’s government
items.b: Just 33.6% of ‘resolvable requests were granted during the first three months of the Sunak Ministry — a record low compared with a 56% rate of information published in full in David Cameron’s first quarter as prime minister, 44% under Theresa May, and 43% under Boris Johnson. The findings have led to accusations of a ‘concealment culture’ within Downing Street that flies in the face of Sunak’s promise for greater integrity, professionalism and accountability.
items.why: a falling FOI grant rate signals weakening transparency and accountability mechanisms for holding government to account.
items.note: FOI treated as accountability mechanism since the story concerns institutional answerability, not the public information environment.

items.h: Liberty take legal action against Home Secretary as anti-protest legislation forced through
items.b: Liberty is pursuing legal action after the Home Secretary forced through highly controversial new protest laws that were previously rejected by the House of Lords during the passage of the Public Order Act , in actions the Lords have described as a ‘constitutional outrage’. Liberty argue the move signals a‘flagrant breach of the separation of powers that exist in our constitution’.
items.why: new protest laws forced through against the Lords' rejection restrict the freedom of assembly while also raising questions about executive overreach and separation of powers.
items.note: Primary beat follows the substantive restriction on protest rights; secondary reflects the constitutional/checks-and-balances angle of overriding the Lords.

items.h: Labour face criticism for failing to back attempts to prevent new protest laws
items.b: Yvette Cooper and the Labour front bench have come under fire for failing to back a ‘Fatal Motion’ which may have scuppered Govt attempts to pass expansive new police protest powers. Baroness Jenny Jones of the Green Party attempted to bring Labour on side, with Labour’s Emily Thornberry MP replying that to kill the bill in the Lords would set a precedent that the ‘Tories could easily use their majority in the Lords to do the same to a Labour government’s laws.
items.why: the opposition's parliamentary tactics in failing to block contested legislation bear on legislative scrutiny and checks on executive power.
items.note: Focus is on parliamentary process and party accountability rather than the protest restriction itself.

items.h: openDemocracy find Tory MP hid directorship at defence firm whilst sitting on defence committee
items.b: Conservative MP Bob Stewart failed to declare their role at a defence firm linked to controversial Azerbaijani businessman Khagani Bashirov, whilst sitting on Parliament’s defence committee, openDemocracy has found. The findings come a week after the same MP was charged with a public order offence over an alleged racially aggravated incident last December.
items.why: an MP concealing a financial interest while serving on a relevant committee undermines standards in public life and conflict-of-interest safeguards.
links: Bob Stewart failed to declare their role at a defence firm
charged with a public order offence

items.h: Bright Blue preparing new report on democratic forms of business ownership
items.b: Bartek Staniszewskvi at Bright Blue reports that they are penning a new report exploring cooperatives, mutuals, employee-owned businesses and community businesses. The report will launch in partnership with Power to Change this October, with a report release in September — contact Bartek for more info .
items.note: This is a forthcoming report on business ownership models, not a story about public political power or participation mechanisms.

items.h: Universal Basic Income of £1,600 to be trialled in two places, Autonomy report
items.b: Taking the UK media cycle by storm earlier last month, Autonomy, in partnership with Big Local, presented plans for large scale UBI pilots in East Finchley, London and Jarrow. The pilots will amount to the first UBI pilots held in England in a major step forward for the policy. Find out more about the pilots via Autonomy .
items.why: a basic income pilot tests changes to economic conditions that bear on people's practical ability to participate in civic and political life.
items.note: Classified under the egalitarian/basic-welfare conditions for participation rather than as general economic policy.
links: presented plans for large scale UBI pilots

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launching their UK Local News Map, July 19th
items.b: The map, currently in Beta , aims to show the provision of local news per local authority in the UK, across print, online, radio and TV. View the map and register for the launch on July 19th, 12pm here .
items.why: mapping local news provision creates new visibility into gaps in the public information environment that citizens rely on for democratic engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new resource that affects the information environment.

items.h: Ofcom investigate GB News and Talk TV over impartiality rules
items.b: Ofcom has launched investigations into GB News and Talk TV as the regulator struggles to play catchup to handle how rightwing television channels are employing serving politicians as presenters, see the Guardian coverage of the story .
items.why: regulatory scrutiny of broadcast impartiality rules affects whether citizens encounter a plural and fair range of political information.
links: see the Guardian coverage of the story

items.h: Conservative Party receive international criticism for charging journalist fee at annual conference
items.b: The Conservative Party has been accused of setting a ‘dangerous precedent’ after it emerged they intend to charge a £137 fee to journalists that want to report at their annual conference. Nearly 300 news organisations, including the Society of Editors , Foreign Press Association , News Media Association , Reporters Without Borders and the European Alliance of News Agencies , signed an open letter to the government criticising what they see as an attempt to restrict public interest journalism.
items.why: restricting or charging journalists to access party conferences narrows the ability of the press to scrutinise and report on political parties, affecting the public information environment voters rely on.

items.h: National Council for the Training of Journalists report reveals lack of diversity in the media
items.b: A new report, Diversity in the Media , from the National Council for the Training of Journalists reveals a startling lack of diversity in the media. More than four in five people (82%) in the media now have the highest educational qualifications, compared to only 38% of all workers. And nearly three-quarters (72%) have parents in the highest, most financially secure professional and managerial occupations, compared to only 44% of all workers.
items.why: a media workforce drawn overwhelmingly from privileged educational and class backgrounds may narrow the range of perspectives and experiences reflected in political coverage, affecting the plurality of public debate.
links: National Council for the Training of Journalists

items.h: New Democracy Network AI & Democracy WhatsApp Group
items.b: Are you interested in applying or experimenting with the new AI large language model tools? Concerned about the impact of AI on democratic processes? Join the Democracy Network’s new WhatsApp Group .
items.note: Internal networking group for practitioners, not a new means of public participation.

items.h: Democracy Network run AI & Democracy How To workshop
items.b: Last week Democracy Network ran a workshop with Hannah O’ Rourke of Campaign Lab looking at the new generation of AI large language model tooling such as Open AI’s ChatGPT. In the session Hannah introduced and explored the tools, showcasing their use cases for democracy organisations — see the slides and view the event recording .
items.note: Event/workshop listing for sector staff, not a public-facing participation tool.

items.h: Joe Coker of Candid.vote produces new UK Politics ChatGPT plugin
items.b: After producing the Candid.vote aggregated dataset earlier this year, Joe Coker quickly moved onto making UK election & candidate datasets interrogable via ChatGPT. The new UK Politics plugin for ChatGPT allows a user to query ChatGPT with up-to-date and references answers about various political subjects, drawing from Democracy Club, TheyWorkForYou and other data sources.
items.why: a new tool making political and candidate information queryable creates a new means for the public to access and engage with information relevant to democratic participation.

items.h: Andrew Gray is running a virtual candidate in the Ainsty & Selby by-election
items.b: Powered by deliberative tool Pol.is , Andrew of Crowd Wisdom is standing on a policy-less platform with their entire stance and policy agenda derived from AI-facilitated deliberation. Andrew has garnered press attention including the Daily Star — see their website for more info .
items.why: a candidate standing in an actual by-election with policy positions derived from AI-facilitated deliberation tests new mechanisms for translating collective input into electoral representation.
items.note: Deliberative process tied to an actual candidacy is assigned to elections per the framework's treatment of deliberation as decision-making machinery.
links: see their website for more info

items.h: Electoral Commission warn time is running out to regulate UK electoral system to keep up with AI
items.b: Last week the Electoral Commission issued warnings to legislators of the perils of ignoring calls to regulate emerging generative AI tech that has the potential to seriously undermine the upcoming 2024 General Election.
items.why: unregulated generative AI could undermine the integrity and conduct of the 2024 General Election, a core electoral administration concern.

items.h: Civic Tech Fieldguide want your favourite AI prompts!
items.b: If you have any success stories or interesting insights from using AI prompts, Civic Tech Field Guide wants to hear about them — share your stories now .
items.note: A call for content submissions, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.h: Scottish Parliament investigating use of AI-assisted automatic speech recognition
items.b: Christopher Gavin and the team at the Scottish Parliament’s digital team are currently appraising the potential use of AI-assisted automatic speech recognition (ASR) for house business in the Parliament.
items.why: it concerns how Parliament records and conducts its official business, affecting the transparency and accountability of legislative proceedings.
items.note: Treated as parliamentary administration rather than a 'not a beat' technology story since it concerns the mechanics of legislative business.

items.h: Civil service leaders consider how ChatGPT could impact the civil service
items.b: Writing in Civil Service World, Jess Bowie interviews Paul Maltby, Director of AI Transformation in Government at Faculty , and Jack Perschke of Content + Cloud , on their thoughts. They say that whilst the technology is currently at the level of an ‘amazing party trick’, we are on the verge of a large scale internet-level transformation . Mass communication using the written word, they write, ‘adjudicated by the high priests of form — journalists, officials, lawyers, whatever — is dead’.
items.note: Speculative commentary about future AI impact on civil service, not a reported change in a democratic mechanism.
links: we are on the verge of a large scale internet-level transformation

items.h: Editors highlight: UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose publish lecture series on Post-Brexit Britain
items.b: This three part lecture series from the UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose , Visiting Professor of Practice in Labour Markets and Innovation, Damon Silvers, unpacks the vice-like growth trap that Britain has laid for itself in the Post-Brexit period. Silvers, the former Policy Director of the U.S AFL-CIO, posits that to escape this trap, the UK will need to fundamentally rethink our entire economic strategy in the neoliberal era — watch it now on YouTube .
links: UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose

items.h: Decider App helps you choose appropriate decision making methods
items.b: Check out the Decider App , a browser based app or Slack integration that helps you choose the group decision making model best suited for your needs.
items.why: it creates a new tool that helps groups choose appropriate collective decision-making methods, expanding practical means for participation.
items.note: Classified under sector capacity-building rule as a new means of participation rather than as formal decision-making machinery.

items.b: The UK Democracy Network maintains a full database of events from across the democracy sector.

items.h: Editors note: In the original version of this digest, a story was included suggesting that the Labour For A New Democracy campaign was working with Led By Donkeys on a banner drop outside the Labour Party HQ, this was incorrect and falsely attributed and has been removed.
items.b: Monthly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network . Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know : hello@democracynetwork.org.uk
Members of the My Vote My Voice coalition hand in #MyVoteMatters petition to Downing Street, 26th July
items.why: the petition concerns the accessibility of voting for disabled voters, a matter of who can practically exercise the franchise.
items.note: Petition mechanism could also fit participation & civic life, but the underlying issue (voting access) anchors it to elections.

items.b: Join the UK Democracy Network’s WhatsApp Community , there are currently 9 active groups on topics ranging from AI & Democracy to Democracy Academics Collaboration.

Thanks to everyone who joined us last week for our Democracy Check-In . We were joined by Flynn Devine — Alan Turing Institute / Recursive Public, Gloria Dawson — Research for Action, Perry Walker — Talk Shop, Rebecca Deegan — I Have A Voice, Myf Nixon — mySociety, Edward Saperia — Newspeak House, Barnaby Fynn — Global People Power and Yvonne Murphy — Omidaze Productions.

items.h: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill returns to Parliament
items.b: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Bill returns to the House of Commons this month, where MPs will vote on a range of amendments from the Lords that seek to close loopholes in tackling economic crime.
