items.h: Together With Refugees plus 200+ charities call for move away from divisive politics in joint statement
items.b: Together With Refugees and more than 200 signatory refugee charities and democracy sector organisations, including Detention Action and the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants , call on the Government that this must mark the turning point away from divisive politics, racist rhetoric and demonising language of communities and refugees — Read and amplify the statement now . Thanks to Compassion in Politics for highlighting this.
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.note: A call-to-sign joint statement urging policy change, without a specific democratic mechanism engaged, falls under excluded sector logistics.
links: Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants
Read and amplify the statement now

items.h: Muslim Council of Britain organising urgent community briefings, highlights Islamophobic comments by Robert Jenrick MP
items.b: The Muslim Council of Britain (MCB) is organising urgent community briefings whilst the race riots continue. The urgent meeting last night included speakers from the London Fire Brigade, Imam Adam Kelwick and representatives of mosques affected by the riots — request the recording here . In an interview this morning, Conservative MP and leadership candidate has called for those shouting “Allahhu Akbar” to be ‘immediately arrested’ , the MCB, Runnymede Trust and allied organisations have called on Jenrick to apologise for this ‘divisive language’ .
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: This matters democratically because political rhetoric that stigmatises a religious minority and civic society's response to it engage freedom of religion and equal protection under the law.
items.note: MP's comments also touch standards in public life, a government & accountability concern.
links: Conservative MP and leadership candidate has called for those shouting “Allahhu Akbar” to be ‘immediately arrested’
have called on Jenrick to apologise for this ‘divisive language’

items.h: Trade Unions across the UK state their opposition to the growing far-right riots
items.b: The Trades Union Congress representing more than 6 million workers, state their total opposition to the far-right movement, framing the growing crisis as a ‘trade union issue’ both in terms of trade unions having been at the heart of the anti-fascist movement in Britain, but also in terms of countering attempts by far-right organisers organising in UK workplaces.
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: This matters democratically because trade unions mobilising against far-right organising in workplaces exercise the freedom of association that underpins civic space.
items.note: Freedom of association for unions/civic organisations places this in rights & civic space rather than participation.

items.h: Institute for Strategic Dialogue focus on Telegram as the organising space for hate-driven violence
items.b: Back in 2020 Institute for Strategic Dialogue analysed the role of Telegram in white supremacist and extremist ecosystems in their report A Safe Space to Hate: White Supremacist Mobilisation on Telegram .
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: This matters democratically because platforms used to organise hate-driven violence shape the public information environment in which political debate takes place.
items.note: References a 2020 report rather than new evidence, but the mechanism concerns platforms as organising space for extremism.
links: A Safe Space to Hate: White Supremacist Mobilisation on Telegram

items.h: CCDH takes aim at social media platforms, calls on UK Govt to enact urgent reforms
items.b: Centre for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) argue social media platforms are e nabling the rising racist violence across the UK , by failing to quell misinformation effectively and through algorithms that privilege incendiary content. CCDH call on the UK Government to enact urgent reforms, amend the Online Safety Act, clamp down on online hate via the Public Order Act, empower researchers with statutory data access rights and other changes — read their report here .
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: it concerns whether the information environment (platform algorithms, misinformation regulation, researcher data access) enables or undermines informed public debate and safety.
links: nabling the rising racist violence across the UK

items.h: UK riots fact checked by Full Fact
items.b: Full Fact are maintaining an up-to-date page for fact checking the ongoing far-right riots , as well as police, government and community response. See Full Fact’s response to the riots here .
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: fact-checking during civil unrest helps preserve a shared factual basis for public debate against misinformation.
links: maintaining an up-to-date page for fact checking the ongoing far-right riots

items.h: Serious and growing concern over role of misinformation and foreign government involvement in recent riots
items.b: Bloomberg reports suspected foreign state-backed actors and UK domestic extremists have coalesced online to stoke racism and incite violence across the UK, the UK Government now believe. Tactics by foreign actors allegedly include using bots and accounts with stolen British identities on X to amplify anti-immigration sentiment, Russian-speaking trolls have also been observed boasting of infiltrating UK far-right Telegram channels. Elon Musk, the owner of X, has made several provocative posts on X , including one saying “civil war is inevitable” that drew sharp criticism from the UK Government.
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: foreign state actors manipulating online discourse to incite violence undermines the integrity of the UK's information environment and political debate.

items.b: The MPs, who are both standing to chair parliament’s science, innovation and technology committee, have stated they intend to press for Musk to be brought before the House to answer questions about his role in the ongoing racist riots.
items.issue: UK Democracy Network Far-Right Response, 8th August 2024
items.why: MPs seeking to summon a powerful private platform owner before Parliament tests mechanisms for holding influential private actors answerable for their effect on public order and debate.
items.note: Treated as accountability since the mechanism is parliamentary scrutiny, not the information environment itself.
links: intend to press for Musk to be brought before the House

items.b: The Civic Power Fund has issued 100 Emergency Action Grants to communities and organisations dealing with the aftermath of the riots. In response to the Islamaphobic and racist riots the fund launched an Emergency Action Fund and was able to issue 100 grants to organisations in less than two weeks following the riots.
items.why: emergency funding sustains civil society organisations' capacity to support communities targeted by racist and Islamophobic violence, preserving their ability to participate in civic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building rather than a routine funding call, given the crisis-response mechanism.

items.h: Institute for Strategic Dialogue examine role of misinformation in far right riots
items.b: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue has tracked the spread of misinformation that led to the far riot riots across the UK, showing how by 3pm the day after the attack, the false name of the attacker had received over 30,000 mentions on X alone, from over 18,000 unique accounts. Self-described ‘breaking news’ accounts and other content aggregators, some of which are monetised on X, are a major problem in the spread of misinformation, says ISD, as they are incentivised to spread sensationalist details to garner engagement, regardless of the truth behind what they say — Read more analysis here .
items.why: unchecked spread of misinformation on social media platforms shaped public understanding of the riots and helped incite real-world political violence, implicating the integrity of the information environment

items.h: 80 anti-racist and migrants’ rights organisations write to Keir Starmer demanding wholesale shift in political culture
items.b: The Runnymede Trust has coordinated an open letter to Keir Starmer calling out the ‘normalised racism and Islamophobia, enabled by mainstream politicians and the British media’, which they suggest has directly contributed to the far right violence across the UK. Combating the spread of the far right and ensuring communities of colour feel safe in the UK must therefore start, they suggest, with a ‘wholesale shift in our political culture, language and policies’.
items.why: civil society organisations are collectively petitioning government for redress and policy change, exercising a core mechanism of civic voice while highlighting systemic discrimination that undermines equal protection
items.note: Classified as petitioning/civic organising rather than pure rights complaint, per participation beat's inclusion of redress of grievances.

items.b: Anti-racist protesters in Lancaster earlier this month (Credit: Manon Cruz/Reuters)
items.note: Photo caption with no substantive claim about a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Unlock Democracy call for better regulation of social media companies
items.b: Unlock Democracy has called on the Government to ‘urgently review’ the laws governing social media companies, suggesting the spates of far right violence are a sign that ‘they clearly aren’t working’. They’ve also called on the government to review the recent laws which have clamped down on peaceful protesting in the UK as the riots have shown the clear difference between violent and non-violent action.
items.why: this matters democratically because it calls for review of the legal framework governing platforms that shape the public information environment and of laws restricting peaceful protest.
items.note: Combines a call on social media regulation (information) with a call on protest law (rights); primary reflects the headline focus.

items.h: Online Safety Act to be reviewed
items.b: Keir Starmer has confirmed that the Online Safety Bill will be reviewed after Mayor of London Sadiq Khan suggested it was unfit for purpose and needed to be revisited. Currently the Online Safety Act gives Ofcom the power to fine social media giants up to 10% of their turnover if they fail to take robust action on the incitement of violence, but the PM suggested that the government would again be looking at the social media realm to ensure it is not a ‘law-free zone’.
items.why: this matters democratically because the review concerns the legal regime governing platform accountability for incitement, shaping the public information environment.
links: confirmed that the Online Safety Bill will be reviewed
suggested it was unfit for purpose

items.h: Byline Times’ Nafeez Ahmed unpacks the complex UK far right networks
items.b: Thanks to Civic Power Fund’s Mohammed Afridi for suggesting this unpleasant if insightful read — Byline Time’s Nafeez Ahmed takes a deep dive into the ‘worrying nexus’ of tech platforms and far-right conspiracy , uncovering the global connections behind the recent racist attacks and riots.
items.why: this matters democratically because investigative journalism exposing far-right networks and their use of tech platforms informs public understanding of threats to the information environment.

items.h: X made over £27k a day from ads near far-right agitators, analysis shows
items.b: Research from The Centre for Countering Digital Hate finds that X made over £27K a day in the week following the UK’s Southport stabbings from ads near posts by far-right disinformation spreaders Andrew Tate, Laurence Fox, and others. These included ads for well-known brands like GlaxoSmithKline, the British Medical Association, and the International Olympic Committee — find out more .
items.why: this matters democratically because it reveals how platform monetisation incentives sustain disinformation spreaders who shape public debate.
items.note: Private commercial practice counted because it materially affects the public information environment.
links: The Centre for Countering Digital Hate

items.h: Stop Funding Hate work to identify companies still advertising on the platform
items.b: While Stop Funding Hate still remains on Twitter / X for the time being, they are now using the site to crowdsource information about which companies are still advertising on the platform .
items.why: this matters democratically because civic pressure on advertisers aims to reduce commercial support for a platform implicated in spreading disinformation and hate.
items.note: Borderline between civic campaigning and the information environment; classified by the underlying target (platform disinformation ecosystem).
links: crowdsource information about which companies are still advertising on the platform

items.h: Big Brother Watch criticise Labour’s plans to expand use of facial recognition technology
items.b: Big Brother Watch has convened a coalition of nearly 30 human rights and racial justice groups, urging Sir Keir Starmer to rethink plans to expand the use of live facial recognition , which they suggest threatens to weaken democratic rights across the country. The Network for Police Monitoring has similarly criticised Labour’s plan for a new ‘standing army’ of riot trained officers, which they suggest will do more to clamp down on legitimate protest rather than stop racist violence.
items.why: this matters democratically because expanded facial recognition surveillance and a specialised riot police force bear on citizens' freedom to protest and be free from state coercion.
links: rethink plans to expand the use of live facial recognition
criticised Labour’s plan for a new ‘standing army’

items.h: Musk could be summoned before Parliament over X’s role in the race riots
items.b: Labour MPs Chi Onwurah and Dawn Butler, who are competing to chair Parliament’s Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, have both expressed an intention to question Musk over his platform’s involvement in the incitement of the riots. Mark Zuckerberg was similarly summoned before Parliament in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, but refused to play ball.
items.why: this matters democratically because Parliament exercising its power to summon a powerful platform owner for scrutiny over incitement is a check on unaccountable private influence over public affairs.

items.h: Civil society groups call for a ‘Build Back Stronger’ inquiry to discuss community rebuilding
items.b: Demos has joined with a range of civil society partners, including Oxfam and the Jo Cox Foundation , to call for a ‘Build Back Stronger’ inquiry to discuss how to go about rebuilding communities in the wake of the riots. They are calling specifically for citizen voices to be included in the inquiry to facilitate local testimonies about what lessons can be learnt.
items.why: it seeks to build a mechanism for citizen testimony and civic input into how communities respond to and recover from the riots, a participatory addition to public inquiry processes.
items.note: Public inquiry is participatory/deliberative in framing rather than pure scrutiny or redress, so classed under participation.
links: call for a ‘Build Back Stronger’ inquiry

items.h: Discussing the riots: Larger Us discuss the importance of difficult conversations
items.b: Recent polling by LargerUs shows that only 7% of people in the UK support the violence we’ve seen on our streets. But of those 7%, two-thirds of them think that most people in Britain do too — meaning there is a big opportunity (and perhaps responsibility) to have those difficult conversations that challenge that assumption, they say. LargerUS has outlined some important steps for anyone who finds themselves in such a situation.
items.why: it addresses social cohesion and civic dialogue that underpin people's willingness and ability to engage constructively in public life.

items.h: Society of Editors welcomes ‘Fake News Initiative’ to help identify online misinformation
items.b: Differentiating between fake news and accurate information online may be taught in primary and secondary schools in the wake of far-right riots across the UK. Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson is considering how to embed critical thinking across multiple subjects in the school curriculum to teach children how to spot misinformation. The Society of Editors welcomed the review suggesting ‘urgent action’ is needed .
items.why: embedding critical thinking about misinformation in the curriculum shapes citizens' future ability to obtain and evaluate meaningful information about public affairs.

items.h: FREE THE PAF
items.b: The Postal Address File is a critically important national dataset, say campaigners. It’s not personal data, it’s a database of every physical postal address in the country. This critical dataset could be used to build the apps, services, platforms and campaigns of tomorrow — but currently it’s locked behind a £6000pa Post Office paywall if you want to use it. Read why James O’Malley thinks this is so important and join the Free the Postcode Address File event at Newspeak House in London on October 1st.
items.note: Advocacy/event notice about open data policy; mechanism connecting it to democratic participation is too indirect to qualify.

items.h: Democracy Club feedback on their election experience with record search numbers
items.b: With over 14 million postcode searches from the UK public, marking a new record, Democracy Club take a look at whether people found what they were looking for , what people thoughts of the platform. Congrats to Democracy Club on such an impressive achievement!
items.why: record use of a voter-facing information platform bears on the practical accessibility of voting and the electoral participation mechanics that determine turnout
items.note: Filed under elections per the standing rule that turnout and voting-access mechanics always sit in elections & decision making.
links: Democracy Club take a look at whether people found what they were looking for

items.h: TEDx Democracy Bootcamp receives over 100 applications
items.b: The initiative supported by The Politics Project and the Civic Power Fund received 114 applications from young people with new ideas on how to change politics for the better. They may soon be reaching out to organisations to ask for you to be involved in the bootcamp they are running in London in October.
items.note: Reports on application numbers to an existing programme rather than a new means of participation or a substantive democracy development.

items.h: Extinction Rebellion to hold ‘Massembly’ demanding a citizens’ assembly on climate justice
items.b: On Saturday 31st of August 1–4pm, Extinction Rebellion is running the biggest People’s Assembly in the UK to decide what steps can be taken to upgrade democracy and allow more public participation in decision making. Their central demand is that the Government must create and be led by a Citizens’ Assembly on Climate and Ecological Justice . Fill in this form if you can attend .
items.why: the campaign demands creation of a citizens' assembly, a form of decision-making machinery that would change how binding collective decisions are reached.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's decision-making machinery rule.
links: Fill in this form if you can attend

items.h: Association of Electoral Administrators pen letter to UK Govt over electoral concerns
items.b: The Association of Electoral Administrators , has written to the new government outlining their concerns over the state of the UK electoral system . The letter suggests that our current system is often too complex to navigate for voters and that recent changes have ‘bolted 21st century user experiences onto 19th century infrastructure’.
items.why: electoral administrators are flagging systemic complexity and infrastructure problems that affect voters' practical ability to participate in well-run elections.
links: outlining their concerns over the state of the UK electoral system

items.h: People Powered run collective book launch, September 13
items.b: On September 13th People Powered are running a co-book launch of two books, Educating for Democracy: The Case for School Participatory Budgeting and Activated Citizenship: The Transformative Power of Citizens’ Assemblies . In the talks they will explore how participatory democracy practices, from school participatory budgeting to citizens’ assemblies, can spark citizen engagement and be integrated throughout a person’s life.
items.note: An event/book launch listing rather than the creation of a new participatory mechanism or reported change.
links: Educating for Democracy: The Case for School Participatory Budgeting
Activated Citizenship: The Transformative Power of Citizens’ Assemblies

items.h: Constitution Unit discuss Labour’s agenda for constitutional reform
items.b: The Constitution Unit’s latest edition of Monitor , their quarterly constitutional review, is now out. The report discusses the early steps Labour has taken towards constitutional reform and praises the pivot in political rhetoric towards a ‘politics of public service’.
items.why: it analyses government moves on constitutional reform, which shapes how executive power is structured and constrained.

items.h: Paris passes legislation drafted by a permanent citizens’ assembly
items.b: On July 10th, The Paris City Council passed into law the recommendations from a municipal citizens’ assembly on homelessness. This marks the first time the Paris City Council has taken up and passed legislation written by citizens who were selected by sortition and who deliberated in an assembly. Check out the insights from this historic first from a civil servant who facilitated the process.
items.why: it is comparative evidence that a permanent citizens' assembly successfully produced binding legislation, relevant to debates about adopting such mechanisms in the UK.
items.note: International case used as comparative evidence for UK deliberative democracy debates.

items.h: Strengthening ties between citizens and their elected representatives; lessons from Belgium
items.b: Last month, Demos published a white paper exploring how the new Labour government could transform democracy using a participatory approach, including the use of citizens’ assemblies. A new article for Democracy Technologies outlines the Belgian approach to ‘Deliberative Committees’ and asks whether this could be an emerging model to learn from.
items.why: it explores deliberative committees and citizens' assemblies as mechanisms for UK decision-making reform.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes fall under elections & decision making, not participation.

items.h: New Local Government Association chair says reset is needed with government
items.b: Louise Gittins, the new Chair of the Local Government Association, likened the relationship between local and national government to being ‘almost like a parent child relationship’ . Gittins said their first priority will be to reset that relationship to allow local governments to deliver on the most pressing needs facing local communities.
items.why: it concerns the structure and power balance between local and national government, part of the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Local government structure/powers stories fall under elections & decision making per boundary rule.
links: the new Chair of the Local Government Association, likened the relationship between local and national government to being ‘almost like a parent child relationship’

items.h: Fearless Cities South Yorkshire, coming this November!
items.b: This November, the internationally acclaimed Fearless Cities summit, first hosted in Barcelona back in 2017, will be coming to the UK and to South Yorkshire for the first time . Fearless Cities brings together the growing international municipalist movement of cities, organisations, citizens and communities who are building new forms of local democracy across the world — tickets are not yet available, but if you’d like to submit a talk or session now is the time .
items.note: Event/conference listing rather than a new means of participation being created.

items.b: Fearless Cities is coming to Sheffield! (Credit: Fearless Cities South Yorkshire)

items.h: Don’t miss Locality 24 in Manchester this November
items.b: Locality’s annual Convention is the biggest community sector event of the year. This year’s event is held in Manchester on 12–13th November. Grab your tickets .
items.note: Ticket/event listing for a sector convention, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: New Local and Reform publish ‘Achieving the Devolution Revolution’ report
items.b: New Local has partnered with the think tank Reform to take a deep dive into what powers are needed to ensure a successful ‘devolution revolution’ in the UK. The paper, What Powers Where? Achieving the Devolution Revolution , sets out design principles and recommendations for whole regional systems to work together and distribute powers at every scale — including the neighbourhood level.
items.why: this concerns the structure and distribution of powers across local, regional and neighbourhood tiers of government, which is the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Local/regional government structure and powers falls under elections & decision making, not participation.
links: What Powers Where? Achieving the Devolution Revolution

items.h: London’s Haringey Community Action Network hosting Markfield Road Festival, September 13
items.b: With the theme of ‘creativity is the greatest rebellion in existence’, Haringey Community Action Network’s festival night aims to highlight the power of creative expression driving social change and fostering community spirit. Check it out now.
items.note: Community festival listing, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: NEON offer new Transformative Organising training
items.b: New Economy Organisers Network will be running their Transformative Organising training in Birmingham on September 28th & 29th, specifically for organisers working toward building the power of local communities to tackle social, environmental and economic injustice in Birmingham and the West Midlands.
items.why: this creates a new training resource intended to build local communities' capacity to organise and exercise collective power.
items.note: Sector capacity-building training counts as a democracy story under the framework's rule.

items.h: Conspiracy charges are increasingly being used to shut down protest, says Netpol
items.b: Following the landmark ruling last month which saw five Just Stop Oil protestors jailed for a total of 21 years, the Network for Police Monitoring has warned that ‘conspiracy to commit public nuisance’ charges are increasingly being used to shut down public protest. With police surveillance on the rise, there is a heightened risk that records of calls, texts, and minutes of meetings could all be used to support conspiracy charges, they suggest.
items.why: the increasing use of conspiracy charges and surveillance to prosecute protestors constrains the legal space for assembly and dissent.
items.note: Protest story concerns legal restriction and policing, so it sits in rights & freedoms rather than participation.
links: Network for Police Monitoring has warned

items.h: Two photo-journalists arrested whilst covering ecological and pro-Palestine protest
items.b: Two photo journalists have been arrested while covering UK protests, in one case before the protest had even taken place. Of particular concern, said the National Union of Journalists , ‘are the instances where the UK Press Card Authority press card has been shown to officers and have been dismissed.’
items.why: the arrest and obstruction of accredited journalists covering protests threatens the public's ability to obtain independent information about contested political events.
items.note: Journalist safety while covering protest sits at the boundary of information & public debate and protest policing.
links: Two photo journalists have been arrested

items.h: E-Visa scheme is pushing UK towards ‘second Windrush scandal’, says Open Rights Group
items.b: By the end of December 2024, the Home Office wants to replace physical documents proving people’s right to live in the UK with e-visas, which will affect up to four million people. Open Rights Group are warning that large numbers of people may struggle to prove their immigration status in the near future due to risk and failures associated with the roll out. On September 2nd they are hosting an event to raise awareness of the serious risks the new legislation poses.
items.why: This matters democratically because a flawed digital ID rollout could strip people of the practical means to prove their legal rights, undermining due process and equal access to justice.
items.note: Framed as a due-process/access-to-rights failure rather than a pure rights-restriction story, so filed under rule of law.

items.h: Unlock Democracy urge Labour to clamp down on MPs’ second jobs
items.b: Unlock Democracy has written to the Chair of the Modernisation Committee urging them to implement stricter rules on MPs’ second jobs. In opposition, Keir Starmer repeatedly called for second jobs to be banned — Unlock Democracy hopes to keep him to this promise to ensure constituent needs come first for MPs.
items.why: This matters democratically because rules on MPs' outside earnings go to standards in public life and whether representatives are answerable primarily to constituents rather than other interests.

items.h: Voter’s delivered ‘final warning’ to UK government on July 4th, says UCL report
items.b: A new report by the UCL Policy Lab and More in Common , based on 60 focus groups and polling with 10,000+ voters, finds the 2024 General Election was a final warning to Britain’s political mainstream. With 3 in 4 now in agreement that Britain is rigged to serve the rich and powerful, the report suggests that the next government must deliver on voters’ desire for fundamental change and implement a culture change to show more respect to ordinary voters.
items.why: This matters democratically because widespread public perception that the political system is rigged for elites reflects on democratic legitimacy and citizens' sense of voice and efficacy.
items.note: Treated as public perception/support-for-democracy evidence rather than an accountability mechanism story.

items.h: Arden Strategies release new identity profiles for Labour Voters
items.b: New polling report 7 Tribes That Make Up Labour’s 2024 Voter Coalition — And The Action Keir Starmer Needs To Take To Stay In Power by Arden Strategies , details the people and voter groups who the PM needs to keep onside, and those whom any prospective opposition would need to target to effectively topple the nascent Labour government.
links: 7 Tribes That Make Up Labour’s 2024 Voter Coalition — And The Action Keir Starmer Needs To Take To Stay In Power

Get in touch via joe@seelaw.co

items.h: Henry Duncan Grants offer unrestricted funding for women-led organisations
items.b: Henry Duncan Grants are offering unrestricted funding for women-led organisations in Scotland that support women & girls within their communities. The funds are open to charities and registered not-for-profit organisations with an annual income of £250,000 or less. Organisations can apply for up to £40,000 across five years (£8,000 per year) in funding. Find out more .
items.note: A funding notice unrelated to democratic mechanisms.

items.b: Two new tenders for English organisations and projects have opened with £50,000 for ‘democratic engagement projects’ with a proven track record of demonstrating impact and £10,000 for ‘democratic innovation approaches’ to pilot new and innovative approaches to democratic engagement. See here for more info .
items.why: this matters democratically because public funding is being made available to create new democratic engagement and innovation projects that expand how people can take part in political life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since the tender explicitly funds new democratic engagement and innovation mechanisms.

items.h: JRCT Power & Accountability Programme opens for new round of funding
items.b: They are anticipating a high demand for this round so before applying, they recommend double checking the programme’s policy areas for specific exclusions and so on. Find out more and register here by 24 October.
items.note: Funding call notice, not a democracy story.

items.b: The research by the Law Family Commission on Civil Society, found that charities with an income of up to £100,000 spend 38% of their total grant income on fundraising applications per year, while those with revenues between £100,000 to £1m spend 35% and larger charities spend 16%. Find out more and read the report .

items.b: Inequality undermines democracy — do you work to change that? This new Democracy Network Power & Voice programme, funded by JRCT , aims to provide tailored support to people and organisations who are working on barriers to democratic engagement created by economic inequality and intersecting forms of discrimination. If you see the strength of working in solidarity with allied people and organisations to affect change, and want to benefit from networking, training or opportunities for collaboration, we’d love to chat — please email Harley@involve.org.uk to find out more and book a place to be p…

items.h: Democracy Network Steering Group to meet for in-person strategy day, October 15th
items.b: Meeting in Central London, the Democracy Network’s recently elected Steering Group will meet to discuss, explore and reflect on the past years work of the Democracy Network to inform a strategy and approach for the next phase of the work to build a stronger, better connected and more impactful democracy sector.
items.note: Internal steering group meeting, organisational admin.

items.h: Democracy Club launch their 2024 Election Report, they’re looking for new board members
items.b: A deep dive into Democracy Club’s local and general election activity across 2024 , the report is a shining testament to Democracy Club’s enduring commitment to improve the availability and accessibility of public election data — in summary, they ‘had a jolly nice time, all things considered’ remarked Peter Keeling, Voting Information Manager at Democracy Club . But that’s not all, they’re now looking for new board members, particularly those with a background in finance, law, or accounting. Get in touch and find out more .
items.note: Report launch reflecting on past activity plus board recruitment notice, treated as organisational admin rather than a new mechanism.

items.h: Civic Power Fund, Politics Project and TEDx to run youth narrative bootcamp
items.b: On the 12th October TEDx , The Politics Project and Civic Power Fund will be running a bootcamp to give narrative training to 40 young people starting new organisations aimed at transforming and reinvigorating UK democracy at Amnesty International UK’s offices in London.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new training and skills for young people to found organisations aimed at increasing civic engagement, expanding the means of participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building programme creating new participatory capacity counts under the framework's carve-out.

items.h: Democracy Classroom Next Steps Strategy Day, 1st of November
items.b: Democracy Classroom is a collaboration between more than 50 non-partisan democracy, education and youth organisations to support young people to engage in elections. Following the election and the change in government, The Politics Project is hosting an in-person day in London for organisations across the youth, schools, and democracy sectors to come together and explore how we plan to work together in the new parliament. Please contact Harriet Andrews for more information via harriet.andrews@thepoliticsproject.org.uk
items.note: Sector coordination/strategy day among organisations, not a new participation resource or reported change.

items.h: Civic Power Fund working to understand Black and Minority led media engagement difficulties
items.b: Civic Power Fund are working with a wide range of media partners to look at why Black and Ethnic Minority organisations find it so difficult to get traction for their work in the media. They are interested to speak to. media organisations interested in addressing this deficit and Black and Minority led campaigning groups who are struggling to get media attention. Can you help?
items.note: A research/call-for-input notice rather than a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: UK Parliament Week: 18th-24th November 2024
items.b: Run by the UK Parliamentary Education and Engagement Team and taking place this November, UK Parliament Week (UKPW) is an annual event, spreading the word about what Parliament is, what it does and how you can get involved. UK Parliament Week (UKPW) is a great opportunity to empower young people to use their voices and participate in their democracy both locally and in Westminster!
items.why: it is a campaign designed to help people, especially young people, understand and take part in parliamentary democracy.
items.note: Sector capacity-building event aimed at boosting civic engagement, so filed under participation.
links: UK Parliamentary Education and Engagement Team

items.h: Involve to celebrate their 20th anniversary next month
items.b: Is the democracy sector maturing? You could definitely argue such — with mySociety hosting its 20th anniversary last year, and now it’s Involve’s turn. The special anniversary event on October 17th is invite-only, featuring a team of panellists exploring the future of public engagement and deliberative decision making and a celebration of Involve’s work over the previous two decades..
items.note: Organisational anniversary celebration, excluded as organisation-as-organisation news.

items.h: Newspeak House launch their 2024 residency programme
items.b: Newspeak House — the London College of Political Technology , is a community hub and event space for political technologists and a new college to nurture emerging talent in the field. With a newly expanded faculty, Newspeak House welcomes 15 students from across the globe to London to study political technology this year — find out more . This weekend last year’s students celebrated completing their course and earning their Fellowship , with student projects ranging from Whatsard , to a new tool for archiving deleted MP tweets (replacing retired Politwoops), 2024 Election Tech Handbook and Org…
items.why: it launches a new training programme creating fresh capacity for people to shape political technology and civic tools that support democratic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation rather than mere organisational news.
links: Newspeak House — the London College of Political Technology

items.h: The All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political and Media Literacy update
items.b: Convened by Shout Out UK (SOUK) , the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political and Media Literacy is dedicated to improving the state of political and media education among young people in the UK. The group has recently broadened its scope to champion media literacy as an essential element of its drive to update the national curriculum to meet the demands of the 21st century. The APPG’s inaugural AGM will take place in October. To stay up-to-date on the APPG, subscribe to the SOUK newsletter .
items.note: Primarily an organisational AGM/update notice rather than a reported change in policy or participation mechanism.
links: All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political and Media Literacy

items.h: Muslim Women Connect launch Roots Fellowship Programme
items.b: The Muslim Women Connect Roots Fellowship Programme is a faith-led development programme is not just about career advancement — it’s about deepening your spiritual relationship, challenging societal stereotypes, and arming you with the support you need to make active contributions to society and speak out on the social issues that matter most to you. The free course is six months long, with 25 fellows, grounded in Islamic values and features a three day in-person residential retreat in Morocco.
items.why: it creates a new fellowship equipping participants to speak out and contribute actively on social issues, expanding civic engagement capacity.
items.note: Counted as sector capacity-building under participation despite its faith-based framing, since it builds civic voice and engagement.
links: Muslim Women Connect Roots Fellowship Programme

items.h: Elect Her forging ahead with roadmap for systematic reform, developing their candidate community
items.b: Hannah, Rosie and Annabel at Elect Her kick off a new programme of support for prospective female political leaders — the new Start Here workshop aims to facilitate discussions with Scottish universities on women and their power — contact Kirsty for details ). But that’s not all, from Councillors Coffee Time, new Peer Support Circles starting in October, to coaching and supporting Fawcett deliver the new woman’s caucus in Parliament, they’ve definitely got their hands full! Contact Annabel for more information or follow their exploits here .
items.why: it creates new training and support pathways that help women take part as candidates and leaders in political life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building programme creating new means of participation.

items.h: Julia Cushion TikTok star AKA how to turn your blogs into popular video summaries
items.b: Last month Julia Cushion, mySociety’s Policy & Advocacy Manager kicked her TikTok fu into gear and earned 10s of thousands of hits on her video on flytipping(!), and another with more than 10,000 views for a video about the sudden reduction in APPGs this year — turns out turning your blog posts into video summaries really works!
items.note: This is organisational content-marketing news, not a change to participation, information plurality or accountability.
links: turns out turning your blog posts into video summaries

items.h: What’s happening with Democracy Box you ask?
items.b: The Democracy Box is a rich 155-page report co-created by young people from across Wales . The report, evidenced by years of youth-led research, stresses the need to abandon the elections-first approach when it comes to the democratic education information gap — and instead provide year round education and information. Yvonne Murphy of Omidaze Productions , who has been diligently working on The Democracy Box for the past decade provides their latest update on progress with the BBC and Electoral Commission.
items.why: it develops a resource aimed at improving year-round democratic education, expanding people's capacity to understand and take part in civic life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building resource under the participation rule.
links: The Democracy Box is a rich 155-page report co-created by young people from across Wales

items.h: Association for Citizenship Teaching seeks feedback from 16–18 year olds on the future of democratic education
items.b: The Association for Citizenship Teaching is conducting nationwide research on the impact of studying Citizenship Studies for democratic engagement, participation, and reduced social inequality. They want to hear from any 16–18 year olds across the country — they don’t have to have studied Citizenship Studies. You can share the online survey here . That’s not all, they’re running an online panel on 14th October on the role of citizenship education in engaging young people in democracy — find out more .
items.note: A feedback survey and panel discussion is sector research/event logistics rather than a new means of participation itself.

items.h: Keseb hosting a range of events on civic power, public leadership and misinformation
items.b: Keseb run a far-reaching Democracy Champions Network, giving democratic innovators, entrepreneurs and leaders the tools, resources and skills they need to demand change, safeguard democratic norms and processes and inspire the next generation — their upcoming Conversation Series, 21st-Century Democracy: Building a Transnational Innovation Ecosystem is running weekly through October, following on the back of their recent SSIR essays , register now.
items.why: it builds a network giving civic leaders tools and skills to safeguard democratic norms and mobilise others, expanding capacity for democratic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building network under the participation rule.

items.h: Co-Production Network for Wales is looking for board members
items.b: Keen to help advance co-production practices in Wales to ensure a fairer and more sustainable society in which everyone’s voice is heard? Then check out this job description and join the Co-Production Network for Wales as a board member. Applications close on the 14th of October.
items.note: Board member recruitment is organisational admin, not a democracy story.

items.h: Stormont votes in favour of lowering the voting age to 16
items.b: Last week the Northern Irish Assembly voted in favour of a motion and amendment to lower the voting age to 16, in line with Scotland and Wales. The motion passed despite opposition from the Democratic Unionist Party and Traditional Unionist Voice. Earlier this month teenagers across Northern Ireland called for lowering the voting age .
items.why: lowering the voting age directly changes the franchise, determining who can exercise the vote in elections.
links: Northern Irish Assembly voted in favour
Earlier this month teenagers across Northern Ireland called for lowering the voting age

items.h: Learnings from the Votes at 16 Launch Conference
items.b: Politics in Action is coordinating a youth-led campaign to lower the voting age to 16 in Northern Ireland. On the 13th of September, Politics in Action hosted world leading experts on Votes at 16, including Dr Jan Eichhorn of the University of Edinburgh, whose research highlighted the increase in voter turnout and the positive voter behaviours associated with lowering the voting age. If you would like to hear more about the insights and discussions from the conference, then please contact Emily via emily@politicsinaction.org .
items.why: the conference concerns a campaign and evidence about lowering the voting age and its effect on turnout, which is franchise and electoral participation.
items.note: Turnout and voting-age campaigning are always filed under elections per the standing rule.

items.h: Labour and Cross-Party MPs join forces to create new All-Party Parliamentary Group for Fair Elections
items.b: A new APPG for Fair Elections has been set up to enhance the integrity of UK democracy. The group, chaired by Labour’s Alex Sobel MP, will focus on replacing First Past the Post with a more proportional voting system, removing dark money and other undemocratic influences from UK politics, and countering disinformation. Fair Vote UK will be the new secretariat for the APPG.
items.why: This matters democratically because the new APPG aims to reshape the electoral system, campaign finance rules and disinformation safeguards that determine how competitive and trustworthy UK elections are.
items.note: Focus on electoral system, dark money and disinformation places it primarily in elections machinery despite being a parliamentary group.
links: APPG for Fair Elections has been set up

items.h: UK Democracy Fund to host lessons learned event on GE2024 tomorrow
items.b: The UK Democracy Fund are convening grantees and key stakeholders tomorrow in London to explore what happened in the 2024 General Election and what can be learnt from the experience.
items.note: Event listing/logistics rather than a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Electoral Commission calls for improvements to Voter ID laws as 16,000 not able to vote at general election
items.b: 16,000 people were unable to vote in the general election due to Voter ID laws, according to new analysis from the Electoral Commission . This represents 0.08% of voters, which is a reduction from the 0.25% at the local elections in May 2023. The Electoral Commission has recommended the government review the list of accepted IDs and has put forward other proposals to ensure fewer voters are impeded by the laws at the next election. Read the report .
items.why: This matters democratically because Voter ID rules directly determine who can exercise their right to vote, and the Electoral Commission's findings and recommendations affect access to the ballot.
links: new analysis from the Electoral Commission

items.h: Compassion in Politics pushing for UK-wide criminalisation of lying in politics
items.b: Compassion in Politics are currently running a 200,000 strong petition to reinforce their campaigning for the criminalisation of lying in politics in the UK — they’ve worked with lawyers on a new Bill for Parliament — see Byline Times coverage . The new Labour Leader of the House of Commons Lucy Powell MP has said the UK does not need a lying bill . Last week the Senedd closed their inquiry into lying in politics .
items.why: This matters democratically because a legal mechanism to police political honesty would change how politicians are held answerable for their public statements.
items.note: Campaign for a lying-in-politics law concerns standards in public life rather than electoral machinery or media plurality specifically.
links: they’ve worked with lawyers on a new Bill for Parliament
Lucy Powell MP has said the UK does not need a lying bill
the Senedd closed their inquiry into lying in politics

items.h: Carnegie UK publish new insights and recommendations on democratic wellbeing
items.b: Back in 2023 Carnegie UK began a programme of engagement to help improve our understanding of participatory and deliberative democracy’s ability to deliver democratic wellbeing, in partnership with their group of 13 ‘Democratic Wellbeing Champions’ . This report captures the insights from that work, the ideas and observations generated and key recommendations for policy makers and campaigners — read the report now .
items.why: This matters democratically because the report offers recommendations on how deliberative and participatory democratic processes can be designed to improve collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative democracy content is anchored to elections_decision_making per the framework's boundary rule, though the item is closer to a research resource.

items.h: Newport residents prepare for 185th Anniversary of the Chartist Newport Rising
items.b: In 1839 thousands of Chartists, campaigning for democracy, the right to vote with a secret ballot, and for the common people to have their voices heard, marched on Newport to rescue fellow imprisoned activists, in the last large scale armed rebellion in the United Kingdom. On the 2nd November, Newport Rising will be hosting a torch lit march through the city, music and community activities to remember their sacrifice — join the rising, grab your ticket .
items.note: Commemorative historical anniversary event, not a report on a current democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Electoral reform remains a strong priority for Liberal Democrats, reports Electoral Reform Society
items.b: Despite fears that electoral reform might slip as a priority for the Lib Dems in light of their historic gains at the general election, the Electoral Reform Society reports that it was a strong theme at their party conference. A conference debate saw the party reaffirm its support for the Single Transferable Vote (STV) — something that has been in every manifesto since 1980. The motion also saw conference reaffirm support for the introduction of voting rights for 16 year olds, scrapping Voter ID laws, and the introduction of a new system of automatic voter registration.
items.why: This matters democratically because the party's stated priorities on proportional representation, voting age, Voter ID and automatic registration bear directly on the electoral system's design and accessibility.

items.h: Talk Shop running Win Win Workshops on 20mph zones
items.b: This month and next, Perry Walker of Talk Shop and Paul Thistlethwaite of Thinking Box are running several of their Win Win Workshops in Torbay, York and Hereford, on 20mph speed limits and the latter on childhood use of smart phones. Contact Perry to find out more about these activities.
items.note: A workshop announcement on local policy topics functions as an event listing rather than reporting a new democratic mechanism.

items.h: Connected by Data & ISWE publish new report on global citizen deliberation and AI
items.b: The new report Global Citizen Deliberation on Artificial Intelligence — Options and design considerations published by ISWE and Connected by Data explores how global citizen deliberation could shape the future of artificial intelligence. The report draws on extensive research, a design lab of in-depth interviews and workshops, and presents a series of options for practitioners and process designers. Download the report .
items.why: exploring citizen deliberation on AI extends direct public input into how emerging technology governance decisions are made.
items.note: Report on deliberative process design maps to elections & decision-making per framework, though its global scope makes UK relevance indirect.
links: Global Citizen Deliberation on Artificial Intelligence — Options and design considerations

items.h: Extinction Rebellion host large-scale community assembly
items.b: Outside Windsor Castle last month, Extinction Rebellion UK ran what they think could well be the UK’s largest community assembly on democracy, the results of which they then fed into the deliberative platform Pol.is , the results of which can be viewed here on XR UK’s Rebel Toolkit . See more info on their next event here .
items.why: a large-scale community assembly feeding into a deliberative platform extends direct citizen input into collective decision-making beyond elections.
items.note: Deliberative assemblies are classified under elections & decision-making, not participation, per framework rule.

items.h: Electoral Reform Society welcomes legislation to remove hereditary Peers from House of Lords
items.b: The government has now published legislation that sets in motion the removal of all 92 hereditary Peers from the House of Lords, revoking a right that has stood in place for 700 years! The Electoral Reform Society is ‘rejoicing that this blight on our democracy will finally be cleared up’, but is calling for further action to create a smaller, fully elected, territorial second chamber.
items.why: removing hereditary peers and reconsidering the composition of the second chamber changes who holds legislative power and how accountable that chamber is to the public.
items.note: Lords reform touches both parliamentary effectiveness (accountability) and calls for an elected chamber (elections); classified primarily as accountability since the news is about legislative composition.

items.h: Compass report outlines role of democratic reform in creating a renewed Britain
items.b: A new report from Compass , The New Settlement for a Better Society , sets out the role democratic reform can play in creating transformational change across the UK. The report calls for stronger democracy in communities and in local economies, a public-serving media, changes to the electoral system, and more — all of this underpinned by a ‘democratic mindset’ that foregrounds participation and inclusion.
items.why: the report proposes reforms to local democracy, electoral systems and media that would reshape the conditions for public participation in political and economic life.
items.note: Report spans multiple beats; classified under participation given its emphasis on community-level democratic mindset and inclusion.
links: The New Settlement for a Better Society

items.h: All Island Better Democracy Network tackling barriers to deliberative engagement
items.b: Last month, the All Island Better Democracy Network came together for a DIY Democracy workshop on how to break down the barriers to deliberative engagement, a valuable and worthwhile practice — but one that can often come with a high price tag! The session left participants with strategies to overcome this and a sense of a new community of practice dedicated to deliberative democracy on the island of Ireland.
items.why: building practitioner capacity to overcome barriers to deliberative engagement expands the practical means available for citizens to take part in collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative engagement practice is classified under elections & decision-making per the framework's treatment of deliberative processes.

items.b: All-Island Better Democracy Network hold DIY Democracy Workshop (Credit: Involve)

items.h: UK Government agrees devolution deals across England
items.b: Subject to parliamentary approval and local consent, devolution deals agreements have been reached in Hull & East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Lancashire, Devin and Torbay . Deputy PM Angela Rayner described the move as the ‘first step of our major ambition to drive forward our devolution revolution’.
items.why: devolution deals transfer governmental powers and decision-making authority to sub-national institutions, restructuring how local democracy operates.
links: devolution deals agreements have been reached in Hull & East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Lancashire, Devin and Torbay

items.h: Research for Action launch new three year Councils in Crisis project
items.b: Gloria Dawson and the team at Research for Action have begun a new 3-year project called Councils in Crisis, where they are exploring how local government financial instability (and the actions taken to mitigate/ remedy it) affect democracy and accountability. They’re open to discussions about this as they’re at an early research stage and currently mapping out what’s at stake. Get in touch with Gloria here .
items.why: examining how council financial instability affects accountability addresses whether local government can be effectively held answerable to the public it serves.
items.note: Focus on financial instability's effect on accountability places this under government accountability rather than local government structure.

items.h: Coming soon: Fearless Cities South Yorkshire, Nov 1–3 2024
items.b: Citizen Network , Opus , Research for Action , Neighbourhood Democracy and Care Full co-organising the upcoming Fearless Cities summit in Sheffield , 1–3 November. Fearless cities is an international gathering of municipal projects, supporting connections between cities, organisations, communities and citizens who are building new public commons and deeper forms of local democracy and care across the world.
items.note: Event listing for a summit, not a reported change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Citizen Network working to establish constitutional convention for Yorkshire
items.b: Earlier this year on April 1st — exactly fifty years since the abolition of the thousand year old Ridings of Yorkshire, over 100 proud citizens and community leaders across Yorkshire signed the Yorkshire Declaration , which was read out loud at the Eye of York. The Declaration called on ending the centralisation of power in London and bringing real power to Yorkshire and the regions. Now, Simon Duffy and the Citizen Network coalition are working to establish a constitutional convention, get updates here .
items.why: it describes an effort to build new regional decision-making machinery through a constitutional convention that would shift power from Westminster to Yorkshire.
items.note: Constitutional conventions and regional governance structures are filed under elections & decision making per the framework.

items.h: Angela Rayner promises greater devolution across Northern England
items.b: Speaking ahead of the Labour Party Conference, Angela Rayner promised to ‘complete devolution in the North’ and said that ‘Northerners would no longer be dictated to by Westminster.’ A new report from the Institute for Government highlights the work still to do to achieve this, as half of England’s population is not covered by any form of devolution. Their report, How the Government can extend devolution to the whole of England , outlines how the government can achieve its aim of devolving power around the country.
items.why: it concerns proposed changes to the structure and reach of devolved government across England.
links: Angela Rayner promised to ‘complete devolution in the North’
How the Government can extend devolution to the whole of England

items.h: Byline Times planning new Media Watch project on state of UK media
items.b: Byline Times is setting up a new project, Byline Media Watch , to identify and analyse the misinformation and bias within the mainstream UK press. The new project is being crowdfunded — view and support the crowdfunding campaign here .
items.why: it creates a new mechanism for scrutinising bias and misinformation in the mainstream press, affecting the public information environment.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building for the information environment rather than a mere funding appeal, since the project itself is the new means of scrutiny.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation announce new Tenacious Journalist Awards
items.b: The awards by Public Interest News Foundation allow for access to between £5,000 to £20,000 to carry out a significant piece of journalism which makes a huge social impact. Deadline for interest is 31st October — apply now .
items.note: A funding/award call for journalists, treated as sector logistics.

items.h: TV broadcast and newspapers seen as most trusted news outlets, despite changing consumption patterns
items.b: A new Ofcom report finds that, for the first time since the 1960s, online sites and apps are now narrowly more popular than TV news — much of this driven by the increased use of social media for daily news updates. However, TV news and newspapers are still seen as the most trusted, accurate, and impartial sources of information.
items.why: it reports a shift in how the public consumes and trusts news sources, affecting the plurality and reliability of the information environment underpinning democratic debate.

items.h: National Union of Journalists passes motion on restoring trust in the media
items.b: The Assistant General Secretary of the NUJ, Seamus Dooley, said at the 2024 Trade Union Congress that the existential crisis in the news industry is prompting an existential crisis of democracy. A motion was passed based on the NUJ’s News Recovery Plan , which outlines a number of steps to reset the media industry, including plans to tackle social media misinformation, improve pay and conditions for freelancers, and reform public ownership models with strengthened public interest in mind.
items.why: the motion targets structural weaknesses in journalism, including misinformation and public ownership models, that bear on the public's access to a plural and reliable information environment.
links: said at the 2024 Trade Union Congress

items.h: TBIJ, Open Democracy and Bristol Cable join press regulator Impress
items.b: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism , Open Democracy and The Bristol Cable — have signed up to independent press regulator Impress , which the regulator calls ‘three of the most innovative publishers’ in the UK. They join more than 200 other — mostly small, online and either local or specialist — member publications to Impress, which is a rival regulator to the Independent Press Standards Organisation which represents most newspaper and magazine publishers in the UK.
items.why: it reflects a shift in the press regulation landscape that shapes standards and accountability within the media environment underpinning public debate.
items.note: Treated as a substantive shift in media regulation rather than routine organisational news.

items.h: New Demos & Liberty report on public attitudes to protest published
items.b: The People’s Town Square on Protest — Behind the Headlines is a new report that uses deliberation for the first time ever to understand what the public really thinks about the right to protest. Demos & Liberty identified a nuanced picture of attitudes which calls into question the rationale for recent anti-protest legislation. The research finds overwhelming support (83%) for the right to peaceful and nonviolent protest The report includes some clear recommendations, including that the Government commission a comprehensive, independent review on the right to protest in Britain. View the report…
items.why: public attitudes toward and legal restrictions on peaceful protest determine whether people can exercise freedom of assembly to challenge and contest public power
items.note: Uses deliberation as a research method, but the substantive issue is protest law and rights rather than decision-making machinery.
links: The People’s Town Square on Protest — Behind the Headlines

items.h: Labour Party faces major freebies scandal
items.b: Free Taylor Swift tickets, clothing passed off as office expenses, senior corporate lobbyists working at the heart of government undeclared , these are just a few of the litany of expenses and freebies detailed by openDemocracy over the last two months. Senior members of the Labour Party have accepted more than £170,000 in gifts and donations since the start of 2023 — and recently elected Labour MPs received more than £80,000 in-kind donations from lobbying firms working on their election campaigns , but due to a rules loophole we will never know the full amount or how widespread this practice…
items.why: undisclosed gifts, donations and undeclared lobbyist access to senior politicians create conflicts of interest that undermine standards in public life and accountability
links: senior corporate lobbyists working at the heart of government undeclared
elected Labour MPs received more than £80,000 in-kind donations from lobbying firms working on their election campaigns

items.h: Tories received four times more campaign funding from unincorporated associations compared to 2019
items.b: Analysis from the Electoral Reform Society finds that the Conservative Party received £375,000 in campaign funding from Unincorporated Associations (UA) in the run-up to the election. This made up approximately 20% of their total funding and equates to roughly four times the amount they received from UAs in 2019. The Conservatives were the only party to receive funding from UAs, which, although legally allowed to donate to UK parties, have attracted widespread criticism due to their opaque internal finances.
items.why: opaque campaign funding channels shape the fairness and transparency of party financing, a core condition for competitive elections
links: Analysis from the Electoral Reform Society

items.h: Ofcom needs ‘emergency powers’ to tackle misinformation, says Centre for Countering Digital Hate
items.b: A new report from Center for Countering Digital Hate , ‘ Social Media’s Role in the UK Riots’ , takes a closer look at the way social media was used to foment online hatred and misinformation. The report recommends a series of amendments to the Online Safety Law, including ‘emergency powers’ for Ofcom to allow the regulator to de-amplify harmful posts. CCDH also published Building a Safe and Accountable Internet this month, setting out the STAR framework ( S afety by Design, T ransparency, A ccountability, R esponsibility), which policymakers can adopt to bring greater levels of accountability…
items.why: unchecked misinformation and hate on social media distorts the public information environment people rely on to make political judgements
links: ‘ Social Media’s Role in the UK Riots’
Building a Safe and Accountable Internet

items.h: Hope Not Hate publish new report on Reform UK
items.b: As the Austrian far-right clinch victory in their national election last week, Hope Not Hate have published a new report Reform UK: Everything the progressive movement needs to know , detailing the rising threat of the far-right party, explaining their strategy, funding and history.
items.why: analysis of a rising political party's strategy and funding bears on political competition and voters' ability to assess electoral options
items.note: Borderline: could be read as media/information analysis rather than electoral competition, so confidence is low.
links: Reform UK: Everything the progressive movement needs to know

items.h: New Compass report looks at far-right riot root causes
items.b: A new report from Compass — After the Riots — takes a closer look at this context, suggesting a clear link between social deprivation and social unrest. Compass is also calling for a Public Inquiry into the Causes and Cures of Political Extremism, to hear the voices of the communities most affected by and vulnerable to extremism.
items.why: calling for a public inquiry into the causes of political extremism is a scrutiny mechanism to hold institutions accountable for addressing root causes
items.note: Public inquiry framing places this in accountability rather than rule of law, per the standing distinction.

items.h: Major win for Full Fact as Daily Express correct false claim following lengthy battle
items.b: On Boxing Day last year, the Daily Express published a false claim in a comment piece which suggested Labour’s policies would lead to the UK taking in an additional 100,000 migrants every year. After a lengthy back-and-forth, which included Full Fact taking the case to the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO), the Express agreed to officially correct the article .
items.why: correcting false political claims in the press protects the integrity of the public information environment that underpins informed democratic debate
links: Express agreed to officially correct the article

items.h: Starmer must make bold changes on ethics, says Institute for Government
items.b: As outrage over Labour’s top brass accepting freebies from wealthy donors grows, the Institute for Government outlines three crucial steps for Starmer to draw a line under the scandal. These include: publishing the updated ministerial code which the new Government has delayed doing, confirming that the independent advisor has the power to investigate breaches of the code (something promised while in opposition), and setting out the details of the new Ethics and Integrity Commission.
items.why: ministerial codes, independent ethics advisers and a proposed integrity commission are mechanisms for holding the executive answerable for its conduct
links: Institute for Government outlines three crucial steps

items.b: Climate activists protest outside North Yorkshire Police (Credit: Gary Calton/The Observer)
items.why: This matters democratically because it depicts citizens exercising the right to protest against state institutions, a core civic liberty.
items.note: Caption accompanies a protest-policing story; classified as protest/assembly under rights per boundary rule.

items.h: Twenty-five conspiracy arrests made during peaceful climate protest at Drax power station
items.b: Last month, the police controversially arrested 25 climate protesters involved in the annual climate camp gathering near Drax Power Station, which burns pellets from rare old-growth forests in the USA . The long running annual gathering of climate activists , includes training and panel discussions — which usually includes peaceful protests targeting carbon / fossil fuel infrastructure. This year, in a major escalation, police intercepted participants on their way to the event and arrested them on conspiracy charges, searching and seizing equipment and vehicles. The arrests were made under rec…
items.why: This matters democratically because new protest laws restricting assembly near infrastructure directly curtail citizens' ability to organise and dissent against state and corporate power.
items.note: Protest story classified as rights/freedoms because the issue is legal restriction, policing and state coercion, not willingness to participate.
links: arrested 25 climate protesters involved in the annual climate camp gathering
burns pellets from rare old-growth forests in the USA
See Network for Police monitoring for more information

items.h: mySociety explores donations and gifts to MPs
items.b: The first financial interests register has been published and mySociety has been busy updating MPs’ profiles accordingly on TheyWorkForYou and making the data easily available in a spreadsheet . Also, keep your eyes peeled as their ‘Who Funds Them’ project is soon getting underway which will provide even greater depth on the financial interests of MPs.
items.why: This matters democratically because a public register of MPs' financial interests, made accessible and searchable, strengthens the ability to hold elected representatives to account for conflicts of interest.

items.h: New AI legislation monitoring platform Seelaw launches
items.b: Seelaw is a new platform which uses AI to help monitor, understand and scrutinise UK legislation. They’re currently working out how to better scrutinise legislative amendments using AI tools. Joe Coker and the team are interested in speaking to anyone who needs to stay up to date and understand the impacts of legislation who can inform the development of the platform and help meet their needs. Get in touch via joe@seelaw.co
items.why: This matters democratically because a new tool that helps the public and civil society scrutinise legislative amendments creates a new means of engaging with the legislative process.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new participation mechanism rather than an accountability story about Parliament itself.

items.h: Campaign Lab runs Campaign Fringe on electoral technology innovation at Labour Party Conference
items.b: Campaign Lab runs a progressive volunteer community aimed at developing and exploring innovations in election and political technology, this year they ran an unofficial fringe event in Liverpool alongside the conference, bringing together a range of organisations from CCDH , to Autonomy Institute , Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK , INQUEST , UCL Policy Lab — and panellists on topics from electoral experiments to tackle the far right, to highlighting impactful electoral tech innovations in 2024.
items.note: Event recap of a conference fringe gathering, not a new resource, tool or mechanism that changes what people can do.
links: Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK

items.h: New AI tool Suffrago running data dashboards for every MP and constituency
items.b: Back during the 2023 Selby & Ainsty By-Election , Andrew Gray and Dr Simon Wallace stood as a candidate on a Polis-powered manifesto , now they’re back with Suffrago . The new tool includes data dashboards for every MP, based on their constituency data, plus a legislation explainer and anonymous quasi-Polis-like voting platform for members of the public to express their views on what is going on in their constituencies and to vote on how their MPs have voted. Launching next month!
items.why: This matters democratically because a new tool letting constituents track and vote on how their MPs have voted creates a new channel for public engagement with elected representatives.
items.note: Classified as a new means of participation under the sector capacity-building rule.
links: a candidate on a Polis-powered manifesto

items.h: Imperial College offering free course in AI for public servants
items.b: See more information on the free course for public servants here .
items.note: A training course announcement for public servants' AI skills, not a mechanism affecting democratic participation, accountability or rights.

items.h: JRRT Vice Chair set to compete in the Commonwealth Powerlifting Federation Championships
items.b: Alison Goldsworthy, Vice Chair of the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust is set to compete in the Commonwealth Powerlifting Federation Championships on the 9th October in South Africa. You can tune to watch her live on Eurosports or follow her instagram to keep up to date on her progress. Good luck Alison!
items.sec: And now for something completely different…
items.note: Personal/organisational news about an individual's sporting activity, not a democracy story.
