items.h: Local Trust, Demos and Centre for Regional Economic and Social Research invite submissions on community regeneration
items.b: Local Trust is running a new essay competition in tandem with Demos and CRESR , looking at innovative ideas on community regeneration. Entrants must submit a 2,500 word essay on the following: ‘What is your policy idea for turning the most socially and economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods in England into thriving communities, what is the evidence behind it, and how might it best be successfully implemented with maximum impact?’ The winner will receive £5,000 and two runners up will receive £1,000. Deadline 10th January 2025. Apply now .
items.note: An essay competition on regeneration policy ideas is sector/calls-to-action content, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Advanced Apprenticeship seeking applicants
items.b: Democracy Network and Happy Ltd are offering a new Level 5 Advanced Apprenticeship for change agents, leaders and managers, delivered by Titus Alexander — find out more information and book a taster session .
items.note: A generic leadership/management apprenticeship, not a tool specifically enabling democratic participation.
links: find out more information and book a taster session

items.h: Are you working with 16–19 year olds? Associate for Citizenship Teaching want to hear from you
items.b: ACT are conducting research on the efficacy of GCSE Citizenship Studies on young people’s levels of democratic engagement and participation — find out more here .
items.note: A call for research participants is sector logistics, not a new means of democratic participation.

items.h: Looking to upgrade your deliberation or facilitation skills? Involve has the training for you
items.b: Involve are running two 3.5 hour long training ‘masterclass’ sessions, Facilitation 101 and Deliberative Democracy 101, at the end of this month. The sessions are donation-based Pay-What-You-Feel, find out more information here .
items.why: training facilitators and citizens in deliberative democracy skills builds new capacity for people to take part in collective decision-making processes.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation, per the framework rule.

items.b: The Autonomy Institute has got funding to work on a new tool to facilitate greater transparency and accountability between the UK Government and its contractors.
items.why: a new tool to increase transparency between government and its contractors strengthens the mechanisms by which public power can be held answerable.

items.b: 50:50 NI’s Hear Her Project has also received £30,100 to implement a new comprehensive training programme designed to address gender disparity in political representation in Northern Ireland.
items.why: a training programme to address gender disparity in political representation improves equal access to political power for an underrepresented group.
items.note: Framed as building equal access to power rather than as a rights/discrimination claim, so placed in participation.

items.b: Police Spies Out of Lives have garnered £87,750 for the duration of the remaining tranches of the Undercover Policing Inquiry, to support their members through the evidential stages of the process and bring public attention to the misogynistic abuse and assault on democracy by political undercover policing.
items.why: supporting victims through the evidential stages of a public inquiry into undercover policing concerns redress for state wrongdoing affecting democratic and personal rights.
items.note: Public inquiry story framed around support for redress rather than scrutiny, so filed under rule of law.

items.b: My Life My Say has received £75,840 in funding to build a largely parliamentary-facing campaign around lowering the voting age.
items.why: a campaign to lower the voting age concerns who is included in the franchise and able to vote.

items.b: Unlock Democracy have won £10,000 to put on a conference in which democracy sector organisations will agree on a set of core campaign proposals, centering on the themes of electoral reform, open and responsive democracy, and a thriving democratic culture.
items.why: a conference bringing democracy sector organisations together to agree shared campaign proposals builds the capacity and coordination of civil society to act on democratic reform.
items.note: Borderline between sector capacity-building and organisational event logistics; treated as capacity-building since it aims to shape future campaigning.

items.h: JRSST Charitable Trust also published their most recent grantees
items.b: The JRSST Charitable Trust is a small charitable trust set up by JRRT in 1955, which operates as a connected but independent Trust. Their grantees included:
items.note: Announcement of grantee list is organisational administrative news, not a reported democratic mechanism.

items.b: Campaign for Freedom of Information Scotland — £29k over 18 months to support a Member’s Bill to reform the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 (FoISA).
items.note: Funding award announcement for advocacy work, not a reported change in FOI law or a participation-building tool.
links: Campaign for Freedom of Information Scotland

items.b: Sarah Shair-Rosenfield at the University of York , who is to undertake work to better understand public attitudes towards abuse and harassment of candidates through a set of survey experiments. The findings of which will help scholars and policymakers understand public reactions to the kinds of threats and violence that are increasingly directed towards political candidates in the UK.
items.note: Academic research funding announcement, sector logistics rather than a reported democratic mechanism change.
links: Sarah Shair-Rosenfield at the University of York

items.b: Spotlight on Corruption , who have received £34,896 to support their work to push for reform to the UK’s framework for upholding political integrity.
items.note: Grant award announcement to an advocacy organisation, not itself a reported reform or participation tool.

items.h: Engender launch new project to understand Scottish women councillors experiences of sexism
items.b: The new research project aims to understand the experiences of everyday sexism, misogyny & VAW within the council environment. Engender is currently in the process of hiring a consultant with an understanding of Scottish local government women’s underrepresentation in politics, and feminist analysis of VAW.
items.note: Launch of a research project studying an issue, not a participation tool or reported policy change.

items.h: UK Democracy Fund host day of grantee reflection focused on lessons learnt from GE2024
items.b: In October, UK Democracy Fund brought together 43 people from their grantee and wider voter engagement community to reflect on GE2024 and look ahead to new challenges posed.
items.note: Event/convening among grantees, organisational activity rather than a democracy story.

items.h: Robert Bosch Stiftung launches new economic inequality fund
items.b: The new fund, which allows UK organisations to apply, has launched a call for proposals for grants between €100,000 to €400,000 per applying organisation or coalition. The funding round closes on 15th December 2024. Check out the Robert Bosch Stiftung Building Power For Economic Justice Fund .
items.note: A funding call for applications, explicitly sector logistics.
links: Check out the Robert Bosch Stiftung Building Power For Economic Justice Fund

items.h: Convening opportunity around the Modernisation Committee
items.b: The Modernisation Committee is a newly announced cross-party committee of MPs that will consider reforms to the House of Commons procedures, standards and working practices. Earlier this month, the Committee launched a call for views . Democracy Network has organised two calls, earlier on Nov 5th, and an upcoming call on Nov 13th ( sign up ) to convene those planning around the new Committee. Unlock Democracy are also working with the Civil Society Alliance and former civil servant Caroline Slocock with a view to submitting a response on the Modernisation Committee.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns a new parliamentary committee reviewing how the House of Commons scrutinises government and regulates its own standards and procedures.
items.note: Wrapped in sector convening logistics, but the underlying fact is a substantive reform process for parliamentary scrutiny.

items.h: Democracy Coworking — Cardiff & London
items.b: Join us in Cardiff for our next Democracy Coworking & Drinks at the Welsh Millenium Centre on November 20th — Register now . London Democracy Coworking continues November 29th at Newspeak House — Register now .
items.note: Pure event listing with no democratic mechanism at stake.

items.h: Democracy Network Christmas Party, 6th December
items.b: The Democracy Network is hosting a Christmas bash in London on the 6th December, replete with nibbles & drinks included in the cost of your ticket — register now!

items.h: Democracy Network Steering Group met for in-person strategy day
items.b: Last month, the Democracy Network Steering Group , elected by members earlier in the year, met to discuss fundraising plans for the network and refreshing the Network’s strategy. Stay tuned for more developments on this soon, plus a blog! They’re meeting again soon later in December.
items.note: Internal organisational strategy meeting, not a democracy story per se.

items.h: The People Act — new online hub for legislative theatre launches
items.b: The People Act is a new hub that brings together legislative theatre case studies, videos, resources, news and more. The new site contains everything you need to get started with Legislative Theatre and to use this playful, innovative and people powered process wherever you are — check it out now .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new resource enabling communities to use legislative theatre as a participatory, deliberative tool to engage with policymaking.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation.

items.h: Association of Democratic Services Officers Conference, 25–26 November
items.b: The Association of Democratic Services Officers annual conference is fast approaching, Diane Sims reports. This year they celebrate their first ever CEO of ADSO and their new report, ‘ Working in a Modern Democracy ’. The report explores what people who work in councils and other organisations think about our changing democracy. ADSO also lauded the new changes to allow for local authorities to hold remote or hybrid meetings, more details below! Find out more information on ADSO and the conference here .
items.why: this matters democratically because new rules allowing remote or hybrid council meetings change the structural machinery through which local government makes collective decisions.
items.note: Local government meeting format is part of the machinery of decision-making, per boundary rule on local/regional government.

items.h: Elect Her upcoming events, new research, evolving roadmap
items.b: Elect Her are now running free training events for women seeking to stand for election in the 2026 Senedd and Scottish Parliament elections. New research suggests parliamentary gender quotas sharply improve maternal mortality rates by as much as 7–12% on a sustained basis! Ongoing concern that women’s representation in Parliament will fall from current 40% numbers in future parliaments, as local and regional levels sit at 34% or less. Editor’s note — key takeaway from today’s Bulletin : Elect Her are advancing their impressive systematic reform roadmap, a considerable piece of work that will h…
items.why: this matters democratically because training and research aimed at increasing women's candidacy and representation affect the representativeness of elected institutions.
items.note: Women's representation in parliament is an explicit elections_decision_making anchor (EIU).
links: parliamentary gender quotas sharply improve maternal mortality rates
email Elect Her for more information

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project MPower candidate training open to applications
items.b: Applications are now open for this year’s MPower political leadership programme run by Migrant Democracy Projec t, to equip first generation migrant political candidates with the skills they need to stand for election — apply here and share the opportunity . Meanwhile, Welwyn Hatfield and Lambeth have become the 14th and 15th local authorities to call on the government to extend the right to vote to all residents .
items.why: this matters democratically because candidate training for migrants and calls to extend the franchise to all residents both concern who can stand for and participate in elections.
items.note: Candidate access and suffrage extension are core elections_decision_making territory.
links: apply here and share the opportunity
right to vote to all residents

items.h: mySociety hiring Head of Fundraising (maternity cover)
items.b: With Alice Williams heading off on maternity (congratulations!), mySociety are seeking a new Head of Fundraising (maternity cover), with a deadline of 15th December — Are you up to the task? Apply now .
items.note: Organisational hiring notice, not a democracy story.
links: Are you up to the task? Apply now

items.h: Black Equity Organisation’s Black Britain Mandate launches
items.b: Black Britain’s Mandate is a new initiative by Black Equity Organisation to reshape the landscape of racial equity in the UK. The mandate puts forward key policy demands aimed at fostering a more just, inclusive, and equitable society for Britain’s Black African, Caribbean, and mixed-heritage communities, they say. Find out more about the project here , watch the launch and read the founding document .
items.why: this matters democratically because the mandate seeks to advance equal access and conditions for political and civic participation for Black communities in the UK.
items.note: Framed as equal access/participation conditions rather than a standalone equality claim.

items.h: UK Parliament Week: 18th-24th November 2024
items.b: Run by the UK Parliamentary Education and Engagement Team and taking place this November, UK Parliament Week (UKPW) is an annual event, spreading the word about what Parliament is, what it does and how you can get involved. UK Parliament Week (UKPW) is a great opportunity to empower young people to use their voices and participate in their democracy both locally and in Westminster!
items.why: it creates a new means for young people to learn about and engage with Parliament, building capacity for democratic participation
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new participation opportunities.
links: UK Parliamentary Education and Engagement Team

items.h: Electoral Commission to publish key report on 2024 General Election this week
items.b: The report to be published this week by the Electoral Commission will include a full analysis of the vote and is recommended reading for those working on or around election activities — keep your eyes peeled.
items.why: an official analysis of a general election's conduct informs assessment of electoral integrity and administration

items.h: Jon Alexander launches new Citizen Collective network
items.b: The new Citizen Collective project kicked off by Jon Alexander, author of CITIZENS , aims to be a community of practice ‘of those leading and learning for a Citizen Future’. The network will include regular introductory calls, a Discord channel, monthly spotlight calls highlighting members and organisations in the community and a regular workshop space to discuss live challenges and questions. Explore and sign up to the Citizen Collective now .
items.why: a new network creates a fresh channel for practitioners to build capacity for citizen-centred participation
items.note: Sector capacity-building: new network counts as creating means of participation.

items.h: Hope Not Hate report identifies drivers of fear and hope in the UK
items.b: The new report, Fear and Hope 2024: The Case for Community Resilience , published by Hope Not Hate , is the latest in their Fear and Hope series spanning more than 13 years. In this latest iteration, they review the past 14 years of public attitudes and provide recommendations for how policymakers can improve the resilience of local identity as a bulwark against the ‘permissive environment’ which is normalising anti-multiculturalism, as well as anti-Muslim and anti-migrant hatred, they say.
items.why: rising anti-Muslim and anti-migrant hatred threatens equal protection and social cohesion that underpin democratic participation
items.note: Report addresses discrimination/hate as a rights issue but borders on general social commentary.
links: Fear and Hope 2024: The Case for Community Resilience
recommendations for how policymakers can improve the resilience of local identity

items.h: Parliament and Newport remembers the Newport Rising
items.b: 185 years ago this week, more than 20 Chartists lost their lives marching on the Westgate Hotel in Newport as thousands descended on the town as part of the fight for the right to vote and the right of ordinary people to have their voices heard. The Newport Rising was the last armed rebellion against authority in Britain and played a key role in the formation of modern British democracy. Jessica Morden, MP for Newport East led the House of Commons in tribute to their sacrifice on the anniversary of the Rising. Earlier this month thousands took part in a torchlit march through the streets of Ne…
items.why: the commemoration recalls the historical struggle for suffrage that established the right to vote central to electoral democracy
items.note: Historical commemoration of the franchise struggle, not a current mechanism change; included cautiously under suffrage.
links: led the House of Commons in tribute to their sacrifice
thousands took part in a torchlit march through the streets of Newport

items.h: Democratic Business Summit to take place in December
items.b: The Centre for Democratic Business , a new Stir to Action project, is hosting the Democratic Business Summit on the 4th of December in Cardiff. With Labour promising to ‘double the size of the co-operative and mutual economy’, the festival this year offers a crucial opportunity to help advance the agenda and ensure Labour invests the funds to grow the sector, they argue. Grab your tickets here .
items.note: Business/co-operative economy event without a clear democratic mechanism at issue.

items.h: Involve celebrates 20 years
items.b: Last month Involve marked its 20th anniversary with an evening of lively discussions, reflection and celebration, bringing together past participants from citizens assemblies, juries, processes and projects to look back on two decades of achievements. Check out their interactive timeline detailing Involve’s work over the period.
items.note: Organisational anniversary/celebration, excluded per rules on organisation news.

items.h: Involve seeking independent evaluator
items.b: The Involve Foundation is seeking an independent evaluator for their new School for Everyday Democracy project . The total budget for this tender is £45,000, funded by the National Lottery Community Fund, with work taking place between December 2024 and March 2028. Find out more about the opportunity here .
items.note: Job/tender listing, sector logistics.

items.h: Common Sense to launch ‘Understanding UK Politics’ politics podcast
items.b: A new podcast from Common Sense hopes to demystify UK politics for listeners. The podcast will cover important things such as how laws are made and what makes the main political parties different from one another. A useful educational tool, the podcast offers a great way for listeners to get hold of the basics — so keep your eyes peeled for the release.
items.why: it creates a new educational resource that helps people understand how laws are made and how parties differ, building civic capacity to engage with politics.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of civic understanding.

items.h: UK election well-run and transparent, say Commonwealth Election Observers
items.b: An Election Assessment Mission Report of the 2024 UK General Election , conducted by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association , has been published based on the observation carried out at 263 polling stations. The Mission expressed high satisfaction with the administration of the election (deemed good or very good in 96% of polling stations), voters’ understanding of procedures (98% good or very good at 98%) and the transparency of the election process (99%).
items.why: independent observer assessment of election administration and transparency speaks directly to electoral integrity.
links: Election Assessment Mission Report of the 2024 UK General Election

items.h: Save the date: Notwestminster is back, Saturday 15th February
items.b: Notwestminster 2025 is a free annual event in Huddersfield for anyone who has something positive to say about local democracy — and everyone who is working to make democracy better wherever you are. Find out more and sign up to their mailing list to stay tuned.
items.note: Save-the-date event listing/mailing-list notice, not a new mechanism for participation.

items.h: Talking Shop Blackwood is re-opening!
items.b: After a hiatus, Talking Shop is back in Blackwood in South Wales, opening from December 2nd 2024. Talking Shop is a democratic and cultural information centre, created by Yvonne Murphy/Omidaze and hosted and facilitated six days a week by trained professional freelance artists and creatives, Democracy Box young co-creators and co-hosts from collaborating and partner organisations. It is a long running experiment of cultural transformation and democratic participation that aims to expand into new towns and cities.
items.why: the relaunch of a civic and cultural space designed to facilitate local democratic participation creates a new means for people to take part in civic life.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building programme reopening rather than a mere event notice.

items.h: Labour Together and New Local discuss avenues for public service devolution
items.b: A new report from New Labour — Public Service Reform and Devolution — looks at the immediate steps Keir Starmer could take to undo the over-centralisation of UK public service provision. Getting this right, they say, could help Labour achieve its growth mission and build stronger and more efficient public services across the country.
items.why: the report addresses the structure and distribution of powers between central and local government, which shapes decision-making authority at the local level.
items.note: Local government structure/powers falls under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: Fearless Cities summit held in Sheffield
items.b: Research for Action , Citizen Network and a whole host of organisations came together to deliver the Fearless Cities summit earlier this month. Find out more on how it went here .
items.note: Event recap without detail on any new participation mechanism created.

items.h: Civic Initiative held NI Citizens Forum on Housing
items.b: The three-day Citizens Forum deliberative process on November 2nd with participants recruited via postal lottery focused on making housing policy recommendations for Northern Ireland. The Civic Initiative is a participatory structure that brings together a wide range of civic society organisations to deliver citizen-led deliberative dialogues. Find out more .
items.why: a lottery-recruited citizens' deliberative forum making policy recommendations is a direct exercise of collective decision-making machinery.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies/deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making.

items.h: Government to allow virtual council attendance, ends councillor home address publishing
items.b: Finally, the long running Local Government Association campaign #DebateNotHate has borne fruit — with Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner announcing councillors home address will no longer be published. They also announced changes to allow for virtual council session attendance in a significant boost for accessibility at the local government level. See the LGA’s writeup .
items.why: allowing virtual council attendance changes the structural mechanics of local government decision-making and improves accessibility for councillors to participate.
items.note: Local government structural change filed under elections & decision making; councillor safety touches personal security as secondary.

items.h: Carnegie Trust report signals lowest ever trust in Scottish government and politics
items.b: The Life in the UK Index published by Carnegie UK measures collective wellbeing across democratic, social, economic and environmental indicators. The research, focused on Scotland, found record low levels of trust in government and politics, with over three quarters feeling they have no influence over decisions that impact the UK. Read the report .
items.why: this matters democratically because public trust in government and people's sense of influence over decisions reflect how accountable and responsive democratic institutions are perceived to be.
items.note: Trust in government is a government_accountability anchor, while 'no influence over decisions' echoes the participation anchor on perceived control over one's life.

items.h: Community Wealth Fund for Cornwall finalise proposal
items.b: The project aims to promote economic democracy and a strong local economy and has received significant support from local community organisations in Cornwall. Cornwall Council were initially very interested in the idea but have now cooled on the plan. View the two page summary or the full proposal here . Contact Gavin Barker of the Cornwall Independent Poverty Forum for more information .
items.why: this matters democratically because community wealth funds redistribute economic resources and control to communities, affecting people's practical capacity to participate in local decisions.
items.note: Economic democracy proposals are classed under participation as conditions for taking part, not as local government structure.
links: Contact Gavin Barker of the Cornwall Independent Poverty Forum for more information

items.h: Federal Trust host discussion on present state of centralisation in UK governance
items.b: Professor John Denham and Glyndwr Jones recently hosted a discussion on the present state of the United Kingdom, arguing that the new government will only be able to bring about economic growth and better public services by the decentralisation of the UK as a whole and a parallel decentralisation of English governance — Explore the work of the Federal Trust here .
items.why: this matters democratically because the balance of centralisation versus devolution determines where collective decision-making power sits across UK government.
links: Explore the work of the Federal Trust here

items.h: Whitehall is ‘resistant’ to greater devolution, says West Midlands Mayor
items.b: The new Mayor for the West Midlands, Richard Parker, has accused the civil service of being ‘resistant’ to government plans for further devolution — although he said Labour’s top brass were ‘absolutely behind the policy’. For an in depth discussion of the devolution agenda and how it is evolving, check out this upcoming online event with UK in a Changing Europe and The Centre on Constitutional Change on November 14th.
items.why: this matters democratically because civil service resistance to devolution plans affects whether decision-making power is actually transferred to regional government as promised.
items.note: Devolution structure is classed under elections_decision_making, with civil service capacity as a secondary accountability angle.

items.h: Democracy Classroom host strategy away day
items.b: Last week, The Politics Project convened over 80 organisations from across the civic education community in the UK, with organisations ranging from the Electoral Commission, to Naked Politics, Education Scotland, Young Muslims in Politics, Association for Citizenship Teachers, Reclaim and more. The day focused on learning and reflection from the 2024 GE and planning and convening around the curriculum review, the campaign to lower the voting age and work around its implementation. See more information about Democracy Classroom .
items.note: A sector convening/strategy day is organisational news rather than a new means of participation being created.

items.b: Democracy Classroom Strategy Away Day (Photo credit: Democracy Classroom)

items.h: Association for Citizenship Teaching are running a survey on the curriculum review
items.b: Earlier this year the Labour Government announced a Curriculum and Assessment Review. Now, the Association for Citizenship Teaching are requesting views on the possible implementation of any new changes. Their campaign Make Space for Citizenship aims to ensure citizenship education enjoys a more prominent role in the new curriculum changes, rather than, as they argue, its somewhat marginalised role at present.
items.why: this matters democratically because embedding citizenship education more prominently in the curriculum builds people's capacity and readiness to take part in civic and political life.

items.h: My Life My Say to campaign to lower the voting age
items.b: At the recent Democracy Classroom strategy day (above), My Life My Say announced their upcoming campaign to build a broad coalition of groups to develop a campaign, co-created and co-led by young people, to push for Votes at 16 and ensure it remains on the government’s agenda. Stay tuned to find out more .
items.why: this matters democratically because lowering the voting age would extend suffrage and change who is entitled to vote in elections.
items.note: Franchise and suffrage campaigns fall under elections_decision_making per the framework anchors.

items.h: The Politics Project to convene sector around implementation of Votes at 16
items.b: With My Life My Say making the case for Votes at 16, The Politics Project will be convening civic education groups to provide information and advice to lawmakers on the implementation on the policy, particularly around the required timing of the legislation. Contact The Politics Project to find out more .
items.why: This matters democratically because expanding the franchise to 16- and 17-year-olds changes who can exercise the vote and how elections are administered.
items.note: Convening sector groups on implementation timing is treated as substantive suffrage reform rather than mere sector logistics.

items.h: Democracy Network and other organisations sign open letter calling for further action on Lords Reform
items.b: The Democracy Network and other organisations including Unlock Democracy , Sortition Foundation , Involve , 38 Degrees , Compass , and others, have signed an open letter published in the Guardian calling on the government to go further in their reform of the House of Lords. Whilst welcoming the proposed end of hereditary Peers, the coalition of organisations want a proper consultation on the future of the Lords — as promised in their manifesto — via a representative citizens’ assembly.
items.why: This matters democratically because it calls for a citizens' assembly to shape reform of a legislative chamber, a direct-democracy mechanism for constitutional change.
items.note: Citizens' assembly call places this under elections & decision making per boundary rule, though Lords composition also touches government accountability.

items.h: Lib Dems plan to force vote on elected House of Lords
items.b: The Liberal Democrats plan to amend the Government’s bill that would end the tradition of hereditary peers and make reforms go further. Labour said in 2022 they would replace the House of Lords with an elected chamber, but these changes did not make it into their manifesto this year, opting for age limits and abolition of hereditary peers.
items.why: This matters democratically because moving to an elected House of Lords changes how legislative power is authorised and who can exercise it.
items.note: Treated as decision-making machinery given the focus on making the chamber elected, with an accountability dimension as secondary.
links: Liberal Democrats plan to amend the Government’s bill

items.h: Electoral Reform Society celebrates recent policy wins
items.b: The government has recently announced that Veterans’ ID cards will now be available for voters to use as ID in the next local elections, and Hereditary Peers will be leaving the House of Lords . The Electoral Reform Society has hailed both as positive democratic changes but urges the government to go further on both agendas by expanding the list of acceptable voter IDs and having an elected second chamber.
items.why: This matters democratically because voter ID rules determine practical access to the ballot and Lords reform changes the composition of a legislative chamber.
items.note: Voter ID is core electoral administration; the Lords element is a secondary accountability angle.
links: Veterans’ ID cards will now be available
Hereditary Peers will be leaving the House of Lords

items.h: Labour should be ‘the tortoise to the last government’s hare’ on law-making, says Institute for Public Policy Research
items.b: A new report from IPPR , Delivery Vs Deliberation? Lessons from the last Parliament , urges the Labour government to carefully consider the impact and delivery of new laws before introducing them. The report takes aim at the record under the Conservatives during which successive administrations brought in legislation that was eventually abandoned, amended, or simply failed to deliver on what was initially promised.
items.why: This matters democratically because how legislation is designed and delivered affects Parliament's capacity for effective scrutiny and accountable law-making.
links: Delivery Vs Deliberation? Lessons from the last Parliament

items.h: Could a more proportional voting system have saved James Cleverly?
items.b: The Conservative Party is the only UK political party to elect their leader using a series of ballots, rather than the ‘Alternative Vote’ system. With James Cleverly crashing out of the Tory leadership race amidst rumours of tactical voting, the Electoral Reform Society discuss whether the more proportional ‘Alternative Vote’ could have produced a fairer outcome. Former Tory MP, Greg Hands, also appeared to be in agreement on the need for change .
items.why: This matters democratically because the electoral system used to choose a major party's leader affects the fairness and representativeness of that competition for office.
links: elect their leader using a series of ballots,
in agreement on the need for change

items.h: Former Conservative Party Chairman calls for internal party voting reform
items.b: Former Conservative Party chairman Greg Hands wrote following the election of Kemi Badenoch as Tory leader: ‘The rules need serious reform. I am not with any of the camps, but it seems tactical voting has taken place on an industrial scale either yesterday, today, or both…It pains me to say it, but one Single Transferable Vote ballot paper — rather than multiple rounds — would probably solve it.’ Electoral Reform Society discuss in a recent blog whether a more proportional system could have produced a fairer outcome.
items.why: This matters democratically because reforming internal party voting rules affects the fairness and representativeness of leadership elections.
links: Electoral Reform Society discuss in a recent blog whether a more proportional system could have produced a fairer outcome.

items.h: Collaborative Democracy Network to host event discussing new citizen white paper on participation, Nov 11th
items.b: The Collaborative Democracy Network is hosting an in-person and online event to discuss the Citizens’ White Paper which sets out why, when and how the government could embed public participation in national policy making. Authors of the White Paper, Demos and Involve , will be speaking alongside others at the event to discuss the current efforts from the government to democratise policy making and rebuild trust in politics. Sign up to the event .
items.why: This matters democratically because embedding public participation mechanisms in national policymaking creates new means for people to take part in political decisions.
items.note: White paper on public participation is treated as sector capacity-building under participation & civic life rather than mere event logistics.
links: hosting an in-person and online event

items.h: How might we take meaningful steps to upgrade democracy? Asks Thinking Box
items.b: This summer 500 people from Extinction Rebellion UK took part in a live ‘Massembly’ in Windsor Great Park and online. But the deliberation process is still ongoing — get involved, vote and propose statements on the Pol.is . The process remains open until the 5th December.
items.why: this matters democratically because deliberative processes like citizens' assemblies are part of the machinery through which collective decisions and political demands are formed and legitimised.
items.note: Deliberative/assembly processes are filed under elections & decision making per framework, not participation.
links: get involved, vote and propose statements on the Pol.is

items.h: Is the bias of the mainstream press impacting Labour’s policy agenda? Unchecked UK investigates
items.b: The power and influence of the mainstream has often forced politicians to reconsider policy and change direction, according to Steve Richard , ex Political Editor of the New Statesman. New research from Unchecked UK explores how mainstream newspaper editorials have covered Labour’s regulatory agenda since July 4th, discussing whether the need to keep the press ‘on side’ is similarly influencing their direction of travel.
items.why: this matters democratically because concentrated press ownership and editorial influence over government policy direction can distort the plurality of political debate and accountability to voters rather than proprietors.

items.h: GB News fined £100,000 by Ofcom for breaking impartiality rules with soft Q&A event with Rishi Sunak
items.b: Ofcom said it has imposed a £100,000 fine on GB News for “breaking due impartiality rules” following a question and answer-style debate with former prime minister Rishi Sunak earlier this year, PA Media reports .
items.why: this matters democratically because broadcast impartiality rules exist to ensure citizens encounter plural political viewpoints rather than one-sided platforming of politicians.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation explore relationships between councils and local news providers
items.b: Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) explore opportunities for improving the relationship between local news outlets and local councils. From public notice reform to local documenters there are many ways of improving local information ecosystems, recently PINF have convened a new Local News Commission to deliberate on recommendations for a more sustainable and thriving local news sector. Sign up to PINF’s newsletters for all the latest .
items.why: this matters democratically because a sustainable local news ecosystem and its relationship with local government affects citizens' ability to access meaningful information about local public affairs.
items.note: Convening a new commission counts as sector capacity-building affecting the information environment.
links: Sign up to PINF’s newsletters for all the latest

items.h: Hacked Off call for Leveson Part Two
items.b: A decade ago, the Leveson Inquiry into corruption, rogue reporters, hacking, bribery and data theft in the British corporate media, was split into two parts — but Part Two was never completed. Hacked Off are now calling for Leveson Part Two .
items.why: this matters democratically because an incomplete inquiry into press corruption and misconduct leaves unresolved questions about accountability within the media that shapes public debate.

items.h: Legal challenge against anti-protest laws continues, reports Liberty and allies
items.b: Liberty and their allies will be at the Court of Appeal the first week of December to defend the ruling of the court earlier in May. Despite some initial reports suggesting otherwise, the new Labour Government is now seeking to appeal Liberty’s High Court victory in May , despite opposing the laws in opposition. Find out more here . Chris Packham recently joined Led By Donkeys in a stunt at HMP Wormwood Scrubs to highlight the recent changes to protest laws, calling on the Government to reverse the changes.
items.why: this matters democratically because legal restrictions on protest directly affect citizens' freedom to assemble and challenge public power.
items.note: Protest restriction via policing/legal challenge is filed under rights & freedoms per boundary rule.
links: Liberty’s High Court victory in May
Chris Packham recently joined Led By Donkeys in a stunt at HMP Wormwood Scrubs

items.h: Undercover Policing Inquiry hears much delayed and damning evidence against controversial spycops unit
items.b: During the most recent hearings last month, exploring spycops deployments between 1983–1992, evidence submitted ‘gives us an idea of why the State wants to keep this stuff secret’ Police Spies Out of Lives suggested. Evidence submitted to the inquiry proves undercover police were sexual predators, fathered children and then the police hid the truth, committed serious crimes, that the police colluded with government to subvert democracy, and that the police acted as corporate spies — campaigners argue in a report on the recent stage of the Inquiry .
items.why: this matters democratically because a public inquiry exposing state collusion, secrecy and abuse by an undercover policing unit tests whether powerful state bodies can be held answerable for subverting democratic norms.
items.note: Public inquiry treated as scrutiny/accountability mechanism per boundary rule.

items.h: 2019 Tory voters are now the least trusting of politicians, according to polling
items.b: New polling from Savanta and Full Fact finds that 59% of voters who support the Conservatives in 2019 say they don’t trust politicians to keep their promises — 10% higher than the UK as a whole. The poll also found that 58% of the public would not consider voting for the Conservatives at future elections, with 1 in 4 Tories saying the same.
items.why: this matters democratically because public trust in politicians keeping their promises reflects the perceived accountability and credibility of the democratic system.
links: polling from Savanta and Full Fact

items.h: NetPol highlight plight of the Newham 3
items.b: The Network for Police Monitoring provides an update on the Newham 3 campaign, of three socialist activists accused of hate crime at a Newham Council meeting, who have been left waiting in limbo for seven months by the Metropolitan Police to hear whether they will face criminal charges. NetPol has the story .
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns state policing and prolonged legal uncertainty facing political activists over speech at a public council meeting, implicating freedom of expression and due process.
items.note: Treated as civic space/policing rather than participation since the story is about state coercion and legal limbo, not willingness to take part.

items.h: Alliance4Europe new report tracks international far right impacts on Southport Riots
items.b: The report by Alliance for Europe , is a product of their work through the Counter Disinformation Network. The report authors analysed more than 11k messages from 1500 different chats and channels posting content related to the riots across a three day period. They revealed that non-UK far right groups played a significant role in inflaming tensions following the Southport murders. Read the report here .
items.why: this matters democratically because it documents how foreign disinformation and information operations shaped public understanding and tensions during a domestic crisis.

items.h: Rebuilding trust in politics — Demos research avenues for change
items.b: A new report from Demos — A Playbook to Rebuild Trust — suggests Labour’s current approach to rebuilding trust falls short. Based on research with their ‘Trustwatch Panel’ — a group of 32 participants who gave their reaction to political events in the run up to the election — the new report diagnoses six key drivers of low trust and sets out recommendations for a better way forward. Check out the write up in Labour List too. Also, recapping from last month, Demos published The People’s Town Square on protest: Looking beyond the headlines , research supported by Liberty that found 83% of the pu…
items.why: this matters democratically because declining public confidence in government and parties bears on whether citizens see democratic institutions as answerable and legitimate.
items.note: Secondary protest-support finding relates to willingness to participate, filed under participation.

items.h: A new anti-corruption messaging guide is published
items.b: Corruption is widely understood to be one of the biggest threats to democracy with concerns of UK corruption reaching an all time high . For campaigners, having a lexicon to raise awareness of this is becoming increasingly important. The National Democratic Institute and the Anti-Corruption & Governance Centre have just developed an ‘Anti-Corruption Messaging Guide’ to do just this, helping campaigners develop and tailor their messaging.
items.why: this matters democratically because it equips campaigners with new capacity to organise and communicate around corruption, a core threat to accountable government.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it creates a new resource enabling civic campaigning.
links: UK corruption reaching an all time high

items.h: New polling and public attitudes tool Suffrago launches
items.b: The new tool Suffrago , builds on the foundations of Pol.is and the Crowd Wisdom project, allows citizens to submit statements about political, social and economic issues and generates new professional grade survey questions from these inputs, quizzing users and building up a representative picture of attitudes in a constituency area. See an example of such insights shared in local Rochdale press recently.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new means for citizens to articulate political attitudes and be heard, expanding avenues for civic participation.
items.note: Not classed as deliberative decision-making machinery since it functions as an attitudes/polling tool rather than a formal citizens' assembly or referendum process.
links: See an example of such insights

items.h: mySociety’s annual TICTeC civic tech conference is back
items.b: Next year’s mySociety TICTeC civic tech conference has just launched and is being held in Belgium, register your tickets now!
items.note: Event/conference listing, not substantive democracy content.

items.h: Full Fact to launch Government Tracker tool to understand if government is delivering on election pledges
items.b: Full Fact is launching a new tool to help voters understand the progress being made on the pledges that delivered them votes. The Tracker, which is currently in the early stages of development, will start with around 50 of the nearly 300 pledges Labour made during their election campaign, with the aim to expand the tool over time to cover every promise the Labour government made during the campaign. Keep your eyes peeled for further updates from the Full Fact team!
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new tool letting citizens track whether an elected government is delivering on its manifesto commitments, strengthening accountability between elections.

items.h: How to leverage AI for Democracy — new essay collection explores this crucial question
items.b: A new set of essays published by the International Forum For Democratic Studies and the National Endowment for Democracy , examines the role AI can play in bolstering democracy. The report also takes stock of the way social media has evolved to undermine democracy in some instances and discusses the safeguards needed to prevent similar issues with AI.
items.why: this matters democratically because it examines how AI and social media technologies could reshape the public information environment on which democratic debate depends.
items.note: Essay collection is discursive rather than a concrete change, so confidence is low.

items.h: Curious about how you can use AI in your organisation? Check out the Civic AI Handbook
items.b: Developed by Edward Saperia at Newspeak House , the Civic AI Handbook , funded by Nesta , is a comprehensive directory covering practices and means by which civic organisations can adopt generative AI. View the handbook . See you next time,
items.why: it creates a new resource helping civic organisations adopt tools that could expand their capacity to support democratic participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building resource launch counts under participation_civic_life.

items.h: Local Trust, Demos and CRESR invite submissions on community regeneration
items.b: Local Trust is running a new essay competition in tandem with Demos and the Centre for Regional Economic and Social Research , looking at innovative ideas on community regeneration. Entrants must submit a 2,500 word essay on the following: ‘What is your policy idea for turning the most socially and economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods in England into thriving communities, what is the evidence behind it, and how might it best be successfully implemented with maximum impact?’ The winner will receive £5,000 and two runners up will receive £1,000. Deadline 10th January 2025. Apply now .

The session is pay what you feel, register your interest in the three day workshop in February 2025 now .

items.b: Earlier this year Google published their €15M Strengthening Democracy in Europe Impact Challenge call for applications to a new large scale fund. Democracy Club, The Politics Project and mySociety teamed up for an almighty project to overhaul UK democratic data architecture and the citizen interface with government and elected bodies. items.b: The Civic Tech Field Guide is the world’s largest collection of projects using tech for the common good, developed and maintained by Matt Stempeck. CTFG is an invaluable resource for thousands of organisations across the globe and features curated directories of 10s of thousands of civic and political technology projects and organisations . The Civic Tech Field Guide receives support from a range of organisations including People Powered , mySociety , NED and many others, including many volunteers — but they need all the help they can get. Get in touch if this is your jam!

items.b: The Swiss Summer School in Democracy Studies and the Deliberative Democracy Summer School series are joining forces next year to create an event for PhD students exploring deliberative democracy in theory and practice. The 2025 Summer School will feature lectures and interactive sessions led by renowned scholars in the field of deliberative democracy and will be a great opportunity to connect with other researchers in this area. Find out more about the course and what you need to do to apply .

items.h: Shout Out UK celebrates Parliament Week
items.b: Shout Out UK distributed 4,500 leaflets and hundreds of posters in a variety of the languages, with materials posted to London foodbanks, libraries and community space — they also hosted three events in schools in London ranging from workshops to assemblies aimed at raising awareness about civic and democratic rights. For more information on the GLA’s Democratic Participation Public Awareness Campaign, contact democracy@london.gov.uk.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: This matters democratically because raising public awareness of civic and democratic rights through community outreach strengthens people's willingness and ability to take part in civic life.

items.h: Scottish Co-production Network celebrates CoPro Week
items.b: The Scottish Co-production Network brought together more than 40 co-producing organisations in Scotland to focus efforts on exploring how to embed co-production as the way to deliver services across Scotland through CoProWeek in November. items.h: Senedd endorses creation of the Innovating Democracy Advisory Group
items.b: Last month the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales published their final report in 2024. The Welsh Government accepted the Commission’s recommendations in full , and they were endorsed by the Senedd. The report recommended an expert panel be created to advise the Welsh Government on expanding the use of democratic innovation and enhance civic engagement in public life. To that end Dr Anwen Elias has now been appointed to head the new Innovating Democracy Advisory Group.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: it establishes a new expert body to advise on expanding deliberative and democratic-innovation mechanisms within Welsh governance
items.note: Deliberative/democratic-innovation bodies are filed under elections & decision making per framework rule.

items.b: Last month the Welsh Government published their comprehensive analysis of the democratic health of community councils and town councils . The report provides a diagnosis of the community council sector in Wales, and a range of ways forward to rejuvenate and rebuild the sector — Read the report here .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition

items.h: UK Government ‘Devolution by default’ to create new era of local power
items.b: The new English Devolution White Paper advocated by Angela Rayner MP, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, is thought to include merging councils and removing district councils in a generational shake up of governance , creating new ‘strategic authorities’.

items.h: Could citizen-involvement unlock English devolution? Involve investigates
items.b: The Government’s English Devolution White Paper is set to be published imminently. To coincide with this, Involve has published a new report, Putting People at the Heart of English Devolution , looking at how involving citizens in decision making could unlock a more effective and democratic approach to devolution. The report sets out five opportunities and practical recommendations for how to do this in order to develop public engagement with this key agenda.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: it examines how citizen involvement mechanisms could shape the design of new devolved decision-making structures
items.note: Citizen involvement in devolution decision-making is classed under elections & decision making, not participation.

items.h: Politics in Action urge importance of moving legislative agenda forward on Votes at 16
items.b: Emily Crudden, Campaigns Organiser at Politics in Action , highlights the importance of moving the legislative agenda forward soon so that 16 year olds can vote in the Northern Ireland Assembly elections in 2027, which can feel like a ways off, but in legislative timeframes is very soon. Back in September four of the five political parties of Northern Ireland called on the UK secretary of state to implement Votes at 16 in the region — Contact Emily for more information .

items.why: it concerns whether the franchise is extended to 16-year-olds for Northern Ireland Assembly elections, a matter of inclusive suffrage.

items.h: 138 MPs vote in favour of Proportional Representation Bill
items.b: Last week, 138 MPs from across all major political parties voted in favour of Sarah Olney MP’s Elections (Proportional Representation) Ten Minute Rule Bill , calling for the use of PR at future elections. The Liberal Democrats were the biggest backers of the bill with 63 of their 72 MPs coming out in support. The vote was only narrowly successful however, with 136 voting against it, including 78 Conservative MPs and 50 Labour MPs.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: it concerns a parliamentary vote on changing the electoral system used to elect representatives.
links: Elections (Proportional Representation) Ten Minute Rule Bill

items.b: The Blueprint for a 21st Century Parliament , published by Compassion in Politics and 50:50 Parliament , provides a framework for quick and low-cost changes to create immediate impacts to make Parliament more inclusive, supportive and effective, while the Modernisation Committee considers longer term structural changes — Read the report .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: it proposes reforms to how Parliament itself functions and scrutinises, affecting its effectiveness as an accountable institution.

items.b: The APPG for Fair Elections launches with more than 100 MPs backing, more than half of them Labour MPs. The group recently published their first report — ‘Free But Not Fair — British elections and how to restore trust in politics’ . The report identifies three main threats to UK democracy which are ; first-past-the-post, dark money, and disinformation — as well as setting out how to solve these crises and improve accountability.

items.h: Brits favour proportional representation over first-past-the-post, according to YouGov polling
items.b: New polling from YouGov reveals that 44% of UK voters favour PR over first-past-the-post, compared to 23% who favour FPTP. This support holds across all voter main voter groups other than the Conservatives. Reform UK: 62% vs 17%, Lib Dems: 58% vs 22%, Labour: 48% vs 24%, Conservative: 39% vs 41%.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: it shows how public preferences over electoral systems relate to the mechanism by which votes translate into seats and representation.

items.h: General election was the most disproportionate on record, says Electoral Reform Society
items.b: The 2024 General Election marked a turning point in British electoral history, becoming the most disproportional election ever recorded in the UK, according to a new report from the Electoral Reform Society . A System out of Step explores how the election was characterised by low voter turnout, record levels of distrust, and an antiquated voting system ultimately warping voter preferences. According to the report, nearly 78% of votes did not directly affect the local outcome in 2024–21.2 million votes in total.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: the proportionality of an electoral system determines how faithfully votes cast translate into political representation.

items.h: Parliament’s Modernisation Committee launches call for evidence
items.b: Parliament’s Modernisation Committee recently launched a call for submissions asking what they should focus on in order to develop their goals of driving up standards, improving working culture, and making parliamentary procedures more effective. If you want to submit your ideas, the deadline for submission is 16th of December and you can submit through their website .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: the effectiveness and standards of parliamentary procedure determine how well Parliament can scrutinise and hold the executive to account.

items.h: Four in ten adults regularly encounter misinformation, says Ofcom report
items.b: According to new research from Ofcom , 44% of adults say they have encountered false or misleading information in the last four weeks. Almost half of people (45%) said they feel they can confidently judge whether sources of information are truthful. But only 30% feel they can confidently judge whether an image, audio or video has been generated by AI.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: the public's ability to identify false or AI-generated information affects whether they can form accurate views of public affairs.

items.h: Labour rules out legislating against use of SLAPPs, despite cross-party pressure
items.b: A cross-party group of MPs has urged the government to take action against the use of SLAPPs due to mounting evidence of their use to shut down public interest journalism. However Justice Minister, Heidi Alexander, has ruled out the possibility of government legislation on this issue during the next parliament. Whilst recognising SLAPPs ‘represent an abuse of our legal system’, they argued they are a ‘complex area and we should not legislate in haste’.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: SLAPPs use the legal system to suppress public-interest journalism, undermining the information environment necessary for democratic debate.
links: ruled out the possibility of government legislation

items.h: Guardian and Observer journalists strike over sale of The Observer
items.b: The Guardian and Observer journalists began a four day strike over what they say is the rushed sale of the Observer newspaper to Tortoise Media. General secretary-elect of the National Union of Journalists , Laura Davison, spoke from the picket line saying, ‘it’s too important for a deal to be done behind closed doors and too important for wider public life. People are calling on management to meaningfully engage with staff…and saying there needs to be proper scrutiny and an opportunity to look at alternatives.”
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: the ownership and editorial independence of a national newspaper affects media plurality and the public's access to diverse reporting.
items.note: Strike action also touches freedom of association but the substantive stake is media ownership and plurality.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation announce shortlist for Tenacious Journalist Award
items.b: PINF has reached the next stage of the Tenacious Journalist Award — a new award celebrating the work and reach of tenacious journalists. A shortlist of 20 applicants has been announced and now it’s up to the judges to pick their winner (who could win £5,000 to 20,000!). Stay tuned for exciting updates soon!
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.note: Award shortlist announcement is organisational news, excluded even though the organisation works on journalism.

items.h: Two short notice £120k Ofcom tenders available
items.b: Ofcom have two 2-year £120k tenders open now, one for kids and one for adults, in conjunction with local news — find out more .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.note: A funding tender listing is sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: UK local and general elections were ‘well-run’, says Electoral Commission report
items.b: The Electoral Commission has published their report into how the UK general elections were conducted, focusing on their management, participant experiences, and lessons for the future. While the elections were generally ‘well-run’ and voter confidence remained high, several key areas for improvement were identified to enhance participation and trust.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: the credibility and administration of elections directly determines whether citizens can trust and exercise their franchise effectively.
links: Electoral Commission has published their report

items.h: Poll finds cross-party support for a cap on donations to political parties
items.b: Opinium polling carried out on behalf of Unlock Democracy finds at least two thirds of Conservative, Labour, Reform, Green and the Liberal Democrat voters support plans to strengthen rules on political donations. Reform voters were most likely to support some sort of cap on donations, with 72% backing stronger rules — despite rumours that Elon Musk plans to donate $100m to the party. Unlock Democracy is campaigning to set the campaign limit at £5,000 .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: campaign finance rules shape whether political competition is fair and free from undue influence by wealthy donors.
links: polling carried out on behalf of Unlock Democracy
rumours that Elon Musk plans to donate

items.h: Politicians ‘inflammatory language’ is driving a crisis of trust, says new report
items.b: A new report sent to Home Secretary Yvette Cooper from a former counter-extremism commissioner, Dame Sara Kahn, calls for politicians to moderate their language to avoid deepening the polarisation and distrust in Britain. In the report, ‘ Societal Threats and Declining Democratic Resilience ’ , Khan warned of a ‘chronic risk of democratic decline’ if politicians continue to use inflammatory language and in some cases actively promote conspiracy theories in order to win votes.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: declining public trust and rising polarisation driven by political rhetoric undermine confidence in government and democratic institutions.
items.note: Focus is on politicians' conduct and public confidence, which anchors to government accountability rather than a specific beat topic.
links: calls for politicians to moderate their language
Societal Threats and Declining Democratic Resilience

items.h: Transparency International outline 50 recommendations for tackling political finance
items.b: With the UK government considering tightening the rules around political finance in the UK, a new set of policy recommendations from Transparency International outlines how this issue can be tackled at a global level. Their 50 ‘actionable recommendations’ set out simple ways to develop a transparent system of political financing, ensuring dodgy actors cannot capture politics for their own ends. Earlier this month Transparency research revealed that almost £1 in every £10 of political donations comes from ‘unknown or questionable sources’ in the UK.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: transparent political financing rules determine whether elections and parties are protected from capture by hidden or unaccountable money.
links: new set of policy recommendations from Transparency International
almost £1 in every £10 of political donations comes from ‘unknown or questionable sources’

items.h: TICTeC 2025 — Call for proposals now open
items.b: mySociety’s annual global civic technology conference will be held in Belgium next June, where call for proposals are now open across their three themes of access to information and open data, democracy, people and politics and climate change — find out more here .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition

items.h: mySociety tonal shift to pro-democracy tech
items.b: Through their upcoming TICTeC conference (above) mySociety are moving to adopt a new framing around their work, Pro-Democracy Tech or PDT , more in line with the current moment, they say. Pro-Democracy Tech describes digital tools aimed at realising and defending democratic values, mySociety state, they unpack this at length in their recent blog post .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.note: Organisational rebranding/framing shift, excluded per rules on organisation-as-organisation news.

items.h: Peer Review, new tool from Tortoise Media
items.b: Peer Review is a new interactive tool produced by Tortoise Media that trawls thousands of public records to shine a light on the House of Lords, its members and the role they play in British democracy. The tool categorises peers into a range of groups, from hereditary to blockers, rebels and absentee peers. It also breaks down their various jobs, positions, financial holdings and property portfolios — Check out Peer Review .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: a public tool that exposes the activities, interests and conduct of unelected legislators strengthens scrutiny and accountability of the House of Lords.
items.note: New transparency tool for scrutinising the legislature, anchored to accountability rather than pure information environment.

items.h: Seelaw launches free tier
items.b: A new app produced by Joe Coker, Seelaw , has now added a free tier so anyone can try it out. For those that aren’t familiar, Seelaw uses AI to scrutinise and predict the impact of legislation, with the aim to make legislation easier to understand.
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.why: a free tool that helps ordinary people understand and engage with legislation expands practical means of civic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation, per framework guidance.

items.h: Introducing the US Democracy Hub
items.b: Impala Digital and the US-based Democracy Funders Network have launched a new resource, the US Democracy Hub , a vast and well maintained resource listing every non-profit organisation working on or around issues related to democracy in the US — check it out .
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.sec: And now for something completely different
items.note: US-focused resource listing organisations, not UK democracy and not a new means of participation itself, more an organisational directory launch.

items.h: Did you know?
items.b: UK election spend from 2001 to 2024 totalled just 3% of this year’s 2024 total US election spend, according to some rough sums by Peter Keeling of Democracy Club. See you next time,
items.issue: UK Democracy Bulletin, December 2024 — Christmas Edition
items.sec: And now for something completely different
items.why: campaign finance scale is part of the machinery of electoral competition and comparative evidence bears on assessing UK election spending regulation.

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust publish latest grant awards
items.b: JRRT is funding a number of new projects to keep an eye on: Black Equity Organisation — Black British Mandate Implementation (Phase II): £73k over one year for the implementation of the recently launched Black British Mandate (BBM) and also to secure the delivery of at least three of its policy demands set out in the mandate within the current parliamentary period. UCL Constitution Unit — Mobilising for House of Commons reform and a restored culture of scrutiny in the 2024 parliament: £56k over one year to conduct work on House of Commons reform in the new parliament, focused on strengthening …

items.h: Join the Democracy Network Summit 2025 in Sheffield, February 28th
items.b: Next week, The Democracy Network is hosting our annual gathering in Sheffield. Join us for a day of connection, collaboration and inspiration at Sheffield Hallam University. Featuring keynote speaker journalist Michael Crick and with sessions spanning the diversity of the democracy sector, we’ve got a packed agenda for you — check out our schedule here .
