items.h: Amna Ahmad to step down as Campaigns Lead at The Democracy Network
items.b: Since November 2022, Amna Ahmad has been leading on the Democracy Network’s campaign workstream. Amna is due to step down at the end of this month to start their new role as the Chief Executive at Inspiring Girls International. She wrote a short message she has asked to communicate to the Network: I am leaving my role at Involve and the Democracy Network. It has been extraordinary to be so deeply involved with developing the DN, particularly engagement and collaboration around campaigns and advocacy work. As a sector, we have come a long way from the initial meetings about campaigns work when …

items.h: Notwestminster 2025 brings together local democracy champions from across the UK
items.b: This weekend’s vibrant Notwestminster hosted a diverse range of groups and communities working to build stronger local democracy. They heard from thriving democratic communities in Test Valley, Coalville CAN and Frome and the incredible impacts these initiatives have locally on the power of local people to transform their communities and places — and much more, including Democracy Club , The Community Councillor Collective , and a variety of examples of local government transformation.
items.note: Event recap describing existing local democracy groups rather than a new mechanism or change.

items.h: New Migrant Democracy Project report maps unenfranchised residents
items.b: The new report What If Everyone Could Vote? from Migrant Democracy Project , funded by the UK Democracy Fund , highlights the extent of unenfranchisement of migrant residents in the UK, and explores the costs of extending the franchise as part of their wider campaign for Residence Based Voting Rights . Read the report now .
items.why: it maps the extent of unenfranchisement among migrant residents and provides evidence for a campaign to extend the franchise to them.

items.h: State of Hate: Hope not Hate to discuss extent of far-right activity in the UK
items.b: Hope not Hate is hosting a webinar on the 19th of March to discuss their latest findings on the state of far-right activity in the UK. The webinar will explore how public attitudes have shifted as a result of the August riots, how anti-migrant activity has changed in 2024 and whether the new Labour government has impacted changing political rhetoric, and much more. Sign up now. .
items.note: Webinar announcement/call to sign up rather than substantive reporting on findings.

items.b: APPG on Political and Media Literacy Launches in Parliament (Photo Credit: Shout Out UK)
items.why: a new parliamentary group aims to build political and media literacy, strengthening citizens' capacity to engage in and scrutinise democratic life.
items.note: Caption mirrors the accompanying story item.

items.h: APPG on Political and Media Literacy Launches in Parliament
items.b: The All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Political and Media Literacy was launched in December, combining the previous APPGs on Political Literacy and Media Literacy. Hosted by Shout Out UK (SOUK) , the launch reception at the Houses of Parliament brought together figures from media, government, education, and academia.
items.why: the launch of a combined APPG on political and media literacy creates a new institutional focus on building citizens' capacity to engage with and scrutinise political information.
items.note: Sits between participation (political literacy) and information (media literacy); classified by primary emphasis on capacity-building for engagement.

items.h: NEON to host in-person social event on the rise of Reform and the far-right
items.b: On the 27th of February, the New Economy Organisers Network is hosting an in-person event where they’ll be joined by Hope not Hate and the journalist and historian Taj Ali to discuss the causes behind the far-right surge in popularity in the UK.
items.note: Event listing/discussion, not a new participation resource or mechanism.

items.h: Naked Politics named as one of 100 Changemakers of 2025
items.b: Naked Politics has kicked off 2025 after being named one of The Big Issue’s 100 Changemakers of 2025. The list celebrates individuals and organisations making a significant impact on society, with Naked Politics being honoured for its innovative media and educational initiatives empowering young people. This recognition highlights their commitment to engaging youth in political discourse and civic education. Congrats Banseka !
items.note: Award nomination for an organisation, excluded as org news.

items.h: Democracy Network training opportunity
items.b: The Democracy Network have teamed up with Titus Alexander and Happy, an innovative training provider, to offer an advanced apprenticeship in Leading Change for Democracy Network members. This provides intensive support for anyone developing a campaign or project at work over a year. It is funded through the Apprenticeship Levy, so is FREE for staff of large organisations and just 5% (£250-£450) for small organisations. Find out more and learn some powerful strategies and & tactics at a free taster session at Happy on the 25th February, 1–3.30 pm. For more details and book your place at the tas…
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new training pathway to build the campaigning and organising capacity of civil society staff engaged in democracy work.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating a new means of participation rather than routine org admin.

items.h: PACAC Select Committee receives flurry of democracy sector submissions
items.b: The Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee’s Review of the 2024 General Election inquiry has received submissions from a range of democracy sector organisations, including submissions from the UK Democracy Fund , which can be found here .
items.why: this matters democratically because parliamentary scrutiny of the 2024 general election's administration can shape future rules governing how elections are run.
links: The Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee’s Review of the 2024 General Election inquiry

items.h: Are you attending TICTeC 2025? Hold off booking transport and accomodation
items.b: mySociety have communicated to attendees of the annual civic tech conference to be held in Belgium, that one of their major donors, the US National Endowment for Democracy, has been affected by President Trump’s freeze on federal funding. TICTeC will go ahead, but might change format — if the funding situation is unlikely to change, they have said they will move to a different format, which may be entirely online.
items.note: Funding/logistics notice about a conference, not about a UK democratic mechanism.

items.h: Newspeak House are looking for new applicants
items.b: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology is currently on the lookout for new applicants for next year’s 2025/2026 intake starting this September. Students will spend a year immersed in communities of practice and undertake the one-year course Introduction to Political Technology course, alongside a range of other activities. Find out more here , residential and non-residential places available. In the past year Newspeak House developed the Election Tech Handbook and the the MP Office Manual and is a thriving hub for political technology hosting hundreds of events every year.
items.note: Recruitment call for an existing course, akin to excluded organisational admin rather than launch of a new resource.
links: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology

items.h: Association of Electoral Administrators Conference sees returning officers descend on Birmingham
items.b: Electoral administrators and Returning Officers gathered in Birmingham for the annual Association of Electoral Administrators Conference , where, amongst other things, The Politics Project and Purpose Union , spoke about the importance of engaging young people and auto-enrolment. See here for more information .
items.why: this matters democratically because electoral administrators discussing auto-enrolment and youth engagement bears directly on voter registration and turnout mechanics.
items.note: Auto-enrolment and registration fall under elections per the turnout boundary rule.

items.h: New Citizen Project to run training on how organisations can embed participation
items.b: The New Citizen Project is running a training programme to help organisations develop methods for increasing participation amongst key audiences — whether that’s citizens, supporters, communities or consumers. Participants will learn how to embrace the ‘Citizen Shift’ and will leave with innovative ways of generating bottom up engagement with their work.
items.why: this matters democratically because the training creates new organisational methods for generating bottom-up civic engagement and participation.
items.note: Counted as sector capacity-building that creates new means of participation.

items.h: People Powered cancel their 2025 conference following US Government cuts
items.b: People Powered’s upcoming conference in Nairobi has been cancelled and is opting for a virtual sessions instead, as they grapple with the funding impacts in relation to recent US Government budget cuts.
items.note: This is organisational news about an event cancellation due to funding, not a democratic mechanism.
links: People Powered’s upcoming conference in Nairobi has been cancelled

items.h: Care Full launching, March 26th
items.b: Ruth Hannan and Hannah Webster have launched Care Full, a new initiative promoting the importance of care in creating a sustainable and just economy. On Wednesday 26th March they will be hosting an event in London alongside Autonomy to launch Care Full into the world. Drop them an email if you are keen to attend the launch event.
items.note: Launch of an economic/care-focused initiative without a clear democratic mechanism.

items.h: Mayday Saxonvale approved!
items.b: Congratulations to the residents of Frome who won their five-year battle to create a community-led development in their town — the UK’s first ever community-led masterplan for development. The decision was made on January 23rd at an Extraordinary Meeting of the Somerset Council Executive. Afterwards, the Leader of the Council was heard saying, “I don’t think I’ve ever been cheered in a planning meeting.”
items.why: this matters democratically because it shows a community organising and campaigning successfully to shape a local development decision through sustained civic engagement.
items.note: Community-led planning success sits between participation and local government decision-making; classified by the mechanism of civic organising achieving voice.
links: won their five-year battle to create a community-led development

items.h: Nine things we learned from the English devolution white paper
items.b: Just before the Christmas break, Labour published the English Devolution White Paper detailing their plans to devolve power across the country. The Institute for Government has combed through the 118 page document and dug out nine key takeaways for how the government intends to usher in this new era of local power.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the structure and powers of local and regional government devolved decision-making.
items.note: Story about structure/powers of local government tiers falls under elections & decision making per framework.

items.h: Politics in Action meets with UK Government leaders on Votes at 16 in Northern Ireland
items.b: Politics in Action supports a youth-led Votes at 16 campaign in Northern Ireland. On December 19th, members met with Hilary Benn MP, Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, who reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to legislating for Votes at 16. He commended the group’s efforts and emphasised the importance of securing legislation in Westminster ahead of the 2027 local and Assembly elections.
items.why: this matters democratically because extending the franchise to 16-year-olds directly affects inclusive suffrage in elections.

items.h: Association for Citizenship Teaching open letter demands Government re-prioritise citizenship studies
items.b: The Association for Citizenship Teaching has coordinated an open letter to the Secretary of State calling for citizenship education to be prioritised in light of the government’s recent Curriculum and Assessment review . The letter has been signed by a range of democracy organisations, academics, MPs and Peers. Add your organisations’ name to the list.
items.why: this matters democratically because citizenship education builds people's capacity and readiness to take part in civic and political life.
items.note: Advocacy for curriculum priority treated as civic engagement capacity-building rather than a policy complaint alone.

items.h: Welcome To Your Vote Week, 10–16 March
items.b: The Electoral Commission’s Welcome To Your Vote Week is an annual event asking schools, colleges, youth groups and universities to celebrate democracy by delivering democratic education with their students and young people. Find out more and sign up to receive the resources here .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new educational resources and activities that help young people engage with democratic life and voting.
items.note: Sector capacity-building initiative for democratic education; touches on turnout but is broader civic engagement programming.
links: The Electoral Commission’s Welcome To Your Vote Week

items.h: The UK Democracy Fund has published a report on introducing Votes at 16
items.b: Written by Dr Christine Huebner of the University of Sheffield and Dr Jan Eichorn of the University of Edinburgh for the UK Democracy Fund , the report aims to provide information on evidence and good practice on lowering the voting age.
items.why: This matters democratically because lowering the voting age would expand the franchise and change who is entitled to choose representatives.

items.h: Naked Politics offer free nationwide in-person school sessions on making change
items.b: Naked Politics is offering free in-person interactive sessions in schools to encourage young people to think about how they can create change in their communities beyond elections. Naked Politics is especially interested in catering to young people of colour, but welcomes all enquiries. If you are interested or have any questions about the sessions, contact Bella Frimpong via bella.frimpong@nakedpolitics.co.uk
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates a new means for young people to learn how to engage in civic and political change beyond voting.

items.h: The Politics Project offering Local Elections 2025 Training
items.b: The upcoming The Politics Project session offers an overview of the most up-to-date information on voting and elections, including strategies and ideas for engaging students in political discussions and an overview of the various resources and support available from across the Democracy Classroom Network to support learning and engagement with the local elections. Contact wendy@thepoliticsproject.org.uk for more information.
items.why: This matters democratically because it builds teacher capacity to help students understand and engage with the electoral process ahead of local elections.
items.note: Turnout-related election training is filed under elections per the turnout rule, with the capacity-building aspect noted as secondary.

items.h: Wales Government Centre describe 2021 Senedd Election as ‘false start’ on Votes at 16
items.b: In a recent report analysing the 2021 Senedd Election , which was the inaugural election of lowering the voting age to 16 in Wales, the Wales Government Centre at Cardiff University described the election as a ‘false start’ with relatively low political engagement among 16 and 17 year olds at a level roughly comparable with over 55s. Read the report here .
items.why: This matters democratically because it provides new evidence on how enfranchising younger voters actually affects electoral participation and turnout.
links: Wales Government Centre at Cardiff University

items.h: Cross-party MPs call for First Past The Post to be scrapped in House of Commons debate
items.b: More than twenty cross-party MPs have condemned Britain’s First Past the Post voting system during a debate in the House of Commons. The debate comes after a majority of MPs voted in favour of proportional representation for the first time ever in December following the first reading of a 10-minute Rule Bill . MPs urged the government to consider changing the UK voting system and asked that a National Commission on Electoral Reform be set up to help facilitate the process.
items.why: This matters democratically because a shift away from First Past the Post would change how votes translate into representation and political competition.
links: condemned Britain’s First Past the Post voting system
first reading of a 10-minute Rule Bill
asked that a National Commission on Electoral Reform be set up

items.h: ‘Citizens in Power’ Network is launched to improve citizen-led decision making
items.b: A new network has been launched to rethink and redesign the way that decisions are made in the cultural and creative sectors. The Citizens in Power Network , made up of 65 members, associates and experts, will run from 2025–27, bringing together key stakeholders to explore how citizen-led decision-making that reflects the diversity of communities can lead to better outcomes. The network will test different approaches to citizen participation centring on the principles of ‘authority giving’, ‘civic lottery’ and ‘deliberation’ — and will advocate for the take up of new models of democratic decis…
items.why: This matters democratically because it develops and tests new deliberative and citizen-led mechanisms for collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative, citizen-led decision-making mechanisms are anchored to elections & decision-making per the framework, despite this network's focus on the cultural sector rather than government.

items.h: IPPR report makes the case for modernising elections
items.b: With the background of the recently established parliamentary Modernisation Committee , IPPR have published a new report fresh for the new year. Modernising Elections: How to get voters back sets out a range of approaches for policy makers to consider and makes the case for reform.
items.why: This matters democratically because it proposes reforms to election administration and processes intended to raise voter turnout.

items.h: Government to consider scrapping Voter ID laws
items.b: At the beginning of January, Angela Rayner hinted at plans that Labour may scrap the Voter ID laws brought in under the Conservative government. Rayner told a select committee hearing that the cases of electoral fraud in the UK are ‘very, very, very minor’ and said the government would ‘look at’ whether to scrap the requirements.
items.why: This matters democratically because changing voter identification requirements directly affects ballot access and electoral integrity safeguards.

items.h: Government must modernise elections to prevent voter disengagement, says leading think tank
items.b: Just one in every two adults living in the country voted in the 2024 general election, with only three in five registered voters casting a ballot. A new report from Institute for Public Policy Research — Modernising Elections: How to get voters back — considers what can be done to address the UK’s woeful election turnout, putting forward three principles for electoral reform that could help tip the balance towards participation. These are: making voting easier, making voting more worthwhile, and creating a strong democratic culture of participation.
items.why: low and declining turnout affects the legitimacy and representativeness of elections, the core mechanism by which citizens choose representatives.
items.note: Turnout is always classified under elections & decision making regardless of framing.
links: Modernising Elections: How to get voters back

items.h: Report launch: Improving Welsh Democracy — Lessons from around the world
items.b: On the 4th of March, the Institute for Welsh Affairs will be launching their new report exploring the potential of democratic innovation to improve Welsh democracy. These innovations are taken from different contexts around the globe where governments have improved their national democracy through interventions boosting participation and citizen deliberation in decision-making.
items.why: the report examines how citizen deliberation and democratic innovation mechanisms could improve how collective decisions are made in Wales.
items.note: Citizens' deliberation and democratic innovation in decision-making are anchored to elections & decision making rather than participation.

items.h: Over 40,000 sign petition calling for proportional representation
items.b: Over 40,000 people have signed a petition calling on the UK government to hold a referendum on introducing proportional representation for elections. Reaching 100,000 signatures will force a parliamentary debate on the matter.
items.why: the petition seeks a referendum on changing the electoral system, directly engaging how votes translate into representation and power.

items.h: Upcoming Water Bill calls for Citizens’ Assembly to decide future of the water industry
items.b: Next month a bill on the future of the water industry will have its second reading in Parliament. The Water Bill , introduced by Clive Lewis MP with the support of Compass , has economic democracy at its heart , calling for a citizens’ assembly to decide the future ownership model for the industry.
items.why: the bill proposes a citizens' assembly to decide the ownership model of a public utility, using direct democratic decision-making machinery.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified as elections & decision-making machinery per the revised framework.
links: has economic democracy at its heart

items.h: How to improve parliamentary scrutiny of legislation: UCL Constitutional Unit event to explore
items.b: The Constitution Unit at the UCL is organising a panel event on the 24th of February to discuss how we can improve parliamentary scrutiny of legislation. With concerns growing in recent years that new laws are too often rushed and/or inadequate, this important seminar explores how we can reverse these trends to put scrutiny at the heart of our democracy.
items.note: This is an event listing about parliamentary scrutiny rather than a report of substantive change or findings.
links: The Constitution Unit at the UCL

items.h: Media Democracy Festival 2025, coming soon
items.b: This May, the Media Reform Coalition are hosting their next gathering, bringing together activists, independent media outlets, journalists, researchers and policymakers to debate how they can transform the media into a more independent, accountable and democratic system that serves the public interest. The event will feature contributions from broadcast journalist Sangita Myska, journalist Peter Oborne, Byline Times editor Hardeep Matharu, the Bristol Cable , We Are The Economy , Impress and many more.
items.note: Event listing/promotion for a festival, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch annual survey of independent news providers
items.b: The annual Public Interest News Foundation survey tracks the number of indie news providers across the UK and provides a great insight into the health and sustainability of the sector. PINF want to hear from any independent news providers with a turnover of less than £2m, so do share the survey link if you know any relevant organisations.
items.note: Call for survey participation is sector logistics/organisational data collection, not a democracy story.

items.h: Society of Editors to hold ‘Media Freedom Conference’ in March
items.b: On Tuesday 25 March 2025, The Society of Editors will host a conference on the theme ‘The Future of News’. Key discussions will include; the sustainability of the local and regional media, progress on restoring police and media relations, and relationships with tech platforms and AI companies. Leading editors and news executives from all sectors of the UK news industry will be there for this important discussion.
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: Want to stay more up to date with Independent News? New Bluesky starter pack is here to help
items.b: The Bristol Cable has put together a starter pack on BlueSky of independent and public interest news providers in the UK and Ireland. If you’re new to BlueSky, this is a great way to get started and follow some of the best independent news outlets around the UK!
items.why: it helps people access a wider range of independent public-interest journalism, supporting media plurality in the information environment.
items.note: Treated as a new means of accessing plural news sources rather than routine sector promotion.

items.h: Tony Blair Institute suggests popularity of the centre ground has dramatically declined
items.b: New analysis by the Tony Blair Institute has found that the popularity of traditional centre-left and centre-right parties across major democratic countries has fallen dramatically from 73% in 2000 to 51% today. The research, based on 12,000 voters globally, suggests that voters have abandoned the centre not because of ideological differences, but because their confidence in the integrity and competence of politicians from established centrist parties has plummeted, no longer seeking the Third Way.
items.why: declining public confidence in the integrity and competence of established parties affects trust in the institutions that hold power to account.
items.note: Focus is on trust/integrity of parties rather than electoral mechanics, so filed under accountability not elections.
links: New analysis by the Tony Blair Institute

items.h: Met Police are behind 95% of the usage of new protest restriction laws
items.b: New data from the Home Office shows that the Met Police were responsible for nearly all of the usage of the new controversial protest restriction laws. Of the 473 recorded uses, 448 were by Met Police officers, with 87.5% of those targeting environmental protesters. Netpol operates a protest solicitors list for anyone facing charges under these new laws.
items.why: the disproportionate use of new protest restriction powers by one police force shows how state coercion can narrow the space for lawful assembly and dissent.
links: New data from the Home Office

items.h: Ending third-party fact checking for Meta platforms will have a ‘chilling effect’, says Full Fact
items.b: Meta, the owners of Facebook, Instagram and Threads, has announced an end to support for third-party fact checking in the United States. The move has been widely condemned by fact checking organisations including Full Fact , who has been part of the third-party checking initiative for six years and has checked 2,596 cases of potential misinformation. They criticised Meta for taking ‘a backward step that risks a chilling effect on the world’.
items.why: withdrawing third-party fact-checking on major platforms affects the public's ability to encounter reliable information and counter disinformation.

items.h: Labour is failing to uphold democratic freedom, according to Human Rights Watch
items.b: Human Rights Watch’s annual report on the state of human rights around the world has criticised the Labour Government for failing to roll back anti-democratic protest laws brought in by the previous Conservative government. Labour is ‘seriously undermining’ democratic rights by failing to do so, they say. The report also finds that across the globe, authoritarian leaders gained ground in the more than 70 elections that took place last year.
items.why: retaining restrictive protest laws limits citizens' ability to organise and dissent, a core civil liberty underpinning democratic contestation.

items.h: More than 40 UK leaders demand law against deliberate factual deception by politicians
items.b: Over 40 politicians, academics, journalists and civil society leaders have called for Westminster to follow Wales’s lead in legislating against deliberate factual deception by politicians. The move, say Compassion in Politics , who coordinated the letter, would be an important step towards addressing the declining rates of trust in politics and is something that carries significant public support.
items.why: legislating against political deception would create a new mechanism for holding politicians answerable for honesty in public life.
links: called for Westminster to follow Wales’s lead in legislating against deliberate factual deception

items.h: Spread of misinformation linked to far-right, according to new study
items.b: Far right movements drive political misinformation, according to a major new study by Petter Törnberg and Juliana Chueri published in the The International Journal of Press/Politics . They analysed 32 million tweets from parliamentarians across 26 countries finding a strong correlation between misinformation, anti-democratic trends and far-right politics.
items.why: evidence linking misinformation spread to political actors bears on the integrity of the public information environment that underpins democratic debate.

items.h: Failure to enact electoral reform was a ‘big regret’, says Justin Trudeau
items.b: After announcing his plans to step down as Prime Minister of Canada, Justin Trudeau conceded that one of his biggest regrets from his ten year tenure was his failure to push forward with electoral reform. Trudeau came to power in 2015 when his Liberal Party won 54.4% of seats in parliament on the basis of just 39.5% of votes cast. Despite promising to do away with the First-Past-The-Post voting system, his government has failed to make headway on this agenda. See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different
items.why: the failure to reform a disproportionate electoral system is comparative evidence about how electoral systems shape representativeness, relevant to UK debates on voting reform.
items.note: International example used as comparative evidence for UK electoral system debates.
links: conceded that one of his biggest regrets
his Liberal Party won 54.4% of seats in parliament

items.b: Monthly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network. Read by 400+ democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know: hello@democracynetwork.org.uk

items.h: UK Government cuts funding to Tell Mama Islamophobia charity
items.b: Founded in 2012, Tell Mama is the UK’s primary reporting service for Islamophobia and until now, has been fully funded by the UK Government to run the service, which supports victims of Islamophobia, and received almost 11,000 reports in 2023–2024. The government is cutting all funding to the service, leaving it facing closure just weeks after it revealed a record number of anti-Muslim hate incidents in Britain. Fiyaz Mughal, the founder of Tell Mama, said its resources were being cut while ‘the far right and ­populists across Europe are growing significantly’. He said: ‘There are going to be …
items.why: this matters democratically because withdrawing state support from a body that documents and addresses anti-Muslim hate affects the personal security and equal protection of a minority group and the civic infrastructure that safeguards their participation in public life
items.note: Classified under rights and civic space because the mechanism is protection from discrimination and hate, not general civil society funding.
links: The government is cutting all funding to the service, leaving it facing closure just weeks after it revealed a record number of anti-Muslim hate incidents

items.h: City Bridge Foundation launches new Standing With Londoners fund
items.b: The new fund focuses on changing the systems that keep people marginalised, they say, while also addressing issues communities face right now. City Bridge Foundation aims to launch the first of their new funding programmes in autumn 2025.
items.note: Treated as a funding call/announcement rather than a concrete new tool for participation, consistent with sector logistics guidance.

items.h: What’s happening to European democracy and what can funders do about it? Asks Philanthropy Europe Association
items.b: Philanthropy Europe Association have produced this in-depth explainer into democratic backsliding across Europe, and how philanthropic organisations can develop appropriate strategies that address the multidimensional challenges democratic backsliding presents. Read the explainer here .
items.note: Explainer resource for funders about strategy, not a UK democratic mechanism being created or changed.

items.h: National Endowment for Democracy suspends activity following US funding freeze
items.b: For the first time in their four decade history, the National Endowment for Democracy is having to suspend support for over 2,000 partners worldwide due to their inability to access congressionally approved funding, with significant impacts for UK and European based organisations. The impact of this is being felt particularly acutely for frontline organisations who are being forced to lay off staff and strip back important operations on the ground.
items.why: this matters democratically because a major funding withdrawal is stripping frontline civil society organisations of the capacity to operate, weakening the civic infrastructure that supports democratic participation.
items.note: Framed as civil society sector capacity rather than a rights restriction, so filed under participation.

items.b: Democracy Network Summit 2025 survivors (Photo Credit: Involve UK)

items.h: Democracy Network Summit brings together democracy sector in Sheffield
items.b: Last month the Democracy Network Summit 2025 brought together more than 120 people from across the Democracy Network for a day of networking, workshops and talks. If you missed the event, you can view the photos here ! Thanks so much to everyone who came.

The Democracy Network is evolving! As our team structure has changed, so too will some of the ways we work — at least for now. While our capacity to respond to individual requests may be more limited for the time being, we remain committed to fostering high-quality discussions and connections. Thank you for being part of the growing Democracy Network community — we look forward to continuing to support and learn with you. As always, if you have any questions — get in touch .

items.h: Democracy Coworking & Games London — March 27–28th
items.b: Join us for Democracy Coworking in London on March 28th — register now here . But that’s not all — next week Patti, Jess and John and gang of the Democracy Board Games Club are back, join them for democracy-themed games & pizza next Thursday evening — sign up here!

items.h: Are you attending/organising around the 2025 party conferences?
items.b: It’s that time of the year again — so if you’re hosting an event, running a panel or drinks reception, or perhaps you’re just attending, add your plans to the Democracy Network party conferences sheet and see who else is working on what and how you could possibly work together — View the spreadsheet here .

items.h: Imagine Belfast, 24–30th March
items.b: Imagine Belfast , the annual festival of politics and ideas, is back for a week of discussions, comedy, film, lectures and more — don’t miss out .

items.h: Sheffield Festival of Debate is back!
items.b: Joe Kriss and the team at the Festival of Debate are back, delivering their huge array of events, talks and community events across Sheffield in April & May — don’t miss it! Get your tickets now!
items.note: Event listing for a returning debate festival, not a democracy story in itself.

items.h: Open Rights Group welcome Henry VIII powers joint letter sign ons
items.b: Jeanette Smith, Head of Fundraising and Projects at the Open Rights Group (ORG), is publishing a new joint letter this week focused on new Henry VIII powers in the Data Use and Access Bill and their threat to election integrity, namely the impending capacity of a future government to change the conditions of how data is processed by political parties during an election period with minimal parliamentary oversight — Email ORG and add your organisation to the joint letter . Open Rights Group also published a damning report earlier this year into UK political parties’ misuse of data — Read the rep…
items.why: new Henry VIII powers would let a future government alter how parties process voter data with minimal parliamentary scrutiny, weakening executive accountability and election integrity safeguards
items.note: Delegated powers issue (accountability) intersects with election data integrity.
links: Email ORG and add your organisation to the joint letter
Moral Hazard: Voter Data Privacy and Politics in Election Canvassing Apps

items.h: My Vote My Voice 2025 campaign launched
items.b: Earlier this month, My Vote My Voice (MVMV) , met with partners and campaigners to share their plans to make the 2025 Local Elections accessible to everyone. MVMV spokespeople shared their vision and experiences of voting, and the campaign shared their ambitious plan for the year and how community groups can get involved to make voting more accessible in 2025 — Watch the webinar of the launch now .
items.why: the campaign works to make local election voting more accessible, directly affecting who can practically exercise the franchise
items.note: Voting accessibility/turnout is always classified under elections per the turnout rule.
links: Watch the webinar of the launch now

items.h: Free taster workshop on campaign strategy
items.b: Titus Alexander is running a free workshop on campaign strategy, using stories and asking questions to create change, in London 1–3.30 pm Tuesday 25 March 2025 . For details and book go to: https://bit.ly/419JUbB . This is a taster for the 12–18 month course to support you carrying out a campaign or project at work, funded through the Apprenticeship Levy, in partnership with the Democracy Network . Come & find out more, & learn something useful.
items.why: the workshop creates a new means for people to learn campaigning skills, expanding practical capacity to take part in civic and political life

items.h: First ever London Democracy Week successful, say Shout Out UK
items.b: Shout Out UK worked to deliver the Greater London Authority’s first ever London Democracy Week, interacting with over 860 people and helping more than 280 people to register to vote in schools and student centres across the capital, through stalls and visiting assemblies and an online presence.
items.why: the initiative registered hundreds of new voters, directly affecting electoral participation and access to the franchise
items.note: Voter registration outreach falls under elections per the turnout/registration rule.

items.h: State of Hate: Hope not Hate to discuss extent of far-right activity in the UK
items.b: Hope not Hate is hosting a webinar on the 19th of March to discuss their latest findings on the state of far-right activity in the UK. The webinar will explore how public attitudes have shifted as a result of the August riots, how anti-migrant activity has changed in 2024 and whether the new Labour government has impacted changing political rhetoric, and much more — Sign up now.
items.note: An invitation to a webinar sharing existing research findings, not a change to democratic participation or institutions.

items.h: Join Ella Baker School of Organising for a special conference on narratives of division
items.b: On June 7th, the Ella Baker School of Organising plans to bring together those who are already doing something, and those that plan to, to ‘innoculate their communities’ from increasing narratives of division within society. The conference will facilitate and encourage participants to think deeper about the challenges, rather than provide a ‘blueprint’ solution, they say — Express your interest in the event here .
items.why: the conference builds organisers' capacity to counter divisive narratives within communities, a form of civic engagement capacity-building
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it aims to equip people to act, not just discuss.
links: Express your interest in the event here

items.h: Assemble following in the footsteps of the Chartists, March 29th
items.b: Assemble are organising a special tour of London historical sites, starting at Kennington Park — the site of the 1848 Chartist demonstration , before taking in Leveller and Suffragette sites, and modern anti-fascist sites, such as the 1936 Battle of Cable Street , where trade unionists, British Jews and socialist groups famously stopped Mosley’s British Union of Fascists from marching through predominantly Jewish neighbourhoods of East London. Find out more .
items.note: A historical walking tour commemorating democratic movements, not a story about current democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Newspeak House are looking for new applicants
items.b: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology is currently on the lookout for new applicants for next year’s 2025/2026 intake starting this September. Students will spend a year immersed in communities of practice and undertake the one-year course Introduction to Political Technology course, alongside a range of other activities. Find out more here , residential and non-residential places available. In the past year Newspeak House developed the Election Tech Handbook and the the MP Office Manual and is a thriving hub for political technology hosting hundreds of events every year.
items.note: Recruitment notice for an existing course, not a new participation mechanism or resource.
links: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology

items.h: Connected by Data unconference on participatory public technologies, 20th March
items.b: Don’t miss Connected by Data’s upcoming unconference Engaging people on data and AI: An unconference on giving people and communities a powerful say on public sector technologies in London this Thursday. If this peaks your interest, get involved in their online community of practice which meets monthly, here .
items.note: Event listing/community promotion rather than a reported democratic development.
links: Engaging people on data and AI: An unconference on giving people and communities a powerful say on public sector technologies

items.h: Generation Rent uncover key data on demographic drivers of voter registration
items.b: Following on from their 2023 analysis of voter registration and census data , Generation Rent set up a data hub with numbers they used at a local level, including a wider set of demographic indicators than used in their earlier analysis — Generation Rent have now updated their hub with the latest data and estimates of eligible voters for each constituency in England & Wales. They welcome any feedback and questions on the work. View the updated voter registration data hub .
items.why: This matters democratically because better data on who is eligible but unregistered helps identify and close gaps in electoral registration, a precondition for exercising the franchise.
links: 2023 analysis of voter registration and census data

items.h: Care Full launching, March 26th
items.b: Ruth Hannan and Hannah Webster are launching Care Full , a new initiative promoting the importance of care in creating a sustainable and just economy. On Wednesday 26th March they will be hosting an event in London alongside Autonomy to launch Care Full into the world. Drop them an email if you are keen to attend the launch event.

items.h: Elect Her making strides on their new Be A Councillor partnership
items.b: Elect Her are working in partnership with a range of organisations, from the Local Government Association (LGA), 50:50 Parliament, the Disability Policy Centre, Operation Black Vote, The Politics Project and the Migrant Democracy Project — with the aim of reaching those who are underrepresented in local government and supporting them to Be A Councillor! Get in touch with Annabel Mullin, Director of Communications at Elect Her, to find out more .
items.why: This matters democratically because a partnership to help underrepresented groups become councillors bears on the representativeness of local elected office and equal access to political power.
items.note: Local office access sits in elections & decision making, with equal-access dimension in participation.
links: Get in touch with Annabel Mullin, Director of Communications at Elect Her, to find out more

items.h: Make Votes Matter hiring a new fundraising manager
items.b: Could you help advance the work of fairer votes in the UK? Apply for this exciting opportunity with Make Votes Matter as their fundraising manager, sourcing the funding streams to progress their work — deadline 24th March, apply now .
items.note: Job advertisement, not a democracy story under the framework's own-organisation exclusion.

items.h: Unhack Democracy launch new REWIRE Substack
items.b: Unhack Democracy run a hope-based mindset shift incubator called REWIRE with 15 social change makers from across Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria, with the goal of developing a cohort of leaders more willing to take risks and develop creative solutions to the issues affecting their societies. As part of this Unhack produce a regular Substack , which you can read here focused on building stronger democracies — they also run regular online events reflecting on the strength of civil society in Eastern Europe, this month’s event featured the former Deputy PM of Ukraine, which you can watch here .
items.note: Focuses on civil society leadership training in Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria, not on UK democracy or comparative evidence bearing on it.

items.h: Democracy Club relaunches archive of over 20,000 election leaflets
items.b: With 36% of all spending by political parties at the 2019 general election going on leaflets, they continue to be a vital campaign material. Thankfully, Democracy Club has done a brilliant job collecting and archiving political leaflets and you can now search the database by region and year of upload.
items.why: This matters democratically because public access to an archive of campaign leaflets increases transparency of the political material used to persuade voters.
items.note: Treated as campaign/political advertising material, placing it in information & public debate rather than pure logistics.

items.h: Phew! TICTeC going ahead as planned, mySociety say
items.b: Following the US Government USAID cut and the ensuing impacts across the globe, mySociety’s TICTeC civic tech conference found their funding having dried up with the collapse of funding for the US-based National Endowment for Democracy. However, all is now well with funding restored and the conference is back on!
items.note: Organisational/funding news about a conference, not a change in democratic mechanism.

items.h: Campaigners welcome a shift in the tone under Labour government, says survey
items.b: The Sheila McKechnie Foundation has launched the results of their ninth Campaigner Survey . The survey asked campaigners about the challenges they face and the evolving landscape in which they work. The general sense amongst campaigners is that the new government has opened up further possibilities for campaigning due to a greater openness and engagement with campaigning organisations.
items.why: the survey reflects the operating conditions and perceived openness available to civil-society campaigners, which shapes their capacity to participate in public policymaking
links: results of their ninth Campaigner Survey

items.h: How to shift ‘Council Culture’ so local councils work with citizens
items.b: A new report from the New Citizenship Project — Council Culture — looks at the cultural changes that need to happen at a local level to bring citizens into the decision making process. By ‘changing the narrative, embedding new rituals, and building totems’, the report set out a pathway to a stronger local democracy.
items.why: the report proposes cultural and procedural changes intended to give citizens a genuine role in local council decision-making
items.note: Focus is on participatory culture-building rather than the formal structure or powers of local government.

items.h: Rathlin Island begins new minipublic
items.b: The Rathlin Citizens Panel is an attempt to answer key questions on the future of Rathlin Island and follows more than ten years of experimentation and work on participatory processes with the islanders, including the development of the only island policy in the UK. Join the upcoming workshop on the 27th March as part of Imagine Belfast Festival to find out more.
items.why: a citizens' panel is a deliberative decision-making process giving residents a formal, binding-adjacent role in shaping policy for their community
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and minipublics are classified under elections & decision making per the framework.
links: Join the upcoming workshop on the 27th March

items.h: Isle of Wight campaign to encourage engagement in elections progressing
items.b: It’s all islands this week, with Ian Boyd of Common Space reporting on their work at Parish Futures , a new campaign to push for greater engagement with the local council and local elections on the Isle of Wight.
items.why: the campaign seeks to raise engagement and turnout in local council elections, which the framework always places under elections & decision making
items.note: Turnout-related campaigns are always classified under elections & decision making regardless of framing.

items.h: Welcome To Your Vote Week, 10–16 March
items.b: The Electoral Commission’s Welcome To Your Vote Week is an annual event asking schools, colleges, youth groups and universities to celebrate democracy by delivering democratic education with their students and young people. Find out more and sign up to receive the resources here (it’s not too late!).
items.why: the initiative aims to build young people's understanding of and future engagement with voting, bearing on electoral participation and turnout
items.note: Recurring annual education event tied to voting; turnout-related framing places it under elections & decision making.
links: The Electoral Commission’s Welcome To Your Vote Week

items.h: Democracy Classroom #ElectionCountdown 2025 kicks off
items.b: Each year Democracy Classroom provides a huge array of resources and information sharing activities prior to the year’s local elections for school students and educators, including more than eight webinars covering various aspects of the election cycle — visit #ElectionCountdown 2025 now for more information.
items.why: the resources help students understand and prepare to participate in the upcoming local election cycle, supporting informed electoral participation
items.note: Recurring annual programme tied directly to elections rather than general civic engagement.

items.h: Young people want to learn more about politics and democracy, new Electoral Commission report
items.b: Young people and children want to learn more about elections and politics in school , according to new research by the Electoral Commission . The research, carried out with people aged 11 to 25, found that nearly three quarters of those surveyed (72%) wanted to be taught more about the subject. “Young people are telling us they want to learn more about democracy and voting — we hear it loud and clear”, said Vijay Rangarajan, Chief Executive at the Electoral Commission — Read the full report .
items.why: evidence that young people want more education about politics and elections bears on future civic engagement and political efficacy, key conditions for participation
links: Young people and children want to learn more about elections and politics in school

items.h: Naked Politics offer free nationwide in-person school sessions on making change
items.b: Naked Politics is offering free in-person interactive sessions in schools to encourage young people to think about how they can create change in their communities beyond elections. Naked Politics is especially interested in catering to young people of colour, but welcomes all enquiries. If you are interested or have any questions about the sessions, contact Bella Frimpong via bella.frimpong@nakedpolitics.co.uk
items.why: it creates a new means for young people to learn how to organise and effect change in their communities, expanding practical avenues for civic participation.

items.h: National Youth Parliament meets for annual session 2025
items.b: On Friday 28 February, more than 300 elected Members of Youth Parliament (MYPs) aged 11–18 met to represent the views of their peers and held debates on a range of topics. Young people from across the UK, British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies gathered on the green benches of the House of Commons Chamber on Friday 28 February for the annual sitting of UK Youth Parliament. They met to discuss motions on whether 16- and 17-year-olds should be allowed to vote in all elections, whether the the National Minimum Wage for every worker under 22 be raised, whether all public transport shou…
items.why: it gives young people a structured forum to debate and voice political concerns, building civic engagement capacity even though it lacks binding decision-making power.
items.note: Youth Parliament is a civic-engagement forum rather than a decision-making body with binding power, so it is filed under participation rather than elections.
links: more than 300 elected Members of Youth Parliament (MYPs) aged 11–18 met to represent the views of their peers

items.h: The Politics Project is after for volunteers for a Youth Steering Group
items.b: The Youth Steering Group is a new initiative designed to give young people a voice in shaping how The Politics Project engages with politics and democracy. They are looking for 14–20 year-olds from across the UK to join them and help shape the organisation’s future projects and programmes. Get in touch if you know someone that might be interested.
items.why: it establishes a new structure giving young people a formal voice in shaping an organisation's civic and democratic engagement work.

items.h: Gen Z don’t actually want a dictatorship — new research debunks recent polling
items.b: A recent widely publicised poll — covered in our previous bulletin — suggested that over half of Gen Z think Britain would be in a better place if ruled by a dictator. But recent research by King’s Policy Institute debunks this claim following extensive research with 2,032 adults between 13 and 27 years old. They tested different versions of the question on Britain as a dictatorship and found that the overall number is more likely to be about 6% .
items.why: it corrects the evidence base on popular support for democracy among young people, a key indicator of the health of democratic legitimacy.
links: tested different versions of the question

items.h: Majority of teachers think curriculum provides insufficient political education, poll shows
items.b: New polling by Teacher Tap finds that 84% of state school teachers don’t believe the current curriculum offers sufficient political education to prepare students for voting in elections. With Labour promising to lower the voting age to 16, the vast majority of teachers across the UK, according to Teacher Tap, feel changes must be made to ensure students are ready for this change.
items.why: it concerns whether civic and political education equips future voters with the knowledge needed to participate meaningfully in elections.
items.note: Tied to the prospective voting age change but the mechanism at issue is educational preparation for participation, not electoral machinery itself.

items.h: Government to publish their approach to electoral reform before the summer recess
items.b: Democracy Minister Rushanara Ali MP has announced that the government will publish its approach to elections and electoral reform before the summer recess. The document will include how they intend to deliver on manifesto commitments and the findings from the review into electoral registration and conduct.
items.why: it signals forthcoming government decisions on electoral registration, conduct and reform that shape how elections are run.

items.h: New law to force political parties to publish diversity data on candidates
items.b: The Government has now confirmed it will begin the process of enacting Section 106 of the Equality Act — a crucial measure that will require political parties to publish diversity data about their candidates. The legislation was written back in 2010 but it has taken 15 years for it to be enacted — something which campaign groups have consistently pointed to as limiting our ability to understand political representation in the UK.
items.why: mandatory publication of candidate diversity data affects transparency around party candidate selection and representativeness of elected institutions.
links: enacting Section 106 of the Equality Act

items.h: Upcoming Electoral Integrity Project workshop on electoral reform
items.b: The Electoral Integrity Project is running a workshop on electoral reform, focused on examining efforts to improve the quality of elections around the world. Find out more information and join the three day online event , running from March 19–21st.
items.note: Event listing/sector logistics rather than a substantive democracy story.

items.h: 4.4 million residents have no right to vote, says new Migrant Democracy Project report
items.b: A new research report, What If Everyone Could Vote? , commissioned by the Migrant Democracy Project and funded by the UK Democracy Fund , finds that 4.4 million residents have no right to vote in general elections, and 1.2 million residents in England and Northern Ireland have no right to vote at all. The report suggests that residence-based voting rights could be implemented as a practical and inexpensive policy solution to combating these disparities in the UK. Read the report now .
items.why: it concerns who is legally entitled to vote in UK elections, a core question of suffrage and inclusive franchise.

items.h: Unlock Democracy’s Resilient Democracy conference launches 5 new campaigning strands
items.b: Unlock Democracy’s Resilient Democracy brought together 28 UK based democracy organisations, who then agreed to work across 5 new campaign strands. These were: promoting Automatic Voter Registration and Votes at 16, improving representation in Parliament, taking foreign money out of politics, tackling deception and improving standards in politics, and finally, establishing a pro democracy institution or campaign. Contact Tom Brake for more details .
items.why: it creates new coordinated civic campaigning capacity aimed at reforms to voter registration, representation, political finance and standards in public life.
items.note: Sector capacity-building launch of campaign strands spans several beat topics; filed as participation per the capacity-building rule.
links: Contact Tom Brake for more details

items.h: Constitution Unit publishes major new report on options for constitutional reform
items.b: The new UCL Constitution Unit report, The Constitutional Landscape: Options for Reform , outlines 31 possible reforms across 6 different areas, from ministerial standards to the future of the Union. Read the report now .
items.why: it sets out proposals for reforming constitutional structures, ministerial standards and executive accountability mechanisms.
items.note: Report spans multiple areas including the Union/devolution; classified primarily under accountability given its focus on constitutional and executive structures.
links: The Constitutional Landscape: Options for Reform

items.h: New guide on introducing Automatic Voter Registration
items.b: Professors Toby S. James and Paul Bernal have produced extensive guidance on how an automatic, or direct, form of voter registration can be implemented across the UK. Read the new report here . The report was funded by the UK Democracy Fund .
items.why: it provides technical guidance on reforming voter registration, a core electoral administration mechanism affecting who can vote.

items.h: The Association of Electoral Administrators publish blueprint for electoral reform
items.b: The Association of Electoral Administrators have published a new set of recommendations, urging the government to implement new changes to update and modernise the British electoral system. Recommendations include earlier deadlines for postal voting, reviewing accepted voter ID formats and changes to polling hours and places — in addition to requests for an independent Royal or Parliamentary Commission review of core election delivery processes and much more, view the report here .
items.why: it proposes reforms to electoral administration such as postal voting deadlines, voter ID and polling arrangements, and calls for independent review of election delivery.

items.h: The Political Technologist held workshop on Democratic AI
items.b: The Political Technologist is a new publication exploring the intersection of technology and civic processes. In this, their second workshop on Democratic AI, they explored the use of AI to enhance group deliberation. Find out more information .
items.note: An event/workshop listing rather than a created resource, tool or change affecting participation.

items.h: ‘Citizens in Power’ Network is launched to improve citizen-led decision making
items.b: A new network has been launched to rethink and redesign the way that decisions are made in the cultural and creative sectors. The Citizens in Power Network , made up of 65 members, associates and experts, will run from 2025–27, bringing together key stakeholders to explore how citizen-led decision-making that reflects the diversity of communities can lead to better outcomes. The network will test different approaches to citizen participation centring on the principles of ‘authority giving’, ‘civic lottery’ and ‘deliberation’ — and will advocate for the take up of new models of democratic decis…
items.why: it establishes a network to test citizen-led deliberative decision-making models, which the framework treats as part of decision-making machinery.
items.note: Deliberative/citizen-led decision-making is filed under elections & decision making per the framework rather than participation, though it is framed here as a capacity-building network.

items.h: Report launch: Improving Welsh Democracy — Lessons from around the world
items.b: On the 4th of March, the Institute for Welsh Affairs launched their new report exploring the potential of democratic innovation to improve Welsh democracy. These innovations are taken from different contexts around the globe where governments have improved their national democracy through interventions boosting participation and citizen deliberation in decision-making.
items.why: it examines democratic innovations, including citizen deliberation in decision-making, to strengthen devolved Welsh democratic institutions.
items.note: Deliberative processes for improving devolved democracy are filed under elections & decision making rather than participation per the framework.

items.h: Demos open letter calls for citizen-led approach to digital rights and tech policy
items.b: Following the AI summit in Paris, Demos issued an open letter calling for the government to develop a citizen-led ‘Declaration of Digital Rights & Principles’ for the UK. The declaration would not be legally binding, but would allow the government to understand and reflect the values of UK citizens in its decisions on tech policy, guiding future policymaking.
items.note: An open letter calling for future citizen-led policy input is an advocacy ask, not a created mechanism or reported change.

items.h: Commission on Political Power launches inquiry into cabinet reform
items.b: The Commission on Political Power has launched an inquiry into what can be done to reform cabinet power as the centre of Government. The first evidence session was held in January with Lord Richard Wilson and Lord Robin Butler, and more sessions on this question to be held in the coming months.
items.why: this matters democratically because it examines how executive power is concentrated and constrained within cabinet government, a core check on the exercise of public power.

items.h: Media Democracy Festival 2025, coming soon
items.b: This May, the Media Reform Coalition are hosting their next gathering, bringing together activists, independent media outlets, journalists, researchers and policymakers to debate how they can transform the media into a more independent, accountable and democratic system that serves the public interest. The event will feature contributions from broadcast journalist Sangita Myska, journalist Peter Oborne, Byline Times editor Hardeep Matharu, the Bristol Cable , We Are The Economy , Impress and many more.
items.note: Event listing/promo, not a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Society of Editors to hold ‘Media Freedom Conference’ in March
items.b: On Tuesday 25 March 2025, The Society of Editors will host a conference on the theme ‘The Future of News’. Key discussions will include; the sustainability of the local and regional media, progress on restoring police and media relations, and relationships with tech platforms and AI companies. Leading editors and news executives from all sectors of the UK news industry will be there for this important discussion.
items.note: Event listing/promo, not a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Want to stay more up to date with Independent News? New Bluesky starter pack is here to help
items.b: The Bristol Cable has put together a starter pack on BlueSky of independent and public interest news providers in the UK and Ireland. If you’re new to BlueSky, this is a great way to get started and follow some of the best independent news outlets around the UK!
items.note: A social media starter pack promoting independent outlets is a promotional resource, not a substantive change to the information environment.

items.h: Indie News Week is back this year from 9th — 15th June 2025
items.b: Under the banner ‘No News is Bad News’, Indie News Week will be returning this year to champion all things independent news. Set up by the Public Interest News Foundation , last year, the Independent News Fund ran alongside the festival, raising £128,000 for the sector. This year will hope to build on the enormous success of last years’ efforts, so reach out if you want to be involved .
items.note: Event/campaign announcement, sector logistics rather than a reported democratic change.
links: Indie News Week will be returning this year
reach out if you want to be involved

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation Local News Commission launching Tues 25th March
items.b: Keep your eyes peeled for Public Interest News Foundation’s (PINF) latest report launch of the Local News Commission, which will be held in Parliament on 25th March.
items.note: Announcement of an upcoming report launch, not yet a substantive finding or change.

items.h: National and local media launch ‘Make it Fair’ campaign to combat AI content theft
items.b: On 25 February, the last day of the government’s consultation on AI copyright issues, regional and national daily newspapers ran the same cover wrap and homepage takeover to raise awareness of the Make It Fair campaign . The campaign aims to boost understanding of the threat posed by AI platforms which ‘scrape’ creative content from the internet without permission or acknowledgement.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the economic sustainability and integrity of journalism, which underpins the public's access to a plural information environment.
items.note: Coordinated media campaign tied to a live government consultation on AI copyright counts as a reported action rather than mere event logistics.

items.h: FediForum unconference highlights the open social web
items.b: With the decline of X, formerly known as Twitter, and a huge outpouring of Twitter users onto federated open platforms, such as Bluesky and Mastodon, the FediForum unconference takes aim at exploring next-generation social media breaking out of the closed silos and connecting the world into a global, open social web. Find out more about FediForum here .
items.note: Event listing for an unconference on decentralized social media, not a UK democracy story or reported change.

items.h: US AID crisis threatens global nonprofit independent media
items.b: The sudden US Government cut-off of more than $268 million worth of agreed US AID grants for nonprofit independent media outlets worldwide is having a severe impact, throwing much of the global nonprofit watchdog sector into crisis, and potentially leaving numerous reporters, contractors, and accountability projects without pay in the weeks and months ahead.
items.why: the sudden loss of funding for independent nonprofit media and watchdog journalism worldwide reduces the plural, public-interest information environment that underpins democratic accountability.
items.note: International funding story counted as comparative evidence bearing on the health of independent journalism relevant to UK debates.
links: US Government cut-off of more than $268 million worth of agreed US AID grants

items.h: Annual State of Protest report published by Network for Police Monitoring & Article 11 Trust
items.b: Published by Article 11 Trust and Network for Police Monitoring , the new Annual State of Protest report, THIS IS REPRESSION , reveals severe protest crackdown in England & Wales. The report states that aggressive police use of new anti-protest laws, coupled with a growing portrayal of protesters as alleged threats to democracy rather than a vital part of public participation, has now grown so routine and so severe that it now amounts to state repression. Register for the report launch on Wednesday 19th March .
items.why: increasingly aggressive policing and legal restriction of protest under new anti-protest laws curtails citizens' freedom of assembly to challenge and contest democratic power.
items.note: Protest policing and legal restriction falls under rights and civic space rather than participation, per the framework's boundary rule.
links: Register for the report launch on Wednesday 19th March

items.h: Journalists targeted by secretive police unit, report Democracy for Sale
items.b: A secretive policing unit, the ‘Central Referral Unit’ (CRU), has been advising police forces across the UK to block requests for information, including those from investigative journalists at Democracy for Sale . Between January and March 2024, the CRU reviewed over 1,700 Freedom of Information (FOI) requests from journalists, researchers, and other requesters and recommended forces reject certain requests and logged requesters’ organisations in a secret database in a major blow to the integrity of freedom of information. MPs and campaigners have branded the CRU as an ‘authoritarian censor’ —…
items.why: a secretive police unit systematically advising forces to block journalists' FOI requests and logging their details undermines the public information environment that enables scrutiny of power.
items.note: FOI story centres on suppression of journalists' access to information rather than institutional answerability, so classed under information & public debate with accountability as secondary.

items.h: Guardian investigation reveals commercial interests in the House of Lords
items.b: A months-long investigation by the Guardian reveals that a number of peers are benefiting from commercial interests, raising questions over the lobbying rules governing the second chamber. The investigation found that: One in 10 Lords get paid to give political advice, multiple peers are being paid by foreign governments and repressive regimes, a Labour peer offered access to ministers and more than £1 in every £14 donated to political parties since 2001 came from those who have sat as peers in the last Parliament.
items.why: peers benefiting from undisclosed commercial and foreign interests while shaping legislation exposes weaknesses in lobbying rules and standards in public life governing the second chamber.

items.h: Ministers draw up plans to limit overseas donations to political parties
items.b: The government is looking to update election laws by limiting party donations from overseas actors. The proposed changes would require foreign companies to generate sufficient revenue or profit within the UK, potentially capping donations based on these financial metrics. For more on this topic, The Constitution Unit will be hosting an event on the 24th of March looking at whether the UK’s regulations around party financing are fit for purpose.
items.why: new rules restricting overseas donations to political parties would change the campaign finance regime that governs fair political competition.
links: government is looking to update election laws

items.h: Beyond Transparency, new report from mySociety
items.b: Fifty volunteers have been helping mySociety comb through the Register of Members’ Financial Interests for all 650 MPs to understand how the rules around financial transparency work in practice. A new report based on the research — Beyond Transparency Four steps to control money in politics — offers four recommendations to better control money in politics. These are; better data collection, stronger checks on information, tighter rules and systematic reform to decrease the role of money in politics.
items.why: recommendations to strengthen checks on MPs' financial interests and reduce the role of money in politics target mechanisms for holding elected representatives to standards of conduct.
links: Beyond Transparency Four steps to control money in politics

items.h: Research for Action to publish new guide on council bankruptcies
items.b: Gloria Dawson and the team at Research for Action are working on a 3-year project on councils in financial crisis, exploring the effects of both bankruptcy and government interventions on democracy and participation. They are planning to publish a new guide to council bankruptcies and government interventions for lay people/campaigners — See here for their incredible work and reports on local government auditing, citizen auditors and accountability failures in local government.
items.why: a new guide equipping lay people and campaigners to understand council bankruptcies and government interventions creates a practical means for citizens to engage with local democratic accountability.
items.note: Classed as capacity-building resource creation rather than a structural local-government story, though the underlying subject touches local government powers.

items.h: New Crime and Policing Bill introduced to Parliament
items.b: A new Crime and Policing Bill was introduced to the House of Commons at the end of February. Netpol has criticised the bill, saying it recycles several anti-protest policies introduced by the Conservatives, including banning smoke flares and making it illegal for protestors to cover their faces at a protest.
items.why: this matters democratically because new legal restrictions on protest tactics such as face coverings and flares affect people's ability to exercise freedom of assembly and challenge state power.
items.note: Protest policing/legal restriction falls under rights & freedoms, not participation.

items.h: Westminster culture of shredding WhatsApp messages is bad for democracy, says New Statesman
items.b: The Covid Inquiry demonstrated to politicians that their private Whatsapp messages could be brought into the public domain through inquiries and FOI requests. Although good for transparency, this has now led to a culture whereby almost all of Westminster uses ‘disappearing messages’ on Whatsapp, reports Will Dunn at the New Statesman . This, he says, is ‘clearly bad for democracy’ as it means communications between politicians and their dealings with journalists are essentially being ‘shredded’.
items.why: this matters democratically because the deliberate destruction of records used to evade FOI and inquiry scrutiny undermines the ability to hold government and politicians answerable for their actions.
links: reports Will Dunn at the New Statesman

items.h: Compassion in Politics campaign to outlaw deception in politics makes progress
items.b: The Welsh Parliament’s Standards Committee has taken up a proposal set out by Compassion in Politics which recommends that candidates and campaign managers who deliberately lie to the public should be guilty of a crime. Having run the campaign for six years, the team is celebrating important progress is being made — and they now have their sights set on Westminster.
items.why: this matters democratically because criminalising deliberate deception by candidates and campaign managers would affect the integrity and fairness of electoral competition.
items.note: Classified under elections as it concerns campaign conduct and electoral integrity rather than general standards in office.
links: proposal set out by Compassion in Politics

items.h: Compass report explores spread of global populism and how to navigate it
items.b: A new report from Compass unpicks the causes behind the surge of global populism and offers guidance to progressives on how to develop an alternative vision that appeals to voters. A ‘combinational, alliance-based politics’ is explored as the way to stop the steady decline towards right extremist politics. See you next time,
items.note: This is a political strategy/ideology report rather than a story about a specific democratic mechanism.

items.b: Monthly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network. Read by 400+ democracy organisations. items.h: Welsh Government extends application deadlines for Democratic Engagement Grant
items.b: The Welsh Government will launch its Democratic Engagement Grant for a further three years with £400,000 being available to support projects in the 2025–26 financial year, through to the end of 2027–28. The grant aims to support local authorities, third sector, and not-for-profit organisations working in Wales to pursue an innovative approach to engaging those typically under-represented in our democracy. This includes but is not limited to:
items.why: this matters democratically because new grant funding creates capacity for organisations to engage under-represented groups in democratic participation.

items.why: this matters democratically because the grant aims to build tools and motivation for people to take part in democratic life.
