items.h: National Endowment for Democracy welcomes first step towards restoring funding
items.b: On March 10th, the National Endowment for Democracy (NED) regained access to congressionally appropriated funds that had been unavailable since late January. The development came after NED’s lawsuit , which they launched soon after they were denied access to $167 million and an additional $72 million already appropriated by Congress.
items.note: Concerns US organisational funding dispute with no stated bearing on UK democracy.

items.h: Aid Transparency Index is put on hold due to lack of funding
items.b: Publish What You Fund says they will not be running the Aid Transparency Index in 2026 due to a lack of funding, with all future editions on hold until funding can be secured. The Index has provided an independent assessment and ranking of the transparency of the world’s largest aid agencies since 2012.
items.note: Organisational funding shortfall halting an index; not UK-specific and reads as organisational news.

items.h: More than 8,619 candidates standing across 1,497 council wards on 1st May, Democracy Club reports
items.b: Following on from this year’s massive volunteer SOPN Day effort — in their latest candidate blog, Peter Keeling from Democracy Club , broke down the numbers and found that, for the first time in modern election history, a party other than Labour, the Lib Dems or the Conservatives are standing candidates in the most seats . Reform is standing 1,705 candidates, compared to the Tories’ 1,687 and Labour’s 1,633 candidates.
items.why: it reports on party competition and candidate access across local elections, a core measure of electoral pluralism.

items.h: Who Targets Me track local election social media spend
items.b: Who Targets Me track social media political advertising spend across multiple countries, including the UK — where it all began back in 2017. See the latest trends in social spend for UK political parties : Reform spent big earlier in the local election cycle and still lead on overall spend, but the race has now narrowed, with ‘Others’ (AKA the Electoral Commission’s adverts) pulling ahead. This data, and monitoring of political advertising via Who Targets Me, is only made possible through their Browser Extension — if you haven’t already, install it today .
items.why: tracking political advertising spend on social media reveals how campaigns seek to shape the information environment voters encounter.
items.note: Political ad spend sits at the boundary of campaign finance (elections) and the information environment (information_debate); classified by the latter as the story concerns platform monitoring.

items.h: Elect Her signal depressing stats on female representation, yet again
items.b: This year’s local election numbers are in, with men making up 67% of candidates, that’s even less women than last time. Annabel Mullin at Elect Her says. The Green Party is ‘winning’ though, fielding just 56% men, whilst Reform are fielding 78% men — these figures show just how important the work of Elect Her and similar organisations are right now. Elect Her are working with Operation Black Vote , 50:50 Parliament , Migrant Democracy Project , The Disability Policy Centre & The Politics Project to support the Local Government Association’s ‘Be a Councillor’ campaign this year. Together they a…
items.why: the gender balance of candidates standing for office affects the representativeness of elected institutions.
links: Local Government Association’s ‘Be a Councillor’ campaign

items.h: Coventry Youth Activists working to get young Disabled people vote-ready
items.b: Coventry Youth Activists (CYA) , a disability-led youth group, have launched a free campaign pack to help young Disabled people , organisations, and their supporters get ready for the upcoming local elections. The campaign, based on lived experiences of barriers like Voter ID confusion and inaccessible polling stations, highlights CYAs unique role as one of the few disability-led, youth-driven initiatives in the UK. Take their Voter Readiness Quiz and amplify their important work on social media now . Reach out to Melissa Smith for more information.
items.why: addressing barriers like Voter ID confusion and inaccessible polling stations directly affects disabled people's practical ability to vote.
items.note: Turnout and access mechanics are always classified under elections per framework rule.
links: amplify their important work on social media now

items.h: Bristol voters confused and apathetic towards mayoral election, reports Bristol Cable
items.b: Bristol Cable’s Isaac Kneebone-Hopkins reports on the state of the mayoral election for the West of England Combined Authority , suggesting that the election is marked by public confusion, a chaotic political environment and a lack of clarity about the political impact of their choices, underlined by the new First Past the Post voting system making the outcome highly unpredictable.
items.why: voter confusion under a newly changed electoral system affects whether people can meaningfully exercise their vote in a mayoral election.
links: Bristol Cable’s Isaac Kneebone-Hopkins reports on the state of the mayoral election for the West of England Combined Authority

items.h: North Warks Council providing information sessions for candidates
items.b: Martyn Harris , Elections and Democratic Services Manager at Nuneaton and Bedworth Borough Council, has been busily organising the local elections in Warwickshire (the ones that are going ahead anyway) — his last set of elections before moving to take up a new post at the Association of Electoral Administrators , congratulations Martyn!
items.note: Primarily a staff-move congratulations notice with routine election administration logistics, not a substantive democracy story.

items.h: First Past the Post changes mean new Mayors can sneak in on low support, say Electoral Reform Society
items.b: As Britain’s voters grapple with changed voting systems this election , Electoral Reform Society highlights the changes under the Elections Act 2022 and shifting the mayoral elections from Supplementary Vote to First Past the Post, and the impacts this will have on the upcoming local elections this week. Experts Professor Rob Ford and Peter Kellner note that it is highly likely mayors will be elected with less public backing than ever before , lower even than 30% they suggest.
items.why: a change from Supplementary Vote to First Past the Post for mayoral elections alters how much public support is needed to win office.
links: Britain’s voters grapple with changed voting systems this election
highlights the changes under the Elections Act 2022

items.h: Democracy Volunteers launch new Observations Podcast
items.b: Democracy Volunteers (DV) new Observations Podcast brings you insightful coverage of elections — past, present, local, national, and international. The podcast explores the stories behind the ballots, speaking with candidates, campaigners, organisers and winners to uncover the narratives you won’t hear anywhere else. Tune in for a deeper look at the elections that shape our world. Check it out now on Spotify , Apple and YouTube )
items.note: A podcast launch is promotional sector content rather than a new mechanism affecting democratic participation or scrutiny.

items.h: UK Supreme Court rules legal definition of a women is based on biological sex
items.b: On 15th April, the UK Supreme Court unanimously ruled that a woman is defined by biological sex under equalities law. The court sided with anti-trans campaign group For Women Scotland , which brought a case against the Scottish government arguing that sex-based protections should only apply to people that are assigned female at birth. Stonewall responded to the ruling, sharing their ‘deep concern at the widespread implications’ of the ruling. Trans cyclist Emily Bridges says the ruling has ‘painted a target’ on the back of trans people . Whilst the law still gives protection against discrimina…
items.why: this matters democratically because a Supreme Court ruling redefines the scope of legal protection against discrimination for a social group, directly affecting equal protection under the law.
items.note: Treated as rights/equal protection per the equality boundary rule rather than participation.
links: UK Supreme Court unanimously ruled that a woman is defined by biological sex

items.h: Keseb publish new primer on building pro-democracy civil society coalitions
items.b: Capturing lessons from interviews with builders and participants of pro-democracy civil society coalitions in Australia, Brazil, France, the Philippines, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States, as well as from the Keseb team’s coalition experiences, the Primer aims to provide actionable insights and a provocation for civil society . It is especially intended for those who are interested in launching, supporting or participating in a coalition to achieve pro-democracy goals. Read it here and find out more about Keseb .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a shared resource to help civil society coalitions organise more effectively to advance democratic goals.
links: the Primer aims to provide actionable insights and a provocation for civil society

items.h: Center for Countering Digital Hate launches new Digital & Information Resilience Training
items.b: Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) have launched a new, free, interactive session designed to help individuals and organisations navigate online hate and disinformation. The new Digital & Information Resilience Training helps participants understand these dynamics and develop strategies to counter online attacks effectively. To find out more contact Risa and arrange a session .
items.why: this matters democratically because it builds new civic capacity to counter disinformation and online hate that degrades public debate.
items.note: Classified under sector capacity-building rule as a new participatory resource, with information environment as secondary.
links: contact Risa and arrange a session

items.h: London Movement Builders Meetup, coming May 8th
items.b: Civic Power Fund , Lush , New Economics Foundation and Common Knowledge are hosting a series of new Movement Builders Meetups. They held their first event in Manchester last week, and are hosting their next in London on May 8th — bringing together London’s infrastructure and movement building organisations to support the work of grassroots organisers and activists. The events are invite only.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new networks and infrastructure to support grassroots organising and civic mobilisation.

items.b: Are you excited by pro-democracy tech? Have you got what it takes to fulfil this specialised role for mySociety ? This new project, pioneered by Assemble , will establish a permanent citizens’ assembly which will have its first sitting in July. The aim is to create a ‘pa…

items.h: Democrafest — new festival celebrating civic participation, early bird ticket release
items.b: On 30th August in Hertfordshire, Democrafest will be a new festival of music and debate, welcoming journalists, authors, organisers and influencers to educate and inspire people to feel empowered by democracy — Book your tickets now .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new public event designed to build engagement and empower people to participate in democratic life.

items.h: Involve are hiring for a new HR lead
items.b: The new Involve People and Culture Lead role will support Involve as the team continues to grow, developing new policies and supporting the organisation to develop an inclusive work environment. Find out more about the role here .
items.note: Organisational HR hiring news, excluded as organisational admin.

items.h: Just Stop Oil are ‘hanging up the high vis’
items.b: After 3 years, 3,300 arrests and 180 imprisonments, Just Stop Oil says they are hanging up the high vis at the end of the month. With an end to all new oil and gas now government policy, the campaign group says they have achieved the goal they originally set out to do. Although they will no longer be protesting on the streets, the group says they will remain vocal in the courts to speak out for those detained.
items.why: this matters democratically because the scale of arrests and imprisonments reflects how the state polices protest and assembly, and the group's shift to courts touches access to justice for detainees.
items.note: Borderline between civic space (protest policing) and organisational campaign news; classified by the protest/policing mechanism.
links: Just Stop Oil says they are hanging up the high vis

items.h: Newspeak House are looking for new applicants
items.b: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology is currently on the lookout for new applicants for next year’s 2025/2026 intake starting this September. Students will spend a year immersed in communities of practice and undertake the one-year course Introduction to Political Technology course, alongside a range of other activities. Find out more here , residential and non-residential places available. In the past year Newspeak House developed the Election Tech Handbook and the the MP Office Manual and is a thriving hub for political technology hosting hundreds of events every year.
items.note: Recruitment for an existing annual course is sector logistics, not a new means of participation being created.
links: Newspeak House — The London College of Political Technology

items.h: The Constitution Unit publish latest round up of UK constitutional developments
items.b: The Constitution Unit has published Monitor 89 — the latest news about constitutional change in the UK. This quarter’s edition focuses on the progress of the bill to scrap hereditary peers, electoral reform, the government’s white paper on English devolution, and much more.
items.why: this matters democratically because it tracks live changes to how the UK allocates and constrains political power, including electoral reform, devolution and House of Lords composition.
items.note: Roundup spans multiple beats (electoral reform/devolution vs Lords reform); classified by the more prominent decision-making machinery angle.

items.h: Novara Media series explores the impact of prison time on activists
items.b: Committed, a new podcast series by Novara Media , explores the stories of five young people currently locked up as political prisoners in Britain as part of recent crackdowns over the past several years on climate protest and direct action movements such as Just Stop Oil and Palestine Action.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns state coercion and imprisonment of people for protest and direct action, bearing directly on the freedom to assemble and dissent.
items.note: Protest is classified under rights/civic space because the mechanism at issue is policing and legal restriction, not willingness to participate.

items.h: Run for Jo — 22 June 2025
items.b: The Run for Jo is part of the Great Get Together weekend and is all about bringing people together and remembering the life of the Batley & Spen MP who was murdered by a far-right extremist in 2016 in the lead up to the EU Referendum. This year’s event falls on 22 June, which would have been Jo’s 51st birthday. Get involved here .
links: murdered by a far-right extremist in 2016

items.h: Active Inquiry running two day legislative theatre in Edinburgh
items.b: The event run by Active Inquiry , last weekend, explored the barriers people face when accessing Historic Environment Scotland’s sites — find out more .
items.note: Event report about heritage-site accessibility, not about democratic power or participation mechanisms.

items.h: Unlock Democracy supporters now top 100,000
items.b: Tom Brake and the team at Unlock Democracy are celebrating topping 100,000 supporters — growing from 20,000 over the past four years. Unlock have led on a range of campaigns in recent years, from pushing for overseas constituencies to addressing foreign funding in politics — last month they convened dozens of democracy campaign organisations in Windsor to align and prioritise around a range of key policy areas.
items.note: Organisational membership milestone counts as org news, not a democracy story.

items.h: The Festival of Debate is back in April and May
items.b: The largest annual UK politics festival — the Festival of Debate — is back this year, with a huge array of events, talks and community events across Sheffield in April & May. Don’t miss it — get your tickets now!

items.h: Leftwing activists less likely to work with political rivals than other groups, study finds
items.b: The new study by More in Common found that the 8–10% of the UK population they class as ‘progressive activists’ both hold very different views to the rest of the UK — and critically — are more likely to disagree, criticise and less likely to work with opposing political blocs. Read the new report here .
items.why: this matters democratically because willingness of politically engaged groups to cooperate across divides affects societal cohesion and the practical functioning of pluralist civic and political life.

items.h: Greenpeace working with The Climate Coalition for Mass Lobby of Parliament
items.b: Building on last year’s Project Climate Vote, Greenpeace are organising a Mass Lobby of Parliament .
items.why: it mobilises citizens to lobby their elected representatives, reflecting willingness to take part in political life
items.note: Lobbying framed as readiness to participate, not legal restriction, so filed under participation rather than rights.

items.h: Senedd establishes Voter Information Platform
items.b: The Senedd has approved the creation of a new Welsh Voter Information Platform — a proposal which originates from the 2024 Elections and Elected Bodies (Wales) Act. The new platform will centralise information related to Welsh elections, breaking down barriers to voting by making it easier for voters to find information about upcoming elections, candidates and polling arrangements.
items.why: it changes how voters can access election information, reducing practical barriers to voting

items.h: Senedd Explained launches
items.b: Maddy Dhesi and Gwion Rhisiart are launching a brand new project to break down Welsh news and politics into accessible bite size chunks, bringing Welsh news closer to anyone who wants it. Check out Senedd Explained now .
items.why: it creates a new source of accessible political information, expanding the public information environment around Welsh politics
items.note: Framed as a news/media project rather than a decision-making tool, so filed under information rather than participation.

items.h: Citizen Network and Neighbourhood Democracy Movement growing democratic governance in Sheffield
items.b: Together, Citizen Network and Neighbourhood Democracy Movement (NDM) have been working to develop democratic governance in Sheffield, working with the council and local authorities to build a plan for 147 neighbourhoods across the city. To this end, Jason Leman of NDM has been preparing new DIY democracy materials — Would you like to know more?
items.why: it builds new civic infrastructure and materials for neighbourhood-level democratic participation
items.note: Involves local council structures but the core story is community capacity-building, not formal electoral structure.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Scottish Government hosts Democracy and Respect Summit
items.b: Transparency International’s Juliet Swann responded to the Summit publishing a new briefing on disinformation in Scotland and what needs to be done to tackle it. First Minister John Swinney said Scotland’s shared values were under ‘huge threat’ from disinformation at the Summit.
items.why: it addresses disinformation's threat to the shared information environment underpinning democratic debate
links: Scotland’s shared values were under ‘huge threat’

items.h: Nominate a councillor for the LGIU Awards
items.b: Celebrate our local democracy with the Local Government Information Unit Awards . The LGIU & CCLA Cllr Awards are the only national Awards to recognise and honour the hard work and dedication of councillors. Nominate a councillor today .
items.note: Award nomination notice, excluded as organisational admin rather than a democracy story.
links: Celebrate our local democracy with the Local Government Information Unit Awards

items.h: Electoral Reform host A Scottish Spring conference
items.b: The conference held last weekend saw contributions from Mark Drakeford, Former First Minister of Wales, Willie Sullivan, Senior Director of Electoral Reform Society Scotland , Esther Roberton, former Coordinator of the Scottish Constitutional Convention and many more. The event aimed to revamp the national conversation about the lessons of the last ten years and build ambition for Scotland’s democratic future.
items.note: Reads as a sector event listing/report rather than reporting a specific democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Southport Community Independents Party is launched promising citizens’ assemblies to decide policy
items.b: Independent MP Jeremy Corbyn and Assemble were in Southport recently to launch a new local political party which will be putting up candidates and running assemblies to decide policy. The Southport Community Independents are hoping to improve bottom up decision making in the local community to give voters a greater stake in local democracy.
items.why: it launches a new political party and proposes citizens' assemblies as a mechanism for collective policy decisions
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and party formation both fall under elections & decision making per framework rules.
links: launch a new local political party

items.h: Labour says it will not be scrapping Voter ID scheme
items.b: The government has said they will not be scrapping the Voter ID scheme despite pressure from democracy campaigners. Democracy minister Rushanara Ali said such a move ‘was not on the table’, and instead said the government is ‘looking to improve the system’.
items.why: voter ID rules directly affect who can exercise the franchise and the accessibility and integrity of elections.
links: not be scrapping the Voter ID scheme

items.h: Commission on Political Power prepares their final report
items.b: In January, the Commission on Political Power launched their final inquiry, this time into reform of the Cabinet. They held evidence sessions with Rt Hon Dominic Grieve KC and Rt Hon Robert Buckland KC; Lord Richard Wilson and Lord Robin Butler; and Rt Hon John McDonnell MP. They also received written submissions from Lord Alex Carlile KC and Lord Wilson of Dinton. You can find out more about the work of the Commission here . The report is being prepared for publication in the summer.
items.why: the inquiry examines how Cabinet power is structured and constrained, bearing on executive accountability.

items.h: Don’t miss Republic Day 2025
items.b: May 10th from midday in Trafalgar Square Central London, Republic are hosting their second ever Republic Day , with live music, entertainment and rousing speeches to ‘bring to life a vision of a better, fairer, more democratic Britain’. Speakers include Baroness Natalie Bennett, former Green Party Leader, storyteller Kelechi Okafor, Rhodes Scholar Yasmin Poole and Norman Baker — author of And What Do You Do? What the royal family don’t want you to know , among others.
items.note: This is an event listing/rally announcement, treated as sector logistics.
links: Republic are hosting their second ever Republic Day
And What Do You Do? What the royal family don’t want you to know

items.h: Constitution Unit report explores options for constitutional reform
items.b: A major new report from The Constitution Unit — The Constitutional Landscape: Options for Reform — provides a concise overview of the current constitutional framework and suggests avenues for reform in 31 areas. The areas of focus include those outlined by the Labour government as a target for reform over the course of the coming parliament.
items.why: it maps options for reforming the constitutional framework that governs how public power is exercised and constrained.
links: The Constitutional Landscape: Options for Reform

items.h: Stop the Lies: How to restore trust in politics — upcoming Compassion in Politics event
items.b: Don’t miss Compassion in Politics upcoming event this Tuesday , in partnership with Reform Political Advertising — featuring speakers such as independent Australian MP Zali Steggall and Adam Price MS — Senedd Member who introduced the recent legislation to disqualify politicians who lie from office.
items.note: This is an event promotion, treated as sector logistics despite touching on political honesty legislation.

items.h: The public square must be protected from poor legislation, says Conservative Home
items.b: Tali Fraser, writing for Conservative Home , warns that small venues across the country could face £10,000 fines if they fail to produce paperwork for new anti-terror plans covering village halls and community centres. Over half (56%) of small venues say these requirements would be difficult to manage due to the heavy burden of time and effort. Conservative Home argues that such legislation threatens civic life , with two-thirds of community centres reporting the new rules would damage their ability to operate.
items.why: new regulatory burdens could restrict the ability of community venues and civic organisations to operate and host public life.
items.note: Concerns civic organisations' operating space, so filed under rights/civic space rather than participation.

items.h: Decolonising deliberative democracy — new open access paper published
items.b: A new open access paper from Ricardo Fabrino Mendonça of Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, and Hans Asenbaum of the University of Canberra entitled ‘Decolonizing deliberative democracy’ argues that deliberative democracy practitioners must confront its colonial legacy. The article offers six actions to deconstruct this legacy and build a truly inclusive and emancipatory form of participatory democracy.
items.why: it addresses how deliberative democratic processes are designed and who is included in collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative democracy is anchored to elections/decision-making per framework, even though this is an academic paper without direct UK application.

items.h: Institute for Government to host reflection on election and electoral reform, 19th May
items.b: The Institute for Government event on the 19th May will bring together journalists, campaigners, the Electoral Commission and others, to discuss proposed reforms from political finance to lowering the voting age — sign up for the event now, but don’t miss their event this week on Wednesday , with Michael Jary, the government’s former lead Non-Executive Director, setting out his views on Whitehall reform.
items.note: Event listing/sign-up notice, treated as sector logistics.
links: their event this week on Wednesday

items.h: What’s to blame for democratic backsliding, the Journal of Democracy asks
items.b: In this month’s Journal of Democracy , leading scholars including Francis Fukuyama debate the root causes of democratic backsliding and what can be done to stop it. Check out the essays now, from why democracies must show they can deliver without sacrificing accountability , to shifting the debate on backsliding away from democracies as failing to deliver socioeconomic goods for citizens, and more about failing to constrain predatory political ambitions .
items.why: it examines the mechanisms—delivery, accountability and constraints on predatory political ambition—that determine whether democracies survive backsliding pressures.
items.note: General scholarly debate on backsliding causes rather than a specific UK institutional development.

items.h: Applications are now open for the School for Everyday Democracy
items.b: Involve and Act Build Change are preparing for their second cohort of The School for Everyday Democracy — a new UK-wide programme to support people who want to create change where they live. They are keen to hear from those who face — or could face — multiple, intersecting barriers to making change. That could mean lacking time or access, juggling caring responsibilities, being underrepresented in decision-making spaces, or simply not feeling like ‘someone who does that sort of thing.’ Share the news with this toolkit — or find out more here .
items.why: it creates a new programme building people's capacity to organise and effect change in their communities, expanding practical means of civic participation.

items.h: TalkShop organise new Win Win Workout on Tackling Disinformation, 6th May
items.b: Perry Walker and the team at TalkShop are organising a new 2.5 hour interactive workshop deep diving into disinformation on Tuesday 6th May online — find out more information and register now .
items.why: it builds public capacity to identify and counter disinformation, which bears on the health of the information environment underpinning public debate.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it creates a new training resource.
links: find out more information and register now

items.h: Media Democracy Festival 2025 is here, 31st May in London
items.b: This year’s Media Reform Coalition annual festival is being held at the University of Westminster on 31st May, with keynotes including Green Party Deputy Leader Zack Polanski and journalist Sangita Myska. Each year the festival brings together activists, independent media organisations, researchers, policy makers and supporters of a more democratic media ecosystem in the UK. Register your ticket now .
items.note: Event listing/ticket announcement, not substantive reporting on a democratic mechanism.

items.h: How to regenerate local news across the UK — new report published
items.b: The Public Interest New Foundation has published a new report — Regenerating Local News in the UK — calling for urgent government action to save local news. The report calls for a Local News Stimulation Fund which will allocate £15m per year for the next 10 years in order to support local news outlets — alongside a host of other measures including tax incentives for the sector and increased regulation of Big Tech.
items.why: it proposes funding and policy measures to sustain local journalism, which underpins the plural information environment citizens need to hold power to account.
links: Regenerating Local News in the UK

items.h: Suffrago recruiting Local Democracy Reports to rebuild local scrutiny
items.b: Last month Suffrago embedded their first ten Local Democracy Reporters across the UK, from Cornwall to Cambridge. These new journalists will be monitoring local stories and sitting in the back of those council planning meetings, paying attention when no one else will. Find out more about Suffrago and their mission to ‘build a new sort of democratic infrastructure’ .
items.why: it creates new local journalism capacity to scrutinise council decision-making, restoring a check on local public power.
links: embedded their first ten Local Democracy Reporters

items.h: Newsmast looking new partners to help pilot their community-focused social media tool
items.b: Saskia Welch at Newsmast Foundation is seeking partners for their new community social media tool — to move away from Big Tech. Would you like to know more?
items.note: A call for partners for an unlaunched tool reads as organisational solicitation rather than a reported democratic development.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: The reach of local media is on the rise, says Starmer
items.b: During an event at the end of March in Downing Street, Keir Starmer praised the vital role played by regional journalism in strengthening local democracy and suggested the reach of local outlets is on the rise. ‘The reach of local regional media is going up’, said the PM, ‘but the pressure is huge and the challenges coming up at the same time’. Starmer encouraged regional outlets to keep holding the government to account, but made no mention of support measures for the struggling sector.
items.why: the strength or weakness of local media affects the plurality of information available to citizens for democratic accountability.
links: praised the vital role played by regional journalism

items.h: Annual State of Protest report published by Network for Police Monitoring & Article 11 Trust
items.b: Published by Article 11 Trust and Network for Police Monitoring , the new Annual State of Protest report, THIS IS REPRESSION , reveals severe protest crackdown in England & Wales. The report states that aggressive police use of new anti-protest laws, coupled with a growing portrayal of protesters as alleged threats to democracy rather than a vital part of public participation, has now grown so routine and so severe that it now amounts to state repression — Download the report .
items.why: it documents how policing and anti-protest laws are restricting the freedom of assembly people need to challenge and contest public power.
items.note: Protest policing/legal restriction falls under rights & freedoms, not participation.

items.b: Friends Meeting House in London (Photo Credit: Quakers in Britain)

items.h: Police raid Friends Meeting House in London
items.b: On 27th March, London Metropolitan Police raided a London Quaker Meeting House, ‘kicking down the door’ and arrested six young people hosting a Youth Demand meeting over concerns for the climate and the Occupied Palestinian Territories. Quakers in Britain strongly condemned the violation of their place of worship which, they say, is a direct result of new ‘stricter protest laws removing virtually all routes to challenge the status quo’, remarking that ‘a threshold has been crossed’ — in a later press statement Quakers in Britain called for civil liberties to be restored . ‘This kind of police …
items.why: a police raid on a place used for organising protest concerns state coercion against freedom of assembly and association.
items.note: Coercive policing of assembly/association sits in rights & freedoms, not participation.
links: Quakers in Britain strongly condemned the violation of their place of worship
Quakers in Britain called for civil liberties to be restored

items.h: Undercover: Exposing the Far Right nominated for BAFTA Best Single Documentary Award
items.b: Undercover: Exposing the Far Right follows the team at Hope Not Hate and their secret cameras to reveal the tactics of the modern far-right. In the wake of the 2024 riots, the film shows how vulnerable communities are targeted, racist ideas mainstreamed and money sought from powerful elites. Watch now on Channel 4 .
items.note: Award nomination for a documentary is treated as promotional/organisational news rather than new democratic evidence.

items.h: Charities and consumer groups marginalised by private sector engagement with ministers, says new report
items.b: A new report from Spotlight on Corruption — Levelling the Playing Field — looks at who has been getting access to ministers, senior officials and special advisers in six of the UK’s government departments principally responsible for economic decision-making. The research finds that business and commercial stakeholders outnumber charity and consumer group stakeholders in meetings by a factor of 23 to 1. The report also finds ‘considerable crossover’ between firms providing corporate hospitality and those getting meetings.
items.why: unequal access to ministers for business versus civil society groups concerns lobbying influence and accountability of government decision-making.

items.h: Full Fact call for greater transparency in policy making to rebuild public trust in politics
items.b: Full Fact launched their manifesto tracking tool four months ago to monitor government progress on their election pledges. However they have found some pledges are ambiguous and difficult to measure — e.g. a promise to recruit ‘ 6,500 new expert teachers in key subjects ’. Full Fact is calling for greater transparency in policy making to ensure manifesto pledges are both comprehensible and measurable so as to avoid further entrenching distrust in our political system.
items.why: calling for transparent, measurable manifesto commitments concerns holding government answerable for its promises.
links: 6,500 new expert teachers in key subjects
calling for greater transparency in policy making

items.h: Unlock Democracy urge the government to ban MPs from accepting gifts
items.b: Following the recent scandals over MPs accepting freebies from private companies — this time involving the Chancellor accepting free gig tickets — Unlock Democracy has written to the government urging them to end this practice. Every scandal, they say, creates a distraction from the proper issues of the day and further damages the increasingly fragile relationship with the electorate.
items.why: restricting MPs' acceptance of gifts concerns standards in public life and conflicts of interest in government accountability.

items.h: Join mySociety’s for TICTeC in Belgium this June
items.b: The world’s leading summit on pro-democracy technology, TICTeC is a unique conference bringing together a mix of tech practitioners, civil society leaders and researchers, to explore and showcase cutting-edge civic and political technology. Book your ticket now .
items.note: Event/ticket listing is sector logistics, not a democracy story.

items.h: Devolved parliamentary registers of interest now on TheyWorkForYou — and mySociety now has a podcast!
items.b: As part of a major update last month, mySociety added devolved parliamentary registers to their already burgeoning suite of data. With this release they’ve shifted their focus away from Westminster, and are publishing the registers of interests for the Scottish Parliament, Senedd/Welsh Parliament, and Northern Ireland Assembly. This includes enhanced UK Parliamentary registers of donations and gifts. That’s not all — did you know mySociety now has a podcast?
items.why: This matters democratically because publishing devolved parliamentary registers of interest increases transparency and public accountability of elected representatives across the UK's nations.
items.note: Treated as an accountability/transparency mechanism (registers of interest) rather than devolved government structure.
links: did you know mySociety now has a podcast?

items.h: Open Council Network launch new service to transcribe and summarise council meetings
items.b: Toby Abel and the team at the Open Council Network are building a new national infrastructure to transform how the public understands local government — using AI to transcribe and summarise council meetings, and working with journalists and communities to publish clear, trusted updates. Contact Toby to find out more .
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates new infrastructure making local council proceedings transparent and accessible to citizens and journalists, akin to local public-interest journalism.
items.note: AI transcription of council meetings is treated as public information infrastructure rather than a participation tool.
links: Contact Toby to find out more

items.h: Explore the wealth of global civic tech resources via the Civic Tech Field Guide
items.b: Built and maintained by Matt Stempeck, the Civic Tech Field Guide is a crowdsourced, global collection of democracy tech, featuring more than 11,000 curated entries, 350+ open source projects, hundreds of jobs and curated civic tech events from across the globe. If you’re into democracy and technology , you need to check this out, right now — subscribe to their newsletter for all the latest.
items.note: A crowdsourced directory of projects, jobs and events is sector logistics, not a reported democratic change.

items.h: Electoral Commission to bring Democracy Club’s polling station finder in-house
items.b: As part of their new 5-year corporate plan, the Electoral Commission (EC) will bring Democracy Club’s WhereDoIVote polling station finder tool in-house . Whilst the EC have financially supported Democracy Club for many years, Democracy Club have long argued that for true sustainability of this work, the tool should be delivered directly by the Electoral Commission.
items.why: This matters democratically because bringing the polling station finder in-house strengthens the institutional sustainability of core electoral administration infrastructure that helps people actually vote.
links: Electoral Commission (EC) will bring Democracy Club’s WhereDoIVote polling station finder tool in-house

items.h: Constitution Unit AI & Democracy webinar, May 15
items.b: The UCL Constitution Unit are hosting a new webinar on AI and democracy, and how it could transform our democratic system — featuring speakers from Harvard University, the Oxford Internet Institute and the Blavatnik School of Government.
items.note: An event listing/webinar announcement, not a reported democratic change.
links: UCL Constitution Unit are hosting a new webinar

items.h: MP Office Manual, in case you missed it!
items.b: Work4Mp highlighted the civic tech project MP Office Manual recently in one of their roundups — the project was developed by a large cross-party group of civic technologists based in Newspeak House aimed at ensuring MPs had well run offices contributing to a flourishing democracy in the UK. The Manual includes advice, tips and procedures gathered from in-depth interviews with current and former MPs, their staff and more than 30+ practitioners. Would you like to know more?
items.note: A resurfaced promotional mention of an existing resource for MP office management, not a new development affecting what people can do.

items.h: Should democracy organisations be rethinking their SEO?
items.b: Ed Saperia at Newspeak House asks, should democracy sector organisations consider the new frontier of AI-assisted search as an opportunity to increase the salience of their organisations and impact, via tools like Promptwatch ?
items.note: A question about organisational marketing strategy, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: The Fiery Spirits, a new book exploring popular protest, parliament and the English Revolution
items.b: This month, author, historian, and activist John Rees published The Fiery Spirits , his second major study of the English Revolution. The book explores the pivotal role of both MPs and street protesters in the English Civil Wars — whose actions ultimately birthed the English Republic and ended absolute monarchy in Britain. It follows Rees’ earlier work, The Leveller Revolution , which traced the Leveller movement’s contributions to the 1640s Putney Debates and their early calls for universal suffrage, centuries ahead of its time. See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: An offbeat historical book review, not a story about how UK public power is currently acquired, exercised or contested.

items.h: Funding available to address racial discrimination in the criminal justice system
items.b: New grants are available from The Baring Foundation to support organisations working on legal action that addresses racial injustice — with a focus on police in schools, repression of protest, and challenging legislation which disproportionately criminalises racialised people. Grants of up to £50,000 for up to 18 months, or up to £90,000 over three years are available. Email by Friday 30 May 2025 to set up a call and apply.
items.note: This is a call to apply for funding, treated as sector logistics rather than a reported change.

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust to fund a range of exciting new projects
items.b: JRRT has announced details of some of the exciting projects they will be funding over the coming year. These include: Black Equity Organisation received £73,148 over one year to implement the Black British Mandate and secure delivery of at least three of its policy demands during the current parliamentary period. The Constitution Unit (University College London) received £56,431 over one year to promote House of Commons reform and restore standards of scrutiny and accountability in the new parliament. Disability Policy Centre received £59,150 over one year to conduct the first-ever research pr…
items.why: new funding builds the capacity of civil society organisations to expand voter registration, monitor parliamentary representativeness, protect journalists from repression, challenge protest policing, and campaign for electoral and constitutional reform, all of which strengthen the infrastructure through which people can take part in and hold power to account.
items.note: A list of newly awarded grants spans several beats; classified under participation as the unifying mechanism of civil-society capacity-building, with secondary beats for the specific project aims.

items.h: Local elections a ‘worrying milestone for democracy’, says Electoral Reform Society
items.b: A ‘worrying milestone’ has been reached in England, says the Electoral Reform Society , as two combined authority mayors were elected on less than 30% of the vote — with one scraping by with just a quarter. In 2021, under the Supplementary Vote system, winning candidates in these regions had nearly 50% of the vote, but the switch to First Past The Post has since dramatically altered the outcome.
items.why: the choice of electoral system directly affects how representative and legitimate elected mayors are, since a switch from Supplementary Vote to First Past The Post let winners take office on far smaller vote shares.

items.h: Petition launched to reform UK voting system after ‘disproportionate’ local election results
items.b: Make Votes Matter , Open Britain , Unlock Democracy and Compass have launched a joint petition calling on the government to reform the voting system after the local elections delivered an ‘unfair and disproportionate’ result. The petition cites the mayoral result in the West of England where Labour won on 25% of the vote and on a 30% voter turnout, meaning just 8% of the local population actually voted for their new mayor.
items.why: a petition calling for voting system reform in response to disproportionate results speaks directly to whether the electoral system translates votes into representative outcomes.

items.h: Local elections a story of ‘unprecedented fragmentation’, say More in Common
items.b: More in Common has broken down the results of the local elections with an extensive analysis of what they mean for the major parties. The key takeaway is that the fragmentation of the electorate means the ‘era of multi-party politics has well and truly arrived’.
items.why: analysis of electoral fragmentation and the shift to multi-party competition bears on the competitiveness and representativeness of the electoral system.

items.h: Women significantly underrepresented at local elections, says Elect Her
items.b: According to Elect Her and Democracy Club , early numbers from the local elections suggest only about 27% of those elected were women. Although gender representation in Parliament is often better than this, the local elections show there is a long road ahead to reach genuine gender parity in politics.
items.why: This matters democratically because the representativeness of locally elected bodies affects whether elected institutions reflect the electorate they govern.
items.note: Representativeness of elected institutions sits in elections & decision making per EIU 'proportion of women in parliament' anchor.
links: According to Elect Her and Democracy Club

items.h: The UK is ‘a real outlier’ due to difficulty of its voter registration process, according to new research
items.b: University of Manchester academics have found the UK is a ‘real outlier internationally’ when it comes to voter registration, based on research with 62 countries. Requirements to actively register to vote, meet strict deadlines and cast a ballot at specific polling stations in person, create a system which is far more onerous than other countries, they say. Labour is currently considering whether to introduce automatic voter registration which campaigners say would enfranchise millions.
items.why: This matters democratically because the ease or difficulty of voter registration directly shapes who can exercise the franchise.

items.h: Is Reform UK about to start benefiting from First Past the Post?
items.b: Following big successes at the local elections and a by-election win in Labour’s heartlands, Nigel Farage can now argue — with growing force — that it is the Conservatives who are splitting the right-wing vote, not the other way around. As suggested in the New Statesman , the First-Past-The-Post voting system could now begin to work in Reform’s favour as right leaning voters think carefully about how to keep out progressive MPs.
items.why: This matters democratically because the electoral system's mechanics shape which parties can compete effectively and how votes translate into seats.

items.h: Democracy Coworking in London, Thursday 19th June
items.b: Don’t miss next month’s Democracy Coworking — sign up here and find out more .
links: sign up here and find out more

items.h: Date set for parliamentary debate on gender recognition ruling, following petition
items.b: A date has been set for a parliamentary debate to discuss the recent ruling to be changed to allow transgender people to be granted gender recognition certificates on the basis of self-identification. This follows a petition which received over 125,000 signatures. It reads ‘we believe the government should change legislation to make it easier for trans people of all ages to change their legal gender without an official diagnosis of gender dysphoria.’
items.why: This matters democratically because a citizen petition triggering a parliamentary debate is a mechanism for redress of grievances and citizen input into government business.
items.note: Petition-triggered debate is filed under participation's petition mechanism rather than the underlying rights topic.

items.h: Vote for Policies to wind down after 15 years
items.b: Vote for Policies has taken the difficult decision to wind down after 15 years, five general elections, and over 4 million users of their policy tracking tool. Founder Matt Chocqueel-Mangan said a combination of declining reach and (welcome) competition from Full Fact’s Government Tracker tool, meant the team could no longer justify the effort. He added that he ‘couldn’t be happier [Full Fact] are taking the baton’.
items.note: News about an organisation's own closure/wind-down is excluded even though its prior work touched civic participation.

items.h: Electoral Commission to take Democracy Club’s ‘polling station finder’ in-house
items.b: Set up over a decade ago, Democracy Club’s polling station finder has been an integral tool in helping voters find out where they can vote. The Electoral Commission has always been a firm believer in the project and has now offered to take it in-house , guaranteeing the long term continuity of the project.
items.why: This matters democratically because ensuring continuity of tools that help voters find their polling station affects practical access to voting.

items.h: Applications for the School of Everyday Democracy are now open
items.b: The ‘School of Everyday Democracy’ , hosted by Involve and Act Build Change , helps equip 100 changemakers with the skills and opportunities to make a real impact in their communities. The successful applicants will form a new collaborative network, sharing ideas and tactics for strengthening democracy on their local patch.
items.why: This matters democratically because the programme creates new capacity and networks for people to engage in and strengthen local democratic life.
items.note: New capacity-building programme counts as a democracy story under the sector capacity-building rule.

items.h: Communicating about democracy under threat — lessons from the US
items.b: Focus group research by Frameworks Institute in the US reveals three major obstacles to communicating about democracy at the moment. A major factor is that concepts like democracy and authoritarianism are difficult for people to relate to, so instead they recommend tapping into feelings of uncertainty, powerlessness and being at the whim of others. They will be undertaking further research in the near future to test these messaging principles — keep your eyes peeled for updates.
items.note: Sector messaging research about how to talk about democracy is not itself a report of a democratic mechanism changing.
links: Focus group research by Frameworks Institute

items.h: Sheila Mckechnie Foundation is looking for a new Chair and Treasurer
items.b: The Chair will hold the Board and staff team to account for SMK’s mission and vision and provide inclusive leadership to the Board. The Treasurer is expected to be the financial expert on the Board, and will provide advice on all financial matters. The deadline for both of these exciting opportunities is 10th of June.
items.note: Organisational recruitment notice, not a democracy story under the framework.

items.h: Republic hold mass protest in Trafalgar Square for ‘Republic Day’
items.b: Republic recently gathered hundreds in Trafalgar Square for ‘Republic Day’. Featuring speeches from Natalie Bennett, Norman Baker and Kelechi Okafor, — and a special appearance by their 30 foot mascot Chuck the Rex — the campaign group called for the abolition of the monarchy and a more democratic future for the UK.
items.why: it demonstrates citizens exercising their willingness and readiness to take part in political demonstration and advocacy for constitutional change.
items.note: Protest coverage is filed under participation because the story is about people's willingness to mobilise, not policing or legal restriction.

items.h: Inquest publish digital archive of state repression and resistance
items.b: In June 2022, INQUEST set out to document its over 40-year history exploring state violence and popular resistance. They have now published a new digital archive , made in partnership with Millipedia , which provides a window onto that important history.
items.note: A historical archive publication is organisational output rather than a current mechanism affecting what people can do.

items.h: Zero Hour launch ‘REAL Change’ campaign
items.b: Zero Hour has launched a new campaign ‘REAL Change’ calling on the government to offer real change on climate on nature policy. The campaign launched 650 open letters to Keir Starmer (one for every constituency in the UK) and has currently generated over 70,000 signatures — the Climate and Nature Bill calls for a temporary Climate and Nature citizens assembly to build consensus around action on climate change.
items.why: it creates new means for citizens to petition government en masse through open letters and signature campaigns, and links to a proposed citizens' assembly on climate policy.
items.note: Citizens' assembly reference is secondary since the primary mechanism reported is the petitioning campaign itself.

items.h: Climate Coalition to host a ‘Mass Lobby’ in June to boost climate action
items.b: The Climate Coalition is set to host a ‘Mass Lobby’ on 9th July which should be a significant moment for democratic engagement on climate. The lobby will bring together citizens from across the country to meet their MPs and demand bold and practical engagement on the climate and nature crisis.
items.why: it creates a new organised opportunity for citizens to directly lobby their MPs, a core mechanism of civic engagement.

items.h: Climate Emergency UK to launch 2025 Council Climate Action Scorecards
items.b: On 17th of June Climate Emergency UK is launching the 2025 Council Climate Action Scorecards , a holistic assessment of all UK councils’ climate work. This is the second edition, so they will be comparing to see what changes in council climate action have happened since the 2023 scorecards . Also, on the 4th of June they will be hosting a pre-launch briefing to discuss the results.
items.why: the scorecards create a tool for holding local councils publicly answerable for their climate performance, a form of transparency and accountability.
items.note: Scorecards function as an accountability mechanism for local government rather than addressing council structure or elections directly.

items.h: Care Full to launch new podcast exploring the power of words
items.b: On Wednesday 27th of May Care Full are launching a new podcast — Words of Affirmation — which will demystify, dismantle and destroy the seeming innocence around words which have entered our everyday lexicon. Each week they’ll choose a new sound bite and explore where it came from and how it holds back from a fairer, more caring society — give it a listen now .
items.note: A podcast exploring language and social framing does not identify a specific mechanism of public power or democratic participation.

items.h: Citizen Network is keen to develop a shared project on constitutional convention
items.b: Simon Duffy from Citizen Network is interested in developing a shared project for a rolling constitutional convention. The project would open up interest around the country and to provoke deeper reflection on what democracy demands. Get in touch if you’re keen to collaborate.
items.note: This is a call for collaboration on a not-yet-existing project, closer to sector networking than a created mechanism.

items.h: Last chance to apply the Newspeak House fellowship programme
items.b: The Newspeak House fellowship programme offers students an opportunity to spend a year immersed in communities of practice and undertake the one-year course ‘Introduction to Political Technology’, alongside a range of other activities. This is the last chance to apply to the 2025/26 intake starting in September.
items.note: An application deadline reminder for an existing fellowship, not the launch of a new participatory mechanism.

items.h: Not1More to explore effectiveness of public inquiries as a method addressing state harm
items.b: Not1More is convening a one-day conference on June 18th bringing together campaigners, lawyers and policy experts from across a broad range of civil society to reflect on their experiences of engaging with public inquiries. This will form part of their wider assessment of the effectiveness of public inquiries as a method for communities seeking justice from state harm.
items.note: This is an event listing for a conference, not itself a reported change in public inquiry mechanisms.

items.h: Safe Landing is running a ‘Visioning Assembly’ to discuss the future of the aviation industry
items.b: Safe Landing is inviting aviation workers and other enthusiasts to a ‘ Visioning Assembly ’ to discuss the future of the industry. The assembly will be in-person in London (exact location TBC) on Saturday 13th of September and will seek to create a transformational vision for the future of air travel that is distinct from the current flightpath.
items.note: An industry-focused stakeholder assembly about aviation's future, not about public political power.

items.h: The People Act to host workshop on legislative theatre
items.b: On June 19th, The People Act: Legislative Theatre will be hosting a free public workshop introducing legislative theatre (with a focus on health, climate and housing policy) at the LSE Festival. The workshop will help anyone seeking new ways to inject accessibility and creativity into decision-making and systems change. And if you’re interested in this, Active Inquiry Theatre are currently working with Historic Environment Scotland to develop a piece of Legislative Theatre to explore accessibility to their sites — email Gavin if you want to come to the performance on the 5th of June.
items.note: A single workshop event listing rather than the launch of a new participatory resource or programme.

items.h: ElectHer working on new ‘Fix the System’ project to improve local democracy
items.b: ElectHer are working on a new project — ‘Fix the System’ — which looks at ways of improving democracy for all. The project will focus on eight major workstreams; Data & Research, Community & Network, Education & Training, Financial Support & Compensation, Transparent & Accountable Processes & Practice, Policies & Legislation, Media & Advocacy, and Normative Standards. If you work in the local democracy space and are interested in changing the system, get in touch with Annabel Mullin.
items.why: this matters democratically because it aims to reform the financial, procedural and legislative barriers that determine who can stand for and access elected local office.
items.note: New capacity-building project on candidate access and party/financial processes, spanning elections machinery and participation capacity.

items.h: Demos launch paper calling for public participation in local planning process
items.b: On 15th May Demos launched a new report — The MIMBY Majority: How to unlock housebuilding with early and representative public participation in planning . The report, supported by the Royal Town Planning Institute , calls for a new approach to public participation in planning decisions to ensure early public involvement which could help anticipate issues earlier and give residents a meaningful opportunity to contribute. You can also check out the recording from the launch event.
items.why: this matters democratically because it proposes new mechanisms for residents to meaningfully participate in local planning decisions that affect their communities.
items.note: Treated as consultation/participation in local decision-making rather than the structure of local government itself.
links: The MIMBY Majority: How to unlock housebuilding with early and representative public participation in planning

items.h: Reform voters are the most likely to trust Citizens’ Assemblies over MPs, according to poll
items.b: New polling for Sortition Foundation shows Reform UK voters are the most likely group to trust Citizens’ Assemblies over MPs, with 69% saying they trust the former compared to just 8% that trust the latter. More broadly, the polling shows that there is broad cross-party support for more citizens’ assemblies with a majority of voters for all major parties trusting them over MPs.
items.why: this matters democratically because it provides evidence on public trust in deliberative decision-making mechanisms like citizens' assemblies relative to elected representatives.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision-making per the framework's deliberative-democracy anchor.

items.h: Improving voter registration through automatic voter registration — new report out
items.b: A new report from Professors Toby S. James and Paul Bernal of the University of East Anglia — Introducing Automatic Voter Registration — describes how AVR could be an effective solution to address democratic inequality. The report, commissioned by the UK Democracy Fund , sets out how AVR would improve the accuracy and completeness of the register, whilst respecting voters’ privacy and saving money.
items.why: automatic voter registration affects the accuracy and completeness of the electoral register, shaping who can actually exercise their franchise

items.h: Polling shows vast majority of public supports a ‘National Commission for Electoral Reform’
items.b: The APPG for Fair Elections — now the biggest ‘All-Party Parliamentary Group’ in Westminster — has revealed brand new polling , showing that a majority (52%) of the public backs its call for a ‘National Commission for Electoral Reform’, whilst just 10% oppose it. They are now calling for the government to act on this widespread support.
items.why: public support for a national commission on electoral reform bears on how the electoral system itself might be restructured
items.note: Treated as electoral system reform advocacy rather than participation, since the subject is the machinery of elections.

items.h: ‌New research show potential detrimental effect of voter ID laws
items.b: Recent research by Dr. Tom Barton of King’s College London highlights the potentially harmful impact of voter ID laws on electoral turnout. The study estimates that during the 2018 Bromley local elections — where voter ID was piloted — around 10,571 people were discouraged from voting and effectively disenfranchised due to the ID requirement. Although Labour has said voter ID reform is not on the table, the Electoral Reform Society is calling for major changes to the ID requirements.
items.why: voter ID requirements can discourage eligible voters from casting a ballot, directly affecting turnout and electoral participation
items.note: Turnout-related stories are always classified under elections & decision making.
links: Electoral Reform Society is calling for major changes

items.h: Indie news providers raise concerns over Local Democracy Reporting Service
items.b: Local news providers have raised concerns about the BBC’s Local Democracy Reporting Service following the recent distribution of new contracts. With over 80% going to three large corporations — National World , Newsquest and Reach — questions are being asked about how to make the service more democratic.
items.why: concentration of local democracy reporting contracts among a few large corporations affects media plurality and the diversity of local political coverage

items.h: Media Democracy Festival 2025 is here, 31st May in London
items.b: This year’s Media Reform Coalition annual festival is being held at the University of Westminster on 31st May, with keynotes including Green Party Deputy Leader Zack Polanski and journalist Sangita Myska. Each year the festival brings together activists, independent media organisations, researchers, policy makers and supporters of a more democratic media ecosystem in the UK. Register your ticket now .
items.note: Event listing/ticket registration, not substantive democracy content.

items.h: House of Lords block Labour’s AI plans in bid to improve copyright protection
items.b: The Society of Editors joined a host of other organisations in calling on the government to amend UK copyright law to protect the creative industry, days before a crucial House of Lords vote on the topic. The upper house then voted against the government plans to allow AI platforms to use copyrighted work without permission — an amendment which was passed by 272 to 125 votes.
items.why: the House of Lords exercising its legislative power to check and amend government AI/copyright plans demonstrates the constraints of one branch on executive policy
items.note: Classified as legislative checks and balances rather than media freedom, since the mechanism is a parliamentary vote constraining government plans.

items.h: Liberty hails major win as anti-protest legislation is quashed
items.b: Positive news for campaigners as the court of appeal upheld the quashing of a key anti-protest regulation which they said was introduced unlawfully. Liberty has been working tirelessly on this. Their director Akiko Hart said the result was a ‘huge win’ which ‘set an important precedent that government ministers must respect the law’.
items.why: a court ruling that the government acted unlawfully in introducing anti-protest regulation reinforces that executive power must operate within the law
items.note: Primary mechanism is judicial constraint on unlawful executive action, with protest rights as a secondary dimension.
links: upheld the quashing of a key anti-protest regulation

items.h: FOI request reveals major lack of transparency around overseas political donations
items.b: A Freedom of Information request from the Byline Times reveals that the Electoral Commission keeps no record of how many overseas donors are financing British political parties. The Commision said they keep no record as to whether donations are coming domestically or from overseas. The finding comes as Reform UK announced they are on the hunt for wealthy non-dom financiers in offshore locations such as Monaco or the UAE, though it should be noted Labour and the Conservatives have both received significant non-dom donations in the past .
items.why: the absence of records on the origin of political donations undermines transparent party financing and safeguards against foreign influence on elections
items.note: Campaign finance transparency is filed under elections; the FOI mechanism also implicates the Electoral Commission's accountability.
links: Electoral Commission keeps no record of how many overseas donors
significant non-dom donations in the past

items.h: Full Fact publishes sixth annual report on the state of UK public debate
items.b: The report by Full Fact examines the current landscape of misinformation in the UK, analysing how recent political shifts have created new challenges for those working to combat false and misleading information. It also considers the roles and responsibilities now facing government, regulators, and online platforms in battling misinformation and upholding high standards political debate.
items.why: it examines how misinformation and platform/regulatory responses shape the quality of public political debate that citizens rely on to make democratic choices.

items.h: Meta’s advertising architecture is a threat to democracy, says new report
items.b: A new report from Open Rights Group tracks how Meta is enabling rogue actors to manipulate elections, spread misinformation and fuel division through its targeted advertising system. The report identifies three broad issues — the transparency problem, the moderation problem and the profiling problem — all of which require a legal or regulatory solution to safeguard democracy against the interference of big tech.
items.why: it documents how a major platform's advertising system can be exploited to manipulate elections and distort the political information environment.

items.h: Social media and search engine platforms are enabling climate denial, says new report
items.b: Centre for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) research shows that climate deniers are strategically spreading disinformation about clean energy online to undermine the environmental solutions. The research suggests social media and search engine platforms are giving climate deniers the tools they need to succeed by damaging people’s trust in science and delaying climate action.
items.note: Concerns platform-enabled science disinformation rather than the public political information environment or electoral processes.

items.h: Demos launch ‘Waves’ — a new tool powered by AI to help deepen citizen deliberation
items.b: Demos has launched what they consider to be the UK’s biggest ever experiment in digital democracy — a new platform, powered by AI, designed to close the gap between councils and citizens. The platform, called Waves , will help identify areas of consensus between otherwise polarised groups on specific topics, and will help digest complex information for participants to make it more accessible. Camden Council and South Staffordshire District Council will be the first to trail the new technology before it is rolled out to others across the country. The project is being delivered by a new coalitio…
items.why: it creates a new deliberative mechanism connecting citizens to local council decision-making, part of the direct/deliberative democracy machinery.
items.note: Deliberative process tools are classified under Elections & decision making per framework rule, not Participation.

items.h: Lessons from the US: Pro Democracy Movement Playbook
items.b: Scott Nakagawa, Co-Founder and Co-Director of the 22nd Century Initiative (22CI) , makes the argument that pro-democracy advocates must pivot from reacting to building — faster, sharper, and at every level. Specific demands tied to institutional change are the key to turning temporary backlash against authoritarianism into permanent democratic renewal, he says. See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: General strategic commentary on movement-building rather than a report of a concrete UK democratic mechanism or change.
