items.h: The Politics Project launch Roadmap to Votes at 16
items.b: Harriet Andrews and the team at The Politics Project launched Roadmap to Votes at 16 , their new showcase of the best ideas, wisdom and practice on Votes at 16 drawn together from across the Democracy Classroom network. Minister for Democracy Rushanara Ali was also in attendance with members of the MHCLG team to support the launch.
items.why: this matters democratically because extending the franchise to 16-year-olds is a direct question of who holds suffrage and can choose representatives.
items.note: Votes at 16 concerns suffrage, which the framework anchors to elections rather than participation.

items.b: Young people from across the UK gather to call for Votes at 16 — Photo Credit: The Politics Project
items.why: this matters democratically because it depicts advocacy for extending suffrage to younger citizens, a core electoral inclusion issue.
items.note: A photo caption tied to the Votes at 16 campaign, placed with elections per the suffrage anchor.

items.h: Join the Shout Out UK Youth Policy Development Group
items.b: If you are a young person yourself, or you know or work with people aged 14–25 who care about their voice being heard in national policy-making, please check out this amazing opportunity from Shout Out UK in partnership with the Paul Hamlyn Foundation. They are looking for 20 people to join a new Youth Policy Development Group. Apply via the following survey link .
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new structured channel for young people's voices to shape national policy-making.
links: Apply via the following survey link

items.h: Pressure on system may put future general election results in doubt, PACAC report finds
items.b: A new report by the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC) says the 2024 General Election was well run but that there are concerns the ‘fabric may not hold’ if a future election result is close, as the system comes under increasing pressure. Chair of PACAC, Simon Hoare MP praised the work of election workers but added: ‘our electoral system is at risk of no longer being able to cope as those running our elections are asked to do more and more. The Government must face up to these issues and ensure we continue to have successful elections in the future. If it does no…
items.why: this matters democratically because strain on the machinery running elections threatens the reliability of future election outcomes and public confidence in them.
links: Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (PACAC)

items.h: The Constitution Society hiring for new Compulsory Voting Campaign Manager
items.b: Have you got what it takes to campaign for Compulsory Voting and push for its introduction in the UK? Deadline for applications 20th August — Apply now .
items.note: A job advert for an organisation, not a reported change to democratic participation itself.

items.h: Rumour mill: Corbyn’s new Your Party apparently considering participatory approaches
items.b: Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana have semi-launched a new party, named Your Party, and have gained 500,000 mailing list supporters in just one week. Sources close to the organising team behind the new project have remarked that people have been talking about assemblies and participatory approaches to their membership to Corbyn and the core team.
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns how a new political movement might structure member participation and internal decision-making, shaping avenues for civic engagement.
items.note: Internal party organising methods, not formal government decision-making machinery, so treated as participation rather than elections/deliberation.

items.h: My Life My Say launch new v.16 campaign
items.b: My Life My Say has launched its national v.16 Campaign with high-profile events in London and Manchester. Hundreds of young people attended, with speakers including Minister Rushanara Ali, Sarah Olney MP, the Mayor of Greater Manchester Andy Burnham, and campaign ambassador Sharon Gaffka. Backed by organisations such as UK Youth Parliament, NUS, and the Electoral Reform Society, v.16 brings together young people, policymakers, and sector leaders to build trust and drive meaningful democratic reform. The campaign aims to form a cross-sector coalition to secure votes at 16 in all UK elections.
items.why: This matters democratically because the campaign seeks to extend the franchise to 16- and 17-year-olds, directly affecting who can exercise the vote.

items.h: David Blunkett argues Govt must strengthen citizenship teaching alongside Votes at 16
items.b: Association for Citizenship Teaching Honorary President Lord Blunkett warns of the perils of not strengthening Citizenship as a national curriculum subject , as lowering the voting age comes into effect.
items.why: This matters democratically because citizenship education builds the civic knowledge and capacity needed for young people to participate meaningfully once the franchise is lowered.
items.note: Sits at the border of votes-at-16 (elections) and civic education (participation); classified by its focus on capacity-building rather than the franchise mechanism itself.
links: warns of the perils of not strengthening Citizenship as a national curriculum subject

items.h: How can young people’s democratic needs be better met? Asks new PYL report
items.b: The Partnership for Young London report, produced in partnership with Royal Holloway University of London, developed by Dr Kaat Smets, Prof. James Sloam and Aine Bennett, offers policy recommendations and an analysis of the ‘polycrisis’ of young political participation in the UK. Read the report now .
items.why: This matters democratically because it analyses the barriers to young people's political participation, bearing on the practical conditions for equal civic engagement.

items.h: Prototyping Hope: Lessons from the REWIRE civil society incubator
items.b: Unhack Democracy & Hope-Based Communications have been partnering to run Rewire Your Mind, Rewire Your Country — a new incubator focused on fundamentally ‘rewiring’ how activists think, feel and act , from reaction to creation, drawing on lessons and experiences across 15 civil society leaders draw from across Hungary, Poland, Bulgaria and Ukraine.
items.note: International civil-society training programme with no evident bearing on UK democracy, and framed as organisational activity rather than a democratic mechanism.
links: Rewire Your Mind, Rewire Your Country — a new incubator focused on fundamentally ‘rewiring’ how activists think, feel and act

items.b: Planning, debating, prototyping — Photo credit: Unhack Democracy
items.note: A photo caption, not substantive content.

items.h: Our House feature in new podcast by Accidental Gods
items.b: Legislative Theatre practitioner Katy Rubin and Oli Whittington of Our House teamed up to unpack the People’s Charter for People Power on the Accidental Gods podcast — Listen now .
items.note: Promotional podcast listing about an organisation's existing work, not a reported democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: July marked Disability Pride Month
items.b: The Greater London Authority are celebrating Disability Pride this month and have released a range of resources for organisations to share and help promote among their supporters and audiences, find out more here .
links: The Greater London Authority are celebrating Disability Pride this month

items.h: More in Common publish new segmentation of British voters and discuss their attitudes to democracy
items.b: A mammoth new report, Shattered Britain , from More in Common has just been published, segmenting UK voters in seven categories based not on how they vote, but based on their values and outlooks on life. Amongst much else, the report looks at what these seven groups think about the functionality of British democracy, their trust in the media, their faith in experts, their likelihood to engage with conspiracy theories, and their overall perception of politics and politicians. The picture they paint is bleak — but essential for campaigners to be aware of.
items.why: it provides new evidence on public trust, perceptions of democracy and engagement with political information that shapes the conditions for civic participation.
items.note: Report spans trust in media and faith in experts but is filed under participation as it centres on public attitudes to democracy itself.

items.h: I Have A Voice launching new Campaigns Committee
items.b: The new Campaign Committee at I Have A Voice will work to support their youth led Politics For All campaign, assisting their youth ambassadors to build the campaign and run events that bring together young people and key decision makers. That’s not at all, their flagship Mentoring Scheme pairs up young people who are considering careers in the world of politics and campaigning with professionals in the sector.
items.why: a new campaigns committee and mentoring scheme create fresh avenues for young people to engage directly with political decision makers.

items.h: New research exploring democracy in the English voluntary sector
items.b: Daniel Haslam at the Open University is starting a new research project ‘Open Societal Challenges’ looking into the actual and perceived roles of voluntary sector organisations (VSOs) in relation to democracy and the democratic deficit. If you are interested in this area and would like to discuss the research in more detail, contact Daniel .
items.note: Announcement of an academic research project without a concrete change to participation mechanisms.

items.h: Involve holds UK’s first Citizens’ Assembly on neighbourhood policing
items.b: In 2024 Involve facilitated a six month project to bring local voices into the debate around how communities are policed. The first of its kind, the project created a Citizens’ Assembly with 50 local residents of Walthamstow to discuss what the future of policing should look like in the area. The final report has just been published — check it out now .
items.why: a citizens' assembly is a deliberative decision-making mechanism through which residents directly shape local policy on policing.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are filed under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: European Cultural Foundation launches new Community Impact Map
items.b: The European Cultural Foundation has created an interactive Community Impact Map that tracks a whole host of grassroots projects across Europe that are connecting people and improving democratic ties. Check out the map to see how over 30 countries are changing from the bottom up.
items.why: the new interactive map creates a resource that helps track and connect grassroots democratic organising across communities.

items.h: Humanity Project to organise popular assemblies in 20 neighbourhoods over the coming years
items.b: RECLAIM officially closed at the end of May — but their legacy lives on. Humanity Project , a national project hosted by Community Organisers , is building on their work of grassroots organising to create ‘Assembly Culture’ — a project over the next two years working in 20 neighbourhoods with local organisations to create a host of bottom up Popular Assemblies to change how decisions are taken at a local level.
items.why: popular assemblies are a deliberative mechanism intended to change how binding local decisions are taken in neighbourhoods.
items.note: Treated as decision-making machinery like citizens' assemblies rather than general civic participation.

items.h: Oxford Democracy Network hosts academic programme on the idea of the ‘people’
items.b: Sumeyye Kocaman, DPhil researcher and founder of the Oxford Democracy Network, reports back on their series of events and discussions around the concept of ‘the people’ . The next portion of their programme will be virtual, held bi-weekly on Thursday afternoons 14:00–16:30 London time from September 4th to April 16th. Their next programme will focus on ‘the elite — get in touch to find out more .
items.note: An academic seminar series on democratic theory, not a mechanism affecting democratic practice.
links: reports back on their series of events and discussions around the concept of ‘the people’
get in touch to find out more

items.h: British politics has entered a new era of polarisation, says Stan Greenberg
items.b: Stan Greenberg — once advisor to Bill Clinton, Nelson Mandela and Tony Blair — has conducted new polling on the state of polarisation in British politics. He finds that there has been a ‘ tectonic shift ’ in how voters perceive political parties. Voters are now solidly split along a liberal and leftist block, and a conservative, nationalist bloc — with voters showing almost no willingness to vote for the opposing bloc.
items.why: deep partisan polarisation into rigid blocs undermines societal cohesion and the fluidity of political competition needed for healthy democratic contestation
items.note: Polarisation framed as bloc-hardening maps to societal cohesion under participation rather than a specific electoral mechanism.

items.h: Democracy: Differently — a new podcast on democracy
items.b: Back for their third episode , podcast host Professor Keith is joined by Prof. Tom Hale (Blavatnik School of Government, University of Oxford), to discuss why democracy struggles with long term challenges like climate change, and what we can do about it. Listen now .

items.h: How to Save Democracy — new podcast out now!
items.b: Jon Alexander from the New Citizen Project and Omezzine Khelifa , an activist in the Tunisian Revolution and subsequently a politician in the country, have launched a new podcast exploring how we can rescue democracy from backsliding and abuse. The first four pilot episodes are out now. To get funding for a full first series they need to demonstrate appetite — so head over, have a listen and make sure to share it around!
items.note: Podcast launch is media content/promotion rather than a new participation tool or mechanism.

items.h: Senedd approves new regulations to support Disabled People standing for office
items.b: Last week, the Welsh Elections Financial Assistance Scheme (Disabled Candidates) Regulations 2025 were approved. These regulations are designed to remove financial barriers that prevent disabled individuals from standing for elected office by covering essential costs such as accessible transport, specialist equipment, and personal support.
items.why: removing financial barriers to standing for office widens who can actually seek elected positions, affecting the representativeness of elected institutions
links: Welsh Elections Financial Assistance Scheme (Disabled Candidates) Regulations 2025

items.b: The Talking Shop in sunny Cwmbran — Photo credit: The Talking Shop

items.h: The Talking Shop On Tour hits the road
items.b: Yvonne Murphy and The Talking Shop team are touring South Wales this week, packing up the kettle, the sofa, the tea trolley and bringing creative conversations to communities. You can catch them in Newport today and Merthyr Tydfil tomorrow.
items.why: a touring community conversation initiative creates new informal opportunities for people to engage in civic dialogue and public life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it creates a new means of community engagement, though the description is thin.

items.h: LGA Debate Not Hate Survey 2025
items.b: The Local Government Association , which represents councils and councillors in England and Wales, has published a new Local Government Association survey of councillors , which has found that 52 per cent report that they have had untrue or misleading information about their political or personal conduct publicly published, with respondents warning of the ‘dangers to democracy’. The report shows persistently high rates of reported abuse and intimidation, with seven in 10 councillors reporting experiencing these issues in the last 12 months and feeling personally at risk while fulfilling their …
items.why: widespread abuse, intimidation and disinformation targeting councillors threatens their personal security and can deter people from standing for or continuing in elected local office
items.note: Personal security of elected officials is the core mechanism, with knock-on effects for willingness to stand noted as secondary.

items.h: Civic Initiative publish new research on the Northern Ireland Citizens’ Forum on Housing
items.b: The research blog by Civic Initiative looks at the use of citizens assemblies in Northern Ireland and whether they could be key to unlocking NI’s potential. Find out more and read the research by Queen’s University Belfast here .
items.why: citizens' assemblies are a deliberative decision-making mechanism that channels public input into binding or influential collective decisions
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Climate Emergency UK launch local council climate actions scorecards
items.b: Climate Emergency UK and mySociety have launched their 2025 Council Climate Scorecards showing the progress all local councils are making around their climate goals. And as this is the second edition of Scorecards, the data allows users to compare their local councillors score to last year. They are also fundraising for the next iteration — please consider donating or sharing the crowdfunding link to your networks . Reform UK recently announced their councils intend to un-declare a climate emergency .
items.why: the scorecards give citizens a tool to compare and hold their local councillors accountable for climate commitments, strengthening local democratic scrutiny.
items.note: Treated as a civic capacity-building tool rather than a story about council structure or powers.
links: please consider donating or sharing the crowdfunding link to your networks
Reform UK recently announced their councils intend to un-declare a climate emergency

items.h: Taxpayer-funded restaurants to make a return
items.b: WW2 style state-sponsored restaurants where deprived families can eat for £3 are making a return . Back during the Second World War, British Restaurants were communal kitchens providing good quality food at low cost as part of an effort at boosting morale and guaranteeing a nourishing diet for all, regardless of class. Two pilot eateries are opening in Dundee and Nottingham, in a bid to provide nutritious meals and space for communities in deprived areas.
links: WW2 style state-sponsored restaurants where deprived families can eat for £3 are making a return

items.h: Campaigners hail major win as First-Past-the-Post to be scrapped for specific elections
items.b: The Government has set out plans in its English Devolution & Community Empowerment Bill to abolish the First Past the Post voting system for mayoral and police & crime commissioner elections. The Electoral Reform Society said the move ‘is a big step in the right direction for improving confidence in our politics’, whilst Labour for a New Democracy said this should be taken as an important sign that the Labour government recognises that First-Past-The-Post is not fit for purpose as an electoral system.
items.why: changing the voting system for mayoral and PCC elections directly affects how votes translate into representative power.
links: Labour for a New Democracy said

items.h: mySociety consider election reform changes
items.b: Alex Parsons at mySociety , who mostly focus their contribution on the democracy between elections, focuses on evaluating the government’s new election strategy in a new blog post .
items.why: the commentary evaluates government proposals to reform election administration and strategy, which shapes how elections are run.

items.h: Demos report calls for new relationship between citizen and state
items.b: A new report — Upgrading Democracy: A new deal to repair the broken relationship between citizen and state — suggests a democratic crisis in Britain and how a new relationship between citizen and state could help solve it. Alongside the ideas in the report, Demos will be working with partners over the coming year to design practical ways to achieve this change.
items.why: the report addresses citizens' sense of voice and efficacy in their relationship with the state, a condition for meaningful participation.
links: Upgrading Democracy: A new deal to repair the broken relationship between citizen and state

items.h: Open Letter calls on UK Government to shift power to local people
items.b: We’re Right Here is coordinating an open letter to the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister calling for a shift in how power is shared. The letter calls for genuine decision-making power to be placed in the hands of local people — not just councils or mayors, but the grassroots organisations, volunteers, and community leaders who know their areas best. Sign it here .
items.why: the campaign seeks to expand the practical ability of grassroots organisations and community members to take part in decision-making.
items.note: Framed around grassroots and community capacity rather than formal local government structure, so classed as participation not elections.

items.h: IPSA to invite members of the public to take part in Citizens’ Forum
items.b: The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (IPSA) has announced that it will be delivering letters to randomly selected households inviting members of the public to take part in a new Citizens’ Forum. In collaboration with the Sortition Foundation and the New Citizen Project , IPSA aims to use this forum to explore public views on how MPs should be paid and how their parliamentary responsibilities should be funded. This deliberate shift towards a more participatory process also seeks to engage people from diverse backgrounds in meaningful conversations about the role and significance of…
items.why: a new deliberative citizens' forum is being created to inform decisions on how MPs are paid and funded, a form of direct democratic input into institutional decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: Compassion in Politics calls for PMQs to be scrapped
items.b: Compassion in Politics has strongly criticised what they say was the ‘calculated humiliation’ of a visibly upset Rachel Reeves earlier this month, as the Leader of the Opposition taunted her saying she was ‘toast’. The campaign group says this behaviour raises fundamental questions about ‘how we do politics’, and they have written to the Speaker of the House calling for PMQs to be scrapped altogether. The organisation says PMQs brings politics into disrepute and has no place in a modern, functioning democracy.
items.why: the call concerns whether PMQs functions as a meaningful mechanism of parliamentary scrutiny and accountability of the executive.

items.h: New polling shows strength of public support for House of Lords reform
items.b: New YouGov polling for the UCL Constitution Unit shows overwhelming support for the government to go further in reforming the House of Lords. They found that 8 in 10 members of the public (79%) want restrictions to make sure the House of Lords doesn’t get any larger, 7 in 10 (71%) said the government should restrict the size of the upper chamber to no bigger than the House of Commons, whilst 6 in 10 supported removing hereditary peers altogether.
items.why: reforming the composition and size of the House of Lords affects how Parliament checks and scrutinises the executive.
items.note: House of Lords reform concerns legislative structure/accountability rather than elected representativeness, so filed under government & accountability.
links: polling for the UCL Constitution Unit

items.h: European Democracy Festival, more details released
items.b: Perry Walker at Talk Shop has announced more details of their prototype European Democracy Festival, coming this autumn. The Festival will see audiences working on a version of the Win Win Workout deliberative tool developed by Talk Shop, focused on two topics, European strategic autonomy and ultra processed food. Get in touch to find out more .
items.note: Event listing for a deliberative-democracy festival with limited UK relevance, not a substantive democracy story.
links: Get in touch to find out more

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch toolkit for collaborative journalism
items.b: Working with academics and grassroots media outlets, the Public Interest News Foundation has developed and launched the Co-Creational News Media Toolkit . The toolkit challenges the top down nature of traditional journalism and outlines a co-creational approach rooted in four core principles: participation, truth-seeking, accountability and care. The new framework has the potential to dramatically change the local media ecosystem by putting communities at the heart of local journalism.
items.why: a new toolkit for collaborative, community-rooted journalism changes how local news is produced and who can shape the public information environment.

items.h: Suffrago hire dozens of Local Democracy Reporters in bid to transform the UK media landscape
items.b: With more than 30 Local Democracy Reporters working for Suffrago across the UK in key constituencies, they are aiming to expand to all 650 constituencies and in so doing transform the information available on local political activity to the average British citizen. Suffrago CEO Andrew Gray asks ‘If any fellow Democracy Network member has a message that they may want to get out, please contact Andrew Gray at andrew.gray@suffrago.org ’.
items.why: expanding local democracy reporting increases the public's access to information about local political decision-making.

items.h: Feeling the chill? Harley Wishart investigates the growing chilling effect on protest rights
items.b: Now a PhD researcher at the University of Brighton, former Democracy Network staffer Harley Wishart is exploring how anti-protest laws are impacting on freedom of expression and assembly — especially for those most at risk of criminalisation. Through their new Substack they’ll be sharing insights on protest, repression and resistance . The work is urgent, Harley says — just six months ago she hosted the panel discussion Feeling the Chill? at The Democracy Network Summit, opinions shared within it have since been criminalised. Follow for their latest insights .
items.why: anti-protest laws and their chilling effect on assembly and expression directly restrict people's freedom to organise and dissent from public power.
items.note: Protest policing/legal restriction falls under rights and freedoms rather than participation willingness.
links: Through their new Substack they’ll be sharing insights on protest, repression and resistance

items.h: RUSI highlight central role of AI in Russian influencing operations
items.b: Generative AI is no longer a concern of the future, the Royal United Services Institute remarks, and is now an active component of Russian-aligned influence operations. The report suggests increasing professionalism of the information war by Russia, emphasising AI as a force multiplier for grassroots cyber operations aimed at overwhelming and destabilising Western digital infrastructure and democratic cultures — Read the report now .
items.why: AI-enabled foreign influence operations threaten the integrity of the information environment citizens rely on to form political judgements.

items.h: Global civil society groups call on UN to establish Special Rapporteur on Democracy
items.b: Although the UN monitors human rights through different rapporteurs, campaigners have pointed out that no specific rapporteur exists to monitor democratic freedoms. 175 civil society organisations and more than 500 activists are now calling on the UN to set up a Special Rapporteur on Democracy which would investigate electoral manipulation, judicial capture and civic space restrictions.
items.why: a UN Special Rapporteur on Democracy would create an international mechanism to scrutinise electoral manipulation, judicial capture and civic space restrictions that affect democratic accountability worldwide.
items.note: International advocacy story with only indirect UK bearing, spanning multiple beats.

items.h: TI-UK to discuss lobbying transparency in Scotland, 3rd Sept
items.b: Join Juliet Swann to discuss lobbying transparency, Scotland’s lobbying register and to find out more about Transparency International UK’s (TI-UK) Open Access tool — which uses AI to enable easier interrogation and comparison of lobbying data at Holyrood and Westminster by topic. Register for the event here .
items.why: greater transparency and tools to interrogate lobbying data at Holyrood and Westminster help hold decision-makers accountable for undue influence.
items.note: Framed as an event but centres on a new accountability tool, so treated as capacity-building rather than mere logistics.

items.h: Donations and Democracy launch UK briefing on UK-US firms backing groups undermining democracy
items.b: Donations and Democracy , a US based group, is an independent non-partisan initiative run by volunteer international lawyers, associated with and advised by the International Advisory Network . They recently published a new report focusing on the connections between UK headquartered firms whose US subsidiaries or member firms have either donated to political actors in the US who voted against certifying the 2020 US election result or PACs which have donated to such campaigns. British firms include PWC, Deloitte, EY, Grant Thornton, GSK, AstraZeneca, BAE Systems, Rolls-Royce Holdings, BP, Briti…
items.note: The report concerns UK-headquartered firms' links to US election-certification opponents, not the exercise of UK public power.

items.h: Far-right mobilisations increase, NetPol release new resources for anti-fascists
items.b: With a rise in far-right mobilisations and violence in recent months, with large fascist mobilisations organised by neo-Nazi groups in Epping and Canary Wharf alarming local communities — Network for Police Monitoring have released new practical advice for those attending anti-fascist protests , focused on keeping your identity secure and first aid.
items.why: it addresses how people can safely exercise protest and assembly rights amid state surveillance and far-right intimidation.
items.note: Protest safety resource sits under rights given its surveillance/security focus rather than pure willingness-to-participate framing.
links: Network for Police Monitoring have released new practical advice for those attending anti-fascist protests

items.h: Police arrest man holding Private Eye cartoon under terrorism charges
items.b: Jon Farley held a placard of a Private Eye cartoon, highlighting what Ian Hislop called ‘hypocrisies of government approach to any sort of action in Gaza’ , and was arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 at a Leeds pro-Palestine demonstration. Farley was bailed and told not to attend any ‘Palestine Action rallies’ and was then later contacted by a counter-terrorism officer who then told him he would face no further action. Hislop (who has not faced arrest for the cartoon) called the arrest ‘mind boggling’ and said the cartoon was ‘quite blatantly an example of freedom of speech on the subject o…
items.why: it shows the state using anti-terrorism powers against an individual's peaceful expression of political dissent, bearing on freedom of speech and protest.
links: Ian Hislop called ‘hypocrisies of government approach to any sort of action in Gaza’

items.b: The offending cartoon — Photo credit: Steve Johnston for the Guardian

items.h: Government ban on public servants speaking at public events is damaging, says Institute for Government
items.b: A new edict from No10 prohibits senior health officials, military leaders and civil servants from speaking openly in public or taking part in any public question and answer sessions. The Director of the Institute for Government , Hannah White, criticised the move saying it comprises one of the most important principles of public life — openness.
items.why: restricting public servants from speaking openly undermines transparency and public accountability of government institutions.

items.h: Labour hasn’t done enough to restore trust since taking office, says Full Fact
items.b: Despite promising to clean up politics and restore faith in the political system, Full Fact says the government has done little to achieve these goals within its first year. Amongst the shortcomings they cite; a failure to establish an Ethics and Integrity Commission, a weak Ministerial Code which is yet to become statutory, and little action to address the crisis of misinformation in Britain . With recent polling pointing to a dire crisis of trust in the political system, more needs to be done, says Full Fact — and fast.
items.why: it assesses whether government has strengthened standards, ethics oversight and transparency mechanisms meant to hold power accountable.
items.note: Misinformation reference is secondary to the core accountability critique.

items.h: Denmark passes new legislation to combat deepfakes
items.b: Denmark made headlines recently following the passing of new legislation which aims to tackle the creation and spread of ‘deepfakes’. The first law of its kind in Europe, it does so by giving people copyright to their own features, thereby strengthening protections against digital imitations of people’s identities.
items.why: new legal protections against deepfakes shape the integrity of the public information environment relevant to political debate.
items.note: Comparative international evidence relevant to UK deepfake/disinformation policy debates.

The faculty welcomed several new members to its ranks including data governance expert Anouk Ruhaak , wargaming expert Alex Vince and chat expert John Evans .

items.h: Campaign Bootcamp
items.b: After nine years of working to better equip those most affected by injustice with the skills, confidence and community they needed to run powerful campaigns, Campaign Bootcamp closed shop in 2022. Campaign Bootcamp was founded in 2013, by a collection of campaigners who were concerned that a lot of high profile campaigning was being led by people who had little to no experience of injustice and inequality. Over 17 bootcamps, training and inspiring more than 1,000 people, they worked to disrupt the UK campaigning space — and have helped build the foundation for the change we see today.
items.note: Retrospective on a now-closed organisation's history is organisational news, not a mechanism change.

items.h: Is it possible to predict voting intention with brain waves?
items.b: Campaign Lab is hosting an event with Dr. Emmanuel Mahieux who will be discussing the insights of a study he did in San Antonio, Texas, in the weeks preceding the 2022 state Governor election. He’ll be discussing whether we can learn anything from electrical brain waves about voters’ political beliefs and if we can predict from this which way undecided voters might swing.

items.b: Hosted by Iona Lawrence and the team at Decelerator , the day conference is a place for those in civil society organisations at times of transition. Whether you’re in an organisation that’s winding down due to financial constraints, or you’re helping someone step away from their role, or you have the feeling ‘something is ending here, I don’t quite know what to do with that — how can I be useful’ — this is the place for you. Birmingham, 15th October, 10 til 4.30pm, sign up now .

items.h: Network for Police Monitoring tips for staying safe on anti-fascist demonstrations
items.b: As far-right rallies and activity proliferate across the UK in recent months, the Network for Police Monitoring have republished their resources for staying safe on anti-fascist protests — check it out now .
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns citizens' practical ability to exercise freedom of assembly and protest safely amid policing and far-right activity.
items.note: Classified under rights/civic space as the concern is safety and policing rather than willingness to demonstrate.

items.h: Democratic disillusionment key to uniting Reform’s voter coalition
items.b: New research from More in Common finds that Reform UK’s potential voter ceiling could be as high as 49% as they could turn out a significant number of non-voters. The report also finds that democratic disillusionment is key in uniting Reform’s voter coalition. Three quarters of Reform voters are dissatisfied with the state of democracy in Britain, and 59% believe the UK is not a genuine democracy at all.
items.why: This matters democratically because it reports on turnout dynamics and how disillusionment with democracy is shaping electoral behaviour and party support.
items.note: Turnout and non-voter behaviour are always filed under elections & decision making per the framework's standing rule.
links: New research from More in Common

items.h: Your Party launch mired in public infighting
items.b: Back in July, the new left wing party Your Party launched, garnering more than 800,000 signups in just a few weeks. Co-led by Zarah Sultana MP and former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn MP, the launch of the party has already spurred the self-organisation of hundreds of burgeoning local groups, and more than 20 large scale regional assemblies are being organised alongside a national conference with participants elected by sortition — developments that could bolster the salience of such methods. However, in a spectacular series of events, the party’s co-leaders engaged in a public spat, alienating …
items.why: This matters democratically because the party's formation, internal leadership conflict and use of sortition-based assemblies affect political competition and experiments in deliberative decision-making.
items.note: Sortition-based national conference and deliberative assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.

items.h: Zack Polanski wins 85% of Green Party leadership vote in landslide poll
items.b: Zack Polanski has won a landslide victory in the Green Party leadership contest, winning over 85% of membership votes in the vote . The dramatic vote signals a change from co-leadership back to a single leader again and a change in policy and communication styles by the party. The Green Party has benefited from a surge in membership in recent weeks, to around 75%, with an additional bounce attributed to the Your Party split between Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana.
items.why: This matters democratically because an internal party leadership election determines the governance and direction of a party that competes in elections.
links: winning over 85% of membership votes in the vote

items.h: Keseb launches the Keseb Democracy Champions’ Pocket Guide
items.b: The new guide by Keseb is a digital resource hub offering key trends, frameworks, and strategic recommendations — distill extensive resource into easy to read modules including ‘Cultivating Pro-democracy Civil Society Coalitions’, ‘Navigating and Countering Closing Civic Space’ and ‘Reimagining and Innovating for Inclusive Democracy’. Read the guide now .
items.why: This matters democratically because the new guide creates a resource to build the capacity of pro-democracy civil society coalitions and civic engagement strategies.

items.h: Demos’ Collaborative Democracy Network returns this autumn — want to join?
items.b: The Collaborative Democracy Network brings together politicians, campaigners, civil society and policy makers to discuss how best to put citizens at the heart of policy making. The group returned this autumn for an event on ‘reimagining the social contract’ which took place on September 18th. Sign up to the network to be part of this evolving conversation and get all the latest news and event info.
items.why: it creates an ongoing forum where citizens, civil society and policymakers shape how policy is made, expanding practical avenues for participation
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building network under the participation beat.

items.h: Open Rights Group to coalesce new NO2ID alliance

items.note: New coalition formation treated as civic-space organising against a surveillance policy.

The free workshops are designed for 15–18 year olds, equipping students with the knowledge, skills and confidence to take part in grassroots democratic action and understand how people power shapes change. Contact Naked Politics’ admin officer Bella Frimpong for more info.
items.why: new free workshops build young people's knowledge and confidence to take part in grassroots democratic action, creating new means of participation
links: Contact Naked Politics’ admin officer Bella Frimpong for more info.

items.h: Scottish Parliament publishes blueprint for deliberative democracy
items.b: The Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee has released a new report setting out a ‘Blueprint for Participation,’ recommending People’s Panels be embedded as a routine part of parliamentary scrutiny. The report highlights evidence that panels build trust, improve scrutiny and broaden citizen involvement, while recognising the need for proper resources and evaluation. If adopted, four panels will be run in the next session (2027–2030), with the Parliament committing to track impact and share learning across Scotland and beyond.
items.why: embedding citizen panels into parliamentary scrutiny expands the deliberative machinery through which collective decisions are shaped and legitimised.
items.note: Deliberative democracy processes are classed under elections_decision_making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: Citizen Participation and Public Petitions Committee

items.b: The new research by Research for Action in collaboration with the University of Sussex proposes a series of urgent recommendations for making council finances less opaque. items.why: opaque council finances undermine the transparency and scrutiny mechanisms citizens and auditors rely on to hold local government answerable for public money.
items.note: Financial transparency of councils treated as an accountability mechanism, with the Local Audit Office also touching local government structure.

items.why: deliberative engagement methods used to shape climate policy extend the machinery through which the public participates in binding collective decisions.

items.b: An end to divisive and set-piece debating traditions to ensure respect, inclusion and genuine accountability
items.why: ending divisive debating traditions in favour of genuine accountability concerns how effectively Parliament scrutinises government and includes its elected members.
items.note: Continuation of the Modernisation Committee submission story; same beat logic as the parent item.

items.h: APPG for fair elections publishes ‘ready to go’ blueprint on electoral reform
items.b: The APPG for Fair Elections has published a proposal for a National Commission on Electoral Reform to address the issues with First Past The Post. The published Terms of Reference suggest ways to independently review how Parliament is elected, promote a national conversation, and build consensus on a way forward. The initiative would also involve establishing a deliberative voters forum as one of the commission’s supporting bodies.
items.why: it proposes an independent review and deliberative process to reform how Parliament is elected, directly addressing the electoral system through which representatives are chosen.
items.note: Deliberative/electoral reform proposals fall under elections_decision_making per the moved boundary rule.
links: published a proposal for a National Commission on Electoral Reform

items.h: English Devolution Bill passes second reading bringing electoral reform a step closer
items.b: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill has passed its second reading by 365 to 164 votes. While the bill covers many areas, democracy campaigners have celebrated in particular that this will bring England a step closer to scrapping First Past The Post for Mayoral and Police Crime Commissioner elections — something which has been in place since 2022. The bill now enters committee stage.
items.why: the bill's progress moves England closer to changing the electoral system used for mayoral and PCC elections, altering how those officials are chosen.
links: English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill

items.h: First ‘House of the People’ meets to set out citizen-led ‘People’s Charter’
items.b: Assemble recently organised the first ‘House of the People’ — a group of 100 people, selected via sortition, who gathered in London to deliberate and debate. The group created the ‘People’s Charter’ setting out a range of policy proposals for the government to adopt including: a wealth tax, strengthening anti-corruption laws, an immediate arms embargo on countries breaking international law, and the long-term decommodification of housing.
items.why: a sortition-based citizens' assembly is a form of deliberative decision-making machinery that produces policy input outside conventional elections.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections_decision_making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: organised the first ‘House of the People’

items.h: New report explores how proportional representation could quell the rise of the populist right
items.b: Compass has released a new report — The Temper Trap: How Proportional Representation Tames the Populist-Right , exploring how PR could moderate Reform UK’s radical agenda. Drawing on international examples from Finland, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands, the report shows how PR can force populist-right parties into coalition governments which helps to water down their more extreme positions.
items.why: the report examines how electoral system design (proportional representation) shapes political competition and the behaviour of parties within government.
links: The Temper Trap: How Proportional Representation Tames the Populist-Right

items.h: Poll shows 16 and 17 year olds support lowering the voting age — but many feel unprepared
items.b: New research from More in Common shows the majority of 16–17 year olds (59%) support lowering the voting age — but there are still big splits amongst this demographic on whether they feel informed enough to vote. Just under half of this age group (46%) said they felt informed enough to vote in an election. Meanwhile, the exact same percentage said they do not feel informed enough. In focus groups, participants called for stronger political education in the school curriculum to prepare young people for the change in legislation.
items.why: the poll concerns extending suffrage to 16-17 year olds, directly bearing on who has the right to vote.

items.h: New report maps the spread of privatisation and calls for greater democratic ownership within UK economy
items.b: Commonwealth has published an expose on the privatisation of key UK industries , suggesting as much as £200bn has been paid to shareholders since they were privatised. The report also states that individual households have been paying a ‘privatisation premium’ of £250 since 2010 alone. The authors call for a radical overhaul of the system to ensure the ‘basics of life are democratic, accountable and run for people rather than profit’.
items.note: This is primarily an economic policy critique of privatisation rather than a story about a specific democratic mechanism or participation capacity.
links: expose on the privatisation of key UK industries

items.h: Reform UK ban DeSmog and New World journalists from party conference
items.b: In a move described as coming straight out of ‘the authoritarian playbook’, Reform UK has come under fire for refusing DeSmog and New World journalists entry to their party conference. Reporters Without Borders said it was ‘shocking to see’ this kind of selective press entry, with the party offering no reasoning behind why the outlets were barred. The move comes shortly after Reform UK’s leader of Nottinghamshire Country Council banned his councillors from speaking to the Nottinghamshire Post following critical coverage of the party in the local newspaper.
items.why: selectively barring journalists from party events restricts press access to political actors, undermining the public information environment needed for scrutiny.
links: refusing DeSmog and New World journalists entry

items.h: Labour Party bans journalists from Labour Party conference, NUJ responds
items.b: Guardian journalist Owen Jones was banned from Labour Party conference this week , reportedly due to his questioning Labour MPs over ‘complicity in genocide’. Similarly Novara Media’s Rivkah Brown also had her press pass removed, whilst journalists from Declassified UK were also denied entry. National Union of Journalists General Secretary Laura Davison responded .
items.why: banning journalists from a major party conference over critical coverage restricts press scrutiny of a political party, affecting the public's access to plural political information.
links: Owen Jones was banned from Labour Party conference this week

items.h: Check out Journalism Support Exchange
items.b: Journalism Support Exchange is a new tool for US based journalists and organisations, thanks Joe Mitchell for sharing this with us.
items.note: US-based tool with no bearing on UK democracy; also organisational sharing news.

items.h: Reform Party bans reporters from talking to council leader
items.b: The Nottingham Post and its online site Nottinghamshire Live have been barred from speaking to Nottinghamshire Council’s Reform council leader Mick Barton . The ban apparently breaches the council’s own codes of conduct. The ban has become global news, even mentioned in the US Congress. Nottinghamshire county council declined to comment, but the Guardian covered the story .
items.why: a council leader unilaterally blocking specific journalists undermines the press's capacity to inform citizens and scrutinise local government decisions.
items.note: Treated primarily as a press-freedom/information-environment story since the ban targets journalists' access, with accountability as a secondary dimension.
links: been barred from speaking to Nottinghamshire Council’s Reform council leader Mick Barton

items.h: How can independent newsrooms unlock charitable status and boost their funding?
items.b: The Charitable Journalism Project has published a new handbook breaking down everything indie newsrooms need to know about unlocking charitable status in the UK. For many local, public-interest publishers, charitable status could unlock vital new funding streams, from grants to donations and tax relief.
items.why: new routes to sustainable funding for independent local journalism help preserve the public-interest reporting citizens rely on to understand and scrutinise public affairs.
items.note: Sector capacity-building applied specifically to journalism sustainability, so filed under the information beat rather than participation.

items.h: X (formerly Twitter) created a staggering amplification of hate during 2024 far-right riots
items.b: False claims on X spread rapidly after the murders in Southport, contributing to violent racist riots across the UK says new Amnesty International research. Amnesty’s analysis links X’s design and policy choices to the amplification of content which incited violence against Muslims and migrants. ‘One year on, even with the arrival of the Online Safety Act, it appears nothing has changed’ — Sacha Deshmukh, Amnesty International UK Chief Executive at Amnesty International UK.
items.why: a platform's design and moderation choices amplifying disinformation and incitement distort the information environment citizens depend on for political judgement.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation launch toolkit for collaborative journalism
items.b: Working with academics and grassroots media outlets, the Public Interest News Foundation has developed and launched the Co-Creational News Media Toolkit . The toolkit challenges the top down nature of traditional journalism and outlines a co-creational approach rooted in four core principles: participation, truth-seeking, accountability and care. The new framework has the potential to dramatically change the local media ecosystem by putting communities at the heart of local journalism.
items.why: a new toolkit changing how local journalism is produced affects the plurality and community accountability of the local media ecosystem underpinning informed citizenship.
items.note: Journalism-focused capacity building, so primarily information beat with a participation secondary given its community co-creation framing.

items.h: Suffrago hire dozens of Local Democracy Reporters in bid to transform the UK media landscape
items.b: With more than 30 Local Democracy Reporters working for Suffrago across the UK in key constituencies, they are aiming to expand to all 650 constituencies and in so doing transform the information available on local political activity to the average British citizen. Suffrago CEO Andrew Gray asks ‘If any fellow Democracy Network member has a message that they may want to get out, please contact Andrew Gray at andrew.gray@suffrago.org ’.
items.why: expanding local democracy reporting increases the information available to citizens about local political decision-making, a precondition for holding local power to account.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation becomes sponsor of APPG for media
items.b: Public Interest News Foundation is now a sponsor of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on media. This means they will join cross party debates on the future of the media sector, enabling them to put independent, local public interest news at the heart of these conversations.
items.note: Organisational news about a group's own institutional affiliations, not a change in democratic mechanism.

items.h: New fund announced to support young investigative journalists in Wales
items.b: Award-winning investigative journalist, Will Hayward, has launched a £10,000 fund to support budding investigative journalists in Wales. Successful applicants will receive between £150 and £500 to support their work which must focus on one of the following topics: climate change and biodiversity loss, poverty, the rise of the far right and/or political extremism, misinformation/disinformation.
items.why: funding investigative journalism on issues like extremism and disinformation sustains the public-interest reporting that underpins informed democratic debate.

items.b: A demonstrator is read his rights by police at a Palestine Action protest, outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool (Photo Credit: PA Wire/PA Images)
items.why: it depicts police enforcement action against a protester, engaging the legal boundaries of freedom of assembly and state coercion.
items.note: Protest policing is classified under rights and civic space per the boundary rule on legal restriction and coercion.

items.h: Pressure grows on government over Palestine Action proscription
items.b: More than a thousand people have now been arrested as part of protests against the proscription of Palestine Action, with more than 867 arrested in a single day last month in London. More than 90 people were arrested outside the Labour Party conference this week alone . Defend Our Juries say that their protests will significantly escalate on 4th October . Metropolitan Police have urged the government to cancel the proscription of Palestine Action after the terrorist attack in Manchester this week.
items.why: mass arrests and police pressure over a proscription decision directly engage the legal limits on freedom of assembly and protest.
items.note: Focus is on policing and state coercion of protest, not willingness to participate, so it sits in rights rather than participation.
links: More than 90 people were arrested outside the Labour Party conference this week alone
Defend Our Juries say that their protests will significantly escalate on 4th October
urged the government to cancel the proscription of Palestine Action

items.h: Equality and Human Rights Commission warns government over human rights compliance
items.b: The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has sent a formal letter to the Home Secretary expressing deep concern that proposed immigration and policing policies risk breaching statutory human rights obligations. The EHRC urges immediate revisions to ensure adequate safeguards, transparency, and compliance with the Equality Act, especially for protected groups, and to facilitate the legal right to protest. The EHRC also raised concerns about police engagement with individuals not linked to any proscribed organisation, such as those simply holding Palestinian flags.
items.why: an independent statutory body is warning that government policy may breach protections for protest rights and equality obligations.
items.note: EHRC acting as an accountability regulator overlaps with government_accountability, but the substantive concern is protest and equality rights.

items.h: Leaked documents suggest Boris Johnson may have used public funds to land private deals
items.b: Documents leaked from Johnson’s private office to Distributed Denial of Secrets — a non-profit that publishes leaked or hacked information — have provoked concern that the ex-Prime Minister used public money to secure private business deals since leaving office. Johnson has received £182,000 through the public duty costs allowance (PDCA) since 2022, which exists to support ex-PMs with public duties. Unlock Democracy is now calling for a full investigation and an assurance that rules and standards will, in the future, be ‘Boris-proofed’.
items.why: it raises questions of whether a former official misused public funds for private gain, engaging standards in public life and conflicts of interest.

items.h: Defend Our Juries launch crowdfunder to defend the rights of jurors
items.b: Defend Our Juries are campaigning to protect and raise awareness of the crucial right of juries to acquit based on conscience, which is currently being severely challenged and undermined, they argue. Find out more information and check out their fundraiser .
items.why: jury nullification is a due process safeguard within the justice system, and a campaign to protect it concerns access to fair adjudication.

items.h: Shooting of Charlie Kirk draws strong condemnation from democracy campaigners
items.b: The killing of Charlie Kirk became another dark day in the history of US political violence. The Index on Censorship called it ‘horrifying’ , reiterating the need to meet difficult view points with ‘words, not bullets.’ The Journal on Democracy has made publically available an article published in October 2024 by Rachel Kleinfeld and Nicole Bibbins Sedaca — How to Prevent Political Violence — which highlights the steps leaders and governments can take to prevent future aggression.
items.why: political violence undermines the personal security and safety needed for open democratic contestation, and the response offers comparative lessons for the UK.
items.note: US-based event included as comparative evidence on political violence relevant to UK democracy debates.
links: The Index on Censorship called it ‘horrifying’

items.b: UKIP leader Nick Tenconi giving a Nazi salute (Photo credit: The London Economic)
items.why: it illustrates a controversy over whether a registered political party should be proscribed, engaging freedom to form and compete as political parties.
items.note: Caption tied to the accompanying proscription story.

items.h: Calls to proscribe UKIP following leader’s Nazi salute last month
items.b: UKIP leader Nick Tenconi and his supporters were filmed making Nazi salutes last month in Bournemouth, leading to calls for the party to be proscribed as a far-right group . Tenconi later responded that there was ‘nothing Nazi-esque about the gesture’ .
items.why: calls to ban a registered political party engage the freedom to form parties and compete for office.
items.note: Party proscription falls under elections and political competition rather than rights of civic organisations.
links: leading to calls for the party to be proscribed as a far-right group

items.h: UK migrants rights organisations encouraged to remove identifiable information
items.b: Migrants rights organisations in the UK are being advised to secure their personally identifiable information from websites, blogs and social media in a general effort to limit or prevent any potential attacks or doxxing from far-right groups. This comes after a steadily increasing number of charities and those who work with them have been attacked directly both online and in some cases in print media.
items.why: it concerns the operating space and safety of civic organisations facing coordinated attacks, which affects their ability to function as part of civil society.

items.h: New tool reveals transparency loopholes around APPG funding
items.b: The Byline Times reports that companies are using funding loopholes to conceal how much money they are funnelling into APPGs. Under current rules, it is impossible to know how much a company is giving to an APPG when they are funding the secretariat, rather than the APPG directly. Byline Times reports that companies such as Lockheed Martin and News UK may be using this loophole to disguise the amount of money they are actually funnelling into specific APPGs. Relatedly, mySociety have been doing a lot of their own work lately analysing APPG memberships .
items.why: it exposes a loophole allowing undisclosed corporate funding to influence parliamentary groups, undermining transparency and accountability mechanisms around lobbying.
links: mySociety have been doing a lot of their own work lately analysing APPG memberships

items.h: Involve highlights UK democracy backsliding
items.b: Involve has warned that the UK’s democracy is in decline, pointing to shrinking civic space and new restrictions on protest. Citing recent arrests at peaceful demonstrations and international watchdogs downgrading the UK’s democratic status, the piece argues the country risks sliding towards authoritarianism. Involve calls for stronger participatory democracy and protection of free expression as essential to reversing this trend.
items.why: it warns of shrinking civic space and new restrictions on protest and assembly, which constrain citizens' ability to organise and dissent.
items.note: Report spans civic space and participation, but protest restriction and policing are the core cited evidence, placing it in rights/civic space.

items.h: Co-designing ‘Waves’ — Local Trust reflects on first steps behind the €1m AI tool project
items.b: For the last few months New Local has been working with democracy organisations and software developers to build ‘Waves’ — an AI tool designed to make it easier and cheaper to gather views and foster deliberation. In this reflective blog New Local discusses the challenges and progress they’ve made in creating what is set to be pioneering new technology for the sector — and what the next steps look like.
items.why: it creates new deliberative machinery intended to be used for gathering public views and fostering deliberation, which the framework treats as decision-making infrastructure.
items.note: Deliberation tools are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.
links: New Local discusses the challenges and progress

items.h: Newspeak House fellows produce range of civic tech tools
items.b: Newspeak House is the London College of Political Technology, a civic and political technology community space and a pioneering residential political technology college for a cohort of twenty students each year. This year students produced a range of projects as part of their final assessments, including Yung-Hsuan Wu’s Not A Stranger AI-powered immigration email drafter tool and Claddagh Niclochlainn’s National Procurement Policy Statement pipeline app .
items.note: This reads as showcasing a fellowship cohort's own projects rather than a launched tool changing public participation.
links: Not A Stranger AI-powered immigration email drafter tool
National Procurement Policy Statement pipeline app

items.b: This year’s incoming Newspeak House students at their orientation weekend (Photo Credit: Newspeak House)

items.h: State.com launches new iOS platform for citizens and MPs
items.b: State uses AI tech to break down the barriers between people and politics, giving everyone a faster, clearer way to be heard, they say. State allows citizens to make statements on issues they care about, and the platform amplifies their voice by connecting it with similar concerns across the UK which MPs then receive as organised insights, enabling them to respond at scale via the platform. Citizens can vote on upcoming legislation, while MPs can send polls directly to their constituents and everyone can see a live priority list of what issues matter most at any given moment, providing the inf…
items.why: it launches a new platform intended to give citizens a direct channel to communicate with and be heard by MPs, expanding the means available for civic participation.
items.note: Includes voting on legislation, which touches decision-making machinery, but primary framing is participatory engagement.

items.h: Nesta’s Zeitgeist tool being prepared for use in citizens assemblies
items.b: Lewis Westbury, a Senior Developer with the Centre for Collective Intelligence Design (CCID) at Nesta, who’s been working on their digital democracy platform Zeitgeist , says they have ambitions to roll out the tool in future citizens assemblies. Zeitgeist has been used in local deliberation on flooding, coastal erosion and water quality with Southend City Council and other areas.
items.why: it develops a digital deliberation tool intended for use in citizens' assemblies, which the framework anchors to decision-making machinery.
items.note: Citizens' assembly tooling is classified under elections & decision making per framework rule.

items.h: Political Studies Association to host January conference on digital democracy
items.b: The Political Studies Association’s Media and Politics Group & Technology, Information and Policy Group are to host Navigating Digital Democracy , a new conference in Bournemouth on 8–9th Jan exploring the intersection of various sectors in shaping democratic practices and governance. The conference will also host a remote-only video conference on the 7th January. Find out more information .
items.note: A conference announcement is event listing/sector logistics, not a change in democratic practice.
links: Political Studies Association’s Media and Politics Group & Technology, Information and Policy Group are to host Navigating Digital Democracy

items.h: Socialudo — Serious play for social change
items.b: Founders Professor Vikki McCall and Professor Alasdair Rutherford set up a new social enterprise to help diverse groups plan and think about how we future-proof society. Socialudo design, develop and deliver serious games to help organisations tackle hard problems. Their flagship game Hopetown sees players take the roles of policy maker, service provider, community group or property developer in a fictional town to better understand how different organisations, service providers and the public interact to improve the lives of the public. See their recent report on how the game fared in Southwa…
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: A serious game/social enterprise for general societal planning does not create a specific democratic participation mechanism.
links: See their recent report on how the game fared in Southwark

items.h: Gaza Project wins the Investigative Journalism For Europe Impact Award
items.b: Manisha Ganguly , Investigations Correspondent at The Guardian, and the team behind the Gaza Project have won the Investigative Journalism For Europe Impact Award (IJ4E). The judge remarked: for its methodological rigour under extreme constraints; its innovative use of satellite analysis and photogrammetry; its collaboration across borders and newsrooms; and its commitment to accountability when accountability is hardest, the IJ4EU jury recognises The Gaza Project with an Impact Award. The Investigative Journalism for Europe Impact Award strengthens the watchdog role of investigative journalis…
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: An award to a journalism project is organisational news, not a change affecting the information environment.
links: Investigative Journalism For Europe Impact Award
