items.h: Electoral Commission to launch pilot scheme on future of youth democratic education
items.b: The Electoral Commission is piloting a new scheme to support young people over the age of 16 to cast their vote . They will be rolling out a whole range of resources and initiatives to do this and are looking for educators, schools and colleges to get involved and bring the content to life. Sign up if you’d like to know more and get involved .
items.why: it creates new educational resources and initiatives aimed at increasing youth voter turnout and understanding of the electoral process.
items.note: Turnout-related engagement always falls under elections & decision making.
links: new scheme to support young people over the age of 16 to cast their vote
Sign up if you’d like to know more and get involved

items.h: Democracy Fund publish new report on voter registration in Black communities
items.b: The report, a partnership between Local Champions CIC and the UK Democracy Fund , looks at the lower voter registration rates among Black communities in the UK and their key learnings from working with Carib Eats , Skate Cabal and The Agency (Battersea Arts Centre) for how to improve democratic engagement among the Black community in the UK.
items.why: it addresses unequal voter registration rates among Black communities, a matter of electoral participation and access to the franchise.
items.note: Voter registration and turnout disparities are classified under elections & decision making per the turnout rule.

items.h: We’re Right Here launches new campaign film
items.b: We’re Right Here’s new film makes the case that the solution to ‘Broken Britain’ can be found in every neighbourhood across the country — within the ‘big hearts and deep knowledge’ of community organisers, groups of neighbours, and grassroots movements. They’re calling for a deeper form of devolution, pushing control downwards and outwards to communities, creating new community rights and powers — and putting the decisions that shape neighbourhoods and futures in the hands of ordinary people. Watch the film and read the story behind it here .
items.why: it campaigns for deeper devolution and new community powers over local decision-making, which concerns the structure of sub-national democratic decision-making.
items.note: Devolution and local control of decision-making falls under elections & decision making, not participation, per the boundary rule on local/regional government.

items.h: Unlock Democracy working on new ‘defensive constitution project’
items.b: Tom Brake, Director of Unlock Democracy , reports they are working on a new ‘defensive constitution project’ with the 99% Organisation , focused on requesting that the government acts to strengthen democratic guardrails. Stay tuned for more on this soon.
items.why: it concerns advocacy to strengthen constitutional checks and safeguards that constrain executive power.

items.h: Electoral Commission hiring first ever digital product owner role
items.b: In this groundbreaking new role as the Electoral Commission’s first ever digital product owner , the successful candidate will be able to develop their own team and pioneer new in-house delivery, running a product that serves millions of voters each year — they’ll also be in the Commission as the first 16 year olds get to vote, and think about automatic voter registration and its role in elections — this is a major new post. Apply now — deadline 2nd November.
items.note: Job advert; excluded even though it references electoral administration.

items.h: Women2Win celebrate 20 years
items.b: Join Women2Win for their 20th anniversary celebrations at The May Fair Hotel in London on November 26th. Women2Win works to support and encourage Conservative women who want to take up public office across the UK.
items.note: Organisational anniversary event, excluded under sector admin rule.
links: Join Women2Win for their 20th anniversary celebrations

items.h: The ‘Coachella of community power’ returns next year
items.b: New Local’s Stronger Things Festival — branded the ‘Coachella of community power’ — is set to return next year in June. Last year 1,200 people joined in-person and online to listen and participate in discussions about the future of local communities. This year they hope to trump that figure so keep your eye out for updates .
items.note: Event listing/promotion rather than a reported democratic mechanism or new participation tool.
links: keep your eye out for updates

items.h: The Politics Project hiring for two new roles
items.b: The team at The Politics Project is growing — they’re looking for applicants for two new roles, a Head of Communications and Networks, and a Partnerships Manager. Both roles are for a fixed-term contract until March 2027 with the possibility of extension. They are London-based, with a minimum of two days per week in the office. The application deadline for both roles is Sunday 9th November 2025. For more information and to apply, see here .
items.note: Job adverts excluded as organisational admin.

items.h: OGP Scotland co-creating next Action Plan
items.b: Open Government Partnership Scotland are in the lead up to co-creating their next action plan, which will include public consultations on trust perception in Scotland — the plan itself will include a trust and transparency strategy, and key planks on anti-corruption and accountability, ethical use of tech and much more besides. Sign up to the OGP Scotland e-bulletin for up to date news .
items.why: it involves co-creating government policy through public consultation, a participatory mechanism shaping transparency and accountability commitments.

items.h: Mapping the migration justice movement, new report
items.b: Natasha Adams has published a new report mapping the migration justice space in the UK, based on interviews and conversations with many across the UK migration justice movement. According to the report, the organisations and groups are over stretched, struggling to cope with keeping organisations and morale afloat while firefighting the onslaught of racist policies and literal death threats, Natasha writes. It needs more unrestricted funding, space for strategic reflection, greater connections and collaborations across the movement and beyond. The report is not public, but you can read a summa…
items.why: it documents the capacity and strain of civil society organisations that enable collective advocacy and participation in public life.
links: The report is not public, but you can read a summary here

items.h: Open Rights Group collecting signatures for inquiry into the ICO
items.b: Beginning next week, Open Rights Group (ORG) will start collecting signatures for an open letter which asks the DSIT select committee to open a formal inquiry about the Information Commissioners Office. ORG are pushing for a full blown inquiry into the ICO’s alleged poor performance on data protection oversight, which is key to protecting the integrity of election campaigners and others from online manipulation. You can find an (almost final) draft of the letter here . The letter will be published later in November, add your organisation to the letter.
items.why: it seeks parliamentary scrutiny of a regulator whose oversight function protects data integrity relevant to fair elections and public debate.
items.note: Inquiry into a regulator's performance is scrutiny (accountability), with electoral integrity and disinformation as secondary threads.

items.h: Trust the People running new online community building course
items.b: Grassroots community organisers Trust the People are running a new four part online course this November sharing democratic tools to help people organise and support their local communities. The course will run every Monday evening for four weeks looking at key concepts such as how to build community, how to support a group, how to develop community assemblies, and more.
items.why: this creates a new tool for people to learn how to organise and build democratic community structures, directly expanding practical means of participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building course counted under participation.

items.h: Compass to host full day member event Charting Our Course this November
items.b: Compass’s upcoming event, Charting Our Course , will be a day of strategy discussion, debate and decision making for the Compass movement. The core theme of the day will be how progressives can organise a popular front against the rise of the far-right. Sign up to join the full day event on November 15th.
items.note: Internal member strategy event, treated as event listing rather than a new means of participation.

items.h: Poland hosts first youth citizens’ assembly on country’s digital future
items.b: The Field of Dialogue Foundation with support from People Powered’s Digital Democracy Accelerator recently launched the first national-level Youth Citizens’ Assembly in Poland’s history. The assembly brought together 32 randomly selected youth from across the country to discuss and debate the sorts of digital policies which the government should implement to ensure technology operates in the public interest.
items.why: citizens' assemblies are deliberative decision-making machinery, and this international example offers comparative evidence relevant to UK democratic innovation practice.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies fall under elections & decision making per framework, even when reported internationally as sector practice.

items.h: Involve to host training sessions on how to facilitate public engagement
items.b: Keen to understand how you can facilitate better public engagement through meaningful discussions in your organisation or community? Involve is hosting two training sessions in November on the 6th and then again on the 13th. There is a price tag on this one, but there are discount options for third sector organisations.
items.why: this creates a new training resource that expands people's practical capacity to facilitate public engagement and deliberation.

items.h: Civic University Network host CiviCon25 in Sheffield
items.b: This year’s Civic University Network conference was the last they’ll hold in Sheffield Hallam before their move to NCCPE in Bristol for next year’s conference. Civic University Network is part of the UK’s National Civic Impact Accelerator (NCIA) and works to help UK universities deepen their civic impact.
items.note: Conference/organisational news about a network's own event, not a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Rebekah McCabe publishes new blog, Assembling Wisdom
items.b: Rebekah McCabe is the Head of Northern Ireland at Involve. Rebekah’s brand new blog Assembling Wisdom is a field notebook from the frontlines of participatory democracy, collating their reflections from citizens’ assemblies and community conversations, training rooms and research projects — and from moments when people surprised each other — and themselves — with generosity or clarity. Sign up for Rebekah’s new blog here .
items.note: Personal blog launch by staff member counts as organisational news, not a democracy story.
links: Rebekah’s brand new blog Assembling Wisdom

items.h: Compassion in Politics hacked by criminals asking for crypto donations
items.b: Supporters of Compassion in Politics (CiP) recently received what they thought to be a distressed email from the organisation which claimed their Stripe payments system had been blocked due to their organisation’s actions highlighting the genocide in Gaza . The email then asked supporters to continue their support via a crypto link. Compassion in Politics quickly became aware of the situation and is taking action to boost their security. Concerned about your organisation’s digital security? Tech coop Common Knowledge is running digital security training for civil society organsiations — find o…
items.note: Cybersecurity/fraud incident affecting an organisation, not a democratic mechanism as such.

items.h: Staying safe from growing racism on UK streets — new guidance published
items.b: Hackney Anti Raids has published advice on how to stay safe on UK streets, especially for migrants who are facing an increased threat of racist attacks. The advice includes what to do if you or those you work with are being filmed and what to do if you are being harassed. Please share with those that would find the resource useful.
items.why: this addresses personal security and protection from racist harassment, bearing on people's ability to safely exercise civic freedoms in public space.
items.note: Treated as rights/civic space given the focus on personal security and discrimination rather than a participation tool.

items.h: New vox pops showcase public attitudes to UK politics and citizens assemblies
items.b: Alisdair Binnie-Lubbock and the team at 858 Project has been out and about on the streets asking people what they think of politics and what they would change if they received a Golden Ticket to join a permanent and powerful citizens’ assembly. Check out and share their new video . They are also crowdfunding for their campaign to scrap the House of Lords and replace it with a citizens assembly.
items.why: it engages public attitudes toward replacing an unelected chamber with a citizens' assembly, a direct-democracy decision-making mechanism
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Record by-election turnout in Caerphilly could be a sign of things to come, says More in Common
items.b: Last weeks’ dramatic by-election in Caerphilly, which saw Plaid Cymru narrowly defeat Reform UK, with support for both Labour and the Tories plummeting, was also notable for local voter turnout. The by-election had the highest turnout the Senedd constituency has ever had , and higher than the national turnout at any Senedd Election. More in Common predict this could be a sign of things to come as tactical voting campaigns and major party campaigns mobilise voters en masse away from Reform UK.
items.why: turnout is a direct measure of electoral participation and the competitiveness of the vote
items.note: Turnout is always classified under elections & decision making regardless of framing.
links: highest turnout the Senedd constituency has ever had

items.h: Institute for Welsh Affairs asks, how can we make the most of a changing Parliament?
items.b: With six months to go until Wales goes to the ballot box to elect a reformed Senedd, the Institute of Welsh Affairs , Electoral Reform Society Cymru , Public Affairs Cymru and the Wales Governance Centre are hosting a one-day event bringing together expert voices and trusted insight to help organisations navigate and prepare for Wales’ changing democratic landscape. Find out more now .
items.note: Sector event listing without a reported change in democratic mechanism.

items.h: Common Weal hosting REVIVE National Conference for Real Land Reform
items.b: As part of the REVIVE coalition, including Friends of the Earth Scotland, The League Against Cruel Sports, OneKind and Raptor Persecution UK — Common Weal are hosting a national conference they’re describing as a landmark event in Scotland’s land reform journey on 8th November. This work builds on last year’s The Big Land Question work , which found just 421 people own half of Scotland’s private land.
items.note: Land reform conference listing; connection to democratic mechanism is too indirect to qualify.
links: Common Weal are hosting a national conference

items.h: Centre for Governance and Scrutiny host all day event on 21st Century Councillors
items.b: Test Valley Borough Council — in partnership with LGC and Birmingham University’s INLOGOV — are hosting a free event, 21st Century Councillors , in Andover on 4 November. The day is designed to give councillors and officers the opportunity to discuss how elected members can adapt, lead and thrive in a rapidly changing landscape that includes local government reorganisation. Find out more .
items.note: Sector event listing for councillors, no reported change to democratic structures or powers.

items.h: Four in five Brits want greater say over local issues, polling finds
items.b: New polling , on behalf of Power To Change , finds that 82% of Britons think it’s important for the government to give local people more control over what happens where they live. When it comes to delivering local change, the most trusted actors are community organisations (36%) followed by the council (19%), whilst just 9% trust central government. And at a national level, just 6% think the government respects their opinion when making decisions that affect the country.
items.why: it shows public demand for shifting decision-making power toward local government and eroding trust in central government's authority
items.note: Local government control falls under elections & decision making per the devolved structures rule, though the poll also touches political efficacy.

items.h: Starmer relaunches ‘Levelling Up’ scheme with new devolved funds and powers
items.b: The Prime Minister is set to announce that 330 deprived areas will receive tens of millions of pounds over a decade to be spent on renewal schemes. Unlike Levelling Up funds of the past, local authorities will be given more autonomy to decide how to spend the funds. Labour is hoping this renewal will bring a boost to deprived areas and help stave off the threat of Reform.
items.why: it devolves funding decisions and powers to local authorities, altering the structure of local decision-making
links: 330 deprived areas will receive tens of millions of pounds

items.h: Demos and UCL Policy launch ‘Nation of Neighbours’ initiative
items.b: ‘Nation of Neighbours’ is a year-long initiative funded by Lloyd’s Bank Foundation and organised by Demos and UCL Policy Lab , which aims to set out a fresh narrative for national renewal. The initiative will show how trusted community organisations hold the key to reconnecting citizens and driving national renewal. Read their first joint statement on this exciting project and its development.
items.why: it launches a new initiative aimed at strengthening community organisations' role in civic engagement
items.note: Sector capacity-building initiative counts as a democracy story under participation & civic life.

items.h: Campaign groups launch ‘Democracy SOS’ calling on government for urgent change
items.b: A new report by Compass , Unlock Democracy and Citizen Network sets out an urgent 8 point plan of action to re-boot our democracy. The authors of the report also sent a letter to Keir Starmer urging him to act on their plan to get his premiership back on track and ensure UK democracy thrives.
items.why: civil society groups are pressing government to reform the mechanisms of electoral and democratic decision-making
items.note: Advocacy for systemic reform rather than a reported change itself.
links: sent a letter to Keir Starmer

items.h: New YouGov MRP poll shows chaotic outcome at next general election
items.b: A new MRP poll published at the end of September puts Reform UK within a whisker of an overall parliamentary majority, winning 48% of available seats. However their overall share of the vote is still just over a quarter of the electorate (27%). Meanwhile the Greens are expected to get 11% of the vote and win just 1% of available seats. The graphs below from Electoral Reform Society show these outcomes in more detail.
items.why: the poll evidence highlights how the electoral system translates votes into seats, a core measure of electoral fairness and representativeness

items.h: CTRLshift to host convention on the future of UK democracy
items.b: On December 2nd in Sheffield, CTRLshift is teaming up with Citizen Network and Our House to hold a convention on the future of democracy in the UK . The event is supported by the National Lottery Community Fund through the Transition Together project. Find out more and book your ticket .
items.note: Event listing for a convention, not itself a reported change to democratic practice.
links: convention on the future of democracy in the UK

items.h: Labour For a New Democracy hold ‘biggest and best attended’ rally at Labour conference
items.b: Labour For a New Democracy , the campaign group pushing for the adoption of proportional representation within the Labour Party, report that they staged their ‘biggest and best attended’ rally for PR ever held at the Labour party conference. MPs, trade unionists, activists and metro mayors were all on the speaker panel, and if you weren’t there in person, you can watch the whole event back online.
items.note: Self-promotional report of rally attendance rather than a substantive reform development.

items.h: Green Party accused of limiting avenues for member participation
items.b: At their recent conference in Bournemouth, The Green Party changed their constitution to allow the leadership to directly issue proposals for members to vote on. Writing in Bright Green , Douglas Rouxel, says the change represents a movement away from their democratic and participatory roots which allows members to shape rather than simply vote on proposals.
items.why: the change to how the Green Party's leadership can set member votes affects internal party democracy, which falls under freedom of association for political parties
items.note: Party internal democracy is classified under elections & decision making per the framework's treatment of parties.

items.h: New report, The Decline of the Constituent-MP relationship — and how to fix it
items.b: A new report from Demos , A Two-Way Street: The decline of the MP-constituent relationship and how to fix it , looks at how MPs’ relationships with their constituents have worsened in recent years, suggesting ways to rebuild it. They propose a new framework to guide interactions between citizens and their representatives, one grounded in principles of ‘inclusivity, participation, reciprocity, accountability, and pragmatism’.
items.why: the report addresses how elected representatives remain answerable and connected to constituents between elections, a core accountability mechanism
links: A Two-Way Street: The decline of the MP-constituent relationship and how to fix it

items.h: Safe Landing host second deliberative event for a vision of sustainable future aviation
items.b: Safe Landing is an organisation dedicated to developing a positive, worker-led vision of the future for sustainable aviation, where everyone can experience the beauty of flying, without harming people or planet. Their latest deliberative workshop for aviation workers saw workers come together for a ‘Visioning Assembly’. They’re still writing up their final report but you can see a short blog & video on it here .
items.note: A private-sector worker visioning exercise, not a public political decision-making process.
links: see a short blog & video on it here

items.h: September council by-elections underscore issues with First-Past-The-Post, campaigners say
items.b: On the 11th of September, six local council by-elections took place across England and Wales. Of those, five elections were won on less than a third of the vote, and in two cases the vote was less than 30%. In our current era of multi-party politics, this system is producing increasingly perverse outcomes, says the Electoral Reform Society . They are campaigning for England and Wales to follow Scotland and Northern Ireland in adopting the Single Transferable Vote, which creates more proportional and fair outcomes.
items.why: low vote-share winners in council by-elections illustrate how the electoral system affects the representativeness of elected local government
links: six local council by-elections took place

items.h: Centre for Constitutional Change on what we can (and can’t learn) from the Germans
items.b: For a long time, German federalism has been viewed internationally as a model of stability. But recent years have seen a more critical discourse emerge, reflecting concerns about the governance, coordination, and resilience of the ‘German model’. Why the Germans Do It Better has given way to Broken Republik . The Centre for Constitutional Change is hosting an event on 11th November, exploring whether German federalism still offers useful lessons for Scotland and the UK — Register now .
items.note: Event listing promoting registration rather than reporting a democracy development.
links: Why the Germans Do It Better

items.h: Less than half of viewers think the BBC is independent of the government, BBC says
items.b: The BBC recently published the results of a mammoth survey of 872,000 audience members. They asked respondents how important certain broadcasting values were, and then asked how effectively they were being met. The biggest gap came on the question of independence from the government of the day with 91% thinking it is important, but just 43% saying they were doing so effectively. The second biggest gap was on whether the BBC reflects people across the UK — 76% said it was important and 51% said they were effectively doing this.
items.why: public confidence in the BBC's independence from government shapes trust in a key part of the UK's public information environment

items.h: Impress launch ‘Ethical Media and Journalism’ course
items.b: Impress , the independent press regulator in the UK, has launched a new course in collaboration with the University of Huddersfield to train journalists to produce content that is accurate and produced with integrity. Chief Executive of Impress, Lexie Kirkconnell-Kawana, said this is a crucial moment for media organisations to enact change given the ‘rising tide of inaccuracies and the poor practises of some plaguing our media and information space’.
items.why: training journalists to produce accurate, integrity-driven content strengthens the quality of public-interest journalism that underpins informed public debate
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building that creates a new means of improving the information environment.

items.h: Nottingham Post takes legal action over Reform UK ban
items.b: A local newspaper, the Nottingham Post , and its online arm, Nottinghamshire Live , have taken legal action against the local Reform run council after the council leader, Mick Barton, refused to speak to its journalists. Barton initially took the unprecedented move to stop speaking to or sending press releases to the Nottingham Post saying the party would not ‘allow misinformation to shape the narrative of our governance’.
items.why: a local council refusing to engage with a newspaper restricts press access and undermines scrutiny of local government by the public-interest press

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation’s Local News Fund backs Newry local journalism
items.b: Ready for a heart warming good news story? Over the past couple of years, Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) has been working with groups and communities across Newry to explore the role that local media plays in the community, and what role a first-of-its-kind Local News Fund can play. Thanks to the generosity of Paul Hamlyn Foundation, PINF were able to fund two pioneering projects to give local journalism a boost in Newry — check out the new projects here .
items.why: funding local journalism projects sustains the local news infrastructure people rely on to know about and scrutinise public affairs
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building for local journalism, not routine organisational funding news.

items.h: Bristol Cable launches world-first new app
items.b: Produced by Freddie and Saskia at the Newsmast Foundation, the Bristol Cable’s new app combines both the Cable’s trusted professional journalism, and a new social network for community connection made up of Bristol Cable members, all in one app. Former PINF Network Manager, now Bristol Cable Operations Lead Jaldeep Katwala unpacks how this changes the game for the Bristol based media co-op .
items.why: a new platform combining local journalism with community connection expands the means by which people access public-interest news and engage with their community
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating new means of accessing local journalism.
links: unpacks how this changes the game for the Bristol based media co-op

items.h: Government to ensure prominence of public service media content on social media
items.b: The Culture Secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said the government will legislate to ensure public service media content is given more prominence on YouTube and other video sharing platforms. The Society of Editors welcomed the news stressing the vital role public service media outlets play in combating fake news, and the importance of this new government initiative to ensure the long-term sustainability of the sector amid a changing media landscape.
items.why: legislating to guarantee prominence for public service media on major platforms shapes what plural, trustworthy information people actually encounter

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation demand big tech pays its share to local news providers
items.b: The Public Interest News Foundation is launching a new campaign to ensure local news providers are compensated by big tech companies like Google News who routinely rely on locally reported news stories on their platforms. Research commissioned by PINF suggests the amount of revenue generated by Google alone from UK news outlets could be as high as £2.2bn. Their new campaign hopes to address this unfair practice to ensure more money is pumped into local journalism.
items.why: a campaign to secure fair compensation from big tech for local news content aims to sustain the local journalism ecosystem essential to public debate
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building campaign to help sustain local journalism.
links: revenue generated by Google alone from UK news

items.h: Pro-palestine protesters awaiting trial in prison to go on hunger strike
items.b: Prisoners for Palestine have said an undisclosed number of inmates will begin an open-ended hunger strike on 2nd November if their demands are not met. A letter detailing their demands, which include immediate bail, lifting the ban on Palestine Action and an end to censorship of their communications, was handed in at the Home Office on Monday by two previously imprisoned activists, Francesca Nadin and Audrey Corno. More than 18 further demonstrations against the proscription of Palestine Action are planned for next month, Defend Our Juries say , as more than 2,100 people have been arrested pen…
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the state's use of proscription, imprisonment and censorship of communications to restrict protest and dissent, core civil liberties for challenging power.
items.note: Protest restriction and state coercion falls under rights & civic space rather than participation.
links: More than 18 further demonstrations against the proscription of Palestine Action are planned for next month, Defend Our Juries say

items.h: The Citizens to take UK government to court over inaction on Russian election interference
items.b: Nathan Gill — a former UKIP and Reform UK politician — was recently charged with eight counts of bribery to promote pro-Russian narratives inside the European Parliament. The Citizens have long been calling for an investigation into Russian interference only to be refused. In 2023 they took the UK government to court over their failure to investigate. With the recent revelations about Gill, they are now preparing for another legal challenge to secure a full scale inquiry into Russian interference in UK elections.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns whether government can be held to account through the courts for failing to investigate foreign interference in UK elections.
items.note: Legal action to compel scrutiny is treated as accountability; electoral integrity is a secondary concern.
links: took the UK government to court

items.h: ID cards precursor to ‘pre-crime’ state, say campaign groups
items.b: Digital ID cards are back on the menu with the Labour government promising to roll them out by the end of parliament. The move has come under intense criticism from civil society groups who were instrumental in killing the original plan fifteen years ago. Open Rights Group said the ID cards would be a ‘bureaucratic nightmare’ and the centralised database would feed AI systems that could create an ‘authoritarian pre-crime state’. Big Brother Watch has launched a petition calling for the scheme to be scrapped, so far amassing just under 165,000 signatures. Another UK Parliament petition has near…
items.why: this matters democratically because a centralised digital ID and surveillance database affects citizens' privacy and freedom from undue state monitoring.

items.h: King Charles defenestrates brother as support for the royal family polls at all time low
items.b: The former Prince Andrew, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, has been stripped of his royal titles and honours in a significant move by the monarch to defend the public image of the royal family, amidst the roiling scandal around the former Prince. Mountbatten Windsor, long implicated in the paedophilia scandal around Jeffrey Epstein, was recently the focus of sex trafficking victim Virginia Giuffre’s new book. Savanta polling this month shows support for the monarchy at its lowest level since records began, at just 46% , down from 51% last year — though recent surveys show 91% of Britons have a …
links: former Prince Andrew, now Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, has been stripped of his royal titles
91% of Britons have a negative opinion of the disgraced former Prince

items.h: Mone £122m repayment over PPE is ‘tip of the iceberg’, say corruption campaigners
items.b: PPE Medpro, the organisation tied to Baroness Mone which supplied faulty PPE during the covid pandemic, has been ordered to repay £122m to the government. The UK Anti-Corruption Coalition welcomed the news but said this was just the tip of the iceberg and the government must continue the fight to reclaim taxpayer money lost during the pandemic.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns holding a public figure accountable for corruption and misuse of taxpayer funds during a public procurement process.
links: UK Anti-Corruption Coalition welcomed the news

items.h: Government under fire for meeting fossil fuel lobbyists 500 times in first year, say Fossil Free Parliament
items.b: Fossil Free Parliament has published research which shows the government met fossil fuel lobbyists over 500 times in their first year — a 48% rise on the number of meetings attended under the Tories. The campaign group said these lobbyists had essentially been given ‘a backstage pass to the government’. Government spokespeople said the findings were misleading as many of these companies have clean energy investments which were often the basis of the discussions. Earlier this year openDemocracy published cutting edge research from InfluenceMap how weak UK lobbying laws allow fossil fuel giants …
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns undue influence of powerful private interests over government policy-making through opaque lobbying.

items.h: Growing far right violence over flags, reports Byline Times
items.b: East Anglia Byline Times report assaults and harassment on members of the public acting to remove ‘divisive flag displays’ in Diss and Norwich, with one man hospitalised and a group of women surrounded and chased . Police took no or limited action in either case, and in Diss accused the women of ‘causing trouble’. While supporters of the so-called Operation Raise the Colours campaign claim the flags show ‘patriotism and unity’, critics see them as symbols of division . British Muslim communities have faced attacks and vandalism of mosques and community spaces , and increasing hatred towards Mu…
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns the state's failure to protect citizens' basic security and freedom from discrimination and intimidation linked to far-right activity.
links: faced attacks and vandalism of mosques and community spaces
as Akeela Ahmed, CEO of the British Muslim Trust — attests

items.h: Greenpeace install prison bars around monuments of civil rights icons
items.b: Yesterday a new Greenpeace stunt saw the team locking up champions of protest — Gandhi, Mandela and Fawcett — to protest at the increasing restrictions of the right to protest in the UK, through the proscription of Palestine Action as a terror group, new laws restricting cumulative and other wide-ranging powers to clamp down on public protest, they argue.
items.why: this matters democratically because the stunt highlights legal and policing restrictions on the right to protest, a core civil liberty underpinning democratic contestation.
items.note: Campaign action about legal restriction on protest, not about willingness to demonstrate, so classed under rights rather than participation.
links: new Greenpeace stunt saw the team locking up champions of protest — Gandhi, Mandela and Fawcett

items.h: New Ethics and Integrity Commission is established and Acoba watchdog abolished
items.b: The much criticised watchdog Acoba (Advisory Committee on Business Appointments) has been scrapped as the government reforms the ethics structure around parliament. A new organisation — the Ethics and Integrity Commission — has also been set up as part of the government’s drive to put accountability at the heart of their parliamentary agenda.
items.why: the ethics infrastructure overseeing former ministers' business appointments and standards in public life is being restructured, directly affecting how public officials are held to account.

items.h: Google cuts all funding to fact checking website Full Fact
items.b: Google has been a major funder of Full Fact , donating over £1million last year to the fact checking organisation. Now they have cut all financial ties to the organisation — a move which echoes Meta’s decision earlier this year to end support for third party fact checkers. Full Fact believes these decisions are motivated by a desire to appease the Trump administration .
items.why: withdrawal of funding from a major fact-checking organisation affects the public's ability to access reliable information about political claims and the wider information environment.

items.h: Tony Blair Institute has received £257 million from CEO of Oracle, investigation finds
items.b: A new investigation by the investigative news Substack ‘ Democracy For Sale ’, finds that The Tony Blair Institute has received £257 million since 2021 from Larry Ellison — the founder of software company, Oracle . Some staff have since left the think tank complaining that the cash injection had led to a form of ‘AI boosterism’ which had turned it into a lobbying vehicle for Ellison.
items.why: large-scale funding of an influential policy institute by a single foreign private individual raises questions about undue private and foreign influence over public policy formation.
items.note: Treated as undue influence by powerful private/foreign interests over public power, per government_accountability anchors.

items.h: Green Party celebrates surging membership numbers, votes to proscribe IDF as terrorist org
items.b: The Green Party of England & Wales how has more than 150,000 members, outstripping all but Labour and Reform. The party is also currently roughly tied with the Labour Party in national polling. Earlier this month, Green Party members voted at their conference for the Israeli Defence Forces to be proscribed as a terrorist organisation. The motion also called for the British government to ‘formally apologise to the people of Palestine for the Balfour Declaration’ and for the establishment of a ‘UN peacekeeping force in the West Bank & Gaza to ensure the safety of Palestinian residents’.
items.why: a surge in party membership reflects growing public engagement in party political life, a core measure of participatory health.
items.note: Polling parity with Labour touches on political competition (elections beat) but membership growth is the dominant participation angle.
links: Green Party members voted at their conference for the Israeli Defence Forces to be proscribed
‘formally apologise to the people of Palestine for the Balfour Declaration’

items.h: Platforms like X ‘failing catastrophically’ to limit reach of extremist posts, new research shows
items.b: Two new studies showcase the ongoing failure of X to limit the reach of harmful content on its platform. Firstly, the Centre for Countering Digital Hate partnered with the Jewish Council for Public Affairs to analyse 679,000 antisemitic posts on X, finding that these hateful posts were viewed a total of 193m times.
items.why: platforms' failure to limit extremist and hateful content shapes the plurality and safety of the public information environment citizens rely on for political debate.

items.b: Another study by CCDH found that posts celebrating the death of Charlie Kirk amassed 52 million views online whilst posts calling for retaliatory violence were viewed 43 million times. The CEO of CCDH, Imran Ahmed, said platforms like X ‘are failing catastrophically to limit the reach of posts that celebrate murder and mayhem.’
items.why: continued failure of platforms to limit incitement to violence and celebration of murder affects the safety and integrity of the public information environment.

items.b: Mick Napier of the Scottish Palestine Solidarity Campaign released after crowds block his arrest, May 2025 Photo credit: Scottish Community and Activist Legal Project
items.note: Bare photo caption with no substantive content.

items.h: Network for Police Monitoring publish new report into policing of Scottish pro-Palestine demos
items.b: The Scottish Community and Activist Legal Project (SCALP) and the Network for Police Monitoring (NetPol) have launched a new report analysing Police Scotland’s response to pro-Palestine demonstrations. The report paints a bleak picture of how fundamental rights of free speech, assembly and protest are being eroded in Scotland, the authors argue, from systematic police violence, police intimidation of organisers and disproportionate use of police resources — Read the report now .
items.why: a report alleging systematic police intimidation and disproportionate policing of protest activity concerns the legal and practical space for assembly and free expression.
items.note: Policing/state coercion of protest places this under rights_freedoms_civic_space rather than participation.
links: The Scottish Community and Activist Legal Project (SCALP)

items.h: Facial recognition tech deployed to Manchester for first time
items.b: Greater Manchester Police announced their first use of the technology last week . Big Brother Watch (BBW) warned of ‘unprecedented expansion’ of facial recognition as ‘worrying for democracy’ back in August, ahead of the country-wide rollout. Rebecca Vincent, Interim Director of BBW, said ‘This unprecedented escalation in the use of facial recognition technology across the UK is alarming, and represents a significant expansion of the surveillance state. Live facial recognition turns every passerby into a walking barcode and treats us all as a nation of suspects.’
items.why: the expansion of live facial recognition surveillance by police affects citizens' privacy and freedom from unwarranted state monitoring, core civil liberties in a democracy.
links: announced their first use of the technology last week

items.h: Government’s new ‘Democracy Taskforce’ accused of evading democratic scrutiny, reports Bylines
items.b: A Freedom of Information request from the Byline Times on the operations of the government’s ‘Defending Democracy Taskforce’ has been sent back with almost all information requests refused. The government body also has little to no information online — no website, social media, meeting minutes, agendas etc — leading to accusations that the taskforce itself is behaving fundamentally undemocratically.
items.why: a government body evading Freedom of Information requests undermines the transparency mechanisms that hold public institutions answerable.
items.note: FOI here concerns institutional answerability, not the information environment, so it sits under government accountability.
links: Freedom of Information request from the Byline Times

items.b: Led By Donkeys team arrested for projecting image onto Windsor Palace (Photo credit: Led By Donkeys)
items.why: arresting protesters for a symbolic act of political expression raises questions about the state's tolerance for dissent and lawful protest.
items.note: Protest policing is classified under rights and freedoms because the story concerns legal restriction and state coercion.

items.h: Arrests after Trump-Epstein Windsor projection are ‘Orweilian’, says Led By Donkeys
items.b: Four arrests were made after the campaign stunt group Led By Donkeys projected an image of Trump and Epstein onto Windsor Castle during the President’s state visit. Led By Donkeys said it was the first time anyone in the group had been arrested for a projection, calling the police response ‘ridiculous’ and ‘Orwellian’.
items.why: police arrests over a political protest stunt implicate freedom of expression and assembly, and the proportionality of state coercion against dissent.
items.note: Classified under rights and freedoms as the story centres on policing response to protest, not willingness to participate.

items.h: Journal of Democracy explores democratic backsliding
items.b: In their latest issue, the Journal of Democracy has selected several key articles exploring the complexities of democratic backsliding and undoing the damage of authoritarian episodes. These include an essay on how pro-democracy opposition parties often adopt the autocratic habits of the regime they replaced , the myth of democratic resilience and how democracies fail to reverse the damage after an authoritarian relapse , recognising democratic backsliding — and case studies from Malawi, Zambia and Gambia.
items.note: This is an academic publication roundup on backsliding in other countries, not a UK-relevant mechanism or reported change.
links: Journal of Democracy has selected several key articles exploring the complexities of democratic backsliding
how pro-democracy opposition parties often adopt the autocratic habits of the regime they replaced
myth of democratic resilience and how democracies fail to reverse the damage after an authoritarian relapse

items.h: mySociety celebrate more than 1.25 million FOI requests on WhatDoTheyKnow
items.b: There are now a record 1,250,876 Freedom of Information requests to 47,172 authorities on WhatDoTheyKnow , since launching in 2008. Unfamiliar with the tool? Check it out now .
items.note: Celebrating a milestone of an existing tool is organisational news, not a launch of new participatory capacity.

items.h: Demos joins call for safeguards around AI technology
items.b: Demos , together with over 200 prominent global figures, has joined calls for international redlines to be placed on unacceptable AI use by the end of 2026. Other signatories include many Nobel laureates, former heads of state, tech leaders, and digital policy organisations.
items.note: General call for AI safety redlines is too broad and not tied to a specific UK democratic mechanism.

items.h: See the latest democracy tech launches, now on Civic Tech Field Guide
items.b: Matt Stempeck, Curator of the Civic Tech Field Guide , has announced CFTG’s latest new feature — a space to monitor all the latest civic technology as it is published and launched — check it out .
items.why: launching a new resource to track civic technology tools creates a new means for people and organisations to discover and use tools that support democratic participation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building since it launches a new feature/platform for tracking civic tech.

items.h: AI minister says the government wants to go ‘further and faster’ with AI
items.b: In an interview with Politico , AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said that alongside healthcare the government intends to ‘put AI in the service of things like our national security’. Starmer previously declared that AI could save the government £45bn in savings and productivity benefits . As the Government moves to hand over these large quantities of public data to AI companies, the Ada Lovelace Institute recently cautioned that there is a long way to go to improve public trust in these companies . The Social Market Foundation has put out a paper on how and why we must take AI regulation seriousl…
items.why: the government's plan to expand AI use and share large quantities of public data with AI companies raises questions about executive transparency, oversight and public trust in how power over that data is exercised.
items.note: Focus is on government data-handling and accountability rather than the information environment as such.
links: declared that AI could save the government £45bn in savings and productivity benefits
there is a long way to go to improve public trust in these companies

items.h: New democratic engagement tool Waves is launched in Camden
items.b: Waves , the new digital engagement tool which has been under development for the last 6 months, has been launched by Demos , New Local , Psi and multiple local authorities. This pilot will be the largest ever UK experiment with digital democracy and they are now looking for people in the Camden area to take part. If you’re a local resident or know one, get involved !
items.why: the pilot creates a new digital mechanism for local residents to engage in civic decision-making, expanding practical means of participation.

items.h: New guide for building public interest technology is published
items.b: The Open Knowledge Foundation has recently published a new field guide for anyone interested in creating public interest technology. The new publication — ‘The Tech We Want — Read This Before You Build’ — is intended to guide readers through the key questions to consider before embarking on a new project, such as thinking about who the tech is for and who will maintain it.
items.note: General technology-building guidance not tied to a specific democratic participation mechanism.
links: ‘The Tech We Want — Read This Before You Build’

items.h: Newspeak House celebrates 10th anniversary this December
items.b: It has almost been a decade since Newspeak House launched as the London College of Political Technology. To mark the occasion, Ed Saperia, Dean of Newspeak, is hosting a fundraiser, conference and Christmas party, all in one — grab your ticket .
items.note: Organisational anniversary/event notice, not a democracy story.
links: fundraiser, conference and Christmas party, all in one — grab your ticket

items.h: Connected by Data working with civil society orgs across AI
items.b: Connected by Data are busy — they’ve launched their Principles for Public Participation in the Procurement of Artificial Intelligence . They held their twelfth meeting of the Data and AI public engagement community of practice, focused on deliberation exercises and how to evaluate them ( see the notes here ). Connected by Data’s Data and AI Civil Society Network meets next week, Tuesday 4th November — find out more .
items.why: the new principles and community of practice build civil society capacity for public participation and deliberation in AI-related decision-making.
items.note: Deliberation exercises border elections_decision_making, but this is sector capacity-building rather than a specific decision-making process.
links: Principles for Public Participation in the Procurement of Artificial Intelligence

items.h: ChatGPT-5 produces more dangerous content than earlier editions, according to campaign group
items.b: The attempt by US parents to sue Open AI for the role Chat-GPT played in encouraging their son to take his life has raised questions about the potential dangers of unregulated AI platforms. The Center for Countering Digital Hate has been investigating whether their latest model ChatGPT-5 is actually safer than previous versions. The results suggest it’s not, as the platform continues to serve up dangerous content to users. The organisation is campaigning for the UK government to put the public’s safety first and properly regulate the emerging technology.
items.note: Concerns AI safety and content harms rather than a democratic mechanism such as the political information environment.
links: US parents to sue Open AI
The Center for Countering Digital Hate

items.h: Inclusivity in Action: Merging Sociocracy and Liberating Structures
items.b: Carl J Rogers argues that inclusive, trust-based teamwork is a competitive advantage in complex environments, and sets out how to pair Sociocracy 3.0 patterns with Liberating Structures’ micro-formats to scale participation. Practical steps include starting small with Liberating Structures, clarifying domains and decision rights, using intent-based leadership, and iterating via regular feedback loops.
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Generic organisational management advice, not tied to UK public power or democratic institutions.
links: sets out how to pair Sociocracy 3.0 patterns with Liberating Structures’

items.h: Churn! Institute for Government launches new policy making boardgame
items.b: Last week marked the successful launch of Churn! The Policy Making Board Game, a groundbreaking collaboration between the University of Roehampton and Institute for Government . This innovative game transforms the complex process of policy-making into a dynamic, hands-on simulation that encourages critical thinking, collaboration, and strategic insight. See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: the game is a new educational resource intended to build public understanding of and engagement with the policy-making process.
items.note: Counted as sector capacity-building creating a new means of civic engagement with policy-making.
