items.h: Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust hiring new Democracy Cooptee for their board
items.b: The Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust (JRCT) wishes to appoint a co-opted member to join our Power and Accountability Committee from April 2026. The committee is looking for someone with experience of issues of democratic accountability and reform in the UK. Apply now .
items.note: Board appointment/hiring notice for an organisation, not a new means of participation.

items.h: New Paul Hamlyn fund will support grassroots social change
items.b: The Paul Hamlyn Foundation has set up a new Ideas and Pioneers Fund which will support individuals and groups exploring ideas for social change. The fund will provide grants of up to £20,000 and a flexible support package for organisations or any legal structure with a turnover of under £150,000. Apply by 2 December.
items.note: General social-change funding, not specifically aimed at democratic participation mechanisms.

items.h: New money for youth organising from the Alliance for Youth Organising
items.b: The Alliance for Youth Organising has launched two new funding opportunities, including up to 10 Anchor Grants of up to £85,000 over two years to organisations supporting the field of youth organising, and 5 Explore Grants of £15,000 for one-off projects exploring gaps in action or understanding for the youth organising field. Apply by 26 January 2026 and 16 February respectively . A B Charitable Trust opens grant applications A B Charitable Trust (ABCT) is open to grant applications of up to £30,000 to support charities working with marginalised and vulnerable groups, find out more and apply …
items.why: this creates new funding infrastructure specifically to support youth organising, a means of civic and political participation.
items.note: Youth organising fund counts as capacity-building for participation; the general marginalised-groups grant (ABCT) is more borderline but bundled here.

items.h: Civic Power Fund is seeking ‘learning partner’ for new infrastructure project
items.b: Civic Power Fund is developing a new project to better understand what infrastructure exists to support civil society organisations with their organising work. The project will determine what infrastructure already exists, what groups are accessing and what gaps remain. They are looking for a Learning Partner to help them deliver this over a period of eighteen months starting in March 2026. Check out the full brief .
items.why: this project aims to map and strengthen infrastructure supporting civil society organising, affecting the capacity of civic groups to participate.

items.h: Tenacious Journalist Awards open for second year
items.b: Designed by Public Interest News Foundation and Changes Ideas to support UK journalists and small news orgs to produce high-impact journalism, prize winners will be awarded £10,000 to work on a new or existing project that seeks real world change. Funded by Changing Ideas, winners will receive up to 8 months’ coaching and mentoring. Check out the full eligibility criteria and apply now .
items.why: this supports public-interest journalism aimed at real-world change, strengthening the information environment underpinning public debate.
links: Public Interest News Foundation and Changes Ideas

items.h: Join Esmée Fairburn Foundation for a pre-application webinar
items.b: On 5th February, Esmée Fairburn will be hosting a Q&A webinar for those organisations interested in applying for support — 2pm, Thursday 5th Feb 2026. Register here .

items.h: City Bridge Foundation publish report into the fund’s slave trade trade history
items.b: City Bridge Foundation , London’s largest independent charitable funder, this week published its new report detailing independent historical research into the links between Bridge House Estates (City Bridge Foundation’s historical and legal name) and the transatlantic traffic in enslaved African people. Find out more here .
items.note: Historical reparations research is organisational history, not a democratic mechanism.

items.h: Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust hiring new Head of Reparations
items.b: After undertaking preliminary research finding showing that the Rowntree company has bought cocoa and other goods produced by enslaved people, and had profited from systems of colonial exploitation, the Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust published a statement outlining their intention to identify meaningful forms of reparation. JRCT is now hiring a Head of Reparations to lead on this work.
items.note: Staff hiring news about an organisation, excluded even where the org works on democracy-adjacent issues.

items.h: Democracy Club and Politics Project begin as new hosts of the Democracy Network
items.b: We’re delighted to announce the Democracy Network is now under new management. Our new hosts, Democracy Club and The Politics Project , are working to support the Network into a new phase. Over the next few months our team will be pausing our usual schedule of activities, instead we’ll be reflecting on what has worked in recent years and where we could improve. We’ll be reaching out to Network members and working with the Steering Group to consult on and co-develop a new strategy and approach. The new hosts were chosen by the elected Democracy Network Steering Group to take on the network, bas…
items.note: News about an organisation's own management/hosting arrangements, not a change to what people can do.

items.h: Curriculum Assessment Review emphasises democracy within the national curriculum
items.b: Last month saw the publication of the Department for Education’s Curriculum and Assessment Review , which places a renewed emphasis on democracy within the national curriculum — including explicit recognition of Votes at 16 within Citizenship education. Organisations across the sector are already working hard to support schools as they respond to this change, Democracy Classroom reports.
items.why: embedding democracy and Votes at 16 in the national curriculum builds young people's capacity and readiness to take part in political life

items.h: UK Government publish National Youth Strategy
items.b: The new National Youth Strategy published by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport sets out plans to support young people, schools and organisations to deliver Votes at 16 — and to invest in resources to ensure young people have the opportunity to engage in politics at a local and national level.
items.why: a government strategy investing in young people's opportunities to engage in politics creates new means of civic participation

items.h: Natasha Adams & Jim Coe ask: How can the UK social change sector meet the moment?
items.b: In a major new report based on more than 60 interviews, 80 conversations and multiple workshops, Natasha Adams and Jim Coe look at how the UK social change space is responding to the rise of the far right. Their research focuses on three key areas — that global power is shifting with powerful international actors promoting authoritarianism and far right policies abroad, that the UK social change sector is not yet responding meaningfully to this new reality, and that UK change orgs need to respond urgently. Their paper Meeting the Moment suggests a framework for a radical, sustained and sector …
items.why: the capacity and strategic response of civil society organisations to authoritarian political trends bears on the health of civic participation
items.note: Borderline: this is sector strategy analysis rather than a concrete new participation mechanism.
links: Read the report and find out more

items.h: IPSA publishes new report on MP’s pay and funding
items.b: The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority convened the New Citizen Project to run sortition-selected demographically representative citizens forum to deliberate on the question How should MPs be paid and funded to best support our democracy? Read the results and the new report based off the forum.
items.why: a sortition-selected citizens' forum deliberating on MP pay is a direct-democracy decision-making mechanism
items.note: Citizens' assemblies/deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule.
links: Read the results and the new report based off the forum.

items.h: Nearly three hundred organisations sign joint statement supporting ECHR
items.b: To mark the 75th anniversary of the Human Rights Act, nearly three hundred organisations including Liberty , Refuge , Parkinson’s UK and the Centre for Military Justice have signed a joint statement calling for a ‘full-throated defence’ of the European Convention on Human Rights and the Human Rights Act. The signatories called on politicians to ‘stop using our human rights as a scapegoat’ and end the politically motivated attacks on these crucial rights.
items.why: This matters democratically because sustained political attacks on the ECHR and Human Rights Act threaten the legal protections that safeguard individual rights and freedoms against state power.

items.h: mySociety celebrate FOI Fest 2026, launch new report on better election data
items.b: Join mySociety’s democracy team for a one-hour discussion diving into the findings of their new report on election donations reporting, Leaky Pipes: Better Election Donation Data . But that’s not all, join the mySociety team for FOI Fest 2026 , celebrating 21 years of Freedom of Information with a one-day conference to discuss its achievements, challenges, and future, in partnership with the FOI Network .
items.why: This matters democratically because transparent, accurate election donation data underpins campaign finance oversight and electoral integrity.
items.note: Report on donation data treated as elections content rather than a pure event listing.
links: Leaky Pipes: Better Election Donation Data

items.h: Politics in Action launch Votes at 16 Campaign Group
items.b: Politics in Action recruited a new Votes at 16 Campaign Group last month and held an inaugural residential of the new group. The new group aims to ensure youth voice remains at the centre of the government’s implementation of Votes at 16.
items.why: This matters democratically because campaigning on votes at 16 concerns who is entitled to vote and thus the scope of the franchise.
items.note: Franchise/suffrage campaign classified under elections rather than participation.

items.h: Applications open for Network Catalyzers Program 2026
items.b: The Democracy & Belonging Forum is launching its second year of the Network Catalyzers Program in 2026. The program’s main goal is to support efforts that boost democratic engagement by overcoming otherness and fostering belonging. Participants in the year-long program will receive extensive support and tailored advice to help them shape their project and achieve this. Find out more about this exciting opportunity and apply by January 14th 2026.
items.why: This matters democratically because the program creates new capacity-building support intended to boost democratic engagement and belonging among communities.

items.h: Social Justice Sector to host conference exploring how to protect and rebuild civic space
items.b: On the 27th of January, Speak Out and Quakers in Britain are hosting an in-person conference to discuss the threats to UK civic space and what social justice organisations can do to protect it. The conference will hear from speakers from Liberty , Greenpeace , New Economics Foundation , Runnymede Trust , Friends of The Earth , and Quakers in Britain . To join in this crucial conversation on the future of UK democracy and campaigning, sign up!
items.note: Treated as an event/conference listing rather than a launched tool or programme.

items.b: APPG on Women in Parliament this month (Photo Credit: Centenary Action)

items.h: APPG on Women in Parliament host session on addressing violence against women and girls
items.b: The APPG on Women in Parliament , Centenary Action and Westminster Foundation for Democracy (WFD) held a special session on 9th December launching WFD’s new methodology for parliaments to address violence against women in politics. The event brought together MPs, researchers, civil society leaders and women with lived experience to explore how the UK can confront VAWP — and strengthen our democracy in the process. Read the new WFD method for institutional action (MINA) now.
items.why: This matters democratically because violence against women in politics deters their participation as candidates and representatives, undermining equal access to political office.
items.note: Gender-based violence in politics treated as a rights/personal-security issue affecting equal participation.
links: Read the new WFD method for institutional action (MINA) now.

items.h: New Art Exchange discuss their use of Citizens’ Assemblies on ITV News
items.b: The New Art Exchange recently appeared on ITV News to discuss their use of citizens’ assemblies to bring local communities into the discussion on culture in Nottingham. The work aims to cement meaningful change in the city by listening to and learning from the views of local residents.
items.why: This matters democratically because citizens' assemblies are a deliberative decision-making mechanism bringing residents directly into local policy discussions.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's revised boundary rule.

items.h: Applications for the Reagan-Fascell Democracy Fellowship are open
items.b: The National Endowment for Democracy (NED) is accepting applications for the Reagan-Fascell Democracy Fellowship . The five month, funded fellowship offers democracy activists, journalists, civil society leaders, and scholars the opportunity to join the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), in Washington, D.C., in order to undertake independent research on democracy in a particular country or region. To apply for this exciting opportunity , send a proposal for your research track to NED by 31st of December.
items.note: Individual fellowship opportunity, akin to a job/research grant listing rather than a new means of public participation.

items.h: Apply for the Patchwork Foundation’s new Masterclass Programme
items.b: Patchwork Foundation are offering a 10 month programme for 18–30 year olds who are passionate about British politics and civil society. The programme will provide participants with access to leading political figures, corporate execs and changemakers, building key professional skills, accessing 1:1 mentoring, and joining a vibrant network of emerging leaders. Apply by now and share the opportunity .
items.why: it creates a new structured pathway for young people to build skills, networks and access needed to take part in political and civic life.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building that expands means of participation, not mere organisational news.
links: Apply by now and share the opportunity

items.h: Final decision on fate of crumbling Parliament building to be delayed until 2030s
items.b: MPs were expected to vote on how to repair the crumbling Parliament building by the end of this year, but that is likely to be significantly delayed beyond Labour’s current term according to MPs familiar with the issue. The building has been suffering from a series of mounting structural problems, but the vote has been delayed with one MP saying the reason is that the cost of repair is a ‘ scary big figure at a time when the government is taking unpalatable decisions and there’s no appetite to put it to MPs .’
items.why: it concerns political reluctance to exercise fiscal authority and make an accountable decision about funding the physical institution of Parliament.
items.note: Borderline: mainly a facilities story, but ties to avoidance of a politically accountable decision.

items.b: Coventry Youth Activists launching their accessible voting campaign in April 2025 (Photo Credit: CYA)
items.note: A photo caption with no substantive content beyond identifying an image.

items.h: Coventry Youth Activists look back on a good year of effective accessible voting campaigns
items.b: Launched in April, the Coventry Youth Activists accessible voting campaign engaged thousands around local elections in Warwickshire and across the country. The campaign aimed to raise awareness of the barriers commonly faced by disabled people trying to vote . CYA believe disabled people should not be locked out of democracy by a voting system that isn’t built for everyone.
items.why: it concerns removing practical barriers that prevent disabled people from exercising their right to vote.
items.note: Accessibility of voting anchors to elections even though delivered via a civic campaign.
links: The campaign aimed to raise awareness of the barriers commonly faced by disabled people trying to vote

items.h: Muslim Youth Engagement Awards mark national moment for youth work
items.b: Organised by Here For Youth , the national Muslim Youth Engagement Awards brought together civil society leaders, funders, policymakers, researchers, mosque leaders and community organisers this month. Chief Executive Officer of Here For Youth, Ayub Seedat , remarked the event felt ‘less like an awards ceremony and more like a line being drawn in the sand’, as Muslim youth organisations acknowledge and celebrate their ecosystem of organisations maturing and professionalising, to the point where they now consistently engage thousands of teenagers every single week.
items.note: An awards ceremony celebrating organisations' growth, not a change to what people can do democratically.

items.h: Podcast Episode: How has the war in Ukraine affected attitudes to democracy?
items.b: The UCL podcast, Uncovering Politics , has a new episode on how the war in Ukraine has affected attitudes to democracy. Do people cling more closely to democratic principles in times of war and crisis, or are they more ready to abandon them? Check out the podcast to find out more .
items.note: A podcast promotion rather than reported findings bearing on UK democracy.

items.h: Police and Crime Commissioners to be scrapped
items.b: Just 20% of voters can name their Police and Crime Commissioner, according to the Home Office, which goes some way to explaining why they are now calling it a ‘failed experiment’ . Thirty seven PCCs were set up twelve years ago by the Conservative government to improve police accountability, but the position is set to be wound up in 2028. The role will move to the elected Mayor’s office or to council leaders.
items.why: it abolishes a directly elected accountability role and transfers police oversight to appointed mayors or council leaders, changing who is elected to exercise that power.
items.note: Structural change to a local elected office falls under elections & decision making.

items.h: Four mayoral elections in 2026 will be postponed
items.b: The government has announced that four mayoral elections in Essex, Hampshire and the Solent, Sussex and Brighton, and Norfolk and Suffolk will be pushed back until 2028. James Cleverly labelled the move a ‘scandalous attempt to subvert democracy’, whilst Reform UK’s Zia Yusef said it was ‘a blatant attempt to stop big Reform wins next May’. Experts at the Institute for Government said the move could not be justified on fairness or democratic grounds .
items.why: postponing scheduled mayoral elections directly affects when and whether voters can choose their representatives at the local level.

items.h: Research for Action to deliver free training on investigating local council finances
items.b: Research for Action is currently looking to develop and deliver a series of free training sessions in early 2026 to explore how local government finance works and how individuals can interrogate council accounts. If you think this would be useful, or have any suggestions for what else to include in the training, get in touch to discuss this further.
items.why: free training that equips citizens to scrutinise council finances creates new means for people to take part in and hold local government accountable.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating new participation tools, classified per capacity-building rule.

items.h: New report says fiscal devolution is a must to address sizeable regional wealth disparities
items.b: The UK has been described as the most regionally unequal country in the developed world, with so much of that due to the heavy centralisation of the UK economy. A new report from The Fairness Foundation — A Fair Share — outlines the path to change, setting out the benefits of widespread fiscal devolution to ensure regional wealth disparities and living standards are addressed.
items.why: the report concerns the powers and fiscal autonomy of regional and local government tiers, which is core decision-making machinery.
items.note: Fiscal devolution treated as structure/powers of sub-national government per boundary rule, not as economic equality condition.

items.h: Democracy Convention convenes in Sheffield
items.b: Earlier this month, Citizen Network , CtrlShift and Our House combined to run a day long workshop on a People’s Charter. You can see the finished charter here . Next year, Citizen Network will be publishing the Charter and inviting people to improve upon it. Our House will be building local People’s Charters with community groups and organisers across the UK, get in touch to get involved .
items.why: building local People's Charters with community groups creates new avenues for civic organising and participation.

items.b: Democracy Convention in Sheffield this month (Photo credit: Citizen Network)

items.h: Speaker commits to making UK first White Ribbon Parliament in the world
items.b: The Speaker of the House of Commons, Sir Lindsay Hoyle MP, has committed to working towards making the UK Parliament the first national White Ribbon accredited Parliament in the world . The White Ribbon campaign aims to end men’s violence against women and girls by encouraging men to never use, excuse, or remain silent about such violence. Prime Minister, Kier Starmer, praised Hoyle for his efforts and said we must now ‘turn that ribbon into action’.
items.note: A symbolic institutional commitment on VAWG, not a mechanism of public power acquisition, exercise or contestation.
links: first national White Ribbon accredited Parliament in the world

items.h: Liberal Democrat Peer calls for laws on election campaign finance to be tightened
items.b: Lib Dem Peer, Chris Rennard, has challenged the government to tackle the changes in election spending that could see a party spend the full £35m in 70 target seats — that amounts to £0.5m per constituency. Rennard called for specific action to address the limits on party spending which were increased by 80% just before the previous election.
items.why: campaign finance limits shape how fairly parties can compete for votes, a core condition of competitive elections.

items.h: New Welsh Election Information Platform to launch in January
items.b: Storm ID was appointed over summer to design and deliver a new digital service that supports voters, candidates and electoral administrators across Wales. The platform, which is set to launch in January, will provide clear, accessible and trusted information about elections in Wales, making information more accessible.
items.why: a new platform providing trusted, accessible election information affects how easily voters, candidates and administrators can engage with the electoral process.
items.note: Election-specific information service classified under elections rather than general information environment.
links: design and deliver a new digital service

items.h: Renters’ Rights Bill gets Royal Assent
items.b: The Renters’ Rights Act , the government’s landmark legislation designed to rebalance the power between tenants and landlords, received Royal Assent on the 27th of October. The legislation will see ‘No Fault Evictions’ banned, will provide tenants with the opportunity to appeal rent-hikes, and will see the creation of a Private Rented Sector Database to help landlords understand their legal obligations. Chief Executive of Generation Rent , Ben Twomey, praised the new laws as ‘ a vital step towards re-balancing power between renters and landlords’. Chief Economics Correspondent at the Financial…
items.note: Tenant-landlord regulation is social/economic policy, not a democratic mechanism of power acquisition, exercise or contestation.

items.h: Gen Z voters get more balanced and varied news diet than most adults, says new report
items.b: A major new study by Demos of Gen Z voters and their online media consumption habits finds that the stereotype of young voters being overwhelmed by untruthful news is simply not true. In fact, many are better informed and receive a more balanced news diet than followers of traditional media. Three quarters of the 700 surveyed said democracy is the best way of running society, and a quarter said the opposite.
items.why: public understanding of politics depends on the balance and plurality of the news environment young voters actually consume, and their reported support for democracy bears on civic engagement.

items.h: Head of Britain’s trade union movement calls for debate on UK press ownership
items.b: The head of the Trade Union Congress , Paul Nowak, has said the time has come for ‘a debate about media plurality and who owns the media’. Speaking to the Byline Times , Nowak warned against allowing Trump’s attacks on the BBC to undermine the broadcaster, and the wider problems of ownership which have emerged in recent years through Musk’s control of X and Paul Marshall’s growing empire .
items.why: concentrated ownership of the press and broadcast media affects whether the public encounters a genuinely plural range of political information and argument.

items.h: Liberal Democrats call for the BBC to be ‘Trump-proofed’
items.b: As President Trump threatens the BBC with a $10billion lawsuit, the Lib Dems have called for the BBC to be protected and says the broadcast must not be bullied into giving the loudest and most divisive voices coverage. They want the special Ofcom rules on balanced coverage at election time to apply all year round to ensure long term impartiality and independence.
items.why: protecting public-service broadcasting from political pressure and extending impartiality rules affects the plurality and independence of the information environment.
links: called for the BBC to be protected

items.h: Compassion in Politics call for government to end use of terror laws against peaceful protesters
items.b: Jennifer Nadel and the Compassion in Politics team sent a letter to the Prime Minister last month, signed by more than 500 Compassion in Politics supporters, calling on the government to end the use of terrorism laws against non-violent protesters. “Peaceful protest is not terrorism; it is a fundamental democratic right” they say in the letter .
items.why: using terrorism legislation against non-violent protesters constrains the freedom of assembly needed to challenge and contest democratic power.
items.note: Protest policing and legal restriction falls under rights and freedoms rather than participation.

items.h: Chilling effect? Harley Wishart investigates what’s happening to protest in the UK
items.b: University of Brighton PhD student Harley Wishart is investigating the implications of recent changes in police doctrine and public order legislation and their impacts or ‘chilling effect’ on the behaviour of activists, protesters, journalists and members of the public — read their Substack here .
items.why: changes to police doctrine and public order law that chill activists, journalists and protesters affect the practical exercise of assembly and expression rights.
items.note: Focus is on legal/policing restriction rather than willingness to participate, so it sits in rights rather than participation.

items.h: Five UN experts condemn Palestine Action ban as ‘unnecessary’ and ‘not justified’
items.b: Four UN Special Rapporteurs and an independent expert have condemned the government’s proscription of Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation. They said the move was ‘unnecessary’, ‘not justified’ and said it was a move associated with authoritarian states. Eight Palestine Action prisoners are currently on hunger strike while awaiting trial. Their lawyers are demanding an urgent meeting with government ministers.
items.why: proscribing a civil-society organisation as terrorist restricts freedom of association and assembly, a core condition for challenging state power.

items.h: Met Police ban UKIP protest in Tower Hamlets due to breach of Public Order Act
items.b: A planned protest in Tower Hamlets at the end of October by the UK Independence Party was banned by the Met Police due to the ‘realistic prospect of serious disorder’. This would have seen the political party breach Section 12 of the Public Order Act , which was introduced by the Conservative government in 2023. Organisers from Stand Up to Racism claimed it as a major victory , but Netpol warned that any use of these powers, even those used against the far right, sets a dangerous precedent of state overreach.
items.why: police use of Public Order Act powers to ban a political party's protest directly restricts the freedom of assembly needed for political contestation.
items.note: Concerns state coercion and policing of assembly, so classified under rights rather than participation.

items.h: Climate protesters given license conditions reserved for extremists
items.b: UK climate protestors that have been released from jail are being given licence conditions that are reserved for extremists , The Guardian reports. One Just Stop Oil protestor was banned from going to any meetings or gatherings, except for worship, without gaining prior permission from her probation officer. These conditions were eventually dropped however, following a legal challenge. Other protestors have been given similar conditions but were banned from even talking about them due to a separate restriction that prohibits contributing ‘directly or indirectly’ to any website.
items.why: it shows the state using coercive licence conditions to restrict protestors' freedom of assembly and expression, narrowing space for lawful dissent.
items.note: Protest policing/legal restriction falls under rights & freedoms per the boundary rule.
links: licence conditions that are reserved for extremists

items.h: Contracts worth £138m awarded to companies that donated to Labour government
items.b: A new study by the The Autonomy Institute has found that the government awarded £138 million worth of contracts in their first year to companies that donated to the party. Dr Susan Hawley, the executive director of Spotlight on Corruption said the findings show ‘a systemic problem with the UK’s absurdly weak handling of conflicts of interest’, and called for systemic solutions to address the problem.
items.why: it raises concerns about conflicts of interest and undue influence of donors over government contracting decisions.

items.h: Police to investigate Reform UK over claims of electoral fraud
items.b: Allegations have emerged that Reform UK broke electoral law last year during the local campaign to win Nigel Farage’s seat of Clacton. The allegations stem from a former aide who suggested Reform UK submitted false election expenses during his campaign and may have spent more than the £20,660 limit. The police are now looking into the matter.
items.why: alleged breaches of campaign spending limits undermine the integrity and fairness of electoral competition.

items.h: Electoral Commission examining government’s drinks receptions with businesses
items.b: The Electoral Commission has confirmed they are looking into whether Labour has applied the law governing political donations correctly in relation to the sponsorship of a series of drinks receptions. Labour has classed these corporate drinks receptions as ‘commercial partnerships’ saying all rules have been complied with. If there is a suspected breach of the law, the Electoral Commission could launch a full scale investigation and can implement fines of up to £20,000.
items.why: scrutiny of how political donation rules are applied affects the transparency and fairness of party financing.
links: applied the law governing political donations correctly

items.h: Former leader of Reform UK in Wales sentenced for taking bribes from pro-Russian groups
items.b: Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform UK in Wales, has been sentenced to ten and half years in prison for taking bribes from a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician to make pro-Russian statements in the European Parliament. Full recap of the story comes from The Citizens . This is just the tip of the iceberg though, says journalist Carole Cadwalladr , as the threats to democracy from Russian interference go far deeper than one man, she suggests.
items.why: a politician taking foreign bribes to influence statements represents undue foreign interference in democratic representation.

items.h: Chinese spying operations amounts to interference in British democracy, says Security Minister
items.b: UK Security Minister, Dan Jarvis, has told MPs to be on high alert to Chinese agents who are contacting MPs and Peers in order to extract information about parliament. Jarvis’ comments came after MI5 launched an official espionage alert, warning that Chinese agents posing as headhunters, or as people working for cover companies, are regularly trying to contact British politicians. Jarvis said the government would not tolerate these ‘covert and calculated’ attempts to interfere in the UK’s sovereign affairs.
items.why: covert foreign interference targeting parliamentarians threatens the independence of democratic institutions from foreign control.
links: told MPs to be on high alert to Chinese agents

items.h: Your Party holds first conference, acrimony continues
items.b: Your Party descended into further infighting and acrimony just before their first conference after Zarah Sultana, the party’s director, was accused of refusing to transfer member donations worth £800,000 to the party. A fortnight later Adnan Hussain MP quit the party due to ‘ persistent infighting ’ . Your Party still went ahead with their founding conference where they published their founding documents and principles based on input from nationwide regional assemblies that took place in October and November.
items.note: Internal party infighting and organisational drama is not itself a democratic mechanism story.
links: descended into further infighting and acrimony
Adnan Hussain MP quit the party

items.h: Reeves’ housing blunder highlights need to double down on standards, says Institute for Government
items.b: Last month the Chancellor, Rachel Reeves, found herself in hot water after it emerged she had failed to manage her housing arrangements properly . Reeves is not the first minister to make such a mistake as both Angela Rayner and Rushanara Ali had to resign earlier this year for similar reasons. The Institute for Government says the government must get serious about cleaning up its image and this starts by upping their game on standards.
items.why: repeated ministerial standards failures and calls for reform bear on accountability mechanisms for conflicts of interest in government.
links: failed to manage her housing arrangements properly

items.h: Brits think UK politics is becoming increasingly unstable, according to More in Common
items.b: Recent polling from More in Common finds that nearly three quarter of Brits (69%) think that UK politics has become more chaotic in the past ten years. Just one quarter of Brits think this current government is stable, whereas 75% say this government is chaotic. A further two thirds (66%) of Brits said they think that politics will never return to normal.
items.why: public confidence in the stability and functioning of government is a core measure of democratic legitimacy and accountability

items.h: Proportion of Brits saying the country feels divided reaches highest point, says King’s Policy Institute
items.b: New polling from the King’s Policy Institute finds that 84% of the public now think that the UK is divided, up 10 percentage points since 2020. Reform is the only party with a majority of voters agreeing that the country is ‘very divided’ (58%), almost double the share of Conservative and Labour voters. Overall, both Conservative and Labour voters still think the UK isn’t unified with 84% and 85% respectively saying the country is divided.
items.why: perceived social division affects societal cohesion and the shared conditions under which people engage in civic and political life

items.h: Republic is fundraising to fund a private prosecution of Andrew Windsor
items.b: Andrew Mountbatten Windsor was officially stripped of his title ‘Prince Andrew’ last month by the King following evidence of his continued relationship with the convicted sex-offender, Jeffery Epstein. The campaign group, Republic , believe this action does not go far enough and is fundraising for a private prosecution of Mr Windsor over allegations of sexual assault, corruption and misconduct in public office. They have currently raised close to £20,000 of their £50,000 target.
items.why: a private prosecution over alleged corruption and misconduct in public office is a mechanism for holding a public figure accountable when state action is seen as insufficient
items.note: Involves both corruption/abuse of office and a legal redress mechanism; classed under accountability as the primary issue is unaddressed misconduct in public office.

items.h: Strong majority believe money and political influence are closely linked, says Transparency International
items.b: New polling from Transparency International finds 84% of people in Britain believe wealthy individuals use political donations to advance their personal interests, a view that is shared across all demographics and a majority of voters from every party. This comes as Reform UK records the largest ever single donation — £9 million pounds from crypto investor Christopher Harborne. The solution is straightforward, says The Fairness Foundation , the UK needs a donation cap to improve transparency and re-build public trust.
items.why: public perceptions of donor influence and record political donations bear directly on transparent party financing and fair political competition

items.h: Scottish government commits to publishing anti-corruption strategy
items.b: The Scottish Government recently committed to publishing its own anti-corruption strategy , a move welcomed by anti-corruption bodies like Transparency International UK . This strategy includes improved provisions for transparency of trust structures ​​which will help prevent kleptocrats and oligarchs investing their gains in Scottish property.
items.why: a formal anti-corruption strategy strengthens safeguards against abuse of office and illicit financial influence over public institutions
links: committed to publishing its own anti-corruption strategy

items.h: Brits divided in their opinions on human rights law, say YouGov
items.b: Recent polling from YouGov finds that Brits are divided in their opinions on human rights law. A third (32%) see human rights law as a positive, 27% say it is neither positive or negative, and 29% say it is a negative. When asked about changing the European Convention on Human Rights so it does not apply in full to cases of asylum and deportation, just under half (45%) said they would support such a move. 27% said they were opposed, and 28% weren’t sure.
items.why: public attitudes toward human rights law and proposals to limit its application constrain the legal protections individuals can rely on against state power

items.h: Lack of enforcement prompts calls for inquiry into UK data protection watchdog
items.b: A group of 73 academics, senior lawyers, data protection experts and organisations including Statewatch and the Good Law Project, have called for an inquiry into the UK data protection watchdog — the Information Commissioner’s Office — over what they are calling a widespread decline in enforcement capacity. After the ICO failed to launch an investigation into the Afghan data breach, the civil liberties group are warning of a ‘deeper structural failure’ in oversight and security.
items.why: a regulator's declining capacity to enforce data protection law weakens oversight of how public and private actors handle personal information and are held answerable for failures
items.note: Touches both regulatory accountability and predictable enforcement; classed under accountability as the story centres on watchdog oversight capacity.

items.h: Did you know the Ostbelgien Model is now five years old?
items.b: Five years ago in Eupen-Malmedy, also known as Ostbelgien, the small cantons of German speaking Belgium, set up the first ever institutionalised form of citizen deliberation, referred to locally as the first ever ‘permanent citizens’ assembly’. Earlier this year the Deliberative Democracy Digest checked in on the research team following its work, here’s what they had to say .
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: a permanent citizens' assembly is institutionalised deliberative decision-making machinery that expands how people exercise collective self-government, offering comparative evidence relevant to UK democratic innovation
items.note: Citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes are classed under elections and decision making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Peer Club launches a co-learning journey for nonprofit leaders
items.b: Peer Club is a small curated circle where experienced nonprofit leaders can slow down, share challenges and grow together across 8 sessions from Jan to Dec 2026. Find out more now .
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Peer learning circle for nonprofit leaders is org capacity-building, not a democratic participation mechanism.

items.h: Naked Politics’ Banseka Kayembe embraced The Dude
items.b: Inspired by Jeff Bridges in The Big Lebowski, Banseka Kayembe left their role at the Parliamentary Digital Service to pursue life at a slower pace, on their own terms. Published in the Guardian last month, Banseka tells their story of leaving behind the busy life, and opting to focus on developing Naked Politics and pursue a measure of inner tranquility. As she says in the piece “if you still think my decision to be jobless was a bad idea, well that’s just, like, your opinion, man.” Good luck Banseka! See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Personal career/lifestyle story about an individual, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: Thirty English councils to delay elections
items.b: Local Government Secretary Steve Reed MP gave 30 councils permission to postpone their elections late last month, after dozens of councils came forward requesting a postponement citing concerns over capacity constraints .
items.why: delaying scheduled local elections directly affects citizens' ability to choose their representatives on a regular, predictable timetable.
links: 30 councils permission to postpone their elections
dozens of councils came forward requesting a postponement

items.h: Election postponement ‘dark days for democracy’, say Unlock Democracy
items.b: As millions see their local elections postponed for a second year in a row, in some areas voters will have gone seven years without any say on their local councillors or how their councils are run. Unlock Democracy highlight more than half of the postponed areas fall within areas where Labour performed poorly in the 2025 General Election .
items.why: mass postponement of local elections denies voters a binding say over their councils, undermining the regularity of electoral accountability.
links: Unlock Democracy highlight more than half of the postponed areas fall within areas where Labour performed poorly in the 2025 General Election

items.h: Array of organisations including Electoral Commission highlight postponement concerns
items.b: The Electoral Commission has stated their disappointment at postponing elections just three months out from election day, whilst the Electoral Reform Society similarly criticise the government for late-stage postponement — reminding the UK government that ‘citizens have the right to expect regular local elections’ . For all the info on postponement, see the Institute for Government’s brief on the upcoming poll . The Speaker of the House, Lindsay Hoyle also remarked elections should go ahead as normal .
items.why: criticism from electoral bodies about late-stage postponement concerns the integrity and predictability of the electoral calendar.
links: Electoral Commission has stated their disappointment
Institute for Government’s brief on the upcoming poll
elections should go ahead as normal

items.h: HOPE not hate organising locally to ‘make elections visible’
items.b: HOPE not hate is launching a new initiative this year called ‘Vote HOPE 2026’ . It is a new project that aims to support people in communities to organise locally, make local elections more visible, and ultimately to act as a bulwark against the expansion of Reform UK and far-right groups, they say.
items.why: a new local organising initiative creates fresh means for communities to engage with and take part in local elections.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating new participation opportunities, though it touches election visibility/turnout.

items.h: Reform UK launches legal challenge over elections, review due 19th Feb
items.b: Reform UK has launched a legal challenge through the High Court over the election postponements, with a review of the case due on 19th February . The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) notes misleading reporting regarding the January 20th local election High Court ruling — that there is no block in place in relation to laying of Statutory Instruments, nor any decision made by the court.
items.why: a legal challenge over whether election postponements were lawfully conducted bears directly on the integrity of the electoral process.
items.note: Court challenge concerns lawfulness of an electoral decision, straddling elections and rule of law.
links: Reform UK has launched a legal challenge through the High Court
review of the case due on 19th February
misleading reporting regarding the January 20th local election High Court ruling

items.h: Max Roche set to leave the Democracy Network team
items.b: A valued member of the Democracy Network family, Max Roche has been working on the project, compiling our monthly bulletins and helping to maintain our various databases and jobs boards for over four years, first at the Centre for Democracy , then Involve — and now with our new hosts Democracy Club and The Politics Project . Max leaves us at the end of this month to take up a new role at the Future Governance Forum — Good luck Max!
items.note: Staff departure/organisational news, not a democracy mechanism story.

items.h: Electoral Commission looking to improve election observation activities
items.b: Are you politically active with a public interest in politics or democracy? Do you work or volunteer for an organisation concerned with democratic rights — but don’t have public political ties? If so, the Electoral Commission would like to hear from you to help improve the transparency of democracy in the UK and work to observe elections and referendums .
items.why: expanding independent election observation capacity strengthens the credibility and transparency of UK elections
items.note: Framed as a volunteer recruitment call but purpose is electoral integrity infrastructure.
links: hear from you to help improve the transparency of democracy in the UK

items.h: mySociety investigates: What’s wrong with donations data?
items.b: Following hot on the heels of their report Beyond Transparency last year, mySociety have published a new report into what they’ve learned — and what they think could be better — about the systems for reporting elections donations. Download now and watch the launch event on YouTube .
items.why: transparent and accurate campaign donations reporting underpins fair political competition and public trust in party financing

items.h: Don’t miss: mySociety’s Freedom of Information Festival
items.b: On Thursday 19th February mySociety will be hosting their first Freedom of Information Festival , co-organised by the FOI Network , with support from the Birckbeck Centre for Political Life and the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust . Grab your ticket now .
items.note: Event listing, sector logistics.

items.h: Remembering Mark Longair
items.b: Mark Longair passed away last month. Mark was the creator of Democracy Club’s candidate crowd-sourcing website, a much valued developer at mySociety — who populated the original Scottish candidate listings on TheyWorkForYou, originator of the UK’s only open geographical dataset of postcode boundaries, and a widely respected figure in the UK civic technology community. See these posts celebrating and remembering Mark Longair — Sym Roe , Anna Powell-Smith , Tom Steinberg , Myfanwy Nixon .
items.note: Obituary/tribute, not a mechanism story.

items.h: UK to chair Open Government Partnership from October, Kevin Keith reports
items.b: UK Open Government Network Chair, Kevin Keith, reports that the UK is to chair the Open Government Partnership from this coming October, marking a significant opportunity for influence and engagement with the global open government movement.
items.why: the UK taking on international leadership of open government commitments creates fresh scrutiny and pressure on domestic transparency and accountability practice

items.h: The Politics Project launch new E-learning platform
items.b: With Votes at 16 just around the corner it’s more important than ever that schools, youth groups and organisations have access to high quality democratic education. Developed with the Electoral Commission, The Politics Project’s new E-learning platform includes training courses on how elections work, who can vote and how to support young people to confidently exercise their democratic rights — check it out now .
items.why: a new e-learning platform teaching young people how elections work and how to exercise voting rights builds capacity for participation ahead of Votes at 16
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating a new tool for democratic participation.
links: new E-learning platform includes training courses

items.b: Filton 24 defendants celebrate their court victory (Photo Credit: Bristol Cable)
items.why: a court acquittal of protest defendants tests due process and the ability of citizens to seek judicial vindication for exercising civil liberties
items.note: Court outcome treated as adjudication/redress rather than the underlying protest right.

items.h: Filton 24 defendants acquitted in ‘powerful affirmation of jury independence and moral courage’
items.b: In August 2024, six people undertook direct action to dismantle military hardware to be exported for use by Israel as part of its ongoing military occupation of Palestine . The group were arrested in counter-terror raids and have been held on remand for two years. The case was originally used to justify the ban against Palestine Action. Last week a crown court jury refused to convict all Filton 24 defendants of every charge they faced , despite ‘extraordinary political pressure’, in what the Bristol Cable have called a ‘powerful affirmation of jury independence and moral courage’ .
items.why: a jury's refusal to convict despite political pressure demonstrates independent adjudication acting as a check on state power, particularly where terrorism law was used against protesters
items.note: Jury independence and due process centre this on rule of law, while the terrorism-labelling of protest is a secondary rights concern.
links: six people undertook direct action to dismantle military hardware
originally used to justify the ban
crown court jury refused to convict all Filton 24 defendants of every charge they faced
Bristol Cable have called a ‘powerful affirmation of jury independence and moral courage’

items.h: Compassion in Politics call on government to end misuse of terror laws
items.b: Following the Filton 24 trial last week, Compassion in Politics’ CEO, Jennifer Nadel, argues this legal victory must be turned into a policy mandate , ending attacks on the right to a trial by jury and ensuring no more terrorism labels for protesters, stating that the crown court victory shows current government policy is ‘fundamentally out of step with public conscience’. Compassion in Politics have started a new open letter calling for the end of terror laws used against nonviolent protesters .
items.why: campaigning to end the use of terrorism legislation against nonviolent protesters concerns the legal boundaries of the right to protest and state coercion of civic dissent
links: argues this legal victory must be turned into a policy mandate
open letter calling for the end of terror laws used against nonviolent protesters

items.b: Are you the right person to join the incredible team at Elect Her ? Find out more about the three board positions and apply now , deadline 27th February.

items.h: Campaign Lab are on the lookout for a new Deputy Director
items.b: Hannah O’Rourke and the team at Campaign Lab are on the lookout for a new and senior member of their team to support their campaign innovation work. Find out more and apply before the 16th February deadline .

items.h: How can the UK social change sector meet the moment? Asks Natasha Adams and Jim Coe
items.b: Natasha Adams and Jim Coe have launched a new report exploring how UK civil society organisations can respond to growing authoritarianism and the rise of the far right. Developed from discussions with more than 140 civil society stakeholders, the report argues organisations need to respond urgently, radically and in a sustained way — find out more .
items.why: the report examines the capacity and readiness of civil society organisations, a key sector for democratic participation, to respond to rising authoritarianism
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building analysis rather than mere organisational news.
links: new report exploring how UK civil society organisations can respond to growing authoritarianism

items.h: Electoral Reform Society Scotland reflect on Dunfermline New City Assembly
items.b: Willie Sullivan, Director of Electoral Reform Society Scotland , reports on the first meeting of the new Dunfermine New City Assembly. Check out Willie’s reflections on the new assembly in Fife .
items.why: a new citizens' assembly is a deliberative decision-making mechanism through which people take part in collective decisions outside standard elections
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the revised framework, not participation.
links: Check out Willie’s reflections on the new assembly in Fife

items.h: Climate Emergency UK hosting Accelerating Local Climate Action Conference
items.b: Climate Emergency UK’s upcoming conference aims to gather climate and democracy sector organisations in support of accelerating council climate action. Their latest report explores the impact of their 2025 Scorecards, looking at how the wealth and governance of a council and public participation accelerates council climate action and policy implementation. Find out more .
items.note: Primarily a climate-action conference and report; governance/participation are explanatory factors for climate outcomes rather than the democratic mechanism itself.
links: aims to gather climate and democracy sector organisations

items.h: Together Alliance aims to provide hope in response to rise of racism and far-right
items.b: A new alliance of hundreds of organisations , including the Muslim Council of Britain, Friends of the Earth, National Union of Students, British Medical Association, Refugee Action, Trades Union Congress, the Security Industry Federation, Social Enterprise UK and many more, with celebrity support ranging from Paloma Faith to Asim Chaudry — have come together to reject narratives of division and racism and unite against far-right politics across the UK. The Together Alliance has announced a march and demonstration on 28 March in London .
items.why: a broad civic alliance organising and mobilising a public demonstration reflects people's willingness to take part in collective political action against far-right politics
items.note: Classified as participation because the story is about mobilisation and readiness to demonstrate, not policing or legal restriction.
links: new alliance of hundreds of organisations

items.h: Hope Not Hate announce new A Million Acts of Hope partnership
items.b: 38 Degrees, Hope Not Hate, the Refugee Council, Good Faith Partnership, faith organisations and community organisations across the UK, are coming together for a week of action 13th — 20th May aimed at inspiring common acts of hope and kindness in communities up and down the country, against those ‘who seek to spread hate and harm our communities’.
items.note: Community anti-hate campaign lacks a specific democratic mechanism beyond general civic goodwill.
links: week of action 13th — 20th May aimed at inspiring common acts of hope and kindness

items.h: Local Policy Innovation Partnership Hub discussion paper outlines new devolution approaches
items.b: In their latest paper, Drs Amy Burnett, Jason Leman and Daniel Ozarow look at the role of town and parish councils and their role in making devolution work for communities . The paper was developed following the National Association of Local Councils’ Power Shift Conference and responds to the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill — Read on for their key findings .
items.why: it examines how devolution structures and the powers of town and parish councils shape local decision-making authority.
items.note: Local government structure and devolution powers are filed under elections & decision making per the boundary rule.

items.h: Taxpayers Alliance cite ‘no taxation without representation’ over council tax rises
items.b: As local authorities delay elections, some without elections for more than seven years, the Tax Payers Alliance recalls the principle of ‘no taxation without representation’ , as 29 postponing councils increase rates.
items.why: councils are raising taxes while postponing the elections that would let residents hold them accountable for that decision.
links: Tax Payers Alliance recalls the principle of ‘no taxation without representation’

items.h: Applications open for 5-year PhD position exploring democratic theory
items.b: The University of Lausanne in Switzerland is looking for a new PhD student to join on a 5-year contract. The prospective doctoral assistant will work with Professor Sandrine Baume on the topic of ‘the relationship between democracy and the life cycle (e.g. old age or youth)’. Application deadline — 15th February .
