links: looking for a new PhD student

items.h: Training course on Citizen Engagement in Policymaking
items.b: Delivered by the EU Competence Centre on Participatory and Deliberative Democracy community of practice, the new training course (open to UK citizens) provides participants with insights into rationales for citizen engagement, principles of good practice, as well as tools for running citizen engagement activities. Registration opens 17th Feb — sign up now .
items.why: it creates a new training resource that builds people's capacity to design and take part in citizen engagement processes.
links: EU Competence Centre on Participatory and Deliberative Democracy

items.h: More in Common polling looks at the state of social cohesion in 2026
items.b: More in Common asked Britons how they felt about the divisions facing the country. Their polling finds Britons see migrants versus those born in the UK as the biggest divide , overtaking class as the top faultline. A record number (64%) say the UK is divided and only 15% feel united, although 55% still think the differences can be bridged.
items.why: it measures societal cohesion and perceived divisions, which shape the conditions under which people feel able to participate together in public life.
items.note: Societal consensus and cohesion is an explicit EIU anchor under participation & civic life.
links: Britons see migrants versus those born in the UK as the biggest divide

items.h: Explore the Kingdom — new tool for discovering constituency data
items.b: Produced by Jethro Reeve the new tool, currently in beta, surfaces constituency data and allows for comparative analyses of data across multiple regions. Check it out now .
items.why: it creates a new way for people to access and compare constituency-level representation data.
items.note: Treated as elections-adjacent tool since the data concerns constituencies and representation.

items.h: UK Parliament to trial citizen-assembly-style events on immigration
items.b: The Home Affairs Committee is partnering with Demos and the Centre for British Democracy at King’s College London to host a series of deliberative events to better understand public attitudes on the trade-offs between legal migration and economic growth. 100 people across three locations will be selected to take part with the hosts keen to understand whether any points of consensus exist on the issue.
items.why: it trials a deliberative, citizens'-assembly-style mechanism for informing binding collective decisions on immigration policy.
items.note: Citizens' assembly-style deliberation is filed under elections & decision making per the revised framework.

items.h: Citizens’ assembly decides on cultural investment in the West of England
items.b: The UK’s first citizens’ assembly on regional culture has published their first report on the West of England. The group has now formed a ‘Citizens for Culture’ panel which has received £100,000 funding from Esmee Fairburn Foundation to pilot ideas to broaden access to arts and culture across the region.
items.why: a citizens' assembly is deliberative decision-making machinery through which residents directly shape public investment choices, extending collective decision-making beyond elections.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections_decision_making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: University of Westminster hosts first ever student and staff citizen assembly
items.b: Dr Graham Smith of the University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy announces the first ever student and staff climate assembly , representing over 20,000 students and 2,000 staff, funded by the Quentin Hogg Trust. At their first meeting, the assembly was welcomed by the University’s President and Vice Chancellor, Peter Bonfield, before design and facilitation lead Sarah Allan led participants through the exciting process — find out more!
items.note: An internal university assembly on climate is an event announcement about a private institution's process, not one bearing on public democratic power.
links: University of Westminster’s Centre for the Study of Democracy

items.h: People Powered publish latest research on impacts of citizens assemblies
items.b: The new research by People Powered details the considerable momentum behind citizens assemblies as an innovative tool for participatory deliberation and agenda setting, drawing from more than 70 studies from across the field. Check out their findings now .
items.note: A research publication summarising the field is organisational/publicity content rather than a change to democratic mechanisms or a new participation tool.

items.h: Demoxis — new Innovate UK civic engagement platform
items.b: Demoxis is an Innovate UK–funded civic engagement platform designed to strengthen communication between verified citizens and the leaders who represent them, turning fragmented public input into clear, structured insight. They’re preparing small, learning-focused pilots with councillors and MPs to test the platform in real communities and refine what works in practice. The Demoxis team would welcome conversations with councils or civic organisations interested in exploring a limited pilot or collaboration.
items.why: a new civic engagement platform creates a structured means for citizens to communicate political input to their representatives, expanding practical avenues for participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building rule: launch of a new participation platform counts as a democracy story under participation_civic_life.

items.h: Upcoming PSA conference on Democratic Innovations & Democratic Futures
items.b: The PSA Participatory and Deliberative Democracy Specialist Group , in collaboration with the Centre for Democratic Futures , are hosting an upcoming conference on participatory and deliberative democracy , to be held at the University of Southampton on 7–8 July 2026.
items.note: Event listing for an academic conference, not a democracy story in itself.
links: PSA Participatory and Deliberative Democracy Specialist Group
upcoming conference on participatory and deliberative democracy

items.h: Two thirds of Labour members support proportional representation, according to new polling
items.b: According to a new poll , 66% of Labour members would support the adoption of proportional representation ahead of the next general election. 77% of members who voted for Lucy Powell in the recent deputy leadership race support the change, compared to just under half (49%) of those who voted for Bidget Phillipson.
items.why: support for proportional representation concerns the electoral system by which votes are translated into seats and political competition is structured.

items.h: Democracy Next launch new paper: Scaling Democratic Innovation
items.b: The new paper — Scaling Democratic Innovations: Features of Effective Catalyst Organisations & Future Frontiers — looks at the often invisible system of networks, capacity building efforts and relationships with power that drive the success of new democratic projects. Based on 22 interviews with key leaders and stakeholders, the report identifies six core features of successful efforts to scale democratic initiatives.
items.note: A meta-level research paper on how organisations scale democratic initiatives, not itself a change to or new means of democratic participation.
links: Scaling Democratic Innovations: Features of Effective Catalyst Organisations & Future Frontiers

items.h: Social media ban must be compatible with votes for 16-years-olds, says Labour MP
items.b: Backbench Labour MP, Josh Dean, told PoliticsHome that whilst he is not against a social media ban for young people, the government needs to carefully consider how it will impact their policy to extend the voting age to 16-year-olds. The 26-year-old MP said the government must work hard to take young people with them so they don’t feel the ban is punitive and unfair.
items.why: the debate concerns extending the franchise to 16-year-olds, a core question of who holds voting rights, intertwined with restrictions on young people's expression.
items.note: Primary mechanism is franchise/voting age extension; the social media ban angle touches rights but is secondary.

items.h: Editors unite to demand action on SLAPPs
items.b: Editors of The Telegraph, Guardian, The Independent, Financial Times, The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, Bloomberg and others, including leading media figures, have signed an open letter calling for the next King’s Speech to limit Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs) targeting journalists, news orgs and whistleblowers — as a matter of urgency.
items.why: SLAPPs threaten investigative journalism and whistleblowing that hold public power accountable, so legal reform to curb them protects the public information environment.
items.note: SLAPPs are treated as an information_debate issue per the framework's press-freedom territory.
links: signed an open letter calling for the next King’s Speech to limit Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation (SLAPPs)

items.h: BBC Charter Review Green Paper ‘blueprint for permanent decline’ say Media Reform Coalition
items.b: The Government’s Green Paper proposals for reform of the BBC call for commercialisation of the BBC funding model, ‘abandonment’ of the BBC’s principles of universality and signify a ‘lack of commitment to democratic accountability’, say the Media Reform Coalition. The landmark paper on BBC Charter renewal has been rushed through via a 12 week online survey, they say. Find out more via the MRC’s in-depth analysis of the proposals .
items.why: changes to the BBC's funding model and governance affect the plurality and independence of public-service media that citizens rely on for political information.
links: The Government’s Green Paper proposals for reform of the BBC

items.h: Demos call for greater public deliberation to ‘future-proof’ BBC
items.b: Demos has published a new paper, Our BBC: A blueprint for a more independent and future-proofed BBC , outlining their vision for how to strengthen the independence and accountability of the BBC. They propose significant reforms to the corporation’s constitution and governance, including embedding public deliberation as a route to deepening resilience. They are now preparing a submission to the Charter Review consultation process.
items.why: proposals to reform BBC governance and accountability structures affect the independence of a major public-service media institution central to public debate.
items.note: Deliberation here concerns BBC internal governance rather than political decision-making machinery, so it stays in information_debate rather than elections_decision_making.
links: Our BBC: A blueprint for a more independent and future-proofed BBC

items.h: Indie News Week is back in 2026
items.b: From Monday 15th to Sunday 21st June, the Public Information News Foundation will be hosting Indie News Week 2026 , returning for its third year in a row. Under the slogan, ‘No News is Bad News’ the campaign will celebrate the vital role local news outlets play in strengthening democracy.
items.why: local news outlets provide the information citizens need to hold local power to account, and campaigns supporting them sustain that part of the media ecosystem.
items.note: Borderline event listing, included as capacity-building around local journalism's democratic role.

items.h: Israeli armed forces responsible for nearly half of all global journalist deaths in 2025
items.b: A new report from Reporters Without Borders (RSF) finds that Israeli military forces killed 43% of all recorded journalist deaths in 2025. Mexico was recorded as the second most dangerous country for journalists last year, with 24% of journalist murders recorded in the country. RSF Director General, Thibaut Bruttin, said of the findings, ‘We must be wary of false notions about reporters: no one gives their lives for journalism, it is taken from them, journalists do not just die, they are killed.’
items.why: the safety of journalists worldwide is a direct indicator of the conditions under which a free press can inform public debate, though this item is not UK-specific.
items.note: International data included as comparative evidence on press freedom rather than a direct UK story.

items.h: Mandelson allegations show urgent need for stronger misconduct laws, say Transparency International
items.b: Jon Norcross and the team at Transparency International UK argue that the Mandelson case underscores how enabling environments for corruption can intersect with other serious abuses, stating the government should accelerate current misconduct reforms to arrest the UK’s declining reputation as a beacon of good governance.
items.why: calls for stronger misconduct laws respond to concerns about corruption and enabling environments that undermine accountability of those holding public office.

items.h: Gordon Brown calls for corruption as new statutory offence
items.b: Gordon Brown has c alled for corruption as a new statutory offence , and that the Ethics and Integrity Commission should be placed on a statutory footing — as Transparency International UK Spotlight on Corruption and others, including the UK Open Government Network , have supported.
items.why: creating a statutory corruption offence and placing an ethics body on statutory footing would strengthen mechanisms for holding officeholders accountable for abuse of office.
links: alled for corruption as a new statutory offence

items.h: Minister commissioned investigation of journalists reporting on Labour Together thinktank
items.b: Parliamentary Secretary for the Cabinet Office, Josh Simons MP, commissioned an investigation into journalists reporting on the activities and finances of Labour Together, according to investigations by Democracy for Sale . Simons hired PR firm APCO for £30,000 to identify journalists’ sources amidst then ongoing reports of discrepancies in their financial reporting, which led to Electoral Commission fines . The PR industry’s professional body has now opened an investigation into APCO following Democracy for Sale’s findings.
items.why: a minister using public funds to identify journalists' confidential sources directly threatens press freedom and the ability of journalists to scrutinise political actors.
items.note: Also engages government_accountability as an apparent misuse of ministerial power and public funds.
links: hired PR firm APCO for £30,000 to identify journalists’ sources
which led to Electoral Commission fines

items.h: Government launches review into foreign interference in politics
items.b: Following the recent prosecution of former MEP Nathan Gill , who took bribes to engage in pro-Russian propaganda, the government has announced an urgent review into foreign interference in UK politics. The review will provide an in-depth assessment of the current financial rules and safeguards, and offer recommendations to further mitigate risks from foreign political interference. A 38 Degrees petition calling on the government to close loopholes in foreign political influencing has amassed nearly 50,000 signatures.
items.why: this matters democratically because it concerns safeguards against foreign powers covertly influencing UK political decision-making and campaign finance.
links: prosecution of former MEP Nathan Gill
38 Degrees petition calling on the government to close loopholes in foreign political influencing

items.h: UK continues slide down corruption rankings, report Transparency International
items.b: In a major new report 2025 Corruptions Perception Index , Transparency International mark the continued backsliding of the UK down global corruption rankings, falling from a score of 71 to 70 in the space of a year. The report highlights a generalised decline among advanced democracies , including the United States, UK, Canada, New Zealand, France and Sweden, combined with parallel trends in scores covering freedom of expression, association and assembly, marking a significant deterioration in civic space. Chair of the Anti-Corruption APPG, MP Phil Brickell, said this “must serve as a wake-up …
items.why: this matters democratically because corruption levels affect whether public power is exercised with integrity and accountability.
links: “must serve as a wake-up call for the Government.”

items.h: Corporate donations to British parties triple over last three elections, report Democracy for Sale
items.b: As the new Elections Bill is introduced, Democracy for Sale found UK parties took £42 million in corporate cash in the year prior to the 2024 election , almost double that of the 2019 election, and triple that of the 2017 poll. Check out the full analysis via Democracy for Sale.
items.why: this matters democratically because the scale of corporate donations to parties affects transparent and fair campaign financing.

items.h: UK civic space under unprecedented threat, Speak Out conference warns
items.b: Held late last month and organised by Speak Out and Quakers in Britain , the London conference gathered charity leaders, civil rights groups and campaigners for a special event focused on declining UK civic space. Paul Parker of Quakers in Britain remarked at the conference: “ UK civic space is at a precipice . When the right to speak out, to organise and to challenge those in power is under attack, we all face a diminished democracy. Healthy democratic debate is an essential prerequisite for peace.”
items.why: this matters democratically because the freedom to organise, speak and challenge power is a precondition for civic participation and debate.
items.note: Conference discussion of standing civic space concerns rather than a new development.
links: UK civic space is at a precipice

items.h: Government to reclassify animal testing sites as ‘national infrastructure’
items.b: Currently passing through the Lords, the Government is set to classify animal testing as ‘national infrastructure’ amending the 2023 Public Order Act via a statutory instrument, which has been widely panned by cross party MPs, civil liberties and animal rights groups. Labour MP John McDonnell has called for a full debate on the matter , saying the proposal sets a dangerous precedent and is a “slippery slope”.
items.why: this matters democratically because reclassifying sites to trigger Public Order Act powers can restrict the legal right to protest and assembly.
items.note: Protest restriction via legal/policing mechanism, not willingness to participate.
links: Government is set to classify animal testing as ‘national infrastructure’
called for a full debate on the matter

items.h: Ofcom and ICO to investigate whether Musk’s X has breached Online Safety Act
items.b: Elon Musk is under pressure again after it emerged that X’s Grok AI tool had produced sexualised images of women and minors. Ofcom has launched a full investigation into whether this constitutes a breach of the Online Safety Act, with the government suggesting they would support the outcome of their investigation, including an outright ban on the platform in the UK. The ICO also launched an investigation into Grok in relation to processing of personal data. 80,000+ have signed a 38 Degrees petition calling for action.
items.why: this matters democratically because regulatory action against a major platform concerns control over the public information environment and safety within it.
links: Ofcom has launched a full investigation
ICO also launched an investigation into Grok

items.h: Naked Politics report on police attitudes towards far right, ignoring reported hate crimes
items.b: Jemima Elliot writing for Naked Politics last month explores how Northumbrian police have acted to ignore far-right hate crime in the city , including Nazi symbology and salutes by far right activists and racial slurs outside of refugee hotels aimed at threatening asylum seekers and counter-demonstrators.
items.why: this matters democratically because uneven police enforcement of the law undermines equality before the law and predictable enforcement.
items.note: Focus is on police non-enforcement, a rule-of-law predictability issue, though personal security rights are also engaged.

items.h: Farage apologises for breaking the MPs’ code of conduct seventeen times
items.b: The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, has issued a public apology after it was revealed that he had broken the MPs’ code of conduct seventeen times. The seventeen breaches amount to over £380,000 of undeclared funds. The Reform leader apologised remarking he is ‘an oddball who does not do computers’.
items.why: this matters democratically because breaches of the MPs' code of conduct and undeclared funds concern standards in public life and accountability of elected representatives.

items.h: ‘Tendrils of Big Tech’ have reached Westminster, says campaigner threatened with US deportation
items.b: The CEO of British NGO Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH), Imran Ahmed, was threatened with deportation from the US on Christmas Eve, despite having a green card allowing him to live in Washington. The US state department announced the sanctions alongside several other European campaigners accusing them of targeting American social media platforms and coercing them into censoring content they oppose.
items.why: a foreign government targeting the leadership of a campaigning NGO for its work holding social media platforms accountable threatens the operating space of civil society and signals possible undue influence by powerful private and foreign actors over public debate.
items.note: Read as civic-space/foreign-influence rather than pure info-debate since the mechanism is state action against an NGO's leader, not the content environment itself.

items.h: Demos investigate: How to safeguard future elections from ‘epistemic security risks’
items.b: Demos is convening leading thinkers to address how to protect the UK’s ‘Epistemic Security’, the resilience of the UK’s information supply chains that British democracy depends on. Their latest briefing looks at the government’s upcoming Elections Bill setting out recommendations to safeguard future elections from the spread of false or unreliable information and the harassment of MPs and candidates.
items.why: recommendations to curb false information and harassment of candidates ahead of an Elections Bill bear on whether voters and candidates can engage in elections free from disinformation and intimidation.
items.note: Straddles information environment and electoral integrity safeguards; classified by its focus on disinformation as the mechanism.

items.h: Dame Sara Khan calls for Patriotic Alternative to be banned as leader attends Russian extreme ethnonationalist conference
items.b: Head of British far right group Patriotic Alternative, Mark Collett, addressed a conference of extreme nationalist groups convened in Russia hosted by Putin-aligned oligarch Alexander Dugin, leading to renewed concern by MPs of political subversion by Russian state-sponsored influence operations. Collett has denied involvement with Russian state actors. Last month, a years-long BBC investigation found PA activists using racial slurs and calling for ‘migrants to be shot’, with Dame Sara Khan calling for the government to urgently ban the far right group . See Hope Not Hate’s report on Patriotic…
items.why: calls to ban a political organisation implicated in extremism and possible foreign-state ties raise questions about the limits of freedom of association and about undue influence by a hostile foreign power over domestic political life.
items.note: Treated as civic-space (association/banning) rather than elections beat since Patriotic Alternative is not contesting elections as a registered party in this story.
links: addressed a conference of extreme nationalist groups convened in Russia
Dame Sara Khan calling for the government to urgently ban the far right group
Hope Not Hate’s report on Patriotic Alternative

items.h: Study finds Youtube algorithm radicalised key members of far right group
items.b: According to new research by City St George University of London , YouTube is a key tool in recruiting far-right activists to the largest British fascist group Patriotic Alternative (PA). Analysing 40 PA activists’ conversion to the far right group, researchers found the YT algorithm played a key role in nudging them towards more radical content .
items.why: evidence that a major platform's recommendation algorithm nudges users toward extremist political content shows how private information infrastructure can shape political radicalisation and public debate.
links: new research by City St George University of London

items.h: Spycop tried to incite activists to firebomb shop, inquiry hears
items.b: As part of the ongoing Spycops inquiry , three anti-fascist activists have accused an undercover police officer of trying to incite them to bomb a shop that was said to be a front for the far-right. The officer, Soracchi, who pretended to be an anti-fascist and socialist campaigner between 2000 and 2006, is due to be questioned by the inquiry next month. To find out more about the inquiry into undercover political policing, see Spycops and Police Spies Out of Our Lives .
items.why: testimony that an undercover officer incited activists to violence tests the lawfulness of covert state surveillance of political activists and the inquiry's ability to deliver redress.
items.note: Classified as rule of law/redress rather than accountability scrutiny since the focus is on wrongdoing and remedy via the inquiry process.
links: Police Spies Out of Our Lives

items.h: Journalists barred from reporting on Reform UK official’s photo shoot
items.b: The Leicester Mercury was barred from reporting on a panel meeting with Reform UK’s Police and Crime Commissioner in Leicestershire, Rupert Matthews, over an alleged email he sent asking a police officer to help him organise a ‘Vladimir Putin-style’ photograph of him on a horse. Despite the Mercury demanding the meeting be held in public, arguing that constituents have a right to know that elected officials are being held to account, the challenge was rejected and the meeting was held in private.
items.why: barring journalists and the public from a meeting with an elected police and crime commissioner undermines the transparency and accountability of elected officials to constituents between elections.
items.note: Primary framed as accountability/transparency of an elected office-holder rather than press freedom per se.

items.b: Democracy across the pond: New York Mayor establishes Office of Mass Engagement Mayor Mamdani has started their new term by creating a new Office of Mass Engagement which promises to transform how New Yorkers are able to participate in democratic decision making.
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: US-based story with no stated bearing on or comparison to UK democratic practice, presented as offbeat curiosity.
links: Democracy across the pond: New York Mayor establishes Office of Mass Engagement
creating a new Office of Mass Engagement

items.h: Political Technology Summit sees civic orgs gather on Berlin
items.b: Over 900 politicians, campaigners, civic and political technologists from over 50 countries gathered in Berlin late last month for Political Tech Summit 2026 , focused on connecting those working across democracy and technology and exploring the impact of technology on democratic politics.
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Event listing/conference notice, not reporting a democratic mechanism or change.

items.h: Issue #78 — March 2026
items.b: Monthly news, jobs, grants and gossip from across the democracy sector, brought to you by James Moulding and Max Roche of the UK Democracy Network. Read by 450+ UK democracy organisations. We read everyone’s newsletters & research so you don’t have to. If you want us to cover yours, let us know: hello@democracynetwork.org.uk

Over the past four years, Max Roche has been a vital part of the team behind this project, working with us to compile our monthly bulletins, maintaining our databases and jobs boards, and providing continuity as the Democracy Bulletin newsletter moved from the Centre for Democracy to Involve and now to Democracy Club and The Politics Project. Across more than 40 issues, he’s helped keep this community informed and connected. Max now moves on to a new role at the Future Governance Forum, where we’re sure his commitment to strengthening democratic practice will continue to make an impact. Thank …
items.sec: Editors note —This edition is Max’s last Democracy Bulletin
