items.h: UK Democracy Fund moving out of JRRT
items.b: In November 2025, the UK Democracy Fund , initially set up by the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust in 2019, moved hosts to JRRT’s connected charitable fund the JRSST Charitable Trust (JRSST-CT) .
items.note: This is organisational/administrative news about a funder's hosting arrangement, not a change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Mozilla Foundation open to applications for new Democracy x AI incubator
items.b: The Mozilla Foundation is looking for technologists who focus on the current state of democracy and see opportunities to strengthen it. By supporting projects that embody and promote democratic principles, the Foundation hopes to demonstrate that AI can be leveraged to create a strengthened democratic ecosystem. Find out more and apply. Deadline: 16 March 2026 .
items.note: A funding call for grant applicants is sector logistics rather than a created means of participation available to the public.

items.h: New John Ellerman Foundation funding coming online
items.b: The John Ellerman Foundation has new funding available , in line with their recently published strategy .
links: John Ellerman Foundation has new funding available

items.h: Power for Democracies share findings on analysis to find most effective democracy charities
items.b: The globally focused effective altruist research organisation Power for Democracies undertook research last year exploring the most effective democracy charities worldwide and their efficacy in countering authoritarianism . The findings are used to make funding recommendations for donors, but may also help researchers and practitioners to improve their understanding of which pro democracy tactics work and under what conditions.
items.note: Research about funder effectiveness is sector/philanthropy analysis, not a change to how UK public power is acquired or contested.
links: most effective democracy charities worldwide and their efficacy in countering authoritarianism

items.h: In case you missed it: JRRT’s new strategy
items.b: Last Autumn Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust launched their major new democratic resilience strategy , guiding their work for the next period. The new strategy marks a significant shift in how JRRT understands its work and will guide funding decisions based on their new five priorities: Money in politics, Voter participation and election systems reform, Political rights — freedom of expression and protest rights, Disinformation and Checks and balances. Read the strategy .
items.note: A funder's internal strategy priorities are organisational news, not itself a change to democratic mechanisms.
links: Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust launched their major new democratic resilience strategy

items.h: Government abandons plans to postpone 30 local elections following legal advice
items.b: The government has u-turned on plans to postpone 30 local elections following a lawsuit from Reform UK which accused the government of attempting to unlawfully restrict local democracy. It is understood Labour u-turned on the plans after receiving legal advice which suggested the postponement could indeed by deemed unlawful. The Electoral Reform Society welcomed the news and called for clarity going forwards on the exceptional circumstances in which governments can lawfully postpone elections.
items.why: it concerns whether the government can lawfully postpone local elections, directly affecting citizens' ability to hold binding elections on schedule.
links: u-turned on plans to postpone 30 local elections
The Electoral Reform Society welcomed the news

items.h: Democracy Club to host UK election data evening in London
items.b: Every year Democracy Club hosts SOPN Day, a massive effort by Democracy Club volunteers to collect and upload all the data on the year’s election candidates published on April 9th via the Statement of Persons Nominated. This year Democracy Club is running an event at Newspeak House , an opportunity to contribute to the effort and meet the people that make it all possible — register now . But that’s not all — see Daisy Brett’s summary of all the councils and seats up for election in this year’s elections.
items.note: This is an event listing/volunteer call rather than a report of a democratic mechanism change.
links: Democracy Club is running an event at Newspeak House
Daisy Brett’s summary of all the councils and seats up for election

items.h: Welcome To Your Vote Week kicks off next week
items.b: Monday 9 March marks the beginning of Welcome to Your Vote Week which is the Electoral Commission’s annual UK wide week to help young people learn about democracy, understand why voting matters and take confident steps to get involved. With the UK government’s commitment to lowering the voting age, this year’s theme is “Why Voting Matters”.
items.why: it is a campaign to raise voter turnout and understanding among young people ahead of a lowered voting age, and turnout campaigns are always classified under elections and decision making.
items.note: Turnout-related campaigns are classified under elections per the standing distinction, even when framed as civic education.

items.h: Green Party by-election win raises concerns over First-Past-The-Post
items.b: Hannah Spencer won the Green Party’s first seat in the north of England in an historic victory in the Gordon and Denton by-election , overturning Labour’s sizable 2024 majority. However, with voter turnout at just 47.5%, and with three major parties competing for the seat, the constituency is now set to be represented by someone who gained just 20% of the available votes — see the Electoral Reform Society’s blog for more information .
items.why: it highlights how the first-past-the-post electoral system can produce representatives with narrow vote shares, raising questions about the representativeness of elected institutions.
links: historic victory in the Gordon and Denton by-election
see the Electoral Reform Society’s blog for more information

items.h: Reform UK accused of breaking electoral law in Gorton and Denton
items.b: The Manchester Mill reports that Reform UK may have broken electoral law in the run up to the recent by-election after residents received a letter from a ‘concerned resident’ who was actually working for Reform UK. In the letter, 74-year-old pensioner Patricia Clegg said she was a long-time Labour voter who would now be backing Reform UK, urging residents to do the same.
items.why: it concerns alleged breaches of electoral law during a by-election campaign, bearing on electoral integrity safeguards.
links: Reform UK may have broken electoral law

items.h: ElectHer is running fortnightly clinics ahead of local elections
items.b: ElectHer is running bi-monthly sessions to help female candidates that are running to become local councillors in May. Her candidate clinics and Ask Her sessions will be available online and there are plenty more resources on their training platform to help prospective candidates. But that’s not all — this year Elect Her have also provided resources for non-candidates to get involved too , through three new toolkits, check them out now and share among your networks.
items.why: it builds capacity for women to stand as candidates, directly affecting candidate access and the representativeness of elected local government.
items.note: Candidate access sits under elections and decision making per the framework anchors, though the capacity-building mechanism also touches participation.
links: Her candidate clinics and Ask Her sessions
Elect Her have also provided resources for non-candidates to get involved too

items.h: Representation of the People Bill announced
items.b: The government has published the long-awaited Elections Bill under a new name — the Representation of The People Bill — which is now in the Committee Stage .
items.why: it reports new legislation reshaping the rules governing how elections are run and representation is structured.

items.h: Government publishes ‘Representation of the People’ Bill
items.b: The Electoral Reform Society welcomed a number of changes including: the expansion of voting rights to 16-year-olds, tightening the rules around political donations, and flexible voting to improve participation. However they warn of a significant missed opportunity in the government’s failure to reform the UK’s voting system. Spotlight on Corruption has similarly highlighted a number of areas where the government could go further including beefing up the Electoral Commission’s independence, introducing a cap on political donations, and ensuring stronger enforcement mechanisms across the board.
items.why: it reports substantive changes to suffrage, campaign finance rules and voting mechanics, alongside calls for stronger Electoral Commission independence and enforcement, which bear on institutional accountability.
items.note: Electoral Commission independence and donation caps touch government accountability as well as core electoral rules.
links: Spotlight on Corruption has similarly highlighted

items.h: Association of Electoral Administrators published handy summary to the Bill
items.b: See the summary produced by the AEA , breaking down the Representation of the People Bill.
items.note: A professional summary resource about a bill, not itself a reported democratic development.

items.h: Working on the Representation of the People Bill? Join the Elections Bill Hub
items.b: Kyle Taylor of Fair Vote UK and a range of organisations are working together to coordinate around the bill. If you’re working on the bill, contact Kyle to get involved .
items.why: it creates a new coordinating hub that helps civil society organisations engage effectively in shaping electoral legislation.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building: a new coordination tool for participation in the legislative process.
links: If you’re working on the bill, contact Kyle to get involved

items.h: Elect Her publish proposed amendments
items.b: Elect Her is proposing a set of amendments to the Representation of the People Bill, focused on transparency, accountability, and sustainable participation. Elect Her are working together with Centenary Action , The Electoral Reform Society , The Jo Cox Foundation , 50:50 Parliament , The Online Safety Act Network and The Fawcett Society to promote these amendments.
items.why: proposed amendments would change transparency, accountability and access rules within electoral law, including provisions bearing on women's representation.
items.note: Focus on amendments to an elections bill places this in elections & decision making rather than participation.

items.h: Campaign win: tech firms must remove intimate images without victims consent from platforms within 48 hours
items.b: End Violence Against Women celebrated a significant win last month. Through an amendment to the Crime and Policing Bill, companies will now be legally required to remove offending intimate content no more than 48 hours after it is flagged to them. Failure to do so will result in major fines of up to 10% of their global operating income.
items.why: new legal duties compel platforms to protect individuals' privacy and personal security from non-consensual image abuse, a rights protection enforced by the state.

items.h: Assisted Dying permitted following Jersey citizens jury
items.b: Last month, the parliament of Jersey voted in favour of the recommendations made by the 2021 Citizens’ Jury on Assisted Dying , which was run by Involve , and the following Jersey Government consultation on the issue.
items.why: a policy decision was reached through a citizens' jury, a deliberative direct-democracy mechanism for binding collective decisions.
items.note: Citizens' juries/assemblies are anchored to elections & decision making per framework rules, not participation.
links: parliament of Jersey voted in favour

items.h: House of Commons Library focus reports on donation changes
items.b: Samuel Power and Eliza Lockhart in their latest House of Commons Library briefings , summarise the new enhanced know-your-donor checks which are to be conducted on political donations following the passage of the Bill. They also look into the current status of cryptocurrency donations and impacts of the government’s new review into financial foreign interference on these donations.
items.why: it reports changes to know-your-donor checks and scrutiny of donations, which govern the transparency and fairness of political campaign finance.

items.h: Open Rights Group takes aim at the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill
items.b: The bill being voted on by MPs today , will see internet services restricted to everyone who cannot prove they are 18 years of age. The bill can also impose curfews so that after a certain time, services can’t be accessed without an ID check. The powers don’t just cover social media, ORG say, but all “internet services’, meaning everything from blogs and websites to online games and apps. Ministers wouldn’t even have to prove that these sites are harmful for children, Open Rights Group argue.
items.why: new legal powers to restrict access to broad categories of internet services affect the public's ability to obtain and encounter information and viewpoints.
items.note: Restrictions on internet access are anchored to the information & public debate beat even though framed as child protection.
links: bill being voted on by MPs today

items.h: Study reveals new young voters political literacy gap
items.b: A new landmark report Young People’s Futures and Democratic Life Project — Votes at 16 by researchers at the University of Nottingham and London Metropolitan University reveals that while British 15-year-olds are eager to participate in democracy, they are being failed by a lack of formal political literacy education. Whilst 61% of newly eligible 14–15 year olds intend on voting at the next election, 26% say they have no real idea about the UK political system or what parties offer.
items.why: it provides new evidence on newly enfranchised young people's intention to vote and understanding of the political system, bearing directly on electoral participation.
items.note: Turnout and voting intention are always classified under elections & decision making per framework rule.
links: Young People’s Futures and Democratic Life Project — Votes at 16

items.h: Campaign for a Fair Banking Act gathers pace
items.b: The Fair Banking Act campaign , which calls for banks to serve all sectors of the community and is modelled on the Community Reinvestment Act in the United States, successfully passed a 10 Minute Rule Bill in Parliament at the end of last month. The motion, which called for the introduction of a Fair Banking Act, was put forward by Gareth Thomas MP and will have its second reading on the 27th of February. Thomas also has an opinion piece in Politics Home on why we need a Fair Banking Act.
items.note: A campaign bill on banking regulation policy, not a story about how democratic power is acquired, exercised or contested.

items.h: New Demos report explores opportunities to revamp outdated parliamentary systems
items.b: Building on their MP Office Manual project in 2024, Hannah O’ Rourke of Campaign Lab and Edward Saperia of Newspeak House explore the intricacies of parliamentary office systems in the new report Democracy on Default Settings , published in partnership with Demos . Revealing the hidden story of the thousands of parliamentary staffers, the report surfaces a range of critical areas in need of reform. Read the report now .
items.why: the capacity and professionalism of parliamentary staff underpins how effectively MPs can scrutinise and hold the executive to account

items.h: Government minister Josh Simons resigns following Democracy for Sale investigation
items.b: Cabinet Office minister and former Labour Together director Josh Simons has resigned following bombshell revelations last month by Democracy for Sale that he commissioned public affairs agency APCO Worldwide to investigate journalists who were looking into the affairs of Labour Together. Peter Geoghegan, Editor-in-Chief of Democracy for Sale, remarked ‘Small journalism outlets really can pack a punch’ .
items.why: a minister resigning after commissioning surveillance of journalists shows accountability mechanisms working against abuse of office and threats to press freedom
links: ‘Small journalism outlets really can pack a punch’

items.h: Inspiring future leaders in Parliament for International Women’s Day
items.b: Centenary Action , CARE International UK and the University of Roehampton’s G-EPIC EU Project held a special APPG Women in Parliament event for International Women’s Day 2026, connecting young women and girls with female MPs, peers and international women’s rights activists. Attendees from organisations including Young Women’s Trust, The Women’s Institute, UN Women UK, Shout Out UK, The Children’s Society, Inspiring Girls UK and Elect Her took part in small group discussions with APPG Co-Chairs Dawn Butler MP and Mims Davies MP, alongside Minister Seema Malhotra and other parliamentarians. The…
items.why: connecting young women with parliamentarians widens pathways into political life and the practical ability of underrepresented groups to take part
links: University of Roehampton’s G-EPIC EU Project

items.h: Republic call for royal inquiry following arrest of disgraced royal
items.b: Republic is calling for an inquiry into the royal household, its secrecy, spending and wider influence, in the wake of the arrest of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. The campaign group also said the inquiry should investigate the complicity of government, civil service, police and the BBC in creating an environment of royal impunity.
items.why: a call for inquiry into royal household secrecy and alleged complicity by government, police and the BBC concerns scrutiny of institutions and unaccountable influence over public power
items.note: Treated as accountability/public inquiry scrutiny rather than a standing complaint about the monarchy itself.

items.h: Jo Cox Civility Commission publish new call to action on abuse and intimidation of elected representatives
items.b: The Jo Cox Civility Commission has published their second call to action on abuse and intimidation of elected representatives , this time focused on the devolved nations. The Commission has identified a range of recommendations across sectors — from central government, to policing, and social media. Whilst significant progress has already been made, they say, they are continuing to campaign for further action.
items.why: abuse and intimidation of elected representatives threatens the personal security and willingness of people to stand for and hold office, undermining political competition
items.note: Torn between personal security (rights) and candidate willingness to stand (elections); classed as rights given the focus on abuse/intimidation itself.

items.h: Hope Not Hate publish this year’s State of Hate report
items.b: State of HATE: It Could Happen Here is the latest annual comprehensive report by Hope Not Hate detailing the analysis of the British far right ecosystem. This year’s report carries a stark warning — The far right is more extreme, bigger and bolder than ever before. The report states that with Reform UK’s rise, growing street protests, and an increasingly hardline rhetoric are combining to reshape the political landscape, while public opinion is shifting and polarisation deepening.
items.why: the growth of far-right street politics and polarisation bears on societal cohesion and the civic conditions underpinning democratic participation
items.note: Could also be filed under civic space given protest and extremism elements; report frames it mainly as societal/political landscape shift.
links: State of HATE: It Could Happen Here

items.h: Are you a councillor? Association of Democratic Services Officers want to hear from YOU
items.b: Association of Democratic Services Officers (ADSO) have launched a councillor survey and a series of councillor focus groups as part of their Working in a Modern Democracy programme to better understand how local officers can adapt to our evolving democracy. Find out more about the vital work of the ADSO .
items.why: a programme to understand and improve how local democratic services support councillors builds capacity for local democratic participation and representation
items.note: Borderline between local government structure (elections) and capacity-building for those who run it (participation); classed as capacity-building programme.

items.h: Civic Punks ask: How do we make government better?
items.b: Derek Alton , former Apolitical Community Lead, Newspeak House alumni and Canadian civic tech/open data evangelist , is turning his attention to building a global network and channel for the people across the world working to innovate and make government better , to share their stories better and learn from one another.
items.note: Professional network launch for practitioners, not a public participation mechanism or organisational news item.
links: building a global network and channel for the people across the world working to innovate and make government better

items.h: Demos is recruiting a Chair of the Board
items.b: Demos is recruiting a new leader to succeed Dame Julie Mellor as Chair of the Demos Board. Check out more information about this exciting opportunity and apply by the 20th of March.
items.note: Organisational staffing/recruitment notice, excluded even for a democracy-focused organisation.

items.h: Our House is expanding
items.b: Join Our House , the new chartists and their campaign for a People’s Charter. They’re looking for an Operations Manager and Comms Manager — find out more and apply now.
items.note: Staff recruitment notice for a campaign organisation, not the campaign mechanism itself.
links: find out more and apply now.

items.h: Independent Forum for Scotland and Common Weal conference, 14 March
items.b: The Independence Forum Scotland , Common Weal and Yes United For Independence are joining forces to organise a Spring Conference on Scotland’s Future , to be held at the Òran Mòr in Glasgow on Saturday 14 March 2026.
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not a new participation mechanism or reported change.
links: organise a Spring Conference on Scotland’s Future

items.h: Partnership announced to support Local Government Reorganisation
items.b: Anthony Collins , the Centre for Governance and Scrutiny (CfGS) and Collaborate CIC — are announcing an informal partnership to support councils on their road to local government reorganisation (LGR). If you’re leading, supporting or advising a place that’s entering LGR, they’d love to hear from you. Please get in touch with Ellen Care at Collaborate CIC .
items.note: Announcement of a consultancy partnership offering advisory support, not itself a change to local government structure or powers.
links: Please get in touch with Ellen Care at Collaborate CIC

items.h: New Citizens’ Assembly in Dunfermline meets to shape city’s future
items.b: A new citizen’s assembly in Dunfermline is offering 35 residents the chance to decide on the future of their city. Participation was allocated through a civic lottery with those involved keen to ensure the process leads to direct outcomes not simply a space for discussion. Read the Electoral Reform Society’s reflections on the assembly.
items.why: a sortition-based citizens' assembly is a new instance of deliberative decision-making machinery shaping local governance outcomes.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's deliberative-process anchor.

items.h: Citizens for Culture Roadshow goes on the road
items.b: Last year the Citizens’ Assembly for Culture met and set out a plan for culture in the West of England. Now, from February to May 2026, Citizens for Culture will run a series of roadshow conversations across the West of England, bringing citizens and a variety of cultural organisations together to explore what the Cultural Plan means in practice.
items.why: the roadshow extends a citizens' assembly's deliberative process into implementation, connecting public input to a public cultural plan.
items.note: Follow-on engagement tied to a citizens' assembly is treated as decision-making machinery, not general participation.
links: Citizens for Culture will run a series of roadshow conversations

items.h: Traveller Movement — new briefing paper on intersecting inequalities
items.b: The Traveller Movement has published a new briefing paper, jointly with the Women’s Budget Group, Uneven Paths: Tackling Intersecting Inequalities Facing Romani (Gypsy), Roma and Irish Traveller Women .
items.why: the briefing documents intersecting discrimination facing specific ethnic and gender groups, bearing on equal protection and social group equality under the law.
items.note: Evidence on group/gender discrimination falls within the rights beat's equality territory rather than being organisational news.
links: Uneven Paths: Tackling Intersecting Inequalities Facing Romani (Gypsy), Roma and Irish Traveller Women

items.h: 1,000 students give their views on the role of AI in education
items.b: Between the 1st of November and the 15th of December, Connected by Data gathered the views of 1,000 students on how schools, government and AI firms should be approaching the role of AI in education. Whilst students see the ability of AI to enhance lessons they were also clear on the importance of student-teacher relationships and don’t want AI tools to be involved in personal, emotional or social support. Check out the full report or see their short video on the findings.

items.h: DemocracyNext is setting up The Assembly Commons
items.b: Two years ago DemocracyNext published an open-access guide on how to create a successful citizens’ assembly. The guide — Assembling the Assembly — has since been viewed over 30,000 times and has been translated into 4 languages. Now they want to turn the guide into an open-access knowledge hub: ‘The Assembly Commons’. If you have used their guide and have feedback on how to shape The Assembly Commons, get in touch .
items.why: a new open-access knowledge hub expands the practical capacity of communities and organisers to run citizens' assemblies, a form of collective decision-making machinery
items.note: Citizens' assembly resources are filed under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: Institute of Welsh Affairs takes a look back on 10 years of the Future Generations Act
items.b: The Institute of Welsh Affairs takes a look back over the last 10 years since the passage of the internationally groundbreaking Wellbeing of Future Generations Act in a new report. Authored by IWA Co-Director Joe Rossiter, the report makes a set of recommendations for the Office of the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales and the next Welsh Government.
items.why: the report evaluates and recommends reforms to an independent oversight body (the Future Generations Commissioner) that holds Welsh Government policy to account
items.note: Borderline: could be read as policy substance rather than a governance mechanism story.

items.h: Academics warn of distorted election results on ‘unprecedented scale’
items.b: Over 50 academics have written to the government warning that their failure to reform the voting system will lead to distorted election results on an ‘unprecedented scale’. The letter was coordinated by the All-Party Parliamentary Group for Fair Elections and campaign group Make Votes Matter .
items.why: the choice of electoral system determines how votes translate into seats and thus how representative and competitive elections are
links: All-Party Parliamentary Group for Fair Elections

items.h: Government announces strengthening of Electoral Commission role
items.b: Steve Reed, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, has announced that the government is to repeal in full the power for Government to impose a strategy and policy statement on the Electoral Commission , and to increase the maximum fines imposed by the EC from £20,000 to £500,000. Additionally, the government will legislate to protect election staff and officials.
items.why: strengthening the independence, enforcement powers and protections of the Electoral Commission affects the integrity and administration of elections
links: government is to repeal in full the power for Government to impose a strategy and policy statement on the Electoral Commission

items.h: Cooperation at the cutting edge, Research for Action investigates
items.b: Gloria Dawson of Research for Action met with the founders of the Cooperation Town Network (an association of 60 community food coops) and Cooperation Manchester , just a couple of examples of the new and exciting initiatives transforming communities as part of a new wave of the cooperative movement building community power. Read and listen to Gloria’s in-depth interviews with the groups .
items.why: grassroots cooperative networks building community power reflect the capacity of civil society and communities to organise and take collective action
items.note: Borderline: cooperative/economic organising rather than explicitly political participation.
links: Read and listen to Gloria’s in-depth interviews with the groups

items.h: Join Shared Future for upcoming webinar on Participatory Budgeting, 17 March
items.b: Shared Future will be running a one hour lunchtime introduction to Participatory Budgeting, focussed on Pride in Places. Taking place on Tuesday 17th March 2026, starting at 12.00pm. Book your place here. Take a deep dive into Shared Future’s latest thinking on Pride in Places and realising community power through participatory budgeting.
items.note: Treated as an event listing rather than a new resource or reported change.
links: Taking place on Tuesday 17th March 2026, starting at 12.00pm. Book your place here.
realising community power through participatory budgeting.

items.h: Dpart publish new research on youth barriers to electoral politics
items.b: In partnership with Bertelsmann Stiftung , the German Dpart think tank have released a new study Hurdles to the ballot box: Why voting is not a Given for young people . The study outlines the structural, individual and contextual barriers that make electoral participation more difficult for young people and is well worth translating to read in full.
items.why: new research on structural barriers to youth voting bears directly on electoral participation and turnout
items.note: Turnout and barriers to voting are always filed under elections & decision making per framework rule.
links: Hurdles to the ballot box: Why voting is not a Given for young people

items.h: New scheme will see £800m of local investment managed by local communities
items.b: The government’s new Pride of Place scheme , launched at the beginning of February, will give local people in 40 communities the opportunity to decide how £20m of funding is spent in their local area. The scheme is being advertised as a way to allow local communities to ‘take back control of their futures’, with the PM saying it is vital to ‘give power, agency and control to the very people who want to improve their community’.
items.why: it creates a participatory budgeting mechanism giving local communities direct control over public resource allocation, expanding practical means of taking part in civic decisions.
items.note: Participatory budgeting is filed under Participation & civic life per framework anchors.

items.h: Votes at 16 — chance for a reset? Asks Advocacy Academy’s Calum Green
items.b: Calum Green, Director of Organising and Campaigning at the Advocacy Academy , explores the potential impacts of lowering the voting age for young people and their relationship with democracy in the UK.
items.why: lowering the voting age would change the franchise, determining who is entitled to participate in elections.
links: potential impacts of lowering the voting age for young people and their relationship with democracy

items.h: Home Office publishes White Paper on future of policing
items.b: A new White Paper published by the Home Office sets out wide-ranging reforms to the future of policing in the UK, including a new national level police force. The Institute for Government praised much of the Home Secretary’s reforms, but said that the plans could see significant power stripped away from local areas leading to less accountability.
items.why: centralising policing under a national force could strip power from locally accountable structures, weakening checks and answerability.
items.note: Touches on local government structure but the central concern raised is loss of accountability.

items.h: Business leaders demand proportional representation to promote economic growth
items.b: In a letter to the Financial Times , over twenty business leaders called for the government to scrap the first-past-the-post voting system. Signed by the Chairman of Virgin Group and others, the authors state: ‘We consider that the electoral system no longer serves the interests of UK business in generating growth.’
items.why: the call to scrap first-past-the-post concerns the electoral system that translates votes into representation.

items.h: New polling shows declining appetite for electoral reform
items.b: The latest polling from the National Centre for Social Research finds the appetite for changing the electoral system has fallen in the last year from 60% to 53%. The biggest decline comes from Reform UK voters (79% to 61%), who may now be aware that their party stands to benefit from first-past-the-post.
items.why: shifting public appetite for electoral reform reflects changing views on the fairness and competitiveness of the electoral system.

items.h: Andy Burnham praises devolution as blueprint for regional prosperity
items.b: In an op-ed for the Guardian, the Mayor of Manchester set out his stall on the importance of devolution as a blueprint for better regional governance and for overcoming ‘the four horsemen of Britain’s apocalypse’: deindustrialisation, privatisation, austerity and Brexit. Centre for Cities Chief Executive Andrew Carter spoke to the Greater Manchester Mayor in an interview last week about his vision for English cities.
items.why: devolution concerns the structure and powers of regional decision-making tiers of government.
items.note: Local/regional government structure is classified under Elections & decision making per boundary rules.
links: Mayor of Manchester set out his stall on the importance of devolution as a blueprint for better regional governance
spoke to the Greater Manchester Mayor in an interview last week

items.h: Competition and Markets Authority delays regulation of Google’s access to news markets
items.b: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has postponed their efforts to regulate Google’s access to UK news markets by another year — a move which the Public Interest News Foundation claims will hurt local news providers. The regulation promised the opportunity for local news providers to negotiate with big tech firms for a share of the profits generated from their reporting, but this has now been put on hold by the delay.
items.why: delaying regulation of big tech's dominance over news distribution affects the plurality and sustainability of the public information environment.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation announce this year’s Tenacious Journalist Award winners
items.b: Together with Changing Ideas , the Public Interest News Foundation announced this year’s Tenacious Journalist Award winners. In a highly competitive process with over 100 applications, 9 exceptional journalists have been chosen to receive a £10k award for their proposed projects including regular 1–2–1 support with a PINF staffer and monthly cohort calls.
items.note: Award announcement is organisational news, not a change to democratic participation mechanisms.

items.h: Leicester Gazette publishes first print edition after two years
items.b: The Leicester Gazette is a fantastic example of a trailblazing award winning independent newspaper . Generating podcasts, regular local stories, local political impact and more than 200,000 unique regular readers. This winter it marked its first publication with 5,000 copies distributed across Leicestershire.
items.why: a thriving independent local newspaper sustains a plural information environment that lets residents scrutinise local political power
links: Leicester Gazette is a fantastic example of a trailblazing award winning independent newspaper

items.h: New standards for police will ensure faster communication with local media
items.b: The police have published new guidance to ensure forces can communicate effectively with the public and the media in the rapidly changing landscape of news consumption. The guidance recognises the vital role established media outlets play in informing local communities and pledges to build constructive and timely relationships with local outlets.
items.why: new guidance shaping how police share information with local media affects the public's ability to obtain meaningful information about public affairs

items.h: Tactical Tech is looking for partners to run training on investigative reporting
items.b: Tactical Tech wants to develop new resources and guidance for budding investigative journalists, including investigation guides, method tutorials and workshop curricula. They are looking for experienced journalists and researchers who can help develop this resource, focusing on areas including AI systems, the climate and information crisis, young people and big tech, and data mapping. Fill out an application form if you want to be part of this paid collaboration.
items.note: This is a call for partners/applications, similar to a funding call, not a launched resource.
links: wants to develop new resources and guidance

items.h: First ever Community Radio Week launched by radio network
items.b: From the 2nd to the 8th of February the UK Community Radio Network held a nationwide celebration of community radio. The week-long event brought together community stations from across the UK to spotlight the importance of community radio with hopes to become an annual event.
items.note: A celebratory awareness week for existing stations, not a new participation mechanism.

items.h: What would a community-first BBC look like?
items.b: With the landmark Charter-Review of the BBC underway, the Public Interest News Foundation has set out a new proposal that would put local people at the heart of the national broadcaster. Their six-part proposal recommends a new partnership agreement between the local news sector and the BBC to set the terms for how the work of local partners is used, as well as local news forums to inform this partnership.
items.why: proposals to reshape the BBC's relationship with local news partners during Charter Review bear on media plurality and public-service journalism's role in informing citizens
links: Public Interest News Foundation has set out

items.h: New book — Bad Influence: How the Internet Hijacked Our Health
items.b: Deborah Cohen discussed their new book Bad Influence: How the Internet Hijacked Our Health at the APPG on Political and Media Literacy recently. Drawing on her experience as Science Editor at ITV News and Health Correspondent at BBC Newsnight, Deborah explores how algorithmic amplification with psychological biases such as fear-driven messaging, motivated reasoning and the Barnum effect, combine to create a potent influence environment with impacts on British politics.
items.why: analysis of algorithmic amplification and psychological manipulation techniques bears on how citizens encounter and are influenced by political information
items.note: Book is framed around health but explicitly claims impacts on British politics.
links: Bad Influence: How the Internet Hijacked Our Health
APPG on Political and Media Literacy

items.h: High Court overturns ‘unlawful’ Palestine Action ban
items.b: In a landmark case the High Court has overturned the government’s proscription of Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation, deeming their categorisation ‘unlawful’. The Co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori, said the ban had massively backfired and called for the organisation to be ‘de-proscribed’. Director of Liberty, Akiko Hart, welcomed the news but said the case exposes a deeper problem about the increasingly blurred line between direct action and terrorism in the eyes of the state . Hart called for a clear definition of terrorism to be outlined to ensure civil liberties and the …
items.why: a court ruling that a government proscription was unlawful demonstrates judicial constraint on executive power and protects the boundary between lawful protest and terrorism designation
items.note: Court process/remedy places this primarily in rule of law, with protest rights as a strong secondary.
links: Please note Palestine Action is a proscribed organisation

items.b: Thousands of protesters have been arrested for holding signs saying they support Palestine Action (Photo Credit: Defend Our Juries)
items.why: mass arrests over signs of support restrict freedom of expression and assembly, core civic-space freedoms needed to contest public power

items.h: High Court upholds acquittal in Quran-burning case
items.b: The National Secular Society has welcomed the High Court’s refusal to overturn the quashing of the conviction of Hamit Coskun for burning a Quran. The court rejected an appeal from the Crown Prosecution Service to reinstate Coskun’s conviction of a religiously aggravated public order offence for burning a Quran in a protest. It said: “We are satisfied that the conclusions arrived at were rationally open to the court”.
items.why: it concerns the extent to which individuals can exercise freedom of expression and religious dissent without criminal sanction, and whether courts uphold that liberty.
items.note: Court ruling on a public order offence engaging expression/religion is filed as rights, with the adjudicating court as secondary.

items.h: Mandelson scandal prompts calls for strengthened accountability in government
items.b: The Mandelson scandal has highlighted the need to tighten the rules at the heart of government, says Open Britain . They say the scandal points to the need for four major reforms: swifter investigations to ensure abuses of power have real consequences, stronger vetting of major political appointments, a clear, enforceable mechanism to remove Peers following serious wrongdoing, and wider democratic reform to ‘stop the rot’ and ensure the public has trust in politicians.
items.why: it concerns whether abuses of power by senior office-holders face real consequences and whether appointment and removal mechanisms hold power to account.

items.h: Investigation reveals lobbying firm selling access to ministers for £30,000
items.b: An openDemocracy investigation reveals that a Labour-linked lobbying firm is selling access to government officials for up to £30,000 . Arden Strategies and Startup Coalition sent out brochures for July’s Future of Tech Summit offering tiered packages of access, including being introduced to key policymakers and attending a ‘private post-conference tech dinner’.
items.why: it exposes paid access to ministers and officials, raising questions about undue private influence over public decision-making.
links: openDemocracy investigation reveals that a Labour-linked lobbying firm is selling access to government officials for up to £30,000

items.h: Female Labour MPs call on Starmer to ‘end the boys club’ in government
items.b: Following the appointment of two men to high office with links to sex offenders, female Labour MPs are calling on Starmer to appoint a woman as First Secretary of State. The role has remained vacant since Starmer’s appointment, with Harriet Harman now urging the PM to use this as an opportunity to address misogyny at the heart of government.
items.why: it concerns how senior public appointments are made and whether they reflect standards of fairness and representation at the heart of government.
items.note: Framed as a call for a specific appointment (public office), so filed under accountability rather than rights, with gender equality as secondary.
links: Harriet Harman now urging the PM

items.h: Anti-SLAPP legislation must be included in King’s Speech, says 127-strong coalition
items.b: 127 newspaper editors, lawyers, academics, campaigners and publishers have signed an open letter to the Prime Minister calling for anti-SLAPP legislation to be included in the next King’s Speech. They describe SLAPPs as a ‘society-wide issue’ that stifles protected speech and participation, calling on the government to implement a ‘society-wide solution’ to the problem.
items.why: SLAPPs are used to suppress public-interest journalism and speech, directly affecting the plurality and freedom of the information environment.

items.h: 15 activists arrested at Quaker’s Friends House in London
items.b: 15 young activists belonging to new group Take Back Power were arrested in a raid on the London Quaker Meeting House. Take Back Power, which describes itself as a non‑violent civil resistance group, claimed responsibility for the Crown Jewels apple crumble stunt last year. A similar operation took place at the Quaker Meeting House last March, when six Youth Demand activists were arrested.
items.why: it concerns state coercion and policing against civic activists exercising freedom of assembly and dissent.
items.note: Protest policing/arrests are filed under rights per the boundary rule on state coercion.

items.h: London’s Met Police four times more likely to arrest when restricting a protest
items.b: Network for Police Monitoring has analysed a new tranche of data released by the Home Office on policing in England and Wales. They found that the Metropolitan Police accounted for 73.5% of all uses of Sections 12 and 14 protest restriction powers in 2024–25 and carried out 92% of related arrests, making it more than four times as likely to arrest under these powers as forces elsewhere in England and Wales. It was also responsible for 100% of restrictions on processions.
items.why: it documents disproportionate use of arrest powers to restrict protest, bearing directly on the practical freedom to assemble.
items.note: Protest restriction/policing data filed under rights per the boundary rule.
links: 73.5% of all uses of Sections 12 and 14 protest restriction powers

items.h: Government must help young voters assess reliable information, says Full Fact
items.b: Full Fact and Internet Matters are calling on parliament to take steps to help younger voters critically assess reliable information online. With the government preparing to lower the voting age to 16, and with only half of 13–17 year olds saying they feel confident reliably assessing the reliability of information online, the organisations say the government needs to do more to allow younger voters to participate fully and confidently.
items.why: it concerns whether young people, soon to gain the vote, can meaningfully assess political information needed to participate as informed citizens.
items.note: Core ask is about information literacy skills, with newly-enfranchised voters as secondary link to elections.

items.h: Banning social media is not the answer to online harm, say Index on Censorship
items.b: The Index on Censorship has called the government’s potential ban on social media for under 16-year-olds a ‘ knee-jerk reaction ’ that ought to be resisted. Despite agreeing with the need to address the harm caused by social media platforms, they argue that these platforms can be a lifeline for marginalised and isolated groups which can help ‘expose state violence, mobilise protest movements and even unseat autocrats.’
items.why: restricting access to social media platforms shapes the public information environment and the tools people use to mobilise, organise and hold power to account.
items.note: Concerns platforms as an information/civic-space mechanism rather than an individual's personal speech.

items.h: Man convicted after threatening to kill editor of local paper
items.b: A 34-year old man has been convicted after threatening to kill the editor of the Pembrokeshire Herald. A local man called the editor on a withheld number and issued a series of death threats to the editor and a local councillor over the publication of a recent article.
items.why: threats against journalists chill public-interest reporting and undermine the safety needed for a free press to inform public debate.

items.h: Open Data Manchester share their Deprivation vs Political Control posters
items.b: The brilliant posters produced by Open Data Manchester have already sold out, but you can print off your own copy via the free online image files of the posters . The posters display Index of Multiple Deprivation data against political control of English local authorities.
items.note: Sharing existing data visualisations is not creation of a new participation mechanism.
links: free online image files of the posters

items.b: Posters by Open Data Manchester (Credit: Open Data Manchester)

items.h: Open Knowledge Foundations marks Open Data Day 2026
items.b: On 11 March, the Open Knowledge Foundation (OKFN) is holding an online conference called ‘The Future of Open Data’ . This event is an official activity for Open Data Day 2026 and marks the start of CKAN’s 20th anniversary celebrations.
items.note: Event listing for an open-data conference; transparency/open-data as such is not a beat.

items.h: Demos call for public participation in regulating AI
items.b: A new report by Demos titled A Declaration on Digital Rights: Embedding human rights in a new deal for the digital age outlines how the current lack of safeguards around the development and use of AI is leaving the public exposed to harm. In the report they set out five recommendations for how this emerging technology should be regulated, including ensuring that there is proper public participation within tech and AI governance decision-making.
items.why: the report calls for embedding public participation into AI governance decision-making, which bears on who gets a say in exercising power over emerging technology.
items.note: Treated as advocacy for a participation mechanism rather than mere tech commentary.
links: A Declaration on Digital Rights: Embedding human rights in a new deal for the digital age

items.h: Debate in France sees possible movement towards direct democracy
items.b: The French Parliament has been seriously considering whether to hand significant power to its citizens . A proposal introduced by MP Marie Pochon calls for the introduction of three new democratic mechanisms: citizen-initiated constitutional amendments, the power for citizens to change laws before they take effect, and a legislative initiative to allow citizens to directly propose new laws. The French National Assembly is continuing to debate the proposals. See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: proposals for citizen-initiated constitutional amendments and direct legislative power are comparative evidence about how direct democracy mechanisms could reshape collective decision-making.
items.note: International comparative example of direct-democracy machinery, relevant per scope rules.
links: hand significant power to its citizens

items.h: London Legal Support Trust celebrate record-breaking 2025 Legal Walk
items.b: The London Legal Support Trust has announced that the 2025 London Legal Walk brought together 19,000 walkers for a 10k through the capital, raising £1 million for frontline free legal advice charities and making it the biggest event in the Walk’s 21-year history. A landmark moment for access to justice fundraising in the sector.
items.note: Fundraising event news about an organisation's own activity, not a mechanism of democratic power.
links: raising £1 million for frontline free legal advice charities

items.h: David Rockefeller Fund CEO makes the urgent case for longer-term democracy funding
items.b: Writing for the National Center for Family Philanthropy , Lourdes Rodríguez, CEO of the David Rockefeller Fund , argues that family and private foundations are uniquely placed to respond quickly to democracy’s needs and should embrace that nimbleness now. She makes the case that democracy funding must go well beyond electoral cycles, covering campaign finance reform, legal costs for civil society and longer grant cycles for pro-democracy organisations. Read the full piece here .
items.note: Opinion piece on funding strategy, no reported mechanism affecting UK democratic power.

items.h: Ford Foundation highlight the power of local “Civic Hubs” in rebuilding rural democracy
items.b: A new piece from the Ford Foundation profiles the Trust for Civic Life’s model of investing in locally led “Civic Hubs” — rooted, trusted organisations that bring communities together to solve shared problems and practice democratic skills from the ground up. Charlie Brown, Executive Director of the Trust for Civic Life , argues that national polarisation is best countered at the local level, and that the sector’s challenge is not a lack of ideas but chronic underfunding of community infrastructure.
items.note: Profile of an existing US funding model rather than a new UK mechanism or programme.

items.h: UK Community Foundations open expressions of interest for Lead the Change youth programme
items.b: Lead the Change, a new three-year initiative supporting young people to strengthen relationships, foster understanding and build belonging in their communities, is now open for expressions of interest . The programme is funded by a partnership of major foundations including BBC Children in Need, Co-op Foundation, Esmée Fairbairn Foundation and The National Lottery Community Fund, and will be delivered locally by 17 community foundations across the UK. Grants will be limited to one or two per eligible place. Find out more about eligibility and how to apply at ukcommunityfoundations.org .
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates new locally-delivered infrastructure to help young people build civic skills, relationships and belonging, expanding the practical means for participation.
items.note: Sector capacity-building creating new means of participation counts under participation_civic_life.

items.h: Electoral Commission registration campaign in full swing
items.b: The Electoral Commission is urging voters to register before the deadline at 11.59pm on Monday 20th April. For full details on the voter registration deadline see the EC’s media breakdown . The Electoral Commission are still looking for a Product Manager to deliver key digital projects for the Commission through this exciting period and into the future — apply now .
items.why: This matters democratically because voter registration determines who is able to exercise the franchise in an election.
links: For full details on the voter registration deadline see the EC’s media breakdown
are still looking for a Product Manager to deliver key digital projects

items.h: Democracy Club to host UK election data evening in London
items.b: Every year Democracy Club hosts SOPN Day, a massive effort by Democracy Club volunteers to collect and upload all the data on the year’s election candidates published on April 9th via the Statement of Persons Nominated. This year Democracy Club is running an event at Newspeak House in East London, an opportunity to contribute to the effort and meet the people that make it all possible — register now for today’s event .
items.why: This matters democratically because collecting and publishing official candidate nomination data underpins the electoral administration that lets voters know their choices.
items.note: Volunteer event supporting election data collection, treated as elections machinery rather than a mere listing.
links: Democracy Club is running an event at Newspeak House

items.h: Democracy Club publish full candidate data for Scottish Parliament elections
items.b: With Scottish Parliamentary elections on 7th May, Democracy Club has added all candidates to its open database, allowing voters to preview their ballot paper by entering their postcode. 437 candidates from 18 parties are contesting constituency seats, with a further 589 candidates from 27 parties standing on the regional lists. Browse the candidates at candidates.democracyclub.org.uk .
items.why: This matters democratically because publishing full candidate data lets voters know who is standing before they vote, supporting informed electoral choice.

items.b: Katie McSherry (wo)manning the stand for Elect Her at the COSLA Spring Conference this month (Photo Credit: Elect Her)

items.h: ElectHer is running fortnightly clinics ahead of local elections
items.b: ElectHer is running bi-monthly sessions to help female candidates that are running to become local councillors in May. Candidate clinics and Ask Her sessions will be available online and there are plenty more resources on their training platform to help prospective candidates. But that’s not all — this year Elect Her have also provided resources for non-candidates to get involved too , through three new toolkits, check them out now and share among your networks.
items.why: training and supporting female candidates for local council office affects who can stand and the representativeness of elected institutions
items.note: Candidate support for elections is treated as electoral machinery (candidate access) rather than generic civic capacity-building.
links: Candidate clinics and Ask Her sessions
Elect Her have also provided resources for non-candidates to get involved too

items.h: My Life My Say host Give an X Live in Hackney ahead of May elections
items.b: My Life My Say and Lime are transforming St John at Hackney Church in London into a youth democracy event on 17th April, featuring a Democracy Café, face-to-face time with decision makers and free food. The event is part of Give an X , the youth voter registration campaign calling on young people to get on the electoral roll before the 20th April deadline. Entry is free. Register now .
items.why: a campaign and event to register young people to vote before a statutory deadline directly affects electoral participation
items.note: Voter registration campaigns always sit under elections per the turnout rule.

items.h: Coventry City Council Elections Team share inclusive voter engagement work ahead of May local elections
items.b: The team at Coventry City Council’s Elections Team has been running a range of targeted voter engagement initiatives ahead of the May local elections, including anonymous registration support for survivors of domestic abuse, outreach to first-time voters, and — after significant GDPR groundwork — direct contact with voters on the sight loss register. The team is also piloting Voting Passports to help voters with disabilities access support at the polls. Martyn Harris at the Elections Team is keen to connect with anyone who has expertise in GIS or data mining for non-specialists, particularly a…
items.why: new outreach, anonymous registration and accessibility pilots directly affect who can register and vote in local elections

items.h: London Decides — New London election analysis insights site launches
items.b: Lowick Hedry in partnership with OnLondon and election expert Lewis Baston and Dave Hill, the new election guide goes borough by borough through all 32 London councils ahead of May’s local elections. With Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, Reform and independents all in play across the capital, the guide covers every candidate, every contest and every significant shift since 2022. It launches on 20th April. Sign up at londondecides.lowickhedry.com to receive it straight to your inbox.
items.why: a detailed guide to every borough contest gives voters the information needed to make informed choices in local elections
items.note: Treated as elections machinery since the guide's purpose is informing voters about specific contests, with a secondary information-environment dimension.
links: new election guide goes borough by borough through all 32 London councils
