items.h: Novara Media and Bureau of Investigative Journalism expose AI character used in far-right political campaigning
items.b: A joint investigation by Novara Media and The Bureau of Investigative Journalism has uncovered links between ‘Danny Bones’ — an AI-generated rapper with nearly three million short-form video views — and Advance UK , a far-right party led by former Reform UK co-deputy leader Ben Habib. Experts describe it as the first known case of an AI character being linked to a political party, with the character used to make interventions in February’s Gorton and Denton by-election. Shout Out UK’s Matteo Bergamini warned that such tactics will “continue to grow in regularity as we get closer to the next ge…
items.why: undisclosed AI-generated political personas used in campaigning can mislead voters and distort the information environment shaping electoral choices

items.h: Working on the Representation of the People Bill? Join the Elections Bill Hub
items.b: Kyle Taylor of Fair Vote UK and a range of organisations are working together to coordinate around the bill. If you’re working on the bill, contact Kyle to get involved .
items.note: A call to join a coordination hub is a networking notice, not a substantive report on the bill's content or effect.
links: If you’re working on the bill, contact Kyle to get involved

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project take Votes for All campaign to Parliament with mass lobby
items.b: NC29 — an amendment to extend voting rights to all UK residents has been tabled by Manuela Perteghella MP, supported by the Migrant Democracy Project . The move comes alongside growing concern about the potential threat to Commonwealth citizens’ existing voting rights, with MDP featured in a Guardian briefing on the issue . Read the amendment here . MDP are boosting the campaign and calling on their supporters to join them for a mass lobby in Parliament . To find out more or get involved, contact Lara Parizotto at lara@migrantdemos.org.uk .
items.why: it concerns who has the legal right to vote, a core determinant of inclusive suffrage in UK elections.
links: MDP featured in a Guardian briefing on the issue
join them for a mass lobby in Parliament

items.h: Elect Her and allies secure three amendments to Representation of the People Bill
items.b: Elect Her’s Annabel Mullin reports they have been working across the women’s sector to push for changes to the Representation of the People Bill, and three of their six proposed amendments are now tabled in Parliament . The amendments span a range of measures to improve women’s political representation, and the organisation is continuing to build support for all six. The amendments represent a joint effort by partners across civil society to bring these amendments, including Centenary Action , The Electoral Reform Society , The Jo Cox Foundation , 50:50 Parliament , The Online Safety Act Netwo…
items.why: the amendments would change electoral rules and candidate/representation mechanisms affecting women's access to elected office.
links: three of their six proposed amendments are now tabled in Parliament

items.h: Transparency International, Unlock Democracy, Spotlight on Corruption and UKACC to push donation cap amendment
items.b: A coalition of organisations are mobilising — including Transparency International , Spotlight on Corruption , Unlock Democracy and the UK Anti-Corruption Coalition — around an amendment to introduce a cap on political donations. Work is ongoing to align the coalition ahead of what promises to be a significant push. Watch this space and if your organisation wants to get involved, contact Tom Brake at tom.brake@unlockdemocracy.org.uk .
items.why: capping political donations directly affects the fairness and transparency of campaign finance in elections.

items.h: Unlock publish report on prisoner voting and secure tabling of franchise extension amendment
items.b: Unlock’s new report, Why Prisoner Voting Matters , sets out how the UK’s current prisoner voting arrangements damage both democracy and rehabilitation prospects. The report finds that 21,000 people in prison in England and Wales struggle to access their existing right to vote — let alone those excluded from it entirely. An amendment — NC9 — has now been tabled to extend the franchise to those serving sentences of four years or less. Read the full report here .
items.why: extending or protecting the franchise for prisoners changes who is legally entitled to vote.

items.h: Glasgow researchers warn immigration reforms will exclude a generation from civic rights
items.b: Researchers at the Glasgow Refugee, Asylum and Migration Network (GRAMNet) published a new analysis warning of long term structural exclusion of asylum seekers and refugees from civic life due to new changes doubling the qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain, a status which serves as a gateway to naturalisation and, with it, the right to vote, stand for office and participate fully in democratic life. Read openDemocracy for the full analysis .
items.why: lengthening the path to settled status delays access to the franchise and the right to stand for office for a whole cohort of residents.
items.note: Focuses on suffrage/civic rights gateway rather than general civic participation, so filed under elections.
links: Glasgow Refugee, Asylum and Migration Network (GRAMNet)
warning of long term structural exclusion of asylum seekers and refugees from civic life

items.h: Rycroft Review published on foreign financial interference in UK politics, as sector calls for government to go further
items.b: The UK Government has published the independent Rycroft Review , commissioned to examine foreign financial influence and interference in UK democracy, and has accepted recommendations to cap political donations from overseas electors at £100,000 a year and ban cryptocurrency donations. The review, led by former Permanent Secretary Philip Rycroft, identifies unlimited donations from UK voters living abroad as a clear vulnerability for foreign money to enter the political system and makes 17 recommendations in total, including new investigative powers for the Electoral Commission. Civil society …
items.why: capping donations and strengthening Electoral Commission powers directly affects the integrity and transparency of campaign finance.
items.note: Foreign interference angle also touches government accountability but the mechanism at issue is campaign finance regulation.
links: cap political donations from overseas electors at £100,000
clear vulnerability for foreign money to enter the political system

items.h: Together Alliance leads largest ever anti-far-right march through central London
items.b: Hundreds of thousands of people marched through central London on 28 March in what organisers called the biggest anti-fascist demonstration in British history . The Together Alliance, backed by around 500 groups including trade unions, antiracism organisations and civil society bodies, converged on Whitehall near the Houses of Parliament. Kevin Courtney, Chairman of the Together Alliance , told the crowd the march “gives us all confidence to carry on.” Amnesty International UK hailed the event as a “historic demonstration” by people calling for a society built on “dignity, compassion and human…
items.why: mass public demonstration reflects citizens' willingness and readiness to take part in political life and express collective voice.
items.note: Framed around turnout and readiness to demonstrate rather than policing or legal restriction, so filed under participation not rights.
links: biggest anti-fascist demonstration in British history

items.h: Democracy Drinks Edinburgh coming up
items.b: Involve’s Kelly McBride and Paul Hirmis are running regular democracy drinks events in Edinburgh, their next event is an election special on 7th May — sign up now . Contact Involve for more information .

items.h: Politics in Action celebrate Votes at 16 announcement after year-long youth-led campaign in Northern Ireland
items.b: Politics in Action have been coordinating a youth-led campaign for Votes at 16 since April 2024, with over 40 young people from across Northern Ireland meeting politicians, academics and policymakers and collaborating with Democracy Classroom on a cross-sector vision for implementation. In July, nine young campaigners travelled to London for a series of events organised by The Politics Project , culminating in the launch of the Roadmap to Votes at 16 in Parliament alongside Minister for Democracy Rushanara Ali MP — the day before the Government announced that 16 and 17-year-olds will be given …
items.why: it extends the suffrage to 16 and 17 year olds, directly expanding who can exercise the franchise in UK elections
links: short film is well worth a watch

items.h: Public Law Project hosting intensive judicial review training in London on 19 May
items.b: The Public Law Project , in partnership with Blackstone Chambers and Linklaters, is running a full-day in-person training on the fundamentals of judicial review , covering grounds for challenge, procedural steps, funding, costs and third-party interventions. The course is aimed at lawyers, NGO staff, campaigners with a legal strategy, and advisers working with marginalised groups. Tickets range from £75 for non-qualified advisers to £175 for private practice, with a discounted rate of £125 for charities and voluntary sector organisations. Register by 19 May .
items.why: it builds campaigners' and advisers' capacity to use judicial review, a legal mechanism for challenging and constraining public power
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building that creates new means to exercise a legal accountability mechanism.
links: full-day in-person training on the fundamentals of judicial review

items.h: Working in Wales? Join Democracy Group Cymru
items.b: Democracy Group Cymru is an information sharing network among organisations working in Wales, convened by Democracy Classroom and the Electoral Reform Society Cymru . So if you’re working on democracy in Wales, don’t miss out on opportunities to share your work, connect with others and collaborate — Join now .
items.note: An information-sharing network for organisations is sector admin rather than a new mechanism for public participation.

items.h: Unlock Democracy celebrate campaign success as Electoral Commission independence set to be restored
items.b: The independence of the Electoral Commission is to be restored, following sustained campaigning by Unlock Democracy, Electoral Reform Society and allies. The Electoral Commission’s independence was curtailed under the 2022 Elections Act — a move widely opposed by civil society organisations at the time — making this a notable reversal. Tom Brake at Unlock Democracy has more detail — get in touch at tom.brake@unlockdemocracy.org.uk .
items.why: restoring the Electoral Commission's independence affects the integrity and impartiality of electoral administration

items.b: Launch of new think tank Verdant Thinking (Photo Credit: Sarah Allan)
items.note: A caption about a think tank launch is organisational news, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: Verdant Thinking launch new think-tank with public participation at its core
items.b: Verdant Thinking , a new think-tank co-directed by Deborah Doane and James Meadway, launched this week with an explicit commitment to shaping its policy work through public participation from the outset. The organisation aims for small-scale, high-quality, issue-focused engagement that starts early in policy development, is iterative and genuinely inclusive — and that builds lasting relationships rather than extracting views. Their first participation-informed report is already out, advocating for a ‘Doge of the left’ .
items.note: This is primarily coverage of a new organisation launching itself, not the creation of a concrete new participation mechanism.
links: first participation-informed report is already out, advocating for a ‘Doge of the left’

items.h: Newspeak House open applications to their year-long fellowship programme
items.b: Newspeak House runs a political technology and social change residential fellowship out of their London campus and community space. Aimed at supporting mid-career technologists, the one-year programme, Introduction to Political Technology , has been running since 2015 — through which participants spend a year immersed in communities of practice — ranging from government, activism, journalism, charities and beyond — enjoying the opportunity to meet thousands of people and participate in a wide range of in-person events at Newspeak House and elsewhere — find out more and apply .
items.note: A professional fellowship for technologists reads as sector training/recruitment rather than a democratic participation mechanism.

items.h: Netpol explore the state of jury equity after landmark Court of Appeal ruling
items.b: The Network for Police Monitoring (Netpol) has published a new explainer on jury equity , the centuries-old principle that allows jurors to acquit according to conscience rather than the strict letter of the law. The piece comes after the Court of Appeal ruled in January on cases involving climate and pro-Palestine protesters . The campaign group Defend Our Juries has warned the ruling is part of a broader effort to curtail juries’ ability to acquit members of social movements. Read the full piece at netpol.org .
items.why: jury equity is a due-process mechanism allowing citizens to check prosecutorial power, and a court ruling narrowing it changes access to that check
items.note: Court ruling on protester juries sits at the boundary of rule of law and protest rights; classified by the judicial mechanism at issue.
links: Court of Appeal ruled in January on cases involving climate and pro-Palestine protesters

items.h: Our House invite sector organisations to Chartist mobilising days in Nottingham and Cardiff
items.b: Our House are running two upcoming mobilising days as part of their People’s Charter campaign, bringing together those who want to build a better democratic settlement. The Nottingham event takes place on Saturday 11th April (11am–4pm) and the Cardiff event on Friday 24th April (1–5pm). Our House also just completed a new hiring process for two new members of the campaign, congratulations to the lucky new starters!
items.note: Event listing and hiring news, not a launched participation resource.

items.h: Advocacy Academy’s Calum Green asks what makes a good organiser?
items.b: With the Advocacy Academy moving to a national footing and hiring new organising roles soon, Calum Green has published a practical framework built around four qualities of organising : curiosity about people, a clear understanding of power, focus on winning real change, and comfort with ambiguity. For youth organising in particular, he argues, supporting young people to discover their leadership potential matters more than identifying leadership that is already there.
items.why: This matters democratically because it develops practical frameworks and capacity for community organising, expanding the means by which people can take part in civic life.
items.note: Treated as a capacity-building resource rather than mere organisational news.
links: Calum Green has published a practical framework built around four qualities of organising

items.h: Act Build Change running online introduction to transformative community organising on 16th April
items.b: Act Build Change is hosting a free-to-members online workshop on 16th April introducing participants to transformative community organising, an approach that combines strategic power-building with collective care. The session covers the fundamentals of what organisers do, how to build teams and movements, and how to sustain that work over the long term. Free for Act Build Change members; £15 for everyone else .
items.why: This matters democratically because the workshop builds new capacity for community organising, expanding practical means of civic participation.
links: Free for Act Build Change members; £15 for everyone else

items.h: Hope Not Hate’s Harry Shukman wins Young Writer of the Year Award
items.b: Harry Shukman from Hope Not Hate put his life on hold to go undercover and expose the far-right in his new book — Year of the Rat. Rubbing shoulders with powerful elites pushing race science as well as the likes of Britain First, Harry spent a year inside far-right networks undercover risking his safety to expose how these groups organise, recruit and normalise extremist ideas. Harry has won the Sunday Times Young Writer of the Year Award for his book Year of the Rat .
items.note: Award win for an individual is organisational/personal news, not a reported democratic mechanism.
links: Harry has won the Sunday Times Young Writer of the Year Award for his book Year of the Rat

items.h: Books galore this month: Shout Out UK to publish new book, Man Enough
items.b: Shout Out UK work on the front lines in schools, working to equip young people with the media literacy tools they need to navigate a fractured digital world. Their new book — Man Enough — published by Souvenir Press, brings together their experience working in this space, and provides parents with a practical roadmap to help parents equip their sons against toxic ‘manfluencer’ culture. The book releases in September 2026.
items.note: Future book announcement functions as organisational publicity rather than a launched participation resource.

items.h: Democracy Matters’ Titus Alexander explores how universities can rebuild democratic culture
items.b: Titus Alexander of Democracy Matters is calling on political scientists and higher education institutions to take a more active role in strengthening democracy. His work argues for politics as social experiment , tracing democratic models from local to global scale. Titus is also working on a new edition of his 1996 book 7 Pillars of Global Apartheid , updated for the current moment. Those interested in the intersection of higher education, polarisation and democratic renewal are encouraged to get in touch directly at titusa03@gmail.com.
items.note: Personal advocacy and book-updating project without a concrete created resource or programme.
links: His work argues for politics as social experiment

items.h: Thinking Box launch six-week online course tackling disinformation, division and democracy
items.b: Thinking Box are running a practical, collaborative course exploring the disinformation crisis and its impact on democratic life. Beyond the Noise runs on Tuesday evenings (7–8.30pm) from 14th April to 19th May. Find out more and apply at thinkingbox.info/beyond-the-noise .
items.why: This matters democratically because the course creates new means for people to understand and resist disinformation's impact on democratic life, building civic capacity.
items.note: Capacity-building course counts as participation & civic life regardless of its disinformation subject matter.
links: Beyond the Noise runs on Tuesday evenings

items.h: James Sherwin-Smith launches campaign to put member democracy back on the ballot at Nationwide
items.b: With 16 million members but only 4% voting annually, Nationwide Building Society is not, its critics argue, living up to its mutual principles. James Sherwin-Smith has submitted 350 member nominations to stand on the ballot for the first time in 21 years. His campaign has secured repeated The Times coverage, and he is also working with ShareAction , the Building Societies Members Association and others to push back against government signals that would allow virtual-only AGMs, a move many in the sector see as a step backwards for member participation. James is keen to connect with others inter…
items.why: This matters democratically because it concerns member voting rights and government policy on AGM formats that shape the practical conditions for participation in mutual governance.
items.note: Private mutual governance counted because government policy on virtual AGMs directly affects conditions for member participation.

items.h: Schumacher Institute launch six-part online series on the politics of transition
items.b: The Schumacher Institute is running a series of six linked online talks exploring the systemic barriers to societal transition, led by Schumacher Fellows Jenneth Parker, Ingrid Stjernquist and Kristin Vala Ragnarsdottir. The opening session on 9th April (4–6pm) focuses squarely on democracy — examining stranded assets and the hollowing out of democratic institutions in the context of sustainability. Register for the Zoom link via info@schumacherinstitute.org.uk .
items.note: Event/webinar listing rather than a reported change or new participation tool.

items.h: Zero Hour builds nationwide campaigner network to drive constituency action on climate
items.b: Campaigning for a citizens’ assembly on climate and nature and the Climate and Nature Bill , Zero Hour has connected over 2,000 campaigners across the UK through constituency WhatsApp groups, coordinating direct MP meetings, with more than 200 meetings delivered so far. The groups are now being used to organise screenings of the newly launching National Emergency Briefing film and campaign . Contact Allan Gray at allangray@zerohour.uk to get involved.
items.why: This matters democratically because building constituency campaigner networks and coordinating direct meetings with MPs creates new civic infrastructure for people to engage with and hold representatives accountable.
items.note: The campaign's ultimate goal (a citizens' assembly) sits in elections_decision_making, but the reported mechanism here is network-building for participation.
links: newly launching National Emergency Briefing film and campaign

items.h: Climate Emergency UK report finds councils with higher spending power deliver better climate action
items.b: A new report from Climate Emergency UK reveals a clear link between local authority funding and climate performance: among single-tier and county councils in England, every £200 per capita increase in spending power is associated with a 0.8% improvement in their Action Scorecard rating. Public appetite for climate action matters too — a one percentage point rise in local support is linked to a 1.9 percentage point improvement in Scorecard performance. The findings add weight to calls for greater local government funding as a lever for meeting climate commitments. Read the full report here .
items.note: This is a climate-policy funding correlation study, not a story about how local democratic power is acquired, exercised or constrained.

items.h: Nets4Dem invite sector to high-level conference on democratic resilience in Brussels
items.b: The Nets4Dem network have invited UK democracy organisations to join them for their upcoming conference Local Action, European Impact: Strengthening Democratic Resilience in Brussels on 5th May, bringing together EU institutions, local government, civil society and researchers to explore how democratic resilience can be built from the ground up. The conference closes with the Nets4Dem Democratic Innovations Awards ceremony — Register now .
items.note: Conference invitation/event listing, sector logistics rather than a reported democratic mechanism or change.
links: Local Action, European Impact: Strengthening Democratic Resilience

items.h: Greater Manchester Combined Authority use citizens’ assembly model to reshape Live Well governance
items.b: The GM Live Well Assembly , which took place 23–25 March, brought together a diverse group randomly selected to reflect the demographics of Greater Manchester to deliberate on how decision-making and resources can shift closer to communities. Steff Riches , GMCA Participation and Insights Manager, described the experience as “pure joy,” reflecting that bringing people together consistently reaffirms that communities are “kind, caring, able to make space” and ready to take responsibility. Recommendations and next steps are expected to be published in the coming weeks.
items.why: This matters democratically because a randomly selected citizens' assembly is being used as deliberative decision-making machinery to reshape how power and resources are allocated locally.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are mapped to elections_decision_making rather than participation under the revised framework.

items.h: International Centre for Sustainability make the case for deliberative technology in UK democratic renewal
items.b: A new briefing paper from Dr Pravar Petkar at the International Centre for Sustainability argues that tools like Pol.is , Decidim and ReMesh can scale participatory and deliberative processes at lower cost than in-person assemblies, making them especially relevant at a time of pressure on public resources. The question, the paper contends, is no longer whether deliberative democracy has value but how to embed it practically and inclusively. Read the paper now or get in touch at pravar@icfs.org.uk .
items.why: This matters democratically because it addresses how deliberative and participatory decision-making processes could be scaled through technology as part of the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative process tools are mapped to elections_decision_making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Talk Shop run world’s first Agree-athon, bringing party leaders together to find common ground
items.b: Perry Walker at Talk Shop convened the leaders and chairs of five parties in Hereford last month for what is believed to be the world’s first ‘Agree-a-thon’, in which each participant proposed a contentious idea and then had to win agreement from the others. The format surfaces common ground by encouraging politicians to separate the rationale behind a policy from the policy itself. Talk Shop are now looking for collaborators to run future Agree-a-thons and partners to test new Win-Win Workouts on AI and inequality. Get in touch at perryw@talkshopuk.org.
items.why: This matters democratically because it is a new democratic-innovation format designed to build political consensus and civic capacity among political leaders.
items.note: Classified as democratic innovation/capacity-building under participation rather than elections since it concerns elite consensus-building, not electoral competition or accountability.

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy report growing momentum for PR
items.b: A wave of Labour MPs have spoken out in favour of Proportional Representation over recent months, with contributions in LabourList , PoliticsHome , Politics.co.uk and Progress . Meanwhile, Anna Dixon MP has asked ministers to consider establishing a National Commission on Electoral Reform, whilst others spoke directly in the Commons chamber during the Second Reading of the Representation of the People Bill.
items.why: This matters democratically because growing political and parliamentary momentum for proportional representation concerns the electoral system through which representatives are chosen.
links: others spoke directly in the Commons chamber

items.h: First Past The Post ‘creaking at the seams’ says Institute for Government
items.b: Hannah White, CEO of the Institute for Government argues that the Gorton & Denton by-election shows FPTP is ‘creaking at the seams’ and argues the importance of adapting the UK’s democratic system to a multiparty future. More than 50 academics and constitutional experts echoed the sentiment in recent weeks, warning that FPTP is not fit for multi-party politics.
items.why: it concerns whether the electoral system (FPTP) can produce genuinely competitive and representative outcomes as party competition fragments.
links: 50 academics and constitutional experts echoed the sentiment

items.h: DemocracyNext explore how young people’s citizens’ assemblies are reshaping democratic participation
items.b: In a new conversation hosted by DemocracyNext , CEO and Founder Claudia Chwalisz speaks with young citizens’ assembly alumni and child rights specialists about what happens when children and young people are given genuine power in democratic decision-making. Watch here .
items.why: citizens' assemblies are part of the machinery of collective decision-making beyond elections, and this discusses extending that machinery to young people.
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule, though this is a discursive video rather than a new mechanism.

items.h: Democracy Narratives Alliance publish landmark research brief on how to talk about democracy
items.b: The Democracy Narratives Alliance , a coalition of more than 35 organisations, researchers and funders, has published a major research brief synthesising evidence from nearly 400 publications on how narratives shape democratic engagement. The brief finds that while large majorities globally say they believe in democracy, record numbers feel it does not work for them, creating space for authoritarian and populist narratives to fill . It maps five dominant narrative types and offers practical guidance on values, framing, audience and messenger, concluding that coordinated, strategic narrative wo…
items.why: it addresses declining popular belief that democracy works and how narrative strategies could sustain public support for and engagement with democratic systems.
links: record numbers feel it does not work for them, creating space for authoritarian and populist narratives to fill

items.h: European Parliament approves EU’s first-ever anti-corruption law
items.b: The European Parliament has passed the Anti-Corruption Directive , establishing binding minimum definitions for nine criminal offences — including bribery, embezzlement and abuse of influence — across all member states. The move marks a significant step toward harmonised integrity standards across Europe.
items.note: EU-level anti-corruption legislation with no stated bearing on or comparison to UK democracy falls outside the UK geography scope.

items.h: Democracy for Sale reveal government spent over £1 million in legal fees fighting Freedom of Information requests
items.b: An investigation by Democracy for Sale has found that Whitehall departments spent more than £1 million on lawyers’ fees fighting Freedom of Information requests at the Information Tribunal in 2024 and 2025. The findings land as anonymously-briefed reports suggest the government may be considering tightening FOI law on national security grounds, with transparency across Whitehall already at its lowest level since records began, departments responding in full to just 29% of FOI requests in 2024. Read the full investigation at Democracy for Sale .
items.why: it shows Whitehall departments spending heavily to resist Freedom of Information requests, undermining a key mechanism for holding government answerable.
items.note: FOI here concerns institutional accountability rather than the wider information environment, so it sits in government & accountability.
links: Read the full investigation at Democracy for Sale

items.h: Protest organisers convicted under Public Order Act amid warnings of chilling effect on civil liberties
items.b: Chris Nineham, Vice-Chair of Stop the War Coalition , and Ben Jamal, Chair of the Palestinian Solidarity Campaign , were convicted at Westminster Magistrates’ Court last week, accused of inciting protesters to breach police-imposed conditions at a 2025 Palestine solidarity march. The case has raised serious concerns over diminishing protest rights . Labour MP John McDonnell said the judgment “stands as an assault on our civil liberties” and the convictions have prompted widespread warnings that prosecuting organisers for ambiguous on-the-day decisions will have a chilling effect on the willing…
items.why: the conviction of protest organisers under the Public Order Act concerns the legal restriction and policing of the right to assembly and dissent.
items.note: This is about legal restriction and policing of protest, not willingness to participate, so it sits in rights & freedoms rather than participation.
links: The case has raised serious concerns over diminishing protest rights

items.h: Netpol warn that “nobody is coming to save us” on protest rights
items.b: The Network for Police Monitoring has published a damning account of a London Assembly session on 28 March, describing it as “quite frankly, an embarrassment,” after most committee members framed demonstrations as a community threat rather than a democratic right. Deputy Mayor for Policing Kaya Comer-Schwartz offered little resistance to the Met’s increasingly draconian approach, NetPol suggested, and denied knowing about Netpol’s campaign demands despite repeated contact. Netpol conclude that resisting the crackdown is now firmly down to campaigners themselves .
items.why: it concerns policing bodies and local government framing lawful protest as a threat rather than a protected democratic freedom, affecting the legal space to assemble and dissent.

items.h: OECD find 19-point gap between anti-corruption rules and their implementation across member countries
items.b: The OECD’s Anti-Corruption and Integrity Outlook 2026 , covering 37 member and 25 partner countries, finds that while governments have strengthened their integrity frameworks, putting those frameworks into practice remains a significant challenge. Across all areas, the average gap between the strength of integrity regulations (63%) and actual implementation (44%) stands at 19 percentage points in OECD countries, with only one in four members tracking the implementation of their own anti-corruption strategies. The report calls for risk-based, results-oriented reform and greater use of digital t…
items.why: the gap between anti-corruption rules and their real-world implementation determines whether public officials can actually be held answerable for abuse of office
items.note: International/comparative OECD evidence rather than UK-specific, but bears on anti-corruption accountability generally.
links: report calls for risk-based, results-oriented reform and greater use of digital tools and AI

items.h: International Civil Society Centre map civil society responses to the global rise of anti-rights movements
items.b: Senior Programme Manager at the International Civil Society Centre Eva Gondor maps how civil society is pushing back against increasingly organised, transnational anti-rights actors reshaping democratic debate through coordinated campaigns, disinformation, and restrictive legislation. Common response strategies include strategic litigation, digital advocacy, narrative work and coalition building, but the mapping finds collective action remains fragmented and reactive. A virtual learning session on narrative change takes place on 15 April .
items.why: the operating space and organising capacity of civil society against coordinated anti-rights campaigns determines whether people can contest attempts to narrow democratic debate and rights
items.note: Global mapping of civic-space pushback, not UK-specific, and includes promotion of a learning session.
links: civil society is pushing back against increasingly organised, transnational anti-rights actors

items.h: US juries find Meta and Google liable for platform harms to children, with implications for UK regulation
items.b: Twin verdicts in US courts this month found tech giants Meta and Google liable for harms to young users on their platforms. The cases are significant not just for their scale but for their legal strategy: for the first time, a case has succeeded by targeting the architecture of the platforms themselves rather than the content users post on them . The verdicts are significant for the UK Government, which is already consulting on whether to restrict addictive design features such as infinite scroll and autoplay under powers linked to the Online Safety Act. The government has signalled it wants t…
items.why: regulatory action over addictive platform design and algorithms shapes how much unaccountable control platforms exercise over the public information environment
items.note: US verdicts feed directly into UK Online Safety Act regulatory debate over platform architecture.
links: Twin verdicts in US courts this month found tech giants Meta and Google liable for harms
platforms themselves rather than the content users post on them

items.h: Catalyst CIC shuts up shop
items.b: Catalyst CIC closed in March 2026 after a deliberate process of winding down. Catalyst shifted over its lifetime from a digital capacity-builder to a convener of the UK tech justice movement and chose to close rather than continue in a state of overstretch, citing thin reserves and a conviction that the next phase of this work should be led by grassroots, by-and-for organisations closer to the communities most affected by tech injustice. In a final reflective piece, the team was candid about the structural barriers they kept hitting : short-term funding cycles, the sector’s bias towards innova…
items.note: News about an organisation closing, not about a change in democratic participation.
links: In a final reflective piece, the team was candid about the structural barriers they kept hitting

items.h: Keep on top of union news via new tool developed by Newspeak House student
items.b: Whathaveunionsdoneforus.uk is a new tool developed by Chris Owen, a current fellowship candidate at the London College of Political Technology . The tool tracks recent union news, wins and updates. For more info, contact Chris .
items.why: a new tool tracking union activity and wins creates a fresh means for people to follow and engage with civic/workplace organising

items.h: Charity Digital Skills Report opens 2026 survey on AI adoption and digital skills
items.b: Now in its tenth year, the annual survey is the sector’s key barometer of digital and AI adoption across UK charities. It takes 15 minutes, all questions are optional, and there’s a chance to win £300 unrestricted funding for your organisation. Take part here: surveymonkey.com/r/CDSR2026
items.note: A sector survey call, not a change affecting participation.

items.b: Join the Democracy Club Slack , the home of election technologists and civic tech practitioners working to support voting systems across the UK.
items.note: A membership invitation to an existing Slack community, akin to sector logistics rather than a new mechanism.

items.h: Unhack Democracy analyse the upcoming Hungarian elections
items.b: Zsofia Banuta and the team at Unhack Democracy performed a scenario analysis exercise together with Tactical Voting and explored the possible situations that might arise from election day in Hungary. Zsofi discusses the results with the Hungarian Népszava newspaper . See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: scenario analysis of election-day dynamics bears on the credibility and machinery of competitive elections, offering comparative evidence relevant to assessing electoral risk

items.h: UK Community Foundations open expressions of interest for Lead the Change youth programme
items.b: Lead the Change, a new three-year initiative supporting young people to strengthen relationships, foster understanding and build belonging in their communities, is now open for expressions of interest . The programme is funded by a partnership of major foundations including BBC Children in Need, Co-op Foundation, Esmée Fairbairn Foundation and The National Lottery Community Fund, and will be delivered locally by 17 community foundations across the UK. Grants will be limited to one or two per eligible place. Find out more about eligibility and how to apply at ukcommunityfoundations.org .
items.note: Youth relationship-building and belonging programme lacks a clear democratic participation or civic-life mechanism.

items.h: Changing Ideas offer £20,000 to support tenacious campaigners through annual awards scheme, nominations close 15 May
items.b: The Tenacious Campaigner Awards , an initiative of Changing Ideas , are offering £20,000 in flexible funding to individual campaigners or small campaign teams, alongside tailored coaching, peer community access, legal and journalistic networks, and wellbeing support. This year the scheme is particularly keen to hear from campaigners holding corporates to account for harm, those working to prevent avoidable deaths, and campaigners based in Scotland. Nominations, which must come from someone familiar with the campaigner’s work rather than the campaigner themselves, closes 15 May 2026. Nominate a…
items.why: this matters democratically because it provides funding and capacity-building support that helps individual campaigners sustain civic action and hold power to account.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building that expands means of civic participation.

items.h: Democracy Re:Boot Camp 2026 opens fully funded applications for young European democracy practitioners, deadline 7 June
items.b: D-Hub’s Democracy Re:Boot Camp returns to the island of Cres, Croatia, 24–28 September, bringing together 30 young people aged 18–28 from across Europe working in organising, journalism, civil society, research or emerging political roles for five days of practical skills, strategic thinking and peer exchange. This year’s edition is anchored around D-Hub’s Anti-Authoritarian Toolkit and is fully funded, covering travel, accommodation and meals. Applications are open to all for the first time and close 7 June. Apply now at democracyreboot.camp .
items.why: this matters democratically because it builds the skills and networks of young people working in civic organising and democracy practice, expanding capacity for civic participation.
items.note: Pan-European rather than UK-specific programme, so UK relevance is indirect.

items.h: Cambridge symposium on protest and peaceful assembly brings together UN Special Rapporteur, Amnesty International and leading scholars
items.b: The Centre of Governance and Human Rights at Cambridge yesterday hosted a full-day symposium on the legal, political and practical dimensions of the right to peaceful assembly, featuring Gina Romero, UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights to Freedom of Peaceful Assembly, alongside legal scholars examining how states regulate and restrict protest. The day concluded with an evening panel and book launch for the Oxford Handbook of Peaceful Assembly , which also featured climate activist Roger Hallam. The symposium was timely given the context of the passage of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which …
items.note: An academic symposium/event listing rather than reporting or capacity-building; touches on protest rights but is sector logistics.

items.h: Public Law Project hosting intensive judicial review training in London on 19 May
items.b: The Public Law Project , in partnership with Blackstone Chambers and Linklaters, is running a full-day in-person training on the fundamentals of judicial review , covering grounds for challenge, procedural steps, funding, costs and third-party interventions. The course is aimed at lawyers, NGO staff, campaigners with a legal strategy, and advisers working with marginalised groups. Tickets range from £75 for non-qualified advisers to £175 for private practice, with a discounted rate of £125 for charities and voluntary sector organisations. Register by 19 May .
items.why: This matters democratically because it builds practical capacity for lawyers, campaigners and marginalised groups to use judicial review, a key mechanism for challenging public power.
items.note: Counted as capacity-building (a training course) rather than mere event logistics.
links: full-day in-person training on the fundamentals of judicial review

items.h: Hope for the Future host sessions on the new Senedd and counter-lobbying this May
items.b: Hope for the Future is running two sessions to help advocates engage with the new Senedd during its crucial first 100 days. They are also hosting a counter-lobbying workshop exploring how people power and democratic engagement can push back against corporate lobbying. Register for the Senedd evening session on the 26 May , and the counter-lobbying workshop on 21st May.
items.why: This matters democratically because it builds advocates' capacity to engage with a newly formed devolved legislature and to counter corporate lobbying, shaping who has effective voice in decision-making.
items.note: Treated as capacity-building workshops under the sector-training rule rather than plain event logistics.

items.h: UCL Policy Lab convene Ecosystem conference, 28 May
items.b: The UCL Policy Lab’s Ecosystem Project is hosting a half-day conference on 28 May, 12:30–4:30pm at UCL East in London, bringing together Miatta Fahnbulleh MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Devolution, Faith and Communities, alongside US scholars Hahrie Han and Gary Gerstle and Australian organiser Amanda Tattersall to explore how progressive movements build power in a contested political moment. Join the waitlist here , or register for the evening community celebration on the same day.
items.note: A discussion conference rather than a course, tool or resource that creates new means of participation.
links: register for the evening community celebration

items.h: Jim Coe and Natasha Adams launch report on NGO responses to far-right authoritarianism, online 20 May
items.b: Following their Meeting the Moment paper, consultants Jim Coe and Natasha Adams are launching “Towards Meaningful Action,” exploring why social change NGOs are struggling to respond fully to far-right authoritarianism and how to address that. Join the online launch on Wednesday 20 May, 10–11:30am BST. Register here .
items.note: A report launch event about an organisation's own research, closer to organisational news than a new participation mechanism.

items.h: Our House to host new event on Building a Disabled People’s Charter, 9 June
items.b: Our House’s June 9th event starts with the a simple basis: any work that claims to speak for disabled people must also include the voices of people with learning disabilities and autistic people. Full stop. That’s why they’re bringing together key voices on Disability rights in the UK , disability rights advocate Martyn Sibley and #MyVoteMyVoice Project Lead Lxx Garcia , together with Mara Livermore , co-lead at Our House to explore the case for a new Disabled People’s Charter. Sign up now!
items.note: An event exploring the case for a charter, not itself a course, tool or campaign creating new participation capacity.

items.h: Migrant Voice host community events across London and Scotland as part of A Million Acts of Hope week
items.b: Migrant Voice are hosting two community gatherings this month as part of A Million Acts of Hope week: “Give Hope a Voice” yesterday in London, a community evening of writing, music and dance with emerging migrant writers in partnership with TogetherintheUK , and “Acts of Kindness” on 20 May online for their Glasgow and Scottish community, where participants will share stories of care and connection and co-create a zine. Sign up for their events here.
items.note: Community cultural gatherings for migrants without a clear democratic decision-making or accountability mechanism at stake.

items.h: Roger Macnair and Luke Flegg convene deliberative democracy symposium
items.b: Roger Macnair and Luke Flegg brought together around 70 organisations from across the UK’s deliberative and participatory democracy ecosystem in London last month for a first-of-its-kind gathering designed to help the deliberative sector better understand itself and begin coordinating more effectively. The event saw participants vote on lightning talks, World Café discussion tables and open space breakouts, with participants encouraged to swap contacts and identify concrete next steps for working across organisational silos.
items.note: A sector networking event/convening rather than a new participation mechanism or resource for the public.

items.h: Bureau of Investigative Journalism launches photography exhibition on offshore financial secrecy
items.b: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism has opened Voices for Transparency , a free exhibition putting human faces to the harm caused by hidden ownership in British Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies. Building on their Enablers project , launched in summer 2020, investigates how the UK and its Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories enable oligarchs, dictators and criminals around the world. Timed to coincide with the UK’s Illicit Finance Summit in June, the exhibition celebrates the role of investigative journalism. The exhibit runs at The Guild Church of St Katharine Cree in Lond…
items.note: An awareness-raising exhibition/event rather than a change to accountability mechanisms or public information infrastructure.

items.h: Open Rights Group warn of national security risk from UK’s reliance on Big Tech
items.b: Open Rights Group have published Tech Giants and Giant Slayers: The Case for Digital Sovereignty and the Digital Commons , the first UK report to make a comprehensive case for a national digital sovereignty strategy. It argues that dependence on a handful of foreign tech corporations for critical digital infrastructure has become an urgent security concern, pointing to the US government’s recent use of tech sanctions against the International Criminal Court, which led Microsoft to shut down email and online banking facilities for ICC members , as a live example of the leverage foreign powers c…
items.why: This matters democratically because reliance on foreign-controlled technology infrastructure could allow foreign powers to exert leverage over UK government functions, undermining the principle that elected UK institutions determine government policy free of external control.

items.h: AI & Democracy Foundation launch Democratic Capabilities Gap Map for the deliberative democracy field
items.b: The AI & Democracy Foundation have published a new open database, the Democratic Capabilities Gap Map , tracking 51 capabilities, 259 research questions, 16 product gaps and 160 resources to identify what it would take to make deliberative democracy ‘truly excellent’ and where the field currently falls short. The resource is designed to help funders, researchers and practitioners direct effort and money toward the gaps that matter most, as enthusiasm and investment in deliberative democracy continues to grow. Explore the map and submit contributions at democracybuild.org .
items.why: This matters democratically because the tool is designed to strengthen the deliberative-democracy field's capacity, directing resources toward improving citizens' assemblies and other collective decision-making processes.
items.note: Deliberative democracy is classified under elections & decision making per framework rules, and the launch of a field-building resource counts as sector capacity-building.

items.h: Carnegie UK find nearly half of MPs believe deliberative democracy undermines their role in new survey of elected members
items.b: Carnegie UK have published new research surveying 203 elected members across Westminster, Holyrood, Stormont and the Senedd on their attitudes to deliberative democracy, finding that 45% of MP respondents believe deliberative processes lack democratic mandates and duplicate the role of elected representatives, while only 21% felt Westminster could act upon their findings. Adam Milne, Senior Policy Advocate at Carnegie UK, argues the findings point to a deeper structural problem in which deliberative processes sit outside the normal machinery of government. Carnegie UK’s forthcoming publication…
items.why: This matters democratically because it surfaces elected representatives' doubts about the mandate and integration of deliberative processes within the machinery of collective decision-making.
items.note: Deliberative democracy and its relationship to elected representatives falls under elections & decision making per framework rules.

items.h: V-Dem Institute names the UK a new autocratiser in its 2026 Democracy Report
items.b: The V-Dem Institute at the University of Gothenburg has classified the UK as one of ten newly identified autocratising countries in its annual Democracy Report 2026 , placing it alongside Croatia, Italy, Slovakia and Slovenia in a group of five European nations newly added to the watchlist. The report, now in its tenth edition, finds that global democracy has regressed to 1978 levels, with 74% of the world’s population now living in autocracies and media censorship identified as the most common tactic used by backsliding governments. Read the full report .
items.why: This matters democratically because being newly classified as autocratising signals a measured weakening of checks on executive power, civil liberties and media freedom in the UK according to a leading comparative democracy index.
items.note: Autocratization spans multiple beats; government accountability chosen as the closest framework anchor for overall regime backsliding.

items.h: Reporters Without Borders ranks UK 18th in 2026 World Press Freedom Index amid global low
items.b: The UK has placed 18th of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index , as global press freedom hits a 25-year low. Key UK flags included transnational threats against Iranian journalists in exile in the UK, SLAPPs aimed at gagging reporters, sustained job cuts, mounting pressure on the BBC and a national newspaper market dominated by just three companies: News UK, Reach, and DMGT. Worldwide, more than half of all countries are now classed as “difficult” or “very serious” for journalism, with the legal indicator showing the sharpest fall. Read the UK Press Freedo…
items.why: This matters democratically because press freedom rankings measure journalists' ability to report on public affairs without intimidation, legal harassment or excessive ownership concentration, which underpins a plural information environment.
links: Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index

items.h: D-HUB launch Anti-Authoritarian Toolkit fight back against democratic backsliding
items.b: Democracy Hub (D-HUB) have launched the Anti-Authoritarian Toolkit , compiling tactics and strategies for resisting “elected authoritarianism” and strengthening democracies. The toolkit includes an Authoritarian Playbook naming the patterns deployed by leaders from Trump to Orbán, a Democratic Playbook curating over 50 counter-tactics, a dedicated volume on Get Out the Vote strategies, and a companion podcast series featuring frontline democracy defenders. Nika Kovač, Executive Director of D-HUB, says the goal is to give practitioners “the tools to engage, inspire, and turn people into agents …
items.why: it creates a new resource equipping practitioners and citizens with tactics to resist democratic backsliding and increase civic participation.
items.note: Toolkit spans multiple beats (GOTV, rights) but its core purpose is building civic capacity to act.

items.h: Working in Wales? Join Democracy Group Cymru
items.b: Democracy Group Cymru is an information sharing network among organisations working in Wales, convened by Democracy Classroom and the Electoral Reform Society Cymru . So if you’re working on democracy in Wales, don’t miss out on opportunities to share your work, connect with others and collaborate — Join now .
items.note: An information-sharing network among organisations is sector admin, not a new means of public participation.

items.h: UK Government opens call for evidence on 7th Open Government National Action Plan
items.b: The government is seeking ideas from civil society and the public for its next National Action Plan for Open Government , covering transparency, accountability, open data, digital governance and public participation, with no limit on the number of submissions. Find out more information about you can submit your ideas .
items.why: the consultation shapes government commitments on transparency, open data and accountability mechanisms that let citizens hold power to account.
items.note: Consultation on an accountability plan; participation is the mechanism but the substance is government transparency.
links: National Action Plan for Open Government

items.h: My Vote My Voice recruiting Democracy Champions
items.b: My Vote My Voice , the campaign run by United Response , Dimensions , Mencap and Ambitious about Autism , is recruiting its next cohort of Democracy Champions to help people with learning disabilities and autistic people take part in elections. Champions, who can be support workers, volunteers, teachers or community organisers, will receive a half-day training session this summer (in-person or online), a toolkit of guides and activities, a certificate, and a grant for delivering sessions in their communities. Travel and care costs are covered and the programme is funded by the Electoral Commis…
items.why: it builds capacity to help people with learning disabilities and autistic people exercise their right to vote, addressing accessibility of the franchise.
items.note: Programme aims at electoral participation/turnout among an underrepresented group, so filed under elections per the turnout rule.
links: recruiting its next cohort of Democracy Champions

items.h: Newspeak House open applications to their year-long fellowship programme
items.b: Newspeak House runs a political technology and social change residential fellowship out of their London campus and community space. Aimed at supporting mid-career technologists, the one-year programme, Introduction to Political Technology , has been running since 2015 — through which participants spend a year immersed in communities of practice — ranging from government, activism, journalism, charities and beyond — enjoying the opportunity to meet thousands of people and participate in a wide range of in-person events at Newspeak House and elsewhere — find out more and apply .
items.note: A career fellowship for technologists is professional development, not a mechanism for public democratic participation.

items.b: ‘Not Your Usual Hustings’ at Dowlais Community Centre, Merthyr (Credit: Boys and Girls Clubs of Wales)
items.why: hustings events allow voters to directly engage with and question candidates seeking office.
items.note: Minimal content (caption only) but topic is an electoral campaigning event.

items.h: Democracy Club publish complete 2026 English local election results dataset covering 18.5 million votes
items.b: Democracy Club have completed their post-election data collection and published the full results of the 2026 English local elections, covering 18.5 million votes cast across all candidates, assembled by their volunteer contributor network from nomination papers and count returns. The dataset, which powers WhoCanIVoteFor and is used by the Electoral Commission , the House of Commons Library and national media, is free to download from the candidates database and represents a decade of local election data that Democracy Club has now built. Review and download the full dataset . Want to get invol…
items.why: publishing a complete, verifiable dataset of local election results supports electoral transparency and underpins tools used by electoral bodies and the public.
links: Review and download the full dataset

items.h: Electoral services teams across the UK complete most complex local elections in years
items.b: As the headlines focus on the results of the 7 May local elections, Laura Burrell , Electoral Services Manager at Kirklees Council , has spoken for many in the profession in paying tribute to the electoral administration workforce behind the count . All-out elections following ward boundary changes are among the most complex polls to deliver, and Burrell described her team’s achievement as the product of “months of late nights, weekends and hours together.” A timely reminder that free and fair elections depend on dedicated public servants working largely out of sight.
items.why: the competence and capacity of electoral administration staff directly determines whether elections are run freely and fairly.

items.h: Who Targets Me find Reform UK’s digital campaign has ‘professionalised’ dramatically since 2024
items.b: Election ad-tracking project Who Targets Me have published new analysis showing Reform UK’s online operation has scaled up sharply during the local, Scottish and Welsh election campaigns. Reform’s main Facebook page ran around 40 ad variations during the 2024 general election, but has run roughly 2,300 in the last month alone, briefly outspending Labour on Meta in the week of 21–28 April, they say. The party is also targeting at postcode level for the first time and routing the bulk of spend through the central party page rather than Nigel Farage personally, who is now outspent by the main acc…
items.why: This matters democratically because campaign spending, targeting and advertising practices affect the fairness and transparency of competition between parties for votes.
items.note: Digital campaign spend/targeting sits at the boundary of campaign finance (elections) and political advertising (information); classified by the campaign-finance mechanism.
links: published new analysis showing Reform UK’s online operation has scaled up sharply

items.h: Jo Cox Foundation warns candidate abuse in May elections worst on record
items.b: Candidates across parties describe a climate of abuse during this year’s local and devolved elections , including death threats and intimidation, with the Green party calling 2026 the worst campaign year in memory. Olivia Field, Chief Executive of the Jo Cox Foundation , said: “Increasingly, people do not feel safe enough to fully participate in politics. Some are choosing not to stand at all, while others are self-censoring or limiting how they engage with voters.” The Electoral Commission will publish its full findings on abuse and intimidation from the 2026 elections in the autumn.
items.why: This matters democratically because intimidation of candidates deters people from standing for office, narrowing political competition and representativeness.
items.note: Candidate safety is filed under elections because it affects willingness to stand, with personal security as a secondary rights dimension.
links: Candidates across parties describe a climate of abuse during this year’s local and devolved elections

items.h: Boys’ and Girls’ Clubs of Wales bring 55 young people face-to-face with Senedd election candidates at youth hustings
items.b: Boys’ and Girls’ Clubs of Wales hosted a ‘Not Your Usual Hustings’ at Dowlais Community Centre on 17 April, bringing 55 young people into roundtable discussions with representatives from seven parties ahead of the Senedd elections, in partnership with Swansea MAD and supported by Cavendish Cymru . Funded through the Welsh Government’s Democratic Engagement Grant , the event used a photo booth, mock voting station and informal activities to create an accessible environment for young people from a range of backgrounds, with additional support from Promo Cymru and the Senedd Commission .
items.why: This matters democratically because it creates new opportunities for young people to engage directly with candidates and understand the electoral process.
links: Boys’ and Girls’ Clubs of Wales

items.h: Electoral Commission confirm smooth polls but flag voter ID data gap and candidate safety concerns ahead of autumn report
items.b: The Electoral Commission described polling day across England, Scotland and Wales as having run smoothly , with more than 17,000 polling places, 25,000 candidates and counts taking place across Great Britain. However, the Commission notes there is currently no legal duty for returning officers in England to collect and report data on the impact of voter ID, meaning the full picture will depend on voluntary local authority disclosure, with the Commission publishing its findings in the autumn.
items.why: This matters democratically because gaps in monitoring voter ID's impact affect the ability to assess and safeguard access to voting.
links: polling day across England, Scotland and Wales as having run smoothly

items.h: Council of Europe observers record voters turned away under voter ID rules
items.b: The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe , conducting its first ever observation mission to the UK, found polling day calm and orderly, with highly committed staff and a high level of trust in electoral processes among voters, candidates and staff. However, observers noted ballot booth layouts were too narrow to guarantee secrecy of the vote, and in England some voters were turned away due to photo ID requirements, while some polling station staff were uncertain about observers’ rights to ask questions. The observers included politicians from Ireland, Poland, Ger…
items.why: This matters democratically because independent observation of polling practices, including voters turned away under ID rules, bears directly on the fairness and accessibility of elections.
links: The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe
highly committed staff and a high level of trust in electoral processes

items.h: The Politics Project support youth hustings and launch #ElectionCountdown resources ahead of 2026 elections
items.b: From Cardiff to Cardigan, The Politics Project’s Host a Hustings Cymru programme , funded by the Welsh Government, helped teachers and youth practitioners organise and deliver their own youth hustings events for the 2026 Senedd elections, providing bilingual resource packs, candidate liaison support and training for young chairs. Their #ElectionCountdown programme , consisting of eight short modules, supported young people across the country to follow elections, register to vote, and learn about candidates and manifestos.
items.why: This matters democratically because these resources build young people's capacity to register, vote and engage with candidates and manifestos.
items.note: Registration content touches elections, but the primary mechanism is civic capacity-building.

items.h: Senedd Explained reach over one million users with volunteer-led 2026 Senedd Election coverage
items.b: Senedd Explained , the civic education platform dedicated to making Welsh politics accessible, deployed a team of volunteers to count locations across Wales on results day last week to deliver live on-the-ground analysis and vox pops with candidates from all six parties elected to the Senedd. Maddy Dhesi, Co-Founder at Senedd Explained, reported that the organisation’s April-May election content reached over one million users, with at least half of that figure recorded on results day alone. Follow Senedd Explained for further analysis and coverage still to come.
items.why: This matters democratically because volunteer-led civic education content helps the public follow and understand election results and candidates.
items.note: Reach statistics are close to organisational promotion, but the underlying activity is civic information provision, so it is treated as capacity-building rather than org news.

items.h: Widespread tactical voting took place during elections, from Hull to Holyrood
items.b: Campaign groups issued tactical voting advice for all but one of the 19 seats contested in Hull, urging voters to back whichever candidate was best placed to beat Reform UK. YouGov research prior to the elections found that 57% of current Green supporters said they would vote tactically for Labour in a direct contest between Labour and Reform, rising to 67% who would switch to the Liberal Democrats in the same scenario. The picture was more complex in Wales, where Nation Cymru and academics from Cardiff University’s Wales Governance Centre noted that the new closed-list proportional system mak…
items.why: This matters democratically because tactical voting behaviour and the design of electoral systems shape how votes translate into political competition and outcomes.

voters to back whichever candidate was best placed to beat Reform

items.h: ADSO opens nominations for its 2026 Democratic Services Awards
items.b: The Association of Democratic Services Officers (ADSO) is inviting nominations for its annual awards, recognising outstanding individuals and teams across the democratic services sector. Categories cover everything from newcomers making an early impact to long-serving professionals who have made a distinguished contribution to local democracy. Nominations close on Friday 22 May, ahead of the ADSO Conference and Awards taking place on 10–11 September. Make your nomination now .
items.note: Sector awards/nomination admin, not a democracy mechanism.

items.h: The Advocacy Academy opens recruitment across seven roles in a major hiring push
items.b: The Brixton-based youth organising charity, Advocacy Academy , which trains young people with lived experience of injustice to drive long-term systemic change, is recruiting for positions spanning organising, campaigns, programme and operations. Roles on offer include a Community Organiser, Head of Digital Organising & Communications, Head of- and Associate Director of Organising & Campaigns (two posts), Head of Spacemaking and Operations, Head of Programme (mat cover), and Senior Leads for their Gender and Climate Coalitions. Deadlines start 18 May 2026 onwards. Browse the full listings on Ch…
items.note: Job listings, excluded as organisational news.

items.h: Bright Blue launches European affiliate to tackle cross-national policy challenges
items.b: Bright Blue , the UK liberal conservative think tank, has established a European arm, Bright Blue Europe , to work on policy issues that require cooperation between multiple national governments, including immigration, populism, energy and democracy. The new outfit is co-founded by Bartek Staniszewski , previously Head of Research at Bright Blue, and Lukas Wick, formerly of the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung , and has affiliates in Germany, Poland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK. A welcome addition for those tracking centre-right thinking on cross-border challenges.
items.note: Launch of a think tank affiliate is organisational news, not a change to democratic mechanisms.

items.h: Thinking Box running six-week online course tackling disinformation, division and democracy
items.b: Thinking Box are running a practical, collaborative course exploring the disinformation crisis and its impact on democratic life. Beyond the Noise runs on Tuesday evenings (7–8.30pm) and has been running from 14th April and will run to 19th May. Find out more and apply at thinkingbox.info/beyond-the-noise .
items.why: it creates a new means for members of the public to build capacity to understand and resist disinformation's effects on democratic life
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation, though the topic (disinformation) also touches the information beat.

items.h: Center for Countering Digital Hate hiring a Research Officer
items.b: The Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) are recruiting a Research Officer to join their UK team, producing written research on digital hate, misinformation and online harms. Applications close on 18 May — Apply now

items.b: Professor Meg Russell is stepping down as Director of the UCL Constitution Unit , a position she has held since 2015. She will be succeeded by Professor Alan Renwick. items.h: Transparency International UK opens membership to new supporters
items.b: Transparency International UK hosted a spring reception in central London last week for its growing community of individual members, looking ahead to a year that takes in June’s Illicit Finance Summit in London, renewed efforts on standards in public life, and the case for stronger governance of rising defence spending across Europe. Daniel Bruce, Chief Executive of Transparency International UK, said members “play an important role in our independence and governance, helping to shape our future.” Sign up as a TIUK member today .

items.h: Unlock Democracy coordinate three campaigns around the Representation of the People Bill and want your help
items.b: Unlock Democracy are coordinating across three fronts as the Representation of the People Bill progresses: working with Transparency International , Spotlight on Corruption and UK Anti-Corruption Coalition to secure a donation cap amendment; pushing the government to commit to a timetable for automatic voter registration that ensures it is in place before the next general election; and supporting a campaign to improve the voting system for UK overseas voters so more ballots are received in time to be counted. If your organisation wants to get involved in any of these campaigns, contact Tom Bra…
items.why: the campaigns target donation caps, automatic voter registration timetables and overseas ballot handling, all mechanisms determining who can vote and how political money is limited.

items.h: Fair Vote UK coordinate joint civil society campaign on political finance ahead of Representation of the People Bill third reading
items.b: Kyle Taylor at Fair Vote UK is pulling together a coalition campaign, which the organisation is calling “Politics Not For Sale,” to push for stronger donation limits in the Representation of the People Bill before its third reading, after Fair Vote UK argued in a recent briefing that the government’s proposed £1 million donation cap “accommodates” rather than addresses the concentration of financial influence in British politics. Organisations interested in joining the coalition can fill in the campaign form and contact Fleur, Campaign Coordinator at Fair Vote UK, at fleur@fairvote.uk.
items.why: it concerns statutory limits on political donations, a safeguard against concentrated financial influence over party competition.
links: joining the coalition can fill in the campaign form

items.h: Centenary Action and partners press DWP minister for clear timeline on disabled candidates fund
items.b: Centenary Action , Disability Rights UK , Girlguiding and the Disability Policy Centre met Sir Stephen Timms MP, Minister of State for Social Security and Disability, last week to discuss barriers facing disabled women seeking elected office. The minister indicated the government’s new fund for disabled candidates should be in place by the end of the year, ahead of the May 2027 elections, but the coalition pressed for a published timeline and for the fund to be placed on a statutory footing through the Representation of the People Bill . They also called for the long-delayed Section 106 of the…
items.why: it concerns whether disabled women have practical access to standing for elected office, and whether that access is protected in law.

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy say results prove First Past the Post has reached breaking point
items.b: Following the May local elections, Labour for a New Democracy have called on the government to urgently establish a National Commission on Electoral Reform , arguing that results across England demonstrated First Past the Post handing majorities to parties on minority vote shares and producing outcomes that are, in the words of Professor Alan Renwick “simply indefensible.” The campaign says a strong caucus of pro-PR Labour MPs is now coordinating through the APPG on Fair Elections and will use the Representation of the People Bill to press for the commission when Parliament returns. Read their…
items.why: it concerns whether the electoral system fairly translates votes into seats and representation, a core question of political competition.
links: Labour for a New Democracy have called on the government to urgently establish a National Commission on Electoral Reform

items.h: CWU backs proportional representation at annual conference, taking pro-PR union Labour affiliates to three quarters
items.b: The Communication Workers’ Union voted at its annual conference on 10 May to back proportional representation, committing the union to reject First Past the Post , support a form of PR that maintains the constituency link, and call on the government to establish an independent Commission on Electoral Reform. Labour for a New Democracy , which worked with union activists to table a motion to CWU conference back in 2022 that triggered a policy review, reports that trade unions representing three quarters of Labour affiliates now back PR, including Unite, Unison, ASLEF, Usdaw and the FBU.
items.why: it reports a shift in organised political support for changing the electoral system used to choose representatives.
links: back proportional representation, committing the union to reject First Past the Post

items.h: Open Britain call for donation caps as Electoral Commission weighs formal investigation into Farage’s £5m gift
items.b: In 2024, Nigel Farage received a £5 million personal gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, and did not declare it at the time; the Electoral Commission is now deciding whether to open a formal investigation, and the matter has been separately referred to Parliament’s standards watchdog. Open Britain argue the case illustrates a wider structural failure, noting that Harborne has donated a reported £12 million to Reform UK across 2025 and early 2026, and that the Representation of the People Bill currently passing through Parliament still contains no meaningful cap on…
items.why: it concerns an undeclared large political donation and the adequacy of donation caps, mechanisms meant to limit concentrated financial influence over elections.

items.b: Quakers in Britain’s Billy Vaughn speaks against the Crime and Policing Bill (Credit: Quakers in Britain)
items.why: it highlights faith-community opposition to legislation restricting the right to protest, a core civil liberty needed to challenge public power.

items.h: Crime and Policing Act 2026 becomes law
items.b: The Crime and Policing Act 2026 has passed into law , introducing a new duty on senior police officers to consider the cumulative impact of repeat protests in the same location when deciding whether to impose conditions, meaning peaceful demonstrations could be restricted not on their own merits but because of previous unrelated protests in the same area. The Act, the third piece of anti-protest legislation in recent years, was passed after MPs voted on 532 amendments in a single day , raising serious concerns about the depth of parliamentary scrutiny given the serious implications for civil l…
items.why: a new statutory power lets police restrict peaceful protests based on unrelated past demonstrations, narrowing the legal space for assembly and dissent.
items.note: Also raises parliamentary scrutiny concerns over rushed amendment process.
