government’s own factsheet on the new law

items.h: Migrant Democracy Project bring 100+ residents to Parliament in mass lobby for Votes for All
items.b: Over 100 residents met with 24 MPs at Parliament on 20 April, organised by Migrant Democracy Project to demand an amendment to the Representation of the People Bill 2026 extending voting rights to all UK residents. Katie, Community Organiser at Migrant Democracy Project, writing in a guest blog for Make Votes Matter last month warned that over 4.4 million people are currently excluded from general elections and over 1.2 million cannot vote at all, and that a counter-amendment to remove the Commonwealth vote entirely makes the fight to defend and extend the franchise urgent.
items.why: campaigners are lobbying to extend or defend suffrage to millions of UK residents currently excluded from voting, directly affecting who can choose representatives.
items.note: Franchise extension sits in elections; the mass lobby event itself touches participation.

items.h: Shared Future CIC warn Pride in Place risks replicating top-down consultation culture without democratic reform
items.b: Jez Hall at Shared Future CIC has published a blog and ten-step guide arguing that the government’s new £5 billion Pride in Place programme , which offers up to £20 million each to over 300 communities over ten years, risks filling gaps left by austerity without achieving a genuine shift of power to residents, if participatory budgeting is not embedded from the start. Read the blog and Jez’s ten recommendations here .
items.why: it concerns whether a major community funding programme genuinely embeds participatory budgeting and shifts power to residents rather than replicating top-down consultation.
items.note: Participatory budgeting and consultation culture are explicitly participation-beat territory.

items.h: Republic lead march on Buckingham Palace calling for abolition of the monarchy
items.b: Over 300 campaigners joined Republic’s Republic Day march on 9 May , marching from Trafalgar Square to the gates of Buckingham Palace to call for abolition of the monarchy, with Graham Smith, Republic’s Chief Executive, noting a significant shift in public sentiment since the death of Queen Elizabeth II. Writer Otto English, speaking at the Trafalgar Square rally, drew a direct link between the local election results and a democracy “broken to such an extent that it needs fixing right to the top.” Demonstrations also took place in Edinburgh and at locations across the UK. View the photos of th…
items.why: it reflects citizens' willingness to demonstrate and voice demands for constitutional change, a measure of civic participation.
items.note: Framed as a demonstration of public readiness to protest rather than a policing/restriction story.

View the photos of the London march

items.h: Transparency International UK calls on incoming MSPs to strengthen Scotland’s lobbying register
items.b: Juliet Swann, Nations & Regions Programme Manager at Transparency International UK , says an early test for Scotland’s new parliamentarians will be whether they tighten the country’s lobbying transparency register, which she notes is a UK outlier simply by existing. Contributing to a Ferret investigation by Karin Goodwin that mapped more than 29,000 lobbying meetings over the last parliamentary term, Swann argues reporting should be extended beyond face-to-face communications and include some indication of financial outlay. Read the full Ferret investigation here .
items.why: strengthening lobbying transparency registers is a mechanism for holding elected officials answerable for undue private influence over policy.
links: Ferret investigation by Karin Goodwin that mapped more than 29,000 lobbying meetings

items.h: Investigative journalist files complaint over Met Commissioner’s letter to Green Party leader
items.b: Investigative journalist Paul Holden has submitted a formal complaint to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over Sir Mark Rowley’s open letter criticising Green Party leader Zack Polanski, arguing the intervention violated the Met’s duty of political impartiality . Holden’s complaint states that the Commissioner “must know that during election periods it is anticipated that civil servants and other public officials will observe customary ‘purdah’ principles,” and that concerns could and should have been raised privately through existing London Assembly channels rather than made public.
items.why: it concerns whether a senior police official breached duties of political impartiality during an election period, a core accountability safeguard.
items.note: Purdah conduct during elections links to elections beat but core issue is official accountability.
links: violated the Met’s duty of political impartiality

items.h: APCO PR executive behind Labour Together journalist dossier leaves firm
items.b: Tom Harper, formerly APCO’s Head of Media Relations in Europe, has left the firm after audio emerged of him instructing a contractor to “get rid of” evidence of APCO’s work for the Labour Party aligned think tank Labour Together, despite a legal notice to preserve records. Harper authored a 58-page dossier alleging without evidence that journalists reporting on Labour Together’s undeclared funding were linked to a “pro-Kremlin network,” a scandal that previously prompted the resignation of cabinet minister Josh Simons . Read Peter Geoghegan’s full report at Democracy for Sale .
items.why: it exposes an unevidenced smear campaign against journalists investigating undeclared political funding, threatening press freedom essential to public scrutiny of power.
items.note: Also touches accountability given the underlying undeclared-funding scandal and evidence destruction.
links: resignation of cabinet minister Josh Simons

One of the men pictured was convicted of assault by beating following the storming of an anti-racism meeting at Holy Trinity Church in Aldershot ; another pictured, Jeremy Stocking, who was present at the church incident but not charged, was acting as a Reform UK election agent in …
items.why: this matters democratically because it raises questions about vetting and integrity of party representatives (an election agent) with links to political violence, bearing on electoral integrity and candidate accountability

items.h: SNP formally adopt cordon sanitaire against Reform UK at Holyrood
items.b: Following the Holyrood elections last week, in which Reform UK and Scottish Labour tied for second place with around 19 MSPs each, First Minister John Swinney has vowed to shun Reform MSPs from any cross-party workings or arrangements at Holyrood, in what amounts to a formal cordon sanitaire. Swinney has branded Reform “a threat to devolution,” and Nigel Farage has previously suggested the Scottish Parliament should be defunded .

items.b: The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has blocked at least seven people from entering the UK ahead of the Unite the Kingdom rally planned for London this weekend, including two American far-right figures: Valentina Gomez, an anti-Muslim influencer and Joey Mannarino. items.b: Researcher Christopher Collins argues in a detailed investigation that a third of all government spending flows through hundreds of arm’s-length bodies that ministers cannot direct, Parliament cannot easily scrutinise, and voters cannot remove, creating the conditions for what he describes as legal corruption. items.b: The Network for Police Monitoring , has issued a call-out for testimony from those present at a counter-protest in Manchester on 18 April, following reports that PAVA spray was deployed against counter-demonstrators during a march by far-right group Britain First . items.b: Catherine Menard, a tech executive with two decades in fraud detection, has written a decoding of the Palantir 22-point manifesto in Byline Times , summarising a book by CEO Alex Karp and legal counsel Nicholas Zamiska titled The Technological Republic: Hard Power, Soft Belief, and the Future of the West . items.b: A new coalition of groups arguing for democratic oversight of AI platforms marched past the London offices of OpenAI, Meta, DeepMind and Google, in what amounts to the biggest AI protest yet held in the UK. The event marked the public debut of Pull the Plug , a UK campaign founded by former film story editor Harry Atkinson and Extinction Rebellion co-founder Frieda Lurken, which calls for legally binding Citizens’ Assemblies to regulate how AI is developed. Co-organised with PauseAI UK , the march brought together safety campaigners, ethics researchers, climate organisers and academics includi…

items.h: Civic Power Fund run authoritarian governance simulation for 80 social justice funders
items.b: Last month Civic Power Fund ran a bespoke simulation game, bringing together 80 UK social justice funders to explore how funding organisations might respond to an increasingly authoritarian UK government. Participants were challenged to navigate strategic trade-offs around a single central question: “faced with an authoritarian government, would your organisation resist or collaborate?” The game was designed and delivered by serious game design studio Stone Paper Scissors .
items.note: An internal strategy simulation for funders does not itself create new means of public participation or report a mechanism change.

items.h: University of Westminster holds first UK university climate assembly
items.b: The University of Westminster Climate Assembly (UWCA) has released its full recommendations report , covering nine areas from interdisciplinary teaching and AI policy to ICT emissions, with 80% of recommendations receiving the support of assembly members. Sarah Allan and Anwen Alias were key to the delivery of the event, find out more about how the event worked .

items.b: For Earth Day on 22 April, Shared Future CIC highlighted their work translating local climate assembly recommendations into citizen action, reflecting this year’s theme of community power. items.b: Safe Landing , the community of aviation workers campaigning for a sustainable industry transition, is proposing Workers’ and Civic Assemblies as the mechanism for engaging both aviation workers and airport-adjacent communities in shaping the future of UK aviation. George Hibberd , former easyJet pilot and Safe Landing co-founder, is lead author of the policy, which will go before the Green Party’s Transport Policy Working Group as a motion at the autumn conference.

items.b: The Evens Foundation have committed €10,000 to civic tech outfit Octree to build and open-source a bridge connecting WhatsApp users directly to the widely used Decidim participation platform . Matt Stempeck, the new Director of Technology & Democracy at the Evens Foundation, sets out a “deceptively straightforward” two-step strategy: go where people already are online, then bridge that organic engagement back to democratic institutions, rather than building new destination sites few will visit. Read the full piece on LinkedIn.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates a new, more accessible channel through which people can engage with a civic participation platform, expanding practical means of taking part.

items.h: BBC plans up to 2,000 job cuts in biggest downsizing in 15 years, with newsroom bearing the steepest reduction
items.b: The BBC is set to cut as many as 2,000 jobs, around 10% of its 21,500 staff, as part of a £600m savings drive over the next three years. BBC News, home to roughly a quarter of the workforce, has been told to expect a 15% cut, above the corporation-wide 10% average . Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told MPs the cuts have had a “very, very strong effect” on staff and are “of real concern to people out in the country”, with affected staff not expected to learn their fate until September. Private Eye journalist Ian Hislop highlighted the fate of the BBC World Service amidst the cuts , saying “we’ve g…

items.b: Migrant Voice began a new round of its London Ambassadors Programme on 18 April , training community members to get migration stories into the media, craft impactful messages and challenge negative stereotypes in public discourse. items.b: With 16-year-olds set to receive the vote under the Representation of the People Bill, The Economist has featured research from the Vote Confident programme exploring how schools can better prepare young people for democratic participation. The piece arrives as civic education capacity across UK schools remains patchy and uneven. Read the Economist piece here (paywall).

items.b: Catherine Day, co-founder of the National Strategy Project and former senior UK Cabinet Office official, has written to the Financial Times arguing that combining technology with deliberative democracy offers far more than improved voting mechanisms, giving millions of people a real voice in complex decisions and helping countries “face reality, make choices and follow through.” Day, who grew up in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, writes that our current system captures political preferences but fails to enable long-term collective decision-making, describing this as “a fatal weakness at …

items.b: The Sudan Digital Archive , a new project developed by Asil Sidahmed and others currently incubated by Newspeak House , is working to preserve the democratic culture of the people of Sudan amidst a devastating genocide and civil war. The digital archive is working to preserve song, community artifacts, messages of support, snippets of memory from the democratic revolution and the transitional government, before its overthrow by Sudanese armed groups. The archive will also securely host public evidence of war crimes for consideration by international courts.

items.b: Amidst the ongoing mass atrocities and genocide in Sudan, the Transnational Institute and the Middle East Research and Information Project have published moving obituaries for Muzan Alneel, the Sudanese writer, researcher and revolutionary organiser who died on 15 April aged 39, on the third anniversary of the outbreak of Sudan’s counterrevolutionary war. items.h: Demos warns AI chatbots get UK election information wrong a third of the time
items.b: Demos’ new report tested leading AI models during the 2026 Scottish pre-election window finding 34.1% of responses contained factual errors, including wrong election dates, faulty voter ID guidance, a hallucinated candidate, and fabricated expenses and nepotism scandals. Accompanying polling suggests one in five UK adults (around 10 million people) used an AI chatbot to find information ahead of the May local and devolved elections, while 49% do not trust these services on election matters, the same level as social media. Authors Jamie Hancock, Senior Researcher in Digital Policy at Demos, and…

items.b: Launched last week in the House of Lords, the paper by Dr Pravar Petkar, Head of Strengthening Democracy Desk at ICFS , with Dr Jyoti Yadav and Surbhi Chakraborty of the Pahlé India Foundation , argues that First Past The Post adversely affects policy scrutiny in both the UK and India through case studies of parliamentary agenda setting, the committee system, and the operation of the whips. The authors call for procedural reforms including a House of Commons Business Committee and changes to the role of the whips, arguing these are needed alongside electoral reform to support Parliament’s demo…
items.why: weakened parliamentary scrutiny mechanisms, including the committee system and whips' operation, reduce Parliament's ability to hold the executive to account
items.note: Paper links electoral system (FPTP) to scrutiny function; primary beat chosen for its focus on parliamentary scrutiny and procedural reform.

items.h: Open Britain calls for public inquiry into foreign interference in UK politics
items.b: Open Britain’s new report, Russian Interference in British Politics , published on 28 May, notes that while the US, France, Germany, Canada and the EU have all established formal investigations into Russian political interference, the UK has never commissioned a comparable inquiry, creating “a serious accountability gap” ahead of the next general election. CEO Mark Kieran said successive governments had “made a political choice not to” investigate; the report calls for a full statutory public inquiry, declassification of the Intelligence and Security Committee’s 2020 Russia Report, a formal in…
items.why: a statutory public inquiry and intelligence-sharing safeguards would hold government and security services accountable for the alleged 'accountability gap' around foreign interference in UK elections.
items.note: Public inquiry framed as accountability scrutiny, with electoral integrity as secondary territory.

items.h: Anthropic calls for coordinated industry pause mechanism as UK campaigns push for democratic control of AI
items.b: Anthropic announced last week that frontier AI developers should agree a coordinated and verifiable way to slow or ‘temporarily pause’ development if systems begin improving themselves faster than society can manage the risks, noting that as of now more than 80% of code merged into its own codebase was authored by its model Claude. The intervention sits alongside growing UK-based campaigning by PauseAI UK and Pull the Plug , which led February’s March Against the Machines in London and argue that AI development should be subject to democratic public control rather than left to corporate decisi…
items.why: campaigners are calling for a citizens' assembly to bring democratic deliberation to decisions about AI development that would otherwise be made solely by private companies.
items.note: Citizens' assembly calls are classed under elections/decision-making machinery, not participation or technology as such.

items.h: APPG on Political and Media Literacy concludes two-week Digital Briefing Series
items.b: The Academic Advisory Group of the APPG on Political and Media Literacy , hosted by Shout Out UK and chaired by Dr James Weinberg, ran its Digital Panel Series over the past fortnight, delivering 30-minute parliamentary briefings from academics on political and media literacy. Sessions covered citizenship education and the “civic gap” Votes at 16, AI-enabled gender violence and deepfakes, mental health influencer content and much more. All sessions were recorded as part of an ongoing public resource; contact Evie at Shout Out UK for access to the recordings.
items.why: it creates a new public resource of parliamentary briefings aimed at building political and media literacy, expanding capacity for informed civic participation.
links: APPG on Political and Media Literacy

items.h: Demos completes ‘Your Voice on Immigration’ deliberative process for Home Affairs Select Committee, with report due in September
items.b: Demos’ Director of Participatory Programmes Miriam Levin reports that a new deliberative process, delivered with King’s College London and the Parliamentary Engagement Team and filmed by Channel 4, brought 35 participants in each of North Tyneside, Leicester and Renfrewshire together to develop principles to guide the Committee’s scrutiny of government policy on workforce migration, with six members of the Committee attending in person. Miriam noted the process was well held and was a great example of disagreeing agreeably in action. The full report and Channel 4 programming are due in Septemb…
items.why: it is a deliberative process feeding directly into a select committee's scrutiny of government policy, which the framework treats as decision-making machinery.
items.note: Deliberative processes are classified under elections & decision making per framework rule, not participation.

items.h: Humanity Project, Octopus Communities and Ambitious Academy host “upside down” youth assembly in Islington
items.b: Writing on their Substack, Clare Farrell of Humanity Project reflects on a recent youth assembly at The Hub (Arsenal Stadium) where young people themselves facilitated conversations with councillors, youth services, local businesses and police, with the process built around a youth-made film about safety and belonging on their estate. The film launches on Friday 19 June, 6–9pm at Collective Acting Studio, Hornsey Road Baths; RSVP info@octopuscommunities.org.uk. Check out the post here.
items.why: it is a deliberative, youth-led assembly structure bringing young people into dialogue with councillors and local decision-makers, functioning as local deliberative decision-making machinery.
items.note: Youth assembly treated as deliberative process per boundary rule, though it also has strong participation/capacity-building character.

items.h: Solidarity Is publishes seven “Solidarity Stances” for organisations navigating authoritarian conditions
items.b: A new resource from the Building Movement Project’s Solidarity Is programme offers seven strategic stances that organisations and networks can adopt in times of heightened chaos and crisis, addressing dilemmas including when to speak out publicly, how to preserve organisational and community safety, and what conditions support bolder action rooted in transformative solidarity practice. Programme leads Deepa Iyer and Adaku Utah discuss the framework in a recent episode of the Solidarity Is This podcast . Download the resource here .
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: it provides civil society organisations with a strategic framework for maintaining organisational capacity and safety under repressive conditions, affecting the sector's ability to operate and organise.
items.note: Generic international resource with no explicit UK grounding, so classification is uncertain.
links: offers seven strategic stances that organisations and networks can adopt

items.h: Democracy27 launches in Brussels with European task force on democratic confidence
items.b: Democracy27 , launched on 2 June, brings together a 15-person task force across ten European countries, chaired by Věra Jourová (former Vice-President of the European Commission) and vice-chaired by Leo Varadkar and Najat Vallaud-Belkacem. Over the coming months it will run citizen consultations, country visits and civil society dialogues exploring why people remain attached to democracy yet lose trust in its institutions. Follow the new project at democracy27.eu . See you next time,
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: it establishes a new European initiative running citizen consultations and civil society dialogues that could offer comparative evidence on public engagement with and trust in democratic institutions.
items.note: International, Brussels-based initiative with no direct UK link; counted as comparative evidence per scope rule but confidence is low.

items.h: Burnham unveils ‘Number 10 North’ announces ‘biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen’
items.b: Speaking at Manchester’s People’s History Museum , Andy Burnham MP -widely tipped to be Prime Minister within weeks - declared Westminster ‘broken’ and called for change ‘in how Britain is governed, not just who governs it’. Partly based on his book Head North , written with Liverpool Mayor Steve Rotherham, Burnham’s blueprint includes a Manchester-based ‘Number 10 North’ to push power and resources out to mayors and local authorities - plus greater public control of water, housing, energy and transport, and a hint at a German-style legal duty to equalise funding across the regions. Read the G…
items.why: it reports a proposed major restructuring of power between central and local/regional government, including new mayoral powers and devolved decision-making authority
items.note: Devolution structure and powers of local/regional government fall under elections & decision making per the boundary rule.
links: analysis of the sweeping new mayoral powers

items.h: Burnham advisor Josh Simons told his account of the journalist monitoring was ‘wrong in numerous important respects’, Democracy for Sale reveals
items.b: A Democracy for Sale investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Khadija Sharife reveals that lawyers for PR firm APCO privately told Josh Simons — who resigned from the Cabinet Office over paying the firm to investigate journalists , and who now co-leads policy for Andy Burnham’s team — that his public account of the affair was ‘wrong in numerous important respects’ and ‘inconsistent with the facts’, having privately called their report ‘incredibly useful’. Green MP Siân Berry is calling for a full investigation into whether Simons breached the Ministerial Code, while Nik Williams of Index on Censor…
items.why: it concerns whether a government adviser's public account of state-linked monitoring of journalists was misleading, raising questions of ministerial accountability, transparency and potential breach of the Ministerial Code
links: resigned from the Cabinet Office over paying the firm to investigate journalists

items.h: Citizen Network’s Simon Duffy sets out an agenda for ‘radical devolution of power away from Westminster’
items.b: In his essay Next Steps for the King of the North , Citizen Network Director Simon Duffy argues the moment demands structural change rather than simply a change of personnel, whoever holds №10. Creeping poverty, insecurity and a deepening sense of injustice demand a proportionate response, Duffy says, highlighting Burnham’s announcement of radical devolution away from Westminster, with community power and public services ‘rooted and accountable to local communities’ as a ‘hopeful path’ at a time when the stakes could not be higher, he says.. Read Simon’s full essay .
items.why: it advocates radical devolution of power away from Westminster toward locally accountable structures, engaging the machinery of regional and local decision-making
items.note: Devolution of power to regions/localities is classified under elections & decision making, not participation, per the boundary rule.
links: Next Steps for the King of the North

items.h: New Statesman’s Alex Niven argues Burnham’s Makerfield win could push radical regional devolution onto the agenda
items.b: Writing in the New Statesman after Andy Burnham’s Makerfield by-election win, Alex Niven (author of The North Will Rise Again ) argues that beneath the ‘King of the North’ branding sits a serious constitutional-regionalist agenda aimed at the UK’s entrenched North-South divide. He points to the Head North manifesto — an elected Senate of the Regions to replace the Lords, a German-style ‘basic law’ guaranteeing fair regional funding, a written constitution, voting reform and expanded regional fiscal powers - as a blueprint for rebalancing power away from Westminster. Read the piece .
items.why: it discusses proposals for constitutional and electoral reform, including an elected regional chamber replacing the Lords and expanded regional fiscal powers, that would restructure how UK political power is allocated and exercised
items.note: Regional/devolved government structure and electoral system reform fall under elections & decision making.

items.h: Localis weigh Burnham’s ‘Number 10 North’
items.b: In a chief executive’s note, Localis ’ Jonathan Werran weighs Andy Burnham’s plan to ‘rewire the state’ around place-based collaboration — arguing the prize hinges on prising economic policy from an over-centralised Treasury and on Burnham’s choice of chancellor, and warning that past attempts, from Wilson’s Department for Economic Affairs to the stalled Levelling Up agenda, foundered on Treasury intransigence. Their report Everything in its right place makes the case for a universal fiscal devolution roadmap for all strategic authorities. Read Werran’s note and the report .
items.why: it concerns the structure and fiscal powers of local and regional government tiers, which determines how devolved decision-making actually functions.
items.note: Devolution structure/powers of local government tiers falls under elections & decision making, not participation.

items.h: UCL Constitution Unit argue Burnham Number 10 needs fewer — and more transparent — special advisers
items.b: Professor Robert Hazell, founder of the Constitution Unit , argues that if Andy Burnham reaches Number 10 he should shrink its team of special advisers — quadrupled from 10 under Thatcher to more than 40 today — in favour of a smaller, more experienced operation. He also revives the Committee on Standards in Public Life ’s call to publish job descriptions and CVs for senior advisers (they argued this in 2001). Read the full story on the Constitution Unit’s blog .
items.why: the size, transparency and appointment process of special advisers affects how ministerial power is exercised and scrutinised.
links: Committee on Standards in Public Life
call to publish job descriptions and CVs for senior advisers
Read the full story on the Constitution Unit’s blog

items.h: Demos welcome Burnham’s devolution turn — and make the case for a ‘democratic delivery model’
items.b: Demos chief executive Polly Curtis has welcomed Andy Burnham’s vision as flipping Keir Starmer’s approach — ‘a clear strategy’ that shifts power away from Whitehall — while cautioning that turning it into a deliverable platform within weeks is ‘a herculean task’. Their New Deal essay Public Service reform: a new democratic delivery model , by Joe Martin, Associate Director of Policy, argues that devolving power from the centre and empowering frontline workers and local institutions can move government ‘from a democratic doom loop towards a democratic hope loop’. Read the essay .
items.why: shifting power away from central government to local institutions changes the machinery through which collective decisions are taken.
items.note: Devolution of power to local/frontline institutions is filed under elections & decision making per the boundary rule.
links: Public Service reform: a new democratic delivery model

items.h: openDemocracy report Burnham plans to make lobbyist James Purnell his chief of staff
items.b: openDemocracy report that Andy Burnham intends to make James Purnell — the former Labour cabinet minister who resigned as CEO of corporate lobbying firm Flint Global the day the story broke — his chief of staff should he become Prime Minister. Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called for Flint’s full client list (which has included Uber, Amazon, BP, Airbnb and Apple) to be published, asking whether Burnham would be willing to take on the corporations Purnell was paid to represent. Read Ethan Shone’s report .
items.why: appointing a former corporate lobbyist to a top government role raises conflicts of interest that bear on undue private influence over public power.

items.h: Common Knowledge outline ‘New Order Manchesterism’ narrative and policy playbook
items.b: Common Knowledge has drafted New Order: Manchesterism, the End of Neoliberalism , a narrative, comms and policy paper for an incoming Burnham administration, framed around ’15 weeks of de-privatisation’. The core argument of the playbook focuses on policy that should treat people ‘like adults and agents in their own lives, not reduced to passivity or spectatorship’.
items.note: This is a policy/comms narrative about substantive economic policy rather than a claim about democratic mechanism.
links: New Order: Manchesterism, the End of Neoliberalism

items.b: The paper details a range of prospective policies, from a publicly owned ride-hailing platform co-governed by drivers, devolution powers empowering local democratically run cooperatives providing local services, to an Irish-style basic income for artists. The paper comes with its own soundtrack (‘read this while listening to New Order… it should feel like the future. It should feel joyful’). Follow Common Knowledge for updates .
items.note: Speculative policy proposals within a comms playbook, not a reported change to democratic institutions or process.

items.h: Democracy for Sale reveal Burnham’s chief of staff ran undeclared lobbying access for corporate clients
items.b: A Democracy for Sale investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Adam Bychawski finds that James Purnell’s firm Flint arranged a March 2025 roundtable between Labour minister Douglas Alexander and corporate clients including Uber, Amazon and Diageo — while declaring almost no lobbying to Westminster’s watchdog across five years. Emails show Flint picked the attendees, set the agenda and hosted the event at its own offices. Green Party deputy leader Rachel Millward has called for Flint’s full client list and all ministerial meetings to be published — read the investigation .
items.why: undeclared corporate lobbying access to ministers undermines transparency and accountability mechanisms meant to check private influence over government.

items.h: Working on the Representation of the People Bill? Join the Elections Bill Hub
items.b: Kyle Taylor of Fair Vote UK and a range of organisations are working together to coordinate around the bill. Activity is proceeding at pace, so if you’re working on the bill, contact Kyle to get involved.
items.why: coordinating civil society input on the Representation of the People Bill shapes the electoral law that governs how people can vote and stand for office.
items.note: Sector capacity-building tied specifically to electoral legislation is filed under elections & decision making.

items.h: Working in Wales? Join Democracy Group Cymru
items.b: Democracy Group Cymru is an information sharing network among organisations working in Wales, convened by Democracy Classroom and the Electoral Reform Society Cymru . So if you’re working on democracy in Wales, don’t miss out on opportunities to share your work, connect with others and collaborate — Join now .
items.note: Organisational networking/membership notice among democracy sector groups, not a change in public participation.

items.h: Social Change Lab and Fossil Free London need you — Have your say on UK protest rights
items.b: Here’s something really useful you can do for democratic rights in the UK, and it takes only 5 minutes. Social Change Lab and Fossil Free London would love you to tell them (anonymously) about your experiences and feelings around protesting in the UK. If you’ve ever attended, or considered attending, a protest, this survey is for you. Your answers will help shape movement strategy and contribute to a parliamentary inquiry on protest laws. Complete the survey here.
items.why: the survey feeds a parliamentary inquiry into protest laws, which determines how far people can lawfully exercise freedom of assembly and dissent in the UK.
items.note: Protest framed as legal restriction/policing issue rather than willingness to participate.

items.h: UK Government opens call for evidence on 7th Open Government National Action Plan
items.b: The government is seeking ideas from civil society and the public for its next National Action Plan for Open Government , covering transparency, accountability, open data, digital governance and public participation, with no limit on the number of submissions. Find out more information about you can submit your ideas .
items.why: the National Action Plan process shapes government commitments on transparency, open data and accountability mechanisms that let citizens and civil society hold institutions answerable.
links: National Action Plan for Open Government

items.h: Esmée Fairbairn Foundation opens youth-led creativity funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
items.b: Esmée Fairbairn Foundation is opening a new youth-led creativity fund for arts and culture organisations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland whose work is led by and for young people underrepresented in the sector. The Foundation expects to make over a dozen grants over the next two years, with applications accepted on a rolling basis. Register for the Q&A webinar on 16 July . Also, Esmée Fairbairn Foundation is looking to appoint two new Trustees to its Board — Applications close on 20 July .
items.note: Arts/culture funding call and trustee recruitment notice, not democratic participation infrastructure.

items.h: The Henry Smith Foundation launches its 2026 funds after giving £61.9m last year
items.b: The Henry Smith Foundation — one of the UK’s largest independent funders — is launching its 2026 funding programmes, having awarded £61.9m to more than 900 organisations reaching 410,000 people in 2024. Their funds focus on support for racially minoritised young people, LGBT+ groups, refugees, people seeking asylum and other migrants. Find out more .
items.note: General charitable funding announcement, not tied to a democratic mechanism.

items.h: People Powered open the Democracy Stories Lab, a global creative competition to reframe democracy
items.b: People Powered and the Democracy Narratives Alliance are launching the Democracy Stories Lab, a worldwide competition for videos, illustrations or graphics that tell fresh stories about voice, fairness and what happens when ordinary people hold real power. Four winners receive $1,000 and five honourable mentions $500, with entries amplified through the Alliance’s partner networks and a global screening. Applications open on 14 July and close on 14 September — apply via the Democracy Stories Lab page .
items.why: the competition creates a new creative campaign encouraging people to engage with and reframe narratives about democratic voice and power, expanding means of civic engagement.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building creating new means of participation rather than pure media/organisational news.
links: — apply via the Democracy Stories Lab page

items.h: Seeds of Liberation offer free grant writing workshops
items.b: Grant writing doesn’t have to feel inaccessible. Whether you’re an artist, organiser, researcher, mutual aid collective, or someone with a vision for your community, this workshop offered by Seeds of Liberation is designed to help you build the skills and confidence to pursue funding without compromising your values. The training takes place over a series of Zoom calls in July — Would you like to know more?
items.note: Generic grant-writing skills training, not specifically building democratic participation capacity.
links: Would you like to know more?

items.h: Regular Democracy Drinks in Edinburgh
items.b: Involve’s Kelly McBride and Paul Hirmis are running regular democracy drinks events in Edinburgh, check their Luma events page for the latest . Contact Involve for more information .

items.h: Upcoming conference on democratic futures and innovation, 6–8 July
items.b: The Participatory and Deliberative Democracy Specialist Group of the Political Studies Association , and the Centre for Democratic Futures are joining forces to revive, for the first time since 2018, a participatory and deliberative democracy conference. This year’s theme is Democratic Innovations, Democratic Futures. Register now and catch the conference .
items.note: Academic conference announcement; event listing rather than a new means of participation.
links: The Participatory and Deliberative Democracy Specialist Group of the Political Studies Association
Register now and catch the conference

items.h: Citizen Infrastructure Builders Club held first online Demo Day, showcasing tools for collective action
items.b: The Citizen Infrastructure Builders Club (CIBC), fiscally hosted by Social Change Nest , research and build what they term ‘citizen infrastructure’ that underpins solidarity and collective action. CIBC held their first online Demo Day last Friday. Five builders presented prototypes including a build-in-public knowledge base of 100+ plain-language articles on democratic innovation.
items.why: this matters democratically because it creates new tools and plain-language resources that help people organise and take collective civic action.
items.note: Treated as sector capacity-building because tools for collective action were launched and showcased, not just an event listing.

items.h: Elect Her run new workshops to get more women standing for election
items.b: Elect Her is ramping up its free online training for prospective candidates, noting that just a third of current councillors are women. Four Wales-focused workshops run in July, with further dates for Scotland and England to follow in September — Book the workshop that suits you. Elect Her are also working with Zoe Franklin MP and the Women’s Democracy Group (WDG) on amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. Elect her will also be hosting an event with Jo Cox Foundation and Centenary Action , and all WDG members, in the Lords, in Sept or Oct (TBC) — stay tuned for updates.
items.why: this matters democratically because it addresses candidate access and the representativeness of elected institutions by training more women to stand for election.
items.note: Candidate training and legislative amendments on representation place this in elections rather than general participation capacity-building.

items.h: The Citizens convene two hearings pressing for a public inquiry into Russian interference
items.b: The Citizens are hosting two free events in Parliament and central London tomorrow Tuesday 7 July, building the case for a full public inquiry into Russian interference in British politics. Speakers include Dominic Grieve, Lord Wallace of Saltaire, Ellie Chowns MP, Marina Litvinenko, Carole Cadwalladr and former MI6 officer Christopher Steele. Places are free but limited — register your interest by emailing info@the-citizens.com.
items.why: this matters democratically because it presses for a public inquiry as a scrutiny mechanism into alleged foreign interference in UK political processes.
items.note: Public inquiry framed as scrutiny (accountability) rather than redress, per the standing distinction on inquiries.

items.h: Campaign Lab convene one-day ‘AI & Campaigning’ conference in London, 16 July
items.b: Campaign Lab is bringing together the people building, funding and deploying AI in campaigns at Newspeak House in London on Thursday 16 July, for live tool demos and Chatham House-rule panels. Sessions ask whether AI can mimic voters well enough to replace asking them, and whether AI persuasion actually works in real campaigns, with speakers drawn from YouGov, Higher Ground Labs and beyond. Places are limited and approval is required — request a spot now.
items.note: Conference announcement about AI and campaigning; discussion event rather than a launched tool or policy change.

items.h: Electoral Integrity Project hosts online elections conference, 6–9 July
items.b: The Electoral Integrity Project holds its annual elections conference starting today til 9 July — free, entirely online, and gathering scholars, election officials and civil-society researchers around contestation, deliberation, participation and electoral justice. Co-convenors Holly Ann Garnett, Toby James (University of East Anglia) and Anthony DeMattee (The Carter Center) have lined up eight thematic panels and two practitioner roundtables, with former election chiefs Lorenzo Córdova Vianello (Mexico) and Jean-Pierre Kingsley (Canada) among the speakers. Register free now.
items.note: Academic/practitioner conference listing, not a reported change or new participation mechanism.

items.h: International Observatory on Participatory Democracy marks its 25th conference with ‘hope and renewal’ in Kraków
items.b: The International Observatory on Participatory Democracy (OIDP) holds its 25th annual conference in Kraków, Poland, from 21–23 September, on the theme ‘Hope and renewal in the face of a global crisis of democracy’. Political leaders, practitioners, academics and civil society from around the world will tackle citizen participation in crises, embedding deliberation in representative government, and local government as a laboratory for democratic innovation — with a Political Declaration to adopt and the OIDP Awards to vote on. Register via oidp.net .
items.note: International conference announcement; event listing rather than a democracy story under the sector-capacity rule.

items.h: Consul Democracy heads to Munich for its 2026 conference on open-source digital democracy
items.b: The Consul Democracy Foundation — whose open-source platform powers participation and direct-democracy processes worldwide — is co-hosting its 2026 conference with the City of Munich from 15–17 September, covering digital democracy, open-source technology and democratic empowerment. Expect demo runs, workshops on designing participation processes, and speakers including Roman Huber (Mehr Demokratie), Sophie Bloemen (Commons Network) and Joe Mathews (Democracy Local). Tickets are donation-based via Open Collective — find out more and book .
items.note: Event listing for a conference, not a new participation resource or mechanism.

items.h: Assemble host online forum on slashing political corruption, Thursday 9 July
items.b: Grassroots campaign Assemble holds the second of its online Charter Forums on Thursday 9 July at 7pm, this one on how to slash political corruption — each forum digs into a top-ranked demand from the first sitting of the House of the People . Speakers are Guardian columnist George Monbiot, Green Party Westminster leader Dr Ellie Chowns MP, and Kamila Kingstone, who leads the Defending Democracy Programme at Spotlight on Corruption . Register via the event page , or read the People’s Charter first.
items.note: An event listing/invitation to attend a discussion forum, not itself a reportable democratic change or new capacity.

items.h: Stevenson Trust for Citizenship plays matchmaker between democracy organisations and academics in Glasgow
items.b: The Stevenson Trust for Citizenship at the University of Glasgow are running a one-day workshop on Friday 4 September pairing civil society and democracy-sector organisations with academics, so each can find the evidence, expertise and collaborators the other has to offer. Drawing on the UK Democracy Network’s own guide to academic-practitioner collaboration , the day features sessions with sector funders and structured matchmaking conversations, with a small travel and accommodation bursary for the 10–12 organisations selected. Express interest by emailing Professor Christopher Carman (christ…
items.note: Sector networking/matchmaking event between organisations, not a change affecting public participation.
