items.h: Common Wealth and Mainstream set out ‘Productive State’ blueprint for public ownership
items.b: A new paper from Labour-aligned pressure group Mainstream , produced by Mathew Lawrence and Alex Williams of think tank Common Wealth , argues government should take direct public ownership of essential sectors such as water, energy and housing rather than relying on regulation or welfare transfers alone. The paper proposes arm’s length public corporations with worker and community representation, distinct from the post-war era nationalisation agenda, and points to former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham’s programme, including the Bee Network bus franchise, as a working model for what it …
items.note: Economic ownership policy proposal, not a mechanism of how public power is acquired, exercised or contested.

items.h: 99% Organisation publish ‘Defensive Constitutional Reform’, a blueprint to defend UK democracy from executive overreach
items.b: The 99% Organisation , with Open Britain and Unlock Democracy , has published Defensive Constitutional Reform — launched in Parliament in late April — setting out safeguards against democratic backsliding and the abuse of executive power. It draws on Professor Andrew Blick of King’s College London and his scenario study Could it Happen Here? The Day a Prime Minister Refuses to Resign , arguing the UK’s largely unwritten, convention-based constitution leaves it dangerously exposed should a future government simply choose to ignore the rules. Download the full report now.
items.why: it proposes safeguards against a prime minister or executive ignoring constitutional conventions and refusing to relinquish power, directly concerning limits on and accountability of executive authority.
links: Could it Happen Here? The Day a Prime Minister Refuses to Resign

items.h: Involve and partners launch the report of the island of Ireland’s first cross-border Citizens’ Jury
items.b: Two Sides, One Conversation: a story of cross-border democracy , the final report of the Carlingford Lough Citizens’ Jury, launched on 26 June — the first time residents from both sides of the Irish border were selected by democratic lottery to reach a verdict on their shared landscape. Convened by The Wheel and NICVA under the Creative Ireland -funded Shifting Tides project, the jury set out recommendations on balancing nature recovery with the economic futures of communities around the lough. Read the report to see what cross-border democracy looks like in practice .
items.why: a citizens' jury selected by democratic lottery reached binding-style recommendations on a shared policy issue, exemplifying deliberative decision-making machinery.
items.note: Citizens' juries/assemblies are classified under elections & decision making per the framework's boundary rule.
links: Two Sides, One Conversation: a story of cross-border democracy

items.h: Westminster Foundation for Democracy publish evidence that democracy underpins security
items.b: Two new independent evidence reviews commissioned by the Westminster Foundation for Democracy argue that democracy is not merely compatible with security but central to delivering it — a timely input at a moment when security dominates the agenda. Presented at the European Partnership for Democracy Annual Conference in Brussels on 9 June, the pair comprise Democracy as a security asset by Katharina Merkel, synthesising more than 30 years of scholarly research globally, and a second review applying that evidence to the European context. Read the reviews on WFD’s site.
items.note: A general evidence review on democracy's relationship to security, not tied to a specific mechanism of UK democratic power.

items.h: Royal Holloway and WFD warn TikTok’s design poses risks to democratic participation
items.b: A new briefing from the London Social Media Observatory at Royal Holloway, University of London , produced with the Westminster Foundation for Democracy , finds TikTok’s highly personalised feeds can fuel polarisation while moderation standards, media-literacy support and researcher access to platform data lag behind. Drawing on a roundtable of 45 policymakers, academics and civil-society figures, lead author Dr Andreu Casas and WFD’s Head of Elections Tanja Hollstein call for more transparent moderation, greater oversight of polarising content, and proper data access for researchers. Read the…
items.why: platform design and moderation choices shape the plural information environment citizens rely on to form political views and can amplify polarisation

items.h: DemocracyNext publish two studies of how multilingual citizens’ assemblies work across Europe
items.b: DemocracyNext has released two new papers on language and technology in transnational deliberation. James MacDonald-Nelson and Hannah Terry give a first-hand account of a citizens’ assembly in Esch-sur-Alzette, Luxembourg, where AI transcription and translation helped bridge language groups, while Hugh Pope draws on interviews with interpreters and members of the EU’s 24-language citizens’ panel. Two more land in July — ‘Deliberative Muscles & AI’ on 9 July, and a report on citizens’ assemblies as democratic infrastructure on 15 July — via DemocracyNext’s Substack and LinkedIn .
items.why: citizens' assemblies and deliberative processes are part of the machinery of collective decision-making the framework anchors to this beat
items.note: Citizens' assemblies are classified under elections & decision-making per the framework's boundary rule, not participation.

items.h: Ethics and Integrity Commission publish their review of lobbying and standards on 9 July
items.b: The Ethics and Integrity Commission — the standards body commissioned by the Prime Minister to examine lobbying, financial disclosure, Business Appointment Rules and access to government — publishes the report of its review on the morning of Thursday 9 July, with the findings going up on its website that day. Unlock Democracy director Tom Brake, who has worked closely with the Commission on its lobbying proposals, flags it as one to watch.
items.why: lobbying rules, financial disclosure and business appointment restrictions determine whether officials can be held answerable for conflicts of interest

items.h: AKO Storytelling Institute find games can build disinformation resilience among the most disengaged audiences
items.b: A new report from the AKO Storytelling Institute at University of the Arts London, with More in Common , finds games can reach audiences most disengaged from mainstream media and most susceptible to disinformation. Rather than drilling facts, it backs ‘psychological literacy’ — helping players see how beliefs form and how emotion and social dynamics shape what we accept as true — and finds games that respect player autonomy, prioritise enjoyment and stay politically neutral work best. Read the ‘On Their Terms’ report and watch the film .
items.why: building resilience to disinformation among disengaged audiences affects whether citizens can access and evaluate accurate political information

items.h: House of Commons Library publish fresh primers on parliamentary confidence and monarchy finances
items.b: The House of Commons Library team has published two new briefings: Commanding confidence explains what ‘confidence of the House’ means in the UK’s largely unwritten constitution — how it is tested, and what happens when a government loses it — while Finances of the Monarchy , updated 5 June, sets out the Sovereign Grant, the Duchies of Lancaster and Cornwall, and royal tax arrangements. Read both via the Commons Library .
items.why: the concept of parliamentary confidence determines whether and how a government can remain in power, a core constitutional accountability mechanism
links: Read both via the Commons Library

items.h: Shared Future and People Powered refresh their guide to participatory budgeting in social housing
items.b: Shared Future CIC has refreshed its practical guide to participatory budgeting in social housing — first published in 2019, updated in July 2025 by authors Jez Hall and Alan Budge, and shared through the global People Powered network. Housing associations, co-operatives and councils, it argues, are uniquely placed to give tenants a direct say over how money is spent — turning a ‘complaints culture’ into collaborative decisions on rents, repairs and improvements. Download the guide now.
items.why: participatory budgeting gives tenants a direct, structured say over public spending decisions that affect their lives

items.h: People Powered share Greater Manchester’s Participation Playbook, a ‘game box’ for local democracy
items.b: Greater Manchester has a new Participation Playbook — a ‘game box’ of methods for residents, policymakers and organisers to co-produce solutions on health, housing and public safety. Commissioned by GM Live Well and created by participatory-democracy practitioners including The People Act and Shared Future CIC , with lead authors including Katy Rubin and Jez Hall, it sets out ‘rules of the game’ for combining participatory tools, alongside a directory of local practitioners. Explore the playbook via People Powered .
items.why: the playbook creates new practical means for residents and policymakers to co-produce local decisions, expanding avenues for civic participation

items.h: KNOCA publish new guidance on communicating climate assemblies for maximum impact
items.b: The Knowledge Network on Climate Assemblies ( KNOCA ) has published new guidance, Communicating Climate Assemblies: Enabling Pathways to Impact , written by Camille Dobler, Head of Research at Missions Publiques . Communication, it argues, should never be an afterthought in a citizens’ assembly — and supporting assembly members to tell their own stories can be a ‘gamechanger’ for an assembly’s influence. Read or download the guidance — and watch the launch discussion .
items.why: guidance on communicating climate assemblies affects the influence and legitimacy of deliberative decision-making processes
items.note: Climate assemblies are deliberative decision-making machinery, classified under elections & decision-making rather than participation.

items.h: DemocracyR&D publish their ‘Year in Deliberation’, charting five trends shaping deliberative democracy
items.b: DemocracyR&D , the global network for deliberative democracy and democratic innovation, has published its latest annual review of where the field is heading. It picks out five trends: the challenges of AI, deliberation’s role in strengthening democratic resilience, widening representation to include children and young people, Indigenous communities and the ‘more-than-human’, deliberation beyond government, and funding sustainability in an age of cuts. Read the report for a global snapshot of deliberative practice.
items.note: A global trends report on the deliberation field, not a UK-specific change or new participatory mechanism.

items.b: MP Jo Cox was murdered 10 years ago during the Brexit referendum campaign (Photo credit: Third Sector)
items.note: Photo caption only, no substantive content.

items.h: Jo Cox Foundation keep ‘more in common’ alive, ten years on
items.b: Ten years ago last month, the MP Jo Cox was murdered in her Batley and Spen constituency. The Jo Cox Foundation marked the anniversary with a Great Get Together of neighbourhood gatherings and an exhibition charting her life, holding fast to her belief that ‘for every act of division, there are hundreds of acts of connection and community’ — and to her words, ‘we are far more united and have far more in common than that which divides us’. Read the Foundation’s reflection or the BBC’s report .
items.note: An anniversary commemoration by an organisation, which the framework excludes as organisational news rather than a change in democratic participation.

items.h: Democracy Club log record use of their voter information tools in 2026
items.b: Democracy Club has published its report on the 2026 local and devolved elections. They recorded more than 10 million postcode searches across WhoCanIVoteFor and WhereDoIVote, an ‘unprecedented’ figure for a local or devolved election, gathered data on some 17,000 polling stations from all 220 participating councils, and supplied the first UK-wide polling-station accessibility data, now feeding Wales’s new official Vote.Wales platform. Read the report via Democracy Club.
items.why: this matters democratically because it reports record use of tools that help people find their polling station and register to vote, and new accessibility data now feeding an official government voting platform, directly affecting the mechanics of electoral access.

items.h: Politics in Action elect new chair ahead of Northern Ireland’s bumper election cycle
items.b: Politics in Action , the Northern Ireland democratic-engagement charity, has elected four new board members — Jeannie McCann steps up as Chairperson, with thanks to retiring chair Richard Ross. The charity says it has never been busier: Assembly and local council elections land in May 2027, 16 and 17 year olds in Northern Ireland will vote in a General Election for the first time, and its Communities CONNECT partnership with the British Council Northern Ireland is now rolling out. Find out more .
items.note: Primarily organisational leadership news (new chair, board members); the franchise extension it mentions is background context, not the reported change.

items.h: Nationwide ‘weaponising’ its Quick Vote, says board challenger James Sherwin-Smith
items.b: James Sherwin-Smith, the first Member Nominated Candidate to stand for the board of Nationwide Building Society since 2005, is contesting a ballot of some 9.3 million members — the largest UK electorate, he says, since the Brexit referendum. He alleges a dozen ‘dirty tricks’ , including a Quick Vote option (used by 87% of the 8% of members who voted last year) that now casts a proxy against him. Advance voting closes on 13 July.
items.note: A private mutual society's internal board election does not materially affect public political power despite the electoral-integrity framing.

items.h: Terror-law reviewers warn national security bill could criminalise journalists and NGOs
items.b: Jonathan Hall KC, the Independent Reviewer of Terrorism Legislation, and his predecessor Lord Anderson of Ipswich have warned that the National Security (State Threats) Bill — expected to become law in early July — could expose foreign correspondents and NGOs to terrorism prosecution for legitimate contact with ‘designated’ groups.
items.why: this matters democratically because new security legislation could criminalise legitimate journalism and civil-society contact with designated groups, chilling the public-interest reporting and NGO activity that underpin public debate.
items.note: Journalists and NGOs both named; classified under information_debate for the press-freedom mechanism with civic-space as secondary.

items.b: Press-freedom bodies including the Society of Editors and Index on Censorship want protection for public-interest journalism written onto the face of the bill, while the Home Office insists journalistic, humanitarian and diplomatic work is already protected. Index’s Nik Williams warns a hastily drafted law ‘could chill or criminalise public interest journalism’ — read the Guardian’s full report .
items.why: this matters democratically because press-freedom bodies are contesting whether a new law adequately protects public-interest journalism from prosecution, a direct question about the legal conditions for a free press.
links: ‘could chill or criminalise public interest journalism’

items.h: Labour for a New Democracy rally cross-party backing for a National Commission on Electoral Reform
items.b: Labour for a New Democracy are coordinating support for an amendment to the Representation of the People Bill, tabled by Labour MP Alex Sobel, that would create a National Commission on Electoral Reform. The amendment has drawn more than 140 signatories from across seven parties — including 81 Labour MPs, a fifth of the parliamentary party — making it, the campaign says, the largest parliamentary intervention in favour of electoral reform to date, at the time of an incoming PR-supporting PM.
items.why: it concerns a parliamentary push to reform the electoral system through which representatives are chosen.

items.h: Unlock make the case for extending the vote to more people in prison
items.b: Unlock argues in its report Why Prisoner Voting Matters that the UK’s near-blanket ban on voting in prison, among the strictest in Europe, harms rehabilitation and weakens democracy. Its Unlock the Vote campaign is backing amendment NC40 to the Representation of the People Bill, which would extend the franchise to everyone in prison serving a sentence of four years or less. Unlock is seeking supportive MPs and Peers — get in touch via policy@unlock.org.uk.
items.why: it concerns who is included in the franchise, a core question of suffrage.

items.h: Byline Times argue UK could regulate political money
items.b: Byline Times chief reporter Josiah Mortimer — formerly of the Electoral Reform Society — argues in the latest of its Crypto-Politics series that regulating political donations is entirely feasible, pointing to Canada, where an independent Chief Electoral Officer answerable only to Parliament can fund and enforce the rules without government interference — unlike the UK’s more constrained Electoral Commission . Byline says the series, tracking cryptocurrency donations and the foreign-interference risks they carry, has already helped prompt a government amendment to the Representation of the Peo…
items.why: it concerns regulation of political donations and campaign finance, a core electoral integrity mechanism.
items.note: Includes a comparison of electoral commission independence, touching accountability.

items.h: 47 strong coalition urges Andy Burnham to ‘reset the narrative’ on online safety
items.b: A 47 strong coalition coordinated by the Online Safety Network calls on Andy Burnham, addressed as the expected incoming Prime Minister, to adopt a ‘much more comprehensive and adaptive approach to online safety and AI regulation’, including a regularly updated Digital Media, Data and Communications Bill built on ‘safety by design’. Signatories including Full Fact , Hope not Hate , the Fawcett Society and the Center for Countering Digital Hate are pressing for restored researcher access to platform data, foundational to ‘the integrity of our information environment and democracy’. Read the coa…
items.why: it concerns regulation of online platforms and researcher access to data that shape the public information environment.
items.note: A policy call rather than an enacted change.

items.h: Reform Political Advertising urge supporters to email their MP over unchecked election ads
items.b: Reform Political Advertising are asking supporters to write to their MPs as the Representation of the People Bill moves through Parliament. The campaign warns that electoral law has barely changed in two decades, leaving a widening ‘regulation gap’ while ‘dark ads’, AI deepfakes and demonstrably false claims go unchecked. They’re asking their supporters to email their MP to back independent regulation of factual claims in electoral advertising.
items.why: it concerns regulation of political advertising within electoral law, affecting fair campaigning conditions.
items.note: Tied explicitly to the Representation of the People Bill; also touches the information environment via deepfakes and dark ads.

items.b: MS’s vote with their and walk out of the Senedd last month (Photo credit: BBC)
items.why: it depicts elected members' conduct and standards within a devolved legislature.
items.note: Minimal caption content; inferred from companion story on Senedd walkout.

items.h: Association of Electoral Administrators warn election teams are in ‘survival’ mode
items.b: Electoral services teams now describe their work as ‘survival’ rather than successful delivery, warns Peter Stanyon, Chief Executive of the Association of Electoral Administrators — after a record 25,000-plus candidates and ballot papers some 750 miles longer than four years ago overwhelmed an already stretched service. He links the strain to falling public trust, intensifying external scrutiny and the mounting complexity of the Elections Act 2022, all driving serious recruitment and retention problems among returning officers. Read the LocalGov interview .
items.why: it concerns the administrative capacity to deliver well-run elections.

items.h: Plaid Cymru, Labour and Green vote with their feet in the Senedd
items.b: Plaid Cymru, Labour and Green members walked out of the Senedd on 17 June during a Reform-initiated debate on scrapping the Welsh Government’s £9m international budget , after Reform MS Joe Martin dismissed the programmes as ‘pointless vanity projects’ and made remarks fellow members condemned as racist. Plaid Cymru’s Zaynub Akbar left first saying ‘I don’t accept any of this and I don’t want to be a part of it’. Daisy Brett unpacks what the episode means for parliamentary standards under the new Plaid-led Welsh Government — read her Senedd Explained explainer .
items.why: it concerns standards of conduct and accountability among elected members within a legislature.
items.note: Focus is on parliamentary standards/conduct, not the structure or powers of devolution, so classed as accountability rather than elections.
links: Reform-initiated debate on scrapping the Welsh Government’s £9m international budget

items.h: Coventry City Council join the national write-out keeping overseas voters on the register
items.b: Returning officers across the country are writing out to the UK’s roughly 200,000 overseas electors, reports Coventry City Council ’s Martyn Harris. Overseas voters can drop off the register between electoral events for purely administrative reasons, losing their vote in UK parliamentary elections and referendums. The aim is to keep them registered, with a postal or proxy vote in place before the next poll — connect with Martyn on LinkedIn .
items.why: it affects whether overseas citizens retain their right to vote in UK elections through registration mechanics.

items.b: Police prepare ahead of Great Israeli Real Estate demonstrations (Photo credit: Netpol)
items.note: A bare photo caption with no reported mechanism or event detail.

items.h: Liberty warn the Met against expanding surveillance tech before oversight in place
items.b: Liberty has responded to the Metropolitan Police Commissioner’s announcement of a major expansion of live facial recognition, drones and AI-powered surveillance across London — a rollout arriving before Parliament has put any dedicated legal framework in place. Ruth Ehrlich, Liberty’s Director of External Relations, said ‘Londoners absolutely have the right to expect that there should be rules that are applied clearly and consistently’. She called for the expansion to be paused until proper oversight, accountability and transparency are in law. Read Liberty’s full response .
items.why: expanding mass surveillance technology without a legal oversight framework threatens privacy and freedom from unaccountable state power.
links: Metropolitan Police Commissioner’s announcement of a major expansion of live facial recognition, drones and AI-powered surveillance

items.h: Netpol warn new protest powers are fuelling ‘growing state of repression’
items.b: Network for Police Monitoring (Netpol) report they are documenting a crackdown on the right to protest ‘happening almost every day, in different ways and in disparate parts of the country’. Campaigns coordinator Kevin Blowe points to recent flashpoints — such as the demonstrations outside the ‘Great Israeli Real Estate Event’ at an Edgware synagogue — as ‘snapshots’ of what he calls a growing state of repression, warning that powers under the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which let police restrict protests that deter access to places of worship, could narrow the right to demonstrate further. Re…
items.why: new legal powers restricting protests narrow the right to assemble and dissent, a core civic freedom.
items.note: Concerns legal restriction and policing of protest, not willingness to participate, so filed under rights not participation.

items.h: MHCLG strip nine councils of planning powers in housebuilding push
items.b: MHCLG has designated nine councils — Cherwell, Dacorum, Epping Forest, Hertsmere and South Tyneside among them — as underperforming on planning, meaning major housing and commercial applicants can now bypass local planning departments and apply straight to the Planning Inspectorate. Council leaders have pushed back — Epping Forest’s Cllr Chris Whitbread called it ‘an attack on local democracy and accountability’ — read William Eichler’s report in LocalGov .
items.why: stripping elected local councils of planning powers shifts decision-making authority away from locally accountable democratic institutions.
items.note: Story concerns the structure and powers of local government tiers, so filed under elections & decision making.
links: — read William Eichler’s report in LocalGov

items.h: mySociety win a standards complaint over an MP’s missing declaration — and share the lessons
items.b: mySociety has won a complaint to the parliamentary standards process over an interest Conservative MP Nick Timothy had failed to declare — spotted via the register-of-interests data behind its TheyWorkForYou service. Their candid write-up covers how an ordinary member of the public can bring a standards complaint, where the process proved opaque or slow, and what would make Parliament’s transparency mechanisms work better. Read what they learned about holding representatives to account.
items.why: testing and improving the parliamentary standards complaints process strengthens mechanisms for holding elected representatives answerable.

items.h: Republic brand palace’s accounts ‘dishonest and misleading’
items.b: Republic , the campaign for an elected head of state, has criticised the royal household’s 2025–26 accounts, arguing they gloss over a near-doubling of the Sovereign Grant and obscure the true cost of the monarchy. Chief executive Graham Smith said ‘another huge hike for royal spending’ came with ‘more spin and gloss and more misdirection on taxes’. Once lost Duchy profits and other costs are counted, the group claims, the real bill to taxpayers exceeds half a billion pounds. Read Republic’s analysis in full .
items.why: scrutiny of public funding transparency for the head of state bears on accountability for the use of public money.
items.note: Treated as an accountability/transparency story about public spending disclosure rather than a standing state of affairs.

items.h: INLOGOV ask why accountability ‘failed to bite’ in the 2026 Tower Hamlets elections
items.b: Writing for the University of Birmingham’s Institute of Local Government Studies , Dr Gulay Icoz examines an ‘accountability paradox’. Despite government intervention over documented governance failures, Tower Hamlets voters returned Lutfur Rahman’s Aspire administration with 73% of the seats on 32% of the vote, they say. The deeper problem, she argues, is not voter apathy but an intervention read locally as ‘external imposition’. Read the piece for an insightful look at local accountability.
items.why: a disproportionate electoral outcome and contested government intervention raise questions about the representativeness and legitimacy of local democratic institutions.
items.note: Combines electoral representativeness with local government accountability; filed primarily under elections given the disproportionality focus.

items.h: CIPFA draft new financial ‘proper practices’ for England’s parish and town councils
items.b: The Smaller Authorities Proper Practices Panel met to consider draft new proper practices, prepared by Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) , for the accounts of England’s parish and town councils — including a new requirement to report borrowing and an end to reporting staff costs separately. The new practices are on track for publication by March 2027, in a sector where weak financial audit remains a persistent local democracy concern. Follow progress via the National Association of Local Councils .
items.why: new financial reporting requirements affect the transparency and audit accountability of parish and town councils' spending of public money.
links: Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA)
Follow progress via the National Association of Local Councils

items.h: NALC women councillors’ network confronts rising harassment and online misogyny
items.b: The National Association of Local Councils ’ women councillors’ network met in late June to confront the rising harassment and intimidation facing women in public life — and its chilling effect on representation. The Local Government Association ’s Ambassador for Civility in Public Life, Cllr Hannah Dalton, briefed members on the Debate Not Hate campaign, and discussion turned to gaps in support and policing and the influence of online misogyny and the ‘manosphere’. Participants set priorities including tackling violence against women and girls and strengthening allyship.
items.why: harassment and online misogyny targeting women councillors threatens their personal security and can deter women from standing for or remaining in public office, undermining representativeness.
items.note: Touches both personal security/discrimination and representativeness of elected bodies; classified by the rights mechanism (harassment, security) as primary.

items.h: Centenary Action mark 98 years of equal votes with a sash for every woman MP
items.b: Centenary Action marked 2 July — 98 years since the Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women equal voting rights with men — by celebrating the women who have since reached Parliament. Working with Re:Make Newport , the campaign has created a personalised sash for every woman MP, each embroidered with her unique number in the history of women elected to Parliament. The newest, Green MP Hannah Spencer, has just received hers — and with women still short of equal representation, celebrate the women MPs who have inspired you via Centenary Action .
items.why: the historic extension of equal suffrage and the ongoing shortfall in women's representation in Parliament bear directly on the representativeness of elected institutions.
items.note: Largely a commemorative campaign item, but touches the representativeness anchor so treated as a low-confidence democracy story.

items.h: UN expert Gina Romero warns digital surveillance is quietly dismantling civil society
items.b: Writing for Tech Policy Press , Gina Romero, UN Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and association, argues that surveillance is not a series of isolated privacy problems but a ‘permanent, interconnected, remote and invisible’ monitoring ecosystem that is eroding the trust collective democratic action depends on.
items.why: pervasive, interconnected surveillance is eroding the trust and operating space that civil society organisations need to exercise freedom of association and assembly.
items.note: International/comparative expert argument treated as bearing on civic space generally, including UK civil society.
links: ‘permanent, interconnected, remote and invisible’ monitoring ecosystem

items.b: Organisations are diverting scarce resources to digital security, lowering their public profile to avoid criminalisation, and even deleting websites and archives to protect staff. She urges governments and companies to assess the cumulative human-rights effects of these systems — read her argument .
items.why: organisations curbing their public profile and deleting archives to avoid surveillance-driven criminalisation shows a chilling effect on the civic space needed for democratic organising.
items.note: Continuation of the same surveillance/civil society argument as the preceding item.

items.h: UCL Constitution Unit give evidence to the Oireachtas on reforming Northern Ireland’s institutions
items.b: The Constitution Unit gave oral evidence to the Oireachtas committee on Good Friday Agreement implementation on 16 June, presenting their proposals for reforming the devolved institutions to improve the quality of governance. Any change, they stressed, would need ‘a large measure of cross-community agreement to command legitimacy’ — and with Alan Whysall warning that ‘Stormont is in trouble’, the case is for substantive rather than superficial reform. Read more via UCL .
items.why: proposals to reform Northern Ireland's devolved institutions concern the structure and legitimacy of a tier of democratic decision-making.
items.note: Devolved institutional structure is classified under elections & decision making per the framework's local/regional/devolved government rule.

items.h: New Economy Brief welcome ‘Pride in Place’ but warn the money is ‘a drop in the ocean’
items.b: A New Economy Brief digest weighs up the government’s £5.8bn Pride in Place programme, which seats residents on Neighbourhood Boards to control local spending across hundreds of deprived areas — a deliberate shift from top-down, competitive funding towards needs-based allocation. Drawing on analysis from JRF , Power to Change , NEF and CLES , it welcomes the community-power principle but warns the money is ‘a drop in the ocean’ against the scale of need — and urges genuine community-led delivery, community wealth-building and participatory budgeting. Read the digest via New Economy Brief.
items.why: Neighbourhood Boards give residents direct control over local public spending, creating a new mechanism for participatory, needs-based decision-making in deprived communities.

items.h: Think Labour call on government to ‘reassert the primacy of democracy over public services’
items.b: Think Labour , a Labour-aligned policy organisation, argues in a new paper, Democratic public services , that government should ‘reassert the primacy of democracy over public services’ — a principle it says ‘has been rolled back in favour of market accountability and regulation’ over recent decades. It makes the case for democratic control and public accountability, rather than market mechanisms, as the organising principle for how public services answer to citizens. Read the paper on Think Labour’s site.
items.why: it argues public services should be organised around democratic accountability to citizens rather than market mechanisms, bearing on how public power over services is checked and answerable.

items.b: Beckie and Wendy of The Bridge at the YHA in Berwick-upon-Tweed (Photo credit: PINF)

items.h: Media Reform Coalition bring people’s assembly to this year’s Media Democracy Festival
items.b: Campaigners, journalists and academics gathered last month at the University of Westminster for this year’s Media Democracy Festival , built around the theme ‘The Future of Public Media’. Alongside keynotes, panels and workshops, the day featured a first-of-its-kind people’s assembly, confronting a moment in which ‘disinformation spreads faster than truth, media ownership continues to concentrate, and public interest journalism faces deep structural challenges’. Keep an eye out for session recordings and write-ups from the Media Reform Coalition .
items.why: a people's assembly is a deliberative decision-making mechanism convened to address concentration of media power and disinformation, which the framework treats as decision-making machinery
items.note: Deliberative process (people's assembly) classified under elections & decision making per boundary rule rather than participation.

items.h: Public Interest News Foundation celebrate a record-breaking Indie News Week
items.b: The Public Interest News Foundation (PINF) reports that its third annual Indie News Week was the biggest yet, with more than 30 independent outlets across England and Wales hosting events in June on why democracy needs indie news — from a Deptford panel and a Leicester freedom-of-information workshop to the launch of a hyperlocal Welsh site in Treorchy. Byline Times editor Hardeep Matharu urged audiences to ‘make hope matter again’ for local news. Sign up via PINF to follow Indie News Week 2027.
items.why: independent and hyperlocal journalism sustains the plural public information environment and local accountability that democratic participation depends on
links: more than 30 independent outlets across England and Wales hosting events in June

items.h: But that’s not all from PINF: Joe Mitchell sat down to record a podcast with ADSO
items.b: The latest Democracy Conversations from the Association of Democratic Services Officers (ADSO) features Joe Mitchell — Deputy Director of the Public Interest News Foundation on why local news is an essential part of local democracy. The conversation takes in how local journalism shapes the relationship between councils and citizens, how new independent titles are doing things differently, and why we can’t simply rely on AI to translate council decision-making. Listen, watch or read the bite-size highlights now .
items.note: Podcast promotion/event listing without a concrete new mechanism or change.
links: Listen, watch or read the bite-size highlights now

items.h: Areeq Chowdhury launches ‘By Any Machine Necessary’ new blog on democratic control of AI
items.b: Technology policy adviser Areeq Chowdhury has launched By Any Machine Necessary , a fortnightly Substack on how the powerful are using technology to reshape society — and how policymakers might ‘regain control’. His opening essay sketches a public-interest agenda for AI, publicly-owned, open-source AI infrastructure, universal digital access, worker representation and a National Data Service — rather than leaving the technology’s direction to a handful of corporations. Subscribe for free to follow the argument.
items.note: Blog launch is opinion/advocacy content on technology policy, a cross-cutting lens not treated as a beat.

items.h: Katy Rubin makes the case for ‘inclusive by design’ democracy that takes emotion seriously
items.b: Writing for Philea , creative civic strategist Katy Rubin of The People Act and academic Alberto Ford argue that mainstream deliberation privileges detached, rational speech — quietly excluding those who cannot emotionally separate themselves from the policies that shape their lives. They contend that ‘unheard emotions’ such as indignation, shame and loneliness are signals of systemic failure, and that embodied, arts-based methods like Legislative Theatre can fold reason, emotion and lived experience into more inclusive problem-solving. Read their call for funders to back the creative infrastr…
items.note: Opinion piece arguing for a deliberation method, without a concrete institutional change or new resource launch.

items.h: Connected by Data wrap up their data and AI community of practice — and gather the lessons
items.b: Connected by Data ’s monthly community of practice for people engaging the public around data and AI has wrapped up after a year and seventeen events, part of its Mohn Westlake Foundation-funded project ‘Giving communities a powerful say in public sector data and AI’ grant. Gavin Freeguard has gathered the lot in two fresh blogs — read the round-up of speakers and resources , then see what comes next for the community.
items.note: Wrap-up of an organisation's own programme and resource round-up, closer to organisational reporting than a new participation mechanism.
links: — read the round-up of speakers and resources

items.h: People Powered and the Democracy Narratives Alliance publish an 11-point agenda to rebuild faith in democracy
items.b: The Democracy Narratives Alliance — a coalition of 40+ organisations convened with People Powered — argues that rebuilding public engagement takes coordinated storytelling, not just better policy, with confidence in democracy falling and autocratic appeals rising. Its new 11-point action agenda spans narrative research across contexts, an AI tool to synthesise guidance for activists, influencer partnerships and a dedicated fund for democracy-narrative work. Read the agenda and join the Alliance via People Powered.
items.why: the coalition is launching new tools, a fund and coordinated campaigns intended to rebuild public engagement with and support for democracy
links: Read the agenda and join the Alliance

items.h: Humanity Project release ‘Love + Power’, a short film on democracy from the ground up
items.b: Humanity Project — the team building ‘assembly culture’ through neighbourhood assemblies and community organising across the UK — has released Love + Power , a three-minute film distilling three years of listening and organising across England and Wales. Directed by filmmaker Nathan Davies, it takes its cue from Martin Luther King Jr.’s line that ‘power without love is reckless and abusive; love without power is sentimental and anemic’ — a glimpse of the community power that can emerge when people come together to shape what happens where they live. Watch and share the film .
items.note: Promotional film release documenting existing organising work, not a new participatory mechanism or accountability change.

items.b: Larpocracy study how live action role playing can build democratic capacity (Photo credit: Larpocracy)
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Caption only, no substantive content.

items.h: MONARCH argue election technology needs independent security assurance, not just testing
items.b: MONARCH — a firm founded by former intelligence chiefs, senior government figures and security scholars — argues that election technology is widely tested but rarely independently verified as secure, compliant and ‘legally defensible’ by assessors with no stake in the result. It says its recent work included a full independent audit — source-code review, penetration testing and end-to-end auditability — of the electronic voting, counting and result-matching systems of a major Middle Eastern democracy of 47 million citizens. Read their case — and ponder where independent assurance fits in the f…
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: this matters democratically because independent verification of election technology's security and legal defensibility bears on the integrity of election administration, a core condition for genuinely competitive and trustworthy elections.
items.note: International case used as comparative evidence about election technology assurance relevant to democratic infrastructure debates.

items.h: National Endowment for Democracy name their 2026 Democracy Award recipients
items.b: The US-based National Endowment for Democracy has named the recipients of its 2026 Democracy Award — themed on First Amendment freedoms to mark America’s 250th anniversary — honouring activists, artists and journalists working under repression. Honourees include anti-war clergy advocate Friede Allen (Russia), imprisoned Cuban dissident artists Félix Navarro, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara and Maykel Castillo Pérez, the Syrian Center for Media and Freedom of Expression, Ethiopia’s Addis Standard , and organisers of Burma’s Spring Revolution. The award will be presented in September at Mount Vernon…
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: Award announcement honouring international activists is not UK-focused and does not itself change any democratic mechanism.

items.h: Larpocracy ask whether live-action role-play can build democratic skills
items.b: Larpocracy , an EU Horizon Europe-funded research project running to December 2027, is investigating whether live-action role-play (LARP) — yes, dressing up and playing a character — can be a serious method for building democratic skills and reviving civic participation where traditional engagement and social media fall short. It runs ‘Designing Democracy’ workshops and seminars (including at the Knutepunkt gathering ) and has begun publishing research on lowering barriers to cultural participation.
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.why: this matters democratically because the project creates new workshop-based methods intended to build civic and democratic participation skills where conventional engagement has failed.
items.note: Sector capacity-building via new programme/workshops counts as participation even though EU-funded rather than UK-specific.

items.h: Civic Data Tech set out to protect the data infrastructure underpinning US democracy
items.b: Civic Data Tech is a new project dedicated to ‘enhancing access to civic information’ — sustaining the often invisible data infrastructure that underpins democratic and civic processes in the United States and across the world, from public records to the datasets that keep citizens informed. It joins a wider movement to keep civic data open, trusted and in the public interest, rather than locked in proprietary hands.
items.sec: And now for something completely different …
items.note: US-focused project launch with no clear bearing on UK democracy or comparative evidence about it.
